[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Define the map $\Residual:\Opendenseset_\alpha\times \mathcal{X}_1\rightarrow \ParaHoelderzero{\alpha}([0,1]\times\R)$
by
\begin{equation}

  \Residual(\gamma,u)
  \coloneqq
  -\partial_su
  -
  \frac12\gamma(s)\mathfrak A(u),
  \qquad 
  \mathfrak A(u)
  \coloneqq
  \partial_{xx}u+g''+s(\partial_xu+g')^2.
\end{equation}
Then, $\Residual$ satisfies the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The map $\Residual$ is well-defined and 
$\Residual\in  C^2
  \bigl(
  \Opendenseset_\alpha\times\mathcal X_1
  ;\, \ParaHoelderzero{\alpha}([0,1]\times\R)
  \bigr)$.
\item For every \(\gamma\in\Opendenseset_\alpha\),
\[
  \Residual(\gamma,\Psi^\gamma-\log\cosh)=0.
\]

\item Let $\mathfrak L_s^u\coloneqq \frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}+s(\partial_x u + g')\partial_x$.
Then,
\begin{align}
  D_\gamma\Residual(\gamma,u)[h]
  &=
  -\frac12 h(s)
  \mathfrak A(u), 
   \\
  D_u\Residual(\gamma,u)[v]
  &=
  -\partial_sv
  -
  \gamma(s)
  \mathfrak L_s^u v,
   \\
  D^2\Residual(\gamma,u)[(h_1,v_1),(h_2,v_2)]
  &=
-
h_1(s)
\mathfrak L_s^u v_2
-
h_2(s)
\mathfrak L_s^u v_1
-
\gamma(s)s\,\partial_xv_1\,\partial_xv_2.

\end{align}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In mathematics, Choquet theory, named after Gustave Choquet, is an area of functional analysis and convex analysis concerned with measures which have support on the extreme points of a convex set C. Roughly speaking, every vector of C should appear as a weighted average of extreme points, a concept made more precise by generalizing the notion of weighted average from a convex combination to an integral taken over the set E of extreme points. Here C is a subset of a real vector space V, and the main thrust of the theory is to treat the cases where V is an infinite-dimensional topological vector space along lines similar to the finite-dimensional case. The main concerns of Gustave Choquet were in potential theory. Choquet theory has become a general paradigm, particularly for treating convex cones as determined by their extreme rays, and so for many different notions of positivity in mathematics.
title: Choquet theory

body:
Assuming the axiom of choice, the closed unit ball B in R^3 can be partitioned into finitely many pieces which can be reassembled by rigid motions (rotations and translations) into two disjoint copies of B; five pieces suffice (Robinson), and four do not. More generally (the strong form) any two bounded subsets of R^n, n >= 3, with nonempty interior are equidecomposable: one can be cut into finitely many pieces and moved by isometries onto the other. The pieces are necessarily non-measurable, so no contradiction with Lebesgue measure arises - the theorem shows that no finitely additive, isometry-invariant measure defined on ALL subsets of R^3 and normalising the ball can exist. In dimensions 1 and 2 the paradox fails: Banach showed that Lebesgue measure on R and R^2 extends to a finitely additive isometry-invariant measure on all subsets, because the isometry groups of R and R^2 are amenable (solvable), while SO(3) contains a free group on two generators, which is the source of the paradox (Hausdorff, 1914). Tarski's theorem (1929) makes this exact: a group action admits a paradoxical decomposition if and only if it carries no finitely additive invariant probability measure, i.e. it is non-amenable. With choice the result is a theorem; in ZF plus the axiom of determinacy, or in Solovay's model, every set of reals is measurable and the decomposition does not exist.

M_N^{(s)}(t)\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{L^1} M_\infty^{(s)}(t),

\mathrm{Var}\bigl(M_\infty^{(s)}(t)\bigr)\ge

\]
In particular, the atomic regime does not collapse to a deterministic discovered-mass curve.

On a finite connected graph with iid Uniform[1,2] edge weights and fixed terminals, define clipped off-edge thresholds a_e in [0,1] so that centered coordinate costs are min(U,a_e)-a_e+a_e^2/2 for U uniform on [0,1]. For a<=b, K(a,b)=a^2[b(2-b)/4-a/6], and K is symmetric. Under independent rate-one coordinate refresh, Var(T)=integral_0^infinity exp(-t)H(t)dt, where H(t)=sum_e E K(a_e(eta),a_e(eta^t)) and only off-edge coordinates are coupled inside H. body: In combinatorics, two Latin squares of the same size (order) are said to be orthogonal if when superimposed the ordered paired entries in the positions are all distinct. A set of Latin squares, all of the same order, all pairs of which are orthogonal is called a set of mutually orthogonal Latin squares. This concept of orthogonality in combinatorics is strongly related to the concept of blocking in statistics, which ensures that independent variables are truly independent with no hidden confounding correlations. "Orthogonal" is thus synonymous with "independent" in that knowing one variable's value gives no further information about another variable's likely value.
title: Mutually orthogonal Latin squares

[Lem 252 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If $\bX:\R^{N'}\to\R^N$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $\bg$ is a standard gaussian in $\R^{N'}$, and $\E[\|\bX(\bg)\|^2] = N$, then for any $\delta > 0$, there exists $c(\delta) > 0$ such that 
    \[
    \P\bigg(
    \bigg|\frac{\|\bX(\bg)\|^2}{N} - 1\bigg|
    \ge \delta\bigg)
    \le e^{-c(\delta)N}\,.\]

\begin{proof}
    Since $\bg \mapsto \|\bX(\bg)\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, it follows from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus} that $\|\bX(\bg)\|-\E\|\bX(\bg)\|$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $2L^2$, and satisfies the concentration bound \eqref{e:lip.subgaus}:
    \[
    \P\bigg( \Big|
    \|\bX(\bg)\| - \E\|\bX(\bg)\|\Big| \ge t
    \bigg) \le 2\exp\bigg\{-\frac{t^2}{2L^2}\bigg\}\,.
    \]
It follows that $\|\bX(\bg)\|$ has variance $O(L^2)$, which implies
    \[
     \frac{O(L^2)}{N}
     \ge
    \frac{\E[\|\bX(\bg)\|^2] - ( \E\|\bX(\bg)\|)^2}{N}
    =1- \frac{ ( \E\|\bX(\bg)\|)^2}{N}\,.
    \]
Combining the last two displays gives the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 252 of arXiv:2608.29416

  \]

[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2608.04644, 'Khinchin's and Chung's Laws of the Iterated Logarithm at Time Zero for the Linear Stochast'] There  is a universal constant $K_0$ such that the following statement holds. Let $S$ be a bounded set and $\{X(s),s\in S\}$ be a separable Gaussian process.
Let $D_X(S) := \sup\left\{d_X(s, t):s, t \in S\right\}$ be the diameter of $S$ in the metric $d_X$. Then for any $u>0$,
\[
\mathbb P\left(\sup_{s,t\in S}   |X(s)-X(t)|\ge K_0\left(u+\int_0^{D_X(S)} \sqrt{\log N(S,d_X;\varepsilon)}  d\varepsilon    \right)  \right)\le \exp\left(-\frac{u^2}{D_X(S)^2}\right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
The model used by Wang-Huang-Li-Wu in arXiv:2609.02728 is Gaussian-feature, online least-squares regression. In the covariance eigenbasis, a feature vector phi has centered Gaussian law N(0,H) with H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2,...) positive trace class, lambda_1>=lambda_2>=...>0. A label is y=<phi,theta_star>+epsilon with epsilon~N(0,sigma^2) independent of phi. The target has finite prediction energy sum_j lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2<infinity; the pairing can equivalently be read as its mean-square-convergent Gaussian series. The population risk is R(theta)=E(<phi,theta>-y)^2/2, and the excess risk is Ecal(theta)=sum_j lambda_j*|theta_j-theta_star_j|^2/2=R(theta)-sigma^2/2. Their source/capacity assumptions are beta>1,s>0, lambda_j asymp j^(-beta) and lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2 asymp j^(-(1+s*beta)), where asymp means upper and lower bounds by fixed positive constants, uniform in j. The label-noise standard deviation sigma is bounded above and away from zero by fixed constants (the constant-order noisy setting). At iteration k a fresh IID batch of B examples, independent of all past batches, gives the AVERAGED gradient g(theta;batch)=B^(-1)*sum_i phi_(k,i)*(<phi_(k,i),theta>-y_(k,i)). For a constant eta>0 and constant rho in[0,1), SGD uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch); Polyak uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch)+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)); Nesterov first sets theta_k_la=theta_k+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)) and uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k_la-eta*g(theta_k_la;batch). The source scaling-law analysis takes theta_0=theta_-1=0. For a one-pass data budget D, take T=D/B updates (or integer rounding at the exponent level), and B=D^(b+o(1)) with fixed b in[0,1). Hyperparameters can depend on D but are constant within each run. This protocol concerns final expected excess risk; it is not a finite-data repeated-epoch protocol, nor a theorem giving explicit constants in the critical-batch trade-off.
Definition of the specific source model; beta>1,s>0,uniform power-law comparison constants.
Fresh independent Gaussian features and independent Gaussian constant-order label noise; averaged minibatch gradients.
Zero initial iterate and zero initial momentum for the scaling-law protocol.

Let F_1,F_2 be identically distributed square-integrable variables with standard deviation s, and G_1,G_2 iid square-integrable variables on the same probability space. Suppose Delta_i=G_i-F_i>=0 have equal means and ||Delta_i||_2<=delta. Then 2(s-2delta)_+^2<=Var(F_1-F_2)<=2(s+2delta)^2. Independence is required only for G_1,G_2, and is not assumed for localization events, errors, or F_1,F_2.

unconditional independence of G_1,G_2
identical F marginals and identical G marginals

[Lemma lem:dtv-U-bound of arXiv:2507.16188, 'The noisy voter model with general initial conditions'] The following holds for every {\upshape\texttt{good}\xspace} collection $\{V_i\}_{i=1}^m$. Let $U_i$ and $\tau_i$ be as in (lem:Xt-from-V-to-U of the paper). Then, for some $C=C(q,\theta,\mathfrak{c}_0,\upalpha)>0$, the $d_{\textsc{tv}}^{\mathsf{x}_0}(U_i,t)$ from (eq:dtv-U-t-def of the paper) satisfy 
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^m d_{\textsc{tv}}^{\mathsf{x}_0}(U_i,t_1-\tau_i)^2 \mathbbm{1}_{\{\tau_i<t_1\}} \right] \leq C(1+t_1^3)e^{4(\log n)^{1-\frac{\upalpha}{2}}}n (\mathcal{A}^{(2)}_{t_1}(\mathsf{x}_0) \vee e^{-4\theta t_1}) + O(n^{-9})\,.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 28 of arXiv:2609.01098, 'Gaussian upper bounds for averaged heat semigroups on graphs'] Let $o\in X$, $n>0$, $r\geq 0$, $C\geq 1$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $q\colon [r,\infty)\to (0,\infty)$ monotone increasing with $q(t)\to\infty$ as $t\to\infty$, and
\[
A\geq  
\left((2C)^{3(2C)^{21n}}\cdot 1\vee  m(B(r)^{\frac{(2C)^{21n}}{q(r)}}\right)^\frac{q(r^2)}{q(r^2)-1}.
\] 
Assume \[
\mathcal{P}_{r}(t,o,o)
 \leq 
\frac{C}{\sqrt[\frac{q(t)}{q(t)-1}]{m(B(\sqrt t))}}
\]
for all $r^2\leq t\leq 2A^4r^2$ and
\[
\frac{m(B_x(s_2))}{m(B_x(s_1))}\leq C\left(\frac{s_2}{s_1}\right)^n
\]
for all $x\in B(2Ar)$ and $r\leq s_1\leq s_2\leq 2A^2r$.
Then, for all $U\subset B(r)$ satisfying $m(U)\geq \varepsilon m(B(r))$, we have 
\[
\lambda(U)
\geq 
\frac{C_n}{A^4r^2}
\left(
\frac{m(B(r))}{m(U)}\right)^{\frac{2}{N}},
\]
where $C_n=\frac{1}{C^{\frac{4}{n}}2^{5+\frac{4}{n}}}$ and 
\[
N\geq n\frac{q(r^2)}{q(r^2)-1}+ \frac{\ln\frac{1}{\epsilon}}{\ln A}+\frac{1}{q(r^2)-1}\ln(1\vee m(B(r))).
\]
title: Theorem 28 of arXiv:2609.01098

[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2506.11918, 'Central limit theorems for the Euler characteristic in the Random Connection Model for hig'] Let $F=\chi_a\big(\Delta_W\big)$.
There are constants $C_i>0$, $i\in\{1,\dots,7\}$, not depending on $W\in\Bf$, such that
\begin{align}
\int_{W^3} \E{ \left( \Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^1F \right)^2 \left( \Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_1,U_1)}^1F \right)^2}^\frac{1}{2} \hspace{4cm} & \nonumber \\
\times \, \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_3,U_3),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^2 \left(\Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_3,U_3),(x_1,U_1)}^2 F\right)^2}^\frac{1}{2}  \; \lambda^3 \, (\d {x}) &\;\leq\; C_1|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_{W^3} \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_3,U_3),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^2 \left(\Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_3,U_3),(x_1,U_1)}^2 F\right)^2} \; \lambda^3 \, (\d {x}) &\;\leq\; C_2|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_W \E{ |\Lambda_{(x,U)}F|^3 } \; \lambda \, (\d x) &\;\leq\; C_3|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_W \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x,U)}F\right)^4 }^\frac{3}{4} \; \lambda \, (\d x) &\;\leq\; C_4|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_W \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x,U)}F\right)^4 } \; \lambda \, (\d x) &\;\leq\; C_5|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_{W^2} 6\; \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1)}F\right)^4 }^\frac{1}{2} \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^4 }^\frac{1}{2} \hspace{3.66cm} & \nonumber \\
+ 3\; \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^4 } \; \lambda^2 \, (\d {x}) &\;\leq\; C_6|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_W \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x,U)}F\right)^4 }^\frac{1}{2} \; \lambda \, (\d x) &\;\leq\; C_7|W|, 
\end{align}
where the integration is to be understood with respect to the points $x_i$.

[Coro 20 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Assume that $0<\alpha<1$, $m\leq0$ a.e. in $\Omega$,
$|\Omega^0|>0$, and $m\in L^\infty(\Omega)$. Suppose that there exist
$\rho_0>0$ and $m_{\rho_0}^-$ such that
\[
\mathcal C_{\rho_0}
:=
\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)<\rho_0\}
\subset\Omega^-,
\qquad
-m(x)\geq m_{\rho_0}^-
\quad\text{a.e. in }\mathcal C_{\rho_0},
\]
and assume that
$\lambda_{1,\Omega}<\lambda_{1,\Omega^0}$.
Then there exist $\varepsilon>0$ and $\rho\in(0,\rho_0)$ such that, for
every
$\lambda\in
(\lambda_{1,\Omega^0}-\varepsilon,\lambda_{1,\Omega^0})$,
\[
u_\lambda^-=0
\quad\text{in }
\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)<\rho\}.
\]
In particular,
\[
\operatorname{supp}u_\lambda^-
\subset
\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\geq\rho\}
\Subset\Omega.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:romiksniady-main of arXiv:2607.24018, 'Jeu de taquin forests \\ and the inverse infinite RSK correspondence'] \begin{enumerate}

\item The Plancherel measure $P$ is the push-forward of the
infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure $\Lambda$ on
$[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ under the map $\RSK(\cdot)$.

\item The jeu de taquin map $J$ is a measure-preserving
transformation on the Plancherel measure space $(\Omega,
\mathcal{F}, P)$.

\item The jeu de taquin map is intertwined with the shift map $S$
on $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ (defined by $S(z_1,z_2,\ldots)=(z_2,z_3,\ldots)$)
by the map $\RSK(\cdot)$, in the sense that the
relation
\[
J \circ \RSK = \RSK\circ S
\]
holds $\Lambda$-almost surely on $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$. 

\item The RSK map $\RSK(\cdot)$ is an isomorphism between
the two measure-preserving dynamical systems $([0,1]^\mathbb{N},
\mathcal{B}, \Lambda, S)$ and $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P, J)$.

\item The inverse map $\RSK^{-1}(\cdot)$ is given explicitly by
\begin{equation} 
\RSK^{-1}(T) = ( \zeta(T), \zeta\circ J(T), \zeta \circ J^2(T), \ldots)
\quad \textrm{for $P$-almost every }T\in \Omega,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}

\zeta(T) =
1 - F\left(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{x_n-y_n}{\sqrt{T_{x_n,y_n}}} \right),
\end{equation}
where $((x_n,y_n))_{n=0}^\infty$ denotes the jeu de taquin
path associated with $T$ as in (equation eq:jdt-path of the paper) and
$F(u)$ is given by
\begin{equation}

F(u) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-2}^u \sqrt{4-s^2} \, ds
\qquad (-2 \le u \le 2).
\end{equation}
(This statement includes the assertion that the limit in
(equation eq:inverse-rsk-firstcoord of the paper) exists and takes a value in $[-2,2]$
$P$-almost surely.)

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:romiksniady-main of arXiv:2607.24018

body:
Every loopless planar graph is properly 4-colourable: its vertices can be coloured with four colours so that adjacent vertices receive different colours. Equivalently, the regions of any map drawn in the plane (each region connected) can be coloured with four colours so that regions sharing a boundary segment differ. Four is best possible (the complete graph K_4 is planar and needs four colours). The five-colour theorem (Heawood 1890) has a short proof; the four-colour theorem was proved by Appel and Haken in 1976 with a computer check of 1,936 reducible configurations, reproved by Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas in 1997 with 633 configurations and 32 discharging rules, and formally verified in the Coq proof assistant by Gonthier in 2005. No proof is known that a human can check unaided; every published proof rests on a machine-checked case analysis.
the graph is planar (embeddable in the plane without crossings) and loopless; multiple edges do not matter for colouring
proper colouring: adjacent vertices differ
the proof is computer-assisted; the sketch names the method and the published verifications

\[
g=S(\alpha*\lambda_v*\overleftarrow{\alpha}),
\]
so $g$ is itself the signature of a bounded-variation path. In the completed graded algebra,
\[
a\e^v a^{-1}=\e^{a v a^{-1}},
\]
so
\[
\log g=a v a^{-1}=\Ad_a v.
\]

PRIVATE NUMERICAL EVIDENCE, not a proof. Lyons (ICM 2014, Question 2.8) asks whether for H = H_1 (+) H_2 orthogonal in l^2(E) there is a coupling of the determinantal projection measures P_{H_1}, P_{H_2} whose union has law P_H. Since the cardinalities are dim H_1, dim H_2 and dim H almost surely, the union must be disjoint, and the question is the nonemptiness of the transportation polytope with the three marginals. Exact LP (HiGHS, minimum total violation) on 1360 random pairs of orthogonal subspaces with |E| in {3,...,6} over all dimension splits, on generic instances with |E| = 7 and 8, on Fourier-mode subspaces of cycles of length 5..8, and on star-space splits in the edge space of K_4 found a feasible coupling with zero violation every time (intake raw/C_lyons_q28_lp_check.json and _structured.json). A structural observation: the naive rule 'sample X_1 from P_{H_1} conditioned on X_1 subset C, set X_2 = C minus X_1' does NOT reproduce the P_{H_2} marginal in general (checked on |E| = 4), so the coupling, when it exists, is not the conditional splitting. Open: a general construction.
Finite E, orthogonal subspaces H_1, H_2
Evidence is computational on |E| <= 8 only
title: Lyons's union-marginal coupling question: transportation polytope feasible in every tested instance, naive conditional splitting fails

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with Stieltjes transform $m(z) = \int \frac{d\mu(t)}{t - z}$, defined and analytic for $\operatorname{Im} z > 0$, with $\operatorname{Im} m(z) > 0$ there. Then for every $a < b$ that are continuity points of $\mu$, $\mu((a, b]) = \lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\pi}\int_a^b \operatorname{Im} m(x + i\eta)\,dx$, and if $\mu$ has a continuous density $f$ at $x$ then $f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} \operatorname{Im} m(x + i\eta)$. The real part has the companion limit $\operatorname{Re} m(x + i\eta) \to \pi H_f(x) := \mathrm{PV}\int \frac{f(t)}{t - x}\,dt$ wherever $f$ is Hölder continuous, so the boundary value $\breve m(x) = \lim_{\eta\downarrow0} m(x + i\eta) = \pi H_f(x) + i\pi f(x)$ (Sokhotski-Plemelj). In particular two measures with the same Stieltjes transform on $\mathbb{C}^+$ coincide, and a sequence of probability measures converges weakly if and only if the Stieltjes transforms converge pointwise on $\mathbb{C}^+$ (to the transform of a probability measure).
mu a finite positive Borel measure on the real line
for the density statement: mu absolutely continuous with a density continuous at x; for the real-part statement: the density Hölder continuous near x

For the zero-boundary GFF on the unit disk, with covariance singularity log(1/|x-y|), let mu_gamma be the GMC of Lebesgue measure defined by the weak limit of 2^(-n*gamma^2/2) exp(gamma*h_{2^(-n)}(y))dy. [Cor 3 of arXiv:2609.01101, '2609.01101'] Let $K$ be a fixed number field, let $L$ be its Galois closure, and set
$$
G=\Gal(L/\Q),\qquad H=\Gal(L/K),\qquad
\rho_K=|H\backslash G/H|.
$$
Assume GRH for $\zeta_L$.  Then, for every fixed real $k>0$ and all
sufficiently large $T$,
\begin{equation}
\int_T^{2T}
\left|\zeta_K\left(\tfrac12+it\right)\right|^{2k}\,dt
\gg_{K,k}
T(\log T)^{\rho_Kk^2}.
\end{equation}
If $K$ is a non-Galois cubic field whose Galois closure has group $S_3$,
then $\rho_K=2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor 3 of arXiv:2609.01101
Corollary 11 of arXiv:2605.20115

[Theorem th:main of arXiv:2510.00214, 'On the local well-posedness of randomly forced reaction-diffusion equations with $\bm{L^2}'] Suppose that $u_0\in L^2[0\,,1]$,
	and that Assumption (cond-dif of the paper) holds. Then, there exists 
	a nonrandom number $t_0>0$ such that 
	(equation SHE:1 of the paper) has a random-field solution $u=u(t\,,x)$ 
	for all $(t\,,x)\in(0\,,t_0]\times[0\,,1]$ that
	satisfies the following:
	\begin{compactenum}[\indent\indent\rm (1)]
	\item $(t\,,x)\mapsto u(t\,,x)$ is a.s.\ continuous on $(0\,,t_0]\times[0\,,1]$;
	\item $\lim_{t\to0+} t^\alpha \|u(t)\|_{C[0,1]}=0$ a.s.\ 
		for every $\alpha>\frac14$, in fact there exists $\gamma=\gamma(b\,,\sigma,\alpha) >0$ such that
		\[
			\E\exp\left\{\gamma\sup_{t\in(0,t_0]}(t^\alpha\|u(t)\|_{C[0,1]})^{2/3}
			\right\}<\infty;
		\]
	\item As $t\to0+$, $\| u(t)-u_0\|_{L^2[0,1]}\to 0$ in probability.
	\end{compactenum}
	Finally, if $v$ is any other continuous random-field solution to (equation SHE:1 of the paper) on 
	the time interval $(0\,,t_0]$ such that 
	$\sup_{s\in(0,t_0]}(s^\alpha\|v(s)\|_{C[0,1]})<\infty$ a.s.~for 
	some $\alpha>\frac14$, then $\mathrm{P}\{u(t)=v(t)\ \forall t\in(0\,,t_0]\}=1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem th:main of arXiv:2510.00214

body: In statistics, sufficiency is a property of a statistic computed on a sample dataset in relation to a parametric model of the dataset. A sufficient statistic for a model parameter contains all of the information that the dataset provides about that parameter. It is closely related to the concepts of an ancillary statistic which contains no information about the model parameters, and of a complete statistic which only contains information about the parameters and no ancillary information.

[Definition 20 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(\iota \colon X \to S\) be a morphism of $\F_p$-stacks.
We say that $X$ is \emph{Hodge--Tate split} (\emph{HT-split}, for short) over $S$ if the homomorphism
\[
\nu_{X/S}^{\sharp} \colon \cO_{X^{(1)}} \to R\nu_{X/S,*}\cO_{(X/S)^{\dR}} \eqdef \OdR{X/S}
\]
is ind-split in $\mcalD_{\qcoh}(X^{(1)})$, where \(X^{(1)}\) is the Frobenius twist of \(X\) over \(S\).

We say that an \(\setF_p\)-stack \(X\) is \emph{HT-split} if $X$ is HT-split over $\Spec(\F_p)$.
title: Definition 20 of arXiv:2609.00567

Let T > 0 and let H: R^n × R^n → R be continuous and satisfy, for some constant C and all x,y,p,q ∈ R^n: (H1) |H(x,p) - H(x,q)| ≤ C|p-q| (H is Lipschitz in p, uniformly in x); (H2) |H(x,p) - H(y,p)| ≤ C|x-y|(1+|p|). Let u and v be bounded and uniformly continuous on R^n × [0,T], with u a viscosity subsolution and v a viscosity supersolution of w_t + H(x,Dw) = 0 in R^n × (0,T). If u(x,0) ≤ v(x,0) for all x ∈ R^n, then u ≤ v on R^n × [0,T]. Consequently the Cauchy problem u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,T), u(·,0) = g, has at most one viscosity solution that is bounded and uniformly continuous on R^n × [0,T].
H continuous with (H1) uniform Lipschitz dependence on p and (H2) |H(x,p)-H(y,p)| ≤ C|x-y|(1+|p|)
u, v bounded AND uniformly continuous on R^n × [0,T] (boundedness or uniform continuity cannot simply be dropped on the unbounded domain without another growth restriction)
u a viscosity subsolution and v a viscosity supersolution in the open strip R^n × (0,T), both continuous up to t = 0
ordering of the initial data everywhere: u(·,0) ≤ v(·,0)

Let Phi be a stationary simple locally finite planar point process with finite positive intensity, bounded Voronoi cells, finite nonempty edge-neighbor sets, no four cocircular points, no three collinear points, and almost surely unique nearest nuclei p_x at deterministic observation points. Define F6(x) as the mean of ((q-p_x)/|q-p_x|)^6 over its Delaunay edge-neighbors. Put C6(x,y)=E[F6(x)conjugate(F6(y))]-E[F6(x)]E[conjugate(F6(y))], V(t)=P(Phi intersect B(0,t) is empty), and alpha(A,B)=sup |P(E intersect H)-P(E)P(H)| over events of the restrictions to A and B. Suppose for D=|x-y|>6r and r>=r0, uniformly in x,y,r, alpha(B(x,3r),B(y,3r))<=Am(1+r)^kappa(1+D-6r)^(-p), and V(t)<=Av exp(-a t^nu) for t>=t0, with p,a,nu>0, kappa>=0, and finite Am,Av. Then |C6(x,y)|=O(D^(-p)(log D)^(kappa/nu)). Thus an eventual lower bound cD^(-eta), c,eta>0, is impossible when p>eta. This is a conditional correlation-transfer result and does not construct a Riesz Gibbs phase.

Let $W \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded measurable set, and let $f$ be a real-valued measurable functional defined on finite simplicial complexes with vertices in $\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{A}$. For $(x, a, t, u) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{A} \times [0, 1] \times \mathbb{M}$, let $\Delta_W^{(x, a, t, u)}$ denote the simplicial complex restricted to $W$ obtained from the augmented Poisson process $\Psi + \delta_{(x, a, t, u)}$. The difference operator $\Lambda_{(x, a, t, u)} f(\Delta_W)$ is defined by $\Lambda_{(x, a, t, u)} f(\Delta_W) := f(\Delta_W^{(x, a, t, u)}) - f(\Delta_{W \setminus \{x\}}^{(x, a, t, u)})$, which measures the exact change in $f$ caused by the addition of the vertex $(x, a)$ with auxiliary randomization marks $(t, u)$.
W is a bounded measurable subset of \mathbb{R}^d
f is a measurable functional on finite simplicial complexes
title: Difference Operator for Simplicial Complex Functionals

Let (X_{n, k}, \mathcal{F}_{n, k})_{1 \le k \le k_n} be a martingale difference array with \mathbb{E}[X_{n, k}^2] < \infty. Suppose that: (1) \sum_{k=1}^{k_n} \mathbb{E}[X_{n, k}^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{n, k-1}] \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} \sigma^2 for some constant \sigma^2 > 0; and (2) for every \epsilon > 0, \sum_{k=1}^{k_n} \mathbb{E}[X_{n, k}^2 \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n, k}| > \epsilon\}} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n, k-1}] \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} 0. Then S_n = \sum_{k=1}^{k_n} X_{n, k} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) as n \to \infty.
(X_{n, k}) martingale difference array
conditional variance converges in probability to \sigma^2
conditional Lindeberg condition holds

G is real-valued on P_2(R^d), admits a first variation V[mu] in C^1(R^d), and for one L>0, |grad V[mu](x)-grad V[nu](y)| <= L(|x-y|+W_2(mu,nu)) for all mu,nu,x,y. G is convex under linear mixing of measures. For the temperature tau>0, F_tau(mu)=G(mu)+tau H(mu), where H(mu)=integral log(dmu/dx) dmu, admits a minimizer mu_tau^*. For every mu in P_2(R^d), Z_mu=integral exp(-V[mu]/tau) dx is finite and positive and nu_mu=Z_mu^(-1) exp(-V[mu]/tau) dx satisfies the uniform logarithmic Sobolev inequality KL(eta||nu_mu) <= I(eta||nu_mu)/(2 rho_tau), with rho_tau>0 independent of mu. Here I(eta||nu)=integral |grad log(deta/dnu)|^2 deta. Let mu_t solve partial_t mu_t=div(mu_t grad V[mu_t])+tau Delta mu_t, with mu_0 in P_2(R^d) and F_tau(mu_0)<infinity. Then for every t>=0, F_tau(mu_t)-F_tau(mu_tau^*) <= exp(-2 tau rho_tau t) [F_tau(mu_0)-F_tau(mu_tau^*)]. This bounds the regularized objective at fixed temperature; it does not give a temperature-uniform rate for G alone.

In a compactly generated tensor-triangulated category $\mathcal{T}$, a localizing $\otimes$-ideal $\mathcal{L}$ is smashing (generated by compact objects) if and only if its support $\operatorname{supp}_*(\mathcal{L})$ is a Thomason closed subset of $\operatorname{Spc}(\mathcal{T}^c)$ (a union of closed subsets with quasi-compact complements).

body:
[Ppn 140 (\hyperlink{proof:p.Ising-IAMP-analysis}{proved in \S\ref{ss:proof.iamp.diffus.limit}}) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] In the setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}, and recalling the notation \eqref{e:state.evol.piecewise}, there exist standard Brownian motions $B$ and $W$ such that the behavior of the state evolution limit \eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments} can be described as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item 
  
The random variables $V^k,Y^k,\prxY^k$ can be written as
  \begin{align*}
  V^k
  &=
        V^0
        +
  \int_{q_0}^{q_0+k\delta}
  s_\delta(t_\delta)
  \,\de B(t),
  \\
  Y^k
  = \breve{Y}(q_0+k\delta)
  &=
        \breve{Y}(q_0)
        +
  \int_{q_0}^{q_0+k\delta}
  \frac{w_{t_\delta}(\prxY(t))}
  {
  \bbE[w_{t_\delta}(\prxY(t))^2]^{1/2}
  }
  \,\de W(t),
  \\
  \prxY^k
  = \prxY(q_0+k\delta)
  &=\prxY^0+
  \int_{q_0}^{q_0+k\delta}
  w_{t_\delta}(\prxY(t))
  \,\de W(t)
  .
  \end{align*}

\item

The random variables $M^k$, $X^k$, $\prxX^k$ can be written as
  \begin{align*}
  M^k
  &=
  \int_{q_0}^{q_0+k\delta} \frac{s_\delta(t_\delta)}{p(t_{\delta})}
  \Big(\sigma_{t_{\delta}}(\prxX(t))-1\Big)
  \,\de B(t);
  \\
  X^k = \breve{X}(q_0+k\delta)
  &=
  \int_{q_0}^{q_0+k\delta}
  s_\delta(t_\delta)
  \sigma_{t_{\delta}}(
  \prxX(t))
  \,\de B(t)
  +
  \int_{q_0}^{q_0+k\delta}
  p'(t_{\delta})^{1/2}
  b_{t_{\delta}}(\prxX(t))
  \,\de t
  \\
  \prxX^k
  =\prxX(q_0+k\delta)
  &=
  \prxX^0
  +
  \int_{q_0}^{q_0+k\delta}
  s_\delta(t_\delta)
  \sigma_{t_{\delta}}
  (\prxX(t))
  \,\de B(t)
  +
  \int_{q_0}^{q_0+k\delta}
  p'(t_{\delta})^{1/2}
  b_{t_{\delta}}
  (\prxX(t))\,\de t
  .\end{align*}
(Recall from Definition~\ref{d:iamp.v1} that $\breve{X}(q_0)=0$.)
\end{enumerate}
Recall $\prxX^0$ and $\prxY^0$
are equidistributed respectively as $X(q_0)$ and $Y(q_0)$ from the SDEs
\eqref{e:IAMP.X.SDE} and \eqref{e:IAMP.Y.SDE}. Moreover $\prxY^0$ is independent of $W$, and $\prxX^0$ is independent of $B$.\footnote{We recall from the discussion after Corollary~\ref{cor:psi-state-evolution} that $N$-dimensional and $M$-dimensional state evolution variables such as $W$ and $B$ are defined on different probability spaces, and can thus be  thought of as independent.} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \hyperlink{proof:p.Ising-IAMP-analysis}{proved in \S\ref{ss:proof.iamp.diffus.limit}}

body: Theorem 2.1. (i) Let G be a graph with bipartition {A, B}. Suppose that, for every subset X of A, there are at least |X| vertices in B which have a neighbour in A [sic: X]. Then G has a matching which covers every vertex in A. (ii) Let M be an n x m matrix. A necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of an injective map f from {1, ..., n} to {1, ..., m} such that M_{i,f(i)} != 0 for all i is that any k rows together have non-zero elements in at least k columns, for 0 <= k <= n. (iii) Let (T_1, ..., T_n) be a family of subsets of S. Suppose that there is a positive integer d such that, for 1 <= k <= n, any k sets from the family contain between them at least k - d elements. Then there is a partial SDR of size n - d; that is, elements a_{i_1}, ..., a_{i_{n-d}} in S such that a_j in T_j for j in {i_1, ..., i_{n-d}} and a_j != a_k for j != k.

body:
For N unit-speed servers with Poisson input N*lambda, independent uniformly chosen destinations, and independent nonnegative job sizes S with rho=lambda*E S<1 and E S^2 finite, the product stationary workload law consists of N independent M/G/1 workloads. The stationary mean workload per server is exactly lambda*E S^2/(2*(1-rho)) for every N. Its first-order 1/N bias and remainder are zero, and off-diagonal covariances are zero. This is the d=1 random-routing case; no zero-bias claim is made for workload-dependent least-of-d routing.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Status: proof written; w346 KEEP pending. This is the d=1 random-routing special case, not a result for interacting least-of-d routing with d>=2.

Consider N rate-one workload servers, a Poisson input of rate N*lambda, independent uniformly chosen routing destinations, and i.i.d. nonnegative job sizes S independent of routing. Assume rho=lambda*E[S]<1 and E[S^2]<infinity. The N workload processes are independent M/G/1 workload processes when started in their product stationary law. For every N, the stationary mean of one server (and of the empirical mean workload) is

    lambda*E[S^2]/(2*(1-rho)).

Consequently its expansion in 1/N has exactly zero bias coefficient and zero remainder for this observable; stationary off-diagonal covariances are zero.

Proof: marked Poisson thinning produces N independent rate-lambda input processes with independent job marks. Each queue drains at rate one while positive and has upward jumps S. Its stability and stationary construction follow from the negative-drift reflected compound-Poisson input. The stationary idle mass is 1-rho by workload balance. For beta(s)=E[e^(-sS)] and L(s)=E[e^(-sW)], the bounded stationary generator test e^(-sW) gives

    0=s*(L(s)-(1-rho))+lambda*(beta(s)-1)*L(s),
    L(s)=(1-rho)*s/(s-lambda+lambda*beta(s)), s>0.

The second-moment assumption gives beta(s)=1-E[S]*s+E[S^2]*s^2/2+o(s^2). Expansion at zero gives L(s)=1-[lambda*E[S^2]/(2*(1-rho))]*s+o(s); the right derivative of a nonnegative variable's Laplace transform identifies its finite mean. Product stationarity proves all finite-N claims. This handles the actual empty-workload boundary, unlike a Gaussian OU control model.

For exponential service sizes of rate mu>lambda, P(W=0)=1-lambda/mu and P(W>x)=(lambda/mu)*exp(-(mu-lambda)*x) for x>=0, so the mean is lambda/(mu*(mu-lambda)). These formulas are a control for implementations of any proposed first-order correction. They do not justify setting the correction to zero under workload-dependent routing.

[Theorem thm: weighted mvt of arXiv:2609.02073, 'Existence of closed non-planar $p$-elasticae'] Let $f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function and let $g: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be an integrable function that does not change sign on the interval $[a, b]$. 
Then there exists at least one point $c \in (a, b)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
    \int_{a}^{b} f(x)g(x) \, dx = f(c) \int_{a}^{b} g(x) \,dx.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition 4 (Covering number and $\epsilon$-net) of arXiv:2608.22636, 'Q-Learning with Stable Infinite-Dimensional \\Linear Function Approximation'] An $\epsilon$-net of $(\mbb L,\rho)$ is a subset $\mfk N\subseteq\mbb L$ such that, for every $\ell\in\mbb L$, there exists $\ell'\in\mfk N$ with $\rho(\ell,\ell')\leq\epsilon$. For $\epsilon>0$, let $\cN_\rho(\epsilon)$ denote the covering number of $\mbb L$ by $\rho$-balls of radius $\epsilon$; that is, $\cN_\rho(\epsilon)$ is the smallest cardinality of any $\epsilon$-net. Moreover, let $\mfk N_\rho(\epsilon)$ denote an $\epsilon$-net satisfying $|\mfk N_\rho(\epsilon)|=\cN_\rho(\epsilon)$.

Let A_1, ..., A_m be events, X_i = 1_{A_i}, U their union, V = span{X_1, ..., X_m} in L2(P), alpha_i = P(A_i) and Sigma_ij = P(A_i and A_j). Then G = alpha^T Sigma^+ alpha (Sigma^+ the Moore-Penrose inverse) equals ||P_V 1_U||^2, the squared norm of the orthogonal projection of 1_U onto V, so P(U) - G = ||1_U - P_V 1_U||^2 >= 0 (Gallot 1966, Kounias 1968). The bound is exact, G = P(U), if and only if 1_U is a linear combination of the X_i almost surely. G = max over c with c^T alpha > 0 of (c^T alpha)^2/(c^T Sigma c), so it is at least the Chung-Erdős value (sum_i alpha_i)^2 / sum_{i,j} Sigma_ij obtained at c = (1, ..., 1).

[Proposition propRepresentation of arXiv:2609.00777, 'Universal murmuration and Hecke augmentation'] The raw symbol-valued augmented data and the ordinary prime data generate the same sigma-field.
Fix a training sample, give each derived coordinate the missing mask of its base coordinate, and fill every numeric column with its training-sample mean.
Within an affine linear model, the imputed panel $X_1+H_2$ has the same column span as the imputed ordinary prime panel together with the selected squares $x_p^2$.
The corresponding statement holds for $X_1+H_3$ and the selected cubes $x_p^3$.
Subsequent columnwise standardization preserves these affine spans for nonconstant columns.

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending. Let d>=1,N>=2d+1,n>=0,K>=2 and 1<=r<K be integers. There are N contexts, K candidates each, d pairs with one arbitrary A and one systematic S context, and N-2d known S contexts. S has all candidates true; A has an independent uniform random r-subset of truths. The factual law p is uniform over contexts, then uniform over true candidates within context. Training supplies n iid uniform context indices and A/S tags, without candidate identities; the partition class has VC dimension d. After training a perfect verifier independently draws a uniform ell-subset of truths in EVERY variable context, including paired S contexts, with 0<=ell<=r; it certifies these identities but gives no orientation tags. It verifies fraction gamma=ell/r of arbitrary truths. The two orientations have the same verifier-output likelihood, so U pairs untouched by training retain both orientations. For arbitrary generators g, require TV(p_Pi,g)<=c in every compatible world, where Pi is the exact partition into nonempty g-probability level sets and p_Pi(y)=p(B)/|B| in each bin B. Define beta=r/K,kappa=1-beta,q=ell/K,alpha=(K-r)/(K-ell),m=U/N,w=(d-U)/N,A0=w*(1-gamma),M0=m*(2-gamma-q). For every c in [0,1], the exact conditional worst-world hallucination frontier is V=alpha*((A0-c)_+ +(A0+M0-c)_+)/2. The oracle given orientations but the same certified identities has value alpha*((d/N)*(1-gamma)-c)_+. The conditional posterior-average game under uniform compatible orientations/supports has the same value. An ERM-version-space generator attains V in every compatible world in expected polynomial bit complexity for rational c. The exact minimax expected value is E[V], where E[z^U]=sum_{j=0}^d binom(d,j)*(z-1)^j*(1-2j/N)^n. At c=(d/N)*(1-gamma), the oracle is zero and V=kappa*U/(2N), with exact expected value kappa*d/(2N)*(1-2/N)^n, half kappa times the minimax expected partition-classification error. For n,d>=1,N=4max(n,d), it lies between (kappa/16)*min(1,d/n) and (kappa/8)*min(1,d/n). At ell=0 it recovers the no-verifier frontier. At ell=r the exact frontier is (kappa*U/N-c)_+/2, so complete arbitrary truth certification without orientation disclosure can still force hallucination at zero calibration error. Candidate T379-C008 v2; OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, proof (unaudited).
Target 2 and its interaction with target 1. Independent checking and

The hardest remaining generalization is ordinary unannotated factual
training, or a verifier revealing unequal numbers of truths per context:
the posterior density ordering used below can then fail.

## Model

Use the paired VC model: integers d>=1,N>=2d+1,n>=0,K>=2 and
1<=r<K; d pairs each have one A and one S context, the rest known S.
All K candidates are true in S; an independent uniform random r-subset
is true in A. The factual law p chooses contexts uniformly, then a true
candidate uniformly. Training is n iid uniform context indices and
their partition tags, with no candidate identities. The class has VC
dimension d. There are U pairs untouched by training. Let a=d/N,
m=U/N and w=a-m. A known partition is not given for untouched pairs.

Fix an integer 0<=ell<=r. A perfect post-training truth-sampling verifier
supplies a uniformly chosen ell-subset of true candidates in EACH of the
2d variable contexts, without disclosing any orientations or other truth
information. In known S contexts it also samples among true candidates,
namely all K. Thus it verifies the fraction gamma=ell/r of arbitrary
truths in every A context, and additionally supplies ell truths per paired
S context. This additional systematic information is explicitly part of
the experiment. The fixed S reservoir needs no queries. Sampling is
without replacement and independent across contexts given the world.

Put beta=r/K, kappa=1-beta, q=ell/K=beta*gamma,
alpha=(K-r)/(K-ell)=kappa/(1-q). Define posterior group masses

 A0=w*(1-gamma),       M0=m*(2-gamma-q).

The proposed exact conditional robust Mis_infinity frontier over ALL
generators is

 V_ell(c,U)=alpha/2 * [(A0-c)_+ +(A0+M0-c)_+],  c in [0,1].       (1)

The oracle with orientations known but the SAME certified truths has
value alpha*[a*(1-gamma)-c]_+. The expected minimax value is E[V_ell],
where U has the original d-pair occupancy law of C004; the verifier does
not reveal orientations. A matching lower bound also holds for coarser
output bins, but only exact levels are asserted for the attaining upper
bound. The specified uniform-posterior average game has the same
conditional value. All claims below remain unaudited derivations.

## Why the verifier does not label the unknown partition

Under a uniform random r-subset R, sample T uniformly among ell-subsets
of R. Every ell-subset of [K] has probability 1/binom(K,ell), since
binom(K-ell,r-ell)/(binom(K,r)*binom(r,ell))=1/binom(K,ell).
This is the same law as a uniform ell-subset from an S context. Hence
the verifier output has identical likelihood under either orientation.
Conditional on it, the untouched pair orientations remain independent
fair bits under the uniform world prior. Each A support is uniform over
r-subsets containing its certified T. Known tags are unchanged.

Let mu=E[p|tags,T] and s(y)=P(y false|tags,T). For uncertified atoms,

 known A:     mu_A=(r-ell)/(N*r*(K-ell)), s=alpha;
 unknown pair:mu_M=(mu_A+1/(N*K))/2,     s=alpha/2;
 known S:     mu=1/(N*K),               s=0.

Certified atoms have risk zero, and their mu is respectively 1/(Nr),
(1/(Nr)+1/(NK))/2, or 1/(NK). Therefore mu is nonincreasing with
positive false-risk level: mu_A<=mu_M<=1/(NK), while certified-safe
atoms have density at least 1/(NK). Let A be all uncertified atoms of
known A contexts; let M be all uncertified atoms of unknown pairs.
Their mu masses are exactly A0 and M0. All other atoms are safe.

## Unrestricted mixed-bin lower bound

For E=A and E=A union M, each atom inside E has mu-density at most
every atom outside E. For any uniform coarsening Pi, this implies
mu_Pi(E)>=mu(E): in a cell with l inside and h outside atoms, writing
their mu sums L,H, the ordering gives L/l<=H/h if both are nonempty,
so l(L+H)/(l+h)>=L. Empty intersections give equality. Sum cells.

For every generator g its output bins Pi(g) are fixed when worlds are
averaged. By linearity and the coordinatewise triangle inequality,
TV(mu_Pi,g)<=E[TV(p_Pi,g)]. A robust or stated posterior-average
calibration budget therefore implies

 g(A)>=(A0-c)_+,     g(A union M)>=(A0+M0-c)_+.

Expected hallucination is alpha*g(A)+(alpha/2)*g(M), exactly alpha/2
times the sum of these two events. This proves (1)'s lower bound for
every g, even bins that mix verified supports, contexts and risk levels.
Worst-world hallucination dominates the posterior average. No restriction
on the competing generator has been inserted into this argument.

## Worldwise attaining generator

Start from mu. Remove tA=min(c,A0) uniformly from A and
tM=min((c-A0)_+,M0) uniformly from M, taking zero from empty groups.
Add tA+tM uniformly to the N-2d fixed S contexts. Leave certified atoms
and all other contexts unchanged. This is nonnegative, normalized and
has TV(mu,g)=tA+tM<=c.

For a known A context, g is constant across its certified atoms and
across its uncertified atoms separately. Each of those groups has the
same p mass as mu in every compatible support. For each unknown pair,
g is constant on all certified atoms of BOTH siblings, and separately
on all uncertified atoms of both siblings. Their pairwise p masses are
respectively ell*(1/K+1/r)/N and (2-ell/K-ell/r)/N, independent of the
orientation and compatible supports. Known S context fibres are constant.
Consequently every exact g-score cell is a union of these invariant-mass
groups (including any merging levels and zero scores). It follows that
p_Pi=mu_Pi in every compatible world. With g_Pi=g,

 Mis_infinity(g,p)=TV(mu_Pi,g_Pi)<=TV(mu,g)<=c.

In known A uncertified groups a fraction alpha of candidates is false;
in unknown-pair uncertified groups a fraction alpha/2 is false. They
are uniform under g, so in EVERY compatible world

 H=alpha*(A0-tA)+(alpha/2)*(M0-tM)=V_ell(c,U).

There are no false certified atoms. The three budget ranges c<=A0,
A0<=c<=A0+M0, and c>=A0+M0 give (1). Empty groups, ell=r, ell=0,
U=0 and zero output bins are included by the stated conventions.

With orientations known, all uncertified A mass is a*(1-gamma), with
constant false-risk alpha. The same tail lower bound and removal
construction give the oracle claimed above. It is not given any
uncertified arbitrary identities beyond those disclosed by the verifier.

## Minimax expectation and informative budgets

Conditional posterior lower bounds integrate under the uniform prior on
orientations and supports, and the maximum over fixed worlds dominates
this average. The construction has the same H=V_ell(U) for every world
and every compatible verifier output. U's distribution is independent of
worlds and outputs because tags reveal a pair iff a training context
touches it, and the verifier conveys no orientation likelihood. These
facts give matching global expected minimax value E[V_ell(U)] under
conditional robust feasibility, without an unjustified sup/expectation
interchange. Its law is

 E[z^U]=sum_{j=0}^d binom(d,j)*(z-1)^j*(1-2j/N)^n,
 E U=d*(1-2/N)^n.

Put T=a*(1-gamma)-c. The exact excess over the known-partition oracle is

 alpha/2 * [(T-m*(1-gamma))_+
           +(T+m*(1-q))_+ -2*T_+].                    (2)

This is nonnegative: split T at -m*(1-q), 0, and m*(1-gamma), using
q<=gamma in the positive middle range. At c=0 it equals
alpha*kappa*gamma*m/2. At the oracle's zero-hallucination threshold
c=a*(1-gamma), the actual value is

 V_ell = alpha*m*(1-q)/2 = kappa*U/(2N).              (3)

Thus its exact expected value is kappa*d/(2N)*(1-2/N)^n, or kappa/2
times the minimax expected classification error R=d/N*(1-2/N)^n of
fair consistent ERM. The verifier does not change R because its law
does not distinguish orientations. It shifts the critical calibration
budget but the generation learning penalty there stays the same.

At ell=0, (1) reduces to C004. At ell=r, every A truth is certified,
but the verifier does not identify which contexts are A. Formula (1)
then becomes (kappa*U/N-c)_+/2. In particular zero calibration error
still costs kappa*U/(2N) unless the tags determine all orientations.
This contrasts with C006's orientation-disclosing full verifier, which
can yield zero hallucination and calibration error when all pairs are
verified. The source of side information, not merely its fact fraction,
must therefore be stated in a frontier claim.

For n,d>=1 choose N=4*max(n,d). Bernoulli's inequality gives
1/2<= (1-2/N)^n <=1. Thus the exact expected value at the threshold
in (3) lies between (kappa/16)*min(1,d/n) and
(kappa/8)*min(1,d/n). These are matching sample-complexity bounds for
this entire annotated VC family, for every allowed verifier fraction;
they do not extend automatically to an arbitrary VC class.

The version space, verifier sets and group counts admit the same efficient
representation as C004/C006. For rational c, group sampling has expected
polynomial bit complexity, with O(n+d+d*ell) explicit data processing.
The probability bound P(U>0)<=d*(1-2/N)^n also applies; U=0 gives the
oracle frontier simultaneously at every c. No independence between
missing-pair indicators is presumed.

[Thm matrix-sharpness of arXiv:2608.29018, 'Sharp Restricted Isometry Thresholds for\\ Global Minima of Rank-Restricted Matrix LASSO'] Fix integers $r_{\star}\ge1$ and $k\ge2$.
Set $t\coloneqq k/r_{\star}$ and
\begin{equation}
\mathsf{C}(t)\coloneqq1+\frac{(3t-4)_{+}}{2-t+\sqrt{t(t-1)_{+}}}.
\end{equation}
If $\delta\ge\delta_{\mathrm{sharp}}(t)+1/r_{\star}$, then:
\begin{itemize}
\item (Matrix) There exist adversarial data $(X_{\star},\mathcal{A},b)$ satisfying
\[
\operatorname{rank}(X_{\star})=r_{\star},\quad\mathcal{A}\in\operatorname{RIP}(\delta,k),\quad b=\mathcal{A}(X_{\star}),
\]
such that every global minimizer $X_{\lambda,r}$ in ((eq:matrix-lasso of the paper))
satisfies 
\begin{equation}
\lambda>0,\;r\ge\mathsf{C}(t)r_{\star}\implies\normF{X_{\lambda,r}-X_{\star}}\ge\normF{X_{\star}}.
\end{equation}
\item (Vector) There exist adversarial data $(x_{\star},A,b)$ satisfying
\[
\normzero{x_{\star}}=r_{\star},\quad A\in\operatorname{rip}(\delta,k),\quad b=Ax_{\star},
\]
such that every global minimizer $x_{\lambda,r}$ in ((eq:vector-lasso of the paper))
satisfies 
\begin{equation}
\lambda>0,\;r\ge\mathsf{C}(t)r_{\star}\implies\normtwo{x_{\lambda,r}-x_{\star}}\ge\normtwo{x_{\star}}.
\end{equation}
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group actions}'] Let \(G\) be a Polish group acting continuously on a Polish space \(X\). For \(x \in X\), \(U \subset X\) open with \(x \in U\) and \(V \subset G\) open with \(1_G \in V\), the \textit{local \(U \text{-} V\)-orbit of} \(x\), denoted \(\mathcal{O}(x,U,V)\), is the set of \(y \in U\) for which there exist \(l \in \mathbb{N}\), \(x = x_1\in U, x_2\in U, \dots x_l = y \in U\) and \(g_1, \dots ,g_{l-1} \in V\) such that \(x_{i+1} = g_i \cdot x_i\) for \(i < l\).

[Prop 11 ($p$-Powers of Derivations on Curves) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] Let $K$ be a generic point of a curve with a coordinate $x$. 
    Let $f\in K$. We define a derivation on $K$ by
    \[
    D=f\frac{\partial}{\partial x}
    \]
    Then, its $p$-power is given by 
    \[
    D^{\circ p}=-b_{p-1} D
    \]
    where $b_{p-1}\in K^p$ is the unique coefficient in the expansion in the $p$-basis $\frac{x^{j}}{(j)!}$ for $0\le j<p$
    \[
    f^{p-1}=b_0+b_1\frac{x}{1!}+\ldots +b_{p-1}\frac{x^{p-1}}{(p-1)!},
    \]
    where $b_i\in K^p$.
title: $p$-Powers of Derivations on Curves

Let $\hat{\tau}_{raw} = \bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0$ be the difference-in-means estimator from an A/B test. The regression-adjusted estimator $\hat{\tau}_{adj} = \hat{\tau}_{raw} - \hat{\beta}^T (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_0)$ asymptotically reduces the estimator variance by a factor of $(1 - R^2)$, where $R^2$ is the coefficient of determination of the regression of potential outcomes on covariates $X$.
Data is obtained from a randomized trial
Pre-treatment covariates X are independent of treatment assignment
Sample size N \to \infty

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); T232-w704-C014 v1. No independent PASS or established novelty/priority. Let m>=2,w>=2 be finite, M a real m-by-2 matrix of rank two, and Sigma a real symmetric positive definite 2-by-2 matrix. Suppose M Sigma has distinct singular values s1>s2>0. For gradient flow B'=-(BA-M)Sigma A^T, A'=-B^T(BA-M)Sigma, form U=(B;A^T) and D=[[0,M Sigma],[Sigma M^T,0]]. Let v1,v2 be positive unit eigenvectors of D. Fix a finite seed U0 with c1=||v1^T U0||>0 and one hidden orthogonal rotation R with v1^T U0 R=(c1,0,...,0). Split U0 R=[z0,X0] and assume c2=v2^T X0 is nonzero. Start at alpha U0 R, let tau=log(1/alpha)/s1, epsilon=alpha^(1-s2/s1), and write U_alpha(t+tau)=[z_alpha(t),X_alpha(t)]. On every fixed shifted compact, z_alpha converges to zbar and X_alpha/epsilon converges to chi c2. With H(P)=[[0,P Sigma],[Sigma P^T,0]], these are the unique weighted-bounded canonical Volterra solutions zbar=c1 exp(s1 t)v1-integral_-infinity^t exp(D(t-u))H(bbar abar^T)zbar du and chi=exp(s2 t)v2-integral_-infinity^t exp(D(t-u))H(bbar abar^T)chi du, where zbar=(bbar;abar). Their backward remainders are O(exp(3s1 t)) and O(exp((2s1+s2)t)), respectively; they extend to every finite time. If Pi projects onto col(M)^perp, then ||Pi B_alpha(physical time)||_F<=alpha||Pi B0||_F for all forward times, and ||Pi (X_alpha)_b/epsilon||_F<=alpha^(s2/s1)||Pi B0||_F. Thus bbar and chi_b belong to col(M), and their ideal equations reduce isometrically to the square target Q^T M for any orthonormal basis Q of col(M). The nondegeneracy assumptions hold almost surely for one fixed iid standard Gaussian seed, then scaled by alpha. This is fixed-compact origin matching, not a full Gaussian saddle passage or an entire normalized-error rate.
m>=2 and w>=2 finite
Sigma symmetric positive definite
rank M=2
s1>s2>0 singular values of M Sigma
fixed finite seed, nonzero top row and nonzero orthogonal second row
one fixed seed subsequently scaled by alpha

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4acbcb4e5c7acd85c682037013616afe960d0f6c9e53e4877e18a62dfc73b704","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4a/4acbcb4e5c7acd85c682037013616afe960d0f6c9e53e4877e18a62dfc73b704.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:d69cab3a62309597bdd696021668bf7b390642f1eda259975dfea1d109804dfb","bundle_entry_key":"rectangular-origin-matching-zero-modes","bundle_id":"population.t232-rectangular-origin-spectrum-arrival-20261021","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"deep linear networks; asymmetric factorization; saddle-to-saddle dynamics","draft":"w704/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.deep_linear_networks:rectangular-origin-matching-zero-modes","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Rectangular origin matching, including zero modes

Claim T232-w704-C014 v1. Kind: moved (origin-matching component of Target 1 only). Status: proof (unaudited). This is not a complete rectangular second-step theorem, and no novelty or priority claim is made. C006 v2 supplies the square precedent, not an independent audit of this extended statement.

## Statement
Let m>=2, w>=2 be finite, M be a real m-by-2 matrix of rank two, and Sigma a real symmetric positive definite 2-by-2 matrix. Suppose M Sigma has distinct positive singular values s1>s2. Define
 D = [[0,M Sigma],[Sigma M^T,0]],
 H(P) = [[0,P Sigma],[Sigma P^T,0]].
Let v1,v2 be orthonormal positive unit eigenvectors of D with eigenvalues s1,s2. Fix a finite seed U0=(B0;A0^T) in R^((m+2)-by-w). Assume c1=||v1^T U0||>0. Fix one hidden orthogonal rotation R with v1^T U0 R=(c1,0,...,0). Write U0 R=[z0,X0] and c2=v2^T X0, and assume c2 is not zero.

For gradient flow B'=-(BA-M)Sigma A^T, A'=-B^T(BA-M)Sigma from alpha U0 R, put tau=log(1/alpha)/s1, epsilon=alpha^(1-s2/s1), and use shifted time t=physical time-tau. Write U_alpha=[z_alpha,X_alpha]. On every fixed compact interval of shifted time,
 z_alpha -> zbar,    X_alpha/epsilon -> chi c2,
where the canonical pair is uniquely prescribed by
 zbar(t)=c1 exp(s1 t)v1 - integral_{-infinity}^t exp(D(t-u)) H(bbar abar^T)zbar(u)du,
 chi(t)=exp(s2 t)v2 - integral_{-infinity}^t exp(D(t-u)) H(bbar abar^T)chi(u)du.
Here zbar=(bbar;abar), with remainder bounds
 zbar-c1 exp(s1 t)v1 = O(exp(3s1 t)),
 chi-exp(s2 t)v2 = O(exp((2s1+s2)t))
as t tends to minus infinity. The constants depend on the fixed seed and data. The solutions extend to every finite shifted time.

Let Q be any m-by-2 orthonormal basis of col(M), and Pi=I-QQ^T. For every physical time >=0,
 ||Pi B_alpha||_F <= alpha ||Pi B0||_F.
Consequently both ideal output components bbar and chi_b lie in col(M), and on every fixed shifted compact
 ||Pi (X_alpha)_b /epsilon||_F <= alpha^(s2/s1)||Pi B0||_F.
In this display B0 may be replaced by B0 R without changing its Frobenius norm. The same hypotheses on c1,c2 hold almost surely for one fixed iid standard Gaussian seed, subsequently scaled by alpha.

## 1. Global existence and the two weighted estimates
The stacked equation is U'=DU-H(BA)U. With sigma=||Sigma||op,
 ||H(BA)||op <= (sigma/2)||U||_F^2.
Loss decreases, hence ||BA||_F is bounded since Sigma is positive definite. K=B^T B-AA^T is conserved and
 ||B^T B||_F^2+||AA^T||_F^2=2||BA||_F^2+||K||_F^2,
 ||B||_F^2+||A||_F^2 <= sqrt(2w)*sqrt(2||BA||_F^2+||K||_F^2).
These identities hold for rectangular B without alteration. For 0<alpha<=1 their right sides are uniformly bounded. Smooth finite-dimensional continuation gives global forward existence.

D has spectrum s1,s2,-s2,-s1 and zero of multiplicity m-2: this follows by a singular value decomposition of M Sigma, whose rank is two. In particular ||exp(Dv)||op<=exp(s1 v) for v>=0. Write K0=||U0||_F and choose a fixed negative T. Variation of constants gives a bootstrap
 ||U_alpha(t)||_F<=2K0 exp(s1 t),  -tau<=t<=T.
Indeed at a first crossing the nonlinear term divided by exp(s1 t) is at most
 (sigma/(4s1))(2K0)^3 exp(2s1 T),
which is strictly smaller than K0 for sufficiently negative T. The initial weighted norm equals K0.

The free dormant block has exactly zero v1 coefficient. Every other eigenvalue, including zero, is <=s2. Its free norm is at most epsilon ||X0||_F exp(s2 t). With C0=2 sigma K0^2, the nonlinear integral operator in the weight epsilon exp(s2 t) has norm at most
 C0 exp(2s1 T)/(s1+s2).
Take T smaller until this is <1/2. Then
 ||X_alpha(t)||_F<=2||X0||_F epsilon exp(s2 t).
The full propagator exp(s1(t-u)) is used for the integral; cancellation of the top coefficient is asserted only for the free term.

## 2. Fixed-compact limits: every free spectral component
On a fixed compact subset of (-infinity,T], the estimates above bound z_alpha, Y_alpha=X_alpha/epsilon, and their derivatives. Subsequential local uniform limits exist by Arzela-Ascoli and diagonal extraction.

For an eigenvalue lambda of D, the active free prefactor is alpha^(1-lambda/s1) exp(lambda t). Thus the v1 component is exactly c1 exp(s1 t); the s2 component has prefactor epsilon; the zero components have prefactor alpha; and the -si components have prefactors alpha^(1+si/s1). All but v1 vanish on fixed compacts.

For the normalized dormant free term the prefactor is alpha^((s2-lambda)/s1) exp(lambda t). The v1 coefficient is identically zero, the s2 coefficient is exactly exp(s2 t)v2 c2, the zero components have prefactor alpha^(s2/s1), and the -si components have prefactors alpha^((s2+si)/s1). All unwanted components vanish. Zero eigenvalues cannot be discarded when asserting a quantitative rate: alpha^(s2/s1) can be slower than the square stable-mode scale alpha^(2s2/s1).

The unnormalized dormant block tends to zero, so the product tends to bbar abar^T. The active integral is bounded by C exp(s1 t) exp(2s1 u); the normalized dormant integral by C exp(s1 t) exp((s1+s2)u). Both are integrable at minus infinity since s1,s2>0. Split at a fixed negative cutoff, pass to local limits on the finite part, and bound the rest by these uniform tails. This gives exactly the two displayed Volterra equations (first with Y in place of chi c2).

## 3. Uniqueness, remainders and continuation
On the bounded active weighted class ||z||<=C exp(s1 t), the cubic nonlinearity is Lipschitz with coefficient C' exp(2s1 u). Its Volterra difference operator has weighted norm at most C' exp(2s1 T)/(2s1). Decrease T until it is <1. The normalized linear dormant operator has norm at most C0 exp(2s1 T)/(s1+s2)<1. Thus both limits are unique in these classes. These bounds also construct chi by contraction about its free vector term, and linearity gives Y=chi c2. All subsequences have the same limits, proving convergence of the full alpha family.

Integrating the respective bounds gives the stated O(exp(3s1 t)) and O(exp((2s1+s2)t)) remainders. The stronger canonical prescription is needed: the mere leading s2 asymptotic alone would permit adding a multiple of zbar. Forward boundedness of the rank-one flow follows from Section 1 with w=1. The chi equation is linear with continuous coefficients, so it exists on each finite forward interval. Fixed finite-interval continuous dependence, applied first to U_alpha and then its normalized linear dormant equation, extends convergence from T to any fixed compact. No growing-time interval is covered.

## 4. Exact output contraction and the reduced ideal pair
Since Pi M=0, E=Pi B solves E'=-EA Sigma A^T. Therefore
 d/dt ||E||_F^2=-2 tr(EA Sigma A^T E^T)=-2||EA Sigma^(1/2)||_F^2<=0.
This proves the uniform transverse bounds in the statement. Fix any finite shifted t; for small alpha it corresponds to a positive physical time. Passing to the limits yields Pi bbar(t)=0 and (Pi chi_b(t))c2=0. Since the fixed row c2 is nonzero, the last equality implies Pi chi_b(t)=0. Thus ideal subspace confinement is established at the backward boundary through actual uniform bounds, rather than inferred merely from finite-time invariance.

Set Mtilde=Q^T M. It is invertible. The ideal equations for (Q^T bbar,abar) and (Q^T chi_b,chi_a) are precisely the square canonical Volterra equations for Mtilde, Sigma; Q is an isometry on their output components, and M Sigma and Mtilde Sigma have the same positive singular values. This identifies the ideal pair, not the finite-alpha projected dynamics over a growing time interval.

## 5. Gaussian event and remaining frontier gap
The two initial eigenrows v1^T U0 and v2^T U0 are independent standard Gaussian rows because v1,v2 are orthonormal and U0 is iid standard Gaussian. The first is nonzero almost surely. Conditional on it, projection of the second onto its hidden orthogonal complement is a nondegenerate Gaussian in dimension w-1>=1 and is nonzero almost surely. This proves c2!=0 without any later-flow independence.

This origin-matching component now extends to all finite m>=2 with two inputs under the displayed assumptions. Rectangular local arrival, full canonical escape, and the complete endpoint composition still require their own dimension checks and independent review. C010 and C012 remain unaudited. A bound on the perpendicular normalized component is not a bound on the entire matching error. No full rectangular rate, complete Target 1 solution, depth>=3 result, or priority finding is asserted.

Sources: proofs/origin_inactive_matching.md (C006 v2, square precedent); proofs/rectangular_output_reduction_route.md (C013 sketch, exact projection algebra). [Corollary 2.6 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Suppose that the hypotheses in Theorem \ref{Theorem: Main}
hold, and that $\msf T_0(t)$ has the asymptotic expansion in \eqref{Equation: Smooth Heat Trace}.
Let $t_1>t_2>\cdots>0$ be a vanishing sequence of positive numbers.
The following holds for any fixed $\ka>0$:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item If $t_n\leq cn^{-1/2-\eps}$ for some fixed $c,\eps>0$, then
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}2\pi t_n\,\msf T_\ka(t_n)=\msf{A}(D)\qquad\text{almost surely}.\]
\item If $t_n\leq cn^{-1-\eps}$ for some fixed $c,\eps>0$, then
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}4\sqrt{2\pi t_n}\left(\tfrac{\msf{A}(D)}{2\pi}t_n^{-1}-\msf T_\ka(t_n)\right)=\msf{L}(\partial D)\qquad\text{almost surely}.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[campaign status: settled_homogeneous_case - author-checked and simulation-validated; verification unreviewed] Consider a homogeneous marked Poisson field of grains of radius r and intensity lambda in R^d moving in straight lines with velocity law mu (the inertial, not Brownian, model). Let K = r_0 B be a ball and a a fixed point, with S_K and S_a their detection times, and let tau = inf{t : r_0 B meets W(t) and a is not in W(t)}, W(t) being the swept region. CLAIM: the joint law of (S_K, S_a), and hence the law of tau, is exact. AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Let U_N and V_N be independent N by M and P by M arrays with fixed centered iid real entry laws, variance one and finite fourth moments. Put A_N=U_N V_N^T/sqrt(N), and let B_N be the same product with independent standard Gaussian factor entries. If P/N->alpha and M/N->beta lie in (0,infinity), then for each fixed s>0, limsup_N [I(A_N;sqrt(s)A_N+G_N)-I(B_N;sqrt(s)B_N+G_N)]/(NP)<=0, with independent standard Gaussian observation noise and natural logarithms. Neither MI limit is assumed to exist. All dimension orderings and a positive mass of zero signal singular values are allowed. The proof uses a conditional rank-two Lindeberg resolvent estimate, concentration, moment bounds giving expected singular-value Wasserstein coupling, and Haar-mixture entropy concavity. It does not prove unconditional all-SNR product-MMSE extremality or a uniform small-SNR expansion.
Fixed centered real iid unit-variance factor laws with finite fourth moments
Independent arrays U_N,V_N and standard Gaussian observation noise
Positive finite limiting aspect ratios P/N and M/N
Fixed s>0 and natural logarithms

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:cc92334215dd5e90e034ea2e8cf2eebd3c5ca51c6a3eba83ca0f5809a74708f1","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/cc/cc92334215dd5e90e034ea2e8cf2eebd3c5ca51c6a3eba83ca0f5809a74708f1.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:4b63b4d5e0e27fb5fc35472ff5eb469e6c139a18443923de29d17fa9cb3919ee","bundle_entry_key":"iid-product-gaussian-mi-all-aspects-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-all-aspect-mi-and-sixth-coefficients-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:iid-product-gaussian-mi-all-aspects-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Gaussian-factor mutual-information comparison at all positive aspect ratios

Target 2, mutual-information part. Proof draft, unaudited; novelty is
unestablished. This extends the monotone-dimension-chain result in
gaussian_mi_wedge.md. It does not establish a formula for the limiting
mutual information or an unconditional all-SNR MMSE comparison.

Let N,P,M tend to infinity with P/N->alpha in (0,infinity) and
M/N->beta in (0,infinity). Let U in R^(N by M), V in R^(P by M)
be independent arrays with centered iid entries of variance one,
using fixed real entry laws with finite fourth moments. Set

 A=UV^T/sqrt(N),   B=U_G V_G^T/sqrt(N),

where the reference factors have independent standard Gaussian entries
and the same dimensions. For every fixed s>0 the claimed inequality is

 limsup [I(A;sqrt(s)A+G)-I(B;sqrt(s)B+G)]/(NP) <=0.          (1)

Noise G has independent standard Gaussian entries. Neither MI limit
needs to be assumed to exist for (1). Thus any existing iid-prior
limiting MI is at most the Gaussian reference limit.

The proof uses a direct global spectral comparison in place of the
dimension-restricted primary product-spectrum theorem. It provides
only global spectral universality; no local eigenvalue result is claimed.

## 1. Rank-two conditional Lindeberg replacement

Put S=UV^T/N, q=N+P, and use the real symmetric linearization

    H(U,V) = [ 0  S ; S^T  0 ],
    m(U,V;z)=q^(-1) Tr (H(U,V)-z I_q)^(-1),

where z has imaginary part eta>0. Every real value of every raw entry
gives a real symmetric H, so its resolvent R has operator norm at
most eta^(-1). This bound is uniform along all real replacement paths.

Condition on V. Differentiating H in one raw entry U_ir gives

    D_ir=N^(-1)[0 e_i v_r^T ; v_r e_i^T 0],

where v_r is the r-th column of V. Its rank is at most two and its
operator norm is ||v_r||/N. In particular it is independent of U_ir.
For the scalar real variable t=U_ir, resolvent differentiation gives

    partial_t^3 m = -6 q^(-1) Tr(R D_ir R D_ir R D_ir R).

The matrix in the trace has rank at most two. The inequalities
|Tr T|<=||T||_nuclear<=rank(T)||T||_op therefore give

    |partial_t^3 m| <= 12 ||v_r||^3/(q N^3 eta^4).       (2)

Taylor's integral remainder at t=0, to degree two, is bounded by
2||v_r||^3 |t|^3/(q N^3 eta^4). Replacing U_ir by an independent
standard Gaussian cancels the constant, linear and quadratic Taylor
terms because the two raw variables have the same first two moments.
The bound (2) is uniform in the other raw entries, including entries
already replaced. Thus a telescoping replacement of all NM entries
is legitimate.

Write a_3=E|U_11|^3, b_3=E|V_11|^3, and g_3=E|G_11|^3<=2.
The deterministic norm inequality

    (sum_{j=1}^P v_j^2)^(3/2) <= P^(1/2) sum_j |v_j|^3

implies E||v_r||^3<=P^(3/2)b_3. Consequently the first replacement
stage has expected normalized-resolvent error at most

    C_U(z)=2 M P^(3/2) b_3(a_3+g_3)/(q N^2 eta^4).       (3)

After this stage U is Gaussian. Replace the PM entries of V by
Gaussians, now conditioning on U. The derivative matrix has norm
||u_r||/N with E||u_r||^3<=N^(3/2)g_3. The second-stage error is

    C_V(z)=2 P M g_3(b_3+g_3)/(q N^(3/2) eta^4).         (4)

Under fixed positive aspect ratios, both (3) and (4) are O(N^-1/2).
Thus for each fixed z in the upper half-plane,

    |E m(U,V;z)-E m(U_G,V_G;z)| <= C_U(z)+C_V(z) ->0.   (5)

Finite fourth moments imply the third moments used here. Taylor's
remainder bound holds for unbounded real raw variables because its
third-derivative bound is uniform in t, and the absolute third moments
are finite. No truncation, unbounded Gaussian exponential moment, or
entrywise central limit theorem is being used.

## 2. Concentration and deterministic subsequential limits

Let r=min(N,P) and mu_A be the empirical probability measure of the
r singular values of S=A/sqrt(N), including any zero singular values
within those r positions. Let nu_A be the eigenvalue measure of H.
The two are related by

    nu_A=(r/q)(mu_A+reflection(mu_A))+(q-2r)delta_0/q.     (6)

The same relation holds for the Gaussian reference. Both r/N and q/N
stay bounded above and away from zero. Equation (5), tightness, and
uniqueness of the Stieltjes transform show that the expected spectral
measures of A and B have the same weak subsequential limits. More
explicitly, take any subsequence and a further subsequence on which
the deterministic expected nu_B converges weakly. Such a subsequence
exists because their second moments are bounded. Equation (5) implies
that expected nu_A has the same limit, by convergence of Stieltjes
transforms. The linear relation (6) transfers the conclusion to the
positive singular-value measures. This argument does not assume that
the full Gaussian spectral sequence has a limit.

To pass from expected to random measures, use independent row blocks
of U and V, exactly as in gaussian_mi_wedge.md. Replacing one row of
either factor changes S by rank at most one, and changes SS^T by rank
at most two. The empirical distribution function of the r squared
singular values therefore changes by at most 2/r. Indeed the N by N
Gram matrix has N-r additional zeros, the same for both configurations,
so its rank inequality rescales from 1/N to 1/r without an extra error.
Efron-Stein gives, for every fixed x,

    Var F_A(x) <= 2(N+P)/r^2 = O(N^-1).                 (7)

The Gaussian factors satisfy the same bound. At continuity points of
each selected deterministic limit, (7) upgrades the expected weak
convergence to weak convergence in probability. Monotonicity of the
distribution functions completes the usual countable-grid argument.

## 3. Moment control upgrades the comparison to expected W2

Let d=NP, b=M/N, T_N=||A||_F^2/d, q_U=E U_11^4,
q_V=E V_11^4. The exact fourth-cumulant patterns give

 E T_N=b,

 d^2 Var T_N = d[2b^2+(M/N^2)(q_U q_V-3)]
     +d(P-1)(M/N^2)(q_U-1)
     +d(N-1)(M/N^2)(q_V-1).                            (8)

Thus T_N-b tends to zero in L^2 for all the aspect ratios under
consideration. The empirical singular second moment is

    integral x^2 dmu_A(x)=(P/r)T_N,

which has a deterministic limit depending only on alpha,beta.
The Gaussian reference has exactly the same limiting second moment.

The uniform fourth singular-moment bound from gaussian_mi_wedge.md
remains valid without a monotone dimension chain. With
C=max(1,|q_U-1|,|q_V-1|,|q_U q_V-3|),

 E[(1/r)Tr(SS^T)^2]
 <= (N/r)[ b^2(NP^2+N^2P+NP)/N^3+C M P^2/N^3 ]=O(1). (9)

As before, the three covariance pairings account for NP^2+N^2P+NP
terms, while every joint fourth cumulant has absolute value at most
CM/N^2 and there are N^2P^2 summands in the fourth trace.
The proof uses no rotation invariance in (8) or (9).

Along each subsequence chosen in Section 2, (9) ensures that the
deterministic limiting singular law has exactly the common second
moment, rather than a smaller one due to lost mass at infinity.
Weak convergence in probability and convergence of second moments
then imply W2 convergence in probability to the same deterministic
subsequential law. This characterization can be seen directly by
matching one-dimensional quantiles: weak convergence gives convergence
of truncated quantiles, and second-moment tail control gives the
remaining L^2 convergence.

The convergence also holds in mean square Wasserstein distance.
Indeed Jensen gives

    E T_N^2 <= E A_11^4
       =3b^2+(M/N^2)(q_U q_V-3)=O(1).

Thus the empirical singular second moments have bounded second
moments. For any selected deterministic limit mu,

    W2(mu_A,mu)^2 <= 2 integral x^2 dmu_A+2 integral x^2 dmu,

so these squared distances are uniformly integrable. The same holds
for B, proving along the selected subsequence that

    E W2(mu_A,mu_B)^2 ->0.                             (10)

If (10) failed along the full sequence, a subsequence with distances
bounded away from zero would admit a further subsequence constructed
in Sections 2-3 on which they tend to zero, a contradiction. Therefore
(10) holds on the full sequence. Independent draws of the two
singular-value vectors are sufficient; no special correlation is needed.

## 4. Haar mixing and entropy continuity finish the proof

Let tilde A be the bi-orthogonal Haar mixture of A. Coupling its
singular values to those of B in sorted order and using the same Haar
left/right matrices gives

    e_N^2=E||tilde A-B||_F^2/(NP)
         =(r/P) E W2(mu_A,mu_B)^2 ->0.                  (11)

The reference B is bi-orthogonally invariant, including when M<r and
there is a macroscopic zero singular-value mass. Such zeros are already
included in the empirical measures and cause no problem in the
coupling. In particular no density or logarithmic singular-value
integrability assumption is being imposed.

Haar-mixture concavity and the Gaussian-smoothed entropy bound in
orbit_comparison.md give the finite-size inequality

    [I(A;sqrt(s)A+G)-I(B;sqrt(s)B+G)]/(NP) <= sqrt(s)e_N.

Equation (11) proves (1) for every fixed positive SNR. This concludes
the mutual-information comparison, subject to independent audit of
the proof.

## MMSE scope

If the Gaussian reference normalized MI converges to a finite i_G(s)
on (0,infinity), the abstract orbit lemma applies for all these aspect
ratios. It gives limsup normalized MMSE_A(s)<=2 i'_{G,-}(s), and
comparison with the reference MMSE at every differentiability point
of i_G, with at most a countable exceptional set. Verifying an
all-SNR differentiability theorem and its hypotheses is still unpaid.
The reference MI existence hypothesis is not used anywhere in (1).

Checks that could fail: rank and norm of the entry derivative D;
the factor 12 in (2) and 1/6 in Taylor's remainder; the different
column lengths P and N in the two replacement stages; concentration
for random rather than expected empirical laws; and uniform
integrability before taking expected W2.
