[Dfn 4. dfn: resistance forms of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Resistance form and resistance metric, [Kigami_12_Resistance]}] 
  
  Let $F$ be a non-empty set.
  A pair $(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})$ is called a \textit{resistance form} on $F$ if it satisfies the following conditions.
  \begin{enumerate} [label=(RF\arabic*), leftmargin = *]
    \item 
          The symbol $\mathcal{F}$ is a linear subspace of the collection of functions $\{ f : F \to \mathbb{R} \}$ 
          containing constants,
          and $\mathcal{E}$ is a non-negative symmetric bilinear form on $\mathcal{F}$
          such that $\mathcal{E}(f,f)=0$ if and only if $f$ is constant on $F$.
    \item 
          Let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation on $\mathcal{F}$ defined by saying $f \sim g$ if and only if $f-g$ is constant on $F$.
          Then $(\mathcal{F}/\sim, \mathcal{E})$ is a Hilbert space.
    \item
          If $x \neq y$, then there exists a function $f \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $f(x) \neq f(y)$.
    \item 
          For any $x, y \in F$,
          \begin{equation} 
            R_{(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})}(x,y)
            \coloneqq
            \sup
            \left\{
            \frac{|f(x) - f(y)|^{2}}{\mathcal{E}(f,f)}
            :
            f \in \mathcal{F},\
            \mathcal{E}(f,f) > 0
            \right\}
            < \infty.
          \end{equation}     
    \item
          If $\bar{f}\coloneqq  (f \wedge 1) \vee 0$,
          then $\bar{f} \in \mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{E}(\bar{f}, \bar{f}) \leq \mathcal{E}(f,f)$ for any $f \in \mathcal{F}$.
  \end{enumerate}
title: Dfn 4. dfn: resistance forms of arXiv:2412.08236

\]

operator/projective cost, while any exposed seed has its displayed

Method: Exact integral manipulation, Palm calculus, mass transport, limiting obstruction or conditional construction Result: Consider two equal radial densities proportional at large r to exp(b*r)*(1+r)^(-a), a>1. On a large L1 sphere, the split at radius s has weight proportional to (1+s)^(-a)*(1+R-s)^(-a). body:
[Lemma lem:tech_extent_lowerbound of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{Y}$ be a nonzero pure-jump L\'evy process on $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\psi_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{u})$ denote its L\'evy-Khintchine exponent and $\nu_{\bm{Y}}$ its L\'evy measure.\\
{\normalfont(a)} If $\bm{Y}$ has finite variation and nonzero drift with direction $\bm{u}_*\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then $|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant cx$ for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $x>0$.\\
{\normalfont(b)} Suppose there exist a locally finite measure $\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with
\[
\nu_{\bm{Y}}(A)
\geqslant \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}\int_{(0,\infty)}\1_A(x\bm{v})\rho(\mathrm{d} x)\sigma(\mathrm{d}\bm{v}),
\qquad A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}).
\]
Define $\Upsilon(x):=\int_{(0,x)}r^2\rho(\mathrm{d} r)$ for $x>0$, and, given any $c\in (0,1)$, suppose that $C_{c,\bm{u}_*}\coloneqq\{\bm{v}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:|\langle \bm{u}_*,\bm{v}\rangle|\geqslant c\}$ has positive $\sigma$-measure $m:=\sigma(C_{c,\bm{u}_*})>0$ for some $\bm{u}_*\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then we have
\[
|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant \frac{c^2m}{3}r^2\Upsilon(x^{-1})
\qquad\text{for all }x>0.
\]
In particular, if $c_\delta:=\inf_{x\in(0,1)}x^{\delta-2}\Upsilon(x)>0$ for some $\delta\in(0,2)$, then $|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant (c_\delta c^2m/3)x^{\delta}$, $x>1$.
title: Lemma lem:tech_extent_lowerbound of arXiv:2411.03609

body:
[Theorem 42 (Physical fourth-moment theorem: exact zero stratum) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $q\ge2$ and
\[
 X_{n,a}=I_q^{W_n}(f_{n,a}),
 \qquad
 \sup_n\sum_{a=1}^dq!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2<\infty.
\]
Write $\Sigma_n=\Cov(X_n)$, fix a free ultrafilter $\mathcal U$, and put
\[
 \xi_a=[f_{n,a}]_{\mathcal U}\in\cH_q,
 \qquad
 \Sigma=\Ulim\Sigma_n,
 \qquad
 \kappa_{n,a}=\E[X_{n,a}^4]-3\E[X_{n,a}^2]^2.
\]
The represented terminal has the intrinsic splitting
\begin{equation}
 T_a=\mathbb U_q^{-1}\xi_a
 =A_a^{\phys}+G_a^{\phys},
 \quad
 A_a^{\phys}=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cD_q}\xi_a,
 \quad
 G_a^{\phys}=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cK_q}\xi_a.
 
\end{equation}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item $\displaystyle\sum_{a=1}^d\mathfrak Q_q(\xi_a)=0$,
 equivalently $\Ulim\sum_a\kappa_{n,a}=0$;
 \item for every $a$ and $1\le r<q$,
 $
  \Ulim\norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,a}}=0
 $;
 \item $\xi_a\in\cK_q$ for every $a$, equivalently
 $P_{\cD_q}\xi=0$;
 \item $A^{\phys}=0$ (equivalently, the limiting active part of
 the reduced Hilbert--Stein trajectory vanishes) and the represented
 laws converge along $\mathcal U$ to $N_d(0,\Sigma)$;
 \item for every $a$,
 $
  \Ulim\E[X_{n,a}^4]=3\Sigma_{aa}^2
 $.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, every mixed proper contraction also
vanishes:
\begin{equation}
 \Ulim\norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,b}}=0
 \qquad(1\le r<q,\ 1\le a,b\le d).
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, there is a finite constant $C_{q,d}$, depending only on
$(q,d)$, such that for every $n$ and $t\in\R^d$,
\begin{equation}
 \left|
  \E e^{it\cdot X_n}
  -e^{-\frac12t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_nt}
 \right|
 \le C_{q,d}|t|^2
 \left(\sum_{a=1}^d\kappa_{n,a}\right)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}
Componentwise, the exact carré-du-champ comparison is
\begin{equation}
 \frac1{3q}\kappa_{n,a}
 \le
 \Var\bigl(\Gamma(X_{n,a},X_{n,a})\bigr)
 \le
 \frac{q-1}{3q}\kappa_{n,a}.
 
\end{equation}
Thus the fourth cumulants detect exactly, and not merely sufficiently,
the disappearance of the decomposable physical sector.

[Corollary C:parabolic-profile of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $\kappa \in (0, 1/2)$ and $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n/m \in [\kappa, \kappa^{-1}]$. Consider the process 
$$
\bar Y(j) = Y(1, j; n, m) - \mu(n, m+1- j), \qquad j\in\llbracket1,m \rrbracket,
$$
and fix a point $j_0 \in [1, (1-\kappa) m]$. Take any $\delta_0 > 0$. There exists some $c > 0$ depending only on $\kappa, \delta_0$, such that for all $\epsilon \in (0, n^{-1/3})$ we have
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{j \in \llbracket1, m \rrbracket} \bar Y(j) - \frac{\delta_0|j-j_0|^2}{m} \ge \epsilon m\right) \le 2\exp(- c \epsilon^{3/2}m). 
$$

[Definition 37 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] \rm
 
 A \([0,\infty]\)-valued function
 $A_t(\omega),\ t \ge 0,\ \omega \in \Omega$
 is a PCAF if the following hold:
 \begin{itemize}
  \item[(A.1)] for each $t \ge 0$, $A_t(\cdot)$ is $\c{F}_t$-measurable,
  \item[(A.2)]
       there exist a set $\Lambda \in \c{F}_{\infty}$ called a defining set, and
       an exceptional set $N \subset E$ such that $\b{P}_x(\Lambda) = 1$
       for any $x \in E \setminus N$ and $\theta_t \Lambda \subset \Lambda$
       for any $t > 0$, and moreover,
       for each $\omega \in \Lambda$, ${A}_0(\omega) = 0$,
       $|A_t(\omega)| < \infty$ for any $t < \zeta(\omega)$,
       $A_t(\omega) = {A}_{\zeta(\omega)}(\omega)$ for any
       $t \ge \zeta(\omega)$ and
       \begin{align}
	{A}_{t + s}(\omega) = {A}_s(\omega) + {A}_t(\theta_s \omega),\
	\text{for any $t,s \ge 0$},
       \end{align}
  \item[(A.3)]
       for each $\omega \in \Lambda$, the map
       $t \mapsto {A}_t(\omega)$ is non-negative and continuous on
       $[0,\infty)$, where $\Lambda$ is the set defined in the above condition.

[Theorem eq:Gaussian-variational of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:gaussian-variational}
There exists \(L_0<\infty\) such that, for every fixed \(L>L_0\),
\(\varepsilon>0\), continuous \(V\) bounded below, and either
\(f\in\mathcal F_m\) or \(f=\ell_\eta\) with fixed \(\eta>0\),
\begin{align}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\Phi_{N,L}^G(V,\varepsilon,f)
 ={}&\frac12\log(2\pi e)+\log a_{\varepsilon,p}\notag\\
 &+\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\left\{-\frac{u^2}{2}-V(u)+\ell_{p,f}(u)\right\}.
 
\end{align}
If in addition \(V\in\mathcal V_m\), the same limit holds with \(G\) replaced
by \(J\) under (thm:bulk-universality of the paper).  For
\(f\in\mathcal F_m\), the same conclusion also follows under
(thm:weibull-bulk of the paper); no uncut \(\ell_\eta\) extension of that
Weibull truncation theorem is claimed. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In abstract algebra, an abelian group $(G,+)$ is called finitely generated if there exist finitely many elements $x_{1},\dots,x_{s}$ in $G$ such that every $x$ in $G$ can be written in the form $x=n_{1}x_{1}+n_{2}x_{2}+\cdots +n_{s}x_{s}$ for some integers $n_{1},\dots,n_{s}$. In this case, we say that the set $\{x_{1},\dots,x_{s}\}$ is a generating set of $G$ or that $x_{1},\dots,x_{s}$ generate $G$. So, finitely generated abelian groups can be thought of as a generalization of cyclic groups.

[Theorem 1 (General mixed-Sellke fluid limit) of arXiv:2608.22122, '2608.22122'] Under the stochastic construction and notation of Section~\ref{sec:model}, for every finite \(T>0\),
\[
\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}
\left\|
\bigl(s_N(t),\iota_N(t),r_N(t),A_N(t)\bigr)
-
\bigl(s(t),\iota(t),r(t),A(t)\bigr)
\right\|
\xlongrightarrow{\Pp}0
\]
as $N\to\infty.$

The deterministic limit is characterized by the  initial-value problem
\[
\dot A(t)
=
\tau\bigl[1-r_0-s_0G(A(t))\bigr]
-\gamma A(t),
\qquad
A(0)=0,
\]
together with
\[
s(t)=s_0G(A(t)),
\]
\[
r(t)=r_0+\frac{\gamma}{\tau}A(t),
\]
and
\[
\iota(t)=1-s(t)-r(t).
\]

Equivalently,
\[
A(t)=\tau\int_0^t\iota(u)\,du.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2607.22416, 'A multi-player optimal stopping game based on a spider Brownian bridge'] Suppose that $p=0.5$, $\mathcal{G}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{1}$ are given by $\mathcal{G}_{1}(z)=z - \alpha$ and $\mathcal{L}_{1}(z)=  \theta z$, and that $\mathcal{G}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{2}$ are given by $\mathcal{G}_{2}(z)=-z - \alpha$ and $\mathcal{L}_{2}(z)=  -\theta z$.
 
The game admits at most three symmetric threshold-type Nash equilibria.

If $\theta \geq 1 + \max \{ 2 \alpha \left[ \alpha + (\alpha^2 + 1)\psi(\alpha) \right], \frac{1}{\alpha}(4+\alpha^2)\psi(\frac{\alpha}{2}) \}$ then there are no symmetric threshold-type Nash equilibria.

If $\theta \leq 1$ then there is a unique symmetric threshold-type Nash equilibria.

There are cases with more than one symmetric threshold-type Nash equilibria.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:e8981610444dc1b08f454063bd40a550617ecb7a9c918c969cc03af20377340d","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/e8/e8981610444dc1b08f454063bd40a550617ecb7a9c918c969cc03af20377340d.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:6b9d792af3bd6b55a5ec302601554d294dc7a463eb6c29de994ef68db0a27580","bundle_entry_key":"tracking-rigidity","bundle_id":"population.adam-active-tracking-preconditioner-rigidity-010","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"adaptive optimization and compact dynamical systems","draft":"w706/bundle_010.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.adam:adam-active-sharpness-convergence-forces-preconditioner-limits-gradient-alignment","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-022 v2; target2; kind moved; independently checked proof.

STATEMENT: ALL POSITIVE TWO-EIGENVALUE DIAGONAL QUADRATICS
Fix eta,epsilon,lambda1,lambda2>0. Run ordinary separately
bias-corrected Adam with b=.9,d=.999, outside-sqrt epsilon and standard
zero moments. Put theta_i=eta*lambda_i/epsilon, g_i=lambda_i*x_i,
P_i,t=sqrt(v_i,t+1/(1-d^(t+1)))+epsilon and

 A_t=eta*[sum_i lambda_i*g_i,t^2/P_i,t^2]
          /[sum_i g_i,t^2/P_i,t],
 S_t=eta*max_i(lambda_i/P_i,t).

Quotient limits are along all defined times, assumed arbitrarily late.
If A_t->38, each physical coordinate approaches EITHER its origin OR
its exact alternating scalar cycle. A cycling coordinate necessarily
has theta_i>38 and position amplitude a_i=eta/38-epsilon/lambda_i>0.
Consequently every corrected variance denominator CONVERGES, without
assuming this convergence. This includes parameters where the scalar cycle linearization has a
unit-modulus multiplier; it also permits stable and unstable cycles.
This conditional classification asserts neither their attraction nor
the generic occurrence of tracking. In particular theta=60 is not
being described as a neutral or attracting cycle.

Moreover the following are equivalent:

 (GAP) A_t->38 and liminf_t S_t>38;

 (GRADIENT) for some permutation(i,j), theta_j>38 and exactly one of
 the following two parameter/gradient conditions holds:

 CYCLE TYPE:
  theta_i>38, |g_i,t|->eta*lambda_i/38-epsilon>0,
  g_j,t/g_i,t->0;                                      (C)

 CRITICAL ORIGIN TYPE:
  theta_i=38, ||g_t||->0,
  g_j,t^2/(g_i,t^2+g_j,t^2)->0.                         (O)

In either type S_t->theta_j>38. Condition(C) forces coordinate i to
its cycle and j to its origin. Condition(O) has both coordinates at
their origins and an asymptotically critical-coordinate gradient.
In particular a persistent asymptotic top gap is IMPOSSIBLE if one
cap is strictly above38 and the other strictly below38. If both caps
are at most38, S_t<=38 at EVERY time, also excluding(GAP).

For epsilon=eta^p, substitute theta_i=eta^(1-p)*lambda_i. At p=1,
the condition is stated solely with the two eigenvalues lambda_i in
place of theta_i, with cycling GRADIENT amplitude eta*(lambda_i/38-1) and
POSITION amplitude eta*(1/38-1/lambda_i).

WHAT THIS CLAIM DOES AND DOES NOT SETTLE
This is an independently checked target2 classification of a POSITIVE ASYMPTOTIC
top-sharpness gap under exact active convergence. Exact022v2 has reviewer PASS.
It does not classify which generic initializations track, does not
give a finite-width band estimate, and does not equate liminf S>38
with the weaker property S_t>38 at every finite time while S_t->38.
The criterion is necessary and sufficient in terms of actual gradient
tails; it does not assert existence of a basin realizing every type.

DEPENDENCIES AND AUDIT
Exact022v2 has independent reviewer PASS,claude-738954b6,21 Oct02:16.
All dependencies are now independently checked:022v1 (033) for both
supercritical caps;012v2 (015) for low-cap decay;023v1 (034),024v2 (037)
and025v1 (036) for mixed caps and strict mixed-range exclusion.
The H.5 six-case inequality used by022v1 remains a cited primary theorem.
The reviewer checked the exhaustive cap partition, denominator limits,
top-limit formula, weighted-versus-gradient fraction comparison and
variance-filter sufficiency. This audit does not cover main021.
Both(C) and(O) require the theta_j>38 coordinate to approach its
linearly unstable origin. This is a criterion for actual asymptotic
trajectories, not a claim that typical starts realize either type.

PROOF
1. Automatic denominator limits.
If both theta_i>38,022v1 gives product origin/cycle convergence with
a nonempty cycling set. If both theta_i<=38,012v2 gives convergence
to the origin in each coordinate. In the remaining mixed range
theta_h>38>=theta_l,024v2 gives origin convergence in the low coordinate
and origin or cycle convergence in the high coordinate. These cases
exhaust all positive eigenvalues, and each gives convergence of P_i.

Let I be the cycling set. Then

 P_i -> eta*lambda_i/38 for i in I,
 P_j -> epsilon for j outside I,
 S_t -> max({38 if I is nonempty} union {theta_j:j outside I}). (1)

The empty maximum is never needed: there are two coordinates.

2. Necessity when the cycling set is nonempty.
If(GAP) holds and I contains both coordinates, (1) gives S_t->38,
a contradiction. Hence I={i}. Its amplitude gives
|g_i,t|->eta*lambda_i/38-epsilon>0 and theta_i>38.
The other coordinate tends to its origin, so g_j/g_i->0.
Equation(1) and(GAP) force theta_j>38. This is(C).

3. Necessity when the cycling set is empty.
Both gradients and variances tend to zero, so P_i->epsilon. If both
caps exceed38, their active weighted mean has liminf at least the
smaller cap>38, contradicting A_t->38. If both caps are at most38,
then S_t<=38 and(GAP) fails. Thus one cap theta_j>38 and the other
theta_i<=38. If theta_i<38,025's strict mixed-cap exclusion contradicts
active convergence. Therefore theta_i=38.

Since both denominators tend to epsilon, along defined times the
active formula, uniformly over relative gradient magnitudes, is

 A_t=38+(theta_j-38)*g_j,t^2/(g_i,t^2+g_j,t^2)+o(1).     (2)

Active convergence and theta_j>38 force the fraction to zero.
Both gradients vanish, so this is exactly(O).

4. Sufficiency of the two gradient conditions.
Under(C), g_j->0 and |g_i| has the positive limit G_i=eta*lambda_i/38
-epsilon. Stable variance recursions give v_i->G_i^2,v_j->0. Hence

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine whether the reflection-positivity chessboard argument can be pushed down from q >= q_c(d) large to q = 3 in d = 3 using improved contour entropy bounds. Result: The Kotecky-Shlosman argument proves a first-order transition when the entropy of contours (bounded by e^{c |contour|}) is beaten by the energy gain, which requires q large enough that log q exceeds a lattice-dependent constant; in d = 3 the best constants give q >= some number in the tens. Improving to q = 3 needs the exact contour entropy, which is not available; numerically the d = 3, q = 3 transition is weakly first order with a tiny latent heat, so any argument must be sharp to within a few percent, beyond what chessboard estimates give. Alternative route through the random-cluster representation: discontinuity is equivalent to non-uniqueness of the infinite-volume random-cluster measure at p_c, i.e. to the wired measure having an infinite cluster at p_c while the free one does not; for q > 4 in d = 2 this was done via the six-vertex transfer matrix, a planar tool. No d = 3 substitute. No result. Obstruction: Contour-entropy constants are far from sharp and the two-dimensional transfer-matrix route has no three-dimensional analogue.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0048-discontinuity-of-the-potts-phase-transition-on-z-d-for-q-3-d-3

body:
Let $S_n = \frac{1}{n} X_n^T X_n$ with $X_n = Z_n \Sigma_n^{1/2}$, where $Z_n$ is $n \times p$ with i.i.d. entries of mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite fourth moment, $\Sigma_n$ is positive semidefinite with $\|\Sigma_n\|$ bounded, $p/n \to c \in (0, \infty)$, and the spectral distribution of $\Sigma_n$ converges weakly to $H$. Let $F^{c,H}$ be the limiting spectral distribution of $S_n$ (the Marchenko-Pastur-Silverstein law) and let $[a, b]$ be a closed interval, $a > 0$, lying outside the support of $F^{c,H}$ and outside the supports of $F^{c_n, H_n}$ for all large $n$ (the finite-$n$ laws built from $c_n = p/n$ and $H_n$). Then almost surely no eigenvalue of $S_n$ lies in $[a, b]$ for all $n$ large enough: $\mathbb{P}(\text{no eigenvalue of } S_n \text{ in } [a, b] \text{ for all large } n) = 1$. Corollary (Bai-Yin 1993, the case $\Sigma = I$): $\lambda_{\max}(S_n) \to (1 + \sqrt c)^2$ and, for $c < 1$, $\lambda_{\min}(S_n) \to (1 - \sqrt c)^2$ almost surely - the Marchenko-Pastur edges - and the finite fourth moment is necessary for the largest eigenvalue to converge. Consequence used throughout: an eigenvalue of a sample covariance strictly above $\sigma^2(1 + \sqrt c)^2$ (by a fixed margin) cannot come from an identity-covariance bulk, which is what licenses the bulk edge as a detection threshold in the spiked model, in Gavish-Donoho denoising, and in the median-based noise estimate.

A probability measure mu on a metric space (M, d) is said to satisfy the T_1 transportation-cost inequality with constant c > 0 (denoted T_1(c)) if for every probability measure nu absolutely continuous with respect to mu, W_1(nu, mu) <= sqrt(2 * c * D_{KL}(nu || mu)), where D_{KL}(nu || mu) = int (dnu/dmu) log(dnu/dmu) dmu is the relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence).
mu is a probability measure on (M, d)
c > 0
title: T_1 Transportation-Cost Inequality

body: In mathematics, the ideal class group (or class group) of an algebraic number field $K$ is the quotient group $J_{K}/P_{K}$ where $J_{K}$ is the group of fractional ideals of the ring of integers of $K$, and $P_{K}$ is its subgroup of principal ideals. The class group is a measure of the extent to which unique factorization fails in the ring of integers of $K$. The order of the group, which is finite, is called the class number of $K$.

[Lemma 16 (properties of precomposition operators) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X=\mathrm{id}+w:\Rn_y\to\Rn_x$ be an orientation-preserving
bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism such that
\[
 \|dX\|_{L^\infty}+\|(dX)^{-1}\|_{L^\infty}\le\mathfrak m,
 \qquad 0<J_-\le\det dX\le J_+.
\]
Put $\Ufield:=dw$ and $\Kmat:=(dX)^{-1}$, and assume
$\Ufield,\Kmat-\mathrm{Id}\in Y^{s-1,1}$.  Recall $\mathcal{C}_{X}^\pm f=f\circ X^\pm$. Then, for every $0\le r\le s$,
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathcal C_Xf\|_{H^r_y}\le C_{\mathrm{comp}}(X,r)\|f\|_{H^r_x},
 \qquad
 \|\mathcal C_X^{-1}u\|_{H^r_x}\le C_{\mathrm{comp}}(X,r)\|u\|_{H^r_y},
\end{equation}
where, with $k(r):=\max\{\lceil r\rceil-1,0\}$,
\[
 C_{\mathrm{comp}}(X,r)\le C(n,s,r,v_{\rm A},\mathfrak m,J_\pm)
 \big(1+\|\Ufield\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}
        +\|\Kmat-\mathrm{Id}\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}\big)^{k(r)}.
\]
If these bounds hold uniformly for $X=X(t)$ on a compact interval $I$ and, in addition,
\[
 w\in C(I;H^s),\qquad
 \Ufield,\Kmat-\mathrm{Id}\in C(I;Y^{s-1,1}),
\]
then $u\in C(I;H^r_y)$ implies
$\mathcal C_{X(t)}^{-1}u(t)\in C(I;H^r_x)$. Independently of the Sobolev
time-regularity hypothesis above, suppose that $X(t)$ and $X(t)^{-1}$ vary
locally uniformly on $I$ and that the Jacobian and bi-Lipschitz bounds are
uniform. Then, for every $1\le q<\infty$, every $t_0\in I$, and every
$g\in L^q$,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{t\in I}\|\mathcal C_{X(t)}^{\pm1}\|_{L^q\to L^q}<\infty,\qquad
 \lim_{t\to t_0}\|\mathcal C_{X(t)}^{\pm1}g
 -\mathcal C_{X(t_0)}^{\pm1}g\|_{L^q}=0.
\end{equation}
title: properties of precomposition operators

[Dfn 99 (SDE coefficients with ideal smoothing) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Abbreviating $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation density of $\vY$, let us define
	\begin{align}
	
	B^i(t,y)
	&\equiv
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,y)}{\rho*\varphi(t,y)}\,,\\
	A^{ij}(t,y)
	&\equiv \frac{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi(t,y)}{\rho*\varphi(t,y)}\,.
	
	\end{align}
Let $\Sigma(t,y)$ be a matrix square root of $A(t,y)$, and let 
$\hvX$ be the solution to the SDE (in $d$ dimensions)
	\beq
	d\hvX(t) = B(t,\hvX(t))\,dt+
		\Sigma(t,\hvX(t))\,dW(t)\,,
	\eeq
where $W$ is a $d$-dimensional standard Brownian motion, with the initial condition that $\hvX(0)$ equidistributed as $\hvY(0)$. \textbf{In the abstract discussion of this section, we assume $B$ and $\Sigma$ are sufficiently regular that $\hvX$ is the unique solution of the SDE.}
title: SDE coefficients with ideal smoothing

Let $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ with $X$ an $n \times p$ design of full column rank (treated as fixed), $E[\varepsilon] = 0$, and $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \Omega = \operatorname{diag}(\omega_1^2, \dots, \omega_n^2)$ - independent errors whose variances may differ across observations. Then the ordinary least-squares estimator $\hat\beta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$ is unbiased and its exact covariance is the sandwich $$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta) = (X^T X)^{-1}\, X^T \Omega X\, (X^T X)^{-1},$$ which reduces to the textbook $\sigma^2 (X^T X)^{-1}$ only when all $\omega_i^2 = \sigma^2$. THEOREM (White, 1980). With $r = y - X\hat\beta$ the residuals, the estimator $\hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}} = (X^T X)^{-1}\big(\sum_i r_i^2 x_i x_i^T\big)(X^T X)^{-1}$ is consistent for $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta)$ in the sense that $n\,\hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}} - n\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta) \to 0$ in probability as $n \to \infty$ with $p$ fixed, under finite fourth moments of the errors and of the regressors (the rows $x_i$ bounded or with $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \|x_i\|^4 = O(1)$) and $\frac{1}{n}X^T X \to$ a positive definite limit. No model for the $\omega_i^2$ is needed. In the ill-conditioned directions of $X^T X$ (nearly collinear regressors) the sandwich can exceed the homoscedastic formula by a large factor when the large residuals fall on the observations that determine those directions; the homoscedastic formula then badly understates the sampling noise of the coefficients.
fixed design X of full column rank
independent errors with mean zero and possibly different variances
finite fourth moments of errors and regressors; (1/n) X'X -> positive definite; p fixed as n -> infinity for the consistency statement

body: A Dirichlet character mod q is a completely multiplicative function chi from the integers to C, periodic with period q, vanishing exactly on integers sharing a factor with q, induced by a homomorphism from the unit group mod q to the circle. Its L-function is L(s, chi) = sum over n >= 1 of chi(n) n^{-s}, absolutely convergent for Re(s) > 1 with an Euler product over primes; for nonprincipal chi it extends holomorphically to C, and L(1, chi) is nonzero - the key analytic input to Dirichlet's theorem.
title: Dirichlet Character and L-Function

Let X be a set. A function mu* from the FULL power set of X to [0, +infinity] is an OUTER MEASURE if (1) mu*(empty set) = 0, (2) it is monotone: A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B), and (3) it is countably subadditive: mu*(union over n >= 1 of A_n) <= sum over n >= 1 of mu*(A_n) for every countable family of subsets A_n of X, MEASURABLE OR NOT. Note that subadditivity is part of the definition in the abstract setting; the mathematical content lies in the fact that the standard constructions produce it. CONSTRUCTION FROM A COVERING FAMILY (a gauge): let E be a family of subsets of X containing the empty set and covering X by countably many of its members, and let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0. Define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k >= 1 of rho(E_k) : E_k in E for all k and A contained in the union of the E_k }, with the convention that the infimum of the empty set is +infinity. Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is the case where E is the family of boxes (or open boxes, or cubes) and rho is the elementary volume. A set A is CARATHEODORY MEASURABLE for mu* if mu*(T) = mu*(T intersect A) + mu*(T minus A) for every test set T; these sets form a sigma-algebra on which mu* restricts to a complete countably additive measure (Caratheodory's theorem). CAUTIONS: an outer measure is defined on all subsets but is in general NOT additive on disjoint sets; it is not a measure on the power set; and the Caratheodory criterion, not the mere inequality in (3), is what recovers additivity.
X is a set and mu* is defined on the entire power set of X
for the construction: E contains the empty set and some countable subfamily of E covers X, so that every subset has at least one admissible cover
rho maps E into [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; no additivity or monotonicity of rho is assumed
countable, not arbitrary, families are used in the subadditivity axiom
title: Outer measure and the outer measure generated by a covering family

body: Let P be a simple polygon (a closed, non-self-intersecting polygonal curve together with its interior) with n vertices. Then floor(n/3) guards, placed at points of P, always suffice to guard the interior of P, meaning every point of P is visible in a straight line, unobstructed by the polygon's boundary, from at least one guard; and for some polygons with n vertices, floor(n/3) guards are also necessary. [Chvatal (1975); see O'Rourke, Art Gallery Theorems and Algorithms]

[Definition eq:deftildeupsilon of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] We define the family of elementary differentials $(\Upsilon^{\tau}: \tau\in\mathfrak{T})$, with $\Upsilon^{\tau} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]$, by using an induction in $\tau$. 
For the base case, we define  $\Upsilon^{\circ} = \big( \Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}\big)_{r \in \N} \in \prod_{r \in \N} \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\circ_{r}]$ by setting, in analogy with (equation eq:elem_diff1_base of the paper), 
\[
\Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}(x_{r}) = V(x_{r})\;.
\]
It is clear that one indeed has $\Upsilon^{\circ_{r}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\circ]$. 
In other words, we could have just fixed a single $r \in \N$, applied the above formula, and then defined $\Upsilon^{\circ} = \pi_{\circ,\circ_{r}} \Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}$ and our construction would be well-defined in that it didn't depend on our initial choice of $r$. 

We now proceed to the inductive step. 
Suppose we have $\tau=[\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k]$, where $k > 0$, the $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k$ are unlabelled, and $[\cdot]$ denotes joining the roots of unlabelled trees at a new unlabelled root. 
Our inductive assumption is that we have been given $\Upsilon^{\circ} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\raisebox{+0.05ex}{\includegraphics[scale=1.5]{figures/Xi.pdf}}]$, and $\Upsilon^{\tau_{j}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}_j]$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant k$.

Next, fix any labelled $\underline{\tau} \in \tau$, and choose any labelled $\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k$ with $\underline{\tau}_j \in \tau_j$, such that $\underline{\tau} = [\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k]_{r}$ (here we use the notation of (equation eq:product_of_trees of the paper), and $r = r(\underline{\tau})$).
For every $\underline{\sigma}\in \{\circ_{r}, \underline{\tau}_1,\cdots,\underline{\tau}_k\}$, we first set
\begin{equs}
   \Upsilon^{\underline{\sigma}} \eqdef \iota_{\sigma,\underline{\sigma}} \Upsilon^{\sigma}\in\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\sigma}]\,.
\end{equs}
We then define $\Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ in analogy with (equation eq:elem_diff1 of the paper) by setting
\begin{equ}
\Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau})})
=
\big( \mathrm{d}^{k} \Upsilon^{\circ_r}(x_{r(\underline{\tau})}) \big) \big[ \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}_{1}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_1)}),\cdots, \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}_{k}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_k)}) \big]\,,
\end{equ}
and finally we can set
\begin{equ}
\Upsilon^{\tau} \eqdef
\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}} \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}}\;.
\end{equ}
In the next lemma we verify that $\Upsilon^{\tau}$ as defined above is well-defined, in that it does not depend on how we realised $\tau$ as the labelled tree $[\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k]_{r}$.

This refutes a general first-moment inference, not the Ising conjecture.

body: A collection B of subsets of a set X is a basis (base) for a topology on X if (i) every point of X lies in at least one member of B, and (ii) whenever a point x lies in the intersection of two members B1, B2 of B, there is a member B3 of B with x in B3 and B3 contained in the intersection of B1 and B2. The topology generated by B consists of exactly those subsets U of X such that every point of U lies in some member of B contained in U; equivalently, the open sets are precisely the unions of subfamilies of B. Conversely, given a topological space (X, T), a subcollection B of T is a basis for T exactly when every open set is a union of members of B.
title: Basis for a topology

body:
Fix an integer n >= 2 and let F_k = I_n(f_k) be a sequence living in the SAME n-th Wiener chaos, with E[F_k^2] = n! ||f_k||^2 converging to sigma^2 > 0. Then the following are EQUIVALENT: (i) F_k converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2); (ii) E[F_k^4] -> 3 sigma^4; (iii) the contractions satisfy || f_k contracted with f_k at r indices || -> 0 for every r = 1, ..., n-1. The theorem replaces the infinitely many moment conditions of the method of moments by a SINGLE fourth-moment condition. The hypothesis that the chaos order n is FIXED and the same for every k is essential and is the standard misquotation: for a general sequence of random variables, or for a sequence whose chaos order drifts, matching the fourth moment says nothing about normality - the fourth moment of a suitable two-point law is also 3 times the square of its variance. Also essential is sigma^2 > 0; degenerating variance is excluded. The quantitative form is due to Nourdin and Peccati via Malliavin-Stein: for F in the n-th chaos with E[F^2] = sigma^2, the total variation distance to N(0, sigma^2) is bounded by a constant depending only on n times the square root of ( E[F^4] - 3 sigma^4 ), so the fourth cumulant controls the rate as well as the limit. [Nualart and Peccati (2005), Ann. Probab. 33; Nourdin and Peccati (2009); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Theorem 5.2.7]
all F_k lie in the SAME fixed chaos of order n >= 2
E[F_k^2] -> sigma^2 > 0
the equivalence is FALSE for sequences not confined to one chaos

Let D be the Malliavin derivative and L the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck generator, so that on the n-th chaos L F = -n F and hence -L^{-1} F = F/n. Stein's method gives, for any F with E[F] = 0 and E[F^2] = sigma^2, the bound d_TV( F, N(0, sigma^2) ) <= (2/sigma^2) sqrt( Var( <D F, -D L^{-1} F> ) ), where <.,.> is the inner product of the underlying Hilbert space. On the n-th chaos this quantity is Var( ||DF||^2 / n ). A direct computation with the product formula for multiple integrals expresses Var( ||DF||^2 / n ) as a positive combination of the squared norms of the contractions in (iii), and the SAME contractions appear in the expansion of the fourth cumulant E[F^4] - 3 sigma^4, again with positive coefficients. Hence E[F^4] - 3 sigma^4 and Var(||DF||^2/n) are comparable up to constants depending only on n, and both vanish exactly when all the contractions vanish. That gives (iii) implies (ii) implies (i) with a rate, and (i) implies (ii) needs in addition the fact that on a fixed chaos all L^q norms are equivalent - the hypercontractive moment comparison - so that convergence in distribution upgrades to convergence of the fourth moment by uniform integrability. Let B be a measurable random real symmetric n-by-n matrix with 0<=B<=I. On real symmetric matrices equipped with the spectral norm define Phi(X)=E[BXB]. For every integer k>=0, the induced operator norm satisfies ||Phi^k-Phi^(k+1)||_(op->op)<=3/(k+1). In particular, for iid orthogonal-projection updates e_(j+1)=P_j e_j, Q=E[I-P_j] and deterministic e_0, one has E[e_k^T Q e_k]<=3||e_0||^2/(k+1). This is independent of dimension, task count, rank and conditioning. For unit row normals and uniform row sampling it gives the full-task randomized Kaczmarz residual. This general inverse-time result was already available in June 2026; the April 2026 O(k^(-3/4-theta)) bound is superseded as a rate frontier.

[Lemma lem:char-eval of arXiv:2410.23944, 'Hitting time mixing for the random transposition walk'] Let $\lambda \vdash n$ and $\tau \in \mathfrak{S}_n$ be a transposition. Then 
\[\chi_{\lambda}(\tau) = - \chi_{\lambda'}(\tau) = d_{\lambda} \binom{n}{2}^{-1}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{\lambda_i}{2} - \binom{\lambda_i'}{2}\bigg).\]
In particular, if $\lambda_1 \geq n - (\log n)^{2}$, then 
    \[\frac{\chi_{\lambda}(\tau)}{d_{\lambda}} = \frac{\binom{\lambda_1}{2}}{\binom{n}{2}} + O(n^{-2+o(1)}) = 1-\frac{2(n-\lambda_1)}{n}+ O(n^{-2+o(1)}).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The language $H$ equals the well-defined concatenation $J.G$.
  \begin{proof}
    To every word $w \in H$ there is a \emph{coupon-counting
    function} $f_w\colon \{ 0, 1, \ldots, \lvert w \rvert \} \to \N$
    that tracks the current number of distinct coupons held.
    This means $f_w(0) = 0$ and $f_w(\lvert w \rvert) = m$.
    Choose the smallest $k$ for which $f(k) = m$ and let
    $j$ be the word formed from the first $k$ letters in $w$.
    Then $w$ has the decomposition $j.g$ for some word $g$
    of length $\lvert w\rvert - k$.
    But since $f(k) = f(\lvert w \rvert) = m$,
    each occurrence of $\D_i$ in $g$ must be eventually followed
    by $\C_i$. Hence $g \in G$. There can be no decomposition $j = u.v$
    with $u \in H$ and $v \neq \varepsilon$ because $k > 0$ was selected minimally.
    This establishes $j \in J$ and $w \in J.G$. Thus $H \subseteq J.G$.

    To show $J.G \subseteq H$, take some $j.g \in J.G$ and
    consider the coupon-counting function $f_{j.g}$.
    Then $f_{j.g}(\lvert j \rvert) = m$ but $g$
    recovers all coupons it drops,
    so $f_{j.g}(\lvert j\rvert + \lvert g \rvert) = 
    f_{j.g}(\lvert j \rvert) = m$. We conclude
    $j.g \in H$ and $H = J.G$.

    We could not have selected a longer word $j' \in J$ in the first
    paragraph because $j' = j.u$ would hold with $u \neq \varepsilon$.
    This gives the contradiction $j' \notin J$.
    So, the factorisation of words $w \mapsto (j, g)$ is unique;
    $J$ and $G$ are well-defined for concatenation.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 7 of arXiv:2605.14206

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $\chi$ is injective. Let $V$ be a $k[G]$-module. Then the following properties hold. 

\medskip
{\bf (1)} If the $k[G]$-module $V$ has a lift $\mathcal V$ to $R$, then we have inequalities
$$\max\bigl(\jmath_V,\sum_{a\in\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z} [\ell_V(a)-\eta_V]\bigl)=\max\bigl(\jmath_V,\dim_k(V)-m\eta_V\bigr)\le r_{\mathcal V}\le\imath_V.$$
Moreover, if the character function $\ell_V$ is constant, then $m\mid r_{\mathcal V}$.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} Suppose that $R$ contains $R_s$. The $k[G]$-module $V$ has a lift $\mathcal V$ to $R$ with $r_{\mathcal V}=0$ if and only if $\ell_V$ is a constant function and $\jmath_V=0$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} Suppose that $R$ contains $R_s$. Let $V_0:=\oplus_{(a,b)\in C_m\times\llbracket1,p^s-1\rrbracket} \mu_V(a,b)U_{a,b}$. Then the following three statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (3.a)} The $k[G]$-module $V$ has a lift to $R$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (3.b)} The $k[G]$-module $V_0$ has a lift to $R$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (3.c)} For each $a\in C_m$ we have an inequality 
\begin{equation}
\ell_{V_0}(a)\le \eta_{V_0}+\ell_{\soc_{k[H]}(V_0)}(a).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let f_n and f be probability density functions with respect to a common sigma-finite measure mu on a measurable space, and suppose f_n converges to f mu-almost everywhere. Then integral of |f_n - f| d mu converges to 0 as n tends to infinity, equivalently the probability measures with densities f_n converge to the probability measure with density f in total variation distance. [standard, e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples]

body: (1) U ≠ C is essential: there is no biholomorphism from C onto D, since any holomorphic map C → D is bounded, hence constant by Liouville's theorem. C and D are the two conformal types of simply connected Riemann surfaces with the sphere. (2) Simple connectivity is essential and is not repaired by 'the domain has no holes that matter'. The punctured disk D minus {0} is not conformally equivalent to D: a biholomorphism F : D minus {0} → D would be bounded, hence extend holomorphically to 0 with |F(0)| ≤ 1; the extension maps the disk into D by the open mapping theorem, so F(0) = F(z1) for some z1 ≠ 0, and openness near both points contradicts injectivity on D minus {0}. Likewise two annuli {1 < |z| < R} and {1 < |z| < R'} are conformally equivalent only when R = R': conformal type has a modulus, so 'both are doubly connected' is not enough. (3) The conclusion is interior. The Riemann map need not extend continuously to the boundary, and when it does it need not be injective there. For the slit disk U = D minus [0,1) (which is simply connected), the inverse of the Riemann map extends continuously to the closed disk, but each point of the open slit is the image of two boundary points, so no homeomorphism of the closures exists. The correct boundary statement is Carathéodory's theorem: if U is bounded by a Jordan curve, then the Riemann map extends to a homeomorphism of the closed domains. (4) Normalization: the map is unique only after fixing F(z0) = 0 and F'(z0) > 0; without it the family of Riemann maps is a three-real-parameter family (compose with any automorphism of D).
title: Pitfall: the Riemann mapping theorem needs simple connectivity, U ≠ C, and says nothing about the boundary

[Defn slith of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] For a closed surface $S$ and a maximal lamination $\lambda$, let $\rho:\pi_1(S) \to \mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be an $n$-pleated representation (as in Definition (defn:pleat of the paper)), pleated along $\lambda$, with an associated $\rho$-equivariant limit map $\xi$ that assigns flags in $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the endpoints of leaves of $\tilde{\lambda}$. The \textit{slithering map} compatible with $\xi$  $$\Sigma:\tilde{\Lambda}^2 \to \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$$ defined on the space of pairs of leaves of $\lambda$, such that $\Sigma(g_1,g_2)$ is a matrix in $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ that takes the transverse pair of flags associated with the endpoints of a leaf $g_2$ to that of a leaf $g_1$ (oriented in parallel), satisfying
\[
\Sigma(g,g)=\mathrm{id}, \qquad
\Sigma(g_1,g_3)=\Sigma(g_1,g_2)\Sigma(g_2,g_3),
\]
whenever $g_2$ separates $g_1$ from $g_3$. When $g_1$ and $g_2$ share an endpoint, $\Sigma(g_1,g_2)$ is the unique unipotent transformation that fixes the flag at the common endpoint and takes the flag at the other endpoint of $g_2$ to the flag at the other endpoint of $g_1$.
title: Slithering map

Let f be twice continuously differentiable on an open interval containing a root x* with f(x*) = 0 and f'(x*) != 0. Then there is a neighborhood U of x* such that for every initial guess x_0 in U, the Newton iterates x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n) are well-defined, remain in U, and converge to x*. Moreover there is a constant C > 0, depending on bounds for |f''| and 1/|f'| on U, such that |x_{n+1} - x*| <= C * |x_n - x*|^2 for all n, i.e. the convergence is locally quadratic.

body:
Let d>=2, B_d={x in R^d:||x||_2<=1}, and 0<epsilon<1/2. A depth-2 sigma network here has the form b_0+sum_{i=1}^w v_i sigma(w_i^T x+b_i), with real finite parameters. Assume sigma:R->R has the following univariate approximation property (Assumption 1): there is a constant c_sigma>=1 such that every L-Lipschitz h:R->R constant outside [-R,R] can, for every delta>0, be uniformly approximated on R to error delta by a+sum_{j=1}^w alpha_j sigma(beta_j z-gamma_j), with w<=c_sigma R L/delta. Let f(x)=phi(||x||_2) be a 1-Lipschitz radial function on B_d. There exists such a network N with sup_{x in B_d}|N(x)-f(x)|<=epsilon and width w<=exp(C_sigma epsilon^(-9) log(d/epsilon)), where C_sigma depends only on sigma. This is the small-error regime of the printed theorem. It does not assert joint polynomial dependence on d and epsilon^(-1), bounded parameter magnitudes, or a training algorithm.
d>=2; 0<epsilon<1/2
f radial and 1-Lipschitz on the Euclidean unit ball
sigma satisfies the complete Assumption 1 property stated above
network parameters unrestricted in magnitude

body: [Theorem 1 of arXiv:1907.02811, 'Network Embedding: on Compression and Learning'] Let T be the 1-step transition probability matrix of vertices V in a graph G and let u,v ∈V . Let Tu and Tv be the transition probability from vertices u and v to other vertices. Then the cosine similarity between Tu and Tv is sim(Tu,Tv) = ∣N(u) ∩N(v)∣.
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:1907.02811: Network Embedding: on Compression and Learning

For groups G and H, a group homomorphism is a map phi:G->H satisfying phi(xy)=phi(x)phi(y) for all x,y in G. Its kernel is ker(phi)={g in G:phi(g)=e_H}, a normal subgroup of G, and its image is im(phi)={phi(g):g in G}, a subgroup of H.
G and H are groups
e_H is the identity element of H
title: Group Homomorphism and Kernel

body:
Let (F_n) be an increasing filtration with F_infinity the sigma-algebra it generates, and let Y be in L^1. Then E[Y | F_n] converges almost surely and in L^1 to E[Y | F_infinity]. Taking Y = 1_A for A in F_infinity gives LEVY'S 0-1 LAW: P(A | F_n) -> 1_A almost surely, so the conditional probability of any event in the limit sigma-algebra converges to 0 or 1. Applied to a tail event of an independent sequence, where F_n is generated by the first n variables and P(A | F_n) = P(A) by independence, this yields Kolmogorov's 0-1 law as a corollary. The theorem is about an INCREASING family; the corresponding statement for a decreasing family is Levy's downward theorem and needs its own proof. The limit is conditional on F_infinity and not on F - the two differ, and writing E[Y | F] would be wrong unless F_infinity = F up to null sets. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorem 14.2]
(F_n) increasing, F_infinity generated by their union
Y integrable

This is a martingale by the tower property, and by the argument in the closure theorem it is uniformly integrable, being a family of conditional expectations of the single integrable Y. Hence X_n converges almost surely and in L^1 to some X_infinity, and X_n = E[X_infinity | F_n]. It remains to identify X_infinity with E[Y | F_infinity]. X_infinity is F_infinity-measurable, being an almost sure limit of F_infinity-measurable variables. For A in F_m the martingale property and L^1 convergence give E[X_infinity 1_A] = E[X_m 1_A] = E[Y 1_A]. The collection of A in F_infinity satisfying E[X_infinity 1_A] = E[Y 1_A] is a lambda-system containing the pi-system consisting of the union of the F_m, which generates F_infinity, so by Dynkin's lemma the identity holds for every A in F_infinity. That is exactly the defining property of E[Y | F_infinity], and conditional expectation is almost surely unique. Let H be a complex Hilbert space and (U(t))_{t∈R} a family of unitary operators on H with U(0) = I, U(t+s) = U(t)U(s) for all s,t ∈ R, and t ↦ U(t)x continuous for each x ∈ H (strong continuity). Then there is a unique self-adjoint, generally unbounded operator A with domain D(A) = { x ∈ H : lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/t exists in H }, defined by iAx = lim_{t→0}(U(t)x − x)/t, such that U(t) = e^{itA} in the sense of the Borel functional calculus. D(A) is dense and invariant under each U(t), and for x ∈ D(A) the map t ↦ U(t)x is differentiable with d/dt U(t)x = iA U(t)x = i U(t) A x. Conversely, every self-adjoint A generates such a group via e^{itA}. Application: A = Δ with domain H²(R^n) is self-adjoint, and the propagator e^{itΔ} of the free Schrödinger equation is the corresponding unitary group; likewise the free wave evolution is a unitary group on Ḣ¹ × L².
H a complex Hilbert space
U(t) unitary for every t, U(0)=I, U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)
strong continuity: t ↦ U(t)x continuous for every x ∈ H

Symmetry: from unitarity, ⟨(U(t)x − x)/t, y⟩ = ⟨x, (U(−t)y − y)/t⟩; passing to the limit shows A is symmetric on D(A). Self-adjointness: the resolvent of A at non-real λ is given by a Laplace transform of the group. Note that |e^{−iλt}| = e^{(Im λ) t}, so the forward integral converges exactly in the LOWER half plane: for Im λ < 0, (A − λ)^{−1}x = −i∫_0^∞ e^{−iλ t}U(t)x dt, and symmetrically for Im λ > 0, (A − λ)^{−1}x = i∫_{−∞}^0 e^{−iλ t}U(t)x dt (here the integrand decays as t → −∞). Either formula exhibits a bounded inverse, so A − λ is surjective for every non-real λ; in particular Ran(A ± i) = H, and a densely defined symmetric operator with Ran(A + i) = Ran(A − i) = H is self-adjoint. Uniqueness of A follows because the generator is determined by the group, and e^{itA} = U(t) then follows from the spectral theorem.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:fffb1239ec08832635ae3099d5b6722b178962b0d45086a4fc87487b379430e7","revision_digest":"sha256:9912107a207ac70d93e85b9b1c20a3238db259eabf01dc54cd86d39bfc304d7b","source_id":"wikipedia:Stone's theorem on one-parameter unitary groups","source_revision":"as-known-2026-09-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 15 (Decomposition of integral over $D_1$) of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] Let $N\ge 1$ and suppose $\pa_tz(u)\geq1/2$ for all $u\in D_1$. Then
\be
\frac{1}{\mathcal Z}\int_{D_1}g(u)e^{-\la z(u)}\dd u = \sum_{k=1}^{N}\la^{-k}\frac{1}{\mathcal Z}\int_{\us(R\e )}\g_k(x)e^{-\la \z(x,0)}\dd x +\Rem_{N+1}^{\Wat},
\ee
where
\be
|\Rem_{N+1}^{\Wat}|\leq 2\mu\left(\|D_{\z}^{N}\g\|_\infty\la^{-N-1}+e^{-R^2d/2}\max_{1\leq k\leq N}\|D_{\z}^{k-1}\g\|_\infty\la^{-k}\right). 
\ee Here, $\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{(x,y)\in \us(R\e)\times[0, (R\e)^2]}|f(x,y)|$.

[Thm exponent of arXiv:2505.24821, 'Asymptotics for the harmonic descent chain and applications to critical beta-splitting tre'] We have that 
    \begin{enumerate}[ref=(\roman*)]
        \item  $x_{n+1} < x_n$ for all $n \geq k$. In particular, for any fixed $k$, the limit $x \coloneqq \lim_{n \to\infty} x_n$ exists.
        \item  For all $n \geq k$, $x_n - x = O(\frac{kx_k}{n-k})$.
        \item 
        For fixed $c \geq 2$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$, and for $k$ sufficiently large, $x_{k+m} \leq \frac{c^\ell x_k}{mh_k}$ for each $m \leq k^{d_\ell}$ where $d_\ell = 1-\frac{1}{c+1} - 2^{-\ell}$.

        \item  For fixed $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $x_n - x = n^{-\gamma_*+o(1)}$, where $\gamma_*$ is the solution to 
        \begin{equation}
        \sum_{i=1}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{i} - \frac{i}{(i+1)(i+1-\gamma)}\right) = 0 
        \end{equation}
        with $1.5 < \gamma_* < 2$.
        \item  For all $\epsilon > 0$ and $k = o(n/\log^3 n)$, there exist $0 < c(k, \epsilon) < C(k, \epsilon) = O_\epsilon(x_k k^{0.01})$ such that $c(k, \epsilon)(n / k)^{-\gamma_*-\epsilon} \leq x_n - x \leq C(k, \epsilon)(n / k)^{-\gamma_*+\epsilon}$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm exponent of arXiv:2505.24821

body: In computational complexity theory, an interactive proof system is an abstract machine that models computation as the exchange of messages between two parties: a prover and a verifier. The parties interact by exchanging messages in order to ascertain whether a given string belongs to a language or not. The prover is assumed to possess unlimited computational resources but cannot be trusted, while the verifier has bounded computation power but is assumed to be always honest. Messages are sent between the verifier and prover until the verifier has an answer to the problem and has "convinced" itself that it is correct.

[Theorem 14 (Homotopy detection under inclusions) of arXiv:2609.01882, '\textbf{Coxeter Descents and Parabolic Homotopy Colimits}\\[2mm] \large A Hochster-type de'] Let $G$ be compact, connected, simply connected, and semisimple, and let $\mathcal K\subseteq\mathcal L\subseteq2^S$. The natural map
\[
  \XK(G)\longrightarrow X_{\mathcal L}(G)
\]
is a homotopy equivalence if and only if, for every $D\subseteq S$, the inclusion
\[
  \mathcal K_D\longrightarrow\mathcal L_D
\]
induces isomorphisms on all augmented reduced integral homology groups, including degree $-1$.

In the synchronous nearest-neighbor particle-hole process on Z^d with iid initial excess eta satisfying P(eta=1)=P(eta=-1)=p, P(eta=0)=1-2p, 0<p<1/2, stationary capacity-one holes and the source coupling conventions, let H_t(x) indicate an unfilled hole and A_t(x) count active particles after round t. For every k distinct sites x_1,...,x_k and every nonnegative measurable function F of the entire active-count field, E[F(A_t) product_i H_t(x_i)] <= [p/(1-p)]^k E[F(A_t)]. In particular E[H_t(x) A_t(z)] <= [p/(1-p)]h_t, where h_t=E H_t(0)=E A_t(0). The estimate holds at each finite t; it does not assert conditional stochastic domination. Novelty: UNCHECKED (mixed-observable extension); deletion method KNOWN. Status: independently checked proof.
0<p<1/2; P(η=±1)=p each and otherwise zero
Stationary capacity-one holes; synchronous finite-time nearest-neighbor dynamics
F nonnegative and depends only on active-count field

Novelty: UNCHECKED. Extension of the KNOWN unvisited-hole deletion argument in source Lemma 8.4 and own C5. No earlier explicit mixed-moment statement found in the limited source searches. This result is valid in all dimensions, but does not give the time-dependent thinning needed by C7.

Use the sparse iid critical law P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p, P(η=0)=1−2p with 0<p<1/2, stationary capacity-one holes and synchronous nearest-neighbor dynamics on Z^d. Let q=p/(1−p). For a finite set K of k distinct sites and any nonnegative measurable function F of the entire active-particle count field at a fixed finite time t,

E[F(A_t) product_{x∈K}H_t(x)]≤q^k E[F(A_t)].

The assertion allows expectations equal to infinity, in which case the inequality is interpreted in the extended nonnegative sense. In particular, with h_t=EH_t(0)=EA_t(0),

E[H_t(x)A_t(z)]≤q h_t,
E[H_t(x)1_{A_t(z)>0}]≤q P(A_t(z)>0)≤q h_t.

No independence or negative association of surviving holes and active particles is claimed.

## Proof

On E_K={H_t(x)=1 for all x∈K}, every specified initial value equals −1 and no particle has arrived at any specified site by time t. For each subset J⊂K replace the initial −1 values at J by zero, leaving every other sign and every walk/stack/tie variable fixed. The modified dynamics agree with the original particle dynamics through t: before a first putative arrival at a modified site, nothing affecting any particle has changed, so such an arrival would also occur in the original dynamics, a contradiction. Hence the active-count field A_t is identical in every image, and F(A_t) is unchanged.

These 2^k images are disjoint, because their initial coordinate assignments on K distinguish exactly which values are zero versus −1. Let c=(1−2p)/p. For a bounded nonnegative F, the image weighted expectation is exactly c^{|J|}E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}], by conditioning on all variables except the k specified initial coordinates. The transformations are injective with the prescribed original values restored. Their union is a subset of the full probability space. Since F is unchanged on each image,

E[F(A_t)]≥sum_{J⊂K}c^{|J|}E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}]
=(1+c)^k E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}]
=q^{−k}E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}].

This proves the inequality for bounded F. Apply it to min(F,m) and use monotone convergence as m→∞ to cover every nonnegative measurable F. The change-of-coordinate argument is finite, even if F depends on infinitely many active counts; at fixed t all specified hole-survival events have finite propagation cones, and the deletion leaves the entire particle evolution unchanged through t.

For F(A)=A(z) or 1_{A(z)>0}, translation invariance and critical signed-density conservation give the displayed specializations. The same moment bound holds at x=z, where the left side is zero. Active counts have finite expectation because the initial particles that can reach a site by t lie in a finite ball and there is at most one initial particle per site.

## Application and limitation

C7's mixed sum has the upper bound q h_t|B_{2R}|. This is useful at R=O(p^−1/d). At R=O(h_t^−1/d), dividing by h_t gives an upper bound of order q/h_t, which grows without limit for fixed p as h_t→0. body: Three hypotheses of the De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theorem are load-bearing, and each fails concretely. (1) Scalar. The theorem is false for systems: De Giorgi (1968) exhibited, for n >= 3, a linear elliptic system with bounded measurable coefficients satisfying the Legendre-Hadamard and even the strong ellipticity condition whose weak solution is u(x) = x |x|^{-gamma} for an explicit gamma with 1 < gamma < n/2 - a solution in H^1 that is unbounded, hence not even locally bounded, let alone Hoelder. So a referee must check that an application of De Giorgi-Nash-Moser or of Moser's Harnack inequality is to a single equation, not to a system, and that the maximum-principle-based truncations used in the proof are available. (2) The energy class u in H^1_loc. A distributional solution whose gradient is only in L^p for some p < 2 need not be bounded. In the plane take A(x) = I + (mu - 1) x x^T/|x|^2 with mu > 1 (uniformly elliptic, bounded, measurable, discontinuous only at the origin). In polar coordinates div(A grad u) = (1/r) d/dr ( r mu u_r ) + (1/r^2) u_{theta theta}, so u = r^s cos(theta) solves the equation away from 0 exactly when mu s^2 = 1. The choice s = -1/sqrt(mu) in (-1,0) gives u = r^{-1/sqrt(mu)} cos(theta), which is unbounded at 0, lies in W^{1,p}_loc precisely for p < 2/(1 + 1/sqrt(mu)) < 2, and is a distributional solution across the origin (the flux through small circles tends to 0 because s > -1). (3) The Hoelder exponent depends on the ellipticity ratio and cannot be improved to Lipschitz. The same coefficients with s = +alpha, i.e. mu = 1/alpha^2, give the H^1 solution u = r^alpha cos(theta) of a uniformly elliptic equation with ellipticity ratio alpha^{-2}: it is exactly C^{0,alpha} at the origin and no better. Hence the exponent alpha(n, Lambda/lambda) in the theorem must degenerate to 0 as Lambda/lambda tends to infinity, and 'bounded measurable coefficients give Lipschitz solutions' is false. Gradient bounds require continuity (or Dini/Hoelder continuity) of the coefficients.
title: Pitfall: De Giorgi-Nash-Moser Needs a Scalar Equation and an Energy-Class Solution

body: [Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] A subshift of finite type $ X \subset A^{G}$ satisfies the $k$-extension property if there exists a finite collection $ \mathcal{F} $ of forbidden patterns for which $ X = X(\mathcal{F})$ and such that any locally allowed pattern $ w$ supported on a set $S \subset G$ which extends to a locally allowed pattern on $ S \cdot \mathbf{B}(k) $, is globally allowed.  $ X$ has finite extension property (FEP) if it satisfies $ k$-extension property for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps is of order n^{1/d_w} with walk dimension d_w > 2 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) of order r^{zeta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. The expected exit time from a ball of radius r is then of order r^{d_f+zeta} (volume times resistance: the Einstein relation d_w = d_f + zeta), so the displacement is of order n^{1/(d_f+zeta)}, subdiffusive when d_f + zeta > 2; the Nash/heat-kernel machinery or a direct expected-exit-time computation turns the two estimates into bounds. In balls of the intrinsic (graph) metric with unit conductances R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) <= r, so zeta <= 1 there: for the high-dimensional incipient infinite cluster the intrinsic volume grows as r^2 and the resistance as r, giving d_w = 3. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.
the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph
a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster
a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure
typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales

        |u(z)| \leq C(1+|z|^2).
    $$
    Then $u(z) = E_z[T(R)]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Cor finite-order of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be a nonconstant planar $p$-harmonic function and $x_0\in\Omega$.  If $u(x_0)=0$, then $u$ has finite vanishing order at $x_0$ in the following sense: either $D u(x_0)\ne0$ and the order is $1$, or $x_0$ is critical and
$$
  |u(x_0+r\theta)|\le Cr^{\lambda_N(p)},
  \qquad
  \sup_{\theta\in\mathbb S^1}|u(x_0+r\theta)|\ge c r^{\lambda_N(p)}
$$
for all sufficiently small $r>0$, with constants $c,C>0$.

body:
[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] For any subclasses \(\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{T}_n\) and \(n\in \mathbb{N}\), the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(\left(\bigcap_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{loc} = \bigcap_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{loc}\) and \(\left(\bigcup_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{loc} \supset \bigcup_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{loc}\).
\item \(\left(\bigcap_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{col} \subset \bigcap_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{col}\) and \(\left(\bigcup_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{col} = \bigcup_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{col}\).
\item If \(\mathcal{T}_1 \subset \mathcal{T}_2\), then \((\mathcal{T}_{1})_{loc} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{2})_{loc}\) and  \((\mathcal{T}_{1})_{col} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{2})_{col}\).
\item For any \(\{F_k\}_k \in \nest\), \(\mathcal{T}_{loc} \subset \mathcal{T}(\{F_k\}) \subset \mathcal{T}_{col}\).
\item \((\mathcal{T}_{loc})_{loc} = \mathcal{T}_{loc}\) and \((\mathcal{T}_{col})_{col} = \mathcal{T}_{col}\).
\item \(\mathcal{T}_{loc} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{loc})_{col} \subset \mathcal{T}_{col}\) and \(\mathcal{T}_{loc} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{col})_{loc} \subset \mathcal{T}_{col}\).
\end{enumerate}

[Coro 13 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Assume that
\(\int_\Omega m(x)\varphi_{1,\Omega}^{\alpha+1}\,dx<0\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[a)]
If $|\Omega^+|>0$, then, as $\lambda\uparrow\lambda^*$,
\[
H_\lambda(u_\lambda^+)
\rightarrow H_{\lambda^*}(u_{\lambda^*}^+),
\qquad
M(u_\lambda^+)
\rightarrow M(u_{\lambda^*}^+).
\]

\item[b)]
If $|\Omega^0\cup\Omega^+|>0$ and condition \textbf{(M)} holds, then
\[
H_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
M(u_\lambda^-)\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{as }\lambda\uparrow\lambda^*.
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2605.03902, 'Bundles of Probability Schemes'] Let $\cA$ be an $\Rr$-subalgebra of $\Rr^{\Omega}$. Then
  \begin{enumerate}[i.]

body: Fix d >= 2 and let E(Z^d) be the set of nearest-neighbour edges of the integer lattice. Assign to each edge e an independent random weight tau_e >= 0 with common distribution F; the collection (tau_e) is the environment. The PASSAGE TIME of a finite lattice path gamma is T(gamma) = sum over the edges of gamma of tau_e, and the passage time between vertices x and y is T(x,y) = inf over finite paths from x to y of T(gamma). T is a random pseudometric on Z^d: it is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and vanishes on the diagonal, but T(x,y) = 0 is possible for x != y when F has an atom at 0. A GEODESIC from x to y is a path attaining the infimum. Geodesics need not exist for a general F, and when F(0) is at least the critical probability p_c(d) the infimum can be 0 and attained by infinitely many paths; when F(0) < p_c a geodesic exists almost surely for every pair, and it is almost surely unique for every pair when F is continuous, since ties then have probability 0. The standing notation in the literature is T(0, x) for the point-to-point time, mu or g for the time constant, chi for the fluctuation exponent and xi for the wandering exponent; the store already records that those exponents are DEFINED differently by different theorems and are not interchangeable. [standard; e.g. Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Chapters 1 and 4]

[Lemma lem:closure of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] For $2\le|S|\le3$ let
$K_S=\operatorname{conv}\{B_{ij}:i,j\in S,\ t_i\ne t_j\}$ (discard $S$ with no valid
pair). Then
\[
  \inf_{\substack{\operatorname{supp} q\subseteq S\\ |\mu(q)|<1}}C(q)
  \;=\;\operatorname{dist}^2\bigl(0,K_S\bigr),
  \qquad
  \inf_{\substack{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le3\\ |\mu(q)|<1}}C(q)
  \;=\;\min_{S}\operatorname{dist}^2(0,K_S) .
\]
For three pairwise distinct directions the interior of the edge-weight
triangle is attained by positive weights (via
$q_1{:}q_2{:}q_3=\frac{d_{23}}{\alpha_{23}}{:}\frac{d_{13}}{\alpha_{13}}
{:}\frac{d_{12}}{\alpha_{12}}$), the vertices by two-point supports, and
non-degenerate edge interiors only as limits with $|\mu|\to1$; if two of the
three directions coincide, the corresponding segment of $K_S$ is attained
exactly. Moreover, for three distinct directions the three points
$B_{ij},B_{ik},B_{jk}$, when distinct, are never collinear over $\mathbb{R}$.

[Definition randomcoveringset of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and consider the probability space
$(\Omega,\mathbb{P})$, where $\Omega:=(\spt\mu)^{\mathbb{N}}$ and $\mathbb{P}:=\mu^{\mathbb{N}}$.
Let $\underline{r}$ be {a} sequence of positive numbers. Given
$\omega \in \Omega$, the \emph{random covering set} generated by the sequence
$\underline{r}$ is the limsup set
\[
E_{\underline{r}}(\omega)\coloneqq\limsup_{k\to\infty}B(\omega_{k},r_k)
  =\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigcup_{k=n}^{\infty}B(\omega_{ k},r_k).
\]

[Lemma 4 (Euclidean score reduction) of arXiv:2609.02362, '\textbf{Farthest-cell triplet entropy: high-dimensional shell limits and hyperbolic curvat'] For the independent query $(R_{0,d},U_{0,d})$ and prototypes
$(R_{i,d},U_{i,d})$, $i=1,2,3$, the farthest-distance ordering is the
ordering of
\begin{equation}
  S_{i,d}
  =
  \lambda_d\xi_{i,d}-Z_{i,d}+r_{i,d},
  \qquad
  Z_{i,d}
  =
  \sqrt d\,\langle U_{0,d},U_{i,d}\rangle.
  
\end{equation}
Conditionally on the prototypes,
\[
  (Z_{1,d},Z_{2,d},Z_{3,d})
  \Rightarrow N(0,I_3)
\]
in probability \cite{diaconisfreedman1987}.  Moreover,
\[
  \max_{1\leq i\leq3}|r_{i,d}|
  \xrightarrow{p}0
\]
when $\lambda_d=O(1)$, whereas
\[
  \frac{1}{\lambda_d}
  \max_{1\leq i\leq3}|r_{i,d}|
  \xrightarrow{p}0
\]
when $\lambda_d\to\infty$.

Let (M,g) be a Riemannian (or pseudo-Riemannian) manifold. There exists a unique affine connection nabla on M, called the Levi-Civita connection of g, that is (1) torsion-free: nabla_X Y - nabla_Y X = [X,Y] for all smooth vector fields X, Y, and (2) compatible with the metric: X(g(Y,Z)) = g(nabla_X Y, Z) + g(Y, nabla_X Z) for all smooth vector fields X, Y, Z.
(M,g) is a smooth Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold

Load-bearing hypothesis: uniqueness in Kruzhkov's theorem is for ENTROPY solutions; the integral (weak) formulation alone, even with Rankine-Hugoniot satisfied at every jump, does not determine the solution. Counterexample 1 (Burgers, f(u) = u^2/2, datum u0 ≡ 0): besides u ≡ 0 the function u(x,t) = 0 for x < -t/2, u = -1 for -t/2 < x < 0, u = 1 for 0 < x < t/2, u = 0 for x > t/2 is a weak solution — every jump satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot (speeds -1/2, 0, 1/2 respectively) — yet it is not an entropy solution (the jump from -1 up to 1 is an expansion shock violating Oleinik/Lax). Counterexample 2 (Burgers with u0 = 0 for x < 0, u0 = 1 for x > 0): the stationary-in-shape expansion shock u = 0 for x < t/2, u = 1 for x > t/2 satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, but the entropy solution is the rarefaction u = 0 for x ≤ 0, u = x/t for 0 ≤ x ≤ t, u = 1 for x ≥ t. In both cases the wrong solutions create information (characteristics emanate from the shock) instead of destroying it, and they are not vanishing-viscosity limits. Auditor's check: a proof that constructs 'a' weak solution and then calls it 'the' solution — or that computes shock speeds from Rankine-Hugoniot without verifying admissibility — is incomplete; check Oleinik's chord condition at every jump (for convex flux: the state must jump DOWN as x increases).
Burgers' equation f(u) = u^2/2 in one dimension
Weak solutions are only required to satisfy the integral identity; jumps must satisfy Rankine-Hugoniot but may still be inadmissible
Uniqueness is restored by the Kruzhkov entropy inequalities (equivalently, for piecewise smooth solutions, by Oleinik's chord condition at each jump)
title: Pitfall: Weak Solutions of a Conservation Law Are Not Unique without an Entropy Condition

body: PageRank (PR) is an algorithm used by Google Search to rank web pages in their search engine results. It is named after both the term "web page" and co-founder Larry Page. PageRank is a way of measuring the importance of website pages. According to Google:PageRank works by counting the number and quality of links to a page to determine a rough estimate of how important the website is. The underlying assumption is that more important websites are likely to receive more links from other websites.
title: PageRank

body: In the theory of abelian groups, the torsion subgroup of an abelian group is the subgroup of consisting of all elements that have finite order. An abelian group is called a torsion group if every element of has finite order and is called torsion-free if every element of except the identity is of infinite order.
title: Torsion subgroup

[Definition of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group actions}'] Let \(X,Y\) be standard Borel spaces and \(E,F\) be two equivalence relations on \(X,Y\) respectively. We say that \(E\) is \textit{Borel reducible} to \(F\) denoted by \(E \leq_B F\), if there exists a Borel mapping \(f: X \to Y\) called a \textit{reduction} such that
    \[x E y \iff f(x) F f(y)\]
    for all \(x,y \in X\). We say that \(E\) is \textit{Borel bireducible} to \(F\) denoted by \(E \sim_B F\), if \(E \leq_B F\) and \(F \leq_B E\). We write \(E <_B F\) if \(E \leq_B F\) and \(F \not \leq_B E\).
title: Unnumbered Definition of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group act'

[Proposition 1 (Functional Blaschke-Santal\'o) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $f:\R^n\to\R_+$ be a measurable function such that $0<\int f <+\infty$. Then, there exists $z\in \R^n$ with the following property: 
\\
for every measurable function $g:\R^n\to\R_+$ and measurable function $\Omega:\R_{+}\to\R_{+}$ satisfying
$$f(x+z)g(y)\le \Omega^{2}(\langle x,y\rangle ) \quad \text{for every } x,y\in \R^n \text{ such that } \langle x,y\rangle >0,$$
        one has
         \begin{equation}
         
         \int_{\R^n} f(x)dx\int_{\R^n} g(y)dy\le
        \left( \int_{\R^n} \Omega({|x|^{2}})dx\right)^2.\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Functional Blaschke-Santal\'o

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(L>0\) and \(a>1\). Define
\(\mathsf A_{a,L}:L^2(B_{a,L},\mathrm dA)\to L^2(0,\infty)\) by
\[
        (\mathsf A_{a,L}f)(\xi)
        :=
        \int_{B_{a,L}}\overline{u_\xi(z)}f(z)\,\mathrm dA(z).
\]
Then \(\mathsf A_{a,L}\) is Hilbert--Schmidt,
\(K_{B_{a,L}}=\mathsf A_{a,L}^*\mathsf A_{a,L}\), and \(K_{B_{a,L}}\) is a
positive trace-class operator with \(\operatorname{tr}(K_{B_{a,L}})=L\lambda_a\).

body:
Let $S = n^{-1} X^T X = \sum_{i=1}^M \lambda_i u_i u_i^T$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\mathbb{R}^M$ with population covariance $\Sigma$, and let $M/n \to c \in (0,1)$. Among rotation-equivariant estimators $\sum_i d_i u_i u_i^T$ the Frobenius-optimal choice is the oracle $d_i^* = u_i^T \Sigma u_i$, whose large-dimensional limit is $\lambda_i / |1 - c - c\lambda_i \breve m_F(\lambda_i)|^2$ with $\breve m_F(\lambda) = \lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} m_F(\lambda + i\eta)$, $m_F(z) = \int dF(t)/(t - z)$ the Stieltjes transform of the limiting sample spectral distribution $F$ (Ledoit-Peche 2011). Writing $\operatorname{Im} \breve m_F(\lambda) = \pi f(\lambda)$ and $\operatorname{Re} \breve m_F(\lambda) = \pi H_f(\lambda)$, $H_f(x) = \pi^{-1} \mathrm{PV}\!\int f(t)/(t - x)\,dt$, the oracle reads $\tilde d_i = \lambda_i / \big[(\pi c \lambda_i f(\lambda_i))^2 + (1 - c - \pi c \lambda_i H_f(\lambda_i))^2\big]$. Ledoit and Wolf (2020) estimate $f$ and $H_f$ from the sample eigenvalues themselves with the Epanechnikov kernel $\kappa(x) = \tfrac{3}{4\sqrt5}(1 - x^2/5)^+$ and the eigenvalue-proportional bandwidth $h_j = \lambda_j n^{-1/3}$: $\tilde f(x) = M^{-1}\sum_j \kappa((x - \lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$ and $\tilde H_f(x) = M^{-1}\sum_j H_\kappa((x - \lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$, where $H_\kappa(x) = -\tfrac{3x}{10\pi} + \tfrac{3}{4\sqrt5\pi}(1 - x^2/5)\log\big|\tfrac{\sqrt5 - x}{\sqrt5 + x}\big|$. The resulting estimator $\hat\Sigma = \sum_i \tilde d_i u_i u_i^T$ has no tuning constant, is positive definite when $c < 1$, and its Frobenius loss (and its minimum-variance-portfolio loss) converges to the oracle's; for $c > 1$ a separate formula handles the $M - n$ null eigenvalues.
rows i.i.d. with finite twelfth moments (the Ledoit-Wolf condition)
M/n -> c in (0,1) for the stated form; the population spectral distribution has compact support (Ledoit-Peche take it bounded away from zero)
the sample eigenvalues are distinct (they are, almost surely)

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved mean-conditioning case of Svante Janson's Problem 20.3 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Let w_j >= 0, w_0 > 0, Phi(z) = sum_{j>=0} w_j z^j, and rho be its radius of convergence. Choose a fixed tau in (0,rho], with Phi(tau) < infinity, and define pi_j = w_j tau^j/Phi(tau), mu = sum j pi_j > 0, and sigma^2 = sum (j-mu)^2 pi_j in (0,infinity). Allow either tau < rho, or tau = rho with finite sigma^2. Let integers m_n satisfy m_n - n mu = O(1), and restrict to feasible sizes. Draw (Y_1,...,Y_n) with probability proportional to product_i w_{Y_i}, conditional on sum_i Y_i = m_n, and put N_d = number of i with Y_i = d. For any fixed finite set D of nonnegative integers, ((N_d-n pi_d)/sqrt(n))_{d in D} converges in distribution to a centered multivariate Gaussian vector. Its diagonal covariance is V_dd = pi_d(1-pi_d) - (d-mu)^2 pi_d^2/sigma^2; for distinct d,e its covariance is V_de = -pi_d pi_e - (d-mu)(e-mu)pi_d pi_e/sigma^2. Degenerate Gaussian coordinates are allowed. In Janson's parameters, Psi(t) = t Phi'(t)/Phi(t), lambda = mu, and nu = lim_{t upward to rho} Psi(t), so the two cases are 0 < lambda < nu and lambda = nu with finite variance. The stronger O(1) centering hypothesis is explicit here; mere convergence m_n/n -> lambda is not being asserted to justify centering by the fixed law pi. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The tilt is fixed, mu > 0, and 0 < sigma^2 < infinity.
m_n-n mu = O(1), with positive conditioning probability.

[Thm A. thm: convergence coupling for fused resistance spaces of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] Let $(F_{n}, R_{n}, \rho_{n}),\, n \geq 1$ and $(F, R, \rho)$ be rooted compact resistance metric spaces.
  Let $(a_{n}^{(i)}, b_{n}^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N}$ and $(a^{(i)}, b^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N}$
  be distinct elements of $F_{n}$ and $F$, respectively.
  Assume that 
  \begin{equation}
    (F_{n}, R_{n}, \rho_{n}, (a_{n}^{(i)}, b_{n}^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N})
    \to     
    (F, R, \rho, (a^{(i)}, b^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N})
  \end{equation}
  in $\mathfrak{M}_{c}(\tau^{2N \text{-}\mathrm{pts}})$.
  Write $(\tilde{F}_{n}, \tilde{R}_{n})$ and $(\tilde{F}, \tilde{R})$ 
  for the resistance metric spaces fused over $\{\{a_{n}^{(i)}, b_{n}^{(i)}\}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ and $\{\{a^{(i)}, b^{(i)}\}\}_{i=1}^{N}$, respectively.
  Let $\pi_{n}: F_{n} \to \tilde{F}_{n}$ and $\pi: F \to \tilde{F}$ be the associated canonical maps,
  and set $\tilde{\rho}_{n} \coloneqq \pi_{n}(\rho_{n})$ and $\tilde{\rho} \coloneqq \pi(\rho)$.
  Then, there exist rooted compact metric spaces $(M, d^{M}, \rho_{M})$ and $(\tilde{M}, d^{\tilde{M}}, \rho_{\tilde{M}})$ 
  satisfying the following:
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (\roman*)]
    \item $(F_{n}, R_{n}, \rho_{n})$ and $(F, R, \rho)$ are embedded isometrically into $(M, d^{M}, \rho_{M})$ 
      in such a way that $\rho_{n} = \rho = \rho_{M}$ as elements of $M$,
      $F_{n} \to F$ in the Hausdorff topology on $M$,
      and $a_{n}^{(i)} \to a^{(i)}$ and $b_{n}^{(i)} \to b^{(i)}$ in $M$;
    \item $(\tilde{F}_{n}, \tilde{R}_{n}, \tilde{\rho}_{n})$ and $(\tilde{F}, \tilde{R}, \tilde{\rho})$ are embedded isometrically into 
      $(\tilde{M}, d^{\tilde{M}}, \rho_{\tilde{M}})$ in such a way that 
      $\tilde{\rho}_{n} = \tilde{\rho} = \rho_{\tilde{M}}$ as elements of $\tilde{M}$ 
      and $\tilde{F}_{n} \to \tilde{F}$ in the Hausdorff topology on $\tilde{M}$;
    \item if we regard $\pi_{n}$ and $\pi$ as elements of $\widehat{C}(M, \tilde{M})$ by the above embeddings,
      then $\pi_{n} \to \pi$ in $\widehat{C}(M, \tilde{M})$.
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm A. thm: convergence coupling for fused resistance spaces of arXiv:2412.08236

[Lemma lem:differential-bound of arXiv:2504.09141, 'Bounds on the distance exponent for higher-dimensional Liouville first passage percolation'] Fix $d \geq 3$. The function $\xi \to \lambda(\xi)$ is $\sqrt{2d}$-Lipschitz on $[0,\infty)$, and thus $\lambda'$ exists for Lebesgue-a.e.~$\xi$. Moreover, for Lebesgue-a.e.~$\xi \geq 0$, we have
    $$
    \max \big{\{} -\xi, \frac{1}{\xi} (\lambda - 1) \big{\}} \leq \lambda' \leq \sqrt{2(d-1)+2\lambda +\xi^2} - \xi.
    $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Independently checked proof (PASS w667 and w668): C003 v1. Let F be a probability on nonempty compact K subset R^d with mean mu and n>=1. Let Z be the n-tuples in K^n whose sum is n*mu. Then F is n-CM iff for every continuous real f on K, integral f dF <= max over Z of average_i f(x_i). Equivalently F belongs to the closed convex hull of the empirical laws n^(-1)sum_i delta_(x_i) for tuples in Z. Compactness of coupling laws preserves the fixed sum and marginals; uniform coordinate permutation makes finite barycenters have identical marginals; Hahn-Banach separation supplies a common potential when the hull excludes F. Empty Z means all formulations fail. For a convex K, the tuple (mu,...,mu) makes Z nonempty. This is a standard marginal-duality specialization, not an existence proof or novelty claim.
