[Lemma l.expdecay of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $Q_1, Q_2$ be two marking functions on finite marked point processes. Let $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ be a marked point process such that the ground process $\mathcal{P}$ satisfies the Palm correlation bound~(equation e:bd_palmcorr of the paper) for $m =1$.
 Suppose for $p\in\mathbb{N}$, $i=1,2$ that there are   fast decreasing functions $\varphi_{i,p}$ as in (equation varphibd of the paper) such that 
\begin{equation}
\sup_{1 \leq n < \infty} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in W_n} \mathbb{P}_{\bk x1p}
\bigl(Q_i(\tilde{x}_1, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n)>r\bigr) \le \varphi_{i,p}(r),\quad r > 0.
\end{equation}
 Then 
for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$ there are fast decreasing functions ~$\tilde\varphi_p$ such that
$$
\sup_{1 \leq n < \infty} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p\in W_n}\mathbb{P}_{\bk x1p}\left( \max_{x \in \mathcal{P}_n :  |x - x_1| \leq Q_1(\tilde{x}_1, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n)} Q_2(\tilde{x}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n) > r \right) \leq   \tilde{\varphi}_p(r), \quad r > 0.
$$
If the assumption (equation e:Q12tails of the paper) holds with the supremum taken up to $n = \infty$, i.e., $\sup_{1 \le n \le \infty}$, then the conclusion  remains valid with  $\sup_{1 \le n \le \infty}$.
title: Tail bounds for the maximum of fast decreasing marks

Let A be an n x n matrix over a field. A has a factorisation A = L U with L unit lower triangular (ones on the diagonal) and U upper triangular if and only if every leading principal submatrix A_k = A[1..k, 1..k], k = 1, ..., n - 1, is invertible (for invertible A this is equivalent to all n leading principal minors being nonzero); when it exists the factorisation is unique for invertible A, and u_kk = det A_k / det A_{k-1}. In general, for every A there is a permutation matrix P with P A = L U (Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting: at each step the row with the largest remaining entry in the pivot column is swapped into the pivot position); for invertible A the factors are then unique given P. The elimination costs 2 n^3 / 3 flops; solving A x = b afterwards costs 2 n^2 by one forward and one back substitution; the determinant is the product of the u_kk times the sign of P. Partial pivoting is backward stable in practice (the growth factor is bounded by 2^{n-1} in the worst case, attained by Wilkinson's example, but is small on almost all matrices), whereas elimination without pivoting can be unstable on matrices with small pivots even when A is well conditioned. Symmetric positive definite matrices need no pivoting (Cholesky); diagonally dominant matrices need none either.

[Lem transprop of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Let $\mathcal N$ be a transparent (weighted planar) network of order $n$, with weight
matrix $A$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If a path in another network reaches sink-$r$ and if the network is concatenated with $\mathcal N$, then it can be continued
through the path $h_r$ without changing its weight. More generally, a vertex-disjoint family reaching pairwise distinct
levels $I\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$ can be continued through the paths
$\{h_r:r\in I\}$, without changing either its weight or its
vertex-disjointness.

\item If $\mathcal N'$ is another transparent network, then the
concatenation $\mathcal N\mathcal N'$ is transparent.

\item Let $D=\emph{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$ be an invertible diagonal matrix.  There is a transparent network with
weight matrix $DAD^{-1}$.  

\item There is a transparent network with weight matrix $SAS^{-1}$ where  $S$ is the side-reversal matrix (see (equation eq:S of the paper)). 
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:BBG-lem5 of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let Assumption~(ass:Wass of the paper) hold. Then, for every $N\ge2$ and every initial
configuration $(x^N_1(0),\ldots,x^N_N(0))\in(\mathbb R^d)^N$, the
$N$-particle SVGD system~(equation eq:svgd-continuous of the paper) associated with the kernel (equation eq:bilinear-matern-kernel of the paper)
has a unique global classical solution. Moreover, there exists
$C\in(0,\infty)$ such that, for all $T>0$,
\[
        \int_0^T \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \|x^N_i(t)\|^2\,dt
        \le
        CT+\frac{C}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N V(x^N_i(0)).
\]
Further, under the initialization in Assumption~(ass:Wass of the paper),
\begin{equation}
        \sup_{N\ge2}
        \mathbb E\left[\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N V(x^N_i(0))\right]
        <\infty .
\end{equation}
The corresponding mean-field equation (equation eq:mf-svgd of the paper)
is globally defined in the weak continuity-equation sense and satisfies, for all
$T>0$,
\[
        \int_0^T \int_{\mathbb R^d}\|x\|^2\,\mu_t(dx)\,dt
        \le
        CT+ C\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)\,\mu_0(dx) < \infty.
\]

Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable map $T: X \to X$ is measure-preserving if $\mu(T^{-1} A) = \mu(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{B}$ (preimages, not images: $T$ need not be injective, and for non-invertible $T$ the condition $\mu(TA) = \mu(A)$ is neither implied nor required). The system is a probability-preserving system when $\mu(X) = 1$. A set $A$ is (strictly) invariant if $T^{-1}A = A$, and invariant mod $\mu$ if $\mu(T^{-1}A \,\triangle\, A) = 0$; every set invariant mod $\mu$ differs from a strictly invariant set by a null set. $T$ is ergodic if every invariant set has measure $0$ or full measure; equivalently (for a probability measure) every measurable $f$ with $f \circ T = f$ a.e. is a.e. constant; equivalently every set $A$ with $T^{-1}A \subset A$ mod $\mu$ (or $T^{-1}A \supset A$ mod $\mu$) has measure 0 or 1. The invariant $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{I} = \{A : T^{-1}A = A\}$ is what the ergodic averages converge to conditional expectations onto. Ergodicity is not the same as mixing (mixing implies ergodic, not conversely: an irrational rotation of the circle is ergodic but not mixing), and it is not preserved by passing to powers ($T^2$ may fail to be ergodic when $T$ is, e.g. the rotation by $1/2$ on two points).
T is measurable
invariance is expressed through preimages T^{-1}A
title: Measure-preserving transformation; ergodicity

On paths 0,...,n, put conductance c_n=1 for odd n and 2 for even n, normalized counting measure, and spatial scale 1/n. Graph metric-measure spaces converge and resistance is between half and all of graph distance. The stationary variable-speed walks accelerated by n^2 have no common limit of finite-dimensional laws: their cosine two-time covariance tends for t>0 to (1/2)exp(-pi^2*t) along odd n and (1/2)exp(-2*pi^2*t) along even n. This weighted-path example diagnoses the need for actual scaled resistance convergence; it is not a counterexample to an IIC scaling limit.

Effective resistance is |i-j|/c_n, so it is uniformly between half and all of graph distance, yet the resistance distance divided by n has no single limit.

Let the continuous-time variable-speed walk have generator L_n h(i)=c_n*sum_{j adjacent i}(h(j)-h(i)), start in its uniform stationary law, and accelerate time by n^2. Its process laws do not have a single scaling limit along all n.

Proof: the nonconstant eigenfunction u_n(i)=cos(pi*(i+1/2)/(n+1)) has eigenvalue -lambda_n, where lambda_n=2*c_n*(1-cos(pi/(n+1))). Its uniform mean is zero and its uniform second moment is 1/2. Thus

    E[u_n(X_0)*u_n(X_(n^2*t))]=(1/2)*exp(-n^2*lambda_n*t).

u_n is uniformly close to the fixed spatial observable cos(pi*i/n). For any fixed t>0, the displayed bounded two-time expectation tends to (1/2)*exp(-pi^2*t) along odd n and (1/2)*exp(-2*pi^2*t) along even n. A common limit of finite-dimensional laws would force the same bounded continuous expectation, a contradiction. Also the endpoint hitting mean from 0 is n(n+1)/(2*c_n), independently confirming the two time constants.

Every graph here is a tree; both volume and resistance orders are controlled. To use a resistance-form convergence theorem for the IIC one must establish actual scaled resistance and measure convergence, matching embedding and time normalization, rather than replace convergence by constant-factor estimates. The example does not assert that the IIC has this alternation, or that its scaling limit fails.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Outer vertex-isoperimetry of regular plane tessellations (18 September 2026) proves that for an infinite (d,f)-regular plane tessellation G with finite d, f >= 3, 1/d + 1/f <= 1/2 and face degree f >= 5, the outer vertex-isoperimetric constant equals the edge-isoperimetric constant: h_V(G) = h_E(G) = (d-2) sqrt(1 - 4/((d-2)(f-2))); in particular h_V(H_{5,5}) = sqrt(5). Together with the triangular and quadrangular cases of Haslegrave and Panagiotis, this answers the finite-faced regular/co-regular part of Question 6.20 of R. Lyons and Y. Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks; arbitrary transitive plane graphs, the further class in the question, are not covered. The proof rests on a general principle: an infinite simple graph of maximum degree Delta has equal edge and outer vertex-isoperimetric constants whenever its edge constant is at least Delta - 3, and the constant 3 is optimal uniformly in the degree. Paper (PDF): https://github.com/yspennstate/outer-vertex-isoperimetry (commit 9dff9a1b89b3); ResearchGate record 414470838. Not refereed.
title: Lyons-Peres Question 6.20 answered for finite-faced regular tessellations: the outer vertex-isoperimetric constant of a (d,f)-regular plane tessellation with f >= 5 is (d-2) sqrt(1 - 4/((d-2)(f-2))) (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/outer-vertex-isoperimetry)

Let V have n elements and X a random subset. The law of X is invariant under all permutations of V if and only if q(A) = P(A subset of X) depends only on |A|, say q(A) = a_|A|. Then P(|X| = r) = p_r = binom(n, r) sum_{j=0}^{n-r} (-1)^j binom(n - r, j) a_{r+j}, and given |X| = r, X is uniform over the r-subsets. A real sequence a_0, ..., a_n is the profile of some exchangeable random subset if and only if a_0 = 1 and every p_r >= 0, and the law is then unique. Monotonicity is not enough: for n = 2, a = (1, 3/5, 1/10) is nonincreasing in [0, 1] but gives p_0 = -1/10.
V finite with n elements

[Definition def:eta-kappa of arXiv:2411.10419, 'Lower bounds on the top Lyapunov exponent for linear PDEs driven by the 2D stochastic Navi'] For any $ \mathbf{q} > 2$ and $ \kappa \in (0, 1] $, we set $\hat M_i = (M_0 - i) \vee \kappa^{-\mathbf{q}}$ and define the  time $ \eta$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item Set $ \tau_{0} =0 $ and then for every $ i \geqslant 0 $:
\begin{equs}[e:def-tau-sigma-i]
\sigma_{i} &= \inf \{ t \geqslant
\tau_{i}  \; \colon \; M^{(2)}_{t} \geqslant \hat M_i \}\wedge \{ 
\tau_{i} + t_{\star}^{\kappa, \delta} (\hat M_i)\} \;,\\
\tau_{i+1} &= \inf \{ t \geqslant  \tau_{i}  \;\colon \; M_{t} \leqslant \hat M_{i+1}\}  \;,
\end{equs}
where $ t_{\star}^{\kappa, \delta} (M)$ is defined in (equation e:tsd of the paper). 
\item Define $ L = \min \{i \geqslant 0\,:\, \hat M_{i} \leqslant \kappa^{- \mathbf{q}} \}$ and the ``final step'' $i_{\mathrm{fin}}= \min \{ i \geqslant 0  \; \colon \; \sigma_{i} < \tau_{i+1} \} \wedge L$.
\item Finally, we set
$\eta = \sigma_{i_{\mathrm{fin}}}$.
\end{itemize}
title: Definition def:eta-kappa of arXiv:2411.10419

body: [Defn def:isotopy of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $C^0$-foliation. A \textbf{$C^0$-isotopy} of $\mathcal{F}$ is a topological isotopy $h_t : M \rightarrow M$ such that $\mathcal{F}_t = h_t(\mathcal{F})$ is a continuous path of $C^0$-foliations. In particular, the plane fields $T \mathcal{F}_t$ exist and vary continuously with $t$. This $C^0$-isotopy is \textbf{$\varepsilon$-small}, if $d\big(h_t(x),x\big)<\varepsilon$ for all $x\in M$ and furthermore $T\mathcal{F}_t$ is $\varepsilon$-close to $T\mathcal{F}$.

[Lemma janson1 of arXiv:2606.09488, 'The temporal stochastic block model'] Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$, $(\lambda_i)_{i\in [r]} \in (\mathbb{R}^+)^r$ and $X_i \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_i)$ be independent random variables. Define
$$ \mu = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{i=1}^r X_i \right] = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{1}{\lambda_i}, \quad \quad \lambda_* = \min_{i \in [r]} \lambda_i. $$
Then, for $\epsilon >0$, we have 
$$ \mathbb{P}\left[ \sum_{i=1}^r X_i \geq (1+\epsilon)\mu \right] \leq (1+\epsilon)^{-1} e^{-\lambda_* \mu (\epsilon-\log(1+\epsilon))}.$$

Define h(D)=N^(-1) sum_i ell_i(b_i+(<G_ij,D>)_(j=1..K)), where each ell_i:R^K->R is convex, nonnegative and twice continuously differentiable. OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T326-w697-C07 v1; independent reviewer PASS pending. For the source augmented K^TQ model with v21 held zero and m21 trained, the scalar-value/factor flow from Q0=K0=alpha I_(d+1), v0=alpha sqrt(d), 0<alpha^3/sqrt(d)<2, is global and bounded for every nonzero finite pool with a nonzero target. The written proof gives matrix/scalar balance, exact input-nullspace retention and a uniform bound on the effective inherited-nullspace contribution. That contribution vanishes uniformly over all training times as alpha->0 at fixed pool/dimension; it also vanishes in fresh-task norm in probability for each fixed positive M as d->infinity with alpha=epsilon/sqrt(d), fixed epsilon in (0,1). Consequently any zero-loss accumulation point selects the minimum-effective-norm interpolant in these limits. IF zero-loss convergence holds, the fixed-M risk still tends to 1+1/M. Zero-loss convergence is explicitly not proved here. In raw coordinates C=E_pool[(Rz)(Rz)^T], T=d[I,0], P projects onto range C, N=I-P, and R=diag(I/d,1). The proof establishes BB^T-A^TA=alpha^2 ee^T, v^2=||A||_F^2 and BN=alpha N. With lambda the smallest positive eigenvalue of C, K0=||TP||_F+sqrt(2L0/lambda), and Zmax=max(2d alpha^2,(2d K0^2)^(1/3)), one has v^2<=Zmax globally. The inherited-nullspace term H=alpha v A N R has normalized fresh-task squared norm at most alpha^2 Zmax^2/d times [1/d^2+(eta-1/d^2)q], with q=e^TNe and eta=(1+rho)^2+2/d. For fixed M and alpha=epsilon/sqrt(d), this bound is O_P(1/d). Zero-loss convergence for M>=2 remains the missing hypothesis for the 1+1/M selector conclusion.

body:
[Ppn 246 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Assume that $L\ge1$ and that condition \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} holds. Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp}  and \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising}, and assume that condition~\eqref{e:w2.coupling.assumption} holds. Then, for the stopping times defined by \eqref{e:trstar.stopping.time}--\eqref{e:trstar.stopping.time.ISING}, we have
	\begin{align*}
	\max_{\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\frac1M \sum_{a=1}^M
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\sigma(q_d,a)^2; \tau(a)<1
	\bigg]
	&\le O(\epsilon) + o_{\trK}(1)\,,\\
	\frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\Ising(q_d,i)^2; 
	\tau^\Ising(i)<1
	\bigg]
	&\le o_{\trK}(1)
	\end{align*}
uniformly over $N$. 

\begin{proof} 
Throughout this proof, we write $\bE_a$ for expectation over a uniformly random index $a\in[M]$, we write $\E$ for expectation over the gaussian disorder, and we write $\E'\equiv \bE_a\E$ for expectation over both. The assumption \eqref{e:w2.coupling.assumption} says that there exists a coupling of $X(1)$ with $Z\sim\mu$ such that
	\[
	\E'\Big[(X(1)-Z)^2\Big]
	\le \epsilon\,.
	\]
We can use this to bound
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	&\frac1M  \sum_{a=1}^M (\E X^\RomI(1,a))^2
	=\frac1M  \sum_{a=1}^M (\E X(1,a))^2
	\le
	\frac1M  \sum_{a=1}^M \E[ X(1,a)^2 ]
	=\E'[ X(1)^2 ] \\
	&\qquad\le 
	2 \E'\Big[ (X(1)-Z)^2  + Z^2\Big]
	\le 2\Big( \epsilon + \E'(Z^2)\Big)
	\le O(1)\,,
	
	\end{align}
where the $O(1)$ indicates a large constant depending only on $\mu$. 
Recall that the $X^{\RomII}$ and $X^{\RomIII}$ processes have mean zero, so $\E X^{\RomI}=\E X$. Next, a straightforward gaussian computation gives the identity
	\[
	\E X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) = p(q_d) \E X^{\RomI}(1,a)\,.
	\]
It follows by combining with the result of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.I.minus.mean} that
	\begin{align*}
	&\frac{1}{M}\sum_{a=1}^M
	\E \bigg[\max_{0\le d\le\dmax} X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)^2\bigg]\\
	&\qquad\le\frac{2}{M}\sum_{a=1}^M
		\E \bigg[\max_{0\le d\le\dmax}
			\Big( X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) - \E X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) \Big)^2
			\bigg]
	+ \frac{2}{M}\sum_{a=1}^M \max_{0\le d\le\dmax} 
		(\E X^{\RomI}(q_d,a))^2 \\
	&\qquad
	\le L^{O(1)}
	+ \frac{1}{M}\sum_{a=1}^M 
		(\E X^{\RomI}(1,a))^2
	\le L^{O(1)} +O(1) \le L^{O(1)}\,.
	\end{align*}

Independent derivation pending w440 review. On the infinite 3-regular tree, iid Bernoulli bond percolation has p_c=1/2 and almost surely no infinite cluster at p_c, but E_{p_c}|C(o)| is infinite. At distance k>=1 there are 3*2^(k-1) vertices, each connected with probability 2^(-k), giving expected connected shell size 3/2. Below p_c, chi(p)=1+3p/(1-2p), which diverges as p increases to p_c. Thus finiteness of susceptibility for every p<p_c cannot be transferred to p=p_c without a further uniform integrability or domination argument; it cannot be assumed as a bridge to critical extinction.
infinite 3-regular tree
iid Bernoulli bonds
critical p=1/2 for the endpoint claim
0<=p<1/2 for the subcritical formula
title: DRAFT: Critical extinction can coexist with infinite susceptibility

[Lemma lem:transfer-minors-master of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $1\leq s\leq k$, and let
$z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(s)}\in\mathbb Z^k$ have coordinate sum zero.  Delete
the same $k-s$ coordinates from every row.  If $Q$ is the resulting
$s\times s$ matrix, then
\begin{equation}
 |\det Q|\leq\prod_{i=1}^s\rho(z^{(i)}).
\end{equation}
In particular, if every $z^{(i)}\in\mathcal D_{h,k}$, then
$|\det Q|\leq h^s$.

body:
[Defn 10 (Broadcasting process) of arXiv:2606.22960, '2606.22960'] Let \((T_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be the tree growth model above. Each vertex carries one of two colours, which we identify with the values \(-1\) and \(1\). The root vertex \(1\) is assigned a random bit \(B_1\in\{-1,1\}\), chosen uniformly at random. For each \(n\geq 1\), once the new vertex \(n+1\) has chosen its parent \(p_{n+1}\), it inherits the bit of its parent with probability \(1-q\) and flips it with probability \(q\), independently of the tree growth and all previous broadcasting steps. Equivalently,
	\[
	B_{n+1}=B_{p_{n+1}}Z_{n+1},
	\]
	where \((Z_n)_{n\geq 2}\) are independent \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued random variables satisfying
	\[
	\mathbb P(Z_n=-1)=q,
	\qquad
	\mathbb P(Z_n=1)=1-q.
	\]
	The parameter \(q\in[0,1]\) is called the bit-flip probability.
title: Broadcasting process

body: [Lemma 1 of arXiv:2511.05218, 'On the Color Discrepancy of Spanning Trees in Random and Randomly Perturbed Graphs'] Fix $\delta>0$. Then for $C$ sufficiently large (depending on $\delta$), the random graph $G\sim G(n,p)$ with $p=C/n$ satisfies the following properties with high probability: (1) For any disjoint sets $V_{1},V_{2}\subseteq V(G)$ with $|V_{1}|,|V_{2}|\geq\delta n$, the induced bipartite subgraph on $V_{1}\cup V_{2}$ contains a matching of size at least $\frac{1}{8}\delta n$. (2) The giant component of $G$ has size at least $(1-\rho)n$, where $\rho\ll\delta$.

body: [Lemma 6 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $A$ and $B$ be sets such that $A\cap B = \varnothing$. title: FPP chi=1/3 campaign, 2026-08-15 fires 9-15: (L2') HOLDS at laptop sizes - the per-block conditional kurtosis SATURATES - and the earlier growth claim was a moving baseline. DECOMPOSITION (elementary, known in kind - cf. Dembin-Elboim-Peled arXiv 2307.01162 on edge influence): resampling block L leaves every path AVOIDING L untouched, so X = min(A,C) and X^L = min(A',C) with the SAME C; on the touching event the geodesic is in the through class so X = A <= C, giving Delta = min(A',C) - A and the exact cap 0 <= (Delta)^+ <= min{(Delta_0)^+, G_L} with G_L = C - A the gap to the best avoiding path. This matters because CRUX 6d.1 (D7) says the engine consumes ONLY the positive part. MEASURED (U[1,2] on Z^2, exact Dijkstra, axis blocks, four occupation points, pre-registered read): A4/(A2^+)^2 = 5.7339 [5.642,5.838], 6.1143 [6.010,6.223], 6.2345 [6.022,6.439], 6.2290 [5.962,6.509] at occupation 3.95 / 6.04 / 10.08 / 14.05, while the reroute fraction goes 0.167 / 0.384 / 0.606 / 0.740. Increments +0.3804, +0.1202, -0.0055: rise, decelerate, flat. A log fit to the first step predicts +0.46 and +0.30 for the next two, so growth is far slower than logarithmic. The two-sided kurtosis - (L2')'s literal statement - is flatter still at 2.9590 / 3.0564 / 3.0854 / 3.1219. THAT IS WHAT (L2') HOLDING LOOKS LIKE. MECHANISM (hypothesis): (Delta)^+ is a mixture under a RANDOM ceiling G, so its level sits elevated (~6.2) against a null of ~3.1-5.1, but once nearly every resample reroutes the mixture stops changing composition and kappa4 saturates as the reroute fraction does - a one-off elevation the engine absorbs into its constant, not a divergence. METHOD CORRECTION THIS SUPERSEDES: the earlier claim that rerouting fattens the engine's functional and grows was an artifact of reporting a DIFFERENCE against a falling null. With four points: the excess grows 4.8x (+0.655 -> +3.135) while the quantity moves 9 percent (5.7339 -> 6.2290) and is flat over the last two, because the null fell 5.0787 -> 3.0944. LIMITS: occupation 4-14 edges against an engine whose hypotheses start near l_0 ~ 1e18; square blocks not the engine's tall thin W ~ sqrt(nQ); one weight law; widest CI at the last point. Saturation over a measured range is evidence for boundedness, never proof. And all of this is (L2'), which is NOT the wall - (L1') is, and nothing here touches it. chi = 1/3 UNMOVED.

Write H_t(x) for an unfilled-hole indicator and h_t=E H_t(0). Assume the source properties h_t tends to zero and h_t>=c0/(t+1) eventually for some c0>0. If for some fixed a>0 and finite C, sum_{0<|z|<=floor(a h_t^(-1/4))} P(H_t(0)=H_t(z)=1) <= C h_t eventually, then limsup_{t->infinity} P(origin strictly nearer an unfilled hole than an active particle)>0. The Palm clustering assumption remains unproved for parking; this is a conditional reduction, not a solution of I0005. Novelty: UNCHECKED (limited primary/source and brain search). Status: independently checked proof.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:8c6e80e635200bb5367f1f9af3cc58b0b5b376e7efb39bf24994618a849425fe","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/8c/8c6e80e635200bb5367f1f9af3cc58b0b5b376e7efb39bf24994618a849425fe.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e0c6a70fae48ddadb045ae4a869b74b238887dd343b37ed6b8e92c14c29ba932","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c9","bundle_id":"population.i0005-palm-reductions-and-comparisons-004","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"interacting particle systems and comparison fields","draft":"w661/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:four-dimensional-parking-finite-palm-clustering-reduction-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C9 v1: bounded Palm clustering suffices for a fixed-law counterexample

Novelty: UNCHECKED. A new-to-this-round reduction using local-priority thinning, finite-time hitting, and hole-loss mass transport. It was compared with the source's proof of Theorem 1.6 and prior own reductions; no assertion of priority. It does not establish its Palm-clustering hypothesis in d4.

Fix one sparse critical law on Z^4 with P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p and P(η=0)=1−2p, where 0<p<1/2 is fixed. Write h_t=P(H_t(0)=1), and F_t for the event that the origin is strictly nearer an unfilled hole than an active particle in graph distance.

Suppose there are fixed a>0 and C<∞ such that for every sufficiently large integer t,

sum_{0<|z|_1≤floor(a h_t^−1/4)} P(H_t(0)=H_t(z)=1) ≤ C h_t.       (PC)

Then limsup_{t→∞}P(F_t)>0. In particular the affirmative limit-to-zero statement is false for that fixed law. The criterion permits any finite C, unlike C2's small Palm neighbor-count condition. It proves a positive limsup, which is enough to contradict convergence to zero; it does not assert a positive liminf.

More precisely, constants κ≥2 and D<∞ depending only on the Z^4 walk can be fixed as below. Let c0>0 be any constant for which h_t≥c0/(t+1) eventually (source Lemma 5.1 permits a universal choice), set A=2/c0, and choose b>0 satisfying

2κb≤a, and b^4≤1/[4AD(1+C)].

Then the lower limit along a sequence of times is at least b^4/[48(1+C)].

## 1. A finite-time one-target hitting estimate

There are κ≥2, c_hit>0 and R0 such that for every integer R≥R0 and every y with |y|_1≤R, a free walk from y hits zero within n=2R² steps before exiting B_{κR}, with probability at least c_hit/R².

To prove this, use the periodic local CLT established in C1. For R²≤j≤2R² on the allowed parity, |y|_2≤R gives p_j(y)≥cR^−4 for all large R, uniformly in y. There are at least cR² allowed times. Hence sum_{j=0}^{2R²}p_j(y)≥c1/R². By the strong Markov property at T0, the expected number of visits after the first hit is at most G(0)=g<∞, so P_y(T0≤2R²)≥c1/(gR²).

The Green-function bound G(z)≤C2/|z|_1² for z≠0 follows from Lawler–Limic, Theorem 4.3.1, or the standard Gaussian heat-kernel sum. Let τ be the first exit from B_{κR}. Conditional on τ<T0, the probability of any subsequent hit is G(X_τ)/g≤C2/(gκ²R²). Strong Markov at τ bounds the probability of hitting by 2R² after an earlier exit by the same number. Choose an integer κ sufficiently large that C2/κ²≤c1/2. Subtracting gives the asserted estimate with c_hit=c1/(2g). All constants are uniform for R≥R0. Put D=1/c_hit.

## 2. Select well-separated holes without requiring isolation in the original field

At time t, attach iid continuous uniform priorities to every lattice site, independently of the process and its future. For a deterministic integer R≥R0, select an unfilled hole x if its priority is the smallest among all unfilled holes within distance 2κR of x. Distinct selected centers have distance greater than 2κR, so their closed balls of radius κR are disjoint. The construction is translation-covariant.

Let i_t be the selected-hole intensity. Conditional on the hole field and H_t(0)=1, selection probability is 1/(1+N), where N counts other holes within 2κR. Therefore Jensen's inequality gives

i_t=h_t E[1/(1+N) | H_t(0)=1]≥h_t/[1+E(N|H_t(0)=1)].

Under (PC), for R=floor(bh_t^−1/4) and 2κb≤a, this is at least h_t/(1+C). These selected centers are not necessarily isolated among all holes; the remaining holes will be helpful for the hole-loss argument.

## 3. A nearby active particle forces some hole loss in its selected ball

Let j_t be the intensity of selected centers with at least one active particle within distance R. Conditional on the complete time-t history and the priorities, choose one such active particle by a translation-covariant rule. For example, order its current displacement and initial-origin displacement relative to the center lexicographically; the set of eligible labels is finite. Its unused future increments remain independent simple-walk steps under the particle-walk construction.

On the event in Step 1 for this particle's free future path relative to the center, at least one hole that was unfilled at time t inside B_{κR}(center) fills by time t+n. Indeed, if the particle settles before reaching the center, its settlement is at a hole inside that ball. If the center's hole has already filled by its arrival, that is already a hole loss in the ball. Otherwise its arrival, possibly in a tie with other particles, fills the center's hole. The free path has not exited the ball before that arrival. Other surviving holes can stop the particle earlier but cannot invalidate the assertion that some hole in the ball fills.

Thus each eligible center has conditional probability at least c_hit/R² of a hole loss in its ball during the window. Independence between different centers is neither required nor asserted.

For each eligible center with such a loss, choose one lost hole in its ball and send one unit of mass from that hole to the center. The balls are disjoint, so a lost hole sends at most one unit. Translation invariance and nonnegative mass transport give

(c_hit/R²)j_t ≤ density of eligible centers witnessing a loss
≤P(H_t(0)=1,H_{t+n}(0)=0)=h_t−h_{t+n}.

Hence j_t≤D R²(h_t−h_{t+2R²}). Capacity one and permanent filling justify the final equality. This bound uses a time-window hole loss, not a hole–active decorrelation estimate.

## 4. Cover sites near the selected centers with no nearby active particle

The good selected centers, those with no active particle within R, have density at least (i_t−j_t)_+. Every site within floor(R/2) of a good center is strictly nearer its hole than every active particle: for such a site w and active site z,

|z−w|_1≥|z−center|_1−|w−center|_1>R−floor(R/2)≥|w−center|_1.

These small balls are disjoint because the selected centers are more than 2κR apart. Sending unit mass from each good center to each site of its small ball therefore yields

P(F_t)≥|B_floor(R/2)|[i_t−D R²(h_t−h_{t+2R²})]_+.

This finite-scale inequality is valid for any deterministic R≥R0 and any translation-covariant separated-hole selection as above.

## 5. There are arbitrarily late windows with controlled inverse-density growth

For the sparse critical law, h_t↓0 and h_t≥c0/(t+1) eventually, by source Corollary 1.3 and Lemma 5.1. Set g_t=1/h_t; it is nondecreasing and g_t≤(t+1)/c0 for all sufficiently large t. For R_t=floor(bg_t^{1/4}) set n_t=2R_t². Eventually R_t≥R0 and n_t≥1.

There are arbitrarily large t with

g_{t+n_t}−g_t≤A n_t, where A=2/c0.

Otherwise, beyond some T the reverse strict inequality would hold at every integer time. Starting at t0=T and iterating t_{k+1}=t_k+n_{t_k} gives t_k→∞ and, by telescoping,

g_{t_k}−g_T>A(t_k−T).

But g_{t_k}≤(t_k+1)/c0. Dividing by t_k and letting k→∞ forces A≤1/c0, a contradiction. No differentiability, smooth density asymptotic or fixed-window independence is used.

At the resulting sequence of times,

h_t−h_{t+n_t}=h_t h_{t+n_t}(g_{t+n_t}−g_t)≤A n_t h_t².

Consequently

j_t≤D R_t² A n_t h_t²=2AD R_t^4 h_t²≤2AD b^4 h_t≤h_t/[2(1+C)].

Since i_t≥h_t/(1+C), good selected-hole density is at least h_t/[2(1+C)] along this sequence. Finally,

h_t|B_floor(R_t/2)|→(2^4/4!)b^4/16=b^4/24.

Step 4 gives the asserted positive subsequential lower bound b^4/[48(1+C)].

## Exact unresolved piece

Proving (PC) for one fixed sparse d4 law would now refute the limit-to-zero statement. It is enough to bound the Palm expected count of other holes in one fixed fraction of the mean-spacing ball by an arbitrary finite constant. No small pair-sum constant, mixed-moment bound, or positive-liminf density estimate beyond the universal inverse-time lower bound is required. C5/C8 supply initial-p estimates that grow like p/h_t on this scale, so they do not prove (PC).

Sources used: arXiv:2609.02820v1, Lemma 5.1/Corollary 1.3, and comparison with Theorem 1.6 proof; Lawler–Limic, author PDF, Theorem 4.3.1; own audited C1 periodic local CLT. The identification of the dual of L^p has two genuine exceptions. (1) p = infinity fails in general: apart from the degenerate case of finitely many atoms all of finite measure (where L^1 = L^infinity is finite-dimensional and the duality is trivially true), L^1 is a proper closed subspace of (L^infinity)*. On [0,1] with Lebesgue measure, C[0,1] embeds isometrically in L^infinity (for continuous functions the sup norm equals the essential sup norm); extend the evaluation functional h -> h(0) from C[0,1] to a norm-one functional Lambda on L^infinity by Hahn-Banach. If Lambda were integration against some g in L^1, then taking continuous h_n with h_n(0) = 1, 0 <= h_n <= 1, supported in [0, 1/n], dominated convergence would give int h_n g -> 0 while Lambda(h_n) = 1. (Concretely, (L^infinity)* is the space of finitely additive bounded measures absolutely continuous with respect to mu.) (2) p = 1 without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) fails: let X = {pt} with mu({pt}) = infinity. Then L^1(mu) = {0}, so (L^1)* = {0}, while L^infinity(mu) is one-dimensional; the canonical map L^infinity -> (L^1)* is not injective, let alone onto. (3) For 0 < p < 1 and mu nonatomic (e.g. Lebesgue on [0,1]) the dual is trivial: (L^p[0,1])* = {0}, so no duality/Hahn-Banach argument survives below p = 1. Only the range 1 < p < infinity is safe for an arbitrary measure space: there L^p is reflexive and (L^p)* = L^{p'} for every measure, whereas L^1 and L^infinity are reflexive only in degenerate finite-dimensional cases.
examples use Lebesgue measure on [0,1] and a one-point space of infinite measure
statements about (L^infinity)* use the axiom of choice via Hahn-Banach
the degenerate exception in (1) is a measure that is a finite sum of atoms of finite measure
title: Pitfall: (L^1)* = L^infinity needs sigma-finiteness, and (L^infinity)* is strictly larger than L^1

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). In two-dimensional critical or near-critical percolation, RSW theory states that if crossing probabilities of n x n squares are uniformly bounded away from 0 as n grows, then crossing probabilities of rho n x n rectangles, for any fixed aspect ratio rho, are also uniformly bounded away from 0 by a constant depending on rho but not on n. The matching bound away from 1 needs the same input for the dual model (at criticality on a self-dual lattice it follows by duality); a lower bound for the primal model alone does not give it, since in the supercritical phase both crossing probabilities tend to 1. The classical proof glues together several square-crossing events using the FKG inequality and translation and reflection symmetry of the lattice. RSW estimates are the essential multi-scale input for proving arm-exponent bounds, conformal-invariance-adjacent results, and, via the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, for establishing sharpness of the phase transition without relying on exact self-duality. RSW does not by itself prove existence of a scaling limit as n -> infinity, does not give the exact value of any crossing probability, only two-sided bounds; and the classical form required exact self-duality (p=1/2 on the square lattice), so extending the theory to general planar lattices or to p != 1/2 required a genuinely new, duality-free argument (Tassion, 2016). Typical failure: Assuming that RSW-type bounded-away-from-0/1 crossing estimates transfer automatically to a new planar model merely because it is monotone and planar; RSW requires either exact self-duality or the more robust but still nontrivial Tassion-style construction, and models without FKG, or with strong enough long-range dependence, can fail to admit the needed gluing arguments even though they look superficially similar to Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Russo, 1978, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Seymour and Welsh, 1978, Annals of Discrete Mathematics; Tassion, 2016, Probability Theory and Related Fields.

This is UNAUDITED. It uses012v2's low-cap convergence,015v3's corrected
scalar countable cycle basin and uniform local capture,023v1's direct
zero-work full-path classification, and025v1's Green origin decay.
The difficult standard-initialization cycle countability in015v3
remains an independent audit burden. Unlike021's singular-floor proof,
this proof needs no source potential or closed-relation singular lift:
the scalar high floor rho=1/lambda_h stays strictly positive.

1. NORMALIZATION, BOUNDEDNESS AND THE LOW COORDINATE
For either coordinate let X=x/eta,M=m/(eta*lambda),
V=v/(eta*lambda)^2,rho=1/lambda. The raw scalar map is

 M'=bM+(1-b)X, V'=dV+(1-d)X^2,

Corrected maps have their ordinary separate clock factors. The
elementary absorbing argument in033 Section1 gives uniform tail
bounds |X|,|M|<=802,V<=802^2, after a start-dependent burn-in.
For high rho in[1/H1,1/H0], the corrected maps converge uniformly
on this compact physical box to the continuous map F_rho in(2).
Claim012v2 gives X_l,M_l,V_l->0 since lambda_l<38, regardless of its
standard initial position.

2. A NARROW ACTIVE BAND IMPOSES A CLOSED SCALAR BAND ON THE OMEGA SET
Suppose limsup |A_t-38|<delta, A_t=eta*C_active,t. Eventually its
defined values lie within delta. Multiply this inequality by the
nonnegative active denominator sum_i g_i^2/P_i. At exact zero gradient
times both extended sides are zero. All coefficients are bounded;
the low coordinate vanishes. For any point (X,M,V) of the high
omega-limit K, taking an adjacent-state limit therefore gives

 X^2*|kappa_rho(X,V)-38|<=delta*X^2,
 kappa_rho(X,V)=1/(sqrt(dV+(1-d)X^2)+rho).                (3)

The harmless positive factor1/(sqrt(V')+rho) was canceled when X!=0;
when X=0 both sides of(3) are zero. Thus(3) remains a closed constraint
at zero positions. K is nonempty compact, F_rho(K)=K, and internally
chain transitive for F_rho. To see the latter, follow a late actual
segment between visits near prescribed x,y in K. Actual tail distance
to K and corrected-map distance to F_rho tend to zero. Project each
segment node into K. Uniform continuity of F_rho bounds each chain
error separately, independently of the segment length.

3. UNIFORM SMALL-BAND REDUCTION TO CRITICAL NEIGHBORHOODS
For delta=0, EVERY full F_rho-path in a compact invariant K satisfying
(3) is a bounded full scalar zero-work path. By023 it is an origin or
cycle path, with a=1/38-rho>0. Hence K is contained in the three
critical states; internal chain transitivity forces one critical orbit.

This exact statement gives a uniform near-critical statement on the
compact rho interval. Fix sufficiently small neighborhoods of the
origin and of the two cycle phases, centered continuously in rho.
For all sufficiently small delta, EVERY compact fully invariant
internally chain-transitive K satisfying(3) lies in their union.
Otherwise take delta_n->0, rho_n converging, and offending K_n. A
Hausdorff subsequence gives K in the common physical compact box.
Uniform convergence F_rho_n->F_rho passes full invariance and(3)
to the limit. It also passes internal chain transitivity: project
the nodes of an arbitrarily fine F_rho_n-chain into K and use uniform
continuity to control each new jump, without accumulating errors.
Thus K is one critical orbit. A selected point outside the chosen
neighborhoods persists outside at the limit, a contradiction.

Choose OUTER neighborhoods first, with these properties uniformly
over rho: they are disjoint; a corrected late step with both ends in
their union cannot change orbit groups or select a wrong cycle phase;
cycle neighborhoods are within015v3's uniform physical capture region;
the origin neighborhood is small enough for the uniform Green estimate
in Section4. Uniform continuity at the separated critical states and
compactness give the nonjump conditions. Use INNER half-radius
neighborhoods for the preceding compactness reduction. For delta small
enough, K lies in the inner union; hence the actual tail lies in the
outer union. Nonjump separation makes it eventually stay in the
origin group or the alternating cycle group.

4. THE ORIGIN ALTERNATIVE CONTRADICTS THE ACTIVE BAND
For high lambda in[H0,H1], the limiting position-pair matrix

 A_h=[[1+b-(1-b)*lambda_h,-b],[1,0]]

has real roots -b<r_s<0,r_u<-1. Their gaps from b and the unit circle
are uniform on the compact high interval. Choose
sup |r_s|<q<nu<b. Eigenbases and inverses are uniformly bounded.
The origin neighborhood and late clocks can be chosen so the actual
position-pair coefficients, throughout that neighborhood, are close
enough to A_h for BOTH Green contractions in036 Section2 (weighted
q and bounded weight1). This argument requires only boundedness and
small coefficient perturbations, NOT prior origin convergence.
Consequently a high-coordinate tail staying in this neighborhood has
|X_h,t|<=C*q^t. Stable raw moment and variance recursions then imply
M_h,V_h->0 as well. Thus both coordinates actually approach their origins.

If the standard low initial position is nonzero,025 gives a subsequence
of active sharpness tending to lambda_l<=L1<38. This is incompatible
with an eventual band delta<(38-L1)/2. We may remove the line x_l,0=0
as a null exceptional set; no assertion on that line is needed here.
Thus the origin alternative is excluded for almost every start.

For clarity, the low-coordinate lower-rate estimate can be chosen
uniformly too: the explicit matrix Q in036 Eq10 is positive definite
for fixed nu<b and every low trace T with |T|<=1+b. It obeys
A_l^T Q A_l=nu^2 Q+A_l^T A_l. On compact low parameters its strict
gain margin is uniform, and actual coefficients approach A_l once
the low coordinate decays. This confirms the rate comparison across
the whole stated low interval, including repeated-root parameters.

range. For fixed eta and lambda_h, its standard initial positions
converging to this corrected cycle form a countable set. Thus full

vertical lines. Together with the removed low-zero line they have

needed. Outside this exceptional set, the assumed strict limsup band
is impossible, proving(1).

Active quotients at finite zero-gradient times can be treated either
by the zero extension used in Section2 or by removing their null
initial lines. For fixed finite time, a nonzero scalar standard initial
position maps analytically to its position on either sign half-line:
positive raw variance after the first update makes all subsequent
square roots analytic. The bounded-increment properness estimate
prevents that analytic function from being identically zero. Its
zeros are countable. Hence the countable union of finite-time zero
events is null, and generic trajectories have all their quotients
defined. Along any specified countable eta sequence, union the null
exceptional sets; an absolutely continuous joint law still assigns
zero mass. This gives the stated simultaneous conclusion.

[Lemma 16 (Properties of Poisson-Voronoi percolation) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a non-compact connected semisimple real Lie group, $(X,d_X)$ be its symmetric space, $\lambda>0$ and $p\in (0,1)$.
    Then $\omega_p^{(\lambda)}$ defines a random closed subset of $X$ which
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[{\rm (i)}] is $G$-invariant and ergodic, and, moreover, is invariant under all isometries of $(X,d_X)$.
        \item[{\rm (ii)}] satisfies the Harris-FKG-inequality.
        \item[{\rm (iii)}] satisfies $\mathbb P\big(o\in \partial \omega_p^{(\lambda)}\big)=0$.
    \end{itemize}
    Moreover, the Voronoi diagram $\mathrm{Vor}(\mathbf{Y}^{(\lambda)})$ consists of compact subsets of $X$.
title: Properties of Poisson-Voronoi percolation

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2506.10522, 'On the Law of the Iterated Logarithm for $m$-dependent stationary random variables under s'] Let $\{X_n; n\ge 1\}$ be a martingale difference sequence in a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ with respect to the
filtration $\{\mathcal F_n\}$ such that $|X_n|\le  m_n$ a.s. for some $\mathcal F_{n-1}$-measurable random variable
$m_n$, with $U_n\to \infty$  and $m_n/\{U_n(\log\log U_n)^{-1/2}\}\to 0$  a.s., where $U_n^2=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2$.  Then
$$ \limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}{U_n(2\log\log U_n)^{1/2}}=1\;\; a.s. $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 2 (Hydrodynamic limit) of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] Let \(\{\mu^n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}\) be a sequence of probability measures on \(\Omega_n\) associated with \(\bm\rho_0\). 
	Then, for every \(t\in[0,T]\), every \(\delta>0\), every \(k\in\{1,2\}\), and every \(f_k\in C^\infty([0,1];\mathbb R) \),
	\[
	\lim_{n\to\infty}
	\mathbb P_{\mu^n}^n
	\left(
	\left|
	X_k^{n,t}(f_k)
	-
	\int_0^1 f_k(u)\rho_k(t,u)\,du
	\right|>\delta
	\right)
	=0,
	\]
	where $ \bm\rho(t,u)
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		\rho_1(t,u)\\
		\rho_2(t,u)
	\end{pmatrix} $
    is the unique weak solution of the reaction-diffusion system with Robin boundary conditions
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{cases}
			\partial_t\bm\rho(t,u)
			=
			\Delta\bm\rho(t,u)+M\bm\rho(t,u),
			& t>0,\ u\in(0,1),\\[0.2cm]
			\partial_u\bm\rho(t,0)
			=
			K_L\bm\rho(t,0)-\bm\alpha,
			& t>0,\\[0.2cm]
			\partial_u\bm\rho(t,1)
			=
			\bm\beta-K_R\bm\rho(t,1),
			& t>0,\\[0.2cm]
			\bm\rho(0,u)=\bm\rho_0(u),
			& u\in[0,1].
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
	Here $ \bm \alpha = \left( \alpha_1,\alpha_2 \right)^{\top} $, $ \bm \beta = \left( \beta_1,\beta_2 \right)^{\top} $, and
	\[
	M=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		-\gamma_1 & \gamma_2\\
		\gamma_1 & -\gamma_2
	\end{pmatrix},
	\qquad
	K_L=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		1-\alpha_2 & \alpha_1\\
		\alpha_2 & 1-\alpha_1
	\end{pmatrix},
	\qquad
	K_R=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		1-\beta_2 & \beta_1\\
		\beta_2 & 1-\beta_1
	\end{pmatrix}.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Hydrodynamic limit

[Lemma lem:bochner-cutoff-approximation of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Suppose Assumptions~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper) and
(ass:bochner-regularity of the paper) hold.  Fix a regular weight $w$ and
$I=(r_0,r_1)$, and consider a field satisfying
\begin{equation*}
 h\in H_{x,w}^1(I)\cap W_{p,\mathrm{loc}}^{1,2}(I\times\mathbb R^d),
 \qquad \mathcal Ph\in L_w^2(I),
 \qquad p>d+2.
\end{equation*}
Fix $0\leq\chi\in C_c^\infty(B_2)$ with $\chi=1$ on $B_1$, and, for
$R\geq1$, set $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$,
$h_R=\chi_Rh$ and $F=\mathcal Ph$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Ph_R
 =\chi_RF-h\mathcal L_t\chi_R-aD_x\chi_R\cdot D_xh
 \quad\text{in distributions},
 
\end{equation}
and, as $R\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 h_R\longrightarrow h\quad\text{in }H_{x,w}^1(I),
 \qquad \mathcal Ph_R\longrightarrow F\quad\text{in }L_w^2(I).
 
\end{equation}
If $\operatorname{Tr}_{r_1}^Xh=\Xi$, then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Tr}_{r_1}^Xh_R=\chi_R(X_{r_1})\Xi,
 \qquad \chi_R(X_{r_1})\Xi\longrightarrow\Xi
 \quad\text{in }L^2(\Omega).
 
\end{equation}
If, in addition,
$\mathfrak B_{J,w}(h)<\infty$ for $J=[s,r]\Subset I$, then
\begin{equation*}
 (D_t^ch_R,\Delta_{\mu,g}h_R,\operatorname{Hess}_gh_R)\longrightarrow
 (D_t^ch,\Delta_{\mu,g}h,\operatorname{Hess}_gh)
 \qquad\text{in }L_w^2(J).
\end{equation*}
The endpoint values and gradients converge in $L^2(\mu_t)$ for
$t\in\{s,r\}$, and
\begin{equation*}
 \int_{J\times\mathbb R^d}\mathscr R_{w,t}(\nabla^gh_R,\nabla^gh_R)\,\mathrm d\mathfrak m
 \longrightarrow
 \int_{J\times\mathbb R^d}\mathscr R_{w,t}(\nabla^gh,\nabla^gh)\,\mathrm d\mathfrak m.
\end{equation*}

body:
Let X be a Banach space and A: D(A) ⊂ X → X linear and densely defined. (1) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0, and A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (2) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) is merely dense for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closable, its closure Ā is dissipative with Ran(λ − Ā) = X for all λ > 0, and Ā generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (3) Conversely, if A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup, then A is densely defined, closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for all λ > 0, and A is dissipative in the strong sense that Re⟨Ax, x*⟩ ≤ 0 for every x ∈ D(A) and every x* ∈ J(x). (4) If X is reflexive, a dissipative A with Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0 is automatically densely defined. (5) Hilbert space corollary: if A is densely defined and closed and both A and A* are dissipative, then A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup; and a densely defined symmetric operator S with S ≤ 0 that is self-adjoint generates the contraction semigroup e^{tS}. Quasi-contractive version: if A − ω is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > ω, then A generates a C_0-semigroup with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ e^{ωt}.
X is a Banach space
A is densely defined (automatic in reflexive X under the range condition)
A is dissipative
a range condition: Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or dense) for some λ_0 > 0

The set of λ > 0 with Ran(λ − A) = X is open (Neumann series: for |λ − λ_0| < λ_0 one has λ − A = (I + (λ − λ_0)(λ_0 − A)^{-1})(λ_0 − A) invertible) and closed in (0, ∞) (the uniform bound 1/λ keeps the range closed), hence equals (0, ∞) by connectedness. Then A is closed, densely defined, with ‖(λ − A)^{-1}‖ ≤ 1/λ, and the contraction case of the Hille-Yosida theorem applies. For (2), dissipativity of a densely defined A implies closability: if x_n → 0 with Ax_n → y, one uses ‖(λ − A)(x_n + λ^{-1}z)‖ ≥ λ‖x_n + λ^{-1}z‖ for z ∈ D(A) and lets n → ∞ then λ → ∞ to force y = 0; the closure is dissipative by continuity of the inequality, and its range is closed and dense, hence all of X. For (3), the semigroup contraction property gives Re⟨Ax, x*⟩ = lim_{t↓0} t^{-1}Re(⟨T(t)x, x*⟩ − ‖x‖²) ≤ lim t^{-1}(‖T(t)x‖‖x‖ − ‖x‖²) ≤ 0.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:0a9e681fc7b5e4b378857c09e96eaf727fa4a68f99189c6accc34e4f8888ba9a","revision_digest":"sha256:9cc7074f8de110e84e704f7481a4bebc14d6b3c2eb606e5b71dc671682f7125e","source_id":"wikipedia:Lumer-Phillips theorem","source_revision":"as-known-2026-09-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Prop ideal equality of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Suppose $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Z}$ are smooth separated Deligne--Mumford stacks of dimension $n$, and there is a representable contraction $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z}$ where the exceptional $\mathcal{E}$ is a smooth irreducible Cartier divisor. 
    Moreover, suppose there is a smooth closed irreducible Deligne--Mumford substack $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{Z}$ such that $(f^{-1}\mathcal{Y}) \simeq \mathcal{E}$ set-theoretically, and $f : \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{E} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{Z} \setminus \mathcal{Y}.$ Then $f^{-1}\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Y}/\mathcal{Z}}.\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{X}\simeq\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{X}(-\mathcal{E})$, as ideal sheaves on $\mathcal{X}$. Here $f^{-1}\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Y}/\mathcal{Z}}\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{X}:=\operatorname{im}(f^\ast\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Y}/\mathcal{Z}}\rightarrow \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{X})$. Furthermore, $\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{X}(-\mathcal{E})$ is relatively ample with respect to $f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$.

Let X be a Banach space, K : X -> X a compact linear operator, and T = I - K. Then: (i) ker T is finite-dimensional and the range of T is closed; (ii) T is injective if and only if it is surjective, and in that case T has a bounded inverse; (iii) dim ker T = dim ker T* where T* = I - K* is the adjoint on the dual X*, and the equation T x = y is solvable exactly when y annihilates ker T* (the closed-range theorem). So either T x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation T x = 0 has a nontrivial finite-dimensional solution space and T x = y is solvable exactly for y orthogonal (in the duality sense) to the finitely many solutions of the adjoint homogeneous equation. For a Hilbert space and a self-adjoint compact K this is the classical alternative for integral equations of the second kind; the same conclusions hold for lambda I - K with any nonzero lambda.
X a Banach space
K compact and linear
the statement is about I - K; for lambda I - K with lambda not zero divide by lambda

body:
[Ppn 132 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $u,v$ be real numbers such that $v\geq u^2 - \bar{\lambda}$, and let $P_1,P_2>0$.
Set
\beq
    \sigma 
    \equiv
    \bigg(
    \frac{P_1v + 2
    (P_1P_2)^{1/2}
    u+P_2}{P_1+P_2}
    \bigg)^{1/2}
\eeq
Then we have the bound
\beq
  u^2 + \Big((v-u^2 + 2\bar{\lambda})^{1/2}-1\Big)^2 
  \ge \bigg(1+\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)(\sigma-1)^2\,.
\eeq
Given any $\sigma\ge0$, if we let $(u,v)$ be defined by the equations
	\[
	u^2 = \frac{P_2}{P_1}(\sigma-1)^2 
	= v-\sigma^2 + 2\bar{\lambda}\,,
	\]
then $(u,v)$ achieves equality in both \eqref{e:sigma.of.u.v} and \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound}. 

\begin{proof}
Denote $\tilde{v}\equiv v-u^2 + 2\bar{\lambda} \ge0$. The above definition of $\sigma$ can then be rewritten as
	\beq    
	(P_1+P_2)\sigma^2
	= P_1 \tilde{v}  +
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)^2\,.
	\eeq
Consider optimizing the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} subject to the constraint 
\eqref{eq:LM-constraint}: the Lagrangian is
	\[
	\mathscr{L}
	= u^2 + \Big(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1\Big)^2 
	+ \lambda
	\bigg\{
	(P_1+P_2)\sigma^2
	- P_1 \tilde{v}  -
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)^2
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The Lagrangian stationarity conditions are
	\begin{align*}
	0&=\frac{\partial\mathscr{L}}
		{\partial u}
	= 2u - 2\lambda (P_1)^{1/2}
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)\,\\
	0&=\frac{\partial\mathscr{L}}
		{\partial\tilde{v}}
	= 1-\frac{1}{\tilde{v}^{1/2}}
	- \lambda P_1\,.
	\end{align*}
Simplifying the above equations gives
	\[
	u
	= \bigg(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)^{1/2}
	 \frac{\lambda P_1}{1-\lambda P_1}
	=
	\bigg(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)^{1/2}
	(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)
	\,.
	\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:LM-constraint} gives $\sigma^2=\tilde{v}$. Substituting this back into the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} gives
	\[
	u^2 + (\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)^2
	= \bigg(1+ \frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)
	(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)^2
	= \bigg(1+ \frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)
	(\sigma-1)^2\,,
	\]
so \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} holds with equality in the case of an interior stationary point. It remains to check the boundary case $\tilde{v}=0$. In this case we have
	\[
	\sigma
	=\bigg|\bigg( \frac{P_1}{P_1+P_2}\bigg)^{1/2} u
	+\bigg( \frac{P_2}{P_1+P_2}\bigg)^{1/2}\bigg|
	\equiv
	\Big| (A_1)^{1/2} u + (A_2)^{1/2}
	\Big|\,,
	\]
with $A_1+A_2=1$. The desired bound \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} then simplifies to
	\begin{align*}
	u^2 + 1
	&= \bigg(\frac{-(A_2)^{1/2}\pm\sigma}{(A_1)^{1/2}}\bigg)^2+1
	= \frac{A_2 + \sigma^2
		\pm 2 (A_2)^{1/2}\sigma}{A_1}
		+1
	= \frac{1+\sigma^2
		\pm 2 (A_2)^{1/2}\sigma}{A_1}
	\\
	&\ge
	\frac{1 + \sigma^2-2\sigma}{A_1}
	= \bigg(1+\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)(\sigma-1)^2\,,
	\end{align*}
which gives the bound for the boundary case $\tilde{v}=0$. This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In mathematics, the probabilistic method is a nonconstructive method, primarily used in combinatorics and pioneered by Paul Erdős, for proving the existence of a prescribed kind of mathematical object. It works by showing that if one randomly chooses objects from a specified class, the probability that the result is of the prescribed kind is strictly greater than zero. Although the proof uses probability, the final conclusion is determined for certain, without any possible error.
title: Probabilistic method

body: Let G be a finite simple graph with maximum vertex degree Delta(G). Then the edge-chromatic number (chromatic index) chi'(G), the minimum number of colors needed to color the edges of G so that no two edges sharing a vertex receive the same color, satisfies Delta(G) <= chi'(G) <= Delta(G) + 1. [Vizing (1964); see Diestel, Graph Theory]
title: Vizing's Theorem (Edge-Chromatic Number)

For infinite noiseless Gaussian least squares with h_j=j^-alpha, alpha>1, (w*_j)^2=C j^(alpha-1-alpha*s), C>0,s>1, zero initial iterate/velocity, fixed finite B and T>=1, let eta>0 and 0<=beta<1 be constant within the run but arbitrarily horizon-dependent, satisfying d_1>0 and S<1 as in C008. Put tau=zeta(alpha), A_T=min(2T(T+1),2BT/tau), J_T=max(1,ceil((4A_T)^(1/alpha))). Then risk>=4C J_T^(-alpha*s)/(9alpha*s). Consequently risk>=c[1+min(BT,T^2)]^-s uniformly in eta,beta,B,T; for B=D^(b+o(1)), the data exponent is at most s min(1,2(1-b)). For fixed B and 1<s<2-1/alpha, even horizon-retuned stable HB cannot improve the exponent s attained by a fixed-step SGD setting. This is a necessary barrier, not an attainable threshold.
alpha>1,s>1,C>0
fresh independent Gaussian mini-batches, noiseless labels
w_0=w_-1=0
B,T positive integers
eta>0,0<=beta<1 constant during each run
global stability: d_1>0, S<1; horizon-dependent choice allowed

[Lemma lem:stationary-derivative-band-partition-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] There exists an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every \(\xi\neq0\), there exist nonnegative \(C^1\) functions
\[
\chi_{\xi,\mathrm{stat}},
\qquad
\chi_{\xi,d}\quad(d\in\mathfrak D_\xi),
\]
on \(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\), where \(\mathfrak D_\xi\) is a finite set of dyadic numbers, satisfying the following properties.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Partition of unity:
\[
\chi_{\xi,\mathrm{stat}}(t)+\sum_{d\in\mathfrak D_\xi}\chi_{\xi,d}(t)=1
\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}).
\]

\item Number of bands:
\[
\#\mathfrak D_\xi\le C(1+\log_2(2+\Lambda)).
\]

\item Stationary tube:
\[
\operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,\mathrm{stat}}
\subset
\{t:\operatorname{dist}(t,Z_\xi)\le C\Lambda^{-1/2}\}.
\]

\item Localization of derivative bands:
for every \(d\in\mathfrak D_\xi\),
\[
C^{-1}\Lambda^{-1/2}\le d\le C,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,d}
\subset
\{t:C^{-1}d\le\operatorname{dist}(t,Z_\xi)\le Cd\}.
\]

\item Derivative size:
on \(\operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,d}\),
\[
C^{-1}\Lambda d\le \lvert\phi_\xi'(t)\rvert\le C\Lambda d.
\]

\item Cutoff derivative:
\[
\lvert\chi_{\xi,d}'(t)\rvert\le Cd^{-1}.
\]

\item Bounded overlap:
\[
\sum_{d\in\mathfrak D_\xi}\mathbf 1_{\operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,d}}(t)\le C
\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}).
\]
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:penalty of arXiv:2608.28007, 'Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression'] Let $C$ have full row rank, $\mathcal A=\{q:Cq=b\}$, and let $G\ge0$ be a
convex quadratic whose restriction to $\mathcal A$ has a unique minimizer
$q_{\mathcal A}$. Assume the Hessian nullspace of $G$ meets $\ker C$ only at
$0$. Then for every $\lambda>0$ the function
$F_\lambda(q)=G(q)+\lambda\lVert Cq-b\rVert^2$ is strictly convex, and its unique
minimizer $q_\lambda$ converges to $q_{\mathcal A}$ as $\lambda\to\infty$.

[Theorem thm:FFR of arXiv:2609.01557, '$L^\infty$ Variational Approximation of the Aubry Set'] Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold and let \(H:T^*M\to\mathbb R\) be a Tonelli Hamiltonian.  
The Mather quotient has vanishing one-dimensional Hausdorff measure in either of the following cases:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
    \item \(\dim M=1\) or \(2\) and \(H\in C^2\);
    \item \(\dim M=3\) and \(H\in C^{k,1}\) for some \(k\geq3\).
\end{enumerate}
That is,
\[
    \mathcal H^1(\mathcal A_M,\delta_M)=0.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition 4 (Granularity) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] A scale may be shared \emph{per-tensor} (one $s$), \emph{per-row} (one $s$ per output row of $W$, the \emph{per-output-channel} weight scale, which the weight-only literature usually just calls \emph{per-channel}, or one $s$ per token row of $X$, the \emph{per-token} activation scale that is the deployed default), \emph{per-column} (one $s$ per input channel, the axis a \emph{per-channel activation} scale shares), or \emph{per-group/block} (contiguous groups of $G$ entries, e.g.\ $G\in\{32,128\}$). Finer granularity lowers distortion at the cost of storing more scales; in the limit a full-precision scale per element would be no compression at all, so a scale must be amortized over a group, which is what makes a single outlier in that group unavoidable. The group size $G$ is the single most important deployment knob and reappears in the block-scaled hardware formats of \Cref{sec:live}.
title: Granularity

[Corollary 32 (Diameter and circle convergence on a persistent large-diameter tail) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be \(\TT^3\), a compact \(\Nil\) torus bundle with nontrivial
unipotent monodromy, or a compact \(\Sol\) torus bundle with hyperbolic
monodromy, and let \(g(t)\), \(t\geq0\), be an immortal Ricci flow on \(M\).
Fix a particular application of
Proposition~\ref{input:bamler-fixed-threshold}, with cutoff \(c_0\) and tail
data \(T_B(c_0),\eps_B^{c_0}\), and suppose that
\[
        \diam(M,g(t))\geq c_0\sqrt t
\]
for every sufficiently large \(t\).  Then there are constants
\(C<\infty\) and \(\ell_\infty>0\) such that
\[
        \diam(M,g(t))\leq C\sqrt t
\]
for all sufficiently large \(t\), and
\begin{equation}
        (M,t^{-1}g(t))\longrightarrow C_{\ell_\infty}
\end{equation}
in the Gromov--Hausdorff sense, where \(C_{\ell_\infty}\) is the metric
circle of length \(\ell_\infty\).

the observable is T_n, the minimal passage time between two opposite sides of an n by n square - a minimum over crossings, not a point-to-point passage time
a curvature assumption on the limit shape (unproven in first-passage percolation)
the edge weights t_e are exponentially distributed
d = 2

WHY A SEPARATE ARGUMENT WAS NEEDED, in the authors' words: 'previous arguments to bound the fluctuations of T(x,y) only give a constant lower bound for those of T_n (even assuming curvature)', so they represent T_n as a minimum of cylinder passage times and use the Markov property to get finer distributional information. The minimum-over-crossings structure is the whole difficulty and the whole difference.
COROLLARY they state: the first polynomial lower bounds on higher central moments of the discrete torus passage time, under the same curvature assumption.
THE MISQUOTE THIS NODE EXISTS TO BLOCK: 'polynomial variance lower bounds are known in FPP'. They are known for this observable, under an unproven curvature assumption, for one weight law (extended by Dembin-Elboim to absolutely continuous laws). Nothing polynomial is known unconditionally for Var T(0,x).
SOURCE: arXiv:2204.06592v1, 'Fluctuation bounds for first-passage percolation on the square, tube, and torus'. Official arXiv API record retrieved by lane P4 on 2026-08-22.
VERIFICATION STATUS: theorem-checked-against-source. The abstract states the observable, the curvature hypothesis, the weight law and the exponent; the proof was not read.
title: Damron-Houdre-Ozdemir (2022): a POLYNOMIAL fluctuation lower bound does exist in planar first-passage percolation, but for a different observable - T_n, the minimal passage time between two opposite sides of an n by n square - under a curvature assumption and for exponentially distributed weights, where the fluctuations of T_n are at least of order n^{1/8-epsilon} for every epsilon > 0. This is NOT a bound on the point-to-point passage time T(0,x), where the best lower bound is still logarithmic.

Let (X_i), i in S, be a finite family with E|prod over A of X_i| finite for every nonempty A, and let the joint cumulants kappa_A be defined by m_A = E[prod over A of X_i] = sum over partitions pi of A of prod over blocks of kappa_B. If S is the disjoint union of nonempty A and C and the vectors (X_i, i in A) and (X_j, j in C) are independent, then kappa_S = 0. Pairwise independence of all the variables does not suffice: for X_1, X_2 independent uniform signs and X_3 = X_1 X_2, the three are pairwise independent but kappa(X_1, X_2, X_3) = 1.

body: CORRECTION to the bounded-density quadratic-form conjecture (2026-09-22 evening): the general (non-separable) universal constant is NOT pi; it is > pi, at least 3*sqrt(2) ~ 4.243. pi is sharp only for the SEPARABLE case. RANK-3 COAREA LEMMA (the real 'why 3'): if (Y1,Y2,Y3) has joint density rho and |lambda_i|>=1 (any signs), then S=sum lambda_i Y_i^2 has density <= C0 ||rho||_inf (C0=pi isotropic). Proof: a rank-3 indefinite form's zero-set is a 2-D cone; resolving Y3, signature (2,1) gives integral u^{-1/2}du (convergent) where a rank-2 indefinite form gives integral u^{-1}=log (unbounded) - the 2-D cone's area element cancels the vertex gradient blowup. General C>pi because a 3-D projection of a high-dim product concentrates (||rho_3D||>1); for (1,1,-1) with uniform min-variance inputs sigma^2=1/12 the Gaussian limit gives p_Q(0)=1/(2 sqrt2 sigma^2)=3 sqrt2, confirmed numerically (rotated (1,1,-1) peak 2.97 at n=3 -> 4.16 at n=40). ROUTE to the general theorem: condition on the other n-3 directions, apply the rank-3 coarea lemma, Fubini => ||p_Q||<=C0*M with M a bound on the conditional 3-D projection density; proving M uniform (Rudelson-Vershynin type) closes it. Supersedes the earlier claim 'general constant is pi'.

[Thm 6 of arXiv:2604.26316, 'Smallest distances between zeros of Gaussian analytic functions'] Given $(z_1,..., z_k) \in M^k\backslash \Delta^{(k)}$ and a partition $\mathcal P=\{I_1,.., I_\ell\}$ of $\{1,..., k\}$ such that the minimal distance $\eta$ between different clusters is at least $\log^2n/\sqrt{n}$, then   the correlation function exhibits the following splitting property,
		\beq
		\rho_k(z_1,.., z_k)=\prod_{I_i \in \mathcal{P}} \rho_{|I_i|}\left(\underline{z}_{I_i}\right)+O\big(n^{-\infty}\big),
		\eeq  
		
		
		
		
		where $n^{-\infty}$ is an error term that decays faster than $n^{-c}$ for any $c>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2608.20613, 'Random walks on wreath products \\and spectral gaps for coloured interchange processes'] Let $\Lambda=(\lambda^\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ be a $G$-multipartition of $n$.  Then the multiplicity of $V_\Lambda$ in $\mathcal P_n(G)$ is $\prod_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\dim\Schur_{\lambda^\gamma}(\C^{d_\gamma})$.  Consequently,
\[
\mathcal P_n(G)
\cong
\bigoplus_{\substack{\Lambda=(\lambda^\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\
\sum_\gamma\abs{\lambda^\gamma}=n\,,\ 
\len(\lambda^\gamma)\leqslant d_\gamma\text{ for every }\gamma}}
\left(
\prod_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\dim\Schur_{\lambda^\gamma}(\C^{d_\gamma})
\right)V_\Lambda .
\]
title: Theorem 11 of arXiv:2608.20613

[Proposition 44 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\alpha \in (\frac{1}{2},1)$, $\delta>0, y \in \T^d$, and $V^{\delta,y}(t,z)$ defined by~\eqref{eq:V delta def}. If for some $K >0$ and all $j \in \N, n \in \{0,1,2\}$, we have the almost sure bound
\[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{\mathcal{C}^0_{x}} \leq K 2^{(n-\alpha)j},\]
    then almost surely there exists a unique solution to~\eqref{eq:V delta ODE} for all $a$, thus~\eqref{eq:V delta flow} almost surely has a unique solution. Further, the unique solution $\Psi^{\delta,y}$ to~\eqref{eq:V delta flow} is almost surely spatially Lipschitz uniformly in $s$ and $t$. That is,
    \[\P\Big(\sup_{s,t\in[0,1]} \|\nabla \Psi^{\delta,y}_{s,t}\|_{\mathcal{C}^0_a} < \infty\Big) = 1.\]

[Proposition 22 (Reducedness and the prefix-signature lift) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space and let $\eta:[0,T]\to E$ be a continuous bounded-variation path. Put
\[
q(t)=\Var(\eta;[0,t]),
\qquad L=q(T),
\]
and let $\bar\eta:[0,L]\to E$ be the variation parametrisation, so that
\[
\eta_t=\bar\eta_{q(t)},
\qquad
\Var(\bar\eta;[u_1,u_2])=u_2-u_1.
\]
When $L=0$, $\bar\eta$ is understood to be constant. Set
\[
r_t=S(\eta|_{[0,t]}),
\qquad 0\leq t\leq T.
\]
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item $\bar\eta$ is the Hambly--Lyons reduced representative of the tree-like equivalence class of $\eta$;
\item every restriction $\eta|_{[s,t]}$ with trivial signature is constant;
\item if $r_s=r_t$ for $0\leq s<t\leq T$, then $\eta|_{[s,t]}$ is constant; equivalently, the prefix-signature lift is injective after constant waiting intervals are collapsed.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, every restriction of a path satisfying these conditions again satisfies them.

[Thm Thm_strongly_convex of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] Let $I\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a nondegenerate interval, $\mu\in\mathbb{R}_+$, and $L: I\to\mathbb{R}$ be a strongly convex function with modulus $\mu$.
Then, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in I$, we have that
 \begin{align*}
  L\left( \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n x_k \right)
     \leqslant \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n L(x_k)
          - \frac{\mu}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n \left(x_k - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n x_j \right)^2.
 \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

CURRENT AUDIT STATUS: independently checked proof, T336-w727-C004 v1; claude-5693aca3 PASS in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. Exact proof SHA256 ac56184efa730025dd3c81b11d4fced2712fb1d3290a9bc2a089ca9a9af705a5. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed. The following original submission text retains historical pre-audit status notices.

For raw inputs in [0,1]^d, every bounded rank-at-most-p GP with coordinatewise K-Lipschitz feature map has an explicit residual ReLU-attention transformer attaining uniform noisy predictive forward KL <= eps over contexts of length <=n and labels bounded by B. Unlike C002, feature computation is counted. The constants, grid size, width, heads, hidden width, and depth are explicit in C004 Sections 1-5. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C004 v1. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 with raw inputs and an explicit Lipschitz feature encoder

Claim T336-w727-C004 v1. Rung: proof (unaudited), subject to recorded checks and dependent on unaudited C002 v1. No Lean certification or independent audit is claimed. This gives a quantitative raw-input subclass of Target 1, rather than assuming exact feature computation outside the size count.

The hardest steps are the explicit residual-MLP encoder and the perturbation budget linking its feature errors to the original GP predictive distribution. The proof does not use a triangle inequality for KL.

## 1. Assumptions and explicit size

Fix integers d,p>=1,n>=0, real s>0, B>=0,R>=0,K>=0,eps>0. The raw domain is X=[0,1]^d. The fixed zero-mean GP prior has kernel k(x,x')=z(x)^T z(x'), where z:X->R^p satisfies ||z(x)||_2<=R and, for each coordinate j,

    |z_j(x)-z_j(x')|<=K ||x-x'||_1.

The observation noise is independent N(0,s). Context labels satisfy |y_i|<=B, and contexts have length t<=n. The target is the predictive law of a new noisy observation. The input encoding supplies only raw coordinates, labels, two binary role flags (context and query), and fixed constants. Zero padding fixes N=n+1 tokens. A padding token has raw coordinates zero and both flags zero; the query has only its query flag set; actual context tokens have only their context flag set. No label is supplied for the query.

Define the following fixed constants:

    S=R+1,
    C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s + S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s > 0,
    eta=min(1, sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)), s sqrt(eps)/(2 C_v), s/(4 C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16),
    m=max(1,ceil(K d sqrt(p)/eta)), J=(m+1)^d, E=3+ceil(log_2 J).

For the solver set

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a residual normalized ReLU-attention transformer (Bai et al. Definition 1 and Definition 2) with

    token width D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    depth L_total=E+T+2=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    tokenwise MLP hidden width at most H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,

whose Gaussian output satisfies forward KL<=eps uniformly over all these raw-input contexts and queries. A dense parameter upper bound is

    L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D.

Fixed affine input placement is not counted; all nonlinear feature computation is counted. Every weight is specified below or in C002 v1 and depends only on the fixed prior feature map (through finitely many grid samples) and the displayed bounds, never on observed contexts, query labels, or future data. This is a real-weight size theorem, not a finite-bit complexity theorem or training guarantee.

## 2. Posterior perturbation caused by an approximate feature map

First suppose a map ztilde satisfies sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=eta<=1. Then ||ztilde||<=R+eta<=S. For any fixed admissible context and query, put

    A=sI+sum_i z_i z_i^T, b=sum_i z_i y_i, q=z(x_*),
    Atilde=sI+sum_i ztilde_i ztilde_i^T, btilde=sum_i ztilde_i y_i, qtilde=ztilde(x_*).

Both matrices are symmetric positive definite with inverse operator norm <=1/s. For vectors u,v,

    ||uu^T-vv^T||_op
      =||(u-v)u^T+v(u-v)^T||_op
      <=||u-v|| (||u||+||v||).

Thus

    ||A-Atilde||<=n(2R+eta)eta<=C_A eta,
    ||b-btilde||<=nB eta, ||b||<=nRB,
    ||A^{-1}-Atilde^{-1}||
      =||A^{-1}(Atilde-A)Atilde^{-1}||<=C_A eta/s^2.

The true and perturbed noisy predictive parameters are

    mu=q^T A^{-1}b, v=s+s q^T A^{-1}q,
    mutilde=qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}btilde,
    vtilde=s+s qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}qtilde.

Both variances are >=s. Add and subtract qtilde^T A^{-1}b and qtilde^T Atilde^{-1}b. Cauchy-Schwarz and the preceding bounds give

    |mu-mutilde|
      <=eta nRB/s + S C_A eta nRB/s^2 + S nB eta/s
      =C_m eta.

For the variance, first replace both q factors while retaining A^{-1}, and then replace the inverse. This gives

    |v-vtilde|
      <=s[eta(R+S)/s+S^2 C_A eta/s^2]=C_v eta.

The definition of eta ensures

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

No probabilistic context distribution or independence between observed features is needed here.

## 3. A finite-grid cone encoder

Let G={0,1/m,...,1}^d, so |G|=J. For each feature coordinate define

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[z_j(a)+K sum_{r=1}^d |x_r-a_r|].

The Lipschitz assumption shows every term in this minimum is >=z_j(x). Choose a nearest grid point coordinate by coordinate; its L1 distance is <=d/(2m). The same Lipschitz bound then gives

    0<=ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)<=Kd/m.

Consequently ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)Kd/m<=eta. This also holds for K=0, when the error is zero and m=1. In particular |ztilde_j(x)|<=||ztilde(x)||<=S on the whole input cube.

The encoder is exact as an implementation of this finite minimum, including all absolute values. It is not a numerical approximation to the finite minimum.

## 4. Exact tokenwise residual-MLP construction

Use the 7p+4 core registers of C002. Add d registers for raw x, Jd zero-initialized absolute-value registers, pJ zero-initialized cone registers, and two role flags. This is D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ. Initially the feature registers z_c,z_q are zero. The core constant is one=1; the variance-output register starts at s, and the query/padding label register is zero. Encoder MLP layers preserve raw x, the flags, and all core constants.

Each MLP has the residual form h^+=h+W2 ReLU(W1 h), with a constant register implementing affine biases. All unspecified matrix entries are zero. The attention block in each encoder layer is the identity (all value matrices zero).

Layer 1 uses 2Jd hidden units for ReLU(x_r-a_r) and ReLU(a_r-x_r), for all a in G,r. Their sums are written into the initially zero absolute-value registers, yielding |x_r-a_r| exactly.

Layer 2 uses Jd identity-ReLU units on the nonnegative absolute registers and one unit on the constant one. Its output matrix writes

    F_{j,a}=z_j(a)+K sum_r |x_r-a_r|

into each initially zero cone register. Negative fixed grid values cause no difficulty: they occur in the output matrix applied to the constant unit.

Next compute the minimum independently for each coordinate j by a balanced binary tournament on the J cone registers. A pair of current registers u,v is replaced in the first slot by

    u-ReLU(u-v)=min(u,v),

leaving the other slot unused thereafter. This is one residual MLP unit: W1 reads u-v and W2 subtracts its ReLU from the u register. Distinct pairs at the same level use disjoint output slots. An unpaired register passes unchanged. After ceil(log_2 J) levels one designated cone slot contains ztilde_j(x). Each level uses at most p floor(J/2) units, bounded by pJ. This works for signed cone values and for every J, not only powers of two.

One final gating layer writes the feature registers. For any |f|<=S and binary flag r define

    g(f,r)=ReLU(f+S(r-1))-ReLU(-f+S(r-1)).

If r=1, this equals f; if r=0, both arguments are <=0 and it equals zero. Apply g to every computed feature with the context flag to populate z_c, and with the query flag to populate z_q. The registers start at zero, so the residual connection adds precisely the desired values. This uses 4p units. Query, padding, and context feature routing now matches C002 exactly. Both flags and the raw x registers are preserved throughout.

There are E=3+ceil(log_2 J) MLP encoder layers. The stated H bounds every hidden width. Biases are realized through the constant register, rather than being omitted from the construction. All grid feature values are fixed weights of the known prior; no context-dependent parameter is selected.

## 5. Solver composition and KL budget

Apply C002 v1 to ztilde with feature bound S and accuracy eps0. Its core 7p+4 registers embed in the larger width D; all additional registers are preserved by zero extension of its matrices. The solver uses its one-head broadcast layer, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout layer. All solver MLPs are identities. The resulting parameters muhat,vhat obey

    vhat>=s,
    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps0)<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |vtilde-vhat|<=s sqrt(eps0)<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Combine these with Section 2 using ordinary triangle inequalities for scalar errors, not for KL:

    |mu-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps),
    |v-vhat|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps)).

Since v,vhat>=s, put h=(v-vhat)/vhat in [-1/2,1/2]. As proved directly in C002 Section 5,

    KL(N(mu,v)||N(muhat,vhat))
      <=(mu-muhat)^2/(2s)+(v-vhat)^2/(2s^2)<=eps.

The depth is E+T+2. There are at most five heads, each with three D-by-D matrices. Counting two D-by-H/H-by-D MLP matrices at every layer, even when they are zero, and a two-coordinate linear readout, gives the stated dense parameter bound.

## 6. What this does and does not settle

This is a quantitative raw-input theorem for every bounded finite-rank GP feature map satisfying the displayed Lipschitz assumption, in every fixed input dimension. It counts the encoder rather than treating it as a free feature oracle. The bound is deliberately explicit and can be very large because J=(m+1)^d.

C003 shows that dropping all raw-feature regularity makes the literal bounded-kernel statement false for continuous Gaussian-output transformers. C004 therefore supplies a precise constructive assumption, while C002 remains the smaller theorem when features are supplied directly.

The finite-grid envelope and ReLU min/max identities are classical elementary constructions, not claims of new approximation theory. The claimed target contribution is their fully costed composition with the accelerated posterior solver and a uniform original-posterior forward-KL budget. C004 remains a proof candidate dependent on C002 until independent review passes both exact versions.
