[Lemma CVtV of arXiv:2504.00512, 'Localization-delocalization transition for a random block matrix model at the edge'] Under the assumptions of Theorem (MixEV of the paper), there exists a constant $\mathfrak c>0$ depending on ${\varepsilon}_A$ and $\delta_A$ such that the following holds for ${\mathfrak t}= N^{-1/3+\mathfrak c}$.  
For any fixed $n\in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a constant $c_n=c_n(\mathfrak c,\delta_A,{\varepsilon}_A)$ such that

\begin{align}
&\left|	\mathbb{E} O\pa{ \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\pa{E^+-\lambda_1^{{\mathfrak t}}},\ldots, \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\pa{E^+-\lambda_n^{{\mathfrak t}}}}\right.\nonumber\\
&\left.-\mathbb{E} O\pa{ \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\left({E^+-\lambda_1}\right),\ldots, \left({DN}\right)^{2/3}\left({E^+-\lambda_n}\right)}   \right|\le N^{-c_n}.
\end{align}
The corresponding result also holds at the left edge $E^-$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition 3.3 (Hypergraph) of arXiv:2505.15746, 'Higher-order Structure Boosts Link Prediction on Temporal Graphs'] A hypergraph can be represented by a tuple (V, H). V = {n1, n2, ...} is the set of nodes. And the set of hyperedges is H = {Ei |Ei ⊆V; 1 ≤ i ≤m}, where Ei is hyperedge and m is the number of hyperedges. Furthermore, in homogeneous graphs, the construction of hyperedges usually relies on the enumeration of maximal cliques (Wang & Kleinberg, 2024).

Use the likelihood-tempered q_lambda and total-data objective J(rho)=-E_rho log p(D|theta) defined above. Let k_s(theta)=p(y|x,theta), m_lambda(s)=E_q_lambda k_s>0 for nu-almost every s, and define the one-sample update qtilde_lambda,s(dtheta)=k_s(theta)q_lambda(dtheta)/m_lambda(s), then qbar_lambda=E_s~nu qtilde_lambda,s. The new likelihood factor is untempered, and each updated posterior is normalized before averaging. Assume the covariance differentiation identity applies to each k_s, B(q_lambda)=E_nu[-log m_lambda] is finite, differentiation through nu is justified by a nu-integrable local envelope for |d log m_lambda/dlambda|, and E_nu E_qtilde_lambda,s |L|<infinity. Then Bprime(lambda)=J(qbar_lambda)-J(q_lambda)=n[Ghat(qbar_lambda,D)-Ghat(q_lambda,D)]. At lambda=1, Bprime(1)=0 iff the two empirical Gibbs losses agree; this is a stationarity criterion, not a minimization theorem. Under the covariance regularity also for f=-L, local CPE Bprime(1)<0 implies that, for every sufficiently small h>0, q_(1+h) has strictly smaller Bayes loss and empirical Gibbs loss than q_1, so q_1 underfits in the authors simultaneous-loss sense. If the finite minimum a=min_theta[-L(theta)] exists, local CPE also forces J(q_1)>a, or Ghat(q_1,D)>a/n.

[Thm 2 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{assump:decay} holds for $W$. Suppose that $\sqrt{N} x_k$  $(1 \leq k \leq N)$ are i.i.d., symmetric, and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables with variance $1$, independent of $W$. Define the likelihood ratios by
\beq
	 \caL(\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2  /\| \bsx \|^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right]
\eeq
and
\beq
	\ol \caL (\SNR) := \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right].
\eeq
Define
\[
	F_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p'(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x, \quad F_d:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p_d'(x))^2}{p_d(x)} \dd x, \quad G_p:= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(p''(x))^2}{p(x)} \dd x.
\]
Then, for any $\SNR \in (0, 1/F_p)$,
\[
	\log \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L), \quad \log \ol \caL(\SNR) \Rightarrow \caN(-\rho_L, 2\rho_L),
\]
as $N \to \infty$, i.e., $\log \caL(\SNR)$ and $\log \ol\caL(\SNR)$ converge in distribution to the Gaussian with mean $-\rho_L$ and the variance $2\rho_L$ as $N \to \infty$, where
\[
	\rho_L:= -\frac{1}{4} \left( \log (1-\SNR F_p) + \SNR(F_p- 2F_d) + \frac{\SNR^2}{4} (2F_p^2 - G_p) \right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 2 of arXiv:2605.07050

body: [Theorem 12 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] Let $\mu$ be a non-atomic measure on $[0,t]\times[\delta,1]$, finite on bounded sets. Suppose that the simple point process $\mathcal{N}$ is such that for any set $\Delta$ which is a finite union of rectangles (32) $P(\mathcal{N}(\Delta)=0)=\exp\{-\mu(\Delta)\}.$ Then $\mathcal{N}$ is a Poisson process with intensity measure $\mu$.

	Set ${\mathbf{b}}=(\PFtrees{{\mathbf{w}}}{n})_{n\geq 1}$.
	Then $({\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{b}})$ is a non-degenerate weight pair.
	For $n\geq 1$ we have $\PFtrees{\mathbf{w}} n=\PFComp{{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{b}}}{n-1}$, and for $T\in\trees_n$ if we write $c(T)=\underline{n}_1 \cdots  \underline{n}_i$ and $\varphi(T)=(T^{[1]},\dots,T^{[i]})$, then
	\begin{align}
	\SimpGen{{\mathbf{w}}}{n}(T)=\PComp{{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{b}}}{n-1}\bigl(c(T)\bigr)\cdot\left(\SimpGen{{\mathbf{w}}}{n_1}\bigl(T^{[1]}\bigr)\cdots \SimpGen{{\mathbf{w}}}{n_i}\bigl(T^{[i]}\bigr)\right).

body: Publication record. P. Thévenin (Electron. J. Probab. 25, 2020, Section 6.2) proved a central limit theorem for the numbers of vertices of fixed outdegree in a subcritical Galton-Watson tree conditioned to have n vertices when the offspring law has a power-law tail, and conjectured that it extends to every subcritical law without exponential moment and every critical law with infinite variance. Y. Shmalo, Non-Gaussian fluctuations of degree counts in conditioned Galton-Watson trees (2026) gives two offspring laws for which the extension fails, an explicit subcritical law with finite third moment and no exponential moment and a critical law with infinite variance: along a sequence of sizes the centred and normalised number of vertices of outdegree one has a non-Gaussian limit, a mixture of two Gaussian laws. The second version (13 October 2026) adds, for Problems 21.2-21.4 of S. Janson, Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation (Probab. Surveys 9, 2012), a joint central limit theorem for the box counts of balls-in-boxes models below the critical density, and at the critical density under a second moment condition when the number of balls exceeds its critical value by at most O(sqrt(n)), and the two-Gaussian mixture for every fringe count with 0 < pi_A < 1, the leaves included. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/non-gaussian-degree-counts (commit 16f5fcef7b00); ResearchGate record 414333267. Not refereed; an outside audit is owed.
title: Thevenin's conjecture (EJP 2020, Section 6.2) refuted, Janson Problems 21.2-21.4 answered in part: non-Gaussian fluctuations of degree counts in conditioned Galton-Watson trees (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/non-gaussian-degree-counts)

[Lem 174 (eighth moment bounds for $X^{\Ising}$, $X^{\trunc,\Ising}$, and $X^{\frozen,\Ising}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The bound of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}
also holds with $X^{\Ising}$ in place of $X^{\RomII}$: for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[\bigg(
	\sum_{\ell=a}^{b-1} 
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_d,
	{i(q_{d+1})})
	\bigg)^8\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4
	\]
for all $0\le a\le b\le \dmax$. The same bound holds with 
$X^{\trunc,\Ising}$ or $X^{\Isplus}$ in place of $X^\Ising$. 

\begin{proof}
Recall from \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising} that
	\[
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_d,i(q_{d+1}))
	= \sqrt{\delta_d}
	({\boldsymbol e}_i,\by(q_{d+1}))
	\]
where ${\boldsymbol e}_i$ is the $i$-th standard basis vector in $\R^N$.
The claim then follows essentially by the argument of Lemma~\ref{l:subgaus.X.II}, replacing $\bar{\bg}(q_d)/N^{1/2}$ with
${\boldsymbol e}_i$. (Moreover, since clearly $\|{\boldsymbol e}_i\|=1$, we can skip the step of restricting to the event that
$\|\bar{\bg}(q_d)\|$ is not atypically large.) It is straightforward to verify that the same argument applies with $X^{\trunc,\Ising}$ or $X^{\Isplus}$ in place of $X^\Ising$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let N be a positive integer, R a commutative ring, f: D(N) -> R and F(n) = sum_{d | n} f(d) for n | N. Then f(n) = sum_{d | n} mu(n/d) F(d) for every n | N, where mu is the arithmetic Moebius function: mu(1) = 1, mu(m) = 0 if p^2 divides m for some prime p, and mu(m) = (-1)^omega(m) for squarefree m, omega(m) the number of distinct prime divisors. Equivalently, with P(n) the set of prime divisors of n, f(n) = sum over S subset of P(n) of (-1)^{|S|} F(n / prod_{p in S} p) (empty product 1).

For rho in [-1, 1], T_rho is the noise operator: T_rho f(x) = E[f(Y)] where the Y_i are independent with P(Y_i = x_i) = (1 + rho)/2, so T_rho chi_S = rho^|S| chi_S. For convex Phi on an interval containing the values of f, Phi(T_rho f(x)) <= T_rho(Phi o f)(x) for every x, and hence E[Phi(T_rho f(X))] <= E[Phi(f(X))] for uniform X. Attributed primary-source theorem, not independently audited here. Let pi_t be the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck evolution of a law pi_0 on R^d with E_pi_0||X||^2<=M_2^2<infinity. Let e be in (0,1], and suppose supplied score estimates s_t have E_pi_t||s_t-grad log pi_t||^2<=e^2 at all relevant times up to T. Require global spatial Lipschitz control of the relative estimated score tilde_s_t(x)=s_t(x)+x: ||tilde_s_t(x)-tilde_s_t(y)||<=beta_tilde_0||x-y||/(1-exp(-2t)) for positive times. With T asymptotic to max{1,log((d+M_2^2)/e^2)}, the analysed denoising diffusion randomized midpoint method with its decaying schedule has output hat_pi and an intermediate pi_approx satisfying KL(pi_approx||hat_pi)<=O_tilde((1+log^2((1 vee beta_tilde_0)(d+M_2^2)))e^2) and W2^2(pi_approx,pi_0)<=O(e^2), using N=Theta_tilde(beta_tilde_0 sqrt(d+M_2^2)/e) steps. The theoretical variant samples each midpoint time tau_k on [0,rho_k h_k] with density proportional to exp(tau_k-h_k), with source-prescribed rho_k<1 sufficiently near 1. The bounds retain the source universal constants and logarithmic factors. The guarantee is hybrid KL/Wasserstein and assumes smooth supplied relative-score estimators; it is not a generic L2-oracle TV bound to unsmoothed data.

body: Let f(n) be a space-constructible function, computable in O(f(n)) space in a way that marks off exactly f(n) cells on inputs of length n, with f(n) >= log n. If g(n) = o(f(n)), then there is a language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using O(f(n)) space that is not decidable by any deterministic Turing machine using O(g(n)) space; equivalently DSPACE(g(n)) is strictly contained in DSPACE(f(n)) whenever the bounds are sufficiently far apart. Thus more memory strictly increases computational power for space-bounded computation. A corresponding nondeterministic space hierarchy theorem also holds.
title: Space hierarchy theorem

$G=(G_{ab})_{1\le a,b\le d}$ be positive semidefinite, and let $q\ge1$.
There are kernels $u_{N,a}\in H^{\odot q}$ such that

 q!\ip{u_{N,a}}{u_{N,b}}&=G_{ab},
 \\
 \norm{u_{N,a}\otimes_ru_{N,b}}&=O(N^{-1/2})
 \qquad(1\le r<q).
 
\end{align}
Consequently $(I_q(u_{N,a}))_{a\le d}\weak N_d(0,G)$.

body:
# Co-scaled noise phases: double descent versus preference for late stopping

T267 / Target 2 / C011 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is an asymptotic phase comparison in C010's restricted model, not
an exact finite-scale two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Model and statement

Keep the four-point design, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher, paired
nonzero initialization and both-layer GD of BOUNDED_RELU_PAIRED.md.
Write alpha=alpha_e and replace label noise +/-2alpha by
+/-2alpha sqrt(rho), for any fixed rho>0. Thus the noise standard deviation
is c_e sqrt(rho), which tends to zero. Each Walsh noise variance is
rho alpha^2. Average clean risk over the sixteen noise patterns as before.
All width limits are over even widths m=2N, before e decreases to zero.

Let b_h be the full-kernel rates of C009, q_h=exp(-b_h), and define

K_e=ceil(e^(-3/2)), T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2)),
E(rho)=rho+2+rho/(1+rho),
L(rho)=2rho+2rho/(1+rho).

For small e, K_e<T_e. The following minima of the ACTUAL nonlinear risk
converge in probability in the iterated width-then-scale sense:

min_(0<=k<=K_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,E(rho)},
min_(K_e<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> L(rho),
min_(0<=k<=T_e) Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2 -> min{3,L(rho)}.

Here convergence means for every epsilon>0, lim_(e->0) limsup_(N->infinity)
P(absolute discrepancy>epsilon)=0. These statements do not control actual
nonlinear risk after T_e or exchange the two limits.

Moreover there are strict descent-rise-descent witnesses at every fixed
rho>0. With k0=ceil(e^(-1/2)),
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), k2=K_e,
k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), their risks divided by alpha^2 converge to

rho+3, E(rho), 2rho+2, L(rho).

Their three limiting strict margins are
1/(1+rho), rho^2/(1+rho), 2/(1+rho).
For all fixed rho<1, the best risk in the late phase is strictly lower
than the best in the early phase with probability tending to one.
For all fixed rho>1, the early phase is strictly better. At rho=1 the
leading phase minima tie at 3; no finite-e ordering is asserted.

Thus rho=1 is the limiting late-versus-early preference boundary in this
model, whereas strict double descent survives on both sides. No lower
critical-noise rate or exact finite-e second threshold is established.

## 2. Exact frozen risk and nonlinear transfer

The frozen zero-output curve is

F_e(k)=Q_e^0(k)/alpha^2
      =rho(1-q0^k)^2
       +sum_(h=1,2,12)[q_h^(2k)+rho(1-q_h^k)^2].

This follows from Walsh Parseval, identical teacher coefficients alpha
and Walsh noise variances rho alpha^2. The paired initialization gives
zero output exactly. Let p_r(q)=q^2+rho(1-q)^2. Completing the square,

p_r(q)=(1+rho)(q-rho/(1+rho))^2+rho/(1+rho).

For each fixed e and rho the labels are bounded; indeed max|y_i| is at
most (3+2sqrt(rho))alpha, which tends to zero. For all sufficiently small
e the residual bound R_0=2 used in C010 is therefore valid. Its pairwise
finite-horizon transfer applies uniformly through T_e (a finite integer
for this fixed e), and over all noise patterns. It follows that

max_(k<=T_e)|Q_(m,e)(k)/alpha^2-F_e(k)| ->0 in probability as N->infinity.

For this step alpha^2 is a FIXED positive number; no uniform-in-e width
bound is inferred. Consequently it suffices to prove the deterministic
frozen limits for the two ranges and the four witnesses.

## 3. Early-phase minimum

At k=0, F_e=3 exactly. At
k1=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b1), the constant mode has learned, q1^k1 tends to
rho/(1+rho), and q2^k1,q12^k1 tend to one. Hence F_e(k1)->E(rho).
These give the upper bound min{3,E(rho)} for the limiting early minimum.

For the lower bound, take any sequence e->0 and early-phase integers
k_e<=K_e. Choose a subsequence such that k_e is bounded or tends to
infinity, and such that b1 k_e converges in [0,infinity].
If k_e is bounded, all nonconstant q_h^k_e tend to one, so liminf F_e>=3.
If k_e tends to infinity, q0^k_e tends to zero. Uniformly for k<=K_e,
b2 k and b12 k tend to zero, since b2 K_e=O(e^(1/2)). Thus the slow-mode
contribution tends to two, while the fast-mode contribution is at least
rho/(1+rho) by the exact completed square. The limit inferior is at least
E(rho), whether the fast scaled time is finite or infinite. This proves
the matching early lower bound. The subsequence argument applies to
minimizers, which exist because the integer range is finite.

## 4. Late-phase minimum

Uniformly for k>=K_e, q0^k and q1^k tend to zero, since b1 K_e tends to
infinity. Their combined risk tends to 2rho, uniformly in this range.
Each of the two slow contributions is bounded below by rho/(1+rho),
so the late minimum has limit inferior at least L(rho).
For k3=floor(log(1+1/rho)/b2), both slow q's tend to rho/(1+rho), because
b12/b2->1. Also K_e<k3<T_e for all small e, since b2 K_e->0 and
b2 T_e->infinity. Thus F_e(k3)->L(rho), proving the matching upper bound.
Combining Sections 3-4 gives the full finite-horizon minimum as
min{3,E(rho),L(rho)}. The simplification in Section 6 proves the stated
min{3,L(rho)} form.

## 5. Strict double-descent witnesses

At k0 all nonconstant modes remain at one and the constant noise mode
has saturated, so F_e(k0)->rho+3. At k1 the limit is E(rho).
At K_e fast q1 tends to zero and the slow q's to one, giving 2rho+2.
At k3 the limit is L(rho). Subtraction gives exactly the three positive
margins in Section 1. This applies to every fixed rho>0, including rho>1.
The strict finite-e margins transfer to nonlinear GD by Section 2.

For rho=0 the frozen curve is sum_(h=1,2,12)q_h^(2k), strictly decreasing.
This zero-noise frozen statement does not imply monotonic actual nonlinear
risk for all times, nor locate a finite-e onset as rho_e tends to zero.
Pointwise positive-rho results must not be promoted to such a uniform
noise-window theorem.

## 6. Which phase wins?

Exact subtraction yields

E(rho)-L(rho)=(2-rho^2)/(1+rho),
L(rho)-3=(rho-1)(2rho+3)/(1+rho).

If 0<rho<1, then L<3 and L<E, so late training beats the entire early
phase, not just its fast-mode stationary point. If rho>1, then L>3,
so the early phase containing k=0 beats the late phase. Also E>3 for
rho>1, since E-3=(rho^2+rho-1)/(1+rho)>0. Consequently the overall
minimum is min{3,L}. At rho=1 the leading early and late values both
are 3, so a finer expansion is needed to decide finite-scale ordering.

Comparing ONLY E and L would instead produce sqrt(2). That would be the
wrong early-stopping boundary because it omits the allowed initialization
time k=0. This is why the early-phase minimization includes every time
from zero rather than only the first fast-signal minimum. The tiny initial
transient may shift the finite-e preference threshold; it does not change
these strict comparisons for rho bounded away from one.

## Scope and source distinction

Stephenson--Lee, arXiv:2108.12006, Section4, EDD-NES/EDD-ES phases and
P3/P4, distinguish onset of double descent from the higher noise level
where early stopping is preferable. This source does not supply this
model's threshold. Our computation is self-contained and restricted to
the paired four-point model. The lower onset at finite scale, its rate,
a full two-threshold window, iid Gaussian inputs, fixed-positive-noise
unit-teacher dynamics, high probability over label noise, and actual
nonlinear convergence after T_e remain open. Mathematical and novelty
review are pending; no independent audit or full Target2 solution.
All paired four-point model definitions and restrictions of C010
Noise-to-signal Walsh variance ratio rho>0 fixed as e decreases; actual noise standard deviation tends to zero
Width tends to infinity before feature scale decreases; nonlinear comparison is only through finite T_e for each fixed e
Clean risk averages over all sixteen training-label-noise sign patterns

[Definition of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] Let  $ (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}) $  be a probability space. 
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item Let $ A, B \in \mathcal{F} $. We say that  $ A, B $ are independent w.r.t $ \mathbb{P} $ if $ \mathbb{P} (A \cap  B) = \mathbb{P} (A) \mathbb{P}(B) $.
        \item Let $ \mathcal{J}_{1} $ and $ \mathcal{J}_{2} $ be two subfamilies of $ \mathcal{F} $. We say that $ \mathcal{J}_{1} $ and $ \mathcal{J}_{2} $ are independent if for all $ (A,B) \in \mathcal{J}_{1} \times \mathcal{J}_{2} $, it holds that $ \mathbb{P}(A \cap B) = \mathbb{P}(A) \mathbb{P}(B) $.
        \item Let $f, g:(\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \rightarrow(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{X}))$ be two random variables. We say that $f$ and $g$  are independent if $\sigma(f)$ and $\sigma(g) $ are independent.
        \item Let $f: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \rightarrow(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{X}))$ be a random variable and $ \mathcal{J} \subset \mathcal{F} $. We say that $f$ and $ \mathcal{J} $  are independent if $\sigma(f)$ and $ \mathcal{J} $ are independent.
    \end{enumerate}

Let Omega be a bounded CONVEX domain in R^n with Lipschitz boundary and let u belong to H^2(Omega) intersected with H_0^1(Omega). Then the integral over Omega of |D^2 u|^2 (the squared Frobenius norm of the Hessian) is at most the integral over Omega of (Laplacian u)^2. The constant is 1, with no dependence on the domain; equality holds when the boundary term that convexity discards vanishes. The inequality gives H^2 a priori bounds for the Dirichlet problem on convex domains with NO smoothness of the boundary beyond Lipschitz, which is exactly why it is the tool of choice on polygons and other corner domains where elliptic regularity theory for smooth boundaries does not apply.
CONVEXITY is what makes the boundary term have a sign - on a non-convex domain the inequality with constant 1 can fail.
Membership in H^2 intersected with H_0^1 is assumed, so the inequality is an a priori estimate, not by itself a regularity theorem;
combined with an approximation argument it yields H^2 regularity of the weak solution on convex domains.

OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; PROOF (UNAUDITED); NO NOVELTY CLAIM. Let K=[0,1]^2, c1=(0,0), c2=(1,0), c3=(0,1), phi_i(x)=max(0,1/2-||x-c_i||_1), and f(x)=sum_i phi_i(x)v_i for unit planar v_i at pairwise angle 120 degrees. Let h:K -> R^m and D:R^m -> R^2 be finite piecewise linear maps with D composed with h=f. Either h has a two-dimensional affine image cell or X=h(K) is an embedded finite graph. In the graph case Z=h(f^{-1}(0))=X intersect D^{-1}(0) is a connected subgraph after finite subdivision, and X minus Z has exactly three connected components. With b the number of edge incidences leaving Z and beta_1(Z)=|E(Z)|-|V(Z)|+1, b>=3. The hidden graph satisfies sum_{v in Z}(deg_X(v)-2)=b-2+2 beta_1(Z)>=1. Therefore some vertex in Z has degree at least three and its incident positive tangent rays span dimension at least two. No constancy of h on final fibres is assumed. Every prefix after the first image-dimension drop in an exact finite PL network has this graph property. Branch vertices may move, and their incident edges may map locally to zero rather than to three positive target legs. The charge identity supplies no weight-cost inequality and does not determine R_infinity.
Exactly the specified square tripod
Finite PL prefix and exact finite PL recovering suffix
Graph conclusion applies when no two-dimensional affine image cell exists
Finite graph subdivision includes all suffix zeros on edges; b counts incidences, not distinct complementary components

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:59c7c0f2933f6adabda3dbeaff99722da9808dc6d40e0d8431ee4f11336e7966","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/59/59c7c0f2933f6adabda3dbeaff99722da9808dc6d40e0d8431ee4f11336e7966.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:b24f52b6592beddac7cceb87b47f4fdb9ce77546ea50d0b23e3e13d57ea588cb","bundle_entry_key":"jacot-hidden-zero-fibre-graph-branching","bundle_id":"population.w715-t276-hidden-zero-fibre-branching-unaudited","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Deep ReLU bottleneck rank and hidden-feature geometry","draft":"w715/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.deep_networks:jacot-hidden-zero-fibre-graph-branching-unaudited","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Intrinsic branching in hidden graph images

T276 Target 2. Proof unaudited. Structural reduction, not a determination
of R_infinity. No novelty claim; the graph degree identity is elementary.

Use the fixed square tripod f:K=[0,1]^2 -> Y. Its corner tents are
phi_i=max(0,1/2-||x-c_i||_1), with c1=(0,0),c2=(1,0),c3=(0,1),
and f=sum_i phi_i v_i for three unit 120-degree planar rays v_i.
Let h:K -> R^m be finite PL, and let D be a finite PL suffix satisfying
D composed with h=f on K. A network prefix and its suffix meet these
conditions, including biases and a final linear output.

THE DICHOTOMY. Either h has a two-dimensional affine image cell, or
X=h(K) is an embedded finite graph. In the latter case Z=h(f^{-1}(0))
is a connected subgraph, X minus Z has exactly three connected components,
and at least one vertex of Z has degree at least three in X. In particular
a common hidden graph branch point exists without assuming fibre constancy.
Its incident edges need not be mapped to three positive target legs locally.

STEP 1: the source pieces. The zero fibre is exactly the convex polygon

 F0=K intersect {x+y>=1/2, x-y<=1/2, y-x<=1/2}.

Indeed, positive tent supports are disjoint, so f can vanish only where
all three tents vanish. The other three pieces U_i={phi_i>0} in K are
nonempty convex relative-open corner triangles. They are exactly the
inverse images of the three positive legs of Y. Thus F0 and every U_i
are connected and K is their disjoint union.

STEP 2: the hidden pieces. Put Z=h(F0), X_i=h(U_i). Exact recovery
implies Z=X intersect D^{-1}(0) and
X_i=X intersect D^{-1}({t v_i:0<t<=1/2}). These four sets are disjoint,
cover X, and are connected as continuous images of connected sets.
Each X_i is relatively open in X minus Z (indeed in X), because a
positive leg is relatively open in Y. Hence X_1,X_2,X_3 are precisely
the three connected components of X minus Z. No assumption that h is
constant on a fibre of f was used.

STEP 3: graph structure. A finite PL map on a two-dimensional polytope
has an image which is a finite union of polytopes of dimension at most 2.
If no image cell is two-dimensional, X is a finite union of segments
and points, and it is connected. Nonconstancy of f excludes a singleton.
Subdivide segment intersections and the breakpoints of D on the segments
to obtain an embedded finite graph Gamma. Since D is affine on each
subdivided edge, its zero set there is an endpoint, the entire edge,
or empty; after also subdividing any interior zero, Z is a subgraph.
It is nonempty, compact, and connected by Step 2.

STEP 4: a branch charge on the distributed zero fibre. Let V_Z,E_Z
be the numbers of vertices and edges of Z. Let b count incidences
at vertices of Z of edges of Gamma which are not edges of Z. An edge
with both endpoints in Z, if present outside Z, is counted twice.
Every one of the three components of X minus Z has an attaching edge,
by connectedness of the finite graph Gamma. Thus b>=3. Degree counting
at vertices of Z gives the exact identity

 sum_{v in V(Z)} (deg_Gamma(v)-2)
       =2 E_Z+b-2 V_Z
       =b-2+2 beta_1(Z) >=1,                                 (1)

where beta_1(Z)=E_Z-V_Z+1>=0 because Z is connected.
Therefore some vertex in Z has degree at least three in Gamma.
In an embedded PL graph, distinct edges incident at a vertex have
distinct initial positive tangent rays: overlapping initial segments
would be one edge after subdivision. Three distinct positive rays
cannot lie in one linear line, so their joint linear span has dimension
at least two. This is a local geometric consequence, not a Jacobian-
rank-two assertion for h (whose image is still one-dimensional).

COROLLARY FOR A WHOLE NETWORK. Let h_j be the successive prefix maps.
The maximum dimension of an affine image cell cannot increase after
composition with a finite PL layer: subdivide the image cells into
the next layer's finitely many affine regions, each of which is mapped
affinely and cannot increase dimension. Since h_0 is the square and
the final image is the tripod, there is a first dimension drop from
2 to 1. Every subsequent prefix has a graph image and obeys (1).
Thus its zero fibre may stay distributed, but each graph stage has
an intrinsic branch vertex on that zero fibre.

WHAT THIS RESOLVES. A previous common-center reduction demanded that
all hidden features collapse each final fibre. That hypothesis is
unnecessary merely to find branching in a one-dimensional hidden image.
The branch point is not necessarily the image of one fixed source point
or a point with three positive target directions. It can change from
layer to layer, and the zero subgraph can contain many edges or cycles.

WHAT REMAINS. The charge in (1) is combinatorial. No inequality here
relates its propagation to squared Frobenius weights or bias cost.
The existing acute-pair telescope still needs its angle hypotheses;
degree three does not supply one common acute pair through all layers.
Also the first dimension drop can be arbitrarily late. This reduction
does not imply R_infinity=2 or any new normalized cost bound.

NEXT: an analytic energy inequality for transitions of these branched
hidden graphs, permitting a distributed zero subgraph and moving vertices.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:1a9028678a56bb0aaf4e5e7234d6a2af63350b6e7af3627f04303a882a5dbc81","revision_digest":"sha256:a019a6d7d8c0a37482ccfa40b04c8c9be16036317ca19b936fc4a62d7931ac28","source_id":"owner-own-work:w715:T276:hidden-graph-branching:v1","source_revision":"Claim w715-T276-hidden-graph-branching version 1, proof (unaudited), 2026-10-20","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Use the network and assumptions below. In particular, (epsilon_n,B)-orthonormal means | ||x_alpha||^2-1 |<=epsilon_n, |x_alpha^T*x_beta|<=epsilon_n for alpha!=beta, ||X||_op<=B, and sum_alpha (||x_alpha||^2-1)^2<=B^2, with constant B and epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0. Put b=E sigma'(Z), Z~N(0,1). For a probability law nu on [0,infinity), let MP_gamma(nu) be its Marcenko-Pastur sample-covariance map with dimension/sample ratio gamma: if a deterministic PSD n-by-n matrix Phi has empirical law nu and G is d-by-n with independent N(0,1/d) entries, n/d->gamma, it is the limiting law of Phi^(1/2)*G^T*G*Phi^(1/2). Equivalently its Stieltjes transform m(z)=integral(lambda-z)^(-1)dMP_gamma(nu)(lambda) solves m(z)=integral[x*(1-gamma-gamma*z*m(z))-z]^(-1)dnu(x), with the Stieltjes branch. Recursively set nu_l=Law(1-b^2+b^2*lambda), lambda~mu_(l-1), and mu_l=MP_gamma_l(nu_l). Then for every fixed l=1,...,L, the empirical eigenvalue distribution of X_l^T*X_l converges weakly almost surely to mu_l. In particular K_CK=X_L^T*X_L has limit mu_L and ||K_CK||_op<=C almost surely for all sufficiently large n. If b=0, mu_l is the ordinary Marcenko-Pastur law with ratio gamma_l. These are bulk limits; convergence of individual extreme eigenvalues to support edges is not asserted.
Fixed integer depth L>=1; n,d_0,...,d_L tend to infinity; n/d_l->gamma_l in (0,infinity) for l=1,...,L.
All weights W_l in R^(d_l by d_(l-1)) and w in R^d_L have independent N(0,1) entries, independent of the input matrices.
sigma:R->R is twice differentiable with globally bounded first and second derivatives. For Z~N(0,1), E sigma(Z)=0 and E sigma(Z)^2=1.
X_0 is (epsilon_n,B)-orthonormal as in the companion definition for constant B, epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0; the ESD of X_0^T X_0 converges to a deterministic probability measure mu_0.
X_l=d_l^(-1/2)*sigma(W_l*X_(l-1)) entrywise, l=1,...,L. The input is fixed, or the stated input conditions hold almost surely independently of the Gaussian weights.

body: In commutative algebra, the Krull dimension of a commutative ring R, named after Wolfgang Krull, is the supremum of the lengths of all chains of prime ideals. The Krull dimension need not be finite even for a Noetherian ring. More generally the Krull dimension can be defined for modules over possibly non-commutative rings as the deviation of the poset of submodules.
title: Krull dimension

[Definition defn:Dd of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For each $d\in \mathbb{N}$, let $\Lambda_d$ be the following directed graph. Its vertices consist of all $(x, a)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \times \mathbb{Z}_{2d}$ with $x+a\in 2\mathbb{Z}$, where $\mathbb{Z}_{2d}=\mathbb{Z}/2d\mathbb{Z}=\{0,\ldots, 2d-1\}$.
For each vertex $(x,a)$, there is a directed edge from it to $(x+1, a+1)$, and a directed edge from it to $(x-1, a+1)$, if $x\ge 1$. (Here our space is periodic, so $a, a + 1$ are understood modulo $2d$).
We let $D_d:\Lambda_d^2\to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ be the resulting directed metric on $\Lambda_d$, i.e., $D_d((x,a), (y,b))$ is the length of the shortest directed path from $(x,a)$ to $(y,b)$.
title: Definition defn:Dd of arXiv:2604.10020

Method: Explicit model calculation, comparison identities and remaining hypothesis obstruction Result: For the density f(x,y)=exp(-x) on x>y>0, E[X*1{D>w}]=(w+2)*exp(-w). The source capacity equation is therefore lambda*(w+2)*exp(-w)=1; a positive root exists when2lambda>1. The planar drift b(x,y)=((1-r^2)x-y,(1-r^2)y+x) has only the equilibrium0 but has an attracting unit-circle orbit. Adding independent noise of size1/sqrtN gives invariant density proportional to exp[N*(r^2-r^4/2)], which concentrates on the circle as N grows, not at the unique equilibrium. The rotational drift is divergence-free and orthogonal to the radial gradient, verifying the invariant density by the Fokker-Planck equation. Its exponent is maximized exactly at r=1. Obstruction: The diffusion is a logical counterexample to an insufficient interchange argument, not to this queue. A queue proof still needs stationary tightness and global attraction or a characterization of all invariant fluid laws, beyond uniqueness of a stationary point. Let m,n be positive integers, x_1,...,x_m and y_1,...,y_m be points in R^n, and let d be a finite-valued metric on R^n. Repeated points are allowed. For 1<=p<infinity set mu=m^(-1) sum_i delta_(x_i) and nu=m^(-1) sum_i delta_(y_i). Then W_p(mu,nu)^p = min_(pi in S_m) m^(-1) sum_i d(x_i,y_(pi(i)))^p. Equivalently the p-Wasserstein distance is the p-th root of this minimum. Thus an optimal Kantorovich cost for two equal-cardinality, equal-weight empirical measures can be attained by a permutation matching. No independence of the two point clouds, or within either cloud, is needed for this deterministic identity. It gives no bound on how small the matching cost is, and does not by itself give a convergence rate for dependent neurons.

Method: Deterministic strong convergence from LPS generators structural calculation Result: Weak freeness plus the usual adjacency norm is insufficient in general. Start with any strongly convergent r-unitary model and append a one-dimensional block in which every generator equals z=exp(i*theta), with cos(theta)=sqrt(2r-1)/r. This block does not change limiting traces and its adjacency eigenvalue is exactly2*sqrt(2r-1). Yet the phase-twisted adjacency polynomial has value2r on that block, above its free norm2*sqrt(2r-1). Check: Normalized trace weight of the added block tends to0. Multiplying each free Haar generator by a fixed phase preserves the free law and norm. [Defn 11 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] For fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, a stochastic kinetic
solution of \eqref{eq:penalized eq} is a nonnegative, almost surely continuous $L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})$-valued $\mathcal{F}_{t}$-predictable function $u_\varepsilon\in L^{1}(\Omega\times[0,T];L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))$ satisfying following properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] Preservation of mass: almost surely for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
    -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_\varepsilon\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\varepsilon^{-1}(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^{+}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_{\mathrm{init}}\phi(0)\mathrm{d}x
\end{align}
\item[(ii)] $\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\in L^{2}(\Omega;L^{2}(Q_T))$,\quad $g(u_\varepsilon)\in L^{1}(\Omega;L^{1}(Q_T;\mathbb{R}^d))$.
\item[(iii)] For every $K\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
[(u_\varepsilon\land K)\lor(1/K)]\in L^{2}(\Omega\times[0,T];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))).
\]
Furthermore, there exists a kinetic measure $m_\varepsilon$ satisfying the following properties.
\item[(iv)] Almost surely as a nonnegative measure, $m_\varepsilon$ satisfies
\[
\delta_{0}(\xi-u_\varepsilon)\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u_\varepsilon|^{2}\leq m_\varepsilon\quad\text{on}\quad\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T].
\]
\item[(v)] (Vanishing)
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\big[m_\varepsilon(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times[N,N+1]\times[0,T))\big]=0.
\]
\item[(vi)] Preservation of energy: for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
&-\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}u_\varepsilon^2(x,s)\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\psi(x,s)(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\\
&+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)|(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+|^2\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+2\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\phi(s)\mathrm{d}m_\varepsilon(\mathbb{T}^d,[0,\infty),s)\nonumber\\
&=\mathbb{E}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}u^2_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\phi(0)\mathrm{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\sigma^2(u_{\varepsilon})(\nabla_{x}\cdot F_{2}-2F_3)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s.\nonumber
\end{align}
\item[(vii)] For every $\phi\in C_{c}^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$, the kinetic function $\chi_\varepsilon$ of $u_\varepsilon$ almost surely satisfies
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi_\varepsilon(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)\nabla_x u_\varepsilon\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)]^{2}\nabla_x u_\varepsilon+\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_\varepsilon(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x\cdot g(u_\varepsilon)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma(u_\varepsilon)\sigma^{\prime}(u_\varepsilon)\nabla_x u_\varepsilon\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma^{2}(u_\varepsilon)F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(u_\varepsilon-\psi)^+\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x\cdot(\sigma(u_\varepsilon)f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k}.\nonumber
\end{align}
\end{itemize}

Let X be a random vector in a real separable Hilbert space with E||X||^2<infinity and covariance H=E[X tensor X]. Assume exact interpolation: Y=<X,theta_star> almost surely for a fixed theta_star in the Hilbert space. Assume R>0 and the operator fourth-moment bound E[||X||^2*(X tensor X)]<=R*H in positive-semidefinite order. Start theta_0=0 and use fresh IID examples with the single-example SGD update theta_(t+1)=theta_t-gamma*(<X_(t+1),theta_t>-Y_(t+1))*X_(t+1), where gamma>0 is constant during the run. Put D=||theta_star||^2 and f_t=E Rcal(theta_t), where Rcal(theta)=E(<X,theta>-Y)^2/2 =||H^(1/2)*(theta-theta_star)||^2/2; the outer expectation is over SGD samples. For each integer horizon T>=2, choose gamma=1/[4*R*ln(T)]. Then E Rcal(theta_T)<=3*R*||theta_star||^2*ln(T)/T. This concerns the final iterate with a horizon-dependent step size held constant for that run. It does not assert the same rate for one fixed step size simultaneously at all horizons, for additive label noise, or for arbitrary interpolating nonquadratic losses. No strong convexity is assumed.

[Definition 16 (Factor of i.i.d.) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Consider a locally finite transitive graph $G=(V,E)$
    (with respect to some group $\Theta\subset\operatorname{Aut}(G)$).
    Let $S$ denote a measurable space,
    and let $\mu$ denote the distribution of a $\Theta$-stationary random field on $S^V$.
    Let $(T,\lambda)$ denote a probability space, and consider $\P:=\lambda^V$.
    A \emph{factor of i.i.d.}\ (FIID) is a map $\phi:T^V\to S^V$
    with the following properties:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\phi$ is measurable with respect to the product $\sigma$-algebras on $T^V$ and $S^V$,
        \item $\phi$ is equivariant with respect to $\Theta$,
        \item If $X\sim\P$, then $\phi(X)\sim\mu$.
    \end{itemize}
title: Factor of i.i.d.

body: [Theorem rep theorem of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Suppose $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Z}$ are smooth separated Deligne--Mumford stacks, and there is a representable contraction morphism $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z}$ whose exceptional $\mathcal{E}$ is a smooth Cartier divisor. Moreover, suppose there is a smooth closed Deligne--Mumford substack $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathcal{Z}$, such that $f^{-1}(\mathcal{Y}) \simeq \mathcal{E}$ set-theoretically, and $f : \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{E} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{Z} \setminus \mathcal{Y}$. Then $f$ is an ordinary blowup with reduced center $\mathcal{Y}$, in particular $f|_{\mathcal{E}} : \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is a projective bundle, and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathcal{E})|_{\mathcal{E}} \simeq \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{E}}(-1) \otimes f^*\mathcal{L}$ for some line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ on $\mathcal{Y}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem rep theorem of arXiv:2609.04023

body:
[Definition def:gamma of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Let $\phi$ be a
		$\mathbb Z$-valued height function on the vertices of a connected domain $V\subset \mathbb Z^2$. Associate to each bond $e\in (\mathbb Z^2)^*$, dual to some edge $(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2$, the gradient $(
abla \phi)_e := \phi_x - \phi_y$, where $x$ is taken to be the 	extsc{north} vertex if $(x,y)$ is vertical and the 	extsc{west} vertex if $(x,y)$ is horizontal. We say the bond $e$ is a \emph{disagreement bond} of $\phi$ if $(
abla\phi)_e
eq 0$ (including when $\phi_x$ or $\phi_y$ are specified by the boundary conditions). A \emph{disagreement polymer}~$\gamma$ is a (maximal) connected component of the disagreement bonds of $\phi$, and we let $\ensuremath{\mathcal P}_\phi$ denote the disagreement polymers in $\phi$. For such a polymer, let $D_i$ be the connected components of $V \setminus \gamma$, noting that by the maximality of $\gamma$, within each $D_i$, all the vertices that are $*$-adjacent to $V\setminus D_i$ must have the same height $h_i$ in~$\phi$. Call the triple $(\gamma, \{D_i\}, \{h_i\})$ a \emph{labeled disagreement polymer}. For brevity,  we denote labeled disagreement polymers by $\gamma$ (omitting the $\{h_i\}$ from the notation).
title: Disagreement polymer

[Proposition 11 of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] Let \(\bm f=(f_1,f_2)^\top\in\mathscr S^\dagger \). The sequence of martingales $ \left\{
	\bm M_t^n(\bm f):0\le t\le T \right\}_{n\in \mathbb{N} }$ converges in 
	the topology of  $ \mathcal D([0,T], \mathbb{R})$, as $ n  \to \infty $, towards a mean-zero Gaussian process \(W_t(\bm f)\) with quadratic variation given by
	\[
	\Phi_{11}+\Phi_{12}+\Phi_{21}+\Phi_{22},
	\]
	where, for \(k=1,2\),
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\Phi_{kk}
		&=
		\int_0^t
		\Bigg\{
		\int_0^1
		2\rho_k(s,u)
		\left(
		1-\rho_k(s,u)
		\right)
		\left(
		\partial_u f_k(u)
		\right)^2
		\,\mathrm du                                     
		+
		\int_0^1
		\left(
		\gamma_1\rho_1(s,u)
		+
		\gamma_2\rho_2(s,u)
		\right)
		f_k(u)^2
		\,\mathrm du                                      \\
		&\quad
		+
		\left(
		\alpha_k\rho_0(s,0)
		+
		\alpha_0\rho_k(s,0)
		\right)
		f_k(0)^2                                  
		+
		\left(
		\beta_k\rho_0(s,1)
		+
		\beta_0\rho_k(s,1)
		\right)
		f_k(1)^2
		\Bigg\}
		\,\mathrm ds,
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	and, for \(k\neq l\),
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\Phi_{kl}
		&=
		-
		\int_0^t
		\Bigg\{
		\int_0^1
		2\rho_1(s,u)\rho_2(s,u)
		\partial_u f_1(u)
		\partial_u f_2(u)
		\,\mathrm du                                      \\
		&\quad
		+
		\int_0^1
		\left(
		\gamma_1\rho_1(s,u)
		+
		\gamma_2\rho_2(s,u)
		\right)
		f_1(u)f_2(u)
		\,du
		\Bigg\}
		\,\mathrm ds .
	\end{aligned}
	\]

Let u: {-1, 1}^n -> R under the uniform measure, with Fourier coefficients u^(S) = E[u chi_S], derivatives D_i u(x) = (u(x with x_i = 1) - u(x with x_i = -1))/2 and total influence I(u) = sum_i E[(D_i u)^2]. Then I(u) - Var(u) = sum over |S| >= 2 of (|S| - 1) u^(S)^2. Hence Var(u) <= I(u) (the Poincare inequality of the cube), with equality iff u is affine, u^(S) = 0 for |S| >= 2. With Pi u = u^(empty) + sum_i u^({i}) x_i the affine part, ||u - Pi u||_2^2 = sum over |S| >= 2 of u^(S)^2 <= I(u) - Var(u), with equality iff u^(S) = 0 for every |S| >= 3.

body: In arithmetic combinatorics, Szemerédi's theorem is a result concerning arithmetic progressions in subsets of the integers. In 1936, Erdős and Turán conjectured that every set of integers A with positive natural density contains a k-term arithmetic progression for every k. Endre Szemerédi proved the conjecture in 1975.
title: Szemerédi's theorem

[Lemma lem:mmean of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Let $z_i\in\mathbb{R}^m$ carry weights $p_i>0$ with $\sum_ip_iz_i=0$, and let
$E=\sum_ip_i\lVert z_i\rVert^2$. Then some convex combination $\delta$ of at most
$m$ of the points satisfies $\Wnorm\delta^2\le E/m^2$. The constant is
attained by the uniformly weighted regular simplex.

Let D_n be the interior of the union of the rectangles [0,a/n]x[0,1], [b/n,1]x[0,1], and [a/n,b/n]x[(m-1/2)/n,(m+1/2)/n]. Each D_n is a simply connected Jordan polygon with fixed corner marks A=(0,1), B=(0,0), C=(1,0), D=(1,1). Its closure Hausdorff distance from the closed unit square is <=k/(2n), its boundary Hausdorff distance is <=b/n, its area loss is k(n-1)/n^2, and its unmarked Caratheodory kernel at (1/2,1/2) is the open unit square. Yet in the induced nearest-neighbor graph on mesh-1/n vertices in its closure, independent bonds p=1/2 give P(AB connects CD)<=2^-k, tending to zero: only the row y=m/n joins the chambers. Canonical square crossings are uniformly positive by classical RSW. The missing marked-prime-end convergence is essential; this example refutes an overstrong approximation bridge, not the properly marked C0017 target.

Let X be a Banach space, Y a normed space, and {T_i : i in I} a family (of any cardinality) of bounded linear operators from X to Y. If the family is pointwise bounded, meaning sup over i of ||T_i(x)|| is finite for every x in X, then it is uniformly bounded: sup over i of the operator norms ||T_i|| is finite. Consequently, if a sequence of bounded operators on a Banach space converges pointwise, the limit operator is bounded. Completeness of the domain is essential.

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2604.09248, '\bfseries Limit laws for longest edges in empty region graphs'] Suppose that the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm:PoisConvAbstract} are satisfied and that $\log(t)+\tau+b>0$. Then, for the point process $\xi_t|_{W \times [b,\infty)\times\LL^d}$, the quantities $E_2$, $E_3$, and $E_4$ in Theorem \ref{thm:BSY} {with $S_{(x,y)}:=S(x,y)\cup\{x,y\}$ for $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d$} are bounded by
    \[
    E_2 \le C_2 \frac{1+ b+ \log(t) + \tau}{e^{2b}t}, \quad E_3 \le \frac{C_3}{e^b(b+\log(t)+\tau)^{\max\{d-2, 1/2\}}},\quad
    E_4 \le \frac{C_{4,1}}{e^b(b+\log(t)+\tau)^{d-1}}+\frac{C_{4,2}}{e^{2b}t}.
    \]
    Here, $C_2$, $C_3$, $C_{4,1}$, and $C_{4,2}$ are constants in $(0,\infty)$ depending only on $d$ and $W$ as well as the constants $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ in Theorem \ref{thm:PoisConvAbstract}. Possible choices are
    \[
    C_2 := \frac{2^{d+1} \kappa_d \alpha^d}{\gamma}\vol(W),\quad C_3 := \begin{cases}
        \frac{4 d \kappa_d^2 M_{d-1}\gamma^{d-2}}{\beta^d(d-2)}\vol(W), & d \ge 3,\\
        {\frac{16\sqrt{2} \pi^{5/2}}{\beta^2\sqrt{\gamma}}\vol(W),} & d = 2,
    \end{cases}\quad
    C_{4,1} := \frac{2^{d+4} d \kappa_d M_{d-1}\gamma^{d-1}}{\beta^d} \vol(W), 
    \]
and $C_{4,2}:=16\vol(W)$, where $M_{d-1} := (2(d-1)/e)^{d-1}$.

body:
[Lemma lem:universal-root of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $X,Z\in\operatorname{End}(W)$ be arbitrary, let $a_1,\ldots,a_N$ be the Kac
orthonormal basis of $W=\mathfrak{so}(n)$, and put $A_i=\operatorname{ad}_{a_i}$.
Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R_i(X,Z)&=\{X,[A_i,Z]\}a_i,&
 U_i(X,Z)&=\{X,Z\}a_i,\\
 E_i(X,Z)&=\{[A_i,X],Z\}a_i,&
 \bar E(X,Z)&=\frac1N\sum_iE_i(X,Z).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10a}
\]
Put $\Psi(T)=\sum_jA_jTa_j$.  Then, with no projection onto curvature
summands,
\[
 \mathcal R_i=A_iU_i-(E_i-\bar E)-\bar E,
 \qquad
 \bar E=\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j+H(X,Z),\qquad V_j=XZa_j,
\tag{3.2.10b}
\]
where
\[
 H(X,Z)=\frac1N\{-X\Psi(Z)+Z\Psi(X)\}.
\tag{3.2.10b$'$}
\]
Moreover, writing $\|\cdot\|_2$ for Hilbert--Schmidt norm,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1N\sum_i\|U_i\|^2
 &\le\frac4N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_j\|V_j\|^2
 &\le\frac1N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_i\|E_i-\bar E\|^2
 &\le\frac{16(n-2)}N\|X\|_2^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.10c}
\]
The residue satisfies
\[
 \|H(X,Z)\|
 \le\frac{\sqrt{n-2}}N
 \bigl(\|X\|_\mathrm{op}\|Z\|_2+\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}\|X\|_2\bigr).
\tag{3.2.10e}
\]
If $X$ and $Z$ are symmetric, then $\Psi(X)=\Psi(Z)=0$, so $H=0$.
The identities and estimates remain valid when all maps are tensored by
an ancillary identity and the Hilbert--Schmidt norm is taken on the
amplified space.

[Lemma lem:interior-dirichlet-gmc-comparison of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] Let $M_{h_D}^{\rm can}$ and $M_{h_U}^{\rm can}$ be the canonical GMC measures
obtained from the construction of Lemma~(lem:canonical-borel-gmc of the paper) on $D$
and $U$, respectively.  Under the coupling above, for every fixed $V\Subset U$,
almost surely,
\begin{equation}
 M_{h_D}^{\rm can}|_V
 =w_{D,U}\,M_{h_U}^{\rm can}|_V,
 \qquad
 w_{D,U}(z)
 :=\exp\!\left(
   \gamma\chi_{D,U}(z)
   -\frac{\gamma^2}{2}\mathbb E[\chi_{D,U}(z)^2]
  \right),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 w_{D,U},\ w_{D,U}^{-1}\in C_b(V).
\end{equation}
In particular, the two measures in
(equation eq:interior-dirichlet-gmc-comparison of the paper) have the same null sets on $V$.

\[
        \Lambda_a'(\theta_a(x))=x,
        \qquad
        J_a(x)=\theta_a(x)x-\Lambda_a(\theta_a(x)).
\]
Moreover, \(J_a\) is differentiable and strictly convex on \((0,\infty)\), with
\(J_a'(x)=\theta_a(x)\) and
\(J_a''(x)=1/\Lambda_a''(\theta_a(x))\). Finally, \(J_a\ge0\) on
\([0,\infty)\), and it vanishes uniquely at
\(\lambda_a=\frac{1}{4\pi}(1-\frac{1}{a})\).

body:
[Proposition 17 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $\chi$ is injective. Let $V$ be a $k[G]$-module with $\ell_V$ constant. Let $a\in C_m$ and $W:=U(a,1)$. We assume that $V$ is constant-indecomposable and we consider a direct sum decomposition into indecomposable $k[G]$-modules $V=\oplus_{i=1}^{\imath_V} U(a_i,b_i)$. Let 
$$J:=\{a_i+\epsilon|i\in\llbracket1,\imath_V\rrbracket\}.$$
Then the following properties hold.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} We have an identity
$$\dim_k\bigl(\Hom_{k[G]}(V,W)\bigr)=\begin{cases}1\quad\textup{if}\quad a\in J\\0\quad\textup{if}\quad a\notin J.\end{cases}$$

{\bf (2)} Let $(c,b)\in\mathbb J_{m,p^s}$. Then 
$$\dim_k\bigl(\Ext^1_{k[G]}(U(c,b),W)\bigr)=\begin{cases}1\quad\textup{if}\quad  a=c+\epsilon\;\textup{and}\;b<p^s\\0\quad\textup{if}\quad a\neq c+\epsilon\;\textup{or}\;b=p^s.\end{cases}$$

{\bf (3)} Suppose that $\jmath_V=0$. Then 
$$\dim_k\bigl(\Hom_{k[G]}(V,W)\bigr)=\dim_k\bigl(\Ext^1_{k[G]}(V,W)\bigr).$$
title: Proposition 17 of arXiv:2609.03191

[Definition def:inf-free-mom-cum of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi^{(0)}, \varphi^{(1)}, \ldots,
  \varphi^{(\nu)})$ be an infinitesimal non-commutative probability space of
  order $\nu$. The infinitesimal free cumulants of order $\nu$ are
  multilinear maps $(\kappa_n^{(0)}, \ldots, \kappa_n^{(\nu)} : \mathcal{A}^n
  \rightarrow \mathbb{C})$ uniquely determined by the following relation: For
  every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $i = 0, \ldots, \nu$ and $(a_1, \ldots, a_k) \in
  \mathcal{A}^k$,
  \begin{equation}
    \varphi^{(i)} (a_1 \ldots a_k) = \sum_{\pi = \{V_1, \ldots, V_p \} \in
    \ensuremath{\operatorname{NC}} (k)} \sum_{\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_p = i}
    \frac{i!}{\lambda_1 ! \ldots \lambda_p !} \prod_{i = 1}^p \kappa_{|V_i
    |}^{(\lambda_i)} (a_1, \ldots, a_k |V_i) . 
  \end{equation}

[Lem 31 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] There exists a constant $C > 1$ such that the following holds, whenever $q \in (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ and $a, b, c \in (1-\varepsilon, 1 + \varepsilon)$, for sufficiently small $\varepsilon \in (0, C^{-1})$. Fix $z_0 = (x_0,y_0) \in \mathfrak{L}_{q;a,b,c}$, and assume that $x_0\ge x^{SW}_{q;a,b,c}$ and that $\ell_{z_0}$ is the southwest edge of $\mathfrak{X}_{a,b,c}$. 
	 
	 \begin{enumerate} 
	 	\item We have that $C^{-1} (\mathfrak{d}_{z_0} \mathfrak{e}_{{z_0};q})^{1/2} \le -\partial_x \mathcal{H}_{q;a,b,c} ({z_0}) \le C (\mathfrak{d}_{z_0} \mathfrak{e}_{{z_0};q})^{1/2}$. 
	 	\item We have that $C^{-1} (\mathfrak{d}_{z_0}^{-1} \mathfrak{e}_{{z_0};q})^{1/2} \le \partial_y \mathcal{H}_{q;a,b,c} ({z_0}) \le C (\mathfrak{d}_{z_0}^{-1} \mathfrak{e}_{{z_0};q})^{1/2}$. 
		\item We have that $C^{-1} \mathfrak{d}_{z_0}^{1/2} \mathfrak{e}_{{z_0};q}^{3/2} \le \mathcal{H}_{q;a,b,c} ({z_0}) \le C \mathfrak{d}_{z_0}^{1/2} \mathfrak{e}_{{z_0};q}^{3/2}$. 
		\item Assume that $z_0 = (x_0,y_0) \in \mathfrak{L}_{q;a,b,c}$ and $\ell_{z_0}$ is the southwest edge of $\mathfrak{X}_{a,b,c}$, but now $ x_0\le x^{SW}_{q;a,b,c}$. Then $C^{-1} (\mathfrak{d}_{z_0} \mathfrak{e}_{{z_0};q})^{1/2} \le -\partial_x \mathcal{H}_{q;a,b,c} ({z_0}) \le C (\mathfrak{d}_{z_0} \mathfrak{e}_{{z_0};q})^{1/2}$ remains valid, but now $C^{-1} \le \partial_y \mathcal{H}_{q;a,b,c} ({z_0}) \le C$ and $C^{-1} \mathfrak{d}_{z_0}^2 \le \mathcal{H}_{q;a,b,c} ({z_0}) \le C \mathfrak{d}_{z_0}^2$. 
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 31 of arXiv:2605.26664

Version 1, Target 2; proof (unaudited). This supplies the named explicit remainder, not a new lognormal law. No novelty claim is made for the partition or connected-graph identities. The law itself is settled in the dossier and prior literature.

Fix k>=2 and c>=0. Let M_t=exp(-5t/2+sqrt(5t)Z), where Z is standard normal, 0<=t<=c. Set a_j=5j(j-1)/2, and let Pi_k denote partitions of [k]. For pi in Pi_k define

    w_pi=(-1)^(|pi|-1)(|pi|-1)!,
    H_pi=sum_(B in pi) a_|B|,
    W_k=sum_(r=1)^k S(k,r)(r-1)!,
    A_(k,s)=(1/s!) sum_(pi in Pi_k) w_pi H_pi^s.

Here S(k,r) is the Stirling number of the second kind and H^0=1 also at H=0. Define cumulants by the finite partition formula, not by an assumed finite moment-generating function. Then for every integer m>=0,

    |kappa_k(M_t)-sum_(s=0)^m A_(k,s)t^s|
       <= W_k exp(a_k c) (a_k t)^(m+1)/(m+1)! .       (1)

All constants are explicit finite sums. In particular, (1) is uniform over all integer L,n with 0<=L<=cn upon setting t=L/n. This is a statement about the limiting-law cumulant evaluated at that t, not a claim that it equals the exact finite-width cumulant.

Proof: E M_t^j=exp(a_j t). Finite moment-cumulant inversion gives

    F_k(t)=kappa_k(M_t)=sum_pi w_pi exp(H_pi t).

Since 0<=H_pi<=a_k, the exponential Taylor remainder for t>=0 is at most exp(a_k c)(a_k t)^(m+1)/(m+1)! termwise. Summing absolute weights proves (1). Every operation is on a finite partition set, so no analyticity of a probability MGF or interchange of an infinite moment series is used.

The coefficients of t^s vanish for s<k-1. To see this, put v=exp(5t)-1. The moment exp(a_jt)=(1+v)^(j choose 2) is the sum of v^|E| over all simple graphs on a fixed j-element set. Each graph uniquely decomposes into connected components. The finite partition moment-cumulant recursion therefore identifies F_k with the sum of v^|E| over connected simple graphs on [k]. Such a graph has at least k-1 edges. The first coefficient is 5^(k-1) times the number of labeled trees (equivalently k^(k-2), by the usual Prüfer encoding). This known identity explains cancellations; inequality (1) does not need tree enumeration.

For a scalar final preactivation Y_t=sqrt(q0 M_t) xi, q0>=0 deterministic and xi an independent standard Gaussian, all odd cumulants vanish and

    kappa_(2k)(Y_t)=(2k-1)!! q0^k F_k(t).

body: Let g be a norm on R^2 that is even in the first coordinate (g(-h, m) = g(h, m)), as every lattice-symmetric FPP limit-shape norm is. For fixed m, the map h -> g((h, m)) is even and convex, hence minimized at h = 0, so g((h, m)) >= g((0, m)) = |m| g(e_2). Consequently, for a dogleg from (0,0) through v = (h, j) to (0, r) with j = r + m, m > 0 (longitudinal overshoot past the far endpoint): g(v) + g((0,r) - v) - g((0,r)) >= (r + m) g(e_2) + m g(e_2) - r g(e_2) = 2 m g(e_2), and symmetrically for j = -m < 0. The dogleg excess grows at least LINEARLY in the overshoot, with the explicit constant 2 g(e_2), using convexity and symmetry alone - no curvature hypothesis of any kind. The bound is tight as h -> 0. Use: in localization arguments it kills union sites with longitudinal overshoot at a rate no curvature assumption needs to fund, letting curvature windows be quoted only where they are literally assumed. Numerical attack: 0 violations in 300,000 trials on an anisotropic convex norm, worst ratio 1.000019.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:e171fa8587e4f09c53cdb48e0409d988c2e40c0c495318429a1a1a79d7447480","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/e1/e171fa8587e4f09c53cdb48e0409d988c2e40c0c495318429a1a1a79d7447480.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:158e3151ac8f31199f8cd7097d37783d2feba9ef7853f1726339ba7279cece99","bundle_entry_key":"li-zhang-arora-theorem54-norm-correct-replacement","bundle_id":"population.t407-draft-norm-correct-theorem54-replacement","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"statistical learning theory","draft":"w693/bundle_009.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.sample_complexity:draft-norm-correct-source-theorem54-replacement-envelope","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Norm-correct replacement bound for the source quadratic regression problem

Status: proof (unaudited). This is a standard rank argument specialized to repair the source normalization, not a novel sample-complexity result. It makes explicit the expected-risk specialization already implicit in JOINT-005 and its queued brain card.

Let d>=1, D=d(d+1)/2, and P consist of x~N(0,I_d) with noiseless target q_alpha(x)=sum_i alpha_i x_i^2, alpha in R^d. The source expected complexity uses E_samples ||A(S)-q_alpha||_L2^2 <=epsilon ||q_alpha||_L2^2 uniformly in alpha.

For every orthogonally equivariant measurable learner A and 0<=epsilon<1, any n satisfying that guarantee necessarily obeys

    n >= ceil(D(1-epsilon)).

There exists an orthogonally equivariant learner that achieves zero error at n=D. Separately, a one-filter square-activation CNN with d scalar patches and only its d readout coefficients trained recovers every q_alpha at n=d. Thus the candidate replacement envelope is

    ceil(D(1-epsilon)) <= inf_(equivariant A) N_star(A,P,epsilon) <=D,
    inf_(specified CNN readout learners) N_star(A,P,epsilon) <=d.

The upper statement is existence of a learner, not an upper bound on every algorithm. No claim is made that the worst-case minimax risk curve equals1-n/D for intermediate n.

## Use the prediction norm, not the faulty source identity

For a real symmetric M, let q_M(x)=x^T M x. The true Gaussian inner product is

    <q_M,q_N>_L2 =2tr(MN)+tr(M)tr(N).

This follows by polarization of the corrected identity in SOURCE-011 (or direct fourth-moment expansion). It is positive definite on Sym(d), so the homogeneous quadratic subspace V has dimension D. Select any orthonormal basis phi_1,...,phi_D in this Hilbert space. The target q_theta=sum_j theta_j phi_j has prediction norm1 for every theta on S^(D-1). No ratio of expectations or uncertain source normalization is used.

Orthogonal equivariance under the Gaussian marginal transfers the learner's uniform normalized guarantee from diagonal targets to every homogeneous symmetric quadratic: diagonalize M and rotate inputs. Source Definition3.2 is sufficient, including for randomized algorithms. Hence a uniform prior on theta in S^(D-1) is a valid lower-bound prior, with exactly unit target prediction norm throughout its support. This transfer is used BEFORE averaging targets.

## Pair targets by a reflection fixing every observed label

Condition on the n input locations, independently of theta. Their evaluation matrix L has entries L_ij=phi_j(x_i) and rank r<=min(n,D). Let P be the Euclidean projection onto its row span, Q=I-P, and T=P-Q=2P-I. Then T is orthogonal, T^2=I and LT=L. The uniform spherical prior is invariant under T. This remains valid for D=1, where S^0 is the uniform two-point law.

Fix the learner's independent random coins. Targets theta and Ttheta produce identical labels and therefore exactly the same output h. If its L2 risk is infinite the lower bound is immediate. Otherwise orthogonally project h onto V, with coefficient vector gamma; projection cannot increase its squared distance from either target. Since theta=Ptheta+Qtheta and Ttheta=Ptheta-Qtheta,

    [||gamma-theta||^2+||gamma-Ttheta||^2]/2
       =||gamma-Ptheta||^2+||Qtheta||^2
       >=||Qtheta||^2.

Averaging over the spherical prior pairs theta and Ttheta without changing their law. Thus conditional average prediction risk is at least E_theta||Qtheta||^2=tr(Q)/D=(D-r)/D. The last equality uses E theta theta^T=I/D, valid also for D=1. Then average over inputs and coins. Since r<=n, the Bayes average risk is at least(1-n/D)_+. The uniform guarantee, transferred to every unit-norm quadratic, bounds that same average by epsilon, so n>=D(1-epsilon); integrality gives the ceiling. All integrands are nonnegative; Tonelli justifies averaging. No independence of conditional labels, posterior density formula, or product of conditional probabilities is assumed.

## Exact interpolation upper bounds

For the equivariant upper, minimize least-squares residual over Sym(d), choosing the unique minimum-Frobenius-norm minimizer. This is defined on every data set and commutes with orthogonal conjugation. At n=D its quadratic design is invertible almost surely: the D inputs e_i and e_i+e_j for i<j give an invertible evaluation matrix, first determining diagonals and then off-diagonals. Therefore its determinant is a nonzero polynomial in the sample coordinates; IID Gaussian inputs avoid its zero set almost surely. Exact recovery holds for every fixed quadratic target, yielding zero normalized expected risk. The zero target causes no division issue: the source guarantee is an inequality against epsilon times its squared norm.

For the CNN, one scalar shared filter w=1 with square activation and d independent readout weights represents sum_i alpha_i x_i^2. At n=d the design of squared coordinates is invertible almost surely, since inputs e_i give identity as a polynomial witness. Solving the readout linear system yields exact recovery for each fixed target. This is a readout-only upper, not a new claim about arbitrary joint-GD initialization. Joint-training candidates remain JOINT-005 and GD-006 v2.

## Verification and scope

The hardest imported source premise is only its model/algorithm definition, not its erroneous LemmaD.8 constant. The reflection identity is a finite algebraic identity and holds for any vector gamma, so it includes improper learners after Hilbert projection. If equivariance is removed, the lower transfer to all homogeneous quadratics fails: the coordinate-aware d-feature learner above is a counterexample to a universal D lower on diagonal targets. If inputs depend on theta, the independent fixed-input reflection prior argument fails. Noisy labels are not covered by the exact interpolation upper.

Primary context: Li-Zhang-Arora arXiv:2010.08515v2 Definition3.2, Theorem5.4 and AppendixD.6 pp21-22. The standard spherical-rank method was already in own JOINT-005/bundles003-004. For the product mean use the bounded-parameter concentration argument on the compact unit sphere: the product of the Gaussian linear forms has a uniformly bounded psi1 norm, and | |a^T s a^T x|-|a^T t a^T x| |<=|a^T x||a^T(s-t)| with psi2 coefficient |a^T x|. Thus the error is also at most e, with failure probability at most c exp(-d m) for m>=C(e)n. Choose e<=delta/[2(2+delta)]. For r>=h+delta, the radial bracket is at least(1-e)-(h+e)/(h+delta)=[delta-e(h+delta+1)]/(h+delta)>=delta/[2(1+delta)]>0. This handles all unbounded radii using concentration only over s on the unit sphere. PROOF (UNAUDITED); novelty unverified. Fix n>=1 integer, T>0, s in (0,1], c0 in [-1,1]. Start a two-input Gram chain with Q0=R0=s and C0=s*c0. Given each completed past, draw n iid centered Gaussian pairs (Ai,Bi) of covariance [[Ql,Cl],[Cl,Rl]], independently of previous layers, and update Qnew=mean tanh(Ai)^2, Rnew=mean tanh(Bi)^2, Cnew=mean tanh(Ai)tanh(Bi). Put Dl=1-Cl/sqrt(Ql*Rl), el=Ql-Rl, Hl=sum(j=1..l)1/j, H0=0; these variances are positive almost surely. Define K=32768*exp((105/2)*(4+T)), A=K*s*exp(3*T), B=264*exp(264*T)*A. For every integer 0<=l<=T*n: ||Ql*Rl*Dl||_2<=A*D0/(l+1), E(el^4)<=B^2*D0^2*Hl^2/n^2, E(el^2*Ql*Rl*Dl)<=A*B*D0^2*Hl/(n*(l+1)), and E(Ql^2*Rl^2*Dl^2)<=A^2*D0^2/(l+1)^2. Consequently sum(l=0..L-1)||el||_4^2<=B*D0*L*HL/n for 1<=L<=T*n. Norms are probability Lp norms. This uses the independently checked finite-width marginal bound T244-w691-C027 v1 and unaudited one-step lemma T250-w712-C013 v1. It closes the two radial mixed sources, not the stochastic angular gap or the full Tensor Programs rate. No Lean certificate is claimed.
Exact zero-bias critical tanh Gaussian Gram chain with fresh iid rows and layers
Deterministic equal initial variances s in (0,1], arbitrary c0 in [-1,1], n>=1 and l<=Tn
C013 v1 one-step fourth moment (unaudited); audited T244 C027 v1 finite marginal moments

Kind: moved. Target: 1 (two-input critical tanh chain).
Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified. This closes a component of
C013, not the full Tensor Programs target or the stochastic angular error.

## Model and statement

Fix n>=1, horizon T>0, and deterministic initial Gram entries
Q_0=R_0=s in (0,1], C_0=s c_0, -1<=c_0<=1. Set D_0=1-c_0.
At each update the n Gaussian pairs (A_i,B_i), conditional on the past,
are iid with covariance matrix [[Q_l,C_l],[C_l,R_l]]. Define
Q_(l+1)=mean tanh(A_i)^2, R_(l+1)=mean tanh(B_i)^2,
C_(l+1)=mean tanh(A_i)tanh(B_i). All layers use fresh rows.
These matrices are positive semidefinite. Marginal variances are strictly
positive almost surely at each finite layer, and bounded by 1.
Write c_l=C_l/sqrt(Q_l R_l), D_l=1-c_l, e_l=Q_l-R_l,
H_l=sum_(j=1)^l 1/j, H_0=0. Norms below are probability Lp norms.

Use the following conservative explicit constants:

    K_T=32768 exp[(105/2)(4+T)],
    A_T=K_T s exp(3T), B_T=264 exp(264T) A_T.

For every integer 0<=l<=Tn,

    ||Q_l R_l D_l||_2 <= A_T D_0/(l+1),                  (1)
    E[e_l^4] <= B_T^2 D_0^2 H_l^2/n^2,                  (2)
    E[e_l^2 Q_l R_l D_l]
       <= A_T B_T D_0^2 H_l/[n(l+1)],                   (3)
    E[Q_l^2 R_l^2 D_l^2] <= A_T^2 D_0^2/(l+1)^2.       (4)

The constants are not claimed sharp. All expectations refer to the actual
coupled chain; Q and R, and their angular gap, are not independent.

## 1. Settled marginal input

We use T244-w691-C027 v1, equations (11)-(12) of
urn:mb-local:70868895e24d4cc2
The exact version has reviewer claude-738954b6 PASS in its CLAIMS record;
the proof file retains its historical unaudited heading. Only its
unconditional finite-width moment bound is used, not its conditional
limiting-law consequence. It applies separately to both marginals here:
their shared rows across inputs do not change either marginal kernel.

For order 4, its nonsingleton partition constant is
C_4=6*3+3*3^2+4*15+105=210, and its c=1/2048.
Equation (12) gives, for 2<=l<=Tn,

    ||Q_l||_4 <= [8/(c l)] exp[C_4(4+T)/4]
                <= K_T/(l+1),

because (l+1)/l<=2. At l=0 and 1 the same last bound follows from
Q_l<=1 and K_T>=2. Identical bounds hold for R_l. We take this audited
scalar result as ground; the argument below concerns the coupled gap.

## 2. Unnormalized distance retains its initial-gap scale

Set P_l=Q_l+R_l-2C_l. This is the empirical squared distance and

    P_l=(sqrt(Q_l)-sqrt(R_l))^2+2sqrt(Q_l R_l)D_l >=0.

Given the past, A_i-B_i are iid N(0,P_l). Since tanh is 1-Lipschitz,

    P_(l+1) <= mean (A_i-B_i)^2.

For any integer p>=1, conditionally on the past,

    E[P_(l+1)^p | past]
       <= P_l^p product_(k=0)^(p-1)(1+2k/n)
       <= P_l^p exp[p(p-1)/n].                         (5)

The product is the exact pth moment of chi-square_n divided by n^p:
it follows from the Gaussian-square mgf (1-2t)^(-n/2), differentiating
p times at zero. When P_l=0 the difference is identically zero and (5)
continues to hold. Iterated conditional expectation, not independence of
states at distinct layers, proves

    E P_l^4 <= P_0^4 exp(12l/n),
    ||P_l||_4 <= P_0 exp(3T)=2sD_0 exp(3T).            (6)

## 3. The second mixed source

Let M_l=||Q_l R_l D_l||_2. The nonnegative distance identity gives
2sqrt(Q_l R_l)D_l<=P_l. Hence, pointwise,

    (Q_l R_l D_l)^2 <= Q_l R_l P_l^2/4
                        <= (Q_l+R_l)^2 P_l^2/16.

Cauchy-Schwarz and the triangle inequality now give

    M_l <= (1/4)||Q_l+R_l||_4 ||P_l||_4
          <= K_T s exp(3T)D_0/(l+1).

This proves (1) and (4), without separating dependent factors.

## 4. Closing C013 and the first mixed source

Use C013 v1 equation (1), with its B=e_l^2+8Q_lR_lD_l and a<=1.
C013 is an explicitly identified unaudited dependency; its finite
one-step estimate is not re-proved here. Put z_l=(E e_l^4)^(1/2).
Cauchy-Schwarz bounds E[e_l^2 Q_lR_lD_l]<=z_l M_l.
Expand C013's B and B^2 and take total expectations to obtain

    z_(l+1)^2 <= (1+18/n+1079/n^2)z_l^2
                  +(144/n+17264/n^2)z_l M_l
                  +69056 M_l^2/n^2.                  (7)

All coefficients and variables on the right are nonnegative. Since
528>=18, 69696>=1079, 528>=144, 139392>=17264, and 69696>=69056,
the right side is at most [(1+264/n)z_l+264M_l/n]^2. Thus

    z_(l+1) <= (1+264/n)z_l+264M_l/n.                 (8)

The equal initial variances give z_0=0. Iterating the deterministic
inequality (8), then applying (1), yields for l<=Tn

    z_l <= (264/n) sum_(j=0)^(l-1)
                    (1+264/n)^(l-1-j) M_j
         <= 264 exp(264T) A_T D_0 H_l/n.

Squaring proves (2). The same Cauchy-Schwarz estimate with (1) gives
(3). At l=0 these statements hold directly. If D_0=0 the paired features
coincide at every layer and all four inequalities hold with zero sides.
The case c_0=-1 is permitted and does not require a positive lower gap.

## Scope and remaining obstruction

The two mixed sources named at the end of C013 are now bounded entirely
in terms of the deterministic initial gap and explicit constants.
For L>=1, sum_(l=0)^(L-1) z_l <=B_T D_0 L H_L/n.
In particular H_L<=1+log L. For 0<eps<1 and L<=n^(1-eps),

    (L/n)(1+log L)
       <= [1+2/(exp(1) eps)] sqrt(L/n),

because sqrt(L/n)<=n^(-eps/2), log L<=log n, and
x exp(-eps x/2)<=2/(exp(1)eps) for x>=0.
Thus this accumulated radial source fits the requested sqrt(L/n)
scale, with eps-dependent constants. It does not by itself prove the
angular recursion, a readout Wasserstein bound, or all of Target 1.
The remaining hard step is the stochastic angular-gap recursion with
predictable products and their inverses: a final product depends on
future innovations, so its moment bound cannot simply be multiplied by
a martingale variance. A valid higher-moment martingale argument (or a
different coupling) is still required. No independence shortcut is used

Every continuous map f from the closed unit ball B^n in R^n to itself has a fixed point: some x with f(x) = x. Convexity and compactness are what matter: the theorem holds for any nonempty compact convex subset of R^n in place of the ball.

In particular any continuous map of a nonempty closed interval [a,b] into itself has a fixed point. The hypotheses cannot be dropped in general: on S^1 in R^2, the half-turn f(x)=-x is continuous and has no fixed point although S^1 is compact; on R^n for n>=1, f(x)=x+v with v nonzero is continuous and has no fixed point although R^n is convex.

    For every $0\le \alpha\le 2/3$, the following hold a.s.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[{\rm(1)}] $C_\alpha$ is compact and path-connected,
        \item[{\rm(2)}] $C\subseteq C_\alpha\subseteq C_\beta$ for every $0\le \beta<\alpha$,
        \item[{\rm(3)}] $\mathcal{B}_R(z)\subseteq C_\alpha$ for every $z\in C$ such that $\mathcal{B}_{6R}(z)\cap A_C=\emptyset$,
        \item[{\rm(4)}] $\partial(C_\alpha)\cap \partial(C_\beta)=\emptyset$ whenever $\alpha\not=\beta$,
        \item[{\rm(5)}] if $D\subseteq \omega^{(\lambda)}_p$ is a cell that belongs to a different cluster than $C$, then $C_\alpha\cap D_\beta=\emptyset$ for every $0<\beta\le 2/3$.
    \end{enumerate}

[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $\mathbf a_*\in D$ be a strict local minimum point of $H$, and choose
$\rho>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
  B_\rho(\mathbf a_*)\Subset D,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  H(\mathbf b)>H(\mathbf a_*)
  \quad
  \bigl(
  \mathbf b\in\overline{B_\rho(\mathbf a_*)}
  \setminus\{\mathbf a_*\}
  \bigr).
\end{equation}
Fix $\kappa,M,R>0$.  Then there exist positive constants
$C$, $\eta_0$, and $\varepsilon_0$, depending only on
$D,\mathbf a_*,\rho,\kappa,M$, and $R$, such that the following holds.

For every $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, let
$\mathbf a_\varepsilon\in B_\rho(\mathbf a_*)$, and let
$\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\in L^\infty(D)$ be nonnegative and satisfy
\[
  \int_D\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\,\mathrm d\mathbf x=\kappa,
  \qquad
  \|\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\|_\infty\leq M\varepsilon^{-2},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\omega_{\varepsilon,0}
  \subset B_{R\varepsilon}(\mathbf a_\varepsilon).
\]
Let $\omega_{\varepsilon,t}$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the corresponding Yudovich
solution of (equation eq:euler-intro of the paper).  If
\begin{equation}
  \eta_{\varepsilon,0}
  :=\mathcal D(\omega_{\varepsilon,0})
  +\kappa^2[H(\mathbf a_\varepsilon)-H(\mathbf a_*)]
  +\varepsilon
  \leq\eta_0,
\end{equation}
then, for every $t\in\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf C(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})\subset B_\rho(\mathbf a_*)
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal D(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})
  +\kappa^2\sup_{\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})}
  [H(\mathbf b)-H(\mathbf a_*)]
  \leq C\eta_{\varepsilon,0}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Quantitative estimates: one vortex

body: The Feynman–Kac formula, named after Richard Feynman and Mark Kac, establishes a link between parabolic partial differential equations and stochastic processes. In 1947, when Kac and Feynman were both faculty members at Cornell University, Kac attended a presentation of Feynman's and remarked that the two of them were working on the same thing from different directions. The Feynman–Kac formula resulted, which proves rigorously a real-valued analogy to Feynman's path integrals. The complex case, needed in quantum mechanics, is still an open question.
title: Feynman–Kac formula

[Lemma lem:independence of arXiv:2606.11951, 'On Skorokhod Problems for Reflected and Singular Stochastic Heat Equations'] Let $x\in (0,1)$. Then it holds that $\beta_x$ and $\beta^{\mathrm{pin},x}$ (as introduced in Definition (def:l_and_bb_pin of the paper)) are independent. Further, the integration formula
    \begin{align}
    	\mathbb{E}\left[ F(\beta) \psi (\beta_x) \right]
    	&= \int_{\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{E}\left[ F(\beta^{\mathrm{pin},x}+y l^x)\right] \psi (y) \, \mathcal{N}(0,x(1-x))(dy) \nonumber\\
    	&= \int_{\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{E}\left[ F(\beta+(y-\beta_x) l^x)\right] \psi (y) \, \mathcal{N}(0,x(1-x))(dy)
    \end{align}
    holds for any $\psi \in C_b(\mathbb{R})$ and any bounded Borel-measurable map $F \colon L \to \mathbb{R}$.

[Theorem 24 (Uniform convergence in probability) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Assume Assumptions~\ref{ass:baseline}--\ref{ass:solutions} and suppose $B,A,S<1$. Then there exists a constant $C>0$, independent of $h$, such that, for every $h>0$, if $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1]$, then
\[
\Pbb\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}>h\right)
\le \frac{C}{h}\left[|x_0-\wt x_0|^{\alpha-1}
+\max\left\{
B^{\frac{\alpha\wt\eta-1}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+1}},
A^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}},
S^{\alpha-1/\wt\eta}
\right\}\right].
\]
If $\wt\eta=1/\alpha$ and $\Theta=\max\{B,A,S\}\in(0,1)$, then
\[
\Pbb\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}>h\right)
\le \frac{C}{h}\left[|x_0-\wt x_0|^{\alpha-1}
+\left(\log\frac1\Theta\right)^{-1}\right].
\]
When $\Theta=0$, the right-hand side is interpreted as $C|x_0-\wt x_0|^{\alpha-1}/h$.

body: [Corollary 4 of arXiv:2609.03495, 'Spectral Characteristics of Autoencoder Parameters as a Vector Representation of Data'] The loss function $\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\psi}_c)$ with the addition of the regularization term ${\|\text{cov}(\mathbf{h}_c) - \mathbf{I}\|^2}$, which decorrelates the vectors $\mathbf{h}_c$ in the hidden space, makes the autoencoder closer in its properties to a VAE, since the covariance matrix of the hidden (latent) representation becomes diagonal, which is characteristic of a VAE. This observation allows the results of Theorem~\ref{theorem:1} to be used as evidence that hypothesis~\ref{statement} holds for both AE and VAE models. \begin{enumerate}[ label = (\roman*) ]

    				j^m

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Explicit model calculation and hypothesis obstruction Result: For constant divergence-free transport fields on a torus or R3, write the equation in Stratonovich form with the matching second-order Ito correction. Let Z_t=sum b_n W_t^n. If v is a deterministic Navier-Stokes solution, u(t,x)=v(t,x+Z_t) solves the corresponding stochastic equation by Ito-Wentzell. Translation is an isometry on Lq and homogeneous Besov norms. Hence in this special commuting case a deterministic local theory transfers without any loss of its spatial smoothness threshold. Check: The quadratic-variation drift is (1/2)sum (b_n dot grad)^2u. Stating this correction is essential: deleting Ito transport without correcting viscosity would solve a different equation. The Leray projection commutes with constant translations. Obstruction: For spatially varying coefficients the flow is not a translation, the transformed Laplacian has random variable coefficients, and the pressure projection no longer simply commutes. No general endpoint estimate or optimality proof is obtained. The2026 high-probability global result uses chosen noise and smoother initial spaces, so its abstract does not settle this question.
