    on the real line and $K\subseteq D$ a compact subset. Let $c_{1}$

    \]
    for all $z,w\in K$.

body:
[Proposition 22 (Isotropic range evolution) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] At level $t$, conditionally on
$(L_t,R_t)=(\ell,r)\in\N^2$, the proposed graft rate is
$\ell+r+1$. If $U$ is uniform on $\{-\ell,\ldots,r\}$ and
$(L_t',R_t')$ is an independent copy of $(L_t,R_t)$, then the proposed
update is
\begin{equation}

        (\ell,r)
        \longmapsto
        \bigl(\max\{\ell,L_t'-U\},\max\{r,R_t'+U\}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Null updates are allowed.

[Proposition of arXiv:2604.17253, 'Large Deviations for the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation with Randomized Quasi-Periodic Ini'] The domain ${\mathrm D}^{(k,\gamma^{(k)})}$ admits a canonical identification with
\begin{align*}
{\mathscr D}^{(k,\gamma^{(k)})}=
\begin{cases}
\prod_{j=1}^d \mathbb{Z}^{\nu_j}, & \gamma^{(k)}=0,\ k\ge1;\\
\prod_{j=1}^d (\mathbb{Z}^{\nu_j})^3, & \gamma^{(1)}=1;\\
\prod_{j=1}^3 {\mathscr D}^{(k-1,\gamma_j^{(k-1)})}, & \gamma^{(k)}\in(\Gamma^{(k-1)})^3,\ k\ge2.
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
This identification is induced by coordinate-wise projection.

More precisely, for each $j=1,\dots,d$, we define the projection
\[
\iota_{x_j}:\left(\prod_{j=1}^d \mathbb{Z}^{\nu_j}\right)^s \to (\mathbb{Z}^{\nu_j})^s,
\quad
\iota_{x_j}\big((q_1^1,\dots,q_d^1),\dots,(q_1^s,\dots,q_d^s)\big)
= (q_j^1,\dots,q_j^s).
\]
The full map $\iota=(\iota_{x_1},\dots,\iota_{x_d})$ induces the above identification. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Given a parametric family {f(.;theta): theta in Theta} and data X, a statistic T(X) is sufficient for theta if the conditional distribution of X given T(X) = t does not depend on theta, for (almost) every value t in the range of T. Equivalently, by the Fisher-Neyman factorization criterion, T is sufficient for theta if and only if the density or pmf factors as f(x;theta) = g(T(x), theta) * h(x) for some functions g >= 0 and h >= 0, where h does not depend on theta.
title: Sufficient Statistic

[Lemma 12 (Kneser) of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $A,B$ be subsets of a locally compact, abelian group $G$ and let $\mu$ 
denote (a version of) the Haar measure on $G$. If there exists an open 
subgroup $H$ such that 
$$
A+B+H=A+B \quad\text{and}\quad \mu(A+B+H) = \mu(A+H) + \mu(B+H)-\mu(H),
$$
then 
$$
\mu(A+B) \geq \mu(A)+\mu(B)-\mu(H).
$$
Otherwise, 
$$
\mu^*(A+B) \geq \mu(A)+\mu(B),
$$
where $\mu^*$ denotes the inner measure induced by $\mu$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Choose positive integers n,L,M,D and D'>=0, parameter bound B>0, token clipping radius R>0, a label bound B_y>=1, and confidence 0<xi<1. Consider fixed-length in-context prediction instances Z=(H,y), with |y|<=B_y almost surely, drawn independently from one meta-distribution. In the paper's setting one first draws a task distribution P, then draws the context and query example iid from P. A transformer has L residual blocks, each consisting of normalized ReLU attention followed by a residual two-layer ReLU MLP; it has token dimension D, at most M attention heads per block, and MLP hidden width at most D'. For S tokens, attention sends h_i to h_i+(1/S) sum_m sum_j ReLU(<Q_m h_i,K_m h_j>) V_m h_j. The MLP sends h to h+W_2 ReLU(W_1 h). Project every input token and every block's output token onto the Euclidean radius-R ball. Read out the designated label coordinate of the final query token and clip it to [-B_y,B_y]. Restrict parameters to the class Theta with norm max_block(max_m{||Q_m||op,||K_m||op}+sum_m ||V_m||op+||W_1||op+||W_2||op)<=B. Write L(theta)=E[(y-prediction_theta(H))^2/2] and let hat theta be any exact empirical minimizer of the same loss over Theta on n independent instances. There is a universal C such that, with probability at least 1-xi, L(hat theta)<=inf_(theta in Theta) L(theta)+C B_y^2 sqrt((L^2(M D^2+D D') log(2+max{B,R,B_y})+log(1/xi))/n). This is an expected loss over the meta-distribution. Source: arXiv:2306.04637, Section 5.1 and Theorem 20, PDF pages 14–15; proof Appendix J.2, PDF page 89. The harmless choice B_y>=1 is stated explicitly here; any smaller valid label bound may be enlarged to one.
n,L,M,D positive integers; D'>=0; B,R>0; B_y>=1; 0<xi<1
The n pretraining instances are iid from the same meta-distribution and the query label is bounded by B_y
Normalized ReLU attention, residual ReLU MLP, input and hidden-token Euclidean projection at radius R, and prediction clipping at B_y
The specified transformer parameter norm is at most B and hat theta is an exact constrained empirical risk minimizer

body: In first-passage percolation on Z^2 with edge weights confined to [a, b] with a > 0, any geodesic from the origin to (0, r) satisfies a DETERMINISTIC bound on its transversal excursion: it never attains transversal level D > r(b - a)/(2a). The proof is elementary counting: reaching transversal level D forces at least r + 2D edges, each of weight at least a, giving passage time at least a(r + 2D), while the straight path gives at most b r; the two are incompatible beyond the stated level. No probabilistic input is used, so the bound holds for every realisation.

Agresti and Veraar, Nonlinear parabolic stochastic evolution equations in critical spaces (journal version 2025, p. 130), Problem 4 asks whether in the variational setting of their Theorem 6.4 there is a constant C_T with E sup_{t <= T} ||u(t)||_H^2 <= C_T (1 + E ||u_0||_H^2) for all u_0 in L^2(Omega; H). Our result (id P0266, 2026-09-08): the bound FAILS, on the authors' own named unresolved example - Allen-Cahn on the one-dimensional torus with one-dimensional quadratic noise, du = (Laplacian u + u - u^3) dt + gamma u^2 dW, at the critical gamma^2 = 2. With deterministic constant data u_0 = a > 0 the solution stays spatially constant, and the substitutions Y = 1/U, Y = e^{-t} V, time change s = (e^{2t} - 1)/2 and R = V / sqrt 2 turn the SDE into R being a four-dimensional Bessel process started at R_0 = 1/(sqrt 2 a), with U_t = e^t / (sqrt 2 R_s). Since sup_{t <= T} U_t^2 >= 1/(2 inf_{s <= S} R_s^2) and a BES(4) enters a ball of radius x with probability of order x^2 (Newtonian capacity), P(sup U^2 > y) is of order 1/y - tail index one - so E sup_{t <= T} ||u(t)||_H^2 = infinity for every T > 0 while E ||u_0||_H^2 = a^2 is finite. Verification as the source words it: checked in the reverse direction by Ito as well; and an instrument note - a first simulation appeared to contradict the x^2 scaling, but refining the steps at fixed x drives P/x^2 toward the exact constant 2.0 (1.204, 1.579, 1.697 at x = 0.2 and 0.725, 1.285, 1.455 at x = 0.1), so the scaling is real. NOT Lean-checked: this one has no finite arithmetic core, being Ito calculus plus a capacity estimate. Prior art not cleared; the source is a year old, so the memo rates this among the likeliest to be genuinely new.

body:
[Corollary cor:iterated-suspension of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $t\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ and put $A^{(0)}=A$.  For each $1\leq i\leq t$, choose an
integer $\ell_i\geq2$ and a specified $c_i$ having a length-$\ell_i$
representation by points of $A^{(i-1)}$ with $\gcd(c_i,\ell_i)=1$, and set
$A^{(i)}=\Sigma_{\ell_i,c_i}A^{(i-1)}$.  Put
$R=\prod_{i=1}^t\ell_i$, with the empty product equal to one.  Then, for
$q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$,
\begin{align}
 \mathcal H_{A^{(t)}}(z)
 &=\mathcal H_A(z)\prod_{i=1}^t[\ell_i]_z,
 \\
 |qA^{(t)}|
 &=\sum_{\substack{0\leq j_i<\ell_i\\
                    j_1+\cdots+j_t\leq q}}
   |(q-j_1-\cdots-j_t)A|,
 \\
 \mathcal K_{A^{(t)}}(z)
 &=\mathcal K_A(z)\prod_{i=1}^t(1-z^{\ell_i}),
 \\
 \mathcal B_{A^{(t)}}(\xi,z)
 &=\mathcal B_A(\xi,z)\prod_{i=1}^t(1+\xi z^{\ell_i}),
 \\
 \operatorname{ndiam}(A^{(t)})&=R\operatorname{ndiam}(A).
 
\end{align}
If every $\ell_i\leq q$, then
\[
 r_q(A^{(t)})=r_q(A)+t,\qquad
 \operatorname{fdim}_q(A^{(t)})=\operatorname{fdim}_q(A).
\]
If the starting projective coordinate ring is ACM, then the ACM property
and Cohen--Macaulay type are preserved.

The construction embeds into every r>=2,p>r and any unequal pair of positive target singular values. Y_*=[[3/5,4/5,0],[0,0,1]].

Y'=M^(-1)Y H(I-Y^TY).

The signal block obeys S'=M^(-1)S diag(1,mu^2)(I-S^TS). At Y_*, the derivative of its determinant is the component of the second row derivative along x:

D'(0) = (1/3) v diag(1,mu^2) x^T
      = (4/25)(mu^2-1) <0.

Compactness of St ensures that the flow through Y_* exists both forward and backward in time. Since D(0)=0 and D'(0)<0, for all sufficiently small delta>0 its determinant is positive at time -delta and negative at time +delta. Start instead at the full-signal-rank frame Y(-delta): it crosses zero after a finite positive time. Strict signs at the two endpoints persist under perturbations of both the initial frame and the SPD parameter M, by continuous dependence on initial conditions and parameters. Thus the crossing is present on an open subset of SPD_2 times St(2,3).

The smooth polar map G=M^(1/2)Y takes this to an open set of full-row-rank 2-by-3 matrices. Every nonempty open subset has positive iid-Gaussian probability. The initial signal block of G is invertible because both M^(1/2) and S_initial are invertible. If M is scalar, or the two positive singular values coincide, the displayed transverse derivative vanishes. This explains why the flat-spectrum arguments do not supply this unequal-spectrum barrier automatically. Let (X, mu) and (Y, nu) be sigma-finite measure spaces, 1 <= p_0 < p_1 <= infinity, and let T be a SUBLINEAR operator defined on L^{p_0}(mu) + L^{p_1}(mu) with values in the measurable functions on Y, which is of WEAK type (p_0, p_0) with constant A_0 and of weak type (p_1, p_1) with constant A_1 (for p_1 = infinity this means ||Tf||_infinity <= A_1 ||f||_infinity). Then for every p with p_0 < p < p_1, T is of strong type (p,p): ||Tf||_{L^p(nu)} <= C ||f||_{L^p(mu)} for all f in L^p(mu), where one may take C = 2 (p/(p - p_0) + p/(p_1 - p))^{1/p} A_0^{1-theta} A_1^{theta} with 1/p = (1-theta)/p_0 + theta/p_1, and the term p/(p_1 - p) is read as 0 when p_1 = infinity. The constant blows up as p tends to p_0 or to p_1, and the conclusion genuinely fails at the endpoints. Off-diagonal version: if T is of weak types (p_0, q_0) and (p_1, q_1) with p_0 not equal to p_1, q_0 not equal to q_1, and p_i <= q_i for i = 0,1, then T is of strong type (p_theta, q_theta) for 0 < theta < 1, with 1/p_theta and 1/q_theta the interpolated exponents.

[Lemma lem:fromboxestointegrals of arXiv:2609.01825, 'On everywhere locally soluble varieties \\ in families over toric bases'] Let $\vec W = (\log (B/X_1), \dots, \log (B/X_k)) = (\log \theta) \vec U_{\!-}$ and $1< \theta \leq 2$. Then for $\gamma > \max_{1\leq l\leq k} \sum_{i=1}^s \frac{\varpi_{li}}{\alpha_i}$ we have
	\begin{multline*}
		\sum_{\vec j \in \cal P(\vec U_{\!-})} \sum_{\vec x \in \cal B_{\vec j}} f(\vec x)
		= c_f \Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^s \alpha_i^{-\ell_i}\Bigr) \int_{\cal P(\vec W)}  \prod_{i=1}^s \mathrm e^{t_i} (1+t_i )^{\ell_i} \,\mathrm d\vec t\\
		+ O\biggl(
		C_f (\log \theta)^{-s} \int_{\cal P(\vec W)} \bigl(1 + \min\nolimits_i t_i\bigr)^{-\delta} \prod_{i=1}^s \mathrm e^{t_i} (1 + t_i)^{\ell_i} \,\mathrm d\vec t
		\biggr)\\
		+ O\biggl(
		C_f \int_{\Xi'} \prod_{i=1}^s \mathrm e^{t_i} (1 + t_i)^{\ell_i} \,\mathrm d\vec t
		\biggr),
	\end{multline*}
	where
	\begin{equation*}
		\Xi' = \cal P(\vec W) \setminus \cal P(\vec W - (\gamma \log \theta, \dots, \gamma \log \theta)).
	\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:fromboxestointegrals of arXiv:2609.01825

body: [Theorem 11 of arXiv:2512.19063, 'Sharp Decoupling Inequalities for the Variances and Second Moments of Sums of Dependent Ra'] With the same setting as Theorem 6, we have a Chebyshev-type inequality for any $t>0$, $\mathbb{P}\left(|S_{n}-\mathbb{E} S_{n}|>t\right)\leq\frac{2\operatorname{Var}(S^{\prime}_{n})}{t^{2}}.$ (15) If in addition $S_{n}\geq 0$ a.s., we have a Paley-Zygmund-type inequality for any $0<\theta<1$, $\mathbb{P}(S_{n}>\theta\,\mathbb{E} S_{n})\geq(1-\theta)^{2}\,\frac{(\mathbb{E} S_{n})^{2}}{2\mathbb{E}{S^{\prime}}_{n}^{2}-(\mathbb{E} S_{n})^{2}}=(1-\theta)^{2}\,\frac{1}{\frac{2\mathbb{E}{S^{\prime}}_{n}^{2}}{(\mathbb{E} S_{n})^{2}}-1}.$

[Lemma 2 (Theorem 7.11, \cite{Fen10}) of arXiv:2605.12475, 'Central limit theorem for the homozygosity of the hierarchical Pitman-Yor process'] Suppose $\bm{X} = (X_1, X_2, \ldots) \sim \PD(\alpha, \theta)$. Let 
\bal
\tilde{H}_m(\alpha, \theta) = \sqrt{\theta}\left( \frac{\theta^{m-1}}{(1 - \alpha)_{(m-1)}}  \sum_{i = 1}^\infty X_i^m - 1 \right), \qquad m \geq 2,
\eal
be the scaled $m$th order homozygosity. Then
\bal
(\tilde{H}_2(\alpha, \theta), \tilde{H}_3(\alpha, \theta), \ldots) \xrightarrow{D} (H_2(\alpha), H_3(\alpha), \ldots)
\eal
as $\theta \to \infty$, where $\bm{H} = (H_2(\alpha), H_3(\alpha), \ldots)$ is a $\R^\infty$-valued random vector such that for all $r \geq 2$, $(H_2(\alpha), \ldots, H_r(\alpha))$ has a multivariate normal distribution with zero mean and covariance matrix
\bal
\cov(H_i(\alpha), H_j(\alpha)) = \frac{(1 - \alpha)_{(i+j-1)}}{(1 - \alpha)_{(i-1)}(1 - \alpha)_{(j-1)}} + \alpha - ij, \qquad i,j = 2, \ldots, r.
\eal (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 7.11, \cite{Fen10}

On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. For rho in [-1, 1], T_rho is the noise operator: T_rho f(x) = E[f(Y)] where the Y_i are independent with P(Y_i = x_i) = (1 + rho)/2, so T_rho chi_S = rho^|S| chi_S. For 0 <= rho <= 1, (1 - rho) Var(f) <= D_rho(f) <= (1 - rho^n) Var(f). For 0 < rho < 1 and nonconstant f, equality on the left holds iff all the nonconstant Walsh mass is at level 1, and on the right iff it is at level n; at rho = 0 and rho = 1 both bounds are equalities for every f. If 0 <= rho < sigma <= 1 then D_rho(f) >= D_sigma(f), strictly when f is not constant. No such monotonicity holds on [-1, 1]: D_rho(x_1 x_2) = 1 - rho^2 increases on [-1, 0].

Let N=N(n) with N/n->c in (0,infinity). For all n,i,j let X_ij^(n) be real independent identically distributed random variables with mean zero, variance one, and E|X_ij^(n)|^(4+epsilon)<infinity for some epsilon>0. Let sigma_ij(n) be deterministic real numbers uniformly bounded in absolute value. Let A_n be deterministic real N-by-n matrices whose row Euclidean norms and column Euclidean norms are uniformly bounded over all n and all rows and columns. Put (Y_n)_ij=sigma_ij(n) X_ij^(n)/sqrt(n) and Sigma_n=Y_n+A_n. For the relevant N,n, write A=A_n and sigma_ij=sigma_ij(n), D_j=diag(sigma_1j^2,...,sigma_Nj^2), and Dtilde_i=diag(sigma_i1^2,...,sigma_in^2). Let S_plus consist of the functions z->integral_[0,infinity) (lambda-z)^(-1) nu(dlambda) for probability measures nu on [0,infinity), analytically continued to C minus [0,infinity). Define the unique S_plus-valued solution psi_i,psitilde_j by psi_i(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(Dtilde_i Ttilde(z))/n)] and psitilde_j(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(D_j T(z))/n)], where Psi=diag(psi_i), Psitilde=diag(psitilde_j), T(z)=[Psi(z)^(-1)-z A Psitilde(z) A^T]^(-1), and Ttilde(z)=[Psitilde(z)^(-1)-z A^T Psi(z) A]^(-1). Both trace terms in these canonical equations use division by n. Let P_n be the empirical eigenvalue probability measure of Sigma_n Sigma_n^T and pi_n the deterministic probability measure with Stieltjes transform tr(T_n(z))/N. Then, for every n, E integral lambda P_n(dlambda) = integral lambda pi_n(dlambda) = (1/(N n)) sum_{i=1}^N sum_{j=1}^n sigma_ij(n)^2 + tr(A_n A_n^T)/N. In particular both first moments are bounded uniformly in n by sigma_max^2+a_max^2, where sigma_max bounds all |sigma_ij(n)| and a_max bounds all row and column Euclidean norms of A_n. The empirical first moment appears under expectation in this equality; the deterministic first-moment identity is exact, not merely asymptotic.

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2608.26084, 'Localic Esakia Duality\\via Conic Frames'] Let~$(X,\leq)$ be a Priestley space. A subset~$C\subseteq X$ is called a \emph{clopen upper set} if~$C$ is clopen and~$\up C= C$. The collection of clopen upper sets is denoted~$\ClopUp(X)$, and forms a distributive lattice under set-theoretic intersections and unions.

	If~$(X,\leq)$ is an Esakia space, then~$\ClopUp(X)$ moreover forms a Heyting algebra, with implication given for clopen upper sets~$A,B\subseteq X$ by~(\cite[\S 2]{bezhanishvili2023FrametheoreticPerspectiveEsakia}):
	\[
	A\to B
	:=
	X\setminus \down (A\setminus B).
	\]

body: [Lemma 6 (Bennett's integral \citep{bennett1948spectra}) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] For a high-resolution quantizer with local step $\Delta(x)$ and input density $p$ whose overload distortion is negligible, as holds in particular when $p$ is supported within the quantizer's granular range, the distortion is $D=\tfrac{1}{12}\int \Delta(x)^2 p(x)\,dx$, the integral taken over that range. For a uniform quantizer ($\Delta$ constant, overload negligible) this reduces to the additive-white-noise model $D=\Delta^2/12$, with quantization error approximately uniform on $[-\Delta/2,\Delta/2]$ and decorrelated from the signal. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (X_n) be a martingale for (F_n) and let (H_n)_{n >= 1} be PREDICTABLE, meaning H_n is F_{n-1}-measurable. Define the transform (H . X)_n = sum_{k=1}^{n} H_k (X_k - X_{k-1}), with (H . X)_0 = 0. If each H_n is bounded (or, more generally, if H_n (X_n - X_{n-1}) is integrable for every n), then (H . X) is a martingale. If (X_n) is a SUPERMARTINGALE and in addition H_n >= 0 for every n, then (H . X) is a supermartingale; the same with submartingale. Predictability is the load-bearing hypothesis: H_n may depend on everything known strictly before time n but not on the outcome at time n. Without it the conclusion is false - taking H_n = sgn(X_n - X_{n-1}) gives (H . X)_n = sum |X_k - X_{k-1}|, which is nondecreasing and not a martingale unless the increments vanish. The nonnegativity requirement in the supermartingale case is also necessary, since multiplying by -1 turns a supermartingale into a submartingale. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Section 10.6]

Its Stieltjes transform, with convention m_nu(zeta)=integral(lambda-zeta)^(-1)dnu(lambda), Im(zeta)>0, is m_nu(zeta)=t_L((c_-1-zeta,c_0,...,c_L),(1,0,...,0)). In particular put a=E[sigma'(Z)^2], q_l=(b^2)^(L-l) and r_plus=sum_(l=0)^(L-1)[a^(L-l)-q_l]. For the scalar-output NTK at initialization, K_NTK=(grad_theta f_theta(X_0))^T*(grad_theta f_theta(X_0)), where f_theta(X_0)=w^T*X_L and theta includes all hidden and readout weights, the limiting transform is m_NTK(zeta)=t_L((r_plus-zeta,q_0,...,q_(L-1),1),(1,0,...,0)). Also ||K_NTK||_op<=C almost surely eventually. This is a bulk law, not a theorem of convergence of individual extreme eigenvalues or of spectra after training.
Fixed integer depth L>=1; n,d_0,...,d_L tend to infinity; n/d_l->gamma_l in (0,infinity) for l=1,...,L.
All weights W_l in R^(d_l by d_(l-1)) and w in R^d_L have independent N(0,1) entries, independent of the input matrices.
sigma:R->R is twice differentiable with globally bounded first and second derivatives. For Z~N(0,1), E sigma(Z)=0 and E sigma(Z)^2=1.
X_0 is (epsilon_n,B)-orthonormal as in the companion definition for constant B, epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0; the ESD of X_0^T X_0 converges to a deterministic probability measure mu_0.
X_l=d_l^(-1/2)*sigma(W_l X_(l-1)); scalar output f_theta(X_0)=w^T X_L; theta contains all hidden and readout weights; K_NTK=(grad_theta f)^T grad_theta f at random initialization.
b=E sigma'(Z) is nonzero, Z~N(0,1).
Explicit input condition: for every column x_alpha, | ||x_alpha||^2-1 |<=epsilon_n; for alpha!=beta, |x_alpha^T*x_beta|<=epsilon_n; ||X_0||_op<=B; sum_alpha (||x_alpha||^2-1)^2<=B^2. B is constant and epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0.

[Theorem teo_fey_kac of arXiv:2605.07832, 'A Bismut -Elworthy formula for BSDEs with degenerate noise'] Let hypotheses (ip_forward of the paper), (ip_forward_agg of the paper) and (ip-psiphi of the paper)
hold true.  Moreover assume that $\phi$ is G\^ateaux differentiable with bounded derivative and that $\psi$ is G\^ateaux differentiable with respect to $x$, $y$ and $z$ \textcolor{red}{with bounded derivatives}. The nonlinear Kolmogorov equation ((Kolmo of the paper)) has a unique mild solution $v$ given by the formula
$$v(t, x) = Y_t^{t,x} ,\qquad     (t, x) \in [0, T ] \times H,$$
where $(X^{t,x},Y ^{t,x} , Z^{ t,x} )$ is the solution to the FBSDE (equation fbsde of the paper). Moreover, we
have, $\mathbb P$-a.s.,
\begin{align}

Y_s^{t,x} = v(s, X_s^{t,x} ),\quad       Z_s^{t,x} =\nabla_x v(s, X_s^{t,x} )\nabla_x  X_s^{t,x}G(s)
\end{align}
and, under our assumptions, there exists a constant $C$, that may depend also on $\nabla_x\phi$,
$\nabla_x\psi$ and $L_\psi$, such that
\begin{equation}
\vert Z_s^{t,x}\vert \leq C.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:from-r-to-l of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] Let the graph $G$ be finite and take $0\le l\le r$. We endow the subdivided graph $G_r$
  with i.i.d.\ edge weights $W_e>0$, $e\in E_r$. Consider the family $W^{(l)}$ of
  corresponding random weights
from Theorem (thm:vrjp-on-G-r-pos-rec of the paper), all realized on the same probability space
with expectation operator ${\mathbb E}$. We abbreviate
$C_\alpha:=2^{-\alpha}\Gamma(\tfrac12-\alpha)/\sqrt{\pi}$
for $0\le\alpha<\frac12$ and ${c_2}:=\gamma+\log 2=1.27036\ldots$, where 
\begin{align}
  
  \gamma=-\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\log t\, dt=0.57721\ldots
\end{align}
denotes the Euler Mascheroni constant. 
For all $\bar e\in E_l$ and $e'\in E_r$, one has
  \begin{align}
    
    {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]
    &\le (2^{-\alpha})^{r-l}{\mathbb E}[W_{e'}^\alpha]
    &\hspace{-1cm}\text{ for } \alpha\in[0,1],\\
    
    {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]
     &\le \frac{1}{C_\alpha}\min_{m\in\{l,\ldots,r\}}\left(C_\alpha 
       (2^{-\alpha})^{r-m}{\mathbb E}[W_{e'}^\alpha]\right)^{2^{m-l}}
     &\hspace{-1cm}\text{ for } \alpha\in[0,\tfrac12),
    \\
      
    {\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{\bar e}]
    &\le \min_{m\in\{l,\ldots,r\}}
      2^{m-l}\left({\mathbb E}[\log W_{e'}]-(r-m)\log 2+{c_2}\right)-{c_2}.
  \end{align}
  Set $m_0:=r-2-\lfloor\alpha^{-1}\log_2(C_\alpha {\mathbb E}[W_{e'}^\alpha])\rfloor$
  and $m_1:=r-2-\lfloor(\log 2)^{-1}({\mathbb E}[\log W_{e'}]+{c_2})\rfloor$.
  If $m_0\in\{l,\ldots,r\}$, a minimizer in (equation eq:combined-alpha of the paper)
  is given by $m=m_0$. If $m_0<l$ or $m_0>r$, it is given by
  $m=l$ or $m=r$, respectively. The analogous statement holds for $m_1$
  with (equation eq:combined-alpha of the paper) replaced by (equation eq:combined-log of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Decay of the effective weights by restriction

[Definition defextgraph of arXiv:2605.10617, 'Logarithmic scaling of selective sweep curves:\\ from tents to houses'] Let $f\in \mathcal D_I$.
  \begin{enumerate}[a)]
    \item 
      The  {\em extended graph} of $f$ is defined as
      $$
        \mathbb G(f)
         := \bigcup_{t\in I}\big(\{t\} \times [\min(f(t-),f(t)), \max(f(t-),f(t))]\big).
      $$
      Thus, in  words from~[K23], the extended graph  ``contains the graph together with the straight lines connecting the two ends of a jump discontinuity''.
    \item 
      A~{\em parametric representation} of (the extended graph of) $f$ is a mapping $\phi$ which maps $[0,1]$ onto $\mathbb G(f)$ and for which $u \mapsto \phi(u)$ is increasing with respect to the total order $\preceq$ on $\mathbb G(f)$ defined by
      $$
        (t_1,x_1)\preceq (t_2,x_2) :\Longleftrightarrow t_1\le t_2
          \mbox{ and } \left(t_1=t_2 \Rightarrow |x_1 - f(t_1-)| \le |x_2 - f(t_1-)|\right).
      $$
  \end{enumerate}
title: Definition defextgraph of arXiv:2605.10617

For independent nearest-neighbor bond percolation on Z^d, d>=2, take plane block centers c_z=L*(z_1,z_2,0,...,0), seed boxes S_z=c_z+[-L,L]^d, and outer boxes D_z(M)=c_z+[-M,M]^d, integers M>=L>=1. Select h_z as the first vertex in S_z reaching the boundary of D_z(M) internally. G_z requires h_z and its four neighboring anchors to exist and h_z to connect to each inside D_z(M+L). Put R=floor(2*(M+L)/L). If p0>0 and P_p0(G_0^c)<800^(-(R+1)^2), finite-product continuity preserves the strict margin at some p1<p0 and compatible anchors give theta_d(p1)>0. Hence the critical failure probability for every fixed pair is at least this threshold. This does not prove critical nonpercolation.

[Lem mass-from-high-to-low of arXiv:2607.05097, 'Asymptotics of Lyapunov Exponents and Phase Transitions for Fluids with Degenerate Forcing'] For every $(\tilde z_0,\tilde v_0) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times S^{n-1}$ and $\eta \in (0, \eta^*(\tilde z_0))$ there is some $\delta, C > 0$ such that for all $(z_0,v_0)$ with $$\|\tilde z_0 - z_0\| + \|\tilde v_0 - v_0\| \leq \delta$$
    and $\epsilon < \delta$ we have
    $$\mathbb{P}\Big(\sup_{t \leq C\ln\epsilon^{-1}} \|P_\eta(z_0)v^\epsilon(t)\| \geq \delta \Big) \geq \delta$$
    (where the process $(z^\epsilon(t), v^\epsilon(t))$ is defined as in (equation eq:zv-def of the paper) with initial condition $(z_0,v_0)$). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition 3 of arXiv:2601.22205, 'Transitive Sets of Mutually Orthogonal Latin Squares'] A Latin square is based on a group if it is isotopic to a Cayley table of a group. A set of cells meeting each row and each column exactly once, whose entries are all distinct, is a transversal of a Latin square. Suppose L = {lij} is the Cayley table of a quasigroup Q = {q0, . . . , qn−1} and T = {(0, j0), . . . , (n −1, jn−1)} is a transversal of L. Then the map θ: Q →Q defined by θ(qi) = qji is a bijection.

[Theorem mainthm of arXiv:2607.05418, 'On the Group Randomness of 0-1 Real Sequences from Binary Linear Codes'] Let $\{\mathcal{C}_n\}$ be a sequence of binary linear codes of length $n$ and dual distance $d_n^\bot$. Let $\widetilde{\Phi}_{\mathcal{C}_n}$ be the $p_n \times n$ 0-1 random matrix as constructed above, with $y:=p_n/n \in (0,1)$ fixed. Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{C}_n}$ be the Gram matrix of $\frac{2}{\sqrt{n}}\widetilde{\Phi}_{\mathcal{C}_n}$, and $\tilde{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}_n}$ denote the spectral measure of $\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{C}_n}$. Assume $d_n^\bot \geq 5$ for all $n$, then as $n \to \infty$,
        $$|\tilde{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}_n}(\mathbf{I})-\varrho_{\mathrm{MP}_y}(\mathbf{I})| \prec n^{-1/4}.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem mainthm of arXiv:2607.05418

[Lem description-of-Pinv of arXiv:2607.05097, 'Asymptotics of Lyapunov Exponents and Phase Transitions for Fluids with Degenerate Forcing'] Let $\mu \in P_{\mathrm{inv}}$ be ergodic. Then there is some $z_0$ such that $\mu(\{z = z_0\}) = 1$. Furthermore, there is some $i$ such that $\mu(\{v \in \operatorname{Span}(\{V_j \mid \Re \lambda_j = \Re \lambda_i\})\}) = 1$, where $V_1,\dots,V_k$ are the generalized eigenspaces of $A(z_0)$ corresponding to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k$. Additionally, we have
$$\int \Lambda(z,v)d\mu(z,v) = \Re \lambda_i \,.$$
In particular, if $\mu(\{P_0(z)v = 0\}) = 0$ then
$$\int \Lambda(z,v)d\mu(z,v) = \lambda(A(z_0)) \,.$$
title: Lem description-of-Pinv of arXiv:2607.05097

body: [Lemma 13 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Fix $\vec{y} \in \weyl_2$ and $b > 0$. Let $U$ be a reverse Brownian motion (with zero drift) on $[0,b]$ with $U(b) = 2^{-1/2}(y_1 + y_2)$ and $V$ an independent 3D Bessel bridge with $V_b=2^{-1/2}(y_1 - y_2)$. Define $B_1 = 2^{-1/2} (U + V)$ and $B_2 = 2^{-1/2}(U-V)$. Then, the law of $(B_1, B_2)$ is given by $\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{pin}}^{b, \vec{y}}$ as in Definition \ref{Def.PinnedPair}.

Let V be a finite set, X a random subset, q(A) = P(A subset of X) and p(B) = P(X = B). Then q(A) = sum over B containing A of p(B), and p(B) = sum over A containing B of (-1)^|A minus B| q(A). If y_k = sum over k-element A of q(A), then y_k = E[binom(|X|, k)], equivalently E[(|X|)_k] = k! y_k with the falling factorial; the law of |X| then follows from the y_k by Jordan's formula.

[Pro Pro1 of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] The following assertions hold.
\begin{itemize}
 \item[(i)] If $n\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$ and $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n$ are exchangeable random variables, then the $(n-1)$-dimensional random vectors
 \[
   (\xi_2,\xi_3,\ldots,\xi_n), \quad (\xi_1,\xi_3,\ldots,\xi_n),\quad \ldots\quad (\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots,\xi_{n-1})
 \]
 have the same distributions.
 
\item[(ii)]
If $h:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a Borel measurable function and $(\xi_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of exchangeable random variables, then $(h(\xi_n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is also exchangeable.

\item[(iii)]
If $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\in\mathbb{R}$, and $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n$ are exchangeable random variables,
 then, for each permutation $\sigma$ of $(1,\ldots,n)$, we have $\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_{\sigma(i)} \xi_i$ has the same distribution as $\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \xi_i$.
\end{itemize}

[Theorem thm:2nd-order-score of arXiv:2607.04514, 'Boundary-layer asymptotics for Gaussian-smoothed singular measures'] Let \(A>0\) and assume (ass:standing of the paper) with \(r\geqslant r_0\) (the value of \(r_0\) is
  specified below for each expansion). Then there exists \(\sigma_0 > 0\) such that, for every
  \((y,\sigma)\in\mathcal Y_{A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\sigma_0}\), \(x=\pi(y)\), \(a = a(y,\sigma)\), it
  holds that
  \begin{align*}
    \boldsymbol{s}_\sigma(y) &= \sigma^{-1}\big(\mathsf S_0(a,x,\sigma) + \sigma \mathsf S_1(a,x,\sigma)
    + \sigma^2\mathscr R_{1,\boldsymbol{s}_\sigma}(a,x,\sigma)\big), \qquad r_0=3 \\
    \mathbf{H}_\sigma(y) &= \sigma^{-2} \big( \mathsf H_0(a,x,\sigma) + \sigma\mathsf H_1(a,x, \sigma)
    + \sigma^2\mathscr R_{1,\mathbf{H}_\sigma}(a,x,\sigma)\big), \qquad r_0=4 \\
    \dot{\boldsymbol{s}}_\sigma(y) &= \sigma^{-2} \big(\dot{\mathsf S}_0 (a,x,\sigma)
    + \sigma \dot{\mathsf S}_1(a,x,\sigma) + \sigma^2\mathscr R_{1,\dot{\boldsymbol{s}}_\sigma}(a,x,\sigma)\big),
    \qquad r_0=4.
  \end{align*}
  Here, the coefficients \(\mathsf S_0\), \(\mathsf S_1\), \(\mathsf H_0\), \(\mathsf H_1\),
  \(\dot{\mathsf S}_0\) and \(\dot{\mathsf S}_1\) are explicitly given in
  (thm:first-order-score of the paper) or by the formulas below and have all mixed derivatives up to order
  \(r-r_0+1\) in the variables \(a\), \(x\), and \(\sigma\), uniformly bounded for
  \(x\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}\), \(\|a\| \leqslant A\), and \(0<\sigma\leqslant\sigma_0\).
  \begin{align*}
    \mathsf S_1 (a,x,\sigma)
    &= \mathbf J_{\theta}^\top (a,x,\sigma) \nabla_{\theta}\mathsf L_0 (a,x)
    + \mathbf J_\nu^\top(a,x,\sigma) \nabla_a\mathsf L_1(a,x), \\
    \mathsf H_1 (a,x,\sigma)
    &= \mathbf J_{\theta}^\top \mathrm{D}_{\theta a}^2\mathsf L_0\,\mathbf J_\nu
    + \mathbf J_\nu^\top \mathrm{D}_{a\theta}^2\mathsf L_0\, \mathbf J_{\theta}
    + \mathbf Q_\nu[\nabla_a\mathsf L_0]
    + \mathbf J_\nu^\top \mathrm{D}_a^2\mathsf L_1\,\mathbf J_\nu, \\
    \dot{\mathsf S}_1 (a,x,\sigma) &= \partial_\sigma{\mathsf
    S}_0(a,x,\sigma) - (\mathrm{D}_a\mathsf S_1(a,x,\sigma))[a].
  \end{align*}
  The functions \(\mathscr R_{1,\boldsymbol{s}_\sigma}\), \(\mathscr R_{1,\mathbf{H}_\sigma}\) and \(\mathscr R_{1,\dot{\boldsymbol{s}}_\sigma}\) have
  all mixed derivatives up to order \(r-r_0\) in the variables \(a\), \(x\), and \(\sigma\),
  uniformly bounded for \(x\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}\), \(\|a\| \leqslant A\), and
  \(0<\sigma\leqslant\sigma_0\). Derivatives in \(x\) are computed in the stratum coordinate
  \(\theta\), after writing \(x=\Phi(\theta,0)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Defn alternativeslippery of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a closed set. A point $\bm{x}\in A$ is \textbf{upwards (resp.~downwards) slippery} in the $k\geq 1$ first coordinates if there is a sequence of points $\bm{x}^j \in A$, $j \geq 0$, converging to $\bm{x}$, such that each $\bm{x}^j$ is an upper (resp.~lower) extremal point in the first $k$ coordinates, the first $k$ coordinates are strictly increasing (resp.~decreasing) with $j$, and the remaining coordinates are nonincreasing (resp.~nondecreasing) with $j$.

Proof (unaudited), elementary Cover-Wendel application; no novelty claimed. For the balanced-sign, zero-threshold ReLU tree committee with fixed even K, a prescribed label-only partition of patterns among sign-compatible hidden units yields a valid strict classifier with probability q(P,N/K)^K, where q(P,n)=2^{1-P} sum_{r=0}^{min(n-1,P-1)} binom(P-1,r). Thus every load a<2/K is constructively feasible with probability tending to one as N tends to infinity at fixed K. At P=2n this procedure succeeds with probability 2^{-K}; above P/n=2 it fails asymptotically. This is a classical Cover-Wendel consequence, not a novelty claim or a nonzero wide-limit lower bound.
K>=2 even; N=Kn; spherical hidden weights of norm sqrt(n)
Independent standard Gaussian inputs across all patterns and disjoint blocks
Fixed balanced readout signs, zero output threshold, ReLU hidden activation, strict correct output signs with no prescribed positive margin
The partition is chosen using labels only and independently of input values; each pattern goes to one unit of the matching readout sign

[Proposition 4 of arXiv:2608.19396, '\bf Penalisation of Two-Dimensional Brownian Motion'] Let $F$ be an integrable random variable defined on the probability space $(\Omega, 
\mathcal{F}_{\infty}, \mathbf{W}^{(2)})$. There exists a continuous martingale $(M_t(F))_{t \geq 0}$, nonnegative if $F \geq 0$, such that for every $t \geq 0$, and every bounded, $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable random variable $Y_t$, 
$$\mathbf{W}^{(2)} (F Y_t) = W^{(2)} (M_t^{(2)} (F) Y_t).$$
Moreover, $W^{(2)}$-almost surely, 
$$M_t^{(2)} (F) = \mathbf{W}^{(2)} (G)$$
where for all $\omega \in \Omega$ such that $\omega_0 = 0$, 
$$G ((\omega_u)_{u \geq 0}) 
= F((\omega'_u)_{u \geq 0})$$
where $\omega'_u = X_u$ for $0 \leq u \leq t$, and 
$\omega'_u = X_t + \omega_{u-t}$ for $u \geq t$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 4 of arXiv:2608.19396

Status: complete author-checked candidate counterexample, 2026-09-06. No independent review and no novelty certification. This is a proposed negative answer to Hasebe, Ueda and Wang, *Log-unimodality for free positive multiplicative Brownian motion*, arXiv:2009.13848v1 (29 September 2020), Problem 4.7, PDF page 11. The published reference is Colloquium Mathematicum 169 (2022), 209-226; the archived version used here is the arXiv version. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13848.

## Claim and normalization

Let \(\nu=(\delta_{1/10}+\delta_{10})/2\). In the source normalization
\[\Sigma_{\sigma_t}(z)=\exp\!\left(\frac t2\frac{z+1}{z-1}\right),\]
the law \(\sigma_t\boxtimes\nu\) is **not log-unimodal for every \(t\ge5\pi\)**. Its initial law has support in the compact interval \([1/10,10]\), so this disproves eventual log-unimodality for arbitrary compactly supported positive initial laws, if the argument and source match survive review.

Log-unimodality means unimodality of the image measure under the logarithm; ordinary unimodality on the positive line is a different claim. The initial law is multiplicatively symmetric but is not log-unimodal. Thus the source theorem for symmetric log-unimodal initial laws does not apply.

## The exact source criterion

Lemma 4.1(3), PDF page 8, says that \(\sigma_t\boxtimes\nu\) is log-unimodal if and only if, for every \(R\in(0,\pi)\), the equation
\[\frac{\sin R}{R}\int_0^\infty\frac{r\xi}{1+r^2\xi^2-2r\xi\cos R}\,d\nu(\xi)=\frac1t\tag{1}\]
has at most two solutions \(r>0\). We use its contrapositive by finding four distinct solutions for one value of \(R\), for each specified \(t\).

Put \(a=\log10\), \(u=\log r\), and
\[K_R(s)=\frac{1}{2(\cosh s-\cos R)},\qquad F_R(u)=\frac{K_R(u-a)+K_R(u+a)}2.\]
The integral in (1) equals \(F_R(u)\), because dividing its integrand's numerator and denominator by \(r\xi\) gives
\[\frac{r\xi}{1+r^2\xi^2-2r\xi\cos R}=\frac1{r\xi+(r\xi)^{-1}-2\cos R}=K_R(\log r+\log\xi).\]
Hence (1) is equivalent to
\[F_R(u)=\frac{R}{t\sin R}.\tag{2}\]
For fixed \(R\in(0,\pi)\), the function \(F_R\) is continuous, positive and even, and tends to zero at both infinities.

## Selecting the level and time

The function \(g(R)=R/\sin R\) is strictly increasing from 1 to infinity on \((0,\pi)\). Indeed
\[g'(R)=\frac{\sin R-R\cos R}{\sin^2R}>0,\]
because the numerator vanishes at zero and has derivative \(R\sin R>0\). Also \(g(\pi/2)=\pi/2\).

For each \(t\ge5\pi\), there is therefore a unique \(R_t\in[\pi/2,\pi)\) with
\[g(R_t)=\frac t{10}.\]
For this choice the right side of (2) is exactly \(1/10\), and \(\cos R_t\le0\).

## Four strict crossings

Since \(\cosh(\log10)=101/20\),
\[F_{R_t}(0)=K_{R_t}(a)=\frac1{2(101/20-\cos R_t)}\le\frac{10}{101}<\frac1{10}.\tag{3}\]
At \(u=a\), the contribution from the centered kernel alone gives
\[F_{R_t}(a)=\frac{K_{R_t}(0)+K_{R_t}(2a)}2\ge\frac1{4(1-\cos R_t)}\ge\frac18>\frac1{10}.\tag{4}\]
The same inequality holds at \(-a\) by evenness. Together with the limits zero at both infinities, (3)-(4) and the intermediate value theorem give a solution of \(F_{R_t}(u)=1/10\) in each of the four disjoint intervals
\[(-\infty,-a),\quad(-a,0),\quad(0,a),\quad(a,\infty).\]
Exponentiation is injective, so these give four distinct positive solutions of (1). Lemma 4.1 proves the claim.

## Separate algebra check in the original variable

The same signs can be checked without hyperbolic functions. At \(r=1\), both atom integrands equal
\[\frac{10}{101-20\cos R}\le\frac{10}{101}<\frac1{10}.\]
At \(r=10\), the atom \(\xi=1/10\) contributes, including its mass one half,
\[\frac1{2(2-2\cos R)}=\frac1{4(1-\cos R)}\ge\frac18.\]
At \(r=1/10\), the atom \(\xi=10\) gives the same lower bound. The integral tends to zero as \(r\downarrow0\) and as \(r\uparrow\infty\). Thus there are crossings in \((0,1/10),(1/10,1),(1,10),(10,\infty)\). These strict rational inequalities include the boundary time \(5\pi\), for which \(R_t=\pi/2\).

## Adversarial checks and limits

The crucial direction is the equivalence in Lemma 4.1, rather than a merely sufficient unimodality condition. Its full statement and proof must remain pinned to the source. The four crossings concern a positive density level, not just multiple extrema in an auxiliary transform. The time is selected separately for each \(t\), as the criterion permits. The upper bound on the central value is uniform for \(R\ge\pi/2\); the lower bound at the two flanks is uniform for all \(R\in(0,\pi)\). No numerical root finder or plot is used as proof. The argument only needs failure for arbitrarily large times; it proves failure for every time in the displayed half-line. It makes no assertion about smaller times or optimality of \(5\pi\).

The large-time mechanism can also be understood from \(K_R(s)\to[4\cosh^2(s/2)]^{-1}\) as \(R\uparrow\pi\): its width does not diverge. A separated two-point mixture of this limiting kernel remains bimodal. This observation motivated the construction; the finite-time rational inequalities above are the proof.

Focused primary-source searches on 6 September 2026 found the original paper, the authors' current publication pages, and Auer's 2026 paper on the law started at one. [Bigthm thm:Main Theorem1 of arXiv:2602.07920, 'On the position matrix of single-shelf shuffle and card guessing'] Fix $n\geq 2$ and let $M$ be the position matrix as defined above. Then, 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item  $\operatorname{ker}(M)=\operatorname{span}\{\eta^{(j)}: 1\leq j\leq  \lfloor n/2\rfloor\}$ where $\eta^{(j)}:=e_j-e_{n-j+1}$, where $e_k$ is the standard $k$-th basis vector $e_k(j)=\delta_k(j)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$. 
    \item For every even integer $0\leq i\leq n-1$, $2^{-i}$ is an eigenvalue of $M$ with multiplicity $1$.
    \item For every even integer $0\leq i\leq n-1$, the vector $\zeta^{(i)}$ is an eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $2^{-i}$, where
    \[
    \zeta^{(i)}(k)= \sum_{t=0}^{i}w_t^{(i)}(k-1)^{\underline{t}}\;,\qquad 1\leq k\leq n
    \]
    and 
    \[w_t^{(i)} =2^{i-t}B_{i-t}\binom{i}{t}(n-t-1)^{\underline{i-t}} = 2^{i-t}B_{i-t}\binom{i}{t}\frac{(n-t-1)!}{(n-i-1)!}\;.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Bigthm thm:Main Theorem1 of arXiv:2602.07920

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2511.09280, 'Random Walk conditioned to stay above a non-flat floor: curvature effects'] Let \(\beta\in (0,1/6)\). There are \(c,n_0,\lambda_0, r_0\geq 0\) such that for any \(n\geq n_0\), any \(\lambda_0\leq \lambda\leq n^{\beta}\), and any \(r_0 \sqrt{\lambda}n^{2/3}\leq k \leq n-r_0 \sqrt{\lambda} n^{2/3}\),
    \begin{equation*}
        P\bigl( W_{k}\geq \lambda n^{1/3}\bigr)
        \geq
        e^{-c\lambda^{3/2}}.
    \end{equation*}
    In particular, \(E(W_k) \geq Cn^{1/3}\) for some \(C>0\) uniform over \(n,k\) as above.
title: Lemma 11 of arXiv:2511.09280

body:
[Theorem T:BddMnt of arXiv:2412.03521, 'On ergodic properties of stochastic PDEs'] Let $u$ be the solution to~(equation E:SHE of the paper) starting from a nonnegative rough
  initial data $\mu$, namely, $\mu$ is is a nonnegative Borel measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$
  such that~(equation A:icon of the paper) holds. Suppose that the diffusion coefficient
  $b(x,u)=b(u)$ satisfies the following degenerate condition:
   \begin{equation}
        b(0) = 0\;, \quad \text{and} \quad
        |b(u_2)-b(u_1)|\le L_b |u_2-u_1|.
      \end{equation}
  Moreover, suppose that $4 L_b^2 \Upsilon (0) < 1$, namely,
  condition~(equation E:Upsilon_0 of the paper) holds and $L_b<(2\Upsilon(0))^{-1/2}$. Then
  \begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}\left[u(t,x)^2\right] \le \frac{J_0^2(t,x)}{L_b^2\left[1-4L_b^2\Upsilon(0)\right]}, \quad \text{for all $t\ge 0$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$},
  \end{align}
  where we recall that $J_0 (t,x)$ is defined by~(equation E:def-J0 of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem T:BddMnt of arXiv:2412.03521

body:
Let (X, B, mu) be a Lebesgue probability space and let P be a measurable partition of X (in Rokhlin's sense, so that the quotient is again a Lebesgue space). Then there is a family of conditional probability measures (mu_P) indexed by the elements P of the partition, uniquely determined mu-almost everywhere, such that mu_P is supported on P for almost every P, the map P -> mu_P(A) is measurable for every A in B, and mu(A) = integral of mu_P(A) with respect to the quotient measure. In particular conditional expectations are given by integration against the conditional measures.
The Lebesgue (standard) space hypothesis is essential: regular conditional probabilities can fail to exist on general measure spaces, and the partition must be MEASURABLE in Rokhlin's sense - the partition of the circle into orbits of an irrational rotation is not, and has no disintegration.

body:
[Theorem thm:conv_BM_limit of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{\Sigma}$ be a symmetric non-negative definite matrix on $\mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ and define $\bm{X}^t=((\bm{\Sigma}\bm{B}_{st}+\bm{S}_{st})/\sqrt{t})_{s\in[0,1]}$ for $t\in(0,1]$ where $(\bm{B}_t)_{t \in [0,1]}$ is a standard Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}^d$ independent of the pure-jump L\'evy process $\bm{S}$ with Blumenthal--Getoor index~$\beta$ (defined in~(equation eq:BG of the paper)).\\
{\nf(a)} Suppose $\beta\in[0,2)$ and fix any $\beta_* \in (\beta,2]$ when $\bm{S}$ is of infinite variation and $\beta_*=1$ otherwise. Then for any $q>0$ with $\mathds{E}[|\bm{X}_1|^q]<\infty$, we have
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{W}_q\big(\bm{X}^t,\bm{\Sigma}\bm{B}\big)
=\mathcal{O}\big(t^{(q\wedge 1)
    (\min\{1/q,1/\beta_*\}-1/2)}\big), 
    \qquad \text{ as }t \downarrow 0.
\end{align*}
{\normalfont(b)} Pick any $\bm{u}_*\in\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}$ and define $C_*\coloneqq |\bm{u}_*|^{-1}|\psi_{\bm{S}}(\bm{u}_*)|>0$. Then for all $q \geqslant 1$, we have 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t_1,\bm{\Sigma}\bm{B}_1)
    \geqslant\frac{C_*}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{t}+ \mathcal{O}(t^{3/2}),
\quad\text{as }t \downarrow 0.
\end{align*}
{\normalfont(c)}  Let $\lambda$ be the largest eigenvalue of $\bm{\Sigma}^2$. Suppose there exist $\delta\in[1,2)$ and vectors $(\bm{u}_r)_{r\in(0,\infty)}$ with $|\bm{u}_r|=r$ satisfying $c\coloneqq\inf_{r>1}r^{-\delta}|\psi_{\bm{S}}(\bm{u}_r)|>0$. Then for any $C_*\in(0,ce^{-\lambda/2})$ we have
$\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t_1,\bm{\Sigma}\bm{B}_1) \geqslant(C_*/\sqrt{2})t^{1-\delta/2}$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:conv_BM_limit of arXiv:2411.03609

Let g be the cutoff planar Gaussian increment field, m=6, h=2pi/m, 0<A<1/m, and U,V independent uniforms on [0,h), independent of g. Put f_A(t)=t+A sin(mt), q_A(x)=f_A(g(x)+V)-f_A(V), theta_A=U+q_A. The map f_A is smooth strictly increasing, |q_A-g|<=2A, and q_A has stationary increments. With v=Var[g(x)-g(y)], Var[q_A(x)-q_A(y)]=v+A^2(1-exp(-m^2v/2)). Yet C_m(x-y)=E exp[i m(theta_A(x)-theta_A(y))] tends to J1(mA)^2>0. Its m-fold phase field is stationary with zero one-point mean. Hence even a smooth bounded monotone perturbation with logarithmic variance correct to O(1) can fail algebraic decay of periodic order. This is not a Riesz Gibbs model or a P0321 solution.

body:
[Theorem thm:ascent of arXiv:2608.24195, '\textbf{A Heterogeneous Mixture of Experts Framework for Interpretable Machine Learning}'] Suppose that:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item the design matrix satisfies $\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{X})=p+1$;
  \item the gating auxiliary function
        \[
          Q_{\mathrm{gate}}(\boldsymbol{\Theta})
          = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{e}
              \tau_{ij}^{(t)}
              \log g_j(\boldsymbol{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\Theta})
        \]
        is twice continuously differentiable.
\end{enumerate}
Define $\boldsymbol{R}^{(t)} = \boldsymbol{T}^{(t)} - \boldsymbol{G}^{(t)}$ and let
\[
  \widehat{\boldsymbol{B}}^{(t)}
  = (\boldsymbol{X}^\top\boldsymbol{X})^{-1} \boldsymbol{X}^\top \boldsymbol{R}^{(t)}.
\]
Further define
\[
  A_t
  = \bigl\langle
      \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\Theta}} Q_{\mathrm{gate}}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(t)}),\,
      \widehat{\boldsymbol{B}}^{(t)}
    \bigr\rangle
\]
and
\[
  C_t
  = \bigl\langle
      \widehat{\boldsymbol{B}}^{(t)},\,
      \nabla^2_{\boldsymbol{\Theta}} Q_{\mathrm{gate}}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^{(t)})\,
      \widehat{\boldsymbol{B}}^{(t)}
    \bigr\rangle,
\]
where $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^{(t)}
= \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(t)} + \eta_t\gamma_t\widehat{\boldsymbol{B}}^{(t)}$ for some
$\eta_t\in(0,1)$.

Then:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $A_t \geq 0$, with strict inequality whenever
        $\boldsymbol{R}^{(t)} \notin \mathrm{Null}(\boldsymbol{P}_{\boldsymbol X})$, where
        $\boldsymbol P_{\boldsymbol X}
         = \boldsymbol X(\boldsymbol X^\top\boldsymbol X)^{-1}\boldsymbol X^\top$;
  \item the update
        $\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(t+1)}
         = \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(t)} + \gamma_t\widehat{\boldsymbol B}^{(t)}$
        satisfies
        $Q_{\mathrm{gate}}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(t+1)})
         > Q_{\mathrm{gate}}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(t)})$
        whenever $0 < \gamma_t < 2A_t / |C_t|$.
\end{enumerate}

body:
Let H^2 be the Hardy space of the unit circle T, realised as the closed subspace of L^2(T) spanned by the exponentials z^n with n >= 0, and let P: L^2(T) -> H^2 be the orthogonal projection. For a continuous symbol phi in C(T) define the Toeplitz operator T_phi on H^2 by T_phi f = P(phi f); the bound ||T_phi|| <= ||phi||_infinity is immediate from ||P|| = 1, and in fact ||T_phi|| = ||phi||_infinity. Then T_phi is Fredholm if and only if phi has no zero on T, and in that case ind T_phi = - wind(phi), the negative of the winding number of the closed curve phi about the origin. In particular T_phi is invertible if and only if phi is nonvanishing with winding number 0, and a Fredholm Toeplitz operator with continuous symbol is never invertible when its winding number is nonzero, even though it may be injective or surjective.
phi is continuous on the unit circle (for merely bounded measurable symbols the criterion is different)
T_phi acts on the Hardy space H^2 of the circle
the winding number is that of the curve phi about 0, defined because phi is nonvanishing

If phi never vanishes, then 1/phi is continuous and T_{1/phi} T_phi - I and T_phi T_{1/phi} - I are compact, so T_phi is Fredholm by Atkinson's theorem. For the index, note ||T_phi - T_psi|| <= ||phi - psi||_infinity, so phi -> T_phi is norm continuous; the winding number classifies the connected components of the nonvanishing continuous functions on T up to homotopy, and phi with winding number n is homotopic within nonvanishing continuous functions to z^n. Along the corresponding norm-continuous path of Fredholm operators the index is constant, so ind T_phi = ind T_{z^n}. Finally T_z is the unilateral shift, with index -1, and T_{z^n} = (T_z)^n has index -n by the composition formula (and for n < 0 it is the adjoint power, of index |n|). The converse (Fredholm forces phi nonvanishing) follows because the map phi -> T_phi + K(H^2) is an isometric embedding of C(T) into the Calkin algebra, so invertibility of the class of T_phi forces invertibility of phi in C(T).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:2225456d23e042d16fa41a4883a1acf0ad8f28160beb6e99ce53d176a31bf47b","revision_digest":"sha256:a336e41f1363f4a04acdf30204d079af81761e9aab33543cfff3898ac6f7532f","source_id":"wikipedia:Toeplitz operator","source_revision":"as-known-2026-09-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2607.06428, 'Impact of spinning on the early-warning signs in non-Markovian stochastic systems'] Let $(W^H_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be a scalar fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index in $H(0,1)$. Then:
\begin{description}
    \item[{\bf(Long-range dependence)}] If $H>1/2$ then 
    \[ \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty \E [W^H_1(W^{H}_{n+1}-W^H_n)]=\infty. \]
    \item[{\bf(Short-range dependence)}] If $H<1/2$ then
    \[ \sum\limits_{n=1}^\infty \E [W^H_1(W^{H}_{n+1}-W^H_n)]<\infty. \]
 \item [(Self-similarity)] Let $a>0$. Then 
 \[ (a^H W^H_t)_{t\geq 0} \stackrel{\text{law}}{=}(W^{H}_{at})_{t\geq 0}. \]
 \item [(Time-inversion)] It holds
 \[ (t^{2H}W^H_{1/t})_{t>0}\stackrel{\text{law}}{=}(W^H_t)_{t> 0}.  \]
\item [(Stationarity of the increments)] For all $h>0$ we have 
\[ (W^{H}_{t+h} -W^H_t )_{t\geq 0} \stackrel{\text{law}}{=} W^H_h. \]
\item [(Regularity of the increments)] The scalar fractional Brownian motion has a version which is $\alpha$-H\"older continuous with $\alpha<H$. 
\end{description} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Then $\pi=\lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \pi_N$ exists and is a probability measure, moreover

body:
[Lem 92 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We have $\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha,0) \subseteq \sM^{\BOGP,\sym}(\alpha,0)$.

\begin{proof}
We repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
\MSRheader\\
\hline
\BOGPdefn{sy}\\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
    By Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.Lip.to.Lip.sym}, it suffices to show $\sym(\sM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0)) \subseteq \sM^{\BOGP,\sym}(\alpha,0)$, where $\sM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0)$ is defined in \eqref{e:sM.Lip.0.chaos}.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ (recall \eqref{e:cM.Lip.0.chaos}), where $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,\epsilon$.
    There exists a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz $((\cA_{N_j})^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ such that
    \[
    \WERR((\cA_{N_j})^\circ,\mu)
    =
        \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu((\cA_{N_j})^\circ), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}((\cA_{N_j})^\circ), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\} \le \epsilon\,,
    \]
    and the correlation functions $\chi_{(\cA_{N_j})^\circ}$ satisfy $\lim_{j\to\infty} \chi_{(\cA_{N_j})^\circ}(0) = 0$ and
    \beq
        
        \chi_{\cA_{N_j}^\circ}(1-\epsilon) \le \epsilon\,.
    \eeq
    That is, we have the same information about the algorithms $((\cA_{N_j})^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:Lip.in.BOGP} (instantiated with $q_0 = 0$), and in addition the estimate \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.sym.chaos}.
    For $\cA_{N_j}$ the perturbation of $(\cA_{N_j})^\circ$ given by Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable},  the estimate \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.sym.chaos} implies
    \[
        \chi_{\cA_{N_j}}(1-\epsilon)
        = \bigg(1-\frac{1}{L^2}\bigg) \chi_{\cA_{N_j}^\circ}(1-\epsilon)
        + \frac{1-\epsilon}{L^2} 
        \le \bigg(1-\frac{1}{L^2}\bigg) \epsilon + \frac{1-\epsilon}{L^2} 
        \le 2\epsilon\,,
    \]
where the last inequality holds for $L$ sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,\epsilon$. By passing to a subsequence of the $j$'s, we may assume that $\chi_{\cA_{N_j}}$ converges both pointwise and in $L^1$ to a limiting function $\chi$, which must then satisfy 
    \[
        \chi(1-2\epsilon) \le \chi(1-\epsilon) \le 2\epsilon\,.
    \]
Therefore $p \equiv \chi^{-1}$ satisfies $p(2\epsilon) \ge 1-2\epsilon$, as required by condition~\ref{it:3.6} (with $2\epsilon$ in place of $\epsilon$).
Arguing identically to the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:Lip.in.BOGP} shows that for some $\hat\epsilon(\epsilon) \ge 2\epsilon$ tending to $0$ as $\epsilon \rightarrow 0$, we have 
    \[
        \cM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
        \subseteq \cB_{\hat\epsilon}\Big(
            \cM^{\BOGP,\chaos}(\alpha,0;\tilde C(L),\hat\epsilon)
        \Big)\,.
    \]
    Taking a union in $L$ and intersection in $\epsilon$, and applying $\sym$ to both sides, shows
    \begin{align*}
       & \sym(\sM^{\Lip,\chaos}(\alpha,0))
        \subseteq \sym\bigg(
        \adjustlimits
            \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(
                \cM^{\BOGP,\chaos}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
            \Big)
        \bigg)\\
       &\qquad \subseteq 
        \adjustlimits
        \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \bigcup_{L>0}
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(
            \sym(\cM^{\BOGP,\chaos}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon))
        \Big)\\
        &\qquad\stackrel{\eqref{e:BOGP.sym.relation}}{=} \adjustlimits
        \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \bigcup_{L>0}
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(
        \cM^{\BOGP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
        \Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:measure.classes.sym.cM}}{=} \sM^{\BOGP,\sym}(\alpha,0)\,.
    \end{align*}
This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let f be holomorphic on a punctured disk {z : 0 < |z - a| < r} (an isolated singularity at a) and let f(z) = Σ_{n in Z} c_n (z - a)^n be its Laurent expansion there. The residue of f at a is Res(f,a) = c_{-1}, equivalently Res(f,a) = (1/2πi) ∫_{|z-a|=ρ} f(z) dz for any 0 < ρ < r, the circle positively oriented (the value is independent of ρ). Computation rules: if a is a pole of order at most m, Res(f,a) = lim_{z→a} (1/(m-1)!) d^{m-1}/dz^{m-1} [(z - a)^m f(z)]; in particular for a simple pole Res(f,a) = lim_{z→a} (z-a) f(z), and if f = g/h with g, h holomorphic near a, h(a) = 0 and h'(a) ≠ 0, then Res(f,a) = g(a)/h'(a). The residue at infinity of a function holomorphic on |z| > R is Res(f,∞) = -(1/2πi)∫_{|z|=ρ} f(z) dz for ρ > R; for a rational function the sum of all residues in C together with the residue at infinity is 0. A removable singularity has residue 0, but residue 0 does not imply removable (example: 1/(z-a)^2).
a is an isolated singularity: f is holomorphic on a punctured disk about a and single-valued there

Owner-own-work draft; proof (unaudited), no novelty claimed. Let x1=(1,1/4), x2=(-1,1/4), both labels +1. Train both layers of the bias-free network f(x)=sum_j v_j ReLU(w_j.x) by gradient flow of summed exponential or logistic loss, with ReLU'(0)=0. Initially every neuron is strictly dead on both examples (D, output arbitrary), or has v_j>0 and lies strictly in A (x1 only), B (x2 only), or C (both active). Assume at least two of A, B, C are occupied.

By continuity of the parameters and losses, this derivative stays strictly positive on incoming C portions of a sufficiently small left neighborhood. Boundary portions are null, and a neuron in this group has not yet strictly exited. Its nonnegative z2 therefore cannot approach zero from above at that time. Every standard initialization 0<|x0|<eta R has a finite first time N
with |x_N|>eta R. While |x_0|,...,|x_t|<=eta R, signs alternate and
 |x_(t+1)|>=q |x_t|.
Consequently N is at most the smallest positive integer with
q^N |x0|>eta R. Equality |x0|=eta R is also harmless; a step leaves it.
This holds for BOTH usual separate bias corrections and uncorrected Adam.

For b=.9 and p=1, every dormant eigenvalue lambda2>38 obeys the premise.
In claim008's diagonal family the active coordinate evolves independently.

an explicit finite escape scale R<1/38-1/lambda2. This does NOT say that
the perturbed trajectory has a particular asymptotic curvature or cannot
later return to a small neighborhood.

 M'=bM+(1-b)X, V'=dV+(1-d)X^2,

where alpha_t=b^(t+1),Vhat'=V'/(1-d^(t+1)) in the corrected case, and
alpha_t=0,Vhat'=V' in the uncorrected case.

Assume past |X_s|<=R, s<=t. The corrected Vhat' is a convex combination
of X_0^2,...,X_t^2 (standard v0=0). Hence sqrt(Vhat')<=R. For the raw
variance its weights sum to 1-d^(t+1)<1, giving the same bound.
Let D=sqrt(Vhat')+rho<=R+rho<c/2.

Induct on the invariant momentum cone
 M X<=0,   |M|<=c |X|,   X!=0.                              (1)
It holds initially since M0=0. Write M=-r X, 0<=r<=c. Then
 M'=h X, h=1-b-br in [c,1-b],
because 1-b-bc=c. Set E=(1-alpha_t)D<=D<=R+rho<c/2.
Now
 X'=-X G, G=h/E-1 >= c/(R+rho)-1=q>1,
so the sign flips and amplitude grows. Moreover
 |M'|/|X'|=hE/(h-E)<=c.

Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This covers arbitrary input/output dimensions and every s>0 at rank one. The chosen constant GD step depends on eps and can be extremely small. It is not a linear-convergence theorem for one step size simultaneously for all accuracies.

Prior work: Kunin, Raventos, Domine, Chen, Klindt, Saxe and Ganguli, Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning, arXiv:2406.06158, Appendix A.2, especially A.2.4 equations (30)-(33), printed p.19, and A.2.5 equation (34), p.20, already give the single-neuron unbalanced gradient-flow solutions and basin boundary under whitened data. With zero output weight, their saddle boundary reduces to w0^T beta_star=0. Gradient-flow convergence from the present initialization is therefore settled, not a new result. The quantitative estimate below uses an equivalent spectral expression for that known flow and an elementary, deliberately conservative finite-horizon Euler-error argument to obtain a specified ordinary GD hitting time. Du-Hu-Lee arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 3.2 instead initializes both rank-one factors with a small Gaussian; it is not the zero/random all-scale theorem here. Literature novelty of the finite-step corollary is unresolved.

## Statement

Let Delta=u v^T, where u in R^m and v in R^p are unit vectors and m,p>=1. Consider simultaneous GD on f(b,a)=||b a^T-Delta||F^2/2, with b0=0 and a0~N(0,s^2 I_p), any s>0. Fix 0<rho<1 and 0<eps<1. Define the following deterministic real constants:

 D=2p s^2/rho, nu_bar=1+D/2,
 U_bar=2+32 nu_bar/(s^2 rho^2),
 V_bar=1+4 sqrt(p)/rho^(3/2),
 T=(1+D) log[16 nu_bar(V_bar+U_bar)/eps],
 R=sqrt(D+4)+2, L=6R^2+1,
 M=(R^2/2+1)R.

Choose any constant step

 0<eta<=min{1,1/M,[eps/(4RM)] exp[-L(T+1)]},

and take N=ceil(T/eta). With probability at least 1-rho over a0,

 ||b_N a_N^T-Delta||F<=eps.

The guarantee includes p>1, a proper input-side rank-one bottleneck, at every initialization scale. The signal condition number is 1. For a rank-one target of singular value lambda>0, use normalized scale s/sqrt(lambda), normalized step eta lambda, and normalized requested error eps/lambda in this statement. It is only a hitting-time guarantee for the prescribed eps, with no efficiency or independently checked proof claim.

## One initial event; no independence multiplication

Write x0=v^T a0 and z0=a0-x0 v. With probability at least 1-rho,

 d=||a0||^2<=D, |x0|>=s rho/2.

Indeed E||a0||^2=ps^2 and Markov bounds the first failure probability by rho/2. The standard normal density is at most 1/sqrt(2pi), so P(|x0|<s rho/2)<=sqrt(2/pi)rho/2<rho/2. Use a union bound; the two events need not be independent. Fix this event. In particular d>0 and x0 is nonzero.

## Known flow in a spectral representation

Both GD and gradient flow keep b in span(u), so write b=beta u and a=x v+z with z orthogonal to v. The normalized gradient flow is

 beta'=x-beta||a||^2,
 x'=beta-beta^2 x,
 z'=-beta^2 z,
 beta(0)=0, x(0)=x0, z(0)=z0.

As in the cited primary source, ||a||^2-beta^2=d is conserved. In Z=(beta,x,z) coordinates define the symmetric block operator

 H_d=[[ -d/2, 1 ],[ 1, d/2 ]] on (beta,x),
 H_d=(d/2)I on the z coordinates.

Then the exact flow is equivalently

 Z'=H_d Z-(||Z||^2/2)Z,
 Z(t)=w(t)/sqrt(1+integral_0^t ||w(tau)||^2 d tau),
 w(t)=exp(t H_d)Z0.

The displayed expression follows by differentiating its positive scalar denominator. It starts at Z0 and solves the same ODE, so uniqueness identifies it with the source's known single-neuron flow; it is not an additional claimed discovery. Its denominator never vanishes. Alternatively, boundedness below gives global existence directly.

Let nu=sqrt(1+d^2/4), g=nu-d/2=1/(nu+d/2). The two eigenvalues of the 2-by-2 block are nu and -nu, with orthonormal eigenvectors e_plus,e_minus. Choose e_plus with positive beta and x entries. Decompose

 w(t)=a_plus e^(nu t)e_plus+a_minus e^(-nu t)e_minus+e^(d t/2)z0.

Because Z0=(0,x0,z0), the spectral projections give

 a_plus^2=x0^2(1+d/(2nu))/2>=x0^2/2,
 a_minus^2=x0^2(1-d/(2nu))/2<=a_plus^2.

In particular a_plus is nonzero. The limiting factors are

 Z_star=sign(a_plus)sqrt(2nu)e_plus,

and their product is the target: the positive eigenvector obeys x/beta=nu+d/2=1/g, while its scaled squared norm is 2nu=g+1/g, hence beta_star^2=g and beta_star x_star=1. Its z component is zero.

## Explicit exponential flow error bound

Let h(t)^2=1+integral_0^t ||w(tau)||^2 d tau and

 Q(t)=h(t)^2/[a_plus^2 e^(2nu t)/(2nu)].

Orthogonality of the three spectral components gives the exact formula

 h(t)^2=1+a_plus^2(e^(2nu t)-1)/(2nu)
          +a_minus^2(1-e^(-2nu t))/(2nu)
          +||z0||^2(e^(d t)-1)/d.

Subtract the leading exponential term. Since 2nu>=2g, ||z0||^2<=d, and a_plus^2>=x0^2/2, it follows that

 |Q(t)-1|<=U e^(-2gt), U=2+8nu/x0^2.

To see every term, the initial constant and the two constant/decaying eigenmode corrections contribute at most (2nu/a_plus^2+1+a_minus^2/a_plus^2)e^(-2nu t), bounded by (4nu/x0^2+2)e^(-2gt). The z integral contributes at most [2nu||z0||^2/(d a_plus^2)]e^(-(2nu-d)t), bounded by (4nu/x0^2)e^(-2gt).

Also, after division of w(t) by a_plus e^(nu t), the nonleading vector has norm at most

 V e^(-gt), V=1+sqrt(2)||z0||/|x0|.

When U e^(-2gt)<=1/2, Q>=1/2, Q^(-1/2)<=sqrt(2) and |Q^(-1/2)-1|<=sqrt(2)|Q-1|. Consequently

 ||Z(t)-Z_star||<=2sqrt(nu)(V+U)e^(-gt).

For completeness, flow loss decreases from f0=1/2, so ||beta a||<=2. The invariant gives beta^2(beta^2+d)<=4, whence beta^2<=2 and ||Z(t)||^2=2beta^2+d<=4+d<=6nu. Also ||Z_star||^2=2nu. The product map is Lipschitz with bound at most ||Z(t)||+||Z_star||<=4sqrt(nu) along the segment between these points, so

 ||beta(t)a(t)-v||<=8nu(V+U)e^(-gt).

On the chosen event, nu<=nu_bar, U<=U_bar, V<=V_bar, and g>=1/(1+D). The definition of T therefore ensures for every t>=T both the required Q condition and

 ||beta(t)a(t)-v||<=eps/2.

For the Q condition explicitly, e^(-gT)<=eps/[16nu_bar(V_bar+U_bar)], so U e^(-2gT)<=U_bar/[256nu_bar^2(V_bar+U_bar)^2]<1/2. This avoids any implicit large-time qualification.

## Rigorous finite-horizon GD transfer

This is an analytical Euler-error bound; no floating-point computation is used or asserted as a certificate. Let F=-grad f for the reduced pair Z=(beta,a), with f=||beta a-v||^2/2. Set H=T+1. The exact flow has ||Z(t)||<=sqrt(D+4)=R-2 for every t>=0. On the whole pair-norm ball of radius R,

 ||F(Z)||<=(R^2/2+1)R=M,
 ||DF(Z)||op<=6R^2+1=L.

The first bound follows from ||beta a-v||<=R^2/2+1. For the second, expand the Hessian quadratic form

 ||d_beta a+beta d_a||^2+2<beta a-v,d_beta d_a>;

its absolute value is at most (3R^2/2+1)(d_beta^2+||d_a||^2), which is smaller than L times that squared norm. The larger L is deliberately conservative.

For one exact-flow step, integration of F and its Lipschitz bound gives the local defect

 ||Z(t+eta)-Z(t)-eta F(Z(t))||<=eta^2 L M/2.

Let E_k=||Z_k^GD-Z(k eta)||. Provided the current GD point is in the radius-R ball, the segment to the flow point is also in it and

 E_(k+1)<=(1+eta L)E_k+eta^2 L M/2.

With E_0=0 this yields

 E_k<=(eta M/2)[(1+eta L)^k-1]
     <=(eta M/2)e^(L H)<=eps/(8R)

whenever k eta<=H. This also closes the ball condition inductively: the exact flow is within R-2 and eps/(8R)<1, so every proposed GD point stays within R-1. No boundedness of the computed GD sequence is assumed without proof.

Since eta<=1, N eta lies in [T,T+1]=[T,H]. The product map (beta,a)->beta a has derivative norm at most R on the radius-R ball, so

 ||beta_N a_N-beta(N eta)a(N eta)||<=R E_N<=eps/8.

Combining the flow error eps/2 and this transfer error gives a GD residual at most 5eps/8<eps. Reintroducing the unit output vector u preserves Frobenius residual norms and proves the statement.

## Limits

The step is constant during this finite run, chosen from deterministic parameters s,p,rho,eps rather than the sampled initializer. It may scale exponentially poorly with T and is not offered as a practical algorithmic rate. Choosing a different eta for a smaller eps is permitted in this theorem; claiming convergence at one fixed eta for all eps would require another argument. The high-probability event is essential and C013 still permits a rare escape event outside it. No expectation statement follows.

The entire rank-one flow component is known from the cited primary paper. The Euler argument is a standard method applied explicitly here, not an assertion of specialist-level novelty. The proper input-side bottleneck at ranks greater than one and arbitrary scales, efficient step/rate dependence, and Target 2 excess risk remain open in this work. body: For 0 < eps < 1 and any integer n, let k be a positive integer with k > 8 log(n)/eps^2 (any k = O(eps^{-2} log n) with a suitable absolute constant suffices). Then for any n points x_1,...,x_n in a Euclidean space of arbitrary dimension there is a linear map f into R^k, obtainable with high probability from a random projection, such that for every pair i, j: (1-eps) ||x_i - x_j||^2 <= ||f(x_i) - f(x_j)||^2 <= (1+eps) ||x_i - x_j||^2. So any n points embed into O(log n / eps^2) dimensions while nearly preserving all pairwise distances. Due to William Johnson and Joram Lindenstrauss.
title: Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma

body: In mathematics, the Cantor function is an example of a function that is continuous, but not absolutely continuous. It is a notorious counterexample in analysis, because it challenges naive intuitions about continuity, derivative, and measure. Although it is continuous everywhere, and has zero derivative almost everywhere, its value still goes from 0 to 1 as its argument goes from 0 to 1. Thus, while the function seems like a constant one that cannot grow, it does indeed monotonically grow.
title: Cantor function

Fix d>=2, unit u, X uniform on the radius-sqrt(d) sphere, Z=X.u, and continuous target q(Z) with q(sqrt(d))>0. Use the aligned exponential model f=integral a exp(b+gamma Z) dmu, w=sqrt(d) gamma u, with all a,b,w trained at original Euclidean learning rate. Initialize a=b=0 and an essentially unbounded positive scale tail: mu(gamma_0>R)>0 for every finite R. There is no common positive interval of finite absolutely continuous aligned characteristics satisfying the actual field almost everywhere, with a defined L-infinity predictor satisfying norm(f_t)_infinity to 0 at initialization. For scales above a fixed threshold, positivity of q near the pole and a hypothetical small predictor imply positive exponential lower bounds for both characteristic forces. The invariant b=a^2/2 then gives d/dt integral_0^a exp(-s^2/2) ds >= A exp(z2 gamma_0), although this transform is bounded by 3 for a>=0. The unbounded tail contradicts every common interval. A scale density proportional to exp(-gamma^4) has every finite quadratic exponential moment and a positive lower density on every compact interval, yet satisfies this obstruction. Pure degree-1 and normalized zonal harmonic targets are included because only positivity near the pole is needed. This does not exclude L2-continuous flows with narrow pole layers, other weak or non-aligned evolutions, or the bounded-scale prepared flows C5/C11, and it is not a ReLU counterexample. body: Lemma (campaign status: proved): Let $A=\{\pm1\}\times A'$ span $\mathbb R\oplus V'$ and suppose $g(s,x)=as+g'(x)$ is sign-valued on $A$. For every $x\in A'$ both $a+g'(x)$ and $-a+g'(x)$ lie in $\{\pm1\}$; therefore either $a=0$ and $g'$ is sign-valued on $A'$, or $|a|=1$ and $g'$ vanishes on the spanning set $A'$, so $g=\pm s$. Hence the projective full dual of a free product is exactly the disjoint union of the free coordinate and the full dual of the reduced factor. Notes: Consequence: deleting or reinserting free coordinates creates NO hidden full-dual form. This is what justifies every occurrence of 'after zero Gale columns are deleted' in the finite reduction -- a hypothesis-preservation lemma, not just a counting one.

The Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is the set of $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ such that $p_{\alpha,\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|<\infty$ for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$. With the countable family of seminorms $p_{\alpha,\beta}$ it is a Frechet space. It contains $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ and the Gaussians $e^{-\pi a|x|^2}$ ($a>0$); it is contained in $L^p(\mathbb R^d)$ for every $1\le p\le\infty$, is dense in $L^p$ for $1\le p<\infty$, and is closed under multiplication by polynomials, differentiation, products and convolution. Its continuous dual $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$ is the space of tempered distributions; the Fourier transform extends to $\mathcal S'$ by $\langle\hat T,\varphi\rangle=\langle T,\hat\varphi\rangle$, which is consistent with the integral definition on $L^1$ and with Plancherel on $L^2$. Note $C_c^\infty$ is not closed under the Fourier transform (a nonzero compactly supported function has a transform that is not compactly supported), while $\mathcal S$ is.

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2605.13727, 'Stochastic evolution equations\\ driven by arbitrary cylindrical Lévy processes'] Let $(\Psi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of $L$-integrable, predictable processes 
	converging to an $L_2(U,H)$-valued predictable process $\Psi$  $P_T$-a.e.  If there exists an $L$-integrable predictable  process $\Upsilon $ satisfying for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ that
	\[(\zeta_L+\eta_L)(\Psi_n(\omega,t)) \leq (\zeta_L+\eta_L)(\Upsilon(\omega,t)) \quad  \text{for $P_T$-a.a.\ $(\omega,t)\in \Omega\times [0,T]$}, \]
	then $\Psi$ is $L$-integrable  and satisfies
	\[\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} d_T^{em}(I(\Psi_n),I(\Psi))=0.\]
title: Theorem 9 of arXiv:2605.13727

Method: A zero-one law for Poisson-coloring frontier dimension structural attempt Result: The dimension event is not visibly a tail event of the independent arriving points. Changing an early point can change the color of infinitely many later descendants, so Kolmogorov zero-one cannot be invoked without a finite-modification invariance proof. The potential route is a regeneration principle producing, inside every surviving interface neighborhood, copies with the full essential supremum of the dimension law; countable-union stability of dimension would then force the maximal value. Check: The mere facts that the frontier is closed and has dimension strictly between1 and2 do not imply determinism: a Bernoulli mixture of two fixed compact fractal curves with different dimensions satisfies those facts and has random dimension. This is a logical control, not a Poisson-coloring counterexample. Obstruction: Independent arrivals do not make recursively inherited colors independent across subregions. A regeneration or local-universality statement strong enough to remove early-history effects is missing.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0231-a-zero-one-law-for-poisson-coloring-frontier-dimension

[Lemma L_Fs of arXiv:2605.15066, 'The critical activation density in graph bootstrap percolation'] Let $A$ be a graph. 
For each edge $e$ in $A$, put $W_e=F_e=e$. 
Recall that, for all other edges $e$ in 
$\langle A\rangle_H\setminus A$, the WGA 
identifies a copy $H_e$ of $H$ completed by $e$ and  
an inclusion-minimal 
subgraph 
\[
W_e=\bigcup_{f\in E(H_e\setminus e)}W_f\subset A
\]
for which $(e,W_e)\in{\mathcal A}(H)$. 
Then, for each such $e$, 
there is some  $e\subset F_e\subseteq W_e\cup e$, for which 
$\rho(e,F_e)\geqslant\rho(H)$ and 
\begin{equation}
v(F_e)-2\leqslant\sum_{f\in E(H_e\setminus e)} v(F_f). 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma L_Fs of arXiv:2605.15066

[Definition 7 (Bernoulli paths and Bernoulli path ensembles) of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] Given $p=(x_p,y_p),q=(x_q,y_q)\in \mathbb T_N+(0,1/(2N))$ such that $x_p<x_q$ and $0 \le y_q-y_p \le x_q-x_p$, we call \emph{Bernoulli path} with endpoints $p,q$ any path $S$ that starts at $p$, ends at $q$ and 
 such that 
 each step of $S$  is either $(1/N,0)$  or $(1/N,1/N)$ (that is, steps are either in the SE or in the  NE direction).
 
    Given $n\in \mathbb N$ and distinct points
    $p_1,\dots,p_n,q_1,\dots,q_n$  of $\mathbb T_N+(0,1/(2N))$ such that all the $p_i$ have
    the same $x-$coordinate  $x_p$ (and the $q_i$ also have all the same $x$-coordinate $x_q>x_p$) and ordered so that the $y-$coordinate of $p_i$ is larger than that of  $p_j$ (resp. the $y$-coordinate of $q_i$
    is larger than that of $q_j$) for $i>j$, we let the \emph{Bernoulli path ensemble} with endpoints
    $p_1,\dots,p_n,q_1,\dots,q_n$ denote the uniform measure on
    $n-$ples     $(S_1,\dots,S_n)$ of non-intersecting (i.e., disjoint) Bernoulli paths, where $S_i$ has endpoints $(p_i,q_i)$. (We assume
    that the points $p_i,q_i,i\le n$ are such that the configuration
    space is nonempty).
title: Bernoulli paths and Bernoulli path ensembles

Independent derivation pending w440 review. Replace every edge of the infinite 3-regular tree with L edges, for a positive integer L, and root at an original vertex. The result T_L is quasi-transitive of maximum degree 3 and has p_c=2^(-1/L)<1. Full subdivided edges are independent coarse bonds of retention p^L, so critical clusters are almost surely finite. For 1<=n<=L the critical probability of reaching graph distance n is 1-(1-2^(-n/L))^3, hence 7/8 at n=L. At radii kL, with u_0=1 and u_(k+1)=u_k-u_k^2/4, the probability is 1-(1-u_(k-1)/2)^3. Reciprocal increments tend to 1/4, so (kL) times this probability tends to 6L. Critical susceptibility is infinite because every original-vertex shell has expected connected count 3/2.

body:
Let Lambda be a compact hyperbolic set for a diffeomorphism f of a manifold. Then for every eps > 0 there is delta > 0 such that every delta-pseudo-orbit in a neighbourhood of Lambda - a sequence (x_n) with d(f(x_n), x_{n+1}) < delta for all n - is eps-SHADOWED by a genuine orbit: there is a point y with d(f^n(y), x_n) < eps for every n. If Lambda is in addition LOCALLY MAXIMAL (isolated) the shadowing point may be taken in Lambda, and if the pseudo-orbit is periodic the shadowing orbit may be taken periodic. Expansiveness of the hyperbolic set makes the shadowing point unique.
Hyperbolicity of the compact invariant set, and delta chosen AFTER eps.
Placing the shadowing orbit inside Lambda requires local maximality - without it the shadowing orbit exists but may leave the set.
Uniqueness uses expansiveness.

Let p and q be probability mass functions on a finite set S with d_TV(p, q) > 0, A = {p > q} and B = {q > p}. For a maximal coupling pi let G_pi be the bipartite graph on A and B with an edge x - y when pi(x, y) > 0. Then pi is an extreme point of the set of maximal couplings if and only if G_pi is a forest. Hence every extreme maximal coupling has at most |A| + |B| - 1 <= |S| - 1 positive off-diagonal entries. The greedy construction, which repeatedly sends the smaller of the remaining row and column masses between the first unfinished points of A and B, produces such a coupling, and if p and q are rational so is every mass it produces.

Consider the zero-bias fully connected Gaussian MLP with L hidden layers of width n, output width k, weight variance reciprocal to input width in every layer, and squared activation sigma(t)=t^2. Set K_1=||x||^2/d and K_(ell+1)=3K_ell^2. Given all L hidden layers, each final preactivation output has conditional variance Sigma=(1/n) sum_j (z_j^(L)(x))^4. This is a restricted specialization of Favaro, Hanin, Marinucci, Nourdin and Peccati, not a new theorem; constants have no asserted uniform dependence on L.

[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2609.02779, '2609.02779'] For the Hamiltonian \eqref{eq:twowell-H}, the critical value is $0$, and
\[
 \widetilde{\A}(H_a)
 =\left\{(0,-a),\left(\frac12,-a\right)\right\}.
\]
The two points are distinct static classes and are hyperbolic equilibria.
Moreover, with
\begin{equation}
\Delta:=\frac a2-A=\frac{B-A}{4}>0,
\end{equation}
the selected critical solution satisfies
\begin{equation}
u_0(0)=0,\qquad
u_0\left(\frac12\right)=-\Delta,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
u_0(x)=\int_0^x\bigl(Q(s)-a\bigr)\,\dd s,
\qquad
u_0'(x)+a=Q(x),
\qquad 0\le x\le\frac12.
