Claim draft w718-T287-029, version 1. Kind: moved; target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). This completes the fixed-iid-law, positive-finite-aspect Target2 comparison provided all earlier dependencies, especially028, pass audit. The dossier parenthetical sign is corrected as instructed: Gaussian maximizes both MI and product MMSE in this asymptotic comparison. Novelty is unestablished. Target1 remains open.

## Statement

Let independent factor arrays U (N by M), V (P by M) have fixed iid real laws with finite second moments, means mu and nu, and variances one. Let P/N->alpha>0, M/N->beta>0 finite. Write X=UV^T/sqrt(N), X_c=(U-mu)(V-nu)^T/sqrt(N), and let B_c be the corresponding centered Gaussian-factor product with unit factor variances. For fixed s>0 and standard Gaussian entry noise, let i_X(s) and m_X(s) denote MI and Bayes product risk divided by NP, respectively. Then

i_X(s)-i_Xc(s)->0,                                     (1)
limsup [i_X(s)-i_Bc(s)]<=0,
limsup [m_X(s)-m_Bc(s)]<=0.                             (2)

If B_mu,nu instead has independent Gaussian factor entries with the same means and variances as U,V, then its MI and risk limits at every s>0 equal those of B_c. Therefore both comparisons (2) also hold against that matching Gaussian prior. At s=0, matching Gaussian and iid risks are exactly (M/N)(1+mu^2+nu^2); both MI values are zero. For non-unit positive factor variances, center and divide each factor by its standard deviation, then rescale SNR and risk. Degenerate zero variance is handled directly by the same projection estimator at s>0 and matching means at zero.

The comparison is asymptotic at fixed SNR and in the limsup sense; the iid-prior risk need not have a limit. It is not a finite-dimensional extremality theorem, nor a result for dimension-dependent priors or means. A centered Gaussian comparator need not dominate noncentered priors exactly at s=0; matched means are essential for that endpoint statement.

## Orthogonal double centering

Put H_N=I_N-1_N1_N^T/N and H_P=I_P-1_P1_P^T/P. Define the orthogonal projection A on the NP-dimensional matrix space by A(T)=H_N T H_P, and Q=I-A. Its complementary dimension is d=N+P-1. Expanding the factors shows exactly

A(X)=A(X_c),                                          (3)

since every term containing either constant-mean factor is killed by the corresponding centering projection. The centered product entries are uncorrelated with variance b_N=M/N: for distinct entry pairs a centered factor expectation vanishes unless both row and column indices coincide, and different latent indices have zero cross expectation. Consequently

E||Q X_c||F^2=b_N d,
E||A X_c-X_c||F^2/(NP)=b_N d/(NP)->0.                  (4)

These require only second moments and independence of the arrays and iid entries. They do not assume independence among the product entries.

## MI carried by the complementary observations

Split Y=sqrt(s)X+G into Y_A and Y_Q. Gaussian noise components on the two orthogonal subspaces are independent standard Gaussian vectors in their respective orthonormal coordinates. The Markov dependence of Y_A on X through A X gives

I(X;Y_A)=I(A X;Y_A),
0<=I(X;Y)-I(A X;Y_A)=I(X;Y_Q|Y_A).

The latter is at most h(Y_Q)-h(G_Q), because conditioning reduces output entropy and the conditional noise given X,Y_A is still G_Q. For any d-dimensional signal T of finite centered second moment, Gaussian maximum entropy and the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality on its covariance eigenvalues give

I(T;sqrt(s)T+G_d)
 <=(d/2)log(1+s E||T-E T||^2/d).

The same upper bound applies to the displayed conditional information. Here

E||Q(X-E X)||F^2 <= E||X-E X||F^2
 =NP b_N(1+mu^2+nu^2).

Therefore

0<=i_X-i_AX
 <= d/(2NP) log(1+s NP b_N(1+mu^2+nu^2)/d)->0.          (5)

The last limit holds because N,P are comparable and d=O(N), so it is O(log N/N). The possibly large deterministic mean of X does not enter this entropy bound. All differential entropies used here are finite after Gaussian smoothing: the second-moment upper bound and the Gaussian-mixture conditional-entropy lower bound apply even for discrete priors.

By (3), i_AX=i_AXc. By (4) and the dimension-uniform Gaussian entropy/W2 continuity estimate of claim006, with the direct projection coupling,

|i_AXc-i_Xc|<=sqrt(s b_N d/(NP))->0.                   (6)

Equations (5)-(6) prove (1), with no independence asserted between the two signal projections. Claim023 gives the centered MI comparison, hence the MI part of (2).

## Fixed-SNR risk upper bound

Use the estimator that estimates A X by its Bayes estimator from Y_A alone, and estimates Q X by Y_Q/sqrt(s). Its two errors lie in orthogonal subspaces, so their squared norms add exactly. Its complementary error has expectation d/s. Hence

m_X(s)<=m_AX(s)+d/(NP s).                              (7)

The Bayes risk m_AX here is for prior A X observed in standard Gaussian ambient noise; its orthogonal noise-only coordinates are independent and contain no information, so it equals the restricted-channel risk used in (7). By (3) its prior is A X_c.

Claim023 couples the ordered singular profiles of X_c to B_c in expected squared per-entry spectral cost tending to zero. Hoffman-Wielandt and (4) show the same coupling for A X_c, by the triangle inequality in the L2 space of ordered singular profiles. Claim006 applies to an arbitrary matrix prior, not just an iid-factor product: Haarizing A X_c can only increase Bayes risk, its Haarized MI limit equals the Gaussian-reference limit by spectral coupling, and that limit is C1 by claim028. Concave secants therefore give

limsup [m_AXc(s)-m_Bc(s)]<=0

at every fixed positive s. Together with (7), this proves the risk part of (2). This proof discards the complementary observations when constructing an upper bound; it does not incorrectly assume that those observations are uninformative about the projected signal.

## Matching noncentered Gaussian comparator

Apply (1) to Gaussian factors with means mu,nu. Their centered product is B_c, so i_Bmu,nu(s)-i_Bc(s)->0 for every fixed s>0. By claim028 the latter information converges to a C1 function. Thus the matching noncentered Gaussian information has the same C1 limit. Its finite-dimensional information functions are concave and differentiable with derivative equal to one half of normalized MMSE. The two-sided secant argument gives m_Bmu,nu(s)-m_Bc(s)->0 for every fixed s>0. It is the Gaussian reference derivative that is taken here, not an inequality between information functions.

At s=0 the Bayes estimator is the prior mean. For each product entry, independence over latent indices gives Var(X_ij)=b_N[(1+mu^2)(1+nu^2)-mu^2nu^2]=b_N(1+mu^2+nu^2). This value depends only on matching means and variances and is exactly the same for the Gaussian comparator. The endpoint need not agree with the limit of positive-SNR asymptotic risks as s decreases to zero, because the low-dimensional mean-related components are learned at every fixed positive SNR. No interchange of these limits is made.

## Zero-variance factors and audit boundary

If one factor variance is zero, that fixed factor is deterministic constant. The random product lies in a subspace of dimension at most max(N,P), so observing it directly yields normalized risk <=max(N,P)/(NP s)->0. All such risks are nonnegative, giving the fixed-positive-SNR Gaussian comparison. The same low-dimensional capacity estimate as (5) makes normalized MI tend to zero. At s=0 the variance formula with the actual second moments gives equality for matching Gaussian factors (including degenerate Gaussian laws). If both variances are positive, the standardization described in the statement reduces exactly to the unit-variance case.

Least trusted: the inherited physical boundary-branch argument025 and its use in the C1 chain rule026. The exact projection and capacity argument here does not certify those dependencies. ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: Even agreement of every one- and two-site marginal need not identify a measure. On Z, partition into triples with a uniformly random phase and use iid uniform even-parity bit triples (000,011,101,110). Every pair of distinct bits is independent Bernoulli(1/2), including pairs across triples. The measure is translation invariant. For three consecutive sites, however, the all-ones probability is (1/3)*0+(2/3)*(1/8)=1/12, whereas iid Bernoulli(1/2) gives 1/8. Thus the pair-correlation experiments cannot distinguish all possible candidate laws. Check: For an aligned triple, 111 is forbidden. In each nonaligned phase the triple crosses a block boundary; two bits from one block are independent and the third is independent of them, giving 1/8. Averaging the three phases gives 1/12. Obstruction: Need a coupling or a characterization using all cylinder events. This auxiliary counterexample refutes only the proposed inference from pair data, not equality of the actual ARW limits.

field $(\zeta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ satisfying
\[
    \Var(\zeta(0))\geq\nu_{0}^2\, ,\qquad \mathbb{E} e^{\theta_{0}|\zeta(0)|}\leq K_{0}\, ,
\]
and every $t\geq t_0$, the planar set
\[
    \{x:u_t(x)>c t^{(4-d)/4}\}
\]
contains an infinite nearest-neighbor component almost surely, where $x$ ranges
over $\mathbb{Z}^2$ if $d=2$, and over $\mathbb{Z}^2\times\{0\}$ if $d=3$.

By $\omega_{h, i}$ we denote the number of $(h,i)$-constrained walks on the rooted infinite $d$-regular tree, while by $\widetilde{\omega}_{h, i}$ we denote the number of $(h,i)$-constrained walks on the rooted infinite $(d - 1)$-ary tree.

body: In combinatorics, a matroid is a structure that abstracts and generalizes the notion of linear independence in vector spaces. There are many equivalent ways to define a matroid axiomatically, the most significant being in terms of: independent sets; bases or circuits; rank functions; closure operators; and closed sets or flats. In the language of partially ordered sets, a finite simple matroid is equivalent to a geometric lattice.

Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y) a bounded linear operator. T is a Fredholm operator if (a) its kernel ker T is finite-dimensional and (b) its range ran T has finite codimension, i.e. the quotient vector space Y / ran T is finite-dimensional. The index of a Fredholm operator is the integer ind T = dim ker T - dim(Y / ran T). The range of a Fredholm operator is automatically closed (a bounded operator between Banach spaces whose range has finite algebraic codimension has closed range), so texts that add 'ran T is closed' to the definition define the same class. For Fredholm T one has dim(Y / ran T) = dim ker T', where T': Y' -> X' is the Banach-space adjoint, so ind T = dim ker T - dim ker T'. Examples on l^2: an invertible operator has index 0; the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is injective with range of codimension 1, so ind S = -1, and its adjoint (the backward shift) has index +1; I + K with K compact has index 0. The set of Fredholm operators X -> Y is written Phi(X,Y).
X and Y are Banach spaces over the same field
T is a bounded linear operator from X to Y
title: Fredholm Operator and Fredholm Index

body:
A ring R (associative, with 1) is semisimple - every left R-module is a direct sum of simple modules, equivalently R is a finite direct sum of simple left modules, equivalently R is left Artinian with zero Jacobson radical - if and only if R is isomorphic to a finite product of matrix rings over division rings: R = M_{n_1}(D_1) x ... x M_{n_r}(D_r). The integers r and n_i and the division rings D_i (up to isomorphism) are determined by R: r is the number of isomorphism classes of simple left R-modules, and the simple module S_i = D_i^{n_i} has End_R(S_i) = D_i (opposite conventions aside). A simple left Artinian ring is a single matrix ring M_n(D). Consequences: for a finite group G and a field k of characteristic not dividing |G| (Maschke), the group algebra k[G] is semisimple, so k[G] = prod M_{n_i}(D_i); over an algebraically closed field the D_i are k itself, the n_i are the degrees of the irreducible representations, r is the number of conjugacy classes, and |G| = sum n_i^2. A commutative semisimple ring is a finite product of fields. Wedderburn's little theorem (finite division rings are fields) then gives: a finite semisimple ring is a product of matrix rings over finite fields.
R associative with identity; 'semisimple' means semisimple as a left module over itself (equivalent to the right-module version)
the division rings need not be commutative (the real quaternions H occur, e.g. in R[Q_8])

\[\frac{\aut H' \cdot X_{H'}(H) \cdot (v(H)-v(H'))!}{\aut H} \in \setz.\]
In particular, for $H \in \mathcal{C}_2\cup\mathcal{C}_3\cup\mathcal{C}_4\cup\mathcal{C}_5$,

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:45ac823e855903243d2b234b934e93c0b867d02662863dbabef7fd7cd064141d","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/45/45ac823e855903243d2b234b934e93c0b867d02662863dbabef7fd7cd064141d.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:a23242ff949ecb817055c8769e4306ca0603b6042513d5cd53131633bf50d399","bundle_entry_key":"bilinear-confidence-full-rank-rotation","bundle_id":"population.t407-draft-gaussian-bilinear-confidence-supplement","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"statistical learning theory","draft":"w693/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.sample_complexity:draft-gaussian-bilinear-orbit-two-point-confidence-lower","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Confidence supplement for the Gaussian bilinear orbit

Status: proof (unaudited). Standard two-point testing, not a novelty claim.
Target 2; supplements LOW-003 v2 without changing that proof or its audit status.

For every d>=2, 0<epsilon<=1/96, and 0<delta<=1/4, any possibly randomized, improper learner achieving population disagreement at most epsilon with probability at least 1-delta for every h_U(a,b)=sign(a^T U b), U in O(d), under independent standard Gaussian a,b, requires

    n >= log(1/delta)/(96 epsilon).

## A pair with dimension-independent disagreement

Let r=floor(d/2), q=2r, P project onto the first q coordinates, and J consist of r standard 2x2 skew rotation blocks and a zero last coordinate if d is odd. Then J^T=-J, J^2=-P. For 0<t<=1/4 put

    U_+(t)=I-P+cos(t)P+sin(t)J,
    U_-(t)=I-P+cos(t)P-sin(t)J.

Both matrices are orthogonal. Conditional on a nonzero b, the normals U_+b and U_-b have equal length ||b|| and distance 2 sin(t)||Pb||. Their angle is therefore

    theta(b)=2 arcsin(sin(t)||Pb||/||b||).

A standard Gaussian a has uniform angular projection onto the span of these normals, so its two sign labels disagree with probability theta(b)/pi. This also holds for coincident normals by continuity. Write u=b/||b||, uniform on the unit sphere. Consequently

    rho_d(t)=(2/pi) E arcsin(sin(t)||Pu||).

When d is even this is exactly 2t/pi. In all dimensions, 0<=||Pu||<=1 and E||Pu||>=E||Pu||^2=q/d>=2/3. Using arcsin(x)>=x, sin(t)>=t/2 and pi<=4 gives

    rho_d(t) >= 2t/(3pi) >= t/6.

Since arcsin(sin(t)||Pu||)<=t, also rho_d(t)<=2t/pi<=t. These are analytic inequalities, uniform in d. Set t=24 epsilon. Then

    4 epsilon <= rho_d(t) <=24 epsilon <=1/4.

## Exact testing overlap, including randomized learners

Let Q_+ and Q_- be the distributions of one labeled observation under these targets, with the same Gaussian input marginal. On their disagreement region D, the two observation distributions have disjoint label support. On D's complement they coincide. For n independent samples their common mass (the integral of the minimum of their densities with respect to a common dominating measure) is exactly

    overlap(Q_+^n,Q_-^n)=(1-rho_d(t))^n.

Indeed, shared labeled samples occur precisely when every input avoids D; that event has marginal probability (1-rho_d(t))^n. Equal-prior optimal testing error is half this mass: pointwise, the cheaper error contribution is half the minimum of the two densities. Adding independent random coins cannot reduce this optimum.

Decode the learner's output by choosing the closer of the two target classifiers in population disagreement, breaking ties arbitrarily. The triangle inequality and separation >=4epsilon imply this decoder is correct whenever the learner's error is <=epsilon. Uniform confidence thus gives testing error <=delta. Hence

    (1-rho_d(t))^n / 2 <=delta,
    n >= log(1/(2delta))/[-log(1-rho_d(t))].

For 0<=rho<=1/4, -log(1-rho)<=rho/(1-rho)<=2rho<=48epsilon. Also delta<=1/4 implies log(1/(2delta))>=log(1/delta)/2. The stated bound follows.

## Relation to the remaining frontier claim

This proves only the confidence contribution. If LOW-003 v2's separately unaudited dimension lower is correct, then for delta<=1/4 and epsilon below a universal constant the two necessary bounds combine as

    n=Omega((d^2+log(1/delta))/epsilon),

because max(A,B)>=(A+B)/2. This would match the independently accepted UP-002 v2 upper order. The combined conclusion remains a candidate until the dimension lower passes independent audit. The hardest outstanding piece remains the source matrix-packing use and conditional-entropy/Fano argument in LOW-003 v2, not this two-point argument.

Primary context: Li-Zhang-Arora, arXiv:2010.08515v2, Lemmas D.2 and D.4. The confidence proof above is self-contained and extends the two-dimensional testing step already in LOW-003 v2 section 5. Let U = <c, X_H> for a set H of hub coordinates with c_h^2 <= |c|^2/2 for every h, and Q = 2 U (L + beta) + sum_{h in H} phi_h(X_h) + lambda V^2 + 2 L <q, X'> + sum_i phi_i(X_i) with the light part as in the single-hub normal form. Then |phi_Q(eta)| <= 8 pi^{3/2} |c|^{-1} |lambda|^{-1/2} |eta|^{-3/2} and ||p_Q||_inf <= 12 (|c|^2 |lambda|)^{-1/3} for all laws and every cross term q. Proof: the hub factor prod_h psi_h(2 eta t c_h + eta b_h) has int dt <= 2 pi/(|eta| |c|) by Hoelder with p_h = |c|^2/c_h^2 (one-dimensional Brascamp-Lieb, shift-invariant), and pairs with the slice bound 2 (4 pi/|eta lambda|)^{1/2}. Roughness of the hub law is an obstruction only when the hub is one coordinate.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked, no independent read.] This is an exactly solved adjacent case of Open Problem 14.12 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). For n>=3 let C_n be the simple cycle on n vertices. Start a particle at every vertex. Each particle independently jumps at rate one to a uniformly chosen neighbor, and particles merge on meeting. Let T_coal be the first time only one particle remains. Then E[T_coal]=(n^2-1)/6. If P is the cycle's discrete-time simple-walk matrix, define its mean spectral hitting-time quantity K=sum_{j=2}^n 1/(1-lambda_j(P)); then K=(n^2-1)/6 also. Thus E[T_coal]=K exactly. Its relaxation time tau_2=1/(1-cos(2pi/n)) satisfies tau_2/K -> 3/pi^2, so this family has the equality conclusion even though the small-relaxation-time hypothesis in the source problem fails. In the extracted optional-stopping proof, EC in a stopping-time subscript denotes the random coalescence time; the final displayed EC denotes its expectation. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
Continuous-time rate-one simple walks; one initial particle per vertex.

neighbour, and particles at the same vertex merge.

Label the $k$ particles round the cycle and let $g_1,\dots,g_k \ge 1$ be the gaps between consecutive
particles, so $\sum_i g_i = n$. Put
$$M \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^k g_i^3 .$$

Take a particle with gap $a$ on its left and $b$ on its right. It steps right at rate $1/2$, sending
$(a,b) \mapsto (a+1,b-1)$, and left at rate $1/2$, sending $(a,b) \mapsto (a-1,b+1)$. The two
increments of $M$ are
$$(3a^2+3a+1) + (-3b^2+3b-1) = 3(a^2-b^2) + 3(a+b),$$
$$(-3a^2+3a-1) + (3b^2+3b+1) = -3(a^2-b^2) + 3(a+b),$$
and the quadratic parts cancel in the average, leaving $3(a+b)$. Each particle jumps at rate one, so
summing over the particles,
$$\mathcal L M \;=\; \sum_{i} 3\,(g_{i-1} + g_i) \;=\; 3\,(n+n) \;=\; 6n,$$
independent of the configuration and of the number of particles. That last point is what makes the
argument work: the drift does not care how far along the coalescence is.

When two particles merge, the gap between them has just become zero and is deleted. Since $0^3 = 0$,
$M$ does not jump at a coalescence, so it is continuous through the whole process.

Hence $M_t - 6nt$ is a martingale. $M$ is bounded by $n^3$ and $EC$ has finite mean, so optional
stopping applies. At time zero all $n$ gaps equal one and $M_0 = n$; at time $EC$ there is one particle
and one gap of size $n$, so $M_{EC} = n^3$. Therefore
$$n^3 - n \;=\; 6n\cdot EC, \qquad EC \;=\; \frac{n^2-1}{6}. \qquad\square$$

[Proposition 6 (Equivariant flows on the quotient) of arXiv:2608.26961, 'Gromov--Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation'] Let \(v:I\times\R^D\to\R^D\) be \(G\)-equivariant and assume that
\eqref{flow-ode} admits a unique flow \(\gamma_t\). Then \(\gamma_t\) induces
the well-defined quotient flow
\[
\bar\gamma_t([x])\coloneqq[\gamma_t(x)].
\]
For every \(\eta\in\mP_2(\R^D)\) and \(t\in I\),
\[
\mathfrak q_\sharp\gamma_{t,\sharp}\eta
=
\bar\gamma_{t,\sharp}\mathfrak q_\sharp\eta.
\]
In particular, if
\(\mathfrak q_\sharp\eta=\mathfrak q_\sharp\widetilde\eta\), then
\[
\mathfrak q_\sharp\gamma_{t,\sharp}\eta
=
\mathfrak q_\sharp\gamma_{t,\sharp}\widetilde\eta,
\]
so the projected curve is independent of the representative lift at time
\(0\).

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); D0007-C008 v1; audits pending. If F=p Uniform[a,b]+(1-p)G with 0<p<1, a<b finite and G bounded-support, then F is n-completely mixable for every sufficiently large integer n. Symmetry is unnecessary and the uniform interval need not contain mean(F). Put ell=b-a, c=(a+b)/2, m=E_G[X], R=B-A for an interval [A,B] supporting G, C=|c-m|+R, and K0=ceil(max(2,6C/ell,2+2C/ell)). Every n>=ceil(K0/p) works. Cyclic quantile strata couple residual coordinates with sum discrepancy at most R. Rounded uniform counts K and conditional affine density tilts absorb the remaining discrepancy; E[delta]=0 restores the exact full marginal. Finite rounding of delta followed by a weak limit at fixed n handles conditional-coupling selection. Therefore a bounded law with a positive density lower bound on just one subinterval is eventually n-CM. This does not cover densities with essential infimum zero on every interval; general D0007 remains unresolved. The established Wang-Wang monotone density criterion is used as stated in Wang arXiv:1411.6190v3 Section 2.2(b), equation (6), p.9; novelty not asserted.

Status: proof (unaudited). Uses the established monotone-density CM criterion and fixed-order weak compactness. Novelty not asserted.

Statement. Let 0<p<1, a<b finite, and let G be any bounded-support probability law, possibly discrete. Then

    F=p Uniform[a,b]+(1-p)G

is n-CM for all sufficiently large integer n. The uniform interval can be anywhere, not necessarily centered at mean(F). Thus any bounded absolutely continuous law whose density is bounded below by a positive constant on even one nondegenerate subinterval is eventually n-CM. No density floor is required elsewhere; symmetry is unnecessary.

An explicit threshold: put ell=b-a, c=(a+b)/2, m=E_G[X], R=B-A for any finite interval [A,B] supporting G, and C=|c-m|+R. Choose the integer

    K0=ceil(max(2,6C/ell,2+2C/ell)).

Every n>=ceil(K0/p) works. The p=1 uniform law is directly CM for all n>=2.

Known theorem used: If a probability law has a monotone density on essential [a,b], it is K-CM iff a+ell/K<=its mean<=b-ell/K. Source: Wang-Wang (2011), doi:10.1016/j.jmva.2011.05.002, stated by Ruodu Wang in arXiv:1411.6190v3 Section 2.2(b), equation (6), p.9. We cite this established theorem rather than reprove it.

1. Bounded-discrepancy coupling for G. For every L>=1, let Q be a quantile of G, with endpoint bounds Q(0)=A and Q(1)=B (values at the endpoints do not affect the law). Draw U uniform on [0,1/L] and form Q(U+(i-1)/L), i=1,...,L. Apply an independent uniform coordinate permutation. Each marginal is G, since the uniformly selected stratum has a uniform quantile argument in [0,1]. The sum S_L does not change under permutation and satisfies

    |S_L-Lm|<=R almost surely.

Indeed monotonicity traps S_L between the lower and upper endpoint sums for the L quantile intervals; Lm lies between the same sums, and their difference telescopes to Q(1)-Q(0)=R. For L=0 take the empty vector and S_0=0. This construction applies to atoms without change.

2. Uniform label counts. Choose K from floor(np) and ceil(np), with expectation np; if np is integer use that fixed count. Set L=n-K. The threshold ensures K>=K0 in every state. Conditional on K draw the G coupling of Step 1, and define

    delta=n*mu-K*c-S_L,
    mu=p*c+(1-p)*m.

Algebra gives delta=(np-K)(c-m)+(Lm-S_L), so |delta|<=C. Also E delta=0 because E K=np and E[S_L|K]=Lm.

3. Monotone uniform tilts absorb the discrepancy. For any K>=K0 and d in [-C,C] define

    t=6d/(K*ell),
    q_{K,d}(x)=(1/ell)[1+t*2(x-c)/ell] on [a,b].

Since |t|<=1 this is a probability density with full essential support [a,b]. It is monotone (increasing for d>0, decreasing for d<0), and its mean is c+t ell/6=c+d/K. Because K>=2+2C/ell,

    |d|<=(K/2-1)ell.

Thus the mean belongs to [a+ell/K,b-ell/K]. The cited theorem supplies a K-CM coupling of q_{K,d}, with sum K*c+d.

4. Avoid any unproved measurable selection. For each mesh eta>0, choose a finite grid in [-C,C] and a measurable rounding function d_eta(delta) with |d_eta(delta)-delta|<=eta and |d_eta(delta)|<=C. If C=0 use the singleton grid {0}. Only finitely many K and rounded d occur. Choose one of the couplings from Step 3 for each pair. Conditional on the G-vector and K use the coupling for d=d_eta(delta), combine its K coordinates with the L G coordinates, and uniformly permute all n coordinates. This is a well-defined Borel probability coupling because there are only finitely many selected kernels.

Its total sum is

    S_L+K*c+d_eta(delta)=n*mu+d_eta(delta)-delta,

so its deviation from n*mu is at most eta.

5. The identical marginals converge exactly to F. A fixed permuted coordinate has G-contribution (1-p)G, since E L/n=1-p and conditional on K every G-coordinate has marginal G. Its uniform-reserve contribution is E[(K/n)q_{K,d_eta(delta)}]. The constant density part is p/ell. The linear part is proportional to

    E[K*t]/n=6 E[d_eta(delta)]/(n*ell).

Since E delta=0, |E d_eta(delta)|<=eta. The L1 norm of this signed linear perturbation is at most 3 eta/(n*ell). Hence the full marginals converge in total variation to F as eta goes to zero. No independence between K and the discrepancy is assumed.

6. Take a fixed-n weak limit. All coordinates are supported on the fixed compact interval spanning [A,B] and [a,b]. Therefore the sequence of n-dimensional couplings as eta decreases to zero has a weakly convergent subsequence. Coordinate projections are continuous, so every limiting marginal is F by Step 5. The continuous sum map and the uniform sum error bound in Step 4 force the limit to have sum n*mu almost surely. Equivalently the expectation of the bounded continuous squared sum error tends to zero. This gives an exact n-complete mix.

7. Local density-floor corollary. If an absolutely continuous bounded-support F has f(x)>=c0>0 almost everywhere on [a,b], set p=c0*(b-a). Subtracting p Uniform[a,b] leaves a nonnegative bounded-support measure of mass 1-p. If p<1 normalize it to G and apply the theorem; if p=1 F is uniform. The global mean need not be the uniform interval center.

Hardest remaining D0007 case: densities with essential infimum zero on every interval, including positive-measure supports containing no interval. Such laws need not contain any interval-uniform component. The proof does not remove this obstacle and does not settle the full problem. such that $\chi|_{(-\infty,1]}=0$ and $\chi|_{[2,\infty)}=1$.
For any $\mu\in[0,1]$ and $t\geqslant0$, 
we define the regularized kernel $G_\mu$, which is given by
   \begin{equs}
       G_\mu(t)\eqdef \chi(t/\mu) \,, \end{equs} 
with the convention that $G_0=G$. 
Finally, we write $\dot G_\mu(t)\eqdef\d_\mu G_\mu(t)$.

[Cor 170 (quenched second moment bounds for $Y^{\RomI}$ and $Y^{\RomI,\frozen}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $N$ large enough, we have
	\beq
	\max\bigg\{
	\bE\Big[\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big]
	: 0 \le d\le \dmax-1
	\bigg\}
    \le L^{O(1)} \delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2
    \,,
    \eeq
with $\MAX_N$ as in Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}. The same bound holds with $\vY^\frozen$ in place of $\vY$. 

\begin{proof} It follows using
Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} that
	\[\bE\Big(
	\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big)
	\le \bE\Big( \Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))^2\Big)
	+ O(\eta)\bigg\{ \bE\Big| \Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	+ \eta\bigg\}\,.\]
From the spatial rerandomization (Definition~\ref{d:rerand}), the index $a(q_{d+1})$ is a uniformly random sample from $[M]$, even if we condition on the gaussian disorder. Thus we can apply Proposition~\ref{p:X.second.mmt.quenched} with $a(q_{d+1})$ in place of $\hat{a}$. Together with Jensen's inequality and \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound}, it implies
	\[
	\bE\Big[\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big]
    \le L^{O(1)}\Big\{ \delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2
    + \eta^2\Big\}
    \le L^{O(1)}\delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2\,,
	\]
using that $\MAX_N\ge1$ and $\eta\ll\delta$ from Assumption~\ref{a:params}. This proves \eqref{e:Y.I.second.quenched}, and the analogous bound for $Y^{\frozen,\RomI}$ follows by the same argument.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: quenched second moment bounds for $Y^{\RomI}$ and $Y^{\RomI,\frozen}$

title: Egorov's theorem

[Definition 12 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Fix $b > 0$ and $\vec{y} \in \weylc_2$. Suppose that $\mu$ is the measure on $\weylc_2 \times \weylc_2$, defined by 
$$\mu(A) = \mathbb{P}\left(((Z,Z),(y_1,y_2)) \in A\right),$$
where $Z$ is a normal random variable with mean  $(y_1 + y_2)/2$ and variance $b/2$. Let $\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{pin}}^{b, \vec{y}}$ be equal to $\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{avoid}}^{a,b,\mu}$ as in (\ref{Eq.RandomBryMeas}) for this choice of $\mu$ and $a = 0$. If $\mathcal{Q} = (\mathcal{Q}_1, \mathcal{Q}_2)$ has law $\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{pin}}^{b, \vec{y}}$, we refer to $\mathcal{Q}$ as a {\em pinned pair of avoiding reverse Brownian motions with boundary data $\vec{y}$} or simply a {\em pinned pair} for short.

body: In the mathematical field of graph theory, Kirchhoff's theorem or Kirchhoff's matrix tree theorem is a theorem about the number of spanning trees in a graph. It states that this number can be computed as any cofactor of the graph's Laplacian matrix. This shows in particular that the number of spanning trees can be computed from the graph data in polynomial time. Kirchhoff's theorem is a generalization of Cayley's formula which provides the number of spanning trees in a complete graph. The theorem is named after the German mathematician Gustav Kirchhoff, who published it in 1847. An English translation of Kirchhoff's paper was published in 1958.
title: Kirchhoff's theorem

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Low-density genealogical limit of branching coalescing walks structural calculation Result: Immediate parent-daughter returns renormalize the branching clock. For two independent simple walks started at neighboring sites in Z^3, their relative walk is a time change of simple walk. The probability they never meet is q=1-G(e,0)/G(0,0)=1/G(0,0), using G(0,0)=1+G(e,0) by the first-step identity and lattice symmetry. Thus a rare branch at rate beta produces a macroscopically surviving split at leading rate beta*q, rather than beta. Check: The equality of the two Green-function expressions follows from translation and reflection symmetry of all six neighbors. It concerns an isolated pair; the chance of interference by other particles has not been set to zero without justification. Obstruction: A thinning heuristic suggests time scaling1/(beta*q), but a proof needs control of third-particle encounters, dependent return episodes and joint Palm genealogies. Stationary balance of split and merge counts does not imply independent Poisson clocks.

body: Vitali covering lemma: from finitely many balls in R^d one can select a pairwise disjoint subfamily whose 5-times dilations cover the union of all the original balls; for infinite families with uniformly bounded radii a countable disjoint subfamily with the same 5x-dilation property exists. body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The logarithmic factor in the tuned constant-step rate of random reshuffling (November 2026), shows that for strongly convex finite sums the logarithmic factor in the last-iterate upper bounds for random reshuffling with a constant step tuned to the number of epochs cannot be removed. On a one-dimensional instance with mu = L n1/n, gradient size G at the minimiser, T = nK steps, initial distance D and Lambda = ln(mu T D/G), every constant step gamma <= 1/L leaves E F(x_K) - F* >= G^2 (Lambda - ln Lambda)^2/(512 mu T^2) once K >= n1(Lambda - ln Lambda)/2, while the step Lambda/(mu T) gives at most G^2 Lambda^2 (1 + o(1))/(8 mu T^2), so the tuned constant-step error is Theta(G^2 ln^2(mu T D/G)/(mu T^2)). The proof computes one epoch exactly; the epoch variance reduces to the variance of a Mann-Whitney statistic. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/rr-constant-step-log-factor (commit 4bc93e1799af). Not refereed.
title: The logarithmic factor in the tuned constant-step rate of random reshuffling cannot be removed (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/rr-constant-step-log-factor)

[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2608.12839, 'Spiking Neural Networks with Elephant Reinforcement'] Assume that the initial laws are translation invariant:
\[
\mu_{i,0}=\mu_0,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.
\]
Then the unique nonlinear RMF solution satisfies
\[
\mu_i(t)=\mu(t),
\qquad
\beta_i(t)=\beta(t),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,
\]
for every \(t\geq0\). Consequently, every representative neuron receives total
input intensity
\[
a(t)=2\beta(t).
\]

body:
[Lem 236 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $1\le \fq < \fp$ and $C > 0$, the spaces $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ and $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric,
are compact.

\begin{proof}
	We will show compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$, as compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$ is proved analogously.
	It suffices to show that every sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ has a subsequence converging in $\bbW_\fq$ to a measure in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$.
	Consider any such sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$.
	The set of measures $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ is clearly tight, so by Prohorov's theorem there exists a weakly convergent subsequence $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$. 
Let $\mu$ be its weak limit. By Skorokhod's theorem, we can find a coupling of random variables $X_j\sim\mu_{n_j}$ and $X\sim\mu$ such that
$X_j\to X$ almost surely. Then, by Fatou's lemma, we have
	\[
		\|\mu\|_{L^\fp}^\fp 
	=\E[|X|^p]^{1/p}
		\le
		\liminf_j \E[|X_j|^p]^{1/p}
		= \liminf_{j\to\infty} \|\mu_{n_j}\|_{L^\fp}^\fp
		 \le C\,,
	\]
	so $\mu \in \cP_\fp(\R,C)$. 
	It remains to show $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$ converges to $\mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
	 Note that for any $\nu \in \cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, Markov's inequality implies
	\[
	\nu(|x|>K) 
	\le \frac{1}{K^\fp}\int
		|x|^\fp \,d\nu
		 \le \frac{C}{K^\fp}\,.
	\]
Combining this with H\"older's inequality gives
	\beq
		\int_{|x|>K} |x|^\fq \,d\nu
		\le \nu(|x|>K)^{1 - \fq/\fp} \bigg(
			\int |x|^\fp \,d\nu
		\bigg)^{\fq/\fp}
		\le \frac{C}{K^{\fp - \fq}}\,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq.tail} and the weak convergence $\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$,
	\begin{align*}
		\limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\bigg|
		&\le \limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			\,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			 \,d\mu
		\bigg|\\
		&\qquad + \limsup_{j\to\infty} \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		+ \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\le \frac{2C}{K^{\fp-\fq}}\,.
	\end{align*}
	Since $K$ was arbitrary, we infer the convergence of $\fq$-th moments
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\E[|X_j|^p]
		=\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		= \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		= \E[|X|^p]\,.\]
This implies that the random variables $\{X_j\}$ are uniformly integrable, so
	\begin{align*}
	&\bbW_\fq(\mu_{n_j}, \mu)^\fq
	\le \E[|X_j-X|^\fq]\\
	&\le\E\Big[
	\max\{|X_j-X|,2K\}^\fq\Big]
	+\E\Big[|X_j| ; |X_j|\ge K\Big]
	+ \E\Big[|X| ; |X|\ge K\Big]
	\\
	&\le o_j(1) + o_K(1)+ o_K(1)\,.
	\end{align*}
Since the left-hand side does not depend on $K$, we conclude that
$\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 236 of arXiv:2608.29416

Let F be a cumulative distribution function on \mathbb{R} and G a differentiable function of bounded variation such that G(-\infty) = 0, G(\infty) = 1, and |G'(x)| \le M for all x. Let \phi_F(t) = \int e^{itx} dF(x) and \phi_G(t) = \int e^{itx} dG(x). Then for any T > 0, \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |F(x) - G(x)| \le \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-T}^T \left| \frac{\phi_F(t) - \phi_G(t)}{t} \right| dt + \frac{24 M}{\pi T}.

G is of bounded variation with bounded derivative |G'| \le M

Let U subset R^n be open, bounded, with Lipschitz boundary, n>=1, and H^1(U)=W^{1,2}(U). Then: (i) if n=1, H^1(U) embeds continuously into C^{0,1/2}(closure(U)); (ii) if n=2, H^1(U) embeds continuously into L^q(U) for every finite q in [1,infinity), but not into L^infinity(U) or C^0(closure(U)) in general; (iii) if n>=3, H^1(U) embeds continuously into L^{2*}(U), 2*=2n/(n-2), i.e. there is C=C(n,U) with ||u||_{L^{2*}(U)} <= C||u||_{H^1(U)} for all u in H^1(U). In every dimension the embedding of H^1(U) into L^q(U) is compact for every q strictly below the borderline exponent (q<2* for n>=3, any finite q for n<=2), by the Rellich-Kondrachov theorem.
U is open, bounded, with Lipschitz boundary
n = dimension >= 1

Let G = (X, Y, E) be a finite bipartite graph and, for S a subset of X, let N(S) be the set of vertices of Y adjacent to some vertex of S. There is a matching saturating every vertex of X if and only if |N(S)| >= |S| for every subset S of X. Equivalently, a finite family of finite sets (A_1, ..., A_m) has a system of distinct representatives (distinct a_i with a_i in A_i) if and only if every k of the sets have a union with at least k elements.

[Lemma bound_waterfall_boundary_L of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] Assume that $\mathsf{t}_l<\mathsf{t}<\mathsf{t}_r$
	and $y=\lfloor L\hspace{1pt} \mathsf{y} \rfloor+\Delta y$, where $\mathsf{y}$ is in the saturation band, that is,
	$\left|\mathsf{y}-\tfrac{\mathsf{S}+\mathsf{t}}{2}\right|\le \tfrac{1}{2}\mathsf{N}$.
	Let $x$ be such that
	$d_{\mathbf{k}}^{S+t}(x;y)>K$.
	For any $\delta>0$,
	sufficiently large fixed $K>0$, all
	$L$ large enough, and
	any configuration $\vec z$ with $x,y\ne z_i$ for all $i$,
	we have
	\begin{equation}
		
		\mathscr{E}_{\mathbf{k}}(x,y\mid T,S,N,t\mid \vec z)
		> \min\bigl\{
			\tfrac18\hspace{1pt} d_{\mathbf{k}}^{S+t}(x;y),
			\delta L
		\bigr\}.
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. For 0 <= t <= n let H_t be the average of Var(E[f | X_T]) over the t-element sets T. Then H_t = sum_{k=1}^t [binom(t, k)/binom(n, k)] W_k, so H_0 = 0, H_n = Var(f) and H_t is nondecreasing in t; and for 1 <= k <= n, W_k = binom(n, k) sum_{t=0}^k (-1)^(k - t) binom(k, t) H_t = binom(n, k) Delta^k H_0 >= 0. The n + 1 averages determine the variance at every interaction order, though not the individual w_S.
independent coordinates with finite ranges
f real valued

[Proposition prop-resample-1 of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $A \subset \mathbb{H}$ be a neighborhood of $\infty$ not containing $i$ such that $\mathbb{H} \backslash A$ is simply connected and  $\partial \mathbb{H} \backslash \overline A$ contains an interval,  and let $\beta = \gamma - \frac W\gamma$. For $(\phi, \eta) \sim M_W$, conditioned on $\phi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash A}$, we have $\phi|_A \stackrel d= h + \mathfrak h + (\frac\beta2 - Q)G_A(\cdot, \infty)$, where $\mathfrak h$ is the harmonic extension of $\phi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash A}$ to $A$ which has normal derivative zero on $\partial A \cap \partial \mathbb{H}$,
	     $h$ is a mixed boundary GFF on $A$ with zero boundary conditions on $\partial A \cap \mathbb{H}$ and free boundary conditions on $\partial A \cap \partial \mathbb{H}$, and $G_A$ is the Green function of $h$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thmFi of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] Let $\phi \in C^1((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^n)$, $b^{jk}=b^{kj}\in
C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for $j,k=1,2,\cdots,n$, 
and $\ell,\Psi \in C^2((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^n)$. 
Let $u$ be an $H^2(G)$-valued, $\mathbf{F}$-adapted process such that $u_t$ is an $L^2(G)$-valued It\^o process. 
Set $\theta = e^\ell$ and $w=\theta u$. 
Then, for a.e.     $x\in G$ and ${\mathbb{P}}$-a.s. $\omega \in \Omega$,

\begin{align}
    \notag
      
    &   \theta \Big ( -2\phi\ell_t w_t + 2\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}\ell_{x_j} w_{x_k} + \Psi w \Big )
    \Big[ \phi du_t - \sum_{j,k=1}^n (b^{jk}u_{x_j})_{x_k} dt \Big]  
    \\ \notag
    & \quad+\sum_{j,k=1}^n \Big[ \sum_{j',k'=1}^n \Big (
    2b^{jk}b^{j'k'}\ell_{x_{j'}}w_{x_j}w_{x_{k'}} -
    b^{jk}b^{j'k'}\ell_{x_j} w_{x_{j'}}w_{x_{k'}}
    \Big )   
    \\ \notag
    &\quad  - 2 \phi b^{jk}\ell_t w_{x_j} w_t + \phi b^{jk}\ell_{x_j} w_t^2  +
    \Psi b^{jk}w_{x_j} w - \Big({\cal A}\ell_{x_j} +
    \frac{\Psi_{x_j}}{2}\Big)b^{jk}w^2 \Big]_{x_k} dt
    \\ \notag
    &\quad +d\Big\{ \phi\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}\ell_t w_{x_j} w_{x_k}-
    2\phi\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}\ell_{x_j}w_{x_k}w_t  + \phi^2\ell_t w_t^2
    - \phi\Psi w_t w 
    \\ \notag 
    & \quad \quad \quad 
    + \Big[ \phi {\cal A}\ell_t +
    \frac{1}{2}(\phi\Psi)_t\Big]w^2 \Big\}   
    \\ \notag
    &   =  \bigg\{ \Big[(\phi^2\ell_{t})_t + \sum_{j,k =1}^n (\phi
    b^{jk}\ell_{x_j})_{x_k} - \phi\Psi \Big]w_t^2   d t
    \\ \notag
    & \quad - 2\sum_{j,k=1}^n \big[(\phi
    b^{jk}\ell_{x_k})_t +
    b^{jk}(\phi\ell_{t})_{x_k}\big]w_{x_j}w_t   d t   
    +\sum_{j,k=1}^n c^{jk}w_{x_j}w_{x_k} d t + Bw^2 d t
    \\
    & \quad 
    + \Big(   -2\phi\ell_tv_t 
    + 2\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}\ell_{x_j}w_{x_k} + \Psi w
    \Big)^2\bigg\} dt + \phi^2\theta^2 \ell_t(du_t)^2,  
\end{align}

where 
\begin{align} \notag
    & {\cal A}\mathop{\buildrel\Delta\over=}\phi (\ell_t^2-\ell_{tt})-\sum_{j,k=1}^n
    (b^{jk}\ell_{x_j}\ell_{x_k}-b^{jk}_{x_k}\ell_{x_j}
    -b^{jk}\ell_{x_jx_k})-\Psi,\\ \notag
       & {\cal B}\mathop{\buildrel\Delta\over=}{\cal A}\Psi+(\phi {\cal A}\ell_t)_t\!-\! \sum_{j,k=1}^n\!({\cal A}
    b^{jk}\ell_{x_j})_{x_k}\! +\!\dfrac 12
    \Big[\big(\phi\Psi\big)_{tt}\!-\!\sum_{j,k=1}^n\!
    \big(b^{jk}\Psi_{x_j}\big)_{x_k}\Big],\\  
      & c^{jk}\mathop{\buildrel\Delta\over=} \big(\phi b^{jk}\ell_t\big)_t\! +\!
    \sum_{j',k'=1}^n\! \Big[2b^{jk'}(b^{j'k}\ell_{x_{j'}})_{x_{k'}}
    \!-\!\big(b^{jk}b^{j'k'}\ell_{x_{j'}}\big)_{x_{k'}}\Big] \!+\! \Psi
    b^{jk}.
\end{align}

Let D be an abelian (v, k, lambda)-difference set in group G. Let p be a prime divisor of k - lambda such that p is coprime to v and p > lambda. Then the map x -> x^p is a multiplier of D: there exists an element g in G such that D^p = {d^p : d in D} = g D.
G is abelian
p divides k - lambda
gcd(p, v) = 1
p > lambda

[Definition def:grafting0 of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Given $\ell \in\N$ and a labelled tree $\underline{\sigma}\in\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$, we define a new labelled tree ${\underline{\sigma}}+\ell \in\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$ to be the labeled tree with node set ${N}(\underline{\sigma}+\ell) \eqdef \{ j + \ell : j \in N(\underline{\sigma})\}$ and such that the \textit{shift by $\ell$} defined as $ N(\underline{\sigma})\ni j \mapsto j+ \ell \in{N}(\underline{\sigma}+\ell)$ belongs to $\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\sigma},\underline{\sigma}+\ell)$ -- in particular, we have $ r(\underline{\sigma}+\ell)= r(\underline{\sigma})+\ell$. 
Note that $\underline{\sigma} + 0 = \underline{\sigma}$. 

Finally, given two labelled trees $\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}\in\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$, we set 
\[
\ell_{\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}}
\eqdef 
 \begin{cases}  
    \max N(\underline{\tau}) + 1& \text{if} \;N(\underline{\tau}) \cap N(\underline{\sigma}) \not = \emptyset\,, \\
    0 & \text{otherwise} \,. \\
\end{cases}
\]
We overload notation, identifying $\ell_{\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}}$ with the shift-isomorphism and write $\ell_{\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}} \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\sigma}, \underline{\sigma} + \ell_{\underline{\tau},\underline{\sigma}})$.

Let (X,d) be a metric space, A a nonempty subset, and 0<kappa<=1. Let f:A->R have finite M_inf=sup_(a in A)|f(a)| and finite Holder seminorm L=sup_(a!=b in A)|f(a)-f(b)|/d(a,b)^kappa, with the seminorm set to zero for a singleton. Then there is F:X->R with F|A=f, sup_X|F|=M_inf and [F]_(kappa,X)=L. Consequently the sum norm ||F||_(BL^kappa(X))=||F||_infinity+[F]_(kappa,X) equals ||f||_(BL^kappa(A)). A construction is g_sup(x)=sup_(a in A)(f(a)-L d(x,a)^kappa), followed by clipping to [inf_A f,sup_A f]. Equivalently, clipping g_inf(x)=inf_(a in A)(f(a)+L d(x,a)^kappa) gives such an extension. In particular kappa=1 gives a globally Lipschitz real-valued extension with the same bound. No closedness of A, completeness of X, compactness, or attainment of the extrema is required.
Arbitrary metric space with finite real-valued distances and a nonempty subset A
Real-valued f bounded on A with finite kappa-Holder seminorm
Exponent 0<kappa<=1, as fixed in primary Definition2.1
Classical real supremum and infimum; singleton seminorm convention zero
For preserving the supremum norm, clip the cone extension to the bounded range interval

Let mu be a positive Radon measure near x with finite positive local mass exponent a. The centered disk potential T(R)=(1/pi) integral_{B_E(x,R)} log(R/|x-y|) mu(dy) is finite and positive for sufficiently small R, and lim_{R->0} log(T(R))/log R=a. This is a Euclidean potential exponent, not a metric Hausdorff dimension or sample-path exit-time theorem.
mu positive Radon near x
mu(B_E(x,r))>0 eventually
finite local exponent a>0

[Theorem 36 (Gram-reduced Hilbert--Stein extraction) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Start from $\bm M^{[0]}=0$.  At every active step, use the reduced
promotion \eqref{bridge:eq:reduced-promotion}, enlarge
$M_{q_*}$ by the orthogonal sum with $V_{q_*}^{\mathrm{red}}$, and
recompute $A,r,\Lambda_q,\mathcal N_q$.  Use one common trajectory and,
for $J\ge2$, stop its level $J$ as soon as
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak H_Q(A,r)
 \le\delta_J,
 \qquad
 \delta_J=\frac{dQa_QR^4}{J}.
 
\end{equation}
Then the terminal modules are nested and satisfy
\begin{align}
 \dim M_q^{[J]}&\le d(J-1),
 \\
 \mathfrak H_Q(A^{[J]},r^{[J]})
 &\le\frac{dQa_QR^4}{J},
 \\
 \Delta_{\mathrm{res}}(r^{[J]})
 +\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}(A^{[J]},r^{[J]})
 &\le\frac{dQ\mu_Qa_QR^4}{J}.
 
\end{align}
At every promotion made before the end of level $J$, the synthesis map
in \eqref{bridge:eq:reduced-promotion} has smallest singular value strictly
larger than
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\delta_J}{dQR}
 =\frac{a_QR^3}{J}.
 
\end{equation}
Thus no Gram mode which vanishes along a fixed level can be promoted after
renormalization.

On [0,1], f(x)=846x/37 for x<=1/6, (264-738x)/37 for 1/6<=x<=1/3, and 18/37 for x>=1/3 is continuous and unimodal with mean 1/3. It satisfies 3P(X>x)<=ceil(1/x)-1 for every x>0, but violates 2P(X>1-t)<=P(X<t) whenever 0<t<4/47 and is not 3-CM. Thus integer tail tests plus unimodality and boundary mean are insufficient.

body: [Lemma lem-resample-inside-ns of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] For $(\phi, \eta) \sim M_W$, the conditional law of $\eta$ given $\phi$ is radial $\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa'}(\rho)$ in $\mathbb{H}$ from $\infty$ to $i$ with force point infinitesimally counterclockwise of $\infty$, where $\rho = \frac4{\gamma^2}W + \frac8{\gamma^2} - 4$.  Furthermore, consider a bounded neighborhood $A\subset \mathbb{H}$ of $i$ such that $\overline A \cap \partial \mathbb{H} = \emptyset$, and let $\alpha = Q - \frac1{2\gamma} (W + 2-\frac{\gamma^2}2)$. Conditioned on $\phi |_{\mathbb{H} \backslash A}$, we have $\phi|_A \stackrel d= h + \mathfrak h + \alpha G_A(\cdot, i)$, where $\mathfrak h$ is the harmonic extension of $\phi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash A}$ to $A$, $h$ is a zero boundary GFF on $A$ and $G_A$ is the Green function of $h$.

body: [campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Salez, Modern aspects of Markov chains: entropy, curvature and the cutoff phenomenon (arXiv:2508.21055), Problem 2.4 (p. 27) asks to prove that cutoff is equivalent to the product condition for random walks on Cayley graphs of abelian groups, presented as a workshop prediction reiterated as [52, Conjecture 1], with no degree bound stated in the printed question. Our result (id P0276, 2026-09-08): the literal statement is FALSE. Take G_d = (Z/2)^d x (Z/m_d) with m_d = 1 + ceil(2^d log d / 4) and S_d = {(e_i, k): i <= d, k nonzero} union {(x, 0): x in the cube, x nonzero} - a simple, connected, undirected, vertex-transitive, unweighted abelian Cayley graph. The cube generators act as a reset Q_d = (2^d Pi_d - I)/(2^d - 1), giving the exact identity q_d(t) = e^{-beta_d t} c_d(alpha_d t) with beta_d chosen so that beta_d T_d tends to 1 (T_d the cube's mixing scale); the distance profile is e^{-s} on 0 < s < 1 and 0 beyond, a continuous decay with NO cutoff, while gap times t_mix is asymptotic to (1/2) log d, which diverges, so the product condition HOLDS. Verification as the source words it: alpha_d tends to 1 and beta_d ~ 4/(d log d) so beta_d T_d tends to 1; the character computation puts the slowest sector at a = 1 giving gap = 2 alpha_d/d + beta_d ~ 2/d; the profile yields t(3/4)/t(1/4) tending to log(4/3) = 0.288, not 1; and the whole-graph error bound |v_d - q_d| <= e^{-alpha_d t} + 1/m_d is correct with both terms vanishing on the relevant scale. A scoped independent review by another agent is on file, checking the full character spectrum, the coupling and the mixing-time brackets, and found no gap in scope. CAVEAT in the memo's own words: the degree is unbounded; Salez's Problem 2.4 as printed carries no degree bound, so the literal statement falls, but whether the workshop question and [52, Conjecture 1] carry one is unchecked. G_d = (Z/2)^d x (Z/m_d), m_d = 1 + ceil(2^d log d / 4) S_d as specified; degree unbounded in d simple, connected, vertex-transitive, unweighted abelian Cayley graph

body:
Let mu_sc be the semicircle law with density (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(4 - x^2) on [-2, 2]. Its Stieltjes transform m(z) = integral (x - z)^{-1} mu_sc(dx) satisfies the self-consistent equation m(z)^2 + z m(z) + 1 = 0 for every z in C^+, equivalently m(z) = -1/( z + m(z) ), and is the UNIQUE solution of that equation with Im m(z) > 0 for z in C^+; explicitly m(z) = ( -z + sqrt(z^2 - 4) )/2 with the branch of the square root chosen so that m(z) is asymptotic to -1/z as |z| tends to infinity. This equation is the fixed point that resolvent proofs of Wigner's theorem converge to: the Schur complement identity applied to the resolvent of a Wigner matrix gives (1/n) tr (H - z)^{-1} approximately equal to -1/(z + (1/n) tr (H - z)^{-1}) up to errors that vanish as n grows, and stability of the fixed point then forces the empirical Stieltjes transform to converge to m. For the Marchenko-Pastur law the analogous equation carries the aspect ratio and reads m(z) = 1/( 1 - y - y z m(z) - z ), a different fixed point that must not be substituted for this one. [standard; e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Section 2.4]

The asymptotic check: for large |z|, s = z sqrt(1 - 4/z^2) is approximately z - 2/z, so m is approximately ( -z + z - 2/z )/2 = -1/z, which matches the required behaviour of the Stieltjes transform of a probability measure. That this m is indeed the transform of the semicircle law follows because the transform of any probability measure satisfies |m(z)| <= 1/Im z and is asymptotic to -1/z, and the quadratic has exactly two roots, only one of which has positive imaginary part on C^+; identifying the measure from m by the inversion formula gives Im m(x + i0) = (1/2) sqrt(4 - x^2) for |x| < 2 and 0 otherwise, so the density is (1/pi) times that, namely (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(4 - x^2), which is the semicircle density. body:
[Theorem 34 of arXiv:2604.13454, 'Invariant and periodic measures in classical spin systems on infinite lattices with highly'] (Harris-Meyn-Tweedie). Let $X(t)$ be a time-homogeneous Markov process on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with transition probability kernel $\mathcal{P}_t$ and infinitesimal generator $\mathscr{L}$. Suppose that following hypotheses are satisfied
		\item[(i)] The Markov process is irreducible, that is, there exists $t_0$(and then for all $t > t_0 $ ) such that
		$$
		\mathcal{P}_{t_0}(x,\Gamma)> 0,
		$$
		for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and nonempty open sets $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^n$.
		\item[(ii)] For any $t> 0$ the Markov semi-group $\mathcal{P}_t(x,dy)$ has a density $p_t(x,y)$, which is a continuous function of $(x,y)$.\\
		Assume there exists a Lyapunov function
		$$
		V:\mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \left[ 0,\infty\right) \xrightarrow{\Vert x \Vert_{\mathbb{R}^n} \rightarrow +\infty}+\infty
		$$
		and constants $C,c> 0$ such that 
		$$
		\mathscr{L}V+cV\leq C.
		$$
		Then there exists unique invariant measure $\mu$ for the process $X(t)$ and there exist constants $K,\alpha > 0$ such that
		$$
		\sup\limits_{\{f:\vert f(x) \vert \leq V(x)\}}\vert \mathcal{P}_tf(a)-\mu (f) \vert \leq KV(a)e^{-\alpha t}
		$$
		for any $a\in \mathbb{R}^n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $\bm{\mathcal{Y}}_N = ((\bm{X}_i)_{i \in [N]}, (\bm{W}_{i, j})_{i, j \in [N]})$ be a dissociated array of particle states and pairwise weights. An Aldous-Hoover representation of $\bm{\mathcal{Y}}_N$ is a triple $((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \pi), \mathsf{X}, \mathsf{W})$ consisting of a latent probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \pi)$ and measurable functions $\mathsf{X}: \Omega \to \mathbb{D}$ and $\mathsf{W}: \Omega \times \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the array is equal in law to the sampling $\bm{X}_i \stackrel{d}{=} \mathsf{X}(\bm{\xi}_i)$ and $\bm{W}_{i, j} \stackrel{d}{=} \mathsf{W}(\bm{\xi}_i, \bm{\xi}_j)$, where $(\bm{\xi}_i)_{i=1}^N$ are independent random variables on $\Omega$ satisfying the averaging condition $\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{Law}(\bm{\xi}_i) = \pi$.
\bm{\mathcal{Y}}_N is a dissociated array
(\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \pi) is a probability space
title: Aldous-Hoover Representation of State-Weight Structures

Let $W$ be a smooth scheme over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let $\mathfrak{d}$ be a finite-dimensional basepoint-free linear system on $W$. 
Then for every $1 \le j \le \dim \mathfrak{d}$ there exists a non-empty Zariski-open subset $\Omega_j \subseteq \mathfrak{d}^{\oplus j}$ such that for $([s_1], [s_2], \ldots, [s_j]) \in \Omega_j$ the zero locus $Z(s_1, \ldots, s_j) \subseteq W$ is either empty or smooth of codimension $j$. [Proposition 26 (Geometric axis and gate decomposition) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let $0\neq v\in V$, and let $g,a\in\Sl(V)$ satisfy
\[
g=a\e^v a^{-1}.
\]
Equip $V$ with an auxiliary Euclidean norm, denoted by $\norm{\cdot}_{\mathrm{Euc}}$, and set
\[
\mathcal{A}=a\mathcal{A}_v
 =\set{a\e^{tv}:t\in\R},
\qquad L_g(x)=gx,
\]
and let $p$ be the metric projection of $1$ onto $\mathcal{A}$. Then, for every $x\in\Sl(V)$,
\begin{align}
 d_{\infty}(x,gx)
 &=2d_{\infty}(x,\mathcal{A})+\norm{v}_{\mathrm{Euc}},
 \\
 \mathcal{A}
 &=\set{x\in\Sl(V):d_{\infty}(x,gx)=\norm{v}_{\mathrm{Euc}}}.
 
\end{align}
Thus $\mathcal{A}$ is the unique minimum-displacement axis of $L_g$ and is independent of the chosen factorisation of $g$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
[1,g]=[1,p]\cup[p,gp]\cup[gp,g],
\end{equation}
where the three pieces meet only at $p$ and $gp$, and
\begin{equation}
gp=p\e^v,
\qquad
g=p\e^v p^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Finally,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{A}\cap[1,g]=[p,gp].
\end{equation}
The first and third pieces in \cref{eq:conjugacy-geodesic-decomposition} degenerate simultaneously.

STATUS: proof (unaudited); owner-own-work draft. For arbitrary n>=2 scalar three-token first-token-query self-attention examples with distinct signed values, negative minimum, positive maximum, and positive signed first token, joint-head logistic GD has two open endpoint-selection basins. Invariant subregions escape for every eta>0; for eta<=min(2/H^2,1/(2D)), every finite initialization outside a null saddle-stable set escapes to one endpoint pattern. Interior and mixed endpoint hard patterns are impossible. Normalized margins are min maxima and min negated minima, so unequal margins give a positive-measure inferior basin.

# Target 1: scalar three-token self-attention under joint training

Version 1, unaudited. Owner own work; novelty not established globally.
This extends the scalar family, not arbitrary vector-valued token geometry.

## Data, model and conclusions

For each i=1,...,n, n>=2, take a label y_i in {-1,+1} and three distinct
signed token values c_ij. Their minimum m_i is negative, maximum M_i positive,
and the FIRST token c_i1 is positive. Let raw tokens x_ij=y_i c_ij and use
the actual first token x_i1 as the self-attention query. With jointly trained
scalar head v and scalar attention weight p, signed prediction is v h_i(p),

 h_i(p)=sum_j c_ij exp(zeta_i c_ij p)/sum_j exp(zeta_i c_ij p),
 zeta_i=c_i1>0.

The loss is average logistic loss. Let
 H=max_i max(|m_i|,|M_i|), D=max_i zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2,
 eta_*=min(2/H^2,1/(2D)).

For every fixed eta in (0,eta_*], simultaneous GD in (v,p) has precisely
three possible limits: the unique finite saddle (0,p_bar), where
mean_i h_i(p_bar)=0; matching-positive escape v,p->+infinity; or
matching-negative escape v,p->-infinity. The saddle's global stable set is
planar null. Both escaping basins are open and nonempty. Their hard selections
are respectively the maximum signed token in EVERY example and the minimum
signed token in EVERY example. No interior token, or mixed pattern of extrema,
is a hard-selection limit in this scalar model. On escaping trajectories
p=O(log |v|), loss->0 and the normalized joint directions are (+1,0),(-1,0).
The corresponding minimum signed margins, normalized by sqrt(v^2+p^2),
are Gamma_+=min_i M_i and Gamma_-=min_i(-m_i).

In addition, for EVERY eta>0 the regions
 Q_+={v>0,p>max_i rho_i}, Q_-={v<0,p<min_i rho_i},
where h_i(rho_i)=0, are forward invariant and satisfy the same respective
escape/margin conclusions. Thus if Gamma_+>Gamma_-, the inferior basin is
open and positive measure even without a step-size restriction. A sufficient
strict inequality is M_i+m_i>0 for every example.

## Scalar softmax link estimates

Write alpha_ij(p) for the three softmax weights. Direct differentiation gives
h_i'=zeta_i[sum alpha_ij c_ij^2-h_i^2]
     =zeta_i sum_{j<l} alpha_ij alpha_il(c_ij-c_il)^2>0.
Also |h_i|<=H, h_i'<=zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2<=D, and h_i tends to m_i,M_i
at the two infinities. Thus each root rho_i exists uniquely.

Let delta be the minimum over i of zeta_i times either adjacent gap of its
sorted three token values. It is strictly positive. For p>=0, the total
softmax mass on nonmaximum tokens is <=2 exp(-delta p).
Variance is no larger than the second moment about the maximum token,
so h_i'(p)<=2D exp(-delta p). Reflecting yields the same upper bound
2D exp(-delta |p|) for p<=0. Every h_i is real analytic, strictly increasing,
bounded, and has exponentially decaying derivative.

## Full-plane trapping and escape

For g_i=(1+exp(v h_i(p)))^-1 put F=mean g_i h_i and G=mean g_i h_i'>0.
GD is v_+=v+eta F, p_+=p+eta vG. The following estimates are identical
to those needed in proof 005, now established for genuine three-token links:

 -H^2/4<=F_v<=0,
 F(0,p)=mean h_i(p)/2=:F_0(p), 0<F_0'<=D/2, G<=D.

There is a unique mean root p_bar. Set u=p-p_bar, A=H^2/4.
In v,u>0, v_+>=(1-eta A)v+eta F_0(p)>0 and p increases; reflecting gives
invariance in v,u<0. In a bad quadrant v>0,u<0, v decreases and u increases
until it exits or converges to the saddle. Double crossing would require

 (1-eta A)v<=eta(D/2)|u|<=eta^2 D^2 v/2,

impossible since eta A<=1/2 and eta D<=1/2. The other bad quadrant is the
reflection. An axis point other than the saddle enters a good quadrant after
one step. A bad-quadrant orbit staying there is bounded and monotone; continuity
of increments gives vG=F=0 at its limit, hence the saddle.

Consider a positive good-quadrant orbit. If p had a finite limit P and v were
bounded, compactness would give G bounded below; Delta p->0 would force v->0,
but F_0(P)>0 contradicts convergence of v to zero. If v were unbounded and
P<=R:=max rho_i, an example with root R has h_j(p)<=0 and therefore g_j>=1/2.
On the compact p interval its derivative is bounded below, so
Delta p>=eta d v/(2n), contradicting finite P. If P>R, eventually all links
are >=c>0; v then increases without bound and
Delta p/Delta v>=d v/H again contradicts finite P. Thus p->infinity.
Eventually all h_i>=c, forcing v->infinity (bounded v would keep the g_i
uniformly positive). Negative escape follows by reflection using -h_i(-p).

This proof also applies directly within Q_+ or Q_- at any eta>0: both
coordinates are monotone from the start and all signed links are positive
after reflection. Only the full-plane trapping argument uses eta_*.

## Rates, margin, and the null exceptional set

On a positive escaping trajectory, h_i>=c>0 eventually, so
Delta p<=eta D v exp(-cv)->0. Moreover
Delta p/Delta v<=2D v exp(-delta p)/c.
Once Delta p<=1, the mean value theorem gives
Delta exp(delta p)<=C v Delta v. Telescoping against v^2 gives
exp(delta p)<=C'(1+v^2), so p=O(log v). Reflection proves the other branch.
Loss and normalized margin limits now follow. For any parameter pair,
the endpoint bounds and sqrt(v^2+p^2)>=|v| show the normalized minimum
margin cannot exceed max(Gamma_+,Gamma_-); the larger branch attains it.

At the saddle, the update Jacobian is
[[1-eta A_s,eta B_s],[eta B_s,1]],
where A_s=mean h_i(p_bar)^2/4<=A and B_s=mean h_i'(p_bar)/2 in (0,D/2].
Its determinant >=7/16 and det(DT-I)<0: one eigenvalue lies in (0,1),
the other exceeds 1. The analytic update map has a Jacobian determinant
not identically zero; the zero set is null. Away from that set its local
inverse maps preserve null sets. By a countable cover, preimages of null
sets are null. The local stable-manifold theorem and countably many iterated
preimages therefore give a null global stable set. Each escaping basin is
the union of preimages of its open good quadrant, hence open. This is the
same null-preimage argument detailed in proofs/003 and 005, not an assumption
that the GD map is globally invertible.

## Which locally optimal selections, and comparison with prior art

For p->+infinity only the largest signed c_ij can dominate; for p->-infinity
only the smallest can dominate. Because all zeta_i>0 these choices must be
consistent across examples. At finite p all weights are strictly positive,
so an interior token cannot become a hard selection. For a fixed v>0, the
maximum-token pattern is the only locally optimal feasible hard selection;
for fixed v<0 the minimum-token pattern is the only one. Both are stable
under joint training, by the open basins above. The minimum pattern can
nevertheless be inferior when comparing the two JOINT normalized margins.

Tarzanagh et al., 2306.13596, Definition 2 (PDF p.5) compares the chosen token
score only to its active SVM neighbors, with a FIXED head. Their Theorem 3
(PDF p.6) gives convergence from cones C_{mu,R} around such locally optimal
directions. It already includes a three-token illustration immediately after
the theorem. The present scalar result is not the discovery of that phenomenon:
it classifies the scalar joint-head basins and excludes mixed/interior hard
patterns in this stated geometry. General vector-valued three-token locally
optimal selections and their joint-head basins remain open here.

## Explicit distinct mixed-label witness

Take signed triples (3/2,1/4,-1/2) and (3/2,1/8,-1), with labels +1,-1.
Raw triples are (3/2,1/4,-1/2),(-3/2,-1/8,1); actual first-token queries
are 3/2,-3/2. Both zeta_i=3/2. H=3/2, D=75/8, eta_*=4/75.
Gamma_+=3/2 and Gamma_-=1/2. The conditions are strict and persist in an
open neighborhood of these data. This witness is illustrative; the theorem
covers the whole family above rather than just this isolated case.
Raw tokens x_ij=y_i c_ij, y_i in {+1,-1}; query=x_i1; c_i1>0, min_j c_ij<0<max_j c_ij, all three c_ij distinct. H=max absolute signed endpoint, D=max_i c_i1(max c_i-min c_i)^2. Train scalar v,p by simultaneous fixed-step Euclidean GD on average logistic loss.

body: In Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory, the Vapnik–Chervonenkis (VC) dimension is a measure of the size of a class of sets. The notion can be extended to classes of binary functions. It is defined as the cardinality of the largest set of points that the function class can shatter—that is, for which all possible binary labelings can be realized by some function in the class. It was originally defined by Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis.
title: Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension

Fix positive integers N,n, arbitrary finite real numbers sigma_ij, and a real N-by-n matrix A_n. For the relevant N,n, write A=A_n and sigma_ij=sigma_ij(n), D_j=diag(sigma_1j^2,...,sigma_Nj^2), and Dtilde_i=diag(sigma_i1^2,...,sigma_in^2). Let S_plus consist of the functions z->integral_[0,infinity) (lambda-z)^(-1) nu(dlambda) for probability measures nu on [0,infinity), analytically continued to C minus [0,infinity). The canonical equations define a unique S_plus-valued solution psi_i,psitilde_j by psi_i(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(Dtilde_i Ttilde(z))/n)] and psitilde_j(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(D_j T(z))/n)], where Psi=diag(psi_i), Psitilde=diag(psitilde_j), T(z)=[Psi(z)^(-1)-z A Psitilde(z) A^T]^(-1), and Ttilde(z)=[Psitilde(z)^(-1)-z A^T Psi(z) A]^(-1). Both trace terms in these canonical equations use division by n. Moreover there are positive matrix-valued measures M and Mtilde on [0,infinity), with total masses I_N and I_n, such that T(z)=integral (lambda-z)^(-1) M(dlambda) and Ttilde(z)=integral (lambda-z)^(-1) Mtilde(dlambda). Positivity here means that the measure of every Borel set is a positive-semidefinite matrix. In particular tr(T)/N and tr(Ttilde)/n are Stieltjes transforms of probability measures. Uniqueness is within this analytic Stieltjes class, rather than among all algebraic roots at one value of z.
N,n positive integers
real deterministic finite profile sigma_ij and real deterministic A_n

body: Let A, B be n x n Hermitian matrices, with eigenvalues of each, and of A+B, listed in decreasing order lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ... >= lambda_n. Weyl's inequality states lambda_{i+j-1}(A+B) <= lambda_i(A) + lambda_j(B) whenever i+j-1 <= n, and lambda_{i+j-n}(A+B) >= lambda_i(A) + lambda_j(B) whenever i+j-n >= 1. Taking j=1 and j=n gives lambda_k(A) + lambda_n(B) <= lambda_k(A+B) <= lambda_k(A) + lambda_1(B) for every k, hence |lambda_k(A+B) - lambda_k(A)| <= ||B|| (operator norm) for all k: eigenvalues are 1-Lipschitz functions of the matrix.

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2604.09248, '\bfseries Limit laws for longest edges in empty region graphs'] Assume the same set-up as in Theorem \ref{th:PoisConv}. Then, for any $t\geq 2$,
$$
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{Kol}}\big(\gamma tL_{t,W}^d-\log(t)-\log(\kappa_d/(2\gamma)),G_W\big) \leq \begin{cases}
        c \log^{-(d-2)}(t), & d \ge 3,\\
        c \log^{-1/2}(t), & d=2,
    \end{cases}
$$
where $G_W$ is a Gumbel distributed random variable with $\PP(G_W\leq s)=\exp(-\vol(W)e^{-s})$ for $s\in\RR$. Here, $c\in(0,\infty)$ is a constant which only depends on $d$, $\vol(W)$, and the parameters of the particular example. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Fix an integer l>=1, and let d_0=d tend to infinity, d_i=d_i(d) tend to infinity for each 1<=i<=l, and d_(l+1)=1. Independently for each layer, let W_i have independent N(0,1/d_(i-1)) entries. Let f_d(x)=W_(l+1) sigma(W_l sigma(...sigma(W_1 x)...)), with sigma applied coordinatewise. Assume sigma is nonconstant and locally Lipschitz, is differentiable almost everywhere with almost-everywhere continuous derivative, and satisfies |sigma'(t)|<=C_sigma(1+|t|^(k-1)) for some fixed integer k>=1. For deterministic x_d of norm sqrt(d), and every increasing positive sequence xi_d tending to infinity, there is a positive deterministic step sequence s_d<=xi_d such that x_s=x_d-sign(f_d(x_d))*s_d*grad f_d(x_d) has ||x_s-x_d||/||x_d|| tending to zero in probability and P(sign(f_d(x_s)) != sign(f_d(x_d))) tending to one. No relative growth restriction between diverging widths is imposed. The theorem does not supply an explicit finite-width rate for the sign-reversal probability. In particular ReLU and profiles d->floor(d^c)->m(d)->1, 0<c<1 and m(d)->infinity, are included.

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2506.22040, '\vspace{-3em} Khinchin inequalities for uniforms on spheres with a deficit'] Let $p \geq 2$. For $a \in \R, v \in \R^d$, $d \geq 2$, we have
\[ 
D_p(a, v) \geq \kappa_{p,d}a^4\cdot\begin{cases}
(|v|^2+2a^2)^{\frac{p-4}{2}}, & 2 \leq p \leq 4, \\
|v|^{p-4}, & p > 4,
\end{cases}
 \]
where 
\[
\kappa_{p,d} = \frac{p(p-2)(p+d-2)(p+d-4)}{4d^2(d+2)}.
\]

body:
Let R be a unique factorization domain with fraction field K. The product of two primitive polynomials in R[x] is primitive; consequently, every primitive polynomial of positive degree is reducible in R[x] if and only if it is reducible in K[x], and R[x] is itself a unique factorization domain.
R is a unique factorization domain
K is the fraction field of R

body:
Symmetric form: let A_1, ..., A_n be events in a probability space, each with P(A_i) <= p, and suppose each A_i is mutually independent of all but at most d of the other events. If e p (d + 1) <= 1 (e the base of natural logarithms), then P(none of the A_i occurs) > 0. General form: if there are numbers x_1, ..., x_n in [0, 1) with P(A_i) <= x_i prod_{j in Gamma(i)} (1 - x_j) for every i, where Gamma(i) is the set of events A_i is not mutually independent of, then P(intersection of the complements) >= prod_i (1 - x_i) > 0.
mutual independence from the events outside the dependency neighbourhood, not merely pairwise independence
e p (d + 1) <= 1 in the symmetric form; the constant e cannot be improved in general

Owner campaign draft, proof (unaudited); no independent audit or novelty assessment. Let d>=5, n>=1, 0<r<=1, h>=0, P0=P on R^d, and M=integral |x-c|^q P(dx)<infinity for fixed c and q>2d/(d-2). Each round draws n conditionally iid centers from rP+(1-r)Pt, with fresh real draws, and Pt+1 is their equal-weight isotropic Gaussian KDE of covariance h^2 I_d. Put z=2^(d/2-2), B=z/(z-1)+8/3, G=1+4/[1-2^(2-q(1-2/d))]. Then sup_t E W2^2(Pt,P) <= [16d B G M^(2/q)n^(-2/d)+2d h^2]/r, including M=0. The same bound holds for independently sampled weighted n+n groups, Pt+1=(r Phat_n+(1-r)Pt_hat_n)*N(0,h^2 I_d), and for exactly m fresh of n total points when r=m/n. The method labels every center by its fresh real-data ancestor. For every cell A, E Lt(A)=P(A) and Var Lt(A)<=P(A)/(n alpha), alpha=1-(1-1/n)(1-r)^2; Gaussian displacement has expected coupling cost at most d h^2/r. An annular dyadic transport bound transfers these dependent-label estimates into the displayed W2 bound. Gaussian increments must be centered, independent, and parent selection must use the KDE weights; real data must be fresh, not a fixed reused dataset. Proofs: C004 v2 and C005 v2, T356/proofs/review/. Classical dyadic architecture is credited to Fournier and Guillin, arXiv:1312.2128v1, Lemmas 5-6 and proof of Theorem 1.

body:
[Corollary 27 of arXiv:2608.30059, 'Multihomogeneous Measures and Stochastic Polar Representations'] For the fixed admissible gauge \(\tau\), with
\(C_\star=(1,2]^q\) and \(d_\alpha=m_\alpha(C_\star)\), set  
\begin{equation}

s_\tau
:=
\varsigma_\tau(\Sigma_\tau)
=
\frac{1}{d_\alpha}
\int_{\{\tau\in C_\star\}}
\chi_\alpha(\tau(x))\,\nu(dx)
=
\frac{\nu\{\tau\in C_\star\}}
{\vartheta_\alpha(C_\star)}
\in(0,\infty].
\end{equation}
Every stochastic representer \(Z\) of \(\nu\) satisfies
\[
\E{\chi_\alpha(R_Z)}=s_\tau.
\]
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item
Some stochastic representer \(Z\) has \(R_Z\perp Y_Z\).

\item
\(s_\tau<\infty\).

\item
\(\nu\{\tau\in C_\star\}<\infty\).
\end{enumerate}

If \(s_\tau<\infty\), put
\[
\bar\alpha:=\sum_{i=1}^q\alpha_i,
\qquad
a_\tau:=s_\tau^{1/\bar\alpha}\boldsymbol1 
\]
and  for any stochastic representer \(Z\)  define
\begin{equation}

\frac{d\mathbb P_Z^\tau}{d\mathbb P}
:=
\frac{\chi_\alpha(R_Z)}{s_\tau},
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}

Z_\tau^\circ
:=
S_{a_\tau}Y_Z
=
S_{a_\tau R_Z^{-1}}Z.
\end{equation}
Under \(\mathbb P_Z^\tau\),
\[
Y_Z\sim\frac{\varsigma_\tau}{s_\tau},
\qquad
\tau(Z_\tau^\circ)=a_\tau,
\qquad
\nu_{Z_\tau^\circ}=\nu,
\]
and
\[
\mathcal L(Z_\tau^\circ)
=
(S_{a_\tau})_\#
\left(\frac{\varsigma_\tau}{s_\tau}\right).
\]
Consequently, every stochastic representer \(W\) satisfying
\(\tau(W)=a_\tau\) almost surely has this law.

Finally, for \(Z\) concentrated on \(E_\tau\) with \(R_Z\perp Y_Z\),
\[
\nu_Z=\nu
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
Y_Z\sim\frac{\varsigma_\tau}{s_\tau}
\ \text{ and }\
\E{\chi_\alpha(R_Z)}=s_\tau.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2608.31101, 'Bang vectors in the real polarization problem:\\ the exact dimensional range'] The Bang-vector prescription is universally valid for systems of $n$ unit vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ if and only if $n\leq14$.

More precisely, for every integer $n\geq15$ there exist unit vectors $v_1,\dots,v_n\in\mathbb R^n$ such that, up to a simultaneous change of all signs,
\[
s=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i
\]
is the unique longest signed sum and
\[
\prod_{i=1}^n
\left|
\left\langle \frac{s}{\|s\|},v_i\right\rangle
\right|
<n^{-n/2}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lem 35 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $j,\ell\in[3]$ with $j\neq\ell$. Recall the functions $m_1,m_2,m_3$ from \eqref{e:freeprob.m.z}, \eqref{e:freeprob.m2.z}, and \eqref{e:freeprob.m3.z}; and let $s_\ell$ denote the inverse of $m_\ell$. For any $z>0$, we have the bounds
    \[
        \iota z^{j/\ell} 
        \le m_j(s_\ell(z))
        \le \bigg(\frac{z}{\iota}\bigg
            )^{j/\ell}\,.
    \]

\begin{proof}
From the definitions \eqref{e:freeprob.m.z}--\eqref{e:freeprob.m3.z}, 
for each $\ell\in[3]$ and for any $z>\hw_1$ we have
    \[
    \frac{\mu_1}{(z-\hw_1)^\ell}
    \le m_\ell(z)=\sum_{j=1}^s
    \frac{\mu_j}{(z-\hw_j)^\ell}
    \le \frac{1}{(z-\hw_1)^\ell}\,.
    \]
Thus, for $t_- = \hw_1 + (\mu_1/z)^{1/\ell}$ and $t_+ = \hw_1 + z^{-1/\ell}$, we have
    \[
        m_\ell(t_+) 
        \le \frac{1}{(t_+ - \hw_1)^\ell}
        = z 
        = \frac{\mu_1}{(t_- - \hw_1)^\ell}
        \le m_\ell(t_-)\,.
    \]
    Since $m_\ell$ is strictly decreasing, this implies $t_- \le s_\ell (z) \le t_+$. Then, since $m_j$ is also strictly decreasing, it follows that
    \[
        \mu_1 z^{j/\ell}
        = \frac{\mu_1}{(t_+ - \hw_1)^j}
        \le m_j(t_+)
        \le m_j(s_\ell (z))
        \le m_j(t_-)
        \le \frac{1}{(t_- - \hw_1)^j}
        = (z/\mu_1)^{j/\ell}\,.
    \]
The conclusion follows by recalling that $\mu_1 \ge \iota$ because $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 35 of arXiv:2608.29416

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Compare the short cycle structure of Z^d and the hypercube to predict the first differing coefficient. Result: The coefficients a_i are determined by the counts of closed non-backtracking walks of length up to 2i in the graph (the lace-expansion diagrams at order i involve random-walk loops of length up to 2i, up to the normalisation by (2d)^i). Z^d and the hypercube both have degree 2d (resp. d, with the appropriate rescaling) and both have girth 4; the number of 4-cycles through a vertex is d(d-1)/2 ... for Z^d: choose two distinct directions, 4 sign patterns give (2d)(2d-2)/2 cycles; for the hypercube choose two coordinates: d(d-1)/2 cycles; after the normalisation by degree these agree to leading order, which is why a_2 agrees. 6-cycles: in Z^d a 6-cycle uses three directions (counts (2d)(2d-2)(2d-4)/...), or two directions with a back-and-forth (which is backtracking-free? a 6-cycle in two directions like ++-+-- exists in Z^2: no, in Z^2 6-cycles do not exist since the square lattice is bipartite with girth 4 and 6-cycles would need ... Z^2 has cycles of length 6? A closed walk of length 6 that is a simple cycle in Z^2 encloses 2 squares: yes, the 2x1 rectangle has perimeter 6. In the hypercube a simple 6-cycle uses exactly three coordinates (a 6-cycle in Q_3 exists); in Z^d a 6-cycle can use two directions (the 2x1 rectangle) or three. The hypercube has no 2x1 rectangle analogue (in Q_d, two coordinates span a 4-cycle only). So the 6-cycle counts differ at relative order 1/d^2: Z^d has extra 6-cycles using only two directions, of number of order d^2 versus the three-direction ones of order d^3; the 1/d^2-relative difference in the 6-cycle count enters the coefficient at order (2d)^{-3} x (1/d^2)... The source says a_3 agrees, consistent with the two-direction 6-cycles being of lower order; they enter at order 1/d beyond a_3's leading diagrams, i.e. at a_4 or a_5. Prediction: the first differing coefficient is a_4 (from the 2x1-rectangle 6-cycles, absent in the hypercube), unless their contribution cancels, in which case a_5. This is a heuristic prediction, not a proof; the source's hint that the proofs in [173, 174] suggest a difference at some i >= 4 is consistent. Key identity: The 2x1-rectangle 6-cycles exist in Z^d but not in the hypercube; their normalised count is one order in 1/d below the three-direction 6-cycles, predicting the first discrepancy at a_4. Obstruction: Not proved; requires the fourth-order lace diagrams on both graphs.
