body: [Corollary cor:blowups-vertex-ramsey of arXiv:2609.00636, 'Forcing monochromatic subdivisions'] The family of closed blowups of trees is vertex-$R_\Delta$-bounded. More precisely, for every integers $d \ge 1$, $s\ge2$ and $k \ge 1$ there is an integer $D$, depending only on $d$, $s$ and $k$, such that for every tree $T$ with $\Delta(T) \le d$ there is a graph $H$ with $\Delta(H) \le D$ in which every $s$-coloring of $V(H)$ contains a monochromatic copy of the closed $k$-blowup~$T[k]$.

body:
[Prop 10 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Let $\lambda_0$ belong to a compact subinterval of
$(\lambda_{1,\Omega},\lambda^*)$ for the branch $u_\lambda^-$, or of
$(-\infty,\lambda^*)$ for the branch $u_\lambda^+$. Then there exist
$\delta>0$ and
$r_i^\pm(\lambda,\lambda_0)=o(|\lambda-\lambda_0|)$, $i=1,2$, such that,
whenever $0<\lambda-\lambda_0<\delta$,
\begin{align}
	-\frac{\lambda-\lambda_0}{2}\|u_\lambda^-\|_2^2+r_1^-(\lambda,\lambda_0)
	&\leq E_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)-E_{\lambda_0}(u_{\lambda_0}^-)
	\notag\\
	&\leq -\frac{\lambda-\lambda_0}{2}\|u_{\lambda_0}^-\|_2^2
	+r_2^-(\lambda,\lambda_0).
	
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
	-\frac{\lambda-\lambda_0}{2}\|u_\lambda^+\|_2^2+r_1^+(\lambda,\lambda_0)
	&\leq E_\lambda(u_\lambda^+)-E_{\lambda_0}(u_{\lambda_0}^+)
	\notag\\
	&\leq -\frac{\lambda-\lambda_0}{2}\|u_{\lambda_0}^+\|_2^2
	+r_2^+(\lambda,\lambda_0).
	
\end{align}
Moreover, for every fixed
$\lambda_0\in(\lambda_{1,\Omega},\lambda^*)$, there exist
$\delta,c_0,C_0>0$ such that, whenever $|\lambda-\lambda_0|<\delta$,
\[
|H_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)|\geq c_0,
\qquad
\|u_\lambda^-\|\leq C_0.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 11 (Thin quantum disk) of arXiv:2608.27630, 'Oriented planar maps and \\ annular mating of trees'] For $W\in(0, \frac{\gamma^2}{2})$, the infinite measure $\mathcal{M}_{2}^{\textup{disk}}(W)$ is defined as follows. First sample a random variable $T$ from the infinite measure $(1-\frac{2}{\gamma^2}W)^{-2}\textup{Leb}_{\mathbb{R}_+}$. Then sample a Poisson point process $\{(u, \mathcal{D}_u)\}$ with intensity $\mathds{1}_{t\in [0,T]}dt\times \mathcal{M}_{2}^{\textup{disk}}(\gamma^2-W)$. Finally consider the ordered (according to the order induced by $u$) collection of doubly-marked thick quantum disks $\{\mathcal{D}_u\}$, called a \emph{thin quantum disk} of weight $W$.
		
		Let $\mathcal{M}_{2}^{\textup{disk}}(W)$ be the law of this ordered collection of doubly-marked quantum disks $\{\mathcal{D}_u\}$.
		The left (resp.\ right) boundary length of a sample from $\mathcal{M}_{2}^{\textup{disk}}(W)$ is defined to be the sum of the left (resp.\ right) boundary lengths of the quantum disks $\{\mathcal{D}_u\}$. A surface sampled from $\mathcal{M}_{2}^{\textup{disk}}(W)$ has two marked points; see Figure~\ref{fig-qt} (left).

STATEMENT
Let 0<b<sqrt(d)<1 and rho>0. Consider a bounded full orbit indexed
by all integers of the raw scalar Adam map

 M_next=b*M+(1-b)*X,
 V_next=d*V+(1-d)*X^2,
 X_next=X-M_next/(sqrt(V_next)+rho), V>=0.

Put D=(1-b)/(2*(1+b)), a=D-rho, and assume 0<rho<D.
Suppose at EVERY integer time

 X_t^2 * [1/(sqrt(V_(t+1))+rho)-1/D] = 0.       (ZW)

Then the full orbit is either the origin, or the exact alternating
cycle (X,M,V)=(+/-a,-/+(1-b)/(1+b)*a,a^2).
No assumption that X stays nonzero, that curvature itself converges,
or that a cycle is hyperbolic is required. This is a zero-work path
classification, stronger than merely classifying constant-curvature
orbits; it is not a claim about all unrestricted Adam orbits.

HARDEST STEP
Exclude isolated exact position zeros on a full zero-work path. The
variance recurrence restricts nonzero amplitudes to two values, while
the momentum recurrence contracts across an isolated zero.

PROOF
If X_t=X_(t+1)=0, the position update gives M_(t+1)=0 and then M_t=0.
The inverse position update gives X_(t-1)=X_t+M_t/(sqrt(V_t)+rho)=0;
the inverse momentum update gives M_(t-1)=0. Repeating backwards and
forwards shows X=M=0 at all times. Then V_next=dV; boundedness at the
negative time end forces V=0. Hence a non-origin full path never has
two consecutive position zeros.

For any nonzero X_t, (ZW) gives V_(t+1)=a^2. If X_t=0, its predecessor
is nonzero, so V_t=a^2 and V_(t+1)=d*a^2. Consequently every variance
along a non-origin path is either a^2 or d*a^2. At any nonzero X_t,
the variance recurrence and V_(t+1)=a^2 imply

 |X_t|=a if X_(t-1)!=0,
 |X_t|=sqrt(1+d)*a if X_(t-1)=0.                 (1)

In particular all nonzero amplitudes are at most sqrt(1+d)*a<2a.

Suppose X_t and X_(t+1) are both nonzero. Their next denominators
are both D, |X_(t+1)|=a, and eliminating the momentum gives

 X_(t+2)=-(1+b)*X_(t+1)-b*X_t.                  (2)

If X_(t+2)=0, then |X_t|=(1+b)*a/b>2a, contradicting (1).
Otherwise |X_(t+2)|=a. If its sign equals that of X_(t+1), (2) requires
|X_t|=(2+b)*a/b>3a, also impossible. Therefore
X_(t+2)=-X_(t+1) and X_t=-X_(t+1). At time t+1 the complete state is

 (X_(t+1),M_(t+1),V_(t+1))
 = (X_(t+1),-2D*X_(t+1),a^2).

This is an exact cycle state. The raw map is injective on physical
states with rho>0: recover X_old=X_new+M_new/(sqrt(V_new)+rho),
then M_old=(M_new-(1-b)*X_old)/b and
V_old=(V_new-(1-d)*X_old^2)/d. Thus the FULL path is that cycle.

The remaining possibility is strict alternation between a nonzero
position and a zero position. Every nonzero amplitude is then the
same number sqrt(1+d)*a by (1). But at a nonzero time t followed by
X_(t+1)=0, the momentum and variance updates give

 X_(t+2)=-k*X_t, k=b*D/(sqrt(d)*a+rho)
                  <=b/sqrt(d)<1,              (3)

because sqrt(d)*a+rho>=sqrt(d)*(a+rho)=sqrt(d)*D.
This contradicts equality of the two nonzero amplitudes. The origin
and exact cycle are therefore the only bounded full (ZW) paths.

The update equations are the standard outside-sqrt raw Adam equations
used in Fong--Yang arXiv2608.20638v2; no convergence theorem from that
paper is invoked. Algebra (2) uses (1-b)/D=2(1+b). Argument (3) is
where b<sqrt(d) is needed. Both time ends and boundedness are essential

Let (X,d) be a compact metric space of diameter at most one, with covering numbers N(X,epsilon)<=epsilon^(-d_x) for 0<epsilon<=1, where d_x>0. Let P be a Borel probability measure, and W:X x X->[0,cmax] a measurable symmetric kernel with 0<cmin<=d_P(x)=integral W(x,y)dP(y) and cmax<=1. Assume there is ONE partition X=X_1 union ... union X_q into q>=1 measurable pieces such that |W(x,y)-W(xprime,y)|<=cLip d(x,xprime) for every y and every x,xprime in the same piece. Let x_1,...,x_n be independent samples from P, and fix 0<rho<=1/2. Let f:X->R be a fixed bounded Borel function, d_X(x)=n^(-1)sum_i W(x,x_i), and D_X(rho)=cmin^(-1)[cLip sqrt(d_x)+(cmax+cLip)sqrt(log(q/rho))]. Define L_P f(x)=integral W(x,y)f(y)/sqrt(d_P(x)d_P(y))dP(y). On the event inf_x d_X(x)>0 define L_X f(x)=n^(-1)sum_i W(x,x_i)f(x_i)/sqrt(d_X(x)d_X(x_i)). There are universal constants C0,C1 such that if n>=C0 D_X(rho)^2, then with probability at least 1-rho, inf_x d_X(x)>=cmin/2 and ||(L_X-L_P)f||_sup <= C1 cmax ||f||_sup D_X(rho)/(cmin sqrt(n)). This is a common-partition restricted version; f is fixed independently of X, while d_X uses the same sample as L_X.

Let G be a finite undirected graph with k>=3 distinct terminals. Its edges are independently open with probabilities in [0,1]. If the terminal partition is all separated with positive probability and all connected with positive probability, then some strictly intermediate terminal partition has positive probability. If its m optional-edge probabilities lie in [epsilon,1-epsilon], 0<epsilon<=1/2, its partition law has total-variation distance at least min(q,1-q,epsilon^m) from the selector law assigning probability q to all connected and 1-q to all separated, for 0<q<1.

Independent Bernoulli edge states.
Quantitative bound additionally assumes all m optional probabilities in [epsilon,1-epsilon].
No conclusion uniform in growing m.

body:
[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2609.01098, 'Gaussian upper bounds for averaged heat semigroups on graphs'] Let $n,r_0,C>0$. Assume that,
for all $x,y\in X$ and $t\geq r^2\geq r_0^2$, we have
\[
\mathcal{P}_r(t,x,y)
 \leq 

C 
\frac{\left(1\vee S^{-2}\sqrt{\rho(B_x(r),B_y(r))^2S^2+t^2}-t\right)^{\frac{n}{2}}}{\sqrt[\frac{2q(t)}{q(t)-1}]{m(B_x(\sqrt t))m(B_y(\sqrt t))}}
 \euler^{-S^{-2}t\zeta(\rho(B_x(r),B_y(r))S/t)}
\]
and  that,
for all $x\in X$ and $r_0\leq r_1\leq r_2$, we have
\begin{equation*}
m(B_x(r_2))\leq C
\left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^{n} m(B_x(r_1)).
\end{equation*}
Then there is a constant $C'=C'(C,n)>0$ such that, for all $\varepsilon\in[0,1)$, $r\geq 1\vee r_0$, and $U\subset B(r)$ satisfying $m(U)\geq \varepsilon m(B(r))$, we have 
\[
\lambda(U)
\geq 
\frac{C'}{r^{2+\varepsilon}}
\left(
\frac{m(B(r))}{m(U)}\right)^{\frac{2}{N}} \left[1\wedge \frac{1}{m(B(r))}\right] ^{\frac{1}{C'q(r^2)}}
\]
 where 
\[
N(r)= n\cdot \frac{q(r^2)}{q(r^2)-1}+ \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\ln \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\cdot \frac{1}{\ln r}+\frac{1}{q(r^2)-1}\cdot \ln(1\vee m(B(r))).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Thm Jankins--Neumann~\cite{JankinsNeumann1985}, Naimi~\cite{Naimi1994} of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Suppose $M=(\text{Pair of pants})\times S^1$, with $\Phi$ the periodic flow in the $S^1$ direction. Then the Jankins--Neumann ziggurat $\mathcal{Z}(\Phi)$ is the subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$ cut out by the following inequality (combined with its sibling obtained by inverting all three coordinates):
for $(r_1,r_2,r_3)\in \mathcal{Z}(\Phi)$,
$$r_3 \leq \sup_{q\geq 1}  \frac{-p_1 - p_2 + 1}q,$$
where $p_1/q \leq r_1$ and $p_2/q \leq r_2$ are the best rational subapproximants of $r_1$ and $r_2$ with denominator $q$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Jankins--Neumann~\cite{JankinsNeumann1985}, Naimi~\cite{Naimi1994}

body:
[Theorem 16 (Mean) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The expectation of $T_{m,p}$ is
  \[
    \E T_{m,p} = m \sum_{\ell = 1}^m \frac{1}{\ell\left(1-p\right)^\ell}.
  \]
  This quantity increases in both $m$ and $p$. Moreover,
  each function $p \mapsto \E T_{m,p}$ is convex.
  \begin{proof}
    Simply take $\E T_{m,p} = M_{T_{m,p}}'(0) = -\Lambda'(0) \, \Lambda(0)^{-2}$.
    The two claims are trivial.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let N>=2,1<=K<=N-1,and1<=t<=N be integers. Let H=Hyp(N,K,t) be the number of successes in t draws without replacement from a population of N containing K successes,and B=Bin(t,K/N). With the usual zero masses outside the hypergeometric support, sum_{w=0}^t |H(w)-B(w)|<=2*(t-1)/sqrt(N-(t-1)). Consequently,for the convention TV(P,Q)=(1/2)*sum_x|P(x)-Q(x)|, TV(H,B)<=(t-1)/sqrt(N-t+1). If t=1 the two laws coincide. Theorem1 is phrased in the regime K/N=p fixed in(0,1) as N tends to infinity;the displayed finite bound follows from its likelihood-ratio proof for each valid N,K,t. In particular,for fixed t and fixed p along integers K=p*N,the L1 distance tends to zero. This is a known source result,not a new convergence theorem.
Finite integers N>=2,1<=K<N,1<=t<=N;standard hypergeometric and binomial count laws.
Natural-log KL;L1 sum differs from total variation by a factor2.
The asymptotic corollary holds t fixed and p=K/N fixed in(0,1) along an integer sequence.

Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. With R_r the block conditional variances, put D_m = (-1)^(m+1) Delta^m R_0 for 1 <= m <= n, and let H_<m be the functions whose Hoeffding components of order m or more vanish. Then D_m = binom(n, m)^(-1) sum_{k=m}^n binom(k, m) W_k and D_m <= dist_2(f, H_<m)^2 <= binom(n, m) D_m; so D_m = 0 if and only if f lies in H_<m. With nonzero tail, the left inequality is an equality exactly when all the tail mass sits at order n, and the right one exactly when it sits at order m. The same holds with Q_r, the average over |A| = r of E[(f(X) - f(X^(A)))^2], since Q_r = 2 R_r: for m = 1 it reads Var(f) <= (1/2) sum_i E[(f(X) - f(X^(i)))^2].

A multi-species stochastic population model X_t = (X_t^1, ..., X_t^d) is stochastically persistent in probability if for every epsilon > 0, there exists delta > 0 such that liminf_{t -> infinity} P(min_{1 <= i <= d} X_t^i >= delta) >= 1 - epsilon whenever min_{1 <= i <= d} X_0^i > 0 almost surely.

body: The characteristic function of a random variable X is phi_X(t) = E[e^{itX}] for t real (the Fourier transform of its distribution). It satisfies phi_X(0) = 1, |phi_X(t)| <= 1, and phi_X is uniformly continuous. It DETERMINES the distribution (uniqueness theorem: equal characteristic functions imply equal laws, via the Fourier inversion formula), and X, Y independent implies phi_{X+Y} = phi_X phi_Y.
title: Characteristic Function

body: [Theorem thm: sbt of arXiv:2507.04505, 'Heights of butterfly trees'] Let $\pi \sim \operatorname{Unif}(\operatorname{B}_{n,s})$ and $h_n^{\operatorname{B}} = h(\mathcal T(\pi))$. Then $h_n^{\operatorname{B}} \sim 2^{X_n} + 2^{n - X_n} - 2$, where $X_n \sim \operatorname{Binom}(n,1/2)$, while $(\log_2 h_n^{\operatorname{B}} - n/2)/(\sqrt n/2)$ converges in distribution to $|Z|$ as $n \to \infty$, where $Z \sim N(0,1)$. In particular, $\mathbb{E} h_{n}^{\operatorname{B}} = 2(3/2)^n - 2 = c N^\alpha \cdot(1 + o(1))$ with $c=2$ and $\alpha = \log_2(3/2) \approx 0.58496$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm: sbt of arXiv:2507.04505

[Thm MPL of arXiv:2506.01746, '\bf Optimal Bregman quantization: existence and uniqueness of optimal quantizers revisited'] $(a)$ {\em General case}  (see e.g.~[Kav1993],~[Struwe1990]). If $\Lambda:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}_+$ ($\Lambda$ for ``landscape'' when $d\!=\!2$) is
a continuously differentiable function satisfying $\displaystyle \lim_{|x|\to +\infty}\Lambda(x)$  $= +\infty$ and if two distinct zeros of $\nabla \Lambda$ are strict local
minima then $\nabla \Lambda$ has  a third zero  which can be in no case a strict  local minimum.

\smallskip
\noindent $(b)$  {\em  Compact case} (see [LambertonP1996],~[Cohort1998],~[LuPag23]). Let $K\!\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be   a
nonempty compact convex set with a nonempty interior $O$, $\mathring{K} = O$. If $\Lambda :K\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is $C^1$
on $O$, $\nabla \Lambda$ admits a continuous extension  on $K$ satisfying $\{\nabla \Lambda=0\}\!\subset \,O$ 
and if, for every small enough $\varepsilon>0$, $(Id-\varepsilon \nabla \Lambda)(O)\!\subset O$, then $\nabla \Lambda$ has at least a third critical point in $K$ which is not a strict local minimum for $\Lambda$ on $K$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Lemma 52 (FIID sparse unique infinite clusters on the symmetric space) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a connected higher rank semisimple real Lie group with property (T) and let $(X,d_X)$ be its symmetric space. Let~$\mathbf Y$ be a Poisson point process $Y$ on $X$ of intensity $1$ together with iid ${\rm Unif}[0,1]$ marks. Then, for every $\eps>0$, there exists $\lambda>0$ such that if $\mathbf Y^{(\lambda)}$ is an independent Poisson point process on $X$ of intensity $\lambda$ equipped with iid ${\rm Unif}[0,1]$ marks,  there is a graph $\mathcal H$ on $Y$ defined as an isometry-equivariant factor of $(\mathbf Y,\mathbf Y^{(\lambda)})$ with a unique infinite cluster and $\mathbb E\big[ {\rm deg}_{\mathcal H(Y_0)}(o) \big]\le\eps$, where $Y_0:=Y\cup\{o\}$.
title: FIID sparse unique infinite clusters on the symmetric space

body: [campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked with a scope caveat; NO independent review - the parent that reviewed it had itself supplied two of the argument's steps, so its review does not certify the amended proof; no Lean] van Handel, The strong convergence phenomenon, arXiv:2507.00346v2 (11 February 2026), Section 6.9, pp. 69-70, asks whether strong convergence of a family of random matrices forces the empirical complex-eigenvalue measures of every noncommutative polynomial to converge to the corresponding limiting Brown measure. Problem 6.9 states it for ARBITRARY strongly convergent families - no independence, no independent entries, no freeness of the limit - and that literal generality is what is addressed. CLAIM: no. Fix an irrational theta and reduced approximants p_j/q_j -> theta; with omega_j = exp(2 pi i p_j / q_j) put U_j e_k = omega_j^k e_k, S e_k = e_{k-1} and V_j = e^{pi i / q_j} S. Then V_j U_j = omega_j U_j V_j, U_j^{q_j} = I, V_j^{q_j} = -I, and det(z I - U_j - V_j) = z^{q_j} exactly, so A_j = U_j + V_j is nilpotent and every empirical eigenvalue measure is delta_0, while the Brown measure of u + v for the limiting irrational-rotation pair is Haar measure on the unit circle (Fang, Jiang, Lin and Xu, arXiv:1210.4771, Theorem 12.2 - a literature dependency, not proved here). The same example blocks any universal lower bound on the limiting spectral radius. Conjugating by an independent Haar unitary makes the family random without changing norms, traces, nilpotency or eigenvalues. THE LOAD-BEARING GAP, named by the record itself: the pair converges to a ROTATION-ALGEBRA pair, not a free pair, and the two have different Brown measures, so the citation has to match the limit the construction actually has; the strong-convergence step is recorded as one of three loose ends. WHAT IS NOT REFUTED: the narrower conjectures for independent Ginibre matrices with adjoints and for free limiting families. Yi Han, arXiv:2606.01664 (June 2026), claims the Ginibre case and is COMPATIBLE with this construction. Do not promote a general counterexample to a result about independent matrix ensembles. FULL CONSTRUCTION AND PROOF: the store holds it as the lemma math:probability.free:candidate-strong-convergence-does-not-force-brown-measure, under a title naming neither the problem nor the campaign; this node is what makes it reachable from the problem id.

[Theorem 29 (Mean) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The first moment of $T_{m, p}$ is
  \[
    \E T_{m, p} = m \, H_m + 
      \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}
      \left[
      (p\,m)^2\left(1-p\right)^{m-1}
      +
      \int_0^1 p^3 \, m^2 \left(m-1\right)
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-2} L(x) \, dx
      \right]
  \]
  where $H_m$ is the $m^\text{th}$ harmonic number
  and $L(x) \coloneqq x + (1-x) \log(1-x)$.
  If $p = p_m$ is an $o(1/m)$ sequence then this becomes
  \[
    \E T_{m, p} = m\,H_m
    + p\,m^2 + \frac{1}{4} \, p^2 \, m^3
    + O\left(p^2 \, m^2\right) + O\left(p^3 \, m^4\right).
  \]
  as $m \to \infty$. If $p \sim c/m$ then
  \[
    \E T_{m, p} = m\,H_m + \left(1 + o(1)\right)
      m \left[ c + c^2 \int_0^1 e^{-cx} \, L(x) \, dx\right].
  \]
  If $p = \omega(1/m)$ then
  \[
    \E T_{m,p} = m\,H_m + \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p} \left(1
    + O\left(\frac{1}{p\,m}\right)\right).
  \]
  In particular, for $p$ constant,
  \begin{align*}
    \E T_{m,p}
    = m \, H_m
    + \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}&\Bigg\{
      1 + \left(-6p + 5 + \frac{1}{p}\right) m^{-1}\\
    &\phantom{\Bigg\{} {} + \left(45\,p^2 - 62\,p + 8 + \frac{7}{p} + \frac{2}{p^2} \right) m^{-2}
      + O\left(m^{-3}\right)
    \Bigg\}.
  \end{align*}
  \begin{proof}
    The difference $T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}$ has \textsc{mgf}
    $I_{m, p}(t)$. Corollary~\ref{thm:mgf} implies
    the \textsc{mgf} of $T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}$
    exists on a neighbourhood of the origin, hence
    $\E [T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}] = \lim_{t \uparrow 0} I_{m,p}'(t)$.
    With the knowledge 
    \begin{equation}
      
      \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left( 1 - x \right)^{m \exp(-t) - m}
      = \log\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right) \, m \, e^{-t}
      \left( 1 - x \right)^{m \exp(-t) - m},
    \end{equation}
    we differentiate the integral expression of
    \eqref{eq:extra term} to find
    \begin{align}
      \notag
      \E \left[T_{m,p} - T_{m,0}\right]
      &= (1-p)^m
      \left[
        1 - \overbrace{\int_0^1 p\, m\left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1}
        \, dx}^{1 - (1-p)^m} 
      \right]^{-2}\\
      \notag
      &\quad \times \int_0^1 p\,m^2 \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1}
      \log\left( \frac{1}{1-x} \right) dx\\
      
      &= \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}
      \int_0^1 (p\,m)^2 \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1}
      \log\left( \frac{1}{1-x} \right) dx.
      \intertext{Notice that $L(x) = x + (1-x) \log(1-x)$
      is an antiderivative of $-\log(1-x)$ that
      increases from $L(0) = 0$ to $L(1) = 1$. Hence, by an
      integration by parts,}
      
      &= \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}
      \left[
      (p\,m)^2\left(1-p\right)^{m-1}
      +
      \int_0^1 p^3 \, m^2 \left(m-1\right)
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-2} L(x) \, dx
      \right].
  \end{align}
    Add on $\E T_{m,0} = m \, H_m$ to find our expression for
    the first moment.

    If $p = o(1/m)$ then use the bound $1 \geq (1-p\,x)^{m-2} \geq e^{O(pm)} = 1 + O(p\,m)$,
    uniform in $x$, within \eqref{eq:diff mean}.
    What remains is straightforward: $\int_0^1 L(x) \, dx = 1/4$ and
    \begin{align*}
      \E \left[T_{m,p} - T_{m,0}\right]
      &= \frac{(p\,m)^2}{p\left(1-p\right)}
      + p^2\,m^3\,(1 + O(1/m))\,(1 + O(p\,m))\,\frac{1}{4}\\
      &= p\,m^2 + O\left(p^2\,m^2\right) + \frac{1}{4} \, p^2 \, m^3
      + O\left(p^2 \,m^2\right) + O\left(p^3 \, m^4\right) + O\left(p^3\,m^3\right).
    \end{align*}
    Remove redundant terms to conclude this case.

    If instead $p \sim c/m$ then by dominated convergence we find

      + \left(1 + o(1)\right) c^2 \, m \int_0^1 e^{-cx} \, L(x) \, dx.

body: Consider a nearly integrable Hamiltonian H(I,theta) = H_0(I) + eps H_1(I,theta) in action-angle coordinates, where H_0 is nondegenerate (its Hessian in I is nonsingular, so the frequency map I -> omega(I) = dH_0/dI is a local diffeomorphism) and H_1 is a sufficiently smooth, classically real-analytic, perturbation. The KAM theorem states that for eps small enough, invariant tori of the unperturbed system whose frequency vector omega(I) is Diophantine (|omega . k| >= c |k|^{-tau} for all nonzero integer vectors k) persist as slightly deformed invariant tori carrying quasi-periodic motion, and the surviving tori occupy a set of measure tending to full measure as eps -> 0. Due to Kolmogorov, Arnold, and Moser.
title: Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser theorem

Let $v, w$ be independent uniformly distributed (Haar) unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^D$ with $D \ge 3$, and let $\rho = \langle v, w\rangle$. Then $Y = 1 - \rho^2$ has the Beta distribution with parameters $\frac{D-1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$, and the singular kernel $(1-\rho^2)^{-1/2}$ has finite mean with the exact value $\mathbb{E}[Y^{-1/2}] = \dfrac{\Gamma(D/2)\,\Gamma((D-2)/2)}{\Gamma((D-1)/2)^2} = 1 + O(1/D)$. This is the benchmark that any corresponding estimate for non-Gaussian residual lines has to reproduce, and having the exact Gaussian value makes a wrong intermediate bound visible immediately.

D >= 3

[Lemma lem:mtfact of arXiv:2608.05089, 'Correlation decay in area-tilted line ensembles'] Suppose that $\Omega$ is a topological space and that $(\nu_N)_{N \in \mathbb{N}}$ are probability measures on $\Omega$
converging weakly to the probability measure $\nu$.
If $f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a bounded continuous function and $A \subseteq \Omega$ is a Borel set
with $\nu(\partial A) = 0$, then
\begin{equation}
    \mu_N(dx) \propto f(x) \ind*{A}(x) \nu_N(dx)
    \qquad \text{converges weakly to} \qquad
    \mu(dx) \propto f(x) \ind*{A}(x) \nu(dx),
\end{equation}
where $\mu_N$ and $\mu$ are normalized to be probability measures.
title: Lemma lem:mtfact of arXiv:2608.05089

Own-work restricted-data theorem, proof unaudited (C006 v2); novelty not established. Fix n,m,d>=1, unit u, labels y_i in {-1,1}, gamma<=r_i<=1 with gamma>0, and x_i=y_i*r_i*u. Let phi(z)=max(z,lambda*z), 0<lambda<1, and f_i=m^-1 sum_j a_j phi(w_j dot x_i). Train BOTH layers simultaneously on average logistic loss with actual step m*eta, eta>0, choosing a derivative in [lambda,1] at zero. Write b_j=w_j dot u, s_j=a_j+b_j, d_j=a_j-b_j; require every s_j(0)!=0. Then all a_j*b_j become positive after finite time; thereafter loss is strictly decreasing and tends to zero. This holds almost surely for iid N(0,sigma^2) initialization of all weights at any sigma>0. An explicit high-probability time bound is as follows. For delta in (0,1) and epsilon in (0,log(2)), define c0=2*eta*lambda*gamma/[max(1,eta)*(1+eta)], c1=eta*lambda*gamma/(1+eta), Pbar=4*sqrt(2)*(m/delta)^(3/2), Bbar=log(2*Pbar)/c0, Kmin=3*lambda*gamma*sigma^2*delta^2/(64*m^2), Fbar=(2*sigma^2/delta)*exp(2*eta*Bbar), T0bar=ceil(Bbar*(1+exp(Fbar))), and Cbar=max(0,log(log(1/epsilon)/Kmin)/(2*c1)). With probability >=1-delta, L_t<=epsilon for every integer t>=T0bar+ceil(n*Cbar/(1-exp(-epsilon))). The same event works for all epsilon. The proof uses exact per-neuron updates s_j^+=(1+k_j)s_j, d_j^+=(1-k_j)d_j, where eta*lambda*gamma*G<=k_j<=eta*G and G is average logistic weight. The cumulative sum of G cannot be finite, since that would bound parameters and hence keep G positive. Ratios contract into |d_j|<=|s_j|/2, fixing all branches and making all margins grow. The probability estimate uses a Gaussian density bound plus Markov and a union bound, not independence between norm and small-ball events. The times can be extremely large; neither Cai et al.'s sharp eta dependence nor convergence for multidirectional data is established. 13149 passing finite exact rational checks support selected algebra only; the analytic theorem remains unaudited. No formal certificate or numerical Gaussian simulation is claimed.
Collinear signed separable data with gamma<=r_i<=1; arbitrary sample count, labels and width.
Literal leaky activation, both layers trained simultaneously, positive arbitrary step and allowed derivative at zero.
Nonzero expanding coordinates deterministically; the quantified Gaussian bound assumes independent equal-variance N(0,sigma^2) coordinates.
Proof (unaudited), C006 v2; no novelty, full-data theorem, sharp Cai rate or formal certificate claimed.

Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. For 0 <= r <= n let R_r be the average over r-element sets A of E Var(f | X_{A^c}). Then R_r = Var(f) - H_{n - r} = sum_{k=1}^n [1 - binom(n - k, r)/binom(n, r)] W_k (the ratio read as 0 when r > n - k), so R_r is nondecreasing in r. If X^(A) keeps X_{A^c} and replaces X_A by an independent draw from its own law, then E Var(f | X_{A^c}) = (1/2) E[(f(X) - f(X^(A)))^2]. In particular n R_1 = sum_i E Var(f | X_{-i}) = sum_k k W_k.
independent coordinates with finite ranges
f real valued

Let Lambda be a compact hyperbolic set for a diffeomorphism f. There exist a neighbourhood U of Lambda and constants C > 0 and delta_0 > 0 such that: whenever a point x and an integer n satisfy f^k(x) in U for 0 <= k <= n and d(f^n(x), x) < delta < delta_0, there is a genuine PERIODIC point p with f^n(p) = p and d(f^k(p), f^k(x)) <= C delta for every 0 <= k <= n. In words, an orbit segment that almost closes up lies uniformly close to an exactly periodic orbit of the same period. This is the standard device for producing many periodic orbits in a hyperbolic set and for approximating invariant measures by measures on periodic orbits.
Hyperbolicity on the compact set, and the whole segment staying in the neighbourhood U.
The period of the produced orbit is exactly n, and closeness is uniform along the segment.

\E\left[\left|\Xi_n\right|^p\right]
\leq L_p
\]
for every \(p\geq1\). Suppose that \(A_n\) has independent entries with common law
\(\Xi_n\) and is almost surely invertible for every \(n\). This last condition is automatic under the density assumption imposed in the triangular-array application below.

There exist constants \(c_{\mathrm{win}},c_{\mathrm{cmp}}>0\) and
\(n_0<\infty\), depending only on a finite collection of the bounds
\(\left(L_p\right)_{p\geq1}\), such that, for every
\[
1\leq m\leq n^{c_{\mathrm{win}}},
\qquad
n\geq n_0,
\]
and every Borel set
\(\Omega\subseteq\left[0,\infty\right)^m\),
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr\left(
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{n,m}^{\mathrm{Gin}}
\in
\Omega\setminus
\partial_{n^{-c_{\mathrm{cmp}}}}\Omega
\right)
-
n^{-c_{\mathrm{cmp}}}
\leq
\Pr\left(
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{n,m}\in\Omega
\right)
\leq
\Pr\left(
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{n,m}^{\mathrm{Gin}}
\in
\Omega\cup
\partial_{n^{-c_{\mathrm{cmp}}}}\Omega
\right)
+
n^{-c_{\mathrm{cmp}}}.
\end{aligned}

\end{equation}
The constants are uniform over all triangular arrays satisfying the displayed moment and circularity conditions.

The Taylor remainder divided by r^2 is at most ||h triple-prime|| infinity*r*(1+cr)^3/6 plus ||h double-prime|| infinity*c^2*r^2/2. {"artifact_digest":"sha256:d7d24572a68ce4263098c324d399774708859cfdac59493b76d5d2697bef2a55","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d7/d7d24572a68ce4263098c324d399774708859cfdac59493b76d5d2697bef2a55.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:cbac8f169ff863a9595053ddefd9aa680d7116085e24b8a5c3f7297ee2ff2704","bundle_entry_key":"scalar-forced-urn-wright-fisher-generator-limit","bundle_id":"population.w336-p0087-checked-attempt-20261010","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"w336/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.reinforcement:scalar-forced-urn-wright-fisher-generator-limit","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# P0087: stationary synchronization and covariance at f=c*r^2

Status: proof written; w346 KEEP pending. This proves a full stationary-law limit, stationary moments and a scalar generator limit under conditional independence. It does not prove the general network's functional diffusion limit or its initial layer.

Assume a fixed finite irreducible row-stochastic Q, its stationary probability row vector pi, p in [0,1]^d, c>0, r>0, f=c*r^2 and r+f<=1. Update

    Z'=(1-r-f)Z+r X+f p,

with conditionally independent X_i given Z, and P(X_i=1|Z)=(QZ)_i. There is a unique stationary law on [0,1]^d. Its mean is z*=f*((r+f)I-rQ)^(-1)p. Write pbar=pi.p and K=sum pi_i^2. As r decreases to zero, its stationary covariance satisfies

    Cov(Z) -> [K*pbar*(1-pbar)/(2c+K)]*1*1^T.

Proof of existence/uniqueness: the transition is Feller on a compact cube. Couple two states using the same independent uniforms for their Bernoulli coordinates. Because 1-r-f>=0, the weighted L1 distance has expected next value at most (1-f) times its present value; use pi Q=pi. Thus stationary laws are unique and the transition contracts in this Wasserstein distance. Taking expectations yields the displayed mean; the matrix is invertible because its eigenvalues have positive real part.

For synchronization, let D=diag(pi), S=pi.Z, and E_Q(z)=z^T D(I-Q)z=(1/2)sum pi_i Q_ij(z_i-z_j)^2. At stationarity, with Delta=r(X-Z)+f(p-Z),

    2r E[E_Q(Z)] = 2f E[<Z,p-Z>_D] + E[||Delta||_D^2]
                   <= 2f+(r+f)^2 = O(r^2).

Irreducibility makes E_Q(z)>=gamma*||z-1*(pi.z)||_D^2 for some fixed gamma>0: the finite symmetric quadratic form has kernel precisely the constants. Hence E||Z-1*S||_D^2=O(r). Also E[S]=pbar exactly, so z*_i tends to pbar.

The martingale innovation for S has conditional variance r^2 sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i); conditional independence is used exactly here. Total variance at stationarity gives

    (2f-f^2) Var(S)=r^2 sum pi_i^2 E[(QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i)].

Synchronization shows (QZ)_i-S tends to zero in L2. The variables are bounded, so for any subsequential limit V of Var(S), division by r^2 gives 2c V=K*(pbar*(1-pbar)-V). Its solution is unique. Every subsequence has that limit, and synchronization gives the full covariance limit.

For the scalar case Q=(1), stationarity gives the exact variance

    Var(Z)=r^2*p*(1-p)/(2f-f^2+r^2)
          =p*(1-p)/(1+2c-c^2*r^2).

For h in C^3([0,1]), the one-step scalar generator divided by r^2 converges uniformly to

    Lh(z)=c(p-z)h'(z)+(1/2)z(1-z)h''(z).

Indeed E[Delta]=c*r^2(p-z), E[Delta^2]=r^2*z(1-z)+c^2*r^4(p-z)^2, and |Delta|<=r+cr^2. Taylor's remainder, divided by r^2, is bounded by ||h'''||_infinity*r*(1+cr)^3/6, with the additional second-order drift term O(r^2). This identifies the candidate Wright-Fisher generator; path tightness and martingale-problem uniqueness are further steps.

Theorem (full stationary law). Under the same fixed-network assumptions and 0<pbar<1, the joint stationary law of Z converges weakly to Y*1, where

    Y ~ Beta(2c*pbar/K, 2c*(1-pbar)/K).

Proof: write S'=S+f*(pbar-S)+r*eta, where eta=pi.(X-QZ), E[eta|Z]=0, |eta|<=1 and E[eta^2|Z]=sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i). For every polynomial h, the stationary Taylor identity divided by r^2 gives

    0=c E[(pbar-S)h'(S)]
      +(1/2)E[sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i)*h''(S)] + O(r).

The drift-square contribution is O(r^2), and the third-order remainder is uniformly O(r). The proved L2 synchronization implies that the sum inside the second term differs from K*S*(1-S) by a quantity tending to zero in L1. Every subsequence has a further weakly convergent subsequence of S because [0,1] is compact. If its limiting moments are mu_k, use h(s)=s^k, k>=1, to obtain

    [2c+K*(k-1)]*mu_k = [2c*pbar+K*(k-1)]*mu_(k-1), mu_0=1.

These are exactly the moments of the displayed beta law: iterating gives the product of (2c*pbar/K+j)/(2c/K+j) for j=0,...,k-1, which also follows by integrating the beta density. A probability law on [0,1] is determined by its moments, since polynomials approximate continuous functions uniformly. Hence all subsequential limits agree and S converges weakly. Synchronization gives Z-S*1 tending to zero in probability, so the joint law converges to Y*1. If pbar=0 or 1, positivity of pi forces every p_i to be that endpoint and the unique stationary law is the corresponding point mass.

This proof uses all polynomial moments, not an inference from the first two moments. It proves convergence of stationary laws, not a limit for trajectories begun away from synchronization. Without conditional independence, the innovation variance changes. For example, Q=J_d/d, constant p, and one shared Bernoulli coin across all coordinates preserve a synchronized state and give the scalar beta parameters 2cp and 2c(1-p), rather than 2cdp and 2cd(1-p).

For reproducible finite checks, the exact covariance identity is

    V=B V B^T+r^2*diag(s*(1-s)-diag(Q V Q^T)),
    B=(1-r-f)I+rQ, s=Q z*.

Checks: the scalar exact formula; first four scalar stationary moments; exact polynomial generators; finite-network covariance systems; first four moments of the exact consensus Markov chain for Q=J_d/d at d=2,3,5; a common-coin control that changes the beta variance. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators (an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, real eigenvalues tending to 0, ||T|| = max |eigenvalue|, min-max characterisation of eigenvalues) requires self-adjointness or at least normality. Compactness alone gives only the Riesz-Schauder picture: the nonzero spectrum consists of eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity accumulating only at 0, and the set of such eigenvalues may be empty. The standard counterexample is the Volterra operator on L^2([0,1]), (V f)(x) = integral from 0 to x of f(t) dt, which is Hilbert-Schmidt (kernel k(x,t) = 1 for t < x, 0 otherwise) hence compact, but has no eigenvalues at all: V f = lambda f with lambda nonzero forces f to be absolutely continuous with f' = f/lambda and f(0) = 0, so f = 0; and V f = 0 forces f = 0 a.e. Thus sigma(V) = {0}, spectral radius 0, while ||V|| = 2/pi; the singular values of V are 1/((n + 1/2) pi), n >= 0, so V is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, and the moduli of its eigenvalues (all zero) are nowhere near its singular values. Consequences for an auditor: (a) 'compact, so expand in eigenfunctions' is invalid without normality; the right substitute is the Schmidt decomposition in singular values, which always exists; (b) 'compact, so the spectral radius equals the norm' is false; (c) Rayleigh-quotient and min-max formulas for eigenvalues are statements about self-adjoint operators and become statements about singular values otherwise; (d) Mercer-type positivity conclusions require a self-adjoint positive kernel, not just an L^2 kernel.
the operator is compact on a Hilbert space

Let X be any full-row-rank p-by-n real design, Delta a fixed m-by-p matrix, and Z=Delta X+E, where the entries of E are independent N(0,sigma^2), sigma>0. body: Green-Tao theorem: The sequence of prime numbers contains arbitrarily long finite arithmetic progressions; that is, for every natural number k >= 1 there exist positive integers a and d such that the k numbers a, a + d, a + 2d, ..., a + (k-1)d are all prime. (The progressions are finite: no infinite arithmetic progression can consist only of primes.) The theorem was proved by Ben Green and Terence Tao in 2004; the proof extends Szemeredi's theorem, via a transference principle, from sets of positive density in the integers to subsets of positive relative density inside a pseudorandom set of almost primes.
title: Green–Tao theorem

[Proposition 18 (Structural properties of the Einstein--Navier--Stokes models) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Consider the system of equations in \autoref{def-prod-areal-flow} under the pressure assumptions~\eqref{hyperbolic-eos-zero}.
Then the following properties hold for sufficiently regular solutions~$(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$.
\bei

\item \emph{Hyperbolicity.} \emph{Under the non-vacuum condition $- \Jbb \cdot \Jbb>0$,} the evolution system consisting of~\eqref{eqchi-evol} and either~\eqref{prod-energy-conservation} or~\eqref{energy-dissip-Sigma} is a first-order hyperbolic system of $12+\dim\mathscr E$ nonlinear balance laws with characteristic cones in the causal cone.

\item \emph{Constraint propagation.}  Given a solution of this hyperbolic system, if the constraints~\eqref{eqchi-constr} on $\log\Omega, K_2, K_3$ are satisfied at initial time they propagate to all future times.

\item \emph{Equivalence property.}
Given such a solution $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$, together with the value of the modular parameter~$\tau$ at one spacetime point and the spatial averages of $G,H$ at initial time, one recovers a unique solution $(g,\beta,\zeta)$ of the Einstein--Navier--Stokes equations, specifically a particle-production relaxation flow (\autoref{def-prod-pot}) or dissipated-energy relaxation flow (\autoref{def-diss-en}).
In particular, the wave equation for the lapse~\eqref{eq:waveconffac-NS} below holds.

\item \emph{Particle-number current.}
The convex current derived from the potential~$\chi$ satisfies
\bel{eq:pot-areal-production}
\aligned
\divuntrois\vNumb_\chi
& = \mathfrak d_{\mathscr B}
\quad && \text{(particle-production areal flow),}
\\
\divuntrois\vNumb_\chi & = 0
\quad && \text{(dissipated-energy areal flow),}
\endaligned
\ee
where $\mathfrak d_{\mathscr B} = \zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}(\beta,\zeta) \geq 0$.

[Theorem 27 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Suppose $U = \sum_{j=0}^\infty u^j$ satisfies Assumption~\ref{asmp:main for refreshing} for some $\beta >0$ and let $\alpha \in (0,1)$ such that $\alpha + \beta/2 > 1$. Let
    \[p >\frac{ \beta}{\alpha + \beta/2-1} \lor \frac{\beta}{\alpha}\]
    and suppose for some $K \geq 1$, 
     we have that for all $j \in \N,$ and  $n \in \{0,1,2\},$
     \begin{equation*}
         \|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega \continuous^0_{t,x}} \leq K 2^{(n-\alpha)j}.
     \end{equation*}
     Then there exist $\delta(\alpha,\beta,p)>0, \gamma(\alpha,\beta,p)>0$, and a random field $M : \T^d \to [1,\infty)$ such that $\gamma \to \infty$ as $p \to \infty$ and
        \begin{enumerate}
         \item almost surely $\sup_{y \in \T^d} |M(y)| < \infty$; in fact $\E \big[\big(\log \log\big(\sup_{y \in \T^d} |M(y)| + e\big)\big)^{\gamma}\big]<\infty$,
         \item $\E \big[\big(\log\big(\|M\|_{L^p_y} + 1\big)\big)^{\gamma}\big]<\infty$,
         \item and for any $y,z \in \T^d$, any $w \in C^{1/2 + \delta}([0,1])$ with $w_0=0$, if we have any solution $X$ to~\eqref{eq:main refreshing ODE 0}, and any solution $\tilde X$ to 
          \begin{equation*}
         \tilde X_t=z+\int_0^t U(s,\tilde X_s)\,ds+w_t,\qquad t\in[0,1],
         \end{equation*}
         then we have the stability estimate on the time interval $[0,1]$,
         \[\|X - \tilde X\|_{C^{1/2 +\delta}_t} \leq M(y)\big(|y-z| + \|w\|_{C^{1/2+\delta}_t}\big),\]
        and, in the case that $w=0$, the expansion/compression estimate for all $t \in [0,1],$
        \[\frac{1}{M(y)} |y-z| \leq |X_t - \tilde X_t| \leq M(y) |y-z|.\]
     \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 27 of arXiv:2608.05931

body: In mathematics, low-rank approximation refers to the process of approximating a given matrix by a matrix of lower rank. More precisely, it is a minimization problem, in which the cost function measures the fit between a given matrix and an approximating matrix, subject to a constraint that the approximating matrix has reduced rank. The problem is used for mathematical modeling and data compression. The rank constraint is related to a constraint on the complexity of a model that fits the data. In applications, often there are other constraints on the approximating matrix apart from the rank constraint, e.g., non-negativity and Hankel structure.
title: Low-rank approximation

body: In mathematics, power iteration (also known as the power method) is an eigenvalue algorithm: given a diagonalizable matrix $A$, the algorithm will produce a number $\lambda$, which is the greatest (in absolute value) eigenvalue of $A$, and a nonzero vector $v$, which is a corresponding eigenvector of $\lambda$, that is, $Av=\lambda v$. The algorithm is also known as the Von Mises iteration.

Fix 0<beta<1. Put h(0)=0, h(n)=n+n^beta for integers n>=1, and T_n=h(n) deterministically. Then h is subadditive, lim_m h(m)/m=1, and E exp(alpha |T_n-E T_n|/n^q)=1 for every n>=1, alpha>0 and q>=0. Nevertheless h(n)-n=n^beta is not O(n^q log n) for q<beta. This is a counterexample to a generic inference, not an iid lattice FPP law.

PRIVATE AUTHOR-CHECKED DRAFT, no independent review. Let n be even, Z_1, Z_2 independent standard Gaussians, (g_i) independent N(0, sigma^2) with sigma small, and X_i = Z_1 + g_i for i <= n/2, X_i = Z_2 + g_i for i > n/2. Then (a) with probability tending to one as sigma -> 0 there are two near-maximal indices with correlation R = 0 (multiple peaks in Chatterjee's sense with deficit |Z_1 - Z_2| of order one), (b) Var(max_i X_i) -> Var(max(Z_1, Z_2)) > 0, so the field is not superconcentrated relative to its variance scale, and (c) the argmax half is determined by sign(Z_1 - Z_2) and is unchanged under Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise of size t unless t exceeds a level of order |Z_1 - Z_2|, so the field is not chaotic. Hence any multiple-peaks condition that admits two peaks cannot be equivalent to chaos or superconcentration; this refutes the two-peak reading of Chatterjee's open problem 6 in 'Chaos, concentration, and multiple valleys' and leaves the growing-number version open.
Gaussian field on n points as specified
Chatterjee's definitions of multiple peaks, superconcentration and chaos

body:
Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity. Scarce calibration (P30, 240 of the calibration rows per cell, split B): P30 (a) HELD: at n = 240 the simplex beats least squares by +14.10 on EMIT (full calibration +8.83); (b) REFUTED: t* averages 0.22 on EMIT and the blend reads -2.61 vs the simplex; (c) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells and the simplex reads +2.27 vs least squares (full calibration -0.18); falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT) TRIGGERED. The observable part of the bias shift (P31): adding t^2 (D_ev - D_cal), the shift in the two bases' mean squared disagreement between the evaluation and calibration rows, to the criterion - P31 (a) REFUTED: the R'-blend reads -0.71 vs the simplex on EMIT split B (R-blend +0.08) and +0.71 on split C (R-blend +0.63); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R'-blend is -0.11 vs the R-blend on split B and -0.12 on split C; (c) REFUTED: mean t** 0.39 against t* 0.33 on EMIT, share of the hindsight optimum 0.07 -> -0.62; falsifier (R'-blend worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 on any corpus or split) TRIGGERED. Per-output mixing weights (P34, the criterion decoupled across outputs): P34 (a) REFUTED: the per-output blend reads -0.41 vs the per-cell blend on EMIT split B and -0.53 on split C; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 -0.02 and -0.08 on split C; (c) REFUTED: on Y2 the share of outputs at t_d = 0 is 0.20 and at t_d >= 0.5 is 0.34; falsifier (per-output worse than per-cell by more than 0.3 anywhere) TRIGGERED. A nearest-neighbour proxy for the bias shift (P35, the simplex's out-of-fold residuals at the nearest calibration rows standing in for its bias at the scored rows): P35 (a) REFUTED: the full-shift blend reads -0.69 vs the R-blend on EMIT split B and -0.12 on split C; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 -0.08 and -0.14 on split C; (c) REFUTED: cross-only vs full on EMIT -0.05 vs -0.62 (split B); falsifier (either variant worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 anywhere) TRIGGERED. Scarce calibration, the ratio-metric criterion (P41, 240 calibration rows, split B, three-vertex form, registered and R_1 choices side by side): P41 (a) HELD: at n_cal = 240 the R_1 blend reads +1.17 vs the simplex on EMIT (within 1.0; the registered three-vertex blend reads -1.83); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R_1 blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells (at least 25); (c) HELD: R_1 vs the registered blend on EMIT +1.38 (at least +1.0); falsifier (R_1 worse than the simplex by more than 2.0 on EMIT) not triggered. So the P30 caveat is confined to the squared-loss criterion; the criterion in the score's own metric keeps the simplex where it should at scarce calibration.

Lindeberg-Levy form: let X_1, X_2, ... be independent identically distributed random variables with mean mu and finite variance sigma^2 > 0, and let bar X_n = (X_1 + ... + X_n) / n. Then sqrt(n) (bar X_n - mu) / sigma converges in distribution to the standard normal law: P(sqrt(n) (bar X_n - mu) / sigma <= x) -> Phi(x) for every real x. Lindeberg-Feller form: for a triangular array of independent, mean-zero rows with s_n^2 = sum_k Var(X_{n,k}), the normalised sums S_n / s_n converge to N(0, 1) provided the Lindeberg condition holds: for every epsilon > 0, (1 / s_n^2) sum_k E[X_{n,k}^2 ; |X_{n,k}| > epsilon s_n] -> 0.
finite, non-zero variance; with infinite variance the limit, when it exists, is a stable law
independence (identically distributed in the Lindeberg-Levy form, the Lindeberg condition otherwise)

[Lemma lem-LF-SLE of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $W \in (0, \frac{\gamma^2}2)$ and $\alpha = Q - \frac W{2\gamma}$. 
	    Sample $(\psi, \eta^\mathrm{wp})$ from $\frac1{2\pi(Q-\alpha)} \mathrm{LF}_{\mathbb C}^{(\alpha, 0), (\gamma, 1), (2Q-\alpha, \infty)} \times \mathrm{SLE}_\kappa^\mathrm{wp}(W-2)$. For each connected component $B$ of $\mathbb{C} \backslash \eta^\mathrm{wp}$, let $p_B$ and $q_B$ be the first and last points of $\partial B$ hit by $\eta^\mathrm{wp}$. Let $\tilde \mathcal{W}$ be the collection of all quantum surfaces $(B, \psi, p_B, q_B)/{\sim_\gamma}$, and  endow $\tilde \mathcal{W}$ with the ordering where $(B_1, \psi, p_{B_1}, q_{B_1})/{\sim_\gamma}$ precedes $(B_2, \psi, p_{B_2}, q_{B_2})/{\sim_\gamma}$ if $\eta^\mathrm{wp}$ hits $q_{B_1}$ for the last time before it hits $q_{B_2}$ for the last time. 
	
	    
	    Let $B_\bullet$ be the connected component of $\mathbb{C} \backslash \eta_0^\mathrm{wp}$ containing $1$, and let $\mathcal{B}_\bullet = (B_\bullet, \psi, 1, p_{B_\bullet}, q_{B_\bullet})/{\sim_\gamma}$. Let $ \mathcal{D} \subset \tilde \mathcal{W}$ (resp.\ $\mathcal{W} \subset \tilde \mathcal{W}$) be the ordered collection of elements that come before (resp.\ after) $(B_\bullet, \psi, p_{B_\bullet}, q_{B_\bullet})/{\sim_\gamma}$. Then the joint law of $(\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{B}_\bullet, \mathcal{W})$ is $(1 - \frac{2W}{\gamma^2})^2 {\mathcal{M}}^\mathrm{disk}_{0,2}(W) \times {\mathcal{M}}^\mathrm{disk}_{1,2}(\gamma^2 - W) \times \mathcal{M}^\mathrm{wed}(W)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked, no independent read.] This is an elementary special case recorded alongside Open Problem 14.12 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). Let K_n be the complete simple graph with n>=2 vertices and start one particle per vertex. Each particle jumps independently at rate one to a uniformly chosen different vertex; particles merge on meeting. If T_coal is the time until one particle remains, then E[T_coal]=sum_{k=2}^n (n-1)/(k(k-1))=(n-1)^2/n. The discrete-time simple-walk matrix has n-1 nonconstant eigenvalues all equal to -1/(n-1), so its spectral mean hitting-time sum K=sum_{j=2}^n 1/(1-lambda_j) is also (n-1)^2/n. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
Complete graph; rate-one simple walks; one initial particle at every vertex.

Let N take values in {0, 1, ..., m} on a probability space, mu = E[N] > 0 and beta = E[binom(N, 2)] = E[N(N-1)/2]; put x = 2 beta / mu and r = 1 + floor(x). The masses p_r = (r mu - 2 beta)/r, p_{r+1} = (2 beta - (r-1) mu)/(r+1) and p_0 = 1 - p_r - p_{r+1} are nonnegative, p_{r+1} = 0 when r = m, and the law on {0, r, r+1} with these masses has the same mu and beta as N and P(> 0) equal to the optimized bound D. So the bound is sharp for every feasible pair (mu, beta).
N is integer valued with 0 <= N <= m
mu = E[N] > 0

For a finite real martingale M_k with M_0=0 and finite fourth moments, put D_k=M_k-M_{k-1}. Then E M_N^4=sum_{k=1}^N(6 E M_{k-1}^2 D_k^2+4 E M_{k-1}D_k^3+E D_k^4). The cubic term need not vanish: if M_1 is a symmetric sign and conditionally on M_1=1, D_2=-1 with probability 2/3 and 2 with probability 1/3, with reversed signs when M_1=-1, then E[M_1D_2^3]=2 and E M_2^4=27. Dropping that term gives 19.

Let p = Bernoulli(a) and q = Bernoulli(b) with a, b in [0, 1]. Every coupling is determined by t = P(X = 1, Y = 1): its table is P(1,1) = t, P(1,0) = a - t, P(0,1) = b - t, P(0,0) = 1 - a - b + t, and these are nonnegative exactly for t in [max(0, a + b - 1), min(a, b)]. The mismatch probability is a + b - 2t, so it takes every value in [|a - b|, 1 - |a + b - 1|], each for exactly one coupling.

[Theorem 23 (Subcritical shape) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Suppose $p = o(1/m)$. Then
  $(T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0})/m \stackrel{P}{\to} 0$ as $m \to \infty$.
  It follows that $(T_{m,p} - m \log{m})/m$ converges
  in law to a standard Gumbel distribution.
  \begin{proof}
    The first claim follows by observing that $\PP(T_{m, 0} = T_{m, p}) = (1-p)^m \to 1$.
    Then Proposition~\ref{thm:classical mgf convergence}
    confirms $m^{-t}\,M_{T_{m,0}}(t/m) \to \Gammaop(1-t)$.
    By Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence} and Definition~\ref{def:Gumbel},
    $(T_{m,0} - m \log{m})/m$ converges in law to a standard Gumbel.
    By Slutsky's theorem, so does $(T_{m,p} - m \log{m})/m$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Subcritical shape

body:
[Lem 130 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $X^1$ and $X^2$ be solutions to SDEs
    \[
    dX^i(t)
    =
    b^i(t,X^i(t))\,dt
    +
    \sigma^i(t,X^i(t))\,dB_t\,,
    \]
such that $X^1(q_*)$ and $X^2(q_*)$ are equidistributed.
Suppose for some finite constant $\oL$ that the SDE coefficients $b^i$ and $\sigma^i$ are uniformly bounded by $\oL$, and moreover are $\oL$-Lipschitz in the space coordinate. Lastly suppose
	\[
    \sup_{(t,x)\in [q_*
    ,1]\times \mathbb R}
    \bigg\{
    \Big|b^1(t,x) - b^2(t,x)\Big|
    +
 	\Big|\sigma^1(t,x)-\sigma^2(t,x)\Big|
    \bigg\}
    \le \epsilon\,.
    \]
Then the marginal laws of $X^1$ and $X^2$ are close in $L^2$-Wasserstein distance for all time: more precisely, there is a coupling of $X^1$ with $X^2$ under which
	\[
	\sup\bigg\{
	\E\bigg[\Big(X^1(t)-X^2(t)\Big)^2\bigg] 
	: t\in[q_*
        ,1]
	\bigg\} \le 
	C(\oL) \epsilon^2\,,
	\]
where $C(\oL)$ denotes a constant depending only on $\oL$.

\begin{proof}
Couple $X^1$ and $X^2$ with the same Brownian motion $B$, and same initial value (almost surely). For this coupling let $Z(t) = X^1(t)-X^2(t)$, and $E(t) = \E[Z(t)^2]$. By It\=o's formula, for any
$0\le t\le t'\le1$, we have
	\[
	E(t')-E(t)
	=\E \int_t^{t'} \bigg\{
		2 Z(s)
		\Big(b^1(s,X^1(s))-b^2(s,X^2(s))
		\Big)
	+\Big( \sigma^1(s,X^1(s))
		-\sigma^2(s,X^2(s))
		\Big)^2
		\bigg\}\,ds\,.
	\]
For $s\in[q_*,1]$, using that $b^1$ and $b^2$ are $\epsilon$-close to one another, and $\oL$-Lipschitz in the space coordinate, gives
	\[
	\Big|b^1(s,X^1(s))-b^2(s,X^2(s))
	\Big|
	\le \oL\Big| X^1(s)-X^2(s)\Big|
		+ \epsilon
	=\oL |Z(s)|
		+ \epsilon\,.
	\]
A similar bound holds with $\sigma^i$ in place of $b^i$. It follows that 
for $[t,t']\subseteq[q_*,1]$, we have
	\[
	E(t')-E(t)
	\le 3
	\E \int_t^{t'}
	\Big(\oL |Z(s)| + \epsilon\Big)^2\,ds
	\le 6 \bigg\{
	\oL^2 \int_t^{t'} E(s)\,ds
	+ \epsilon^2 (t'-t)
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The claimed bound follows from Gr\"onwall's inequality. More precisely, we can use the form stated in \cite[Lem.~6.1]{MR1071170} which says that if for all $t\in[q_*
    ,1]$ we have
	\[
	E(t) \le a(t) +\int_{q_0}^t b(s) E(s)\,ds
	\]
with $a,b$ continuous nonnegative functions, then it holds that
	\[
	E(1)
	\leq 
	E(q_*)
	+
	\int_{q_*
        }^1
	a(s)b(s)
	\exp
	\lt(
	\int_s^1 b(r)\,dr
	\rt)\,ds.
	\]
In our setting $E(q_*)=0$, $b(t)=6\oL^2$, and $a(t)=6\epsilon^2(t-q_*)$. Therefore
$a(1) \le 6\epsilon^2$, and the claimed bound follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 130 of arXiv:2608.29416

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical, priority and target-scope audit pending. # Neutral truth/false bundles defeat the smaller-count hypothesis

T379-C016 v2, proof (unaudited), exact checks PASS; independent audit pending.
Targets 1/2: auxiliary-route failure, no target score claimed.

For every integer m>=5 and N>=3 set K=3m,r=3(m-1),d=1. In the two
variable contexts L,R suppose the known truth unions have sizes
s=2(m-1),t=r, respectively. There are N-2 fixed known S contexts.
No partition tags are supplied. Both orientations remain compatible:
if L is A its r-support contains C_L of size s; if R is A its support
is exactly C_R of size r. Such unions have positive probability from
actual untagged factual samples with ell=0, e.g. one occurrence of
every known truth, n=s+r. The identities can be permuted within each
context without affecting the construction or source probabilities.

Put lambda=1/(NK). Partition the variable-context atoms as follows:

* B: all K-s=m+2 atoms outside C_L and two atoms outside C_R;
* T: all s known L truths and any s of the known R truths;
* Z: the remaining m-1 known R truths and its one remaining outside atom.

B has m+4 atoms; T has 4(m-1); Z has m. In either orientation and
for EVERY compatible residual L support, their source masses are

 p(B)=lambda*(m+2),
 p(T)=lambda*(4m-2),
 p(Z)=lambda*m.

For B, if L is A its residual true count is r-s=m-1, so
p(B)=(m-1)/(Nr)+2/(NK)=lambda*(m+2). If R is A the same mass comes
from K-s systematic L atoms and no R truths. T's mass is always
s/(Nr)+s/(NK). Z's mass is (m-1)/(Nr)=m/(NK) when R is A and is
also m/(NK) when R is S. This checks invariance directly from p.

Define g as the uniform coarsening of these groups:

 g(B atom)=lambda*(m+2)/(m+4)=q,
 g(T atom)=lambda*(2m-1)/(2(m-1)),
 g(Z atom)=lambda,
 g(fixed S atom)=lambda.

The total is one and all probabilities are nonnegative. Equal lambda
scores merge Z and fixed S; their source masses remain invariant.
Thus g is source Mis_infinity=0 for every compatible world, not just
on average or conditional on a correct orientation prediction.

If L is A all three false atoms lie in B, giving H_L=3q.
If R is A two false atoms lie in B and one in Z, giving H_R=2q+lambda.
Since q<lambda, the worst-world false mass is

 max H=lambda*(3m+8)/(m+4).                              (1)

C016 v1 conjectured that the smaller known count alone gives the exact
value. Here h=s yields that conjectured value

 V_small=3lambda*(m+1)/(m+2).

The actual feasible worst risk (1) is strictly smaller, by

 V_small-max H=lambda*(m-4)/((m+2)(m+4))>0.               (2)

For m=5,N=3 these are 2/35 versus 23/405, gap 1/2835.
This refutes the entire proposed smaller-count formula; it does not
establish the optimal risk in this family. In particular the nine
complete small-alphabet score-partition checks were consistent with
the conjecture but insufficient to prove it. No general lower bound
was promoted from those computations.

The neutral Z group contains truths and possible falsehoods in exactly
the systematic true-density ratio. Its p mass is orientation-invariant
even though the known truth counts are unequal. This mechanism is
invisible to a rule that discards all surplus known truths. A general
unequal-count frontier must account for invariant weighted count
identities, not merely the minimum count or posterior risk ordering.
This is a route obstruction, not a solution of the unrestricted target.
Primary calibration basis: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2.

Verification: logs/neutral_bin_counterexample_check.json records 33
exact rational parameter cases and 582 compatible-world source-bin
calibration checks. It exhausts residual L supports for m=5,6,7;
larger m use the displayed general cardinality proof plus one
representative support, without claiming exhaustive enumeration there.
N>=3,K>=2,1<=r<K,0<=s,t<=r integers
One arbitrary and one systematic context, remaining contexts known S; source uniform contexts then uniform truths
Known truth identities from actual untagged factual samples and optional verifier; all compatible supports/orientations allowed
Robust source exact-level zero miscalibration; arbitrary generators

[Lem LM51 of arXiv:2608.16170, '\bf On hitting time distributions of Markov processes with sub-Gaussian heat kernel bounds'] Assume that the Borel right process $X$ satisfies  (AC), (H2a) and (H2b). Let $B\in \mathscr{B}^n(E)$ be such that $\overline{B}$ is compact in $E$. Then for any $\lambda>0$ ($\lambda\geq 0$ if $X$ is transient), there exists a unique positive  measure $\nu^{(\lambda)}_B$ on $E$ such that 
\[
   p_B^{(\lambda)}(x)
   =\int_E u_\lambda(x,y)\nu^{(\lambda)}_B(\mathrm{d} y),\quad \forall x\in E. 
\]
Moreover, $\nu^{(\lambda)}_B$ is finite and concentrated on $\overline{B}$.

[Lemma 7 (Shifted trace quadratic form) of arXiv:2609.03958, '2609.03958'] Let $n\geq 2$ and $K\geq 0$. Suppose that $\lambda\in \Gamma_2$ satisfies $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\geq -K$ and $\sigma_2(\lambda)=f$ with $f_0\leq f\leq f_1$ for two constants $f_1\geq f_0>0$ and that $$\ell_i:=\sigma_1(\lambda)-\lambda_i,\ \ \ i=1,\ldots,n.$$
Then there exist  some constants $C>0$ and $J_0>0$ depending only on $n$, $K$, $f_0$ and $f_1$ such that  
\begin{equation}
 z_k^2+3\sum_{i\ne k}z_i^2
 -\left[1+\frac{7}{6}\frac{\ell_k}{\sigma_1(\lambda)+J_0}\right]
       \left(\sum_iz_i\right)^2
 \geq-C\left(\sum_i\ell_iz_i\right)^2
\end{equation}
 for  any $1\leq k\leq n$ and $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\R^n$.

Let mu be a nonnegative Borel measure on R such that every polynomial is absolutely integrable and integral q(t)^2 dmu(t)>0 for every nonzero real polynomial q. Let p_j be its monic orthogonal polynomial of degree j, with p_0=1. For any integer n>=1 and any real alpha, p_n+alpha p_(n-1) has n distinct real roots r_1<...<r_n. For every integer k with 0<=k<n, the polynomial product_(i=1)^k(t-r_i) has strictly positive coefficients in the basis p_0,...,p_k. The product for k=0 is 1. The ordering from the smallest roots is essential; no restriction alpha>=0 is imposed, and no corresponding assertion is made for k=n. This is Theorem3.1 of Cohn-Kumar math/0607446v2.

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Let U in R^(N by M) and V in R^(P by M) be independent arrays with fixed centered symmetric iid real entry laws, variance one and finite absolute fourteenth moments. Put X=UV^T/sqrt(N), d=NP,b=M/N, and let C_j be the ordered joint cumulant tensor of vec(X). Write T4=sum_(a,b,c,d,e,f) C4(a,b,c,d) C4(a,b,e,f) C4(c,d,e,f). For standard independent Gaussian G and all s>=0, I(X;sqrt(s)X+G)=dbs/2-db^2s^2/4+db^3s^3/6+(-db^4/8-||C4||_F^2/48)s^4+(db^5/10+b||C4||_F^2/12)s^5+(-db^6/12-5b^2||C4||_F^2/24-||C6||_F^2/1440+T4/48)s^6+R(s), with |R(s)|<=3041280 E||vec(X)||^14 s^7. If P/N->alpha>0 and M/N->beta>0 finitely, the coefficients of s^j in I/d tend for j=1,...,6 to beta/2,-beta^2/4,beta^3/6,-(beta^4+alpha beta^2)/8,beta^5/10+alpha beta^3/2, and -beta^6/12-5alpha beta^4/4-alpha^2 beta^2/12+alpha(1+alpha)beta^3/12, respectively. These limits are independent of the symmetric factor laws. The proof includes complete exact enumeration of 2197 fourth-cumulant triangle terms. The remainder is finite-dimensional and grows with dimension: this does not identify Taylor coefficients of the thermodynamic MI or justify exchanging limits.
Independent fixed real symmetric iid factor laws
Centered unit variance and finite absolute fourteenth moments
Positive finite limiting aspect ratios only for the coefficient-limit conclusion
Independent standard Gaussian noise, nats
Finite exact combinatorial enumeration in scripts/check_sixth_order.py is part of this unaudited proof

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:7f62f0f5d229c4d4fab7cc3df9b0697a63db7d47b0312fb44c0aed13c14c9b55","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/7f/7f62f0f5d229c4d4fab7cc3df9b0697a63db7d47b0312fb44c0aed13c14c9b55.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:4b63b4d5e0e27fb5fc35472ff5eb469e6c139a18443923de29d17fa9cb3919ee","bundle_entry_key":"iid-product-mi-sixth-coefficient-limits-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-all-aspect-mi-and-sixth-coefficients-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:iid-product-mi-sixth-coefficient-limits-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Prior independence of the first six finite-size MI coefficient limits

Target 1. Computer-assisted proof draft, unaudited. The finite diagram
enumeration is scripts/check_sixth_order.py; its run artifact must say
PASS before this draft is entered as a proved claim. Novelty is
unestablished. This is a theorem about limits of finite-size Taylor
coefficients. It does not interchange the Taylor expansion and the
large-matrix limit.

## Statement and explicit finite-size remainder

Let U in R^(N by M) and V in R^(P by M) have independent iid entries,
with fixed symmetric real laws, mean zero, variance one and finite
absolute fourteenth moments. The laws of U and V need not coincide.
Let X=UV^T/sqrt(N), d=NP and b=M/N. For independent standard Gaussian
noise G define I_N(s)=I(X;sqrt(s)X+G), in nats. Let C_j be the ordered
joint cumulant tensor of order j of vec(X), and put

 T_4 = sum_(a,b,c,d,e,f) C_4(a,b,c,d) C_4(a,b,e,f) C_4(c,d,e,f).

The vector input is centrally symmetric, Cov(vec X)=b I_d. Its exact
finite-dimensional Taylor polynomial through order six is

 I_N(s) = db s/2 -db^2 s^2/4 +db^3 s^3/6
   +(-db^4/8-||C_4||_F^2/48)s^4
   +(db^5/10+b||C_4||_F^2/12)s^5
   +(-db^6/12-5b^2||C_4||_F^2/24
       -||C_6||_F^2/1440+T_4/48)s^6 + R_N(s),        (1)

with the explicit bound, for all s>=0,

 |R_N(s)| <= 3041280 E||vec X||^14 s^7.              (2)

One completely factorized bound in (2) is

 E||vec X||^14 <= d^7 M^14 N^(-7)
                         E|U_11|^14 E|V_11|^14.    (3)

Let P/N->alpha in (0,infinity), M/N->beta in (0,infinity).
The coefficient of s^j in I_N(s)/d tends, for j=1,...,6, to

 c_1=beta/2,
 c_2=-beta^2/4,
 c_3=beta^3/6,
 c_4=-(beta^4+alpha beta^2)/8,
 c_5=beta^5/10+alpha beta^3/2,
 c_6=-beta^6/12-5alpha beta^4/4-alpha^2 beta^2/12
                         +alpha(1+alpha)beta^3/12. (4)

In particular none of these coefficient limits depends on the fourth
cumulant, or any higher moment, of either symmetric factor law.

## 1. Finite-dimensional Gaussian-channel coefficient extraction

First let the centrally symmetric vector X be bounded and isotropic.
Standardize the output by its covariance (1+bs)I. Relative to standard
Gaussian measure its density is 1+q_s. The Hermite generating identity is

 E exp(t.W_s-||t||^2/2)
   = exp[sum_(j>=3) C_j:t^j (s/(1+bs))^(j/2)/j!],

interpreted for coefficient extraction at zero; odd tensors vanish.
Consequently the Hermite chaos components of degrees four and six are

 q_[4] = (s/(1+bs))^2 (C_4:H_4)/4!,
 q_[6] = (s/(1+bs))^3 (C_6:H_6)/6!.

There is no degree-two component. Higher components begin at s^4.
Hermite orthogonality kills their cross terms with degrees four and six
in integral q_s^2. The entropy expansion is

 D((1+q_s)gamma || gamma)
        = (1/2) integral q_s^2 -(1/6) integral q_s^3 +O(s^7).

These local expansions are justified for bounded X in any fixed
dimension: the Mehler-density bound and Gaussian hypercontractivity
used in bounded_prior_expansion.md bound the chaos tails in L^4 for
s in a sufficiently small interval. In particular ||q_s||_4=O(s^2),
and the entropy Taylor error after the cubic term is O(||q_s||_4^4).
The scalar remainder divided by |q|^4 is bounded on [-1,infinity),
with its continuous value at q=0, so the possible endpoint q=-1
does not invalidate this argument. All constants here are allowed
to depend on the fixed bounded input and dimension.

The quadratic terms are

 ||C_4||^2 s^4/[48(1+bs)^4]
       +||C_6||^2 s^6/[1440(1+bs)^6].

For the cubic degree-four contribution, Wick pairing connects the
three Hermite factors by two edges between each pair of factors.
There are choose(4,2)^3 (2!)^3=1728 such pairings. After division by
(4!)^3 and by the entropy coefficient 6, its contribution to D is

                      -T_4 s^6/48+O(s^7).

Use I_N(s)=d log(1+bs)/2-D, and expand the displayed denominators.
This gives exactly the polynomial (1).

For its explicit remainder use the already derived posterior-replica
streaming identity in finite_moment_expansion.md. For
F(s)=E||E[X|sqrt(s)X+G]||^2, that identity bounds the k-th derivative by

 |F^(k)(s)| <= 2^k (2k)! E||X||^(2k+2).

At k=6, I_N^(7)=-F^(6)/2 gives the Taylor remainder constant
2^6 (12)!/[2(7)!]=3041280. This uses the combinatorial coefficient
bound, not an enumeration of a growing replica polynomial. It holds
on every finite SNR interval for bounded X. Symmetric norm truncation
followed by covariance whitening preserves central symmetry and
converges in L^14 to X. The finite-moment approximation argument in
finite_moment_expansion.md therefore extends (1)-(2) to finite
fourteenth moments: the polynomial tensors and remainder bounds
converge, and Gaussian-smoothed output entropy is continuous.

Finally (3) follows by Jensen first over the d coordinates and then
over the M summands in each product entry. Independence of the U and
V entry in one summand factors the fourteenth absolute moment.

## 2. Sixth-cumulant norm: its only leading terms are simple cycles

Write W_ij=u_i v_j for a single rank-one summand. Additivity and
scaling of cumulants give C_6(X)=(M/N^3) C_6(W).
Expand each U- and V-moment by its set partitions. Since the laws
are symmetric, all blocks have even size at least two. For six
positions the possible block sizes are (2,2,2), (4,2), (6).
Their coefficients are products of factor cumulants.

Each row partition imposes equality of the row indices in its blocks;
each column partition imposes the corresponding column equalities.
Non-Gaussian factor cumulants require a block of size four or six,
so there are at most two free row indices, or at most two free column
indices, in every such term. In the squared norm a second copy can
only merge index classes. Hence any term involving a higher factor
cumulant has at most five free indices and total degree at most five
in N,P. This argument applies after the moment-cumulant subtraction,
which changes coefficients but never releases an index constraint.

Terms with six free indices must have three row pairs and three
column pairs in both copies, identical respectively across copies.
For a row pairing p and column pairing q, the coefficient in C_6(W)
is one precisely when their union is a connected six-cycle. One can
see this without a limiting argument: if p,q have one shared pair,
the (4,2) subtraction cancels the moment; if p=q, the coefficient is
1-3+2=0; if their union is connected, no proper moment partition can
be factored off, so its coefficient is one.

There are 15 row pairings and eight connected column pairings for
each, giving 120. The exact script checks every one of the 225 pairs.
Consequently, with constants depending only on the fixed moments,

 ||C_6(W)||^2 =120 N^3 P^3 +polynomial of total degree <=5,
 ||C_6(X)||^2/(NP) ->120 beta^2 alpha^2.              (5)

## 3. Three fourth cumulants: complete exact index enumeration

Let k_U=E u^4-3 and k_V=E v^4-3. For the three pairings p of four
positions write delta_p(i) for its row equalities, and delta_all(i)
for equality of all four rows. The exact identity is

 C_4(W) = sum_(p!=q) delta_p(i)delta_q(j)
       +k_U delta_all(i) sum_q delta_q(j)
       +k_V delta_all(j) sum_p delta_p(i)
       +k_U k_V delta_all(i)delta_all(j).             (6)

There are 6+3+3+1=13 terms. This is just the fourth moment of u times
the fourth moment of v, minus the three covariance pairings.

In T_4(W) the three tensors use the six entry positions
(0,1,2,3), (0,1,4,5), (2,3,4,5). The script expands all 13^3 choices
in (6). Union-find separately counts the free row and column indices.
Each choice contributes exactly
N^(row classes) P^(column classes) k_U^u k_V^v.
These are integer symbolic monomials; negative numerical values of
k_U or k_V do not affect the identity.

The full polynomial is saved in logs/sixth_order_checks.json. Its
only terms of total degree at least five are

                      4 N^3 P^2+4 N^2 P^3.         (7)

Every term containing k_U or k_V has degree at most four. This is
the only computer-assisted enumeration in the proof; it is complete,
uses exact integers, has no numerical tolerance, and fits in a few
kilobytes. Its script and complete output permit every case to be
checked from (6), with no downloaded code or stochastic step.

As C_4(X)=(M/N^2)C_4(W), equation (7) implies

                T_4(X)/(NP)->4 beta^3 alpha(1+alpha). (8)

## 4. Conclusion and limitation

The fourth-cumulant norm already computed in the dossier's settled
ground, and explicitly in finite_moment_expansion.md, gives
||C_4(X)||^2/(NP)->6 beta^2 alpha. Combine this with (5),(8) and
the exact finite-size polynomial (1) to obtain all coefficients (4).

No step above asserts a size-independent bound on (2) or (3). Their
constants grow with dimension. We have not proved that the limiting
MI is six times differentiable at zero, or that its coefficients are
the limits in (4). The hardest unpaid piece of Target 1 remains a
uniform small-SNR remainder or another argument justifying the
exchange of limits. It is also open here whether all fixed-order
coefficient limits are prior independent. These findings do not
establish the conjectured universal low-SNR phase.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:1799c3714831f68ac6b63c1958639d4969ff2adb0a37bb467a220be02f1ba043","revision_digest":"sha256:ac60b259c3cb9a46e43edf02cfecb06d5cf753cb873eeff53a96bbfc3a7ad50b","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:iid-product-mi-sixth-coefficient-limits-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

For a finite star with at least one leaf and positive edge lengths, and a nearest-unvisited walk that stops after all vertices are visited, every random start distribution satisfies sd(L)/E L<=1/(2*sqrt(6)). For at least two leaves, write S for the sum of all edge lengths and w_1>=w_2 for the largest two. All lengths lie in [2S-w_1-w_2,2S-w_1], whose endpoint ratio is at most 3/2. A one-leaf star has constant positive length and coefficient zero. The constant is sharp over arbitrary start distributions; the uniform-start case is included but no optimality claim for that subclass is made. This does not prove an absolute bound for arbitrary graphs.

body: A function f: [a, b] -> R has bounded variation if its total variation V(f; [a, b]) = sup over all partitions a = x_0 < x_1 < ... < x_n = b of sum_{i=1}^{n} |f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})| is finite; the space of such functions is BV[a, b]. Facts (Jordan, Lebesgue): (1) f is of bounded variation if and only if f = g - h with g and h nondecreasing on [a, b] (Jordan decomposition; one may take g(x) = V(f; [a, x]), the variation function, and h = g - f, both nondecreasing); (2) a BV function is bounded, has one-sided limits at every point, has at most countably many discontinuities, all of them jumps, and is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere with f' integrable and integral_a^b |f'(x)| dx <= V(f; [a, b]), with equality if and only if f is absolutely continuous; (3) monotone functions and Lipschitz functions are BV (a Lipschitz function with constant L has V <= L (b - a)), while a continuous function need not be: x sin(1/x) on (0, 1] (extended by 0) has infinite variation, and the Cantor function is continuous, nondecreasing, BV, yet has f' = 0 almost everywhere with total variation 1 (so it is not absolutely continuous); (4) BV[a, b] is a Banach space under ||f|| = |f(a)| + V(f; [a, b]); (5) f is BV exactly when the Riemann-Stieltjes integral integral_a^b g df exists for every continuous g, and then g -> integral g df is a bounded linear functional on C[a, b] of norm V(f; [a, b]) - the Riesz representation of the dual of C[a, b] (normalised BV functions correspond to finite signed Borel measures). In higher dimensions BV functions are those whose distributional gradient is a finite vector measure.

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: in the Calderon-Zygmund theory for Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu the leading coefficients must be continuous (uniform continuity on the relevant compact set), or at least of vanishing mean oscillation; only then does the freezing-and-absorption step work for every 1 < p < infinity. Mere measurable uniform ellipticity is not enough, and the failure is not a technicality: both the estimate and uniqueness fail. Counterexample (Gilbarg-Serrin type): on the unit ball B_1 in R^n, n >= 2, fix lambda in (0,1) and set a^{ij}(x) = delta^{ij} + beta x_i x_j/|x|^2 with 1 + beta = (n-1)/(1 - lambda) > 0. These coefficients are bounded, symmetric, uniformly elliptic (eigenvalues 1 with multiplicity n-1 and (n-1)/(1-lambda)) and continuous except at the origin. For radial u, D_{ij}u = u''(r) x_i x_j/r^2 + (u'(r)/r)(delta_{ij} - x_i x_j/r^2), hence Lu = (1 + beta) u'' + (n-1) u'/r, and u(x) = |x|^lambda gives Lu = r^{lambda - 2} [ (1 + beta) lambda(lambda - 1) + (n-1) lambda ] = 0. Now w = |x|^lambda - 1 lies in W^{2,p}(B_1) for every p < n/(2 - lambda), lies in W^{1,p}_0(B_1) for those p, satisfies Lw = 0 almost everywhere, and is not identically zero (w(0) = -1). Consequences: the Dirichlet problem is not uniquely solvable in W^{2,p} intersect W^{1,p}_0 for p < n/(2 - lambda), so no global estimate ||w||_{W^{2,p}} <= C ||Lw||_{L^p} can hold there; the maximum principle also fails for such strong solutions (w attains its minimum -1 at an interior point while Lw = 0 and w = 0 on the boundary). Note n/(2 - lambda) < n and lambda may be taken as close to 1 as desired, so the failure reaches every exponent below n. What survives with only measurable coefficients: the Aleksandrov-Bakelman-Pucci estimate and Krylov-Safonov theory, both of which require the solution to be in W^{2,n}_loc - which is exactly the class this example escapes.
title: Pitfall: W^{2,p} Estimates Need Continuous (or VMO) Leading Coefficients
