Let A_n (n = 1, 2, ...) and A be self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space H, each on its own dense domain; the domains are not assumed equal or even comparable. One says A_n -> A in the STRONG RESOLVENT SENSE if for every psi in H and every z in C with nonzero imaginary part, (A_n - z)^(-1) psi converges in norm to (A - z)^(-1) psi. Because each operator is self-adjoint, the resolvent (A_n - z)^(-1) is bounded with norm at most 1 / |Im z|, so the family is uniformly bounded and it is enough to verify the convergence for a SINGLE non-real z: one z in the upper half plane suffices, the conjugate point following by taking adjoints and the remaining z by the resolvent identity together with the uniform bound. The NORM RESOLVENT SENSE is the same statement with convergence in operator norm; it implies the strong resolvent sense and is strictly stronger. Practical criterion: if all the A_n and A are essentially self-adjoint on a common core D and A_n psi -> A psi for every psi in D, then A_n -> A in the strong resolvent sense. Without such a hypothesis convergence on a dense subspace says nothing, which is precisely why the resolvent formulation, and not naive pointwise convergence of unbounded operators, is the notion that interacts with the spectral theorem.
H is a complex Hilbert space
every A_n and A is self-adjoint (so the resolvent set contains C minus R and the resolvent norm bound 1/|Im z| holds)
no relation between the domains of the A_n and of A is assumed
convergence is of the resolvents, applied to a fixed vector (strong) or in operator norm (norm)
title: Strong and norm resolvent convergence of self-adjoint operators

body: Brownian motion is the random motion of particles suspended in a medium. The traditional mathematical formulation of Brownian motion is that of the Wiener process, which is often itself called "Brownian motion", even in mathematical sources.
title: Brownian motion

body:
A measurable function f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty) is regularly varying at infinity with index \rho \in \mathbb{R} (written f \in RV_\rho) if for every x > 0, \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{f(t x)}{f(t)} = x^\rho. When \rho = 0, f is called slowly varying at infinity (f \in SV). Every regularly varying function can be factored as f(x) = x^\rho L(x) where L is slowly varying.
f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty) is measurable
title: Regularly Varying Function (Karamata)

body: Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random Hermitian d by d matrices with E[X_k] = 0 and ||X_k||_op <= R almost surely for every k, and let sigma^2 = ||sum_{k=1}^n E[X_k^2]||_op. Then for every t >= 0, P(||sum_{k=1}^n X_k||_op >= t) <= 2d exp(- t^2 / (2 (sigma^2 + R t / 3))). [Tropp, An Introduction to Matrix Concentration Inequalities (2015)]
title: Matrix Bernstein Inequality

body: In mathematics, specifically group theory, Cauchy's theorem states that if G is a finite group and p is a prime number dividing the order of G, then G contains an element of order p. That is, there is x in G such that p is the smallest positive integer with xp = e, where e is the identity element of G. It is named after Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who discovered it in 1845.
title: Cauchy's theorem (group theory)

Let Omega in R^n be a connected open set (bounded or not) and let Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + sum b^i D_i u + c u be uniformly elliptic with bounded coefficients on each open subset with compact closure in Omega (lambda > 0 there). Let u be in C^2(Omega) with Lu >= 0 in Omega. (a) If c = 0 and u attains its supremum over Omega at an interior point, then u is constant. (b) If c <= 0 and u attains a nonnegative maximum over Omega at an interior point, then u is constant. Dually, a supersolution (Lu <= 0) attaining an interior infimum (a nonpositive minimum when c <= 0) is constant.

AUTHOR PROOF; independent audit pending. Let G be a finite undirected graph with vertices o,b, a nonempty relay set A, a vertex v, and a_star in A. If every o-to-A path and every a_star-to-b path contains v, then in every edge configuration {o connects to A,a_star connects to b} is contained in {o connects to b,o connects to A}. For independent Bernoulli edge states with arbitrary edge probabilities in [0,1], P(o connects to b)>=P(o connects to A)min_{a in A}P(a connects to b). Connection means an open path in G.
The two separator hypotheses hold for deterministic G,v,a_star

[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Let $h\in Z\hat C(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)$, $R\in  C(\Delta_T^2;B_\alpha)$ and $\hat\delta R = h$. For $\tau\in[0,T]$, define $r^\tau := \Theta_\tau R$.
Then $(r^\tau)_{\tau\in[0,T]}$ is a compatible frozen increment family over $h$.
Moreover, if $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and $R\in E^{\gamma}(\Delta_T^2; B_\alpha)$, then for every
$0<\varepsilon<\gamma$,
\[
\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{\gamma-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon;\tau}\le M_{\alpha+\varepsilon,T}\|R\|_{\gamma-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon};
\]
if $R\in E_{\log}^{1}(\Delta_T^2; B_\alpha)$, then for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
\[
\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{1-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon;\tau}\le M_{\alpha+\varepsilon,T} \|R\|_{1-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon},
\]
and $ \sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{1,\log;\tau,\alpha}\le M_{\alpha,T}\|R\|_{1,\log;\alpha}$.

Let Omega be a compact full-dimensional polytope in R^din and g:R^din -> R^dout a continuous finite piecewise affine map. For width n, take networks F=fu composed with (id+fL) composed with ... composed with (id+f1) composed with fe, with affine embedding fe and unembedding fu, and fl(z)=Wl,2 ReLU(Wl,1 z+bl,1)+bl,2. Define C(L,n,lambda;g) as the infimum, over parameters computing g exactly on Omega, of (||Wu||_F^2+||We||_F^2)/2 + (lambda/2) sum_{l=1}^L (||Wl,1||_F^2+||Wl,2||_F^2); all biases are unpenalized. Let rJ be the maximum rank of Jg(x) at differentiability points in the interior of Omega, and let rBN be the least integer k admitting a finite continuous piecewise affine factorization g|Omega=h2 composed with h1 through R^k. For every sufficiently large fixed n depending on g and Omega, rJ <= liminf_{lambda->0+} liminf_{L->infinity} C(L,n,lambda;g)/(lambda log(1/lambda)) and limsup_{lambda->0+} limsup_{L->infinity} C(L,n,lambda;g)/(lambda log(1/lambda)) <= rBN. These bounds do not assert rJ=rBN or that either normalized limit equals rBN. They concern residual connections, unpenalized biases, and an ordered depth-then-lambda limit; they do not determine the plain-network depth-normalized cost R_infinity of a branching tripod. This is a restricted-domain, liminf/limsup formulation of Boix-Adsera Theorem 3.3, equations (3.1)-(3.2), arXiv:2501.19149v1, Section 3, printed pp.6-8.

g continuous finite piecewise affine
fixed width sufficiently large depending on g and Omega
two-layer residual blocks; affine external embedding and unembedding

L tends to infinity before lambda tends to zero

[Theorem 4 (Random regular graphs: averaged version) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(d\ge 3\), \(u\in[0,1]\), and \(\theta>0\). Let \(G_n\) be the random \(d\)-regular graph on \(n\) vertices, and let \(p_{d,n}\) denote its law. Assume
\begin{equation}
d>2c_{\theta,u}
=
2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).

\end{equation}
Then there exist \(\eta>0\), \(s>0\), and \(c>0\) such that for every \(a\ge 0\),
\[
p_{d,n}\!\left(
\frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t \ge c
\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2604.23133, 'High-Precision Framework for Expected Hitting Times Analysis in the Dice-Sum Process'] Let $p_n$ denote the probability of ever hitting $n$, and let $q_n = 1 - p_n$ denote the probability of skipping (or missing) $n$.  
Then
\[
\frac{2}{7} - \varepsilon_n \le p_n \le \frac{2}{7} + \varepsilon_n,
\qquad
\frac{5}{7} - \varepsilon_n \le q_n \le \frac{5}{7} + \varepsilon_n,
\]
where $\varepsilon_n := \tfrac{5}{7}\,|w_+|^{\,n}$ and $|w_+| = 0.7302499667.$

body: [Defn 27 (Similarity) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] We say that two multicycles $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are similar and write $\gamma \sim \gamma'$ if the following holds: for any nodes $i$ and $j$, $m^\gamma_{ij} > 0$ iff $m^{\gamma'}_{ij} > 0$, and the difference of the multiplicities $|m^\gamma_{ij} - m^{\gamma'}_{ij}|$ is even.

[Corollary Erntogan of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $\lambda_1 (N), \lambda_2 (N) \in \hat{U} (N)$
  be two sequences of signatures such that for $i = 1, 2$,
  \[ \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{m}}_N [\lambda_i (N)]
     =\mathbf{m}_i, \]
  where $\mathbf{m}_1, \mathbf{m}_2$ are two probability measures and the
  above convergence is weak. Moreover, let $\pi (N) = \pi^{\lambda_1 (N)}
  \otimes \pi^{\lambda_2 (N)}$. Then, for $\lambda (N) \in \hat{U}
  (N)$ chosen at random with respect to $\varrho^{\pi (N)}$, the random
  measures $\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{m}}_N [\lambda (N)]$ converge, as $N \rightarrow
  \infty$, in the sense of moments, in probability to a deterministic
  probability measure which one denotes by $\mathbf{m}_1 \otimes \mathbf{m}_2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
The Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind are defined on [-1, 1] by T_n(cos theta) = cos(n theta), n = 0, 1, 2, ...; equivalently T_0 = 1, T_1 = x and T_{n+1}(x) = 2 x T_n(x) - T_{n-1}(x). Facts: (1) T_n is a polynomial of degree n with leading coefficient 2^{n-1} for n >= 1, and T_n(x) = ((x + sqrt(x^2 - 1))^n + (x - sqrt(x^2 - 1))^n) / 2 for all real x (cosh(n arccosh x) for x >= 1); (2) |T_n(x)| <= 1 on [-1, 1], with T_n(cos(k pi / n)) = (-1)^k at the n + 1 extremal points and zeros at cos((2k - 1) pi / (2n)), k = 1..n, all in (-1, 1); (3) orthogonality: integral_{-1}^{1} T_m(x) T_n(x) dx / sqrt(1 - x^2) = 0 for m != n, pi for m = n = 0, pi/2 for m = n >= 1; (4) MINIMAX (Chebyshev): among all monic polynomials of degree n, 2^{1-n} T_n has the smallest maximum absolute value on [-1, 1], namely 2^{1-n}, and it is the unique minimiser; equivalently x^n is best approximated in the sup norm on [-1, 1] by polynomials of degree < n with error 2^{1-n}; (5) Chebyshev interpolation at the zeros of T_{n+1} has Lebesgue constant O(log n) and the Chebyshev series of a Lipschitz function converges uniformly, which is why Chebyshev nodes replace equispaced nodes (Runge's phenomenon) in numerical analysis. The polynomials of the second kind U_n are defined by U_n(cos theta) sin theta = sin((n+1) theta) and satisfy the same recurrence with U_1 = 2x.
real variable on [-1, 1] for the extremal statements; the polynomials themselves are defined on all of R and C

[Theorem kpartW1 of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let Assumption~(ass:w1-normalized-matern of the paper) hold and suppose the joint initial law of the particles is exchangeable. For fixed \(k\ge1\), define
the random \(k\)-fold empirical occupation measure
\[
        \widehat\mu_T^{N,k}
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T (\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}\,dt,
        \qquad
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T \mu_t^{\otimes k}\,dt,
\]
where
\[
(\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}
:=
\frac{1}{(N)_k}
\sum_{\substack{1\le i_1,\ldots,i_k\le N\\
i_1,\ldots,i_k\ {\rm distinct}}}
\delta_{\bigl(x_{i_1}^N(t),\ldots,x_{i_k}^N(t)\bigr)},
\qquad
(N)_k:=N(N-1)\cdots(N-k+1).
\]
Let \(W_1^{(k)}\) be the Wasserstein distance on \((\mathbb R^d)^k\)
associated with the product cost
\(
        d_k(x,y):=\sum_{\ell=1}^k \|x_\ell-y_\ell\| .
\)
Then, with $\gamma$ as in Theorem~(prop:uniform-time-averaged-w1 of the paper),
\begin{equation}
\lim_{M \to \infty} \, \limsup_{N \to \infty}\,\sup_{T>0}
\mathbb P\left(
W_1^{(k)}
\left(
\widehat\mu_T^{N,k},
\overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
\right)
>
M(\log \log N)^{-\gamma/2}
\right)=0.
\end{equation}
Moreover, suppose the initial distributions satisfy (equation Gaussexp of the paper). 
Define, for $k \ge 1$,
\[
        \bar\mu_T^{N,k}
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T
        \mathcal L(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))\,dt,
        \qquad
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T \mu_t^{\otimes k}\,dt ,
\]
where $L(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))$ denotes the joint law of $(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))$.
Then there is \(C_k<\infty\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\begin{equation}
        \sup_{T>0}
        W_1^{(k)}
        \left(
        \bar\mu_T^{N,k},
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        \right)
        \le
        C_k(\log\log N)^{-\gamma/2}.
\end{equation}

DRAFT proof (unaudited), T421-W706-003 v1. For scalar uncorrected full-batch Adam on f(x)=lambda*x^2/2, lambda>0, eta>0, beta1=9/10, beta2=999/1000 and epsilon>0 outside the square root, put rho=epsilon/(eta lambda). For 0<rho<1/38 the known sign-alternating cycle has amplitude |x|=eta*(1/38-rho), momentum m=opposite-sign lambda*|x|/19, and v=lambda^2*x^2. Its local linear stability holds exactly when 358811/13673160 < rho < 1/38. For 0<rho<358811/13673160 it is linearly unstable; equality is a nonhyperbolic boundary. Therefore epsilon=eta and both eigenvalues of a positive diagonal quadratic in (38,13673160/358811) give locally attracting product cycles with eta active curvature and eta top sharpness tending to 38 in their full-state basin. This does not prove entry from standard m0=v0=0. With epsilon=eta^p, p>1, fixed lambda makes this particular cycle unstable for all sufficiently small eta. This does not exclude tracking by other attractors.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:c34565020f6762c4ef10401c2d5459eb044f9bc81b465563692d14b312326883","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/c3/c34565020f6762c4ef10401c2d5459eb044f9bc81b465563692d14b312326883.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:dd247e5a77daa1f0968c03ea4a8aabcc303754d27a319322f822fb79b3745c38","bundle_entry_key":"cycle-stability","bundle_id":"population.t421-adam-curvature-source-scope-and-cycle-stability-001","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"deterministic adaptive optimization","draft":"w706/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.adam:adam-default-betas-outside-sqrt-two-cycle-exact-stability-interval-w706","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-003 v1; target 1; kind special; rung proof (unaudited).

This concerns a whole epsilon/step ratio interval, but NOT the dossier's
standard initialization. It does not yet score as a random-initialization theorem.

Let beta1=9/10, beta2=999/1000 and f(x)=lambda*x^2/2, lambda>0.
Put X=x/eta, M=m/(eta lambda), V=v/(eta lambda)^2, rho=epsilon/(eta lambda).
Uncorrected Adam becomes
 M'=b M+(1-b)X, V'=d V+(1-d)X^2,
 X'=X-M'/(sqrt(V')+rho).
For 0<rho<1/38 its sign-alternating two-cycle is
 (X,M,V)=(a,-a/19,a^2) <-> (-a,a/19,a^2), a=1/38-rho>0.
The cycle's unnormalized preconditioned curvature satisfies eta C=38 exactly.
This cycle existence is known (Fong-Yang Prop.3.1), not new work here.

The explicit local stability interval computed here is
       rho_* < rho < 1/38, rho_*=358811/13673160.
In particular at p=1 (epsilon=eta) this means
       38 < lambda < 13673160/358811.
Both eigenvalues of a two-dimensional diagonal quadratic in this open interval
give an attracting product two-cycle (either relative sign), so every trajectory
in its local state-space basin has eta C_t ->38 and eta S_t ->38.
For p>1, rho=eta^(p-1)/lambda ->0, hence the same exact two-cycle is
linearly unstable for all sufficiently small eta. This rules out assuming
that cycle's attraction; it does NOT disprove curvature tracking via other orbits.

Derivative and exact test. At the positive phase, ordering (X,M,V),
J_+ = [[-1399/500-19*rho/250, -171/5, 18981/500],
       [1/10, 9/10, 0],
       [1/19000-rho/500, 0, 999/1000]].
For R=diag(-1,-1,1), J_-=R J_+ R, so D(F^2)=J_-J_+=(RJ_+)^2.
Thus Schur stability is equivalent to all roots of
 P(z)=z^3-(28970+760rho)/10000*z^2
          +(27999-684rho)/10000*z-8991/10000
lying in the open unit disk. All coefficients and calculations are rational.

Write P=z^3+A z^2+B z+C and define
 Q(z)=(P(z)-C z^3 P(1/z))/z=q0*z^2+q1*z+q2.
Here |C|=8991/10000<1,
 q0=19161919/100000000,
 q1=-(13749844rho+37960991)/100000000,
 q2=-9(151924rho-216897)/10000000.
Schur reduction gives P Schur iff Q Schur; for a real quadratic with q0>0,
this is equivalent to q0-q2>0, q0+q2>0, Q(1)>0 and Q(-1)>0.
Their exact factors are
 q0-q2=(13673160rho-358811)/100000000,
 q0+q2=1999(19351-6840rho)/100000000,
 Q(1)=360829(1-38rho)/50000000,
 Q(-1)=1009(19rho+18990)/25000000.
Over 0<rho<1/38, only the first can fail, giving the stated interval.
At rho=rho_* a conjugate pair lies on the unit circle; no hyperbolic
attraction or instability claim is made at this boundary.

Why the Schur test applies (proof, not a numerical eigenvalue test):
For monic real P with |C|<1, on |z|=1 its reciprocal polynomial P*(z)
has |P*|=|P|. If P is Schur, Rouché applied to P-C P* shows zQ
has all three roots in the disk, so Q is Schur. Conversely,
(1-C^2)P=zQ+C Q*, where Q*(z)=z^2Q(1/z).
If Q is Schur, Rouché compares zQ and C Q* on the unit circle and
shows P is Schur. The quadratic conditions follow by mapping the disk
to the left half-plane: (1-s)^2 Q((1+s)/(1-s)) has coefficients
Q(-1), 2(q0-q2), Q(1); their positivity is the real quadratic Hurwitz
criterion. Necessity and sufficiency follow also directly from a real
root pair or a complex conjugate pair. The extra q0+q2>0 is redundant
given Q(1),Q(-1)>0 but retained for a standard symmetric formulation.

Checks run: independent all-rho symbolic differentiation in a>0 variables;
nonlinear cycle identity; independent determinant expansion of the polynomial;
all Schur factors; denominator positivity (D=1/38 and a>0).
The exact boundary factorization is
 P(z)=(10000z-8991)(179910z^2-359801z+179910)/1799100000
at rho_*, and P(z)=(z-1)(10z-9)(1000z-999)/10000 at rho=1/38.
The first quadratic has unit root product and negative discriminant.
For 0<rho<rho_* no root can lie on the unit circle: a non-real unit pair
would imply q2=q0, and real unit roots are excluded by P(1),P(-1)!=0.
Since Schur stability fails there, a root has modulus strictly above 1.
The exact checks are in scripts/verify_cycle.py and logs/cycle_exact.json.
Lean key-step check timed out after 60s; no Lean certificate is claimed.
Numerical roots in the exploratory log are illustrative only.

Prior work: Bock-Weiss arXiv:2210.02070v1, Section 3 pp.4-7, derives
cycle existence and numerically studies stability, with epsilon INSIDE
the square root, unlike this row. Their p.5 notes analytical stable-eigenvalue
estimates were not obtained. Their Experiment 1 (p.8) observes the standard
beta cycle is unstable. Thus instability near rho=0 is known qualitatively;
the outside-sqrt rational transition above is the concrete calculation here.
No exhaustive novelty claim has been made.

Initialization gap: all local-basin statements concern the full (x,m,v)
state near the nonzero cycle, not m0=v0=0 and arbitrary random x0.
For corrected Adam, the intended extension is a tail basin at sufficiently

[Lemma NEW-l:pre-Gron of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Consider Lipschitz diffusion  coefficients $(b,\sigma)$ as defined in Definition~(NEW-d:lip_assum of the paper). Let $\{X[x]\}_{x\in{\cal X }}$ and $\{X'[x]\}_{x\in{\cal X }}$ be two families of  continuous  processes in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ adapted to the filtration generated by the family of i.i.d. standard Brownian motions $\{Z_x(\cdot)\}_{x \in {\cal X }}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$ on $[0,t_0]$ 
and $\mathbb{E} [\|X[x]\|^2]<\infty$, $\mathbb{E} [\|X'[x]\|^2]<\infty$ for all  $x\in{\cal X }$.
Consider  the family of stochastic processes $\{Y[x]\}_{x\in{\cal X }}$ on $\mathbb {M} $, defined on $[0,t_0]$ by
\begin{equation}
   
Y(x,t):= Y(x,0)+\int_0^t b(t, X[x], X[N_x])\, \mathrm{d} t + \sigma(t, X[x], X[N_x])\, \mathrm{d} Z_x(t),
\end{equation}
along with the family of stochastic processes $Y'(x,t)$ on $\mathbb {M} $ defined as above but with $X'$ instead of $X$.
These processes are indexed by the vertices $x\in{\cal X }$, they utilize the graph neighborhood $N_x=\{y\in{\cal X }:y\sim x\}$ on a given graph $\Psi({\cal X })$
and they share the same initial conditions $Y(x,0)=Y'(x,0)$.
Then for any $x\in{\cal X }$ and $t\in[0,t_0]$, we have
\begin{equation}

\mathbb{E}  [\| Y[x,t] - Y'[x,t] \|^2]
\le 32\max(t,1)K_t^2\int_{0}^t \max_{y\in\mathfrak{B}_1(x)} \mathbb{E}  [\| X[y,s] - X'[y,s] \|^2]\, \mathrm{d} s,
\end{equation}
where $\mathfrak{B}_1(x)$  is graph ball on  $\Psi({\cal X })$ of radius $1$ centered at~$x$
and where $K_t$ is the Lipschitz diffusion constant given in Definition \ref
{NEW-d:lip_assum}.
title: (Pre-)Gr\"onwall inequality for interacting diffusions

[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked only, no independent read.] This is a restricted negative answer to the question in Chapter 4 of David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html), recorded as intake row I0024. The question asks whether the relaxation time can be characterized exactly as an infimum over flows, that is, whether one of the chapter's flow inequalities (Sinclair's bound, the Diaconis-Stroock bound) can be made an identity. For a finite irreducible reversible transition matrix P, let its eigenvalues be 1=lambda_1>lambda_2>=... and define the relaxation time tau_2=1/(1-lambda_2), equivalently the inverse spectral gap of the rate-one continuous-time generator P-I. Suppose Q(P) is the finite attained optimum of a finite linear program in flow variables whose objective and constraint coefficients are well-defined rational functions, with rational coefficients, of the entries of P. If P has rational entries, then Q(P) is rational. Such a rule cannot equal tau_2 for every rational reversible P. The witness is the simple walk on the path P_6 with vertices 0,...,5, which moves deterministically at the endpoints and with probability 1/2 to each neighbor in the interior. It has lambda_2=cos(pi/5)=(1+sqrt(5))/4 and tau_2=3+sqrt(5), which is irrational. A genuinely nonlinear flow characterization is not excluded. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The flow optimization is finite, feasible, has finite optimum, and has rational data on rational P.
tau_2 uses the second-largest eigenvalue, not the absolute spectral radius.

Let $S = \sum_i \lambda_i u_i u_i^T$ be the sample covariance of $n$ observations in $\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $\Sigma$, $p/n \to c \in (0, 1)$, in the setting of the Marchenko-Pastur-Silverstein theorem. Consider rotation-equivariant estimators $\hat\Sigma = \sum_i d_i u_i u_i^T$ and the global minimum-variance portfolio $\hat w = \hat\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}/(\mathbf{1}^T\hat\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1})$ built from them, scored by its true out-of-sample variance $\hat w^T \Sigma \hat w$. Ledoit and Wolf (2017) show: (i) the finite-sample oracle for this loss is $d_i^{\mathrm{mv}} = 1 / (u_i^T \Sigma^{-1} u_i)$ (the 'inverse' oracle), whereas the Frobenius-loss oracle is $d_i^{\mathrm{fro}} = u_i^T \Sigma u_i$; (ii) in the large-dimensional limit both oracles converge to the SAME nonlinear shrinkage $\tilde d_i = \lambda_i / |1 - c - c\lambda_i \breve m_F(\lambda_i)|^2$ (the Ledoit-Peche formula), because the Ledoit-Peche limits of the two quadratic forms $u_i^T\Sigma u_i$ and $u_i^T\Sigma^{-1}u_i$ are reciprocal to each other; so the nonlinear shrinkage estimator that is optimal for estimating the covariance in Frobenius loss is also asymptotically optimal for the minimum-variance portfolio - neither too much shrinkage (the linear shrinkage's) nor too little (the sample covariance's). In the ensemble-stacking application, this is the statement that the Ledoit-Peche cleaning of the error covariance is the right cleaning for the sum-to-one (unconstrained-sign) stack, whose weights are exactly a global minimum-variance portfolio.
the Marchenko-Pastur-Silverstein setting (i.i.d. rows with finite twelfth moments in Ledoit-Wolf's statement), p/n -> c in (0, 1)
estimators restricted to the rotation-equivariant class (sample eigenvectors kept)
the identity making the two oracles' limits reciprocal is cited from the paper, not re-derived above

Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d, d >= 2, with edge-weight law nu. Assume the two conditions (i) E min{ t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d } < infinity, where the t_i are 2d independent copies of tau_e - equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity where Y is the MINIMUM of 2d copies, the two being the same because x -> x^d is increasing on [0, infinity) - and (ii) F(0) < p_c(d). Let B(t) = {x : T(0, x) <= t}, the random ball. Then there is a DETERMINISTIC, convex, COMPACT set B_nu in R^d with NON-EMPTY INTERIOR, symmetric about the axes, such that for every eps > 0, P( (1-eps) B_nu is contained in B(t)/t which is contained in (1+eps) B_nu for all large t ) = 1. The set B_nu is the unit ball of the time constant. Condition (i) is NOT merely convenient: if it fails then for every C > 0 the sum over x of P(m(x) > C|x|) diverges, where m(x) is the minimum weight over the edges at x, and Borel-Cantelli forces T(0,x)/|x| > C for infinitely many x almost surely, so the shape statement itself fails. Condition (ii) is what keeps the shape bounded: if F(0) >= p_c then zero-weight edges percolate, the time constant vanishes and B_nu is all of R^d. What is NOT known, and is repeatedly imported elsewhere as an unproven hypothesis: whether the boundary of B_nu is STRICTLY CONVEX, whether it is DIFFERENTIABLE, and whether it has uniformly positive CURVATURE. Those are open for every non-degenerate weight distribution in every dimension, which is why the Newman-Piza exponent bounds and the directed-geodesic results carry non-constructive curvature or differentiability hypotheses. B_nu is not computed explicitly for any non-trivial F. [Cox and Durrett (1981), verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 2.2]
i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d, d >= 2
F(0) < p_c(d), so the time constant is a norm and the shape is bounded
E min{t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d} < infinity, equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity for Y the minimum of 2d independent copies of tau_e - and this condition is necessary, not just sufficient
no curvature, strict convexity or differentiability of B_nu is asserted; those are open

The time constant mu exists by the subadditive ergodic theorem and is a norm under F(0) < p_c. The upgrade from the one-directional limit to a uniform statement over all directions has two ingredients. First, a uniform version of the ray limits: convexity of mu and the almost sure convergence along each rational direction combine, via a covering of the unit sphere by finitely many directions and the Lipschitz property of mu, to give sup over unit vectors of |T(0, [tx])/t - mu(x)| -> 0 provided one can control the passage times at the intermediate lattice points. Second, and this is where the moment condition enters, one must rule out that some vertex within distance t of the origin has an anomalously large passage time. The number of such vertices is of order t^d, so a union bound requires the tail P(T(0,x) > eps|x|) to be summable against t^{d-1} dt, which is exactly what E[Y^d] < infinity provides via the greedy-path bound T(0,x) <= sum of minimum outgoing weights along a path. If that moment fails, isolated vertices with huge passage times appear at density high enough that the shape statement fails in its almost sure form. body:
Erdos (1947): R(k,k) > 2^{k/2} for every k >= 3. Colour the edges of the complete graph on n vertices red or blue independently and uniformly at random. The expected number of monochromatic k-cliques is C(n,k) 2^{1 - C(k,2)}; when n = floor(2^{k/2}) this expectation is below 1 for k >= 3, so some colouring has no monochromatic k-clique, and R(k,k) > n. This is the first-moment method (a union bound over the C(n,k) cliques); only linearity of expectation is used, and no clique needs to be independent of another. With Stirling's formula the same count gives R(k,k) >= (1 + o(1)) (k / (e sqrt 2)) 2^{k/2}; the Lovasz local lemma (Spencer 1975) improves the constant to (1 + o(1)) (sqrt 2 / e) k 2^{k/2} and nothing better than the exponent k/2 is known. The upper bound side is separate: R(k,k) <= 4^k from Erdos-Szekeres, improved to (4 - epsilon)^k by Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe (2023).
k >= 3 (for k = 2 the bound is trivial)
the random colouring is uniform and independent over edges; the argument uses only the expectation
the bound is on the diagonal Ramsey number; the off-diagonal case R(3,k) has a different order, of k^2 / log k

Let W,W_1,...,W_L be real D-by-D matrices, L>=1, and 1<=R<=D an integer. Put B=W_L...W_1 and E=W-B. Fix a singular value decomposition of E and use its nested truncations LR_j(E), with LR_0=0 and LR_j=E beyond the rank. Assume every W_l is nonsingular and B+LR_j(E) is nonsingular for every integer 0<=j<=R(L-1). Then min_{rank(Delta_l)<=R} ||(W_L+Delta_L)...(W_1+Delta_1)-W||_2 = sigma_(RL+1)(E), where ||.||_2 is the operator norm and singular values beyond D are zero. The minimum is attained with the product equal to B+LR_(RL)(E). In particular, R>=ceil(rank(E)/L) permits exact equality of the product with W. The target W itself need not be nonsingular unless the stated partial-sum hypothesis forces it.

Each frozen weight is invertible
All specified nested low-rank corrected full products are invertible

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:c58d87cfdd7a30a9a3ed515a2b008b56bd788248ab1f5858e689e6e258b4487e","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/c5/c58d87cfdd7a30a9a3ed515a2b008b56bd788248ab1f5858e689e6e258b4487e.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9548f3adc68903b67cd441efcd18bebcb2f7ac02a496d314a765992a9a4498a7","bundle_entry_key":"rectangular-heat-spectral-entropy-c1-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-rectangular-reference-c1-and-noncentered-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_009.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:rectangular-heat-spectral-entropy-c1-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Rectangular heat entropy chain rule under explicit regularity

Claim draft w718-T287-026, version 1. Kind: moved; target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). This is a supporting analytic lemma, not a completed MI calibration or Target 2 claim. Novelty is unestablished.

## Hypotheses and conclusion

Let gamma in (0,1), a=(1-gamma)/gamma. Suppose t maps to rho_t is a family of even probability measures on an open interval J, satisfying the conclusions of supporting claim 025. More explicitly, on every compact subinterval:

1. The laws have densities p_t, a common compact support in [-R,-epsilon] union [epsilon,R], and uniformly bounded Cauchy transforms up to the real boundary. Set H_t(x)=Re integral (x+i0-y)^(-1)rho_t(dy).
2. At each t0, p_t(x) and H_t(x) converge to p_t0(x) and H_t0(x) for almost every x as t tends to t0. Both are uniformly bounded on the common support.
3. With V_t(x)=H_t(x)+a/(2x), the integrated weak transport equation holds for every C1 test f:

integral f d rho_v-integral f d rho_u
 = integral_u^v integral f' V_t d rho_t dt.               (1)

Define Sigma(rho)=double-integral log|x-y|rho(dx)rho(dy) and

E_gamma(rho)=gamma Sigma(rho)+(1-gamma)integral log|x|rho(dx).

Then E_gamma(rho_t) is continuously differentiable and

d E_gamma(rho_t)/dt
 =2 gamma integral [H_t(x)+a/(2x)]^2 rho_t(dx)
 =Phi_gamma(t)/2,                                       (2)

where Phi_gamma(t)=4 gamma integral V_t^2 d rho_t is finite and continuous. These statements apply to the real Gaussian-product heat laws once claim 025 is accepted. They do not rely on equality of two definitions of rectangular free entropy or Fisher information.

## Smooth-kernel chain rule

Fix a compact time interval [u,v] inside J. Uniform boundedness and the gap imply |V_t|<=L on the common support. Equation (1) implies W1(rho_t,rho_s)<=L|t-s|: apply it to smooth tests of derivative norm at most one, approximate Lipschitz tests uniformly on the containing compact interval by convolution, and use the dual formula for one-dimensional W1 (equivalently its elementary distribution-function characterization).

For e>0 put K_e(x,y)=(1/2)log((x-y)^2+e^2) and Sigma_e(rho)=double-integral K_e d rho d rho. This kernel is smooth on the containing compact square. Let delta_h=rho_(t+h)-rho_t. Expanding the quadratic functional gives

Sigma_e(rho_(t+h))-Sigma_e(rho_t)
 =2 double-integral K_e(x,y)delta_h(dx)rho_t(dy)
  +double-integral K_e(x,y)delta_h(dx)delta_h(dy).         (3)

The last term is O(W1(rho_(t+h),rho_t)^2)=O(h^2). Indeed choose an optimal coupling pi of the two laws; write that term as the integral against pi tensor pi of the mixed difference K_e(x',y')-K_e(x',y)-K_e(x,y')+K_e(x,y). Its absolute value is bounded by ||partial_x partial_y K_e||infinity times integral |x'-x||y'-y|d(pi tensor pi), which equals that constant times W1^2.

The fixed test f_t(x)=integral K_e(x,y)rho_t(dy) is smooth, with derivative

f_t'(x)=H_e,t(x)=Re g(x+i e,t).

For any fixed C1 test, the right-hand integrand in (1) is continuous in time by hypothesis 2 and dominated convergence, since V_t p_t is bounded and supported in a common compact set. Hence its integral is differentiable at every t. Divide (3) by h and pass to zero to obtain

d Sigma_e(rho_t)/dt=2 integral H_e,t(x) V_t(x)rho_t(dx).  (4)

The derivative is continuous in t. For example H_e,t is jointly continuous and bounded on the compact support by weak continuity, which follows from (1), while V_t p_t converges almost everywhere and is uniformly bounded.

## Remove the logarithmic regularization

If p_t<=C, then uniformly in t,

0<=Sigma_e(rho_t)-Sigma(rho_t)
 <= C integral_R (1/2)log(1+e^2/x^2)dx
 = C pi e.                                             (5)

To check the integral, differentiate it in e>0 to get integral e/(x^2+e^2)dx=pi and use scaling, or monotone convergence to zero as e decreases to zero. Compact support and bounded density also show directly that Sigma is finite; its positive part is bounded by the support diameter and its negative logarithmic part is integrable.

The uniform Cauchy bound gives a bound on |H_e,t| on the common support, independent of small e and t. At each t, H_e,t converges almost everywhere to H_t. The functions involved are measurable in (t,x) (for H_t take a pointwise boundary limit where it exists and zero on the null complement). Fubini therefore permits dominated convergence over time and space. Integrate (4) over [u,v], use (5) at the endpoints, and let e tend to zero:

Sigma(rho_v)-Sigma(rho_u)
 =2 integral_u^v integral H_t V_t d rho_t dt.            (6)

The integrand is continuous in t by hypothesis 2, common support and uniform bounds. Thus (6) proves continuous differentiability, rather than simply an almost-everywhere derivative.

## The origin term and the square

On a neighborhood of the common support, log|x| is smooth and has derivative 1/x. Extend it to a global C1 test across the unused gap, and apply (1). This gives

d/dt integral log|x|rho_t(dx)=integral V_t(x)/x rho_t(dx), (7)

again continuously in t. Combining (6) and (7), and using gamma a=1-gamma, gives

E_gamma'=integral [2 gamma H_t+(1-gamma)/x] V_t d rho_t
         =2 gamma integral V_t^2 d rho_t.

The same pointwise convergence and uniform bounds show that integral V_t^2 p_t dx is continuous. This proves (2).

## Controls and exact scope

For dilation D_c rho (the law of cX, c>0), direct substitution in the two logarithms gives E_gamma(D_c rho)=E_gamma(rho)+log c. A Gaussian-entry signal with entry variance beta/n simply replaces t by beta+t and gives Phi_gamma=1/(beta+t). These controls check the factors of gamma and two. body: The Gamma function Gamma(z) = integral from 0 to infinity of t^(z-1) e^(-t) dt, convergent for Re(z) > 0, extends the factorial to the complex plane. It satisfies the functional equation Gamma(z+1) = z Gamma(z) (integration by parts), so Gamma(n) = (n-1)! for positive integers n; it continues meromorphically to all of C with simple poles at the non-positive integers, and Gamma(1/2) = sqrt(pi). By the Bohr-Mollerup theorem it is the unique log-convex function on the positive reals with value 1 at 1 that satisfies the functional equation. Stirling's approximation is the asymptotics of Gamma (equivalently of the factorial) for large argument.

[Lemma 5 ({Lemma 3.5 in \cite{vanwerde2024recovering}}) of arXiv:2512.02661, 'Worst-case mixing estimates for Brownian motion with semipermeable barriers'] Suppose that $\delta < 1/2$.
	Then, for every $x_0 \in \bbR^2$, there is at most one barrier $B_i$ which intersects $\sB(x_0,r_{\delta})$.
	Moreover, if such a $B_i$ exists, then there exists a unit vector $ \hatn \in \bbR^2$ depending on $x_0$ and $B_i$ with the following properties:
	\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin = 2em, label = (\arabic*)]
		\item There exists some $\mathfrak{c}\in \bbR$ such that $\lvert \langle  y, \hatn\rangle - \mathfrak{c} \rvert <  4\delta r_\delta$ for every $y\in B_i\cap \sB(x_0, r_\delta)$.
		\item One has $\Vert \vec{n}_i(y)-  \hatn \Vert < 2\delta$ for every $y\in B_i \cap \sB(x_0, r_\delta)$.
		\item Every point $z \in \sB(x_0, r_\delta)$ on the positive side of $B_i$ satisfies $ \langle  z, \hatn\rangle > \mathfrak{c} -  4\delta r_\delta$.
		      Similarly, it holds for every $z\in \sB(x_0, r_\delta)$ on the negative side of $B_i$ that $ \langle  z, \hatn\rangle < \mathfrak{c}  +  4\delta r_\delta$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\wedge \xi \lrcorner H-\mathcal{L}_{\xi }^{2}.

AUTHOR-CHECKED PARTIAL OBSTRUCTION, NOT INDEPENDENTLY REVIEWED. For the heat semigroup with generator Delta on the unit two-torus, integral_0^infinity exp(-t)*||p_t(x,.)-p_t(y,.)||_2^2 dt is infinite when y-x=(1/2,0). Thus this illustrative metric formula can fail even when an ordinary Feller topology exists. For a symmetric Markov semigroup with finite integrated heat trace G(t) for t>0, the weight w(t)=exp(-t)/(1+G(2t)) instead yields finite Hilbert row norm almost everywhere. This alone does not establish the Feller-topology compactification conjecture.

The suggested unweighted heat-kernel metric can be infinite in a basic admissible example. For Brownian motion on the two-torus, the squared row-distance integrated against exp(-t)dt equals sum_(k in Z^2) |1-exp(2pi*i*k.h)|^2/[1+8pi^2*|k|^2]. At h=(1/2,0), every odd k1 has numerator4. Each dyadic annulus contains order N^2 such terms of order N^-2, so the series diverges. A repair is to use w(t)=exp(-t)/(1+G(2t)), where G is the integrated diagonal heat trace: Fubini gives finite weighted row norm for almost every state.

Second check. Parseval computes the row norm exactly; integrating the nonnegative Fourier series is justified by Tonelli. For the repaired weight, the average row squared norm is integral w(t)*G(2t)dt<=1. This produces an almost-everywhere finite Hilbert-space pseudometric after identifying indistinguishable rows.

Limits. Brownian motion already has a good usual topology, so the divergence refutes only the illustrative formula, not the existence conjecture. Completing a heat-kernel embedding can add states; proving valid transition kernels and the Feller property on that completion is still missing.

body: In mathematics, Galois cohomology is the study of the group cohomology of Galois modules, that is, the application of homological algebra to modules for Galois groups. A Galois group G associated with a field extension L/K acts in a natural way on some abelian groups, for example those constructed directly from L, but also through other Galois representations that may be derived by more abstract means. Galois cohomology accounts for the way in which taking Galois-invariant elements fails to be an exact functor.
title: Galois cohomology

\]
is continuous and maps bounded closed subsets of \(\mathcal D\) into

\[

and assume that
\begin{equation}
 x\neq\Phi(x,t)
 \qquad
 \text{for every }(x,t)\in\partial\mathcal O,
\end{equation}
where the boundary is taken relative to \(X\times[0,1]\).  If
\[
 \mathcal O_t:=\{x\in X:(x,t)\in\mathcal O\},
 \qquad
 \Phi_t(x):=\Phi(x,t),
\]
then
\[
 \deg(\operatorname{Id}-\Phi_t,\mathcal O_t,0)
\]
is well defined and independent of \(t\).  The degree of an empty
slice is understood to be zero.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Transfer the branching-random-walk identification of the limit to the random model of zeta, and locate the arithmetic obstruction. Result: For the random Euler-product model (45) of the source, the maximum over h in [0,1] is a maximum of a log-correlated non-Gaussian field with the multiscale structure (47)-(50), and the general theory (Arguin's Section 3, and the DRZ-type universality for the maximum) gives convergence of the centred maximum to a randomly shifted Gumbel whose shift is the log of the total mass of the critical multiplicative chaos of the field, provided (i) the increments have exponential moments with the right Gaussian-like rate (true for the random model), and (ii) a second-moment computation at the level of the critical chaos with the derivative-martingale normalisation. For the random model this is plausibly within reach of existing tools (it is the content of what the random model's community calls the 'full FHK conjecture for the random model'), and I believe the identification of the limiting law for the random model is still not written; the Gumbel convolution structure would follow from the cluster structure at the maximum, which for a non-Gaussian field requires the local limit theorem for the increments, available via the prime-sum large deviations. For the actual zeta function the obstruction is arithmetic: the increments at different scales are only asymptotically independent, and the identification of the limit law needs the joint law of the increments at the finest scales (primes near T), which the moment method cannot control at the required precision. Recorded: for the random model the limit is predicted to be the standard randomly shifted Gumbel with the critical chaos of the Euler-product field; for zeta the same is conjectured and the finest-scale dependence is the gap. Obstruction: Fine-scale dependence of the prime sums prevents the local limit theorem needed to identify the cluster structure.

body: The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem is a fundamental result of mathematical analysis giving necessary and sufficient conditions to decide whether every sequence of a given family of real-valued continuous functions defined on a closed and bounded interval has a uniformly convergent subsequence. The main condition is the equicontinuity of the family of functions. The theorem is the basis of many proofs in mathematics, including that of the Peano existence theorem in the theory of ordinary differential equations, Montel's theorem in complex analysis, and the Peter–Weyl theorem in harmonic analysis and various results concerning compactness of integral operators.
title: Arzelà–Ascoli theorem

[Corollary 18 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Buildings being relayed by a given building.}
    
Conditional on $\zone(\alpha, \beta)$ the buildings in $\zone(\alpha, \beta)$ form an inhomogeneous PPP of intensity
\[\tilde{\lambda} = \lambda \rm{d}x\otimes \mathcal{L}. \]

body: Schwarz lemma: Let D = {z in C : |z| < 1} be the open unit disk and let f : D -> D be a holomorphic map with f(0) = 0. Then |f(z)| <= |z| for every z in D, and |f'(0)| <= 1. Moreover, if |f(z_0)| = |z_0| for some z_0 in D with z_0 nonzero, or if |f'(0)| = 1, then f is a rotation, i.e. f(z) = a z for some constant a with |a| = 1. (The Schwarz-Pick-Ahlfors generalization in complex differential geometry estimates the pointwise norm of a holomorphic map f : M -> N between Hermitian manifolds under curvature bounds: for instance, if M is complete Kaehler with Ricci curvature bounded below by -K_1 and N has holomorphic sectional curvature bounded above by -K_2 < 0, then the squared norm of df is bounded by K_1 / K_2.)
title: Schwarz lemma

\[
c\,\|a\|\le \tau(a)\le C\,\|a\|.

Consequently, for every $x$ in a Hilbert $\mathcal A$-module $(\mathbb H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal A})$,
\[
c\,\|x\|_{\mathcal A}^2\le \|x\|_{\tau}^2\le C\,\|x\|_{\mathcal A}^2,
\qquad
\|x\|_{\tau}^2:=\tau(\langle x,x\rangle_{\mathcal A}).
\]

body:
Let D be either the Euclidean square [0,1]^2 or a smooth connected compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary and with Riemannian volume one. Let m be its volume probability measure and use the Euclidean distance on the square and intrinsic Riemannian distance on the manifold. Let X_1,X_2,... be independent samples with law m and mu_n=(1/n)sum_(i=1)^n delta_(X_i). Then lim_(n->infinity) (n/log n) E[W_2(mu_n,m)^2]=1/(4 pi). For the bipartite assertion restrict D to [0,1]^2 or to the standard flat unit torus R^2/Z^2. Let Y_1,Y_2,... be an independent second iid sample with law m and nu_n=(1/n)sum_(i=1)^n delta_(Y_i). Then lim_(n->infinity) (n/log n) E[W_2(mu_n,nu_n)^2]=1/(2 pi). W_2 uses squared metric cost before taking its square root; the expectations here are expectations of that squared distance. The manifold semi-discrete branch and the square/flat-torus bipartite branch have different stated domain scopes. Source: Luigi Ambrosio, Federico Stra and Dario Trevisan, A PDE approach to a 2-dimensional matching problem, arXiv:1611.04960v1, Theorem 1.1, PDF p3, with connectedness and metric conventions in Section 3.
Uniform volume sampling on the unit square, or on a smooth connected compact boundaryless Riemannian surface of volume one
The square uses its Euclidean metric; the manifold uses intrinsic Riemannian distance
All samples are iid; in the bipartite assertion the two samples are independent
The bipartite assertion is restricted to the square or the standard flat unit torus
Natural logarithm; expectation of squared quadratic Wasserstein distance

[Lemma 3 (Stability of the atomic part under convolution) of arXiv:2605.30121, 'Improved Survival Results for the One-Dimensional Renewal Contact Process'] Let $\mu$ be an interarrival distribution. Then for every $n\ge0$ the atomic part of $\mu^{*n}$ equals the $n$-fold convolution of the atomic part of $\mu$, i.e.
\[
\bigl(\mu^{*n}\bigr)_{\mathrm{at}} = \mu_{\mathrm{at}}^{*n}.
\]
Consequently, the atomic part of the renewal measure $U=\sum_{n\ge0}\mu^{*n}$ is
\[
U_{\mathrm{at}}=\sum_{n\ge0}\mu_{\mathrm{at}}^{*n}.
\]

[Lemma 25 of arXiv:2608.16752, 'Absorption Probabilities for Random Convex Hulls: Distribution-Freeness via the Wall-Cross'] Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite family of pairwise distinct affine hyperplanes in
$\mathbb R^n$, and let $x,y\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal L}H$.
Then there exists a piecewise linear path $\gamma\colon[-1,1]\to\mathbb R^n$ with
$\gamma(-1)=x$ and $\gamma(1)=y$ which meets $\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal L}H$ at
finitely many times $t_1 < \dots< t_L$ only,  and such that $\gamma(t_i)$
lies on exactly one hyperplane of $\mathcal L$ for every $i\in\{1,\dots,L\}$.

Let Omega subset S^{n-1} be a closed subset of the unit sphere in R^n, and let E be a random subspace of R^n of dimension n - m chosen uniformly according to the Haar measure on the Grassmannian. Define the Gaussian width w(Omega) = E_g[ sup_{x in Omega} g^T x ] where g ~ N(0, I_n). If w(Omega) < a_m where a_m = E[||h||_2] for h ~ N(0, I_m), then P(E intersect Omega = emptyset) >= 1 - 3.5 * exp(- (a_m - w(Omega))^2 / 2).

In the source translation-invariant particle-hole instruction-stack construction on Z^d, d>=3, assume fresh independent uniform nearest-neighbor instructions rho_j(y) are revealed only after they are determined used, and m_t=E U_t(y)<infinity at a fixed finite t. For G_s(x)=sum_n s^n p_n(x), 0<s<1, define M_t^s(x) in L2 by summing [G_s(rho_j(y)-x)-(P G_s)(y-x)] over used instructions j<=U_t(y) and all departure sites y. As s increases to one these martingales have an L2 limit M_t with mean zero and covariance m_t[2G(z-x)-1{x=z}], where G is full-space SRW Green. Its variance is m_t(2G(0)-1). Deterministic tests retain energy cancellation; no Gaussian law or obstacle-conditioned influence bound is asserted. Novelty: KNOWN martingale/resolvent method; UNCHECKED exact parking covariance statement. Status: independently checked proof.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:5385d3ade4e16776b0fdce1ed11b761993122aecf026cfe15667f68cf47c6706","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/53/5385d3ade4e16776b0fdce1ed11b761993122aecf026cfe15667f68cf47c6706.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:55088415a049af5e8a9143cfc14291cb5e0f4cfd2f31ee7339c148e76a5f0314","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c17","bundle_id":"population.i0005-correlation-energy-and-active-moments-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"parking and comparison fields","draft":"w661/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:particle-hole-deterministic-green-instruction-noise-covariance-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C17 v1: deterministic Green-potential instruction-noise covariance

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN martingale isometry/resolvent
method; UNCHECKED separate prior appearance of this exact parking identity.
This statement concerns the actual process, but deterministic test functions
only. No Gaussian law or conditional influence estimate is asserted.

Consider a translation-invariant particle-hole process in the source's
instruction-stack construction on Z^d, d>=3. Instructions rho_j(y) are
independent uniform nearest neighbors of their departure site y, revealed
only once preceding history determines they are used (source Lemma 4.3).
Let U_t(y) count used instructions through a fixed finite t and assume
E U_t(y)=m_t<infinity. For instance the source's bounded sparse critical
law has these properties. Write P for the SRW transition operator and
G(x)=sum_{n>=0}p_n(x). For 0<r<1 let G_r(x)=sum_{n>=0}r^n p_n(x).
Define, initially by finite departure-site sums and then in L2,

    M_t^r(x)=sum_y sum_{j<=U_t(y)}
               [G_r(rho_j(y)-x)-(P G_r)(y-x)].

There is an L2 limit M_t(x) as r increases to one. It has mean zero and

    E[M_t(x)M_t(z)]=m_t[2G(z-x)-1{x=z}].

In particular Var(M_t(x))=m_t(2G(0)-1). The d4 logarithmic divergence of
sum_y G(y)^2 does not occur in this deterministic instruction-noise
variance. This does not remove the initial-value contribution in the
source's two-hole proof or justify replacing its random conditional
influence functions by deterministic ones.

## 1. Deterministic test-function isometry

For f in l2(Z^d), define the analogous sum

    M_t(f)=sum_y sum_{j<=U_t(y)}[f(rho_j(y))-(Pf)(y)].

For a finite set of departure sites this has mean zero. Distinct used
instruction increments are orthogonal: reveal them chronologically, each
after the history determines that it is read, as in the source Lemma 4.3.
Their conditional means are zero and their conditional variances at y are
P(f^2)(y)-(Pf(y))^2. The indicator that instruction j is used is decided
before revealing that instruction, so summing its conditional variance
is legitimate even though U_t is random.

This orthogonality can also be implemented in a finite backward time-t
cone covering any two finite departure-site sums, then expanded; bounded
sparse initial data gives a deterministic finite bound on relevant
departures in that cone. Thus the finite sums have variance

    sum_y E U_t(y)[P(f^2)(y)-(Pf(y))^2]
             =m_t sum_y[P(f^2)(y)-(Pf(y))^2].

The sum is finite for f in l2, since P is an l2 contraction. Consequently
finite departure-site truncations form an L2 Cauchy net. Its limit obeys

    E M_t(f)M_t(h)=m_t[<f,h>-<Pf,Ph>]

by polarization, for real l2 functions f,h. Translation invariance enters
only through E U_t(y)=m_t; it is not an independence assumption about U_t.

## 2. Abel Green functions and Fourier normalization

On the torus [-pi,pi]^d with normalized Lebesgue measure, the one-step
Fourier multiplier is lambda(theta)=d^(-1)sum_i cos(theta_i).
The multiplier of G_r is (1-r lambda)^(-1), a bounded l2 function for
r<1. For f(y)=G_r(y-x), h(y)=G_s(y-z), the isometry gives the Fourier
kernel with multiplier

    (1-lambda^2)/[(1-r lambda)(1-s lambda)].

Near theta=0, 1-lambda is comparable to |theta|^2. Thus
(1+lambda)/(1-lambda) is integrable precisely for d>2. For lambda>=0,
the preceding multiplier is at most (1+lambda)/(1-lambda). For lambda<0
both denominators are at least one and the multiplier is at most one.
These give an integrable dominant bound independent of r,s.

Dominated convergence therefore applies as r,s increase to one. In
particular the variances of M_t^r(x)-M_t^s(x), expressed using their two
variances and covariance, tend to zero. This proves the asserted L2 limit.

## 3. Exact limiting kernel

The limiting Fourier multiplier simplifies to

    (1-lambda^2)/(1-lambda)^2
       =(1+lambda)/(1-lambda)=2/(1-lambda)-1.

The inverse Fourier transform of (1-lambda)^(-1) is the full-space SRW
Green function: one can first use r<1 and then dominated convergence,
or use its defining nonnegative transition series and transience. The
constant multiplier one is the delta at zero. Hence the covariance is
exactly m_t(2G(z-x)-1{x=z}), proving the statement.

The period-two point lambda=-1 causes no singularity here. This argument
does not apply an aperiodic local CLT. Domain, operator and boundary
conventions are full-space discrete-time SRW, with no killing; obstacle
or killed Green functions would require their own energy calculation.

## Remaining route

Source Proposition 8.3 bounds instruction covariance for conditional
hole-survival influences by products q_x q_z, losing gradient cancellation.
The identity above retains cancellation for deterministic Green tests.
It suggests asking for a conditional or averaged influence-energy bound,
but it does not prove one. C12's permanent-trap example excludes a simple
uniform pointwise free-gradient bound. Even a successful instruction-energy
estimate would still leave the d4 initial-scenery convolution to control.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, On a contractivity question of Neri and Pinto for generalized Polya urns (2026). For a balanced d-colour generalized Polya urn with replacement matrix R and balance lambda, Neri and Pinto (arXiv:2607.07309, Remark 3.7) asked whether the form w -> <w(R - lambda I), w> is negative definite on the sum-zero hyperplane H for the Euclidean inner product on all d coordinates or on the first d - 1 (their Proposition 3.6 with p = d or p = d - 1). For two colours both readings hold for every irreducible urn, with constant R_01 + R_10. For every d >= 3 there is an irreducible d-colour urn with nonnegative integer entries for which both readings fail under every ordering of the colours (balance 6 for d >= 4, balance 100 for d = 3), and a six-colour example of balance 6 whose non-principal eigenvalues all have real part below lambda/2. If gamma is the largest real part of a non-principal eigenvalue, the Lyapunov equation on H gives for every A < lambda - gamma an adapted inner product with contraction rate A, and none does better than lambda - gamma; so the rate theorem of Neri and Pinto applies to every tenable irreducible urn with an adapted inner product, and their fast-rate theorem exactly when gamma < lambda/2. Symbolic checks and a Lean 4 file verify the examples. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/urn-euclidean-contractivity (commit 10af47e51a1a). Not refereed.
title: Euclidean contractivity of generalized Polya urns holds for two colours and fails for every d >= 3, on a question of Neri and Pinto (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/urn-euclidean-contractivity)

[Theorem thmCarlemanFinal of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] Let $u$ be an $H^2_{\rm loc}(G)$-valued $\mathbf{F}$-adapted process such that $u_t$ is an $L^2_{\rm loc}(G)$-valued It\^o process. 
Set $ \ell = s \varphi^{-1} $ with $ \varphi $ given by (weight1 of the paper), $\theta = e^\ell$ and $w=\theta u$. 
Then there exists $ \tau_{0} >0 $ such that for all $0< \tau \leq \tau_{0} $ and $u$ supported  in $Q_{\tau}$, there exist positive constants ${\cal C} $, $ \lambda_{0} $ and   $s_0$, such that for all $ \lambda \geq \lambda_{0} $ and  $s \geq s_0$, it holds that 

\begin{align}
&  {\mathbb{E}}\int_{Q_\tau}\theta \big( -2\sigma\ell_t w_t +
2\nabla\ell\cdot\nabla w \big)
\big( \sigma du_t - \Delta u dt \big)dx\nonumber  \\
& \geq {\cal C} {\mathbb{E}}\int_{Q_\tau} \Big[s\lambda^2
\varphi^{-\lambda-2}(|\nabla w|^2+w_t^2)+
s^3\lambda^4 \varphi^{-3\lambda-4}w^2 \Big]dxdt \\
& \quad + {\mathbb{E}}\int_{Q_\tau}\big( -2\sigma \ell_tw_t +
2\nabla\ell\cdot \nabla w \big)^2 dxdt + {\cal C}
{\mathbb{E}}\int_{Q_\tau}\sigma^2\theta^2\ell_t(du_t)^2dx. \nonumber
\end{align}
title: Theorem thmCarlemanFinal of arXiv:2411.05534

[Proposition 10 (Uniqueness of coefficients for orthonormal unit systems) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Let $S=\{h_i\}_{i\in I}\subset\mathbb H$ be $\mathcal A$-orthonormal with
$\langle h_i,h_i\rangle_{\mathcal A}=1_{\mathcal A}$, and assume the inner product is
continuous with respect to norm convergence.
Assume $f=\sum_{i\in I} a_i h_i$ with convergence in norm, where $(a_i)\subset\mathcal A$.
Then necessarily $a_i=\langle f,h_i\rangle_{\mathcal A}$ for all $i$.

body: The Borel–Cantelli lemma is a result in measure theory. It is often stated in the context of probability theory, where it is used to study whether, in a given sequence of events, a finite or infinite number of these events occur. The statement of the lemma is often split into two parts:The first Borel–Cantelli lemma, which states that if the sum of the probabilities of the events is finite, then the probability that infinitely many of them occur is 0. This result holds for any sequence of events, without additional assumptions; The second Borel–Cantelli lemma, which states that if the events are independent and the sum of their probabilities is infinite, then the probability that infinitely many of them occur is 1.

body:
Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ and $\sigma_Nf=\frac1{N+1}\sum_{k=0}^NS_kf=f*F_N$ its Fejer (Cesaro) means. (a) If $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb T$, then $\sigma_Nf\to f$ uniformly on $\mathbb T$. (b) If $f\in L^p(\mathbb T)$, $1\le p<\infty$, then $\|\sigma_Nf-f\|_p\to0$; always $\|\sigma_Nf\|_p\le\|f\|_p$ for $1\le p\le\infty$. (c) If the one-sided limits $f(x^\pm)$ exist at $x$, then $\sigma_Nf(x)\to\frac12(f(x^+)+f(x^-))$. (d) (Fejer-Lebesgue) $\sigma_Nf(x)\to f(x)$ at every Lebesgue point of $f$, hence almost everywhere. Consequences: trigonometric polynomials are dense in $C(\mathbb T)$ (Weierstrass) and in $L^p(\mathbb T)$ for $1\le p<\infty$; and if the Fourier series of $f$ converges at $x$ (in the symmetric sense) then its sum is the Fejer limit, e.g. it equals $f(x)$ at a continuity point. The contrast with the partial sums $S_Nf$, which can diverge for continuous $f$, is entirely due to $F_N\ge0$ versus $\|D_N\|_1\to\infty$.
f is 1-periodic and integrable over a period
(a): f continuous on the circle
(b): f in L^p(T), 1 <= p < infinity
(c): the one-sided limits of f at x exist

[Theorem 3 (Left Edge) of arXiv:2511.12623, 'The eigenvector bead process'] Fix integers $K, \ell \ge 1$, and let $q = N/T \in (0,1)$ be kept fixed in the asymptotic regime $N,T \to \infty$.
Consider a Wishart matrix $W_{N+K}$, and let $\{\lambda_j^{(s)}\}_{j}$ denote its increasingly ordered eigenvalues at level $s$. Then the array of rescaled left-edge increments
\[
\left(
-\frac{\sqrt{q}}{1-\sqrt{q}}\bigl(\lambda_{1}^{(s+1)} - \lambda_{1}^{(s)}\bigr),\,
-\frac{\sqrt{q}}{1-\sqrt{q}}\bigl(\lambda_{2}^{(s+1)} - \lambda_{2}^{(s)}\bigr),\,
\dots,\,
-\frac{\sqrt{q}}{1-\sqrt{q}}\bigl(\lambda_{\ell}^{(s+1)} - \lambda_{\ell}^{(s)}\bigr)
\right)_{0 \le s \le K-1}
\]
converges in distribution, as $N,T \to \infty$, to a random array with independent
Gamma-distributed entries on $(0,\infty)$ having density
\( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\, x^{-1/2} e^{-x/2}.
\)
Moreover, this array is independent of the array of the $\ell$ smallest eigenvalues,
\(
\left(
\lambda_{1}^{(0)},\,
\lambda_{2}^{(0)},\,
\dots,\,
\lambda_{\ell}^{(0)}
\right).
\) (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending. # A genuine zero-budget global averaging obstruction from repeated facts

T379-C020 v2, proof (unaudited), exact all-world checks PASS; audit pending.
Target 1, secondary target 2: auxiliary-route obstruction, not an exact
global frontier. This concerns actual iid training, not only an
artificial conditional posterior or a handpicked world.

## Experiment and objectives

Fix any N>=5. Set d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0,n=6. There are two A/S pairs,
one A and one S each, and N-4 fixed S contexts. A has an arbitrary
uniform two-element truth support; S has all three truths. Source p
chooses contexts uniformly and then truths uniformly. Observe six
iid factual samples WITHOUT orientation labels or verifier information.
Require every data-dependent generator to have source Mis_infinity=0
in EVERY world compatible with its observed facts, at exact score bins.

For data D let V(D) be the conditional minimum over robustly calibrated
generators of their maximum compatible-world false mass. Let

 B_N=E_w[V(D)],
 Gamma_N=inf_policy max_fixed_world w E_w[H(policy(D))].

B_N is independent of the fixed actual world w: sibling permutations
and within-context candidate permutations map any world to any other,
preserve the model and compatibility, and carry source calibration,
false mass and V(D) with them. The data laws are carried along by the
same bijections. Thus V(D)'s distribution is identical in all worlds.

The candidate strict inequality is

 Gamma_N <= B_N-5/(1008*N^7) < B_N.                      (1)

No numerical value of B_N or Gamma_N is claimed. The point is that
expected conditional worst-world risk overstates global expected
minimax risk even at ZERO source calibration budget.

## Finite conditional selectors exist

There are finitely many actual worlds and finitely many score
partitions of the NK atoms. For a zero-calibrated g its score partition
Pi satisfies g=p_w,Pi for every compatible w, so a fixed Pi admits at
most one such g. Merging equal-score cells preserves this property.
The one-cell uniform generator is always feasible, so each V(D) is
attained among finitely many candidates. Choose any deterministic
conditional minimizer g*_D by a fixed tie rule. This selector is an
existence construction, not a claim of computational efficiency.
For every actual w it satisfies H_w(g*_D)<=V(D) pointwise.
Datasets incompatible with every source world may use the uniform
fallback; they have probability zero under every actual world.

## Observable rare event and its conditional value

Let E be the event that all six samples have this pattern:

* Four copies of ONE candidate in ONE context of one pair;
* one fact in each of the two contexts of the other pair;
* no other observations.

The pair roles, repeated context, candidate identities and sample
order are unrestricted. E is recognizable from the data alone.
Its known-truth counts are (1,0) in the repeated pair and (1,1) in
the other pair, all strictly below r=2. Thus C017's exact zero-budget
frontier, with pairwise minima 0 and 1, gives

 V(D)=1/(3N)+7/(24N)=5/(8N) on E.                        (2)

For clarity, the (1,0) pair's zero-calibrated bins must contain whole
contexts: support swaps make each uncertified set constant-score and
orientation invariance with the zero-known sibling leaves no known
truths available to peel from that context. Forgetting the repeated
fact therefore preserves all source-bin and false-count information.
The resulting balanced (0,0)/(1,1) game has artificial mean densities
1/(3N),7/(24N) on its residual groups, with false risks 1/6,1/4;
safe densities are higher. The per-bin low-density tail argument
gives the lower value (2), and the invariant-group mean attains it
worldwise. This is a conditional worst-world assertion, not an
actual-orientation posterior calculation.

## A causal calibrated generator on E

Let x be the observed four-repeat context. Let a,b be the two contexts
of the other pair and let their single observed candidates be c_a,c_b.
Form B from ALL THREE atoms of x plus the four atoms of a,b other
than c_a,c_b. Its source mass is 1/N+7/(6N)=13/(6N) in every
compatible world; its seven atoms get score q=13/(42N).
Give the two observed atoms in a,b score 5/(12N). Give every other
atom score lambda=1/(3N), including the untouched sibling of x and
all fixed S contexts. The group masses sum to one. All source group
masses are invariant across orientations and supports, so exact-score
mergers preserve source Mis_infinity=0. The rule uses observed context
counts and observed truths only; it never reads the hidden orientation.

If x is actually A, false mass is H_A=2q=13/(21N).
If x is actually S, false mass is H_S=q+lambda=9/(14N).
These identities hold for every compatible truth-support choice.

## Fixed-world event probabilities, not a posterior shortcut

In ANY fixed actual world, summing over the repeated candidate
identity gives repeated-four-fact weights proportional to

 r*(1/(Nr))^4=1/(N^4*r^3) for the A context,
 K*(1/(NK))^4=1/(N^4*K^3) for the S context.

Consequently, conditional on E, the repeated context is actually A
with probability K^3/(K^3+r^3)=27/35, uniformly in every fixed world.
The exponent is THREE, not four: the number of available true
candidate identities must be included. The other pair's one sample
per context contributes 1/N^2 after its identities are summed out.

There are two choices of repeated pair and 6!/(4!1!1!)=30 orders.
Thus in every fixed world

 P_w(E)=60/N^6*(1/8+1/27)=175/(18N^6),                  (3)
 E_w[H_pool|E]=(27/35)*13/(21N)+(8/35)*9/(14N)
             =153/(245N),
 V(E)-E_w[H_pool|E]=1/(1960N).                           (4)

These are ordinary disjoint-event sums under the fixed sampling law;
no independence of learned events or hidden labels is assumed.

## Global policy and strict separation

Use the explicit pooling generator on E and g*_D otherwise. Every
outcome is robustly zero-calibrated. For every fixed actual world,

 E_w H <= E_w[1_{not E}V(D)]+P_w(E)*153/(245N)
       =B_N-P_w(E)/(1960N)
       =B_N-5/(1008N^7).

Taking the maximum over w proves (1). At N=5 the exact strict gap
certified by this construction is 1/15750000. This is an upper bound
on Gamma_N relative to B_N, not an exact value for either objective.

The result complements C014's positive-budget example and C015's
single-outcome pointwise control. Here the improvement is realized
under actual iid data, uniformly for EVERY fixed world, at zero
budget. A global expected lower bound must therefore use a valid
fixed-prior/per-world argument rather than average conditional maxima.
Primary statistic: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9.
Independent mathematical, priority and target-scope audit pending.

Exact verification: logs/zero_budget_global_separation_check.json
checks all 36 fixed worlds and all 108 rare-event histograms for
N=5,6,9, totaling 6480 positive-probability source-calibration checks
and 108 exact event expectation checks. Another 108 checks verify
whole-source-family transitive relabeling. In every fixed world some
event outcomes worsen risk, so the improvement is genuinely in
expectation. A three-repeat fault produces the wrong sign in all
108 world/parameter cases. The general finite-selector and symmetry
proof supplies the global conclusion; neither B_N nor Gamma_N is
estimated numerically.
N>=5,d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0,n=6; two A/S pairs and remaining known S contexts
Actual iid factual samples without tags; p uniform on contexts then true candidates; all A truth supports allowed
Each data-dependent generator robustly exact-level source-calibrated at zero in every compatible world
Conditional V(D) maximizes after data; global Gamma_N maximizes over a fixed world before data

In arXiv:2609.02818, Brysiewicz and Sinn emphasize that the principal computational cost of the quadratic isolation test is solving a system of quadratic forms in s = nullity(J_F(p)) variables. When the corank of the Jacobian is small relative to the ambient dimension n, s is small, circumventing the doubly-exponential or combinatorial complexity of standard Groebner basis algorithms.
s = nullity(J_F(p)) is significantly smaller than ambient dimension n
title: Complexity Governed by Jacobian Nullity

continuous speed curves r_1,r_2 on [0,S], with r_i(0)=0 and r_i(b)>0 for b>0.

Let a finite nonempty binary-labeled data set (x_i,y_i), y_i in {-1,+1}, and a real-valued predictor Phi(theta;x) with theta in R^d be given. For each fixed x, theta -> Phi(theta;x) is locally Lipschitz and admits the chain rule: for every locally absolutely continuous arc z, (Phi(z(t);x))'=<h,z'(t)> for every h in its Clarke subdifferential at z(t), for almost every t. Assume common positive homogeneity degree L>0: Phi(a theta;x)=a^L Phi(theta;x) for every a>0. Put q_i(theta)=y_i Phi(theta;x_i), q_min(theta)=min_i q_i(theta), and E(theta)=sum_i exp(-q_i(theta)), without averaging by sample size. Let theta:[0,infinity)->R^d be a locally absolutely continuous Clarke gradient-flow trajectory satisfying theta'(t) in -partial^C E(theta(t)) almost everywhere. Assume there is a finite t0 with E(theta(t0))<1. For t>=t0 put r(t)=||theta(t)||_2, gamma_bar(theta)=q_min(theta)/||theta||_2^L, and gamma_tilde(theta)=-log E(theta)/||theta||_2^L. The norm stays positive. For almost every t>t0, d gamma_tilde(theta(t))/dt>=0; if the normalized direction has nonzero derivative then that derivative is strictly positive. Moreover gamma_bar-log(N)/r^L<=gamma_tilde<=gamma_bar, E(theta(t))->0, and r(t)->infinity. The two margins converge to the same finite positive limit. The theorem makes gamma_tilde monotone; it does not assert that gamma_bar itself is monotone. These are the gradient-flow conclusions under (A1)-(A4), not a discrete ReLU gradient-descent theorem.

Positive homogeneity of a common degree L>0

Independence Metropolis-Hastings proposing the exact prior has stationary acceptance alpha_y <= (2 sqrt(2)/3)^d exp(-||y||^2/12). From the explicit 2-warm law nu_y=pi_y conditioned on x_1<=y_1/2, TV(nu_y K_y^t,pi_y)>=1/2-t(2 sqrt(2)/3)^d exp(-||y||^2/12) for integer t>=0. For even d=2n, t<=(9/8)^n/4 implies TV>=1/4. Thus the Target 1 condition cannot justify polynomial mixing of this particular prior-refresh route, even with exact prior samples and scores. The posterior has a direct linear-time exact sampler; this is not computational hardness or a new Gaussian sampling result.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:b43fdc8114af9e5c135e4064e82cd8703c575911806e0ca88ee18060fe81f4c3","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/b4/b43fdc8114af9e5c135e4064e82cd8703c575911806e0ca88ee18060fe81f4c3.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:17d4eeb3112f750db06d3480af82140912cf8393886c4cdb51a43450adfc061f","bundle_entry_key":"draft-prior-refresh-metropolis-gaussian-obstruction","bundle_id":"population.t411-prior-refresh-metropolis-obstruction-005","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"posterior sampling; Metropolis-Hastings; Hellinger affinity; warm starts","draft":"w740/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.sampling:draft-prior-refresh-metropolis-gaussian-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C010: exact prior samples do not make prior-refresh Metropolis mix quickly

Version 2, 20 October 2026. Target 1; kind: route-failure.
Status: proof (unaudited). A proved obstruction to one algorithmic route, not a target solution, posterior hardness result, or novelty claim.

## 1. Statement

Let the prior be q=N(0,I_d), A=I_d, and observation noise N(0,I_d). Then C_LS(q)=1 in the convention Ent(f^2)<=2 C_LS E||grad f||^2, and ||A||^2 C_LS/sigma^2=1. At every observation y, the posterior is

    pi_y=N(y/2,I_d/2).

Consider ONLY the independence Metropolis-Hastings kernel K_y proposing a fresh independent sample from q at each step, with the exact likelihood acceptance rule. Exact prior samples and exact scores are available in this example. Its stationary acceptance probability alpha_y satisfies

    alpha_y <= h_y := (2 sqrt(2)/3)^d exp(-||y||^2/12).

There is an explicit initial law nu_y with density at most 2 relative to pi_y such that for every integer t>=0,

    TV(nu_y K_y^t,pi_y) >= 1/2 - t h_y.

For even d=2n, every t<=(9/8)^n/4 therefore has TV error at least 1/4. This is exponential in dimension, uniformly over all observations. For every fixed c>0 the parameter condition 1<=c log d holds in sufficiently large dimension. Hence that condition cannot justify polynomial mixing of this prior-refresh correction strategy, even from a 2-warm start.

This does NOT rule out a general posterior algorithm or an algorithm using different proposals. In this example an independent posterior sample is simply y/2+G/sqrt(2), so there is an explicit linear-time exact sampler. The obstruction concerns the proposed route under strong access, not Gaussian posterior sampling as a research contribution.

## 2. Stationary acceptance and Hellinger affinity

For strictly positive densities pi,q, let w=pi/q. The accepted off-diagonal stationary flow density for independence Metropolis is

    J(x,z)=pi(x)q(z) min(1,w(z)/w(x))
          =min(pi(x)q(z),pi(z)q(x)).

The Gaussian proposals are nonatomic, so accepting and moving coincide almost surely. Thus the mean acceptance is alpha=integral J(x,z) dx dz. Using min(a,b)<=sqrt(ab), Tonelli's theorem and nonnegativity,

    alpha <= [integral sqrt(pi(x)q(x)) dx]^2.

The integral in brackets is Hellinger affinity; no conversion between the competing normalizations of Hellinger distance is used. All densities are positive and integrate to one, so the displayed integrals exist and the bound is at most one.

For pi=N(m,I_d/2), q=N(0,I_d), the square root density product is

    sqrt(pi(x)q(x)) = 2^(-d/4) pi_constant^(-d/2)
                     exp(-||x-m||^2/2-||x||^2/4).

Here pi_constant denotes the number 3.14159..., not the posterior. Completing the square gives

    ||x-m||^2/2+||x||^2/4
      = (3/4)||x-2m/3||^2+||m||^2/6.

Integrating the resulting Gaussian yields affinity

    (2 sqrt(2)/3)^(d/2) exp(-||m||^2/6).

Its square is (2 sqrt(2)/3)^d exp(-||m||^2/3). Substituting m=y/2 proves the stated h_y. The posterior formula itself follows by completing the square in exp(-||x||^2/2-||y-x||^2/2), a classical Gaussian baseline already recalled from the brain.

## 3. A 2-warm initial law and the TV lower bound

Take B_y={x: x_1<=y_1/2}; pi_y(B_y)=1/2. Define nu_y=pi_y(.|B_y), whose density relative to pi_y is 2 on B_y and zero elsewhere. Write

    Q_y=integral_{B_y x B_y^c} J(x,z) dx dz.

Symmetry of J implies equal reverse flow, and these two disjoint regions imply 2Q_y<=alpha_y. Start a stationary chain with X_0~pi_y. Conditioning this entire path on X_0 in B_y gives exactly the chain started from nu_y, since the transition kernel is unchanged. If that conditional chain is outside B_y at time t, it must have crossed from B_y to B_y^c at one of the first t transitions. A union bound on the UNCONDITIONED stationary path therefore gives

    P_nu_y(X_t in B_y^c)
      <= 2 sum_{k=0}^{t-1} P_pi_y(X_k in B_y, X_{k+1} in B_y^c)
      = 2t Q_y <= t alpha_y <= t h_y.

The factor two is exactly 1/pi_y(B_y). No independence of crossing events or conditional stationarity is asserted. Consequently

    TV(nu_y K_y^t,pi_y)
      >= (nu_y K_y^t)(B_y)-pi_y(B_y)
      >= 1/2-t h_y.

For d=2n, h_y<=(8/9)^n. Multiplication by t<=(9/8)^n/4 proves the claimed 1/4 lower bound. At t=0 the statement correctly gives TV=1/2.

## 4. Independent exact finite checks

At y=0 the likelihood weight decreases strictly with ||x||. Swapping x,z in the two equal parts of the acceptance integral gives

    alpha_0=2 P(||Z||^2<=||X||^2),
    X~N(0,I_d/2), Z~N(0,I_d), independent.

For d=2n, independent U=||Z||^2 and V=2||X||^2 are chi-square(2n), so U/(U+V) has Beta(n,n) density. The event U<=V/2 is exactly U/(U+V)<=1/3. Thus

    alpha_0=2 integral_0^(1/3) t^(n-1)(1-t)^(n-1) dt / B(n,n).

Expand (1-t)^(n-1) by the binomial theorem. Every integral is rational; B(n,n)=((n-1)!)^2/(2n-1)!. The saved script evaluates these finite sums with Fraction arithmetic, independently checking the acceptance upper bound for n=1,...,32. This is a finite diagnostic, not the proof for every dimension; Sections 2 and 3 give that proof.

Two controls record the exact scope: A=0 gives pi=q and acceptance one; proposing pi_y directly also gives acceptance one and exact mixing after one step. Neither control contradicts the lower bound, which concerns only the specified prior-refresh proposal with A=I and sigma=1.

## 5. Exact failure point and remaining alternatives

The failed step would be: infer polynomial overlap of prior proposals with the posterior from the operator ratio ||A||^2 C_LS/sigma^2 alone. Here that ratio is one but squared Hellinger affinity decays exponentially. A minorization or acceptance argument for the unmodified prior proposal therefore cannot supply the desired dimension-independent polynomial bound.

Local, transport-adapted, or tempered proposals remain possible. A tempering route would still require efficient sampling along its intermediate measures; a generic posterior-LSI inheritance shortcut is already excluded by C004 and is not rechecked here. C009 separately excludes TV identification from only finite-cutoff approximate forward scores. Together these facts identify two genuinely different limitations: insufficient score information under one interface, and an exponentially poor proposal under a stronger interface. Neither proves computational hardness for Target 1 with exact scores and unrestricted algorithmic choices.

The remaining formulation question for the reviewer is whether Target 1 supplies exact prior scores including time zero, a prior sampling oracle, or only the primary paper's finite-cutoff L2-accurate forward-score networks. Only the last model is addressed by C009. No claim of an open-problem solution should be recorded until this interface is explicit.

Least trusted proof step for audit: the factor-two conditioning/union-bound argument in Section 3. 	\mu(\lambda,x)\sim   \lambda^{-p}\sum_{k\ge0}   C_{p+k}\frac{m_k(x)}{k!}\lambda^{-k}, \quad \text{as $\lambda\gg1$},
\end{equation}
where $m_k(x)=  \partial_s^km|_{s=0} $, 
and $C_{p+k}:= e^{\i \pi (p+k)/2}\Gamma(p+k) = i^{k}p(p+1)\dots (p+k-1)C_p $. In particular, 
\[
\mu(\lambda,x)\sim   {C_p}\, \lambda^{-p} m_0(x)\big(1+O(\lambda^{-1})\big) , \quad C_p := e^{\i\pi p/2} \Gamma(p).
\]
