metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:0e0f575a67ab79154e4b9f27c0969e1aaa9de2b2dc30ab02f9279406be0b9960","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/0e/0e0f575a67ab79154e4b9f27c0969e1aaa9de2b2dc30ab02f9279406be0b9960.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:ddb8be3e8545350ce2cc636e9297135b54bd2da8198fdd3570d719dbfce84b0c","bundle_entry_key":"corank-large-scale","bundle_id":"population.t419-corank-one-all-ranks-large-scale-gd-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"LoRA population GD and large unbalanced initialization","draft":"w705/bundle_011.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-corank-one-input-all-ranks-large-gaussian-scale-gd-rate","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C022 v2: large-scale GD for the proper input co-rank-one family

Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.

This uses the published sufficient-deficiency-margin idea of Min, Tarmoun, Vidal and Mallada (arXiv:2105.06351, Corollary 5, p.10), the known invariant output span (Zhang, Liu and Chen, arXiv:2502.01235, Theorem 3.1/C.10), and the discrete imbalance/descent method of Du, Hu and Lee (arXiv:1806.00900, Appendix B, Claim B.1). None of these citations alone supplies the theorem below. Kunin et al., arXiv:2406.06158, Appendix A.2.4 and Theorem 4.2, give related unbalanced flow results under different structural assumptions. Prior searches did not establish novelty. The hardest step here is the finite-time fast/slow comparison in section 4, with constants that close its induction before using the endpoint bounds. It is proved below, but has not received an independent audit.

## Statement

Let r>=2, p=r+1, m>=r+1. Let Delta be a real m-by-p matrix with exactly r nonzero singular values, each equal to 1. Let G be r-by-p with independent standard normal entries. Set B_0=0, A_0=sG and perform simultaneous factor GD on q=||BA-Delta||F^2/2:

 B_next=B-eta(BA-Delta)A^T,
 A_next=A-eta B^T(BA-Delta).

For any 0<rho<1 define the positive, deterministic constants

 d=rho/3, c0=10r/d, a=1/(c0 sqrt(r)), b=sqrt(rp/d), xi=d^3/(9p),
 K0=sqrt(r)(b^2+1+4sqrt(r)), gamma=1/(6K0+1),
 T=ceil[log(8sqrt(r)/xi)/(gamma a^2)],
 Q=sqrt(r)/a, Q1=Q+1, b1=b+1,
 L=b1^2+2Qb1+1, H=Q1(Q1b1+sqrt(r)), Z=b1+Q,
 E=gamma H T exp(gamma L T), S=max{1,(8ZE/xi)^(1/4)}.

For every s>=S choose the single fixed step eta=gamma/s^2. With probability at least 1-rho, simultaneously for all integer t>=T,

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F <= exp[-gamma xi^2(t-T)/(32s^4 K0)].

In particular, for every 0<eps<1 the residual is at most eps once

 t >= T + ceil[(32s^4 K0/(gamma xi^2)) log(1/eps)].

The step and the success event do not depend on eps. The scale threshold is finite but extremely conservative; no efficient numerical magnitude or useful practical threshold is asserted. This is a whole family at every rank, with a proper rank bottleneck on both input and output sides, but only condition number 1 and input co-rank 1. General aspect ratios, general spectra, moderate scales, expected risk and Target 2 are not asserted.

## 1. One Gaussian event; no independence multiplication

Write v0 for a fixed unit vector spanning ker(Delta), so Delta^T Delta=I-v0 v0^T. The following three events hold jointly with probability at least 1-3d=1-rho:

 sigma_min(G)>=a, ||G||F<=b, and |z^T v0|^2>=xi,

where z is any unit representative of the one-dimensional ker(G). Its sign does not matter.

For completeness the smallest-singular-value bound needs only a square submatrix, without a random-matrix theorem. Let H0 be the first r columns of G. It is nonsingular almost surely. For its j-th column, let delta_j be its distance from the span of the other columns. Conditional on those other columns, delta_j has the distribution |N(0,1)|. The j-th row of H0^{-1} has norm delta_j^{-1}, by its unit pairing with column j and zero pairing with all other columns. If sigma_min(H0)<a then ||H0^{-1}||F>1/a, and some row has norm >1/(a sqrt(r)). Thus some delta_j<a sqrt(r). A union bound and the normal density bound give

 Pr[sigma_min(H0)<a] <= r sqrt(2/pi) a sqrt(r) < d,

since a=d/(10r^(3/2)). Also GG^T dominates H0 H0^T, so the same lower bound holds for sigma_min(G). Markov gives Pr[||G||F>b]<=rp/b^2=d.

Gaussian right orthogonal invariance implies that the kernel line of G is uniformly distributed over unoriented lines in R^p. Indeed G O has the same law as G for every orthogonal O, and its kernel is O^T ker(G); the rotation-invariant probability on lines is the line of a uniform sphere vector. Consequently |z^T v0| has the law of |g_1|/||g|| for a standard Gaussian vector g in R^p, after rotating v0 to the first coordinate. This distributional representation makes no claim about independence from the preceding two events. The normal density bound gives Pr[|g_1|<d/2]<=d/sqrt(2pi)<d/2; Markov gives Pr[||g||^2>2p/d]<=d/2. Outside their union,

 |g_1|/||g|| >= d^(3/2)/(2sqrt(2p)) > d^(3/2)/(3sqrt(p))=sqrt(xi).

Thus the third event fails with probability at most d. A union bound over all three events finishes this section. Henceforth fix any G in their intersection.

## 2. Global descent and a factor bound

Use the deterministic boundedness lemma C014, whose proof is appended to the queued card and saved in proofs/C014_empirical_boundedness.md. Here C=I, D=W=Delta, q0=r/2,

 J=||A0 A0^T||F+1 <=s^2 b^2+1,
 R=||Delta||F+sqrt(2q0)=2sqrt(r),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R)<=s^2 K0,

where the last inequality uses s>=1. Since K0>=4r and gamma=1/(6K0+1), eta=gamma/s^2 <=1/(1+r). Also

 eta(6K+1) <= gamma(6K0+1/s^2) <=1.

Both hypotheses of C014 hold. Therefore, at every iterate,

 q_next<=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2,
 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=K<=s^2 K0.

These bounds hold before and after the fast phase. C014 proves them without assuming bounded iterates: descent is first proved on the segment to the proposed step in a factor ball of twice the current radius, then the telescoping Gram drift returns the endpoint to the original radius. Merely assuming a local Lipschitz constant along the unknown trajectory would not suffice.

## 3. The exactly solvable frozen-feature phase

Keep the input factor fixed at G and let Ubar_0=0,

 Ubar_next=Ubar-gamma(Ubar G-Delta)G^T.

Let M=GG^T, P=G^T M^{-1}G=I-zz^T, and Ustar=Delta G^T M^{-1}. Then

 Ubar_t=Ustar[I-(I-gamma M)^t],
 ||Ubar_t||F<=||Ustar||F<=sqrt(r)/a=Q.

Indeed M is symmetric with eigenvalues in [a^2,b^2], and gamma b^2<1, so the bracket has operator norm at most 1. Its multiplication on the right of Ustar does not require Ustar and M to commute. An SVD of G also shows

 ||Ubar_t G-Delta P||F <=sqrt(r)(1-gamma a^2)^t
                              <=sqrt(r) exp(-gamma a^2 t).

The irreducible frozen residual satisfies

 ||Delta(I-P)||F^2=||Delta z||^2
                 =1-(v0^T z)^2 <=1-xi.

Consequently its norm is at most sqrt(1-xi)<=1-xi/2. At t=T the transient term is at most xi/8, and the triangle inequality yields

 ||Ubar_T G-Delta||F<=1-3xi/8.

This is the place where p=r+1 and the equal singular values are used. A generic random row space in higher input co-rank need not achieve a frozen residual strictly below the smallest nonzero singular value.

## 4. Actual GD stays close for the finite fast phase

Set U_t=s B_t, V_t=A_t/s and epsilon=s^{-4}. Direct substitution in simultaneous GD gives the exact recurrences

 U_next=U-gamma(UV-Delta)V^T,
 V_next=V-gamma epsilon U^T(UV-Delta).

The initial conditions are U0=Ubar0=0, V0=G. Define

 d_t=||U_t-Ubar_t||F+||V_t-G||F.

Whenever d_t<=1, the current factors obey ||U||F<=Q1 and ||V||F<=b1. Expanding the difference of the fast gradients gives the exact matrix identity

 (UV-Delta)V^T-(Ubar G-Delta)G^T
 = (U-Ubar)VV^T + Ubar(VV^T-GG^T) - Delta(V-G)^T.

Using ||VV^T-GG^T||F <= (||V||op+||G||op)||V-G||F, ||Delta||op=1, and ||Ubar||F<=Q, its norm is at most

 b1^2 ||U-Ubar||F + (2Qb1+1)||V-G||F <=L d_t.

The slow gradient satisfies

 ||U^T(UV-Delta)||F <=Q1(Q1 b1+sqrt(r))=H.

The two updates therefore give

 d_(t+1) <=(1+gamma L)d_t+gamma epsilon H

at every current point with d_t<=1. Starting at d0=0, induction yields for 0<=t<=T

 d_t <=epsilon gamma H t exp(gamma L t) <=epsilon E<=xi/(8Z)<1.

To avoid a circular bootstrap: the displayed estimate at time t only invokes d_(t-1)<=1; the geometric-sum solution of the recurrence bounds the proposed next distance by epsilon E, which is strictly less than 1. Thus each new endpoint is admissible before the next recurrence is used. The last inequality is exactly the definition of S and s>=S.

Moreover

 ||UV-Ubar G||F <=||U-Ubar||F ||V||op + ||Ubar||op ||V-G||F
                 <=Z d_t<=xi/8.

At time T the actual population residual e_T therefore satisfies

 e_T=||B_T A_T-Delta||F=||U_T V_T-Delta||F<=1-xi/4.

## 5. Persistent positive margin and one fixed-step rate

Write Delta=U_D S0 where U_D has r orthonormal columns and S0 S0^T=I_r. Because B0=0 and both Delta and B_t lie in col(U_D), the B update preserves that subspace. Thus B_t=U_D R_t for a square r-by-r matrix R_t at every time, and

 e_t=||R_t A_t-S0||F.

Global descent from section 2 implies e_t<=1-xi/4 for all t>=T. Weyl's singular-value inequality then gives sigma_min(R_t A_t)>=xi/4, where the minimum here is the smallest of the r singular values of the r-by-p product. For square R_t and any A_t,

 sigma_min(R_t A_t)<=sigma_min(R_t)||A_t||op.

For example apply the transpose to a unit vector minimizing ||R_t^T x||. Since ||A_t||op<=s sqrt(K0), it follows that

 sigma_min(R_t)>=xi/(4s sqrt(K0)).

The A-gradient is R_t^T(R_t A_t-S0), so

 ||grad q||F^2 >=||grad_A q||F^2
               >=xi^2 e_t^2/(16s^2 K0).

Using q=e_t^2/2 and section 2 gives

 e_(t+1)^2 <=[1-gamma xi^2/(16s^4 K0)]e_t^2.

The bracket is in (0,1), as follows directly from s>=1, xi<1 and gamma<1. Iterating and using sqrt(1-x)<=exp(-x/2), and e_T<=1, proves the statement. Every update throughout this proof uses the same eta; no change of step at T or dependence on requested accuracy is hidden.

## Scope and strongest failure tests

If ker(G) is orthogonal to ker(Delta), the frozen residual can equal 1 and this route gives no positive margin. That is a measure-zero alignment, but its near-neighborhood explains the confidence-dependent xi and large S. If input co-rank exceeds one, the frozen Frobenius residual can exceed 1 even with a generic Gaussian row space; the present argument then fails. If target singular values are unequal, the same test must compare the frozen residual to sigma_r(Delta), not to 1; no general-spectrum assertion follows from this proof. Replacing the actual second update by frozen features forever would prove a different algorithm and is not done here. Positive-noise finite-sample dynamics have no exact invariant target output span, so this proof does not answer Target 2.

Exact rational recurrence/projector checks are auxiliary algebra checks only. They do not certify the Gaussian event, estimates at arbitrary real parameters, independent correctness, or novelty. Independent reviewer audit is required on version 2.


Full deterministic C014 boundedness component:
# T419-C014 v1: empirical GD boundedness with an initialization-dependent step

Kind: bound. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This is an explicit anisotropic version of the published Gram-imbalance/descent method, not a solution of Target 2. It proves a trajectory component without assuming the iterates are bounded. The prior source is Du-Hu-Lee, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 2.2 and Appendix B, Claim B.1; its full convergence theorems have different initialization/step hypotheses. C009 already identifies the exact covariance metric and C010 the positive-noise empirical landscape.

## Statement

Let C be any real positive definite p-by-p matrix, D any real m-by-p matrix, and r>=1. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op, ell=||D||op, W=D C^(-1), and

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.

## Exact identities and product/factor bounds

Let G=BA C-D. The two factor gradients are G_B=G A^T and G_A=B^T G. With E_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t the first-order cross terms cancel exactly, giving

 E_(t+1)-E_t=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 ||E_(t+1)-E_t||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

This cancellation only uses dependence on BA and does not require isotropic C. Also

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 <=r [||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

To verify it, write P=B^TB,Q=AA^T. Scalar trace Cauchy-Schwarz gives (tr(P+Q))^2<=r tr((P+Q)^2), and cyclicity of trace gives tr((P+Q)^2)=||P-Q||F^2+4 tr(PQ), tr(PQ)=||BA||F^2. No commutation is assumed.

When q<=q0, positivity of C gives ||BA-W||F<=sqrt(2q0/lambda), hence ||BA||F<=R. If additionally ||E-E0||F<=1, then ||E||F<=J, so the preceding trace bound implies

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=sqrt(r) sqrt(J^2+4R^2)<=K.

The initialization meets these conditions and therefore has pair norm at most sqrt(K).

## Descent established before closing the boundedness induction

Suppose at the current iterate the pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have valid descent inequalities. Then

 ||grad q||F<=||BA C-D||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(Kc/2+ell)sqrt(K).

Because eta<=1/(6Kc+ell), the proposed next point has pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The connecting segment also lies in that ball. On that ball the Hessian quadratic form in a perturbation (dB,dA) is

 ||(dB A+B dA) C^(1/2)||F^2+2<BA C-D,dB dA>.

Its absolute value is at most

 [c(||A||op^2+||B||op^2)+||BA C-D||op]
 times (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2)
 <=[4Kc+(2Kc+ell)] (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2).

Here the first summand uses Cauchy-Schwarz on dB A+B dA; the cross term uses |<G,dB dA>|<=||G||op||dB||F||dA||F. Thus the Hessian operator norm on the segment is at most L. Taylor's theorem along that segment proves

 q_next<=q-eta||grad q||F^2+(L eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2
        <=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2.

In particular q_next<=q0. Telescoping the descent inequalities, including the proposed step, and using q>=0 yields

 sum_(j=0)^t eta^2||grad q_j||F^2<=2eta q0
 <=2q0/(1+2q0)<1.

Summing the imbalance increments now proves ||E_next-E0||F<=2eta q0<1. The product/factor bound therefore puts the endpoint back in the smaller ball of pair radius sqrt(K). This closes the induction without assuming a bound before proving descent on the required larger segment. The q0=0 case is included: both gradients vanish, the sequence is constant, and all inequalities still hold.

## Consequences and exact remaining gap

Telescoping for every finite horizon gives the infinite summability bound. A nonnegative summable sequence tends to zero, so the gradients vanish. Bounded finite-dimensional factor pairs have convergent subsequences; gradient continuity makes every subsequential limit critical. The running-minimum bound follows by averaging the finite sum. These statements do not require that the entire sequence converges to one point.

For B0=0 and a Gaussian A0, this provides an allowed positive step after observing the initialization, conditional on every full-row-rank design. It does not supply a single positive step independent of the unbounded Gaussian initializer. C013 shows that unconditional expected-limit risk with such an initialization-independent fixed step can diverge even at rank one.

Combining this bound with the already verified empirical strict-saddle landscape C010 is insufficient to conclude global optimization. One must additionally show that the specified zero/Gaussian initialization does not approach a nonglobal critical point, with all hypotheses of a saddle-avoidance theorem checked for its lower-dimensional initial support and step rule. Vanishing gradients do not establish that. Even convergence almost surely would not by itself justify passing to expected population risk; a failure-tail/integrability or finite-stopping argument is separately required. The usual full-ambient absolutely-continuous random-initialization theorem cannot simply be cited for the plane B0=0.

Independent reviewer audit and any novelty assessment remain pending. Owner-own-work proof draft (unaudited), no novelty priority claimed. For every oracle O there is one uniform family P_L^O with polynomial-time Boolean unnormalized weights, an explicit normalizer, exact polynomial-time normalized point probabilities and an exact uniform polynomial-time sampler, for which polynomial-time cumulative-probability evaluation implies NP^O=P^O. At L=2d+1 take C,b,w of lengths d,1,d and give weight one iff b=V_d^O(C,w), where V is a polynomial-time universal time-bounded oracle verifier. The normalizer is 2^(2d). Two CDF values recover the number of accepting witnesses: 2^(2d)[F(C,1,1^d)-F(C,0,1^d)]. Additive error at most 2^(-(L+2)) per value still decides whether this integer is positive. Strict CDFs work as well by adding the known point mass. Other lengths are dummy point masses. Thus easy point probabilities, even with exact sampling, cannot alone establish a cumulative-computability hypothesis under NP^O not contained in P^O/poly. This is not an AR KL lower bound and does not refute the PSamp extension of average-case completeness.
Standard deterministic polynomial-time universal oracle-verifier simulation
Lexicographic CDF on fixed-length binary strings; exact CDF or specified exponential additive accuracy

Fix any oracle O. There is a single uniform length-indexed family P_L^O
with polynomial-time 0/1 weights, known normalizer, polynomial-time exact
normalized point probabilities, and a uniform exact polynomial-time sampler,
such that polynomial-time evaluation of its lexicographic CDF would imply
NP^O=P^O. Even additive CDF precision 2^(-(L+2)) suffices for this collapse.
Therefore in any oracle sought by Target 2, this family is not in PComp^O
under the cumulative-probability convention of Bogdanov-Trevisan Definition 2.
This is NOT an AR KL lower bound, or an obstruction to samplable-distribution
extensions of average-case completeness.

## Uniform verifier and exact law

Let V_d^O(C,w) be a fixed universal, polynomial-time, Boolean oracle verifier
on pairs of d-bit strings. Interpret C as a self-delimited deterministic oracle
verifier program M and input x followed by padding. On malformed encodings
return zero. Otherwise simulate M(x,w) for at most d simulated steps and
return its accept bit, with timeout returning zero. This universal simulation
takes polynomial time in d, including oracle-query lengths. The verifier can
ignore unused witness bits. Its accepted-C language

    {C : exists w in {0,1}^d with V_d^O(C,w)=1}

contains a polynomial-time encoding of every NP^O problem: for its fixed
verifier, on input x choose d polynomially large enough for its code, x,
witness length and running time, and pad C to that length. Wrap the original
verifier to use just its prescribed witness prefix; surplus witness bits
are ignored. This padding is computable in polynomial time and does not
require deciding the NP predicate. Thus deciding positivity for all C decides
every NP^O language. Only this universal-verifier property is needed below.

At L=2d+1, d>=1, use words C b w, with |C|=|w|=d and |b|=1. Set their
weight to one iff b=V_d^O(C,w), otherwise zero. There is exactly one supported
word for each pair (C,w), so the normalizer is exactly 2^(2d). Every supported
word has probability 2^(-2d). An exact sampler chooses C and w uniformly and
outputs C V_d^O(C,w) w. At even lengths and the finitely many unused lengths,
put all mass at the all-zero word. Both the weight evaluator and the sampler
are single uniform polynomial-time oracle algorithms, without any NP oracle.

## Two CDF evaluations decide the verifier's existential predicate

Let F_L(z)=Pr[X lexicographically <= z] on L-bit words. For a fixed C let

    z_0=C 0 1^d,       z_1=C 1 1^d,
    K(C)=number of w with V_d^O(C,w)=1.

All words with first block preceding C occur in both CDFs and cancel.
F_L(z_0) includes the whole C,0 block; F_L(z_1) additionally includes the
whole C,1 block, and no later first block. Consequently, exactly,

    K(C) = 2^(2d) [F_L(z_1)-F_L(z_0)].                 (1)

Polynomial-time exact CDF evaluation therefore decides whether K(C)>0,
which by the encoding above implies NP^O=P^O. More robustly, if each CDF
value is computed with absolute error at most 2^(-(2d+3)), scaling their
difference as in (1) gives error at most 1/4. Comparing the result to 1/2
correctly distinguishes the integer K=0 from K>=1. Here 2d+3=L+2, so a
precision evaluator with runtime polynomial in L and requested bit precision
also yields the same collapse. This precision requirement is exponential
in L; inverse-polynomial absolute CDF accuracy alone is not enough for this
argument. In particular it does not imply a KL lower bound.

## Exact implication for the literature bridge

Bogdanov and Trevisan, Average-Case Complexity (2006), arXiv cs/0606037,
PDF page 17, Definition 2, define PComp through polynomial-time computation
of cumulative probabilities, and explicitly note that point probabilities
are then computable. Their implication is in that direction. The example
above excludes reversing it under NP^O not contained in P^O/poly, even after
adding exact samplability and a known normalizer. It is stronger than merely
not knowing how to normalize the weights, since the example's normalizer is
already explicit.

Thus our efficiently weighted-law hypothesis cannot simply be substituted
for PComp in a cited average-case theorem. The same survey separately gives
an extension from PComp to samplable distributions (section 1.1.5, citing
Impagliazzo-Levin); our example IS samplable, so it does not refute that
extension. Whether ALL efficiently weighted laws can be sampled in the
reported IR2 oracle, or whether direct AR approximation avoids sampling,
remains unresolved. No [IR2] construction has been obtained. The hardest
open piece remains final-oracle weighted-law coverage together with NP
circuit hardness. Target 2 remains OPEN.

The finite checks validate the two-CDF endpoint identity and rounding
threshold on small relations. They do not establish the complexity reduction
by enumeration. No independent audit or formal proof certificate is claimed.

## CDF endpoint convention clarification (version 2)

If the source writes a strict cumulative sum G(z)=Pr[X<z], our F(z) is
G(z)+P_L(z). The point mass is already polynomial-time exactly computable
in this construction. Thus a strict CDF evaluator gives the non-strict CDF
used in (1) with the same precision and polynomial overhead. This implication
does not rely on how a lexicographic successor is represented, including the
last supported word. The CDF-hardness conclusion therefore covers either
endpoint convention. [Definition Permutation Symmetric Property of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] Suppose ${\bf F}({\bf x})$ is a degree-d homogeneous multilinear polynomial random matrix, i.e.,\xspace
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right),
$$
where $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n}$ is a multi-indexed sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. ${\bf F}({\bf x})$ is permutation symmetric if ${\bf A}_{i_1, \dots, i_d} = {\bf A}_{i_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, i_{\sigma(d)}}$ for any permutation $\sigma \in \mathfrak{S}_d$ and any $(i_1, \dots, i_d) \in {\mathcal T}^d_n$.

[Proposition intro-ordinal of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, let $\underline{r}$ be a positive nonincreasing sequence, and  
let $C\subseteq \spt \mu$ be compact. Define compact sets $C_0^{\gamma}$ for
each ordinal number $\gamma$ as follows: 
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[i)] Set $C_0^0:=C$.
  \item[ii)] If $C_0^{\gamma}$ has been defined, set 
             $C_0^{\gamma+1}:=\Jmurz(C_0^{\gamma})$.
  \item[iii)] If $\lambda$ is a nonzero limit ordinal and $C_0^{\gamma}$ has been defined for 
              every $\gamma<\lambda$, set 
        \[
        C_0^{\lambda}:=\bigcap_{\gamma<\lambda}C_0^{\gamma}.
        \]
\end{enumerate}        
Then there exists a countable ordinal $\beta_0$ such that 
$C_0^{\beta_0+1}=C_0^{\beta_0}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (X_t) and (Y_t) be CENTRED Gaussian processes indexed by a finite set T. SUDAKOV-FERNIQUE: if E[(X_s - X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s - Y_t)^2] for all s, t in T, then E[ sup_t X_t ] <= E[ sup_t Y_t ]. Note that only the increment variances are compared and the individual variances may differ; the conclusion is about EXPECTED suprema only. SLEPIAN: if in addition E[X_t^2] = E[Y_t^2] for every t - so that the increment comparison is equivalent to E[X_s X_t] >= E[Y_s Y_t] for all s, t - then the stronger distributional conclusion P( sup_t X_t >= u ) <= P( sup_t Y_t >= u ) holds for every u, and indeed the whole joint law is stochastically ordered coordinatewise. Slepian's extra hypothesis of equal variances is not decorative: without it the distributional conclusion is false, while the Sudakov-Fernique conclusion about expectations survives. Both require CENTRED and GAUSSIAN; there is no comparable general statement for non-Gaussian processes. The finite index set is a convenience; both extend to separable processes by approximation. [Slepian (1962), Sudakov (1971), Fernique (1975); see Adler and Taylor, Random Fields and Geometry, Chapter 2, or Boucheron-Lugosi-Massart Section 13.3]
both processes centred and Gaussian
Sudakov-Fernique: increment variances compared; conclusion only for expected suprema
Slepian: additionally equal pointwise variances; conclusion is distributional

Differentiating F(u) = E[ f(Z(u)) ] and applying the Gaussian integration by parts identity E[ Z_s g(Z) ] = sum_t Sigma(u)_{st} E[ d g / d z_t ] gives F'(u) = (1/2) sum_{s,t} ( Sigma^X_{st} - Sigma^Y_{st} ) E[ d^2 f / dz_s dz_t ]. For the soft maximum the diagonal and off-diagonal second derivatives combine so that F'(u) can be written as a sum over pairs s != t of ( E[(X_s - X_t)^2] - E[(Y_s - Y_t)^2] ) times a NONPOSITIVE quantity, using that the row sums of the Hessian of f_beta vanish because f_beta is invariant under adding a constant to all coordinates. The hypothesis makes each such term nonnegative in the right direction, so F is monotone and F(1) <= F(0). Letting beta -> infinity gives E sup X <= E sup Y. For Slepian, run the same interpolation with f a smooth approximation to the indicator of the orthant {z_t < u for all t}, whose mixed second derivatives are nonnegative; the equal-variance hypothesis kills the diagonal terms, which is exactly what the orthant test function needs and what the soft maximum did not.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:65bc8bd338d9119f2b8ee6c53a7945a71c4d874c489921ae4c702fb50c6fd474","revision_digest":"sha256:b4b2e0be77f5756917d65ef45275366760a72b9a8c024ebef3f9c4928a398295","source_id":"rederived:claude-8e06e1f7-M9","source_revision":"re-derived-2026-08-22; the statement and the hypothesis distinction were checked by the author; the interpolation proof is written at sketch level, with the sign bookkeeping in the soft-maximum step asserted rather than expanded","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

\[
\rho_t:=\rho_{\xi_0}+t(\rho_{\xi_1}-\rho_{\xi_0})
\quad \text{and}\quad

Suppose that Assumption~\ref{ass:regular-interior} holds on \(J\Subset(0,a_{\xi_\star})\) for \(\xi_\circ=\xi_\star\) and uniformly along the path \((\xi_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\), i.e.,

Then, if 
\[
G(r):=\int_1^r (\rho_1(u)-\rho_0(u))\,du 
=0

\]
and
\[
\Vert G\Vert_\infty

Let G be a connected d-regular graph on n vertices with adjacency eigenvalues d = lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ... >= lambda_n >= -d. G is Ramanujan if every eigenvalue other than +-d satisfies |lambda| <= 2 sqrt(d - 1); the number 2 sqrt(d-1) is the spectral radius of the infinite d-regular tree. Alon-Boppana theorem: for every fixed d >= 3 and every epsilon > 0, every d-regular graph with sufficiently many vertices has lambda_2 >= 2 sqrt(d - 1) - epsilon; more precisely lambda_2 >= 2 sqrt(d-1) (1 - O(1/ log^2 n)) (Friedman; Nilli). So Ramanujan graphs are the best possible spectral expanders. Existence: Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak (1988) and independently Margulis constructed explicit infinite families of (p+1)-regular Ramanujan graphs for every prime p congruent to 1 mod 4 (Cayley graphs of PSL(2, Z/qZ) or PGL(2, Z/qZ) according to the Legendre symbol of p modulo q, the eigenvalue bound coming from the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture for modular forms proved by Deligne), later extended to all prime powers (Morgenstern 1994); Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava proved by the method of interlacing families, non-constructively, that infinite families of bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree d >= 3 exist (Ann. Math. 2015, via 2-lifts) and then that bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree exist on every even number of vertices (interlacing families IV, 2018); Friedman (2008) proved Alon's conjecture that a random d-regular graph is nearly Ramanujan, lambda_2 <= 2 sqrt(d-1) + epsilon with high probability, and Bordenave (2020) gave a shorter proof. Ramanujan graphs give the optimal expander mixing lemma constant and near-optimal derandomisation gadgets.
d >= 3, G connected and d-regular (bipartite graphs have lambda_n = -d, which is excluded from the Ramanujan condition together with +d)
the Alon-Boppana bound is asymptotic in n for fixed d
existence results are cited, not proved

[Defn def:downwards-closed of arXiv:2412.09535, 'Local limit theorem for joint subgraph counts'] A finite set of non-$\kone$ connected graphs $\mathcal{H}$ is \emph{downwards closed} if for all $H \in \mathcal{H}$ and $H' \preceq H$ with $H'$ connected and not $\kone$, we have $H' \in \mathcal{H}$. In this case, it is true that if $H' \preceq H \in \mathcal{H}$, all components of $H'$ are in $\mathcal{H} \cup \set{\kone}$; thus (prop:linrel of the paper) implies that
\[\setr[X_H \colon H \in \mathcal{H} \cup \set{\kone}] = \setr[\gamma_H \colon H \in \mathcal{H} \cup \set{\kone}].\]
Call this algebra $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{H}}$.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4d0dd9163c5404d1fe99c89990ea2a179ab857eff446b8793059554d2ce64afd","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4d/4d0dd9163c5404d1fe99c89990ea2a179ab857eff446b8793059554d2ce64afd.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:3b007cc8327fbde1dc2d15b8b99bd1e58252354dfd1268b792a572d9599c9123","bundle_entry_key":"transition-kappa-common-hessian","bundle_id":"population.t362-transition-kappa-005","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"optimization; random reshuffling; transition condition number; optimal constant step","draft":"w732/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.randomreshuffling:common-hessian-random-reshuffling-exact-transition-condition-number-optimizer","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Target 1: the exact transition path kappa=4T/log(T)

Status: proof draft (unaudited). This is an exact transition path, not a theorem for every sequence with kappa*log(T)/T->4. No priority claim.

## Statement

Use the normalized common-Hessian model of C001 with fixed n>=2, fixed deterministic x0!=0,y0, fixed zero-sum linear terms of mean squares s1>=0,s2>0, and fresh independent uniform epoch permutations shared across coordinates. For T=nK->infinity set exactly kappa=4T/log T. Put ell=log T, m=log ell and

    D_n = n/(n-1) if n is even,
          (n+1)/n if n is odd.

Then the globally minimized final-epoch expected function error P_T obeys

    min_{eta>=0} P_T(eta) ~ s2*D_n*ell^2/(16*T*m).         (1)

Every sequence of global minimizers has

    kappa*eta_T = 2 - (4+o(1))*m/ell.                    (2)

The exact transition path is essential to the proof; subleading changes in kappa can change the competing transient scale.

## Endpoint residue

In the settled recursion put q=kappa*eta, a=1-q,

    W_n(q)=sum_{0<=i<j<n}(a^i-a^j)^2,
    J_n(q)=q^2*W_n(q)/[2(n-1)(1-a^(2n))],  0<q<2.

The stiff variance is exactly (s2/kappa)*J_n(q)*(1-a^(2T)). At q=2, the n powers (-1)^i have floor(n/2) of one parity and ceil(n/2) of the other. Thus

    W_n(2)=4*floor(n/2)*ceil(n/2)
          = n^2 (n even), or n^2-1 (n odd).

For delta=2-q->0 positively, 1-a^(2n)=1-(1-delta)^(2n)~2n*delta. Hence

    delta*J_n(2-delta) -> W_n(2)/[n(n-1)] = D_n.         (3)

Here n is fixed; n-1>0 and the stationary denominator is positive on (0,2). The finite-horizon variance, including q=2 and q>2, is always

    R_T = [s2*q^2*W_n(q)/(2(n-1)*kappa)]
                *sum_{r=0}^{K-1}(1-q)^(2nr).             (4)

## Upper bound

1. Choose z_c=2m-3log m, delta_c=2z_c/ell and q_c=2-delta_c. For all sufficiently large T, z_c>0, delta_c->0 and delta_c*T->infinity. Thus 0<q_c<2. From (3)-(4),

    R_T(eta_c) ~ s2*D_n/(kappa*delta_c)
              = s2*D_n*ell^2/(8*T*z_c)
              ~ s2*D_n*ell^2/(16*T*m).                 (5)

We used (1-delta_c)^(2T)<=exp(-2delta_c*T)->0.

2. Let A=x0^2/2>0. Since eta_c=q_c/kappa and T/kappa^2->0, the flat deterministic contribution is

    A*(1-eta_c)^(2T)
       = (A/T)*exp(z_c+O(T/kappa^2))
       ~ A*ell^2/(T*m^3),                               (6)

which is o(ell^2/(T*m)). The identity -2q_c*T/kappa=-ell+z_c uses the exact definition kappa=4T/ell, not merely its leading ratio.

The stiff deterministic term is at most (kappa*y0^2/2)*exp(-2delta_c*T), negligible compared with the scale in (5). Indeed delta_c*T is of order T*m/ell, which dominates log T, whereas the logarithms of kappa and the reciprocal target scale are O(log T). The flat variance is O(eta_c^3)=O(ell^3/T^3), also negligible. Thus the minimum is at most (1+o(1)) times (5), and tends to zero.

## Localization of every unrestricted global optimizer

3. A global minimizer exists because the exact error is a continuous coercive polynomial: the last epoch and pair (0,1) in (4) give P_T>=s2*q^4/[2(n-1)*kappa]. Write q_T=kappa*eta_T for any sequence of global minimizers. Eventually q_T<2. In fact if q_T>=2, then W_n(q_T)>=q_T^2 and every term of the geometric sum in (4) is >=1, so

    P_T(eta_T) >= 8*s2*K/[(n-1)*kappa]
                 = [2*s2/(n(n-1))]*ell ->infinity,

contradicting the vanishing upper bound. This excludes all unstable steps, not only those close to the endpoint.

4. For 0<=q_T<2, eta_T->0 and T*eta_T^2=O(ell^2/T)->0. Uniformly in this interval the flat transient equals

    A*exp(-q_T*ell/2+o(1)).

If q_T<=2-epsilon along a subsequence for any fixed epsilon>0, that transient is at least A*T^(-1+epsilon/2)*exp(o(1)), exceeding the candidate bound of order ell^2/(T*m). Therefore q_T->2 from below. Set delta_T=2-q_T->0.

5. Necessarily delta_T*T->infinity. Otherwise take a subsequence on which delta_T*T<=M. For large T on that subsequence delta_T<=1/2 and log(1-delta_T)>=-2delta_T. Every summand in (4) is then at least

    (1-delta_T)^(2n(K-1)) >= exp(-4delta_T*T)>=exp(-4M).

Since q_T->2 and W_n(q_T)>=q_T^2, (4) gives P_T>=const*K/kappa, diverging like ell. This contradicts the upper bound. The constant can depend on M but is strictly positive. Hence (3) applies and the finite-horizon variance multiplier tends to one.

## Optimization on the transition scale

6. Define z_T=delta_T*ell/2>0. By the endpoint residue and step 5,

    R_T(eta_T) = (1+o(1))*s2*D_n*ell^2/(8*T*z_T).        (7)

The flat transient is (A/T)*exp(z_T+o(1)), by the same uniform expansion used in step 4. Comparing this transient with the upper bound gives

    z_T <= 2m-log m+O(1),                               (8)

so limsup z_T/m<=2. Comparing (7) with that upper bound gives liminf z_T/m>=2. Consequently z_T/m->2, which is (2). Substitution into (7), combined with the upper bound, proves (1). All other objective contributions are nonnegative, so no cancellation or exchange of expectation and minimization is required.

## Hypotheses and unpaid step

x0!=0 is used in (8); if initialization is exactly the optimum, eta=0 gives zero error and (1) would fail. s2>0 is used in every noise localization and in (7); with no stiff noise the endpoint pole is absent. Fixed n is used in (3) and the stationary estimates. n>=2 makes n-1 positive. Independent epoch permutations enter the inherited recursion; coordinate-noise independence is not needed because the objective is diagonal. Exact kappa=4T/log T is used in (6) and (8).

This proves a named-target-1 transition path in draft form. General sequences satisfying only kappa*log(T)/T->4 remain unpaid, as do general finite-sum Hessians and the full T362 obstruction. Independent audit should focus on the uniform all-minimizer localization in steps 3-5 and the two comparisons in step 6. Exact finite algebra checks are checks of (3)-(4), not certificates of the asymptotic theorem. \[
R(p):=\left| k \in \{0,...,n\} : \, f_p(k)=f_p(k+1)\right|.
\] 
similarily, we define the number of \emph{up-turns} by
\[
U(p):=\left| k \in \{0,...,n\} : \, f_p(k)<f_p(k+1)\right|,
\] 
and the number of \emph{down-turns} by
\[
D(p):=\left| k \in \{0,...,n\} : \, f_p(k)>f_p(k+1)\right|.
\]

[Theo 4 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] i) For all $F\in D_h( \R^{2n})$,  we have, 
  
    
      $$ F(X) =  ( \pi h)^{-n} \int _{\R^{2n}}e^{ - \frac {1 }  {h}   |X-T|^2 }
      H_hF(T) dT, $$

      $$  H_hF(T) =  ( 4 \pi h)^{-n}   \int _{\R^{2n}} 
       F^{\rm ext} \Big(  T+\frac{Z}{2} , T-\frac{Z}{2}\Big ) 
      e^{ - \frac {1 }  {4h}   |Z|^2 } dZ,$$

    ii) The operator $H_h$ maps $D_h (\R^{2n})$ into

    iii)  Let  $F\in D_h( \R^{2n})$. There exists a function $\widetilde F$ on $\C^{2n} \simeq \R^{4n} $ which is holomorphic in the following sense,     
    \be (\partial _1 + i \partial _2 ) \widetilde F = 0,\
    (\partial _3  + i \partial _4 ) \widetilde F = 0
  \ee 
    
   with a restriction to $\R^{2n}$ 
     equals to $F$, that is to say,  $\widetilde F (x , 0, \xi , 0) = F(x , \xi)$. Moreover, for $X,Y\in\R^{2n}$,
      
      \be   | \widetilde F (X+iY) |  \leq 
    ( 4 \pi h)^{-n}   \Vert \psi_F \Vert _{L^1 (\R^{2n})}

that is to say, for any $(x_1 , x_2 , x_3 , x_4)\in\R^{4n}$,

 \frac {x+y} {2} ,   \frac {\xi - \eta } {2} ,

 If $\widetilde F$ is satisfying  (\ref{Cauchy-Riem}) then $F^{\rm ext}$

[Prop P:half-space-horizon-marginals of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] As $n\to\infty$, the process $R^{(n)}$ has a distributional limit $R^{\mathsf{DL}}=\{R^{\mathsf{DL}}_i\}_{i=1}^k$, under the uniform-on-compact topology. 
    We can describe the process $R^{\mathsf{DL}}$ explicitly as follows.
	
Let $\mathcal{B} = (\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_2, \ldots, \mathcal{B}_{2k})$ be $2k$ independent Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ of diffusivity $2$, drift $\lambda_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_i, i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket$ and $-\lambda_i$ for $\mathcal{B}_{2k+1-i}$. Next, let $\{X(-i, j) : i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket, j \in \llbracketi +1, 2k +1 - i \rrbracket\}$ be an array of exponential random variables, independent of each other and $\mathcal B$, satisfying 
\[
X(-i, j) \sim \begin{cases}
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 - \lambda_j/2), \qquad &j \in \llbracketi + 1, k \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 + \lambda_{2k + 1 -j}/2), \qquad &j\in\llbracketk + 1, 2k - i \rrbracket, \\
\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i/2 - \rho), \qquad &j=2k + 1- i.
\end{cases}
\]
We turn this array into a 
sequence of cadlag functions $X = (X_1, \dots, X_{2k})$ on $(-\infty, 0]$ by the rule that $X_j(0) = 0$ for all $j$, and the measure $dX$ has atoms of size $X(-i, j)$ at each coordinate $(-i, j)$ where $X(-i, j)$ is defined (and is supported on these points). Equivalently, the path $X_j$ has a jump of size $X(-i, j)$ at location $-i$.

Let $X \mathcal{B}$ be the concatenation of $X$ and $\mathcal{B}$. (See Figure (fig:hfsh of the paper) for an illustration.) Then:
$$
R^{\mathsf{DL}}_i(x) = \begin{cases}
X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; x, 2k) - X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; 0, 2k), \qquad &x \ge 0, \\
X\mathcal{B}^{\Delta_{2k+1}}(-i, i; |x|, 2k) - X\mathcal{B}(-i, i; 0, 2k), \qquad &x \le 0.
\end{cases}
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop P:half-space-horizon-marginals of arXiv:2604.10020

satisfies the fast \textnormal{BL}-mixing correlation condition for $p$ and $q$, that is to say (equation e.mppmixing of the paper) holds  for $f \in \textnormal{BL}((\mathbb{K}')^{p})$, $g \in \textnormal{BL}((\mathbb{K}')^{q}),$ and some fast decreasing function $\omega_{p+q}$. 
\item   Part~(i.BL-iterated-marks of the paper)
 above remains valid if
$\xi$ satisfies fast \textnormal{BL}~cluster-localization---that is,
conditions~(equation Lp-stab-infinite-weak1 of the paper) and~(equation Lp-stab-infinite-weak2 of the paper)---on
$\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ for  $p,q$, and $p+q$.

 \item  If 
  $\xi$ is fast stabilizing on $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ as in (equation stab-infinite of the paper) (via stopping sets) for $p,q$ and $p+q$, 
then  $\dbtilde\mathcal{P}$ has fast $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations for $p$ and $q$, i.e., (equation e.mppmixing of the paper) holds for $f \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^{p})$, $g \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^{q}),$ and some fast decreasing function $\omega_{p+q}$.
\end{enumerate}
In  all cases~(i.BL-iterated-marks of the paper), (i.BLc-iterated-marks of the paper), and~(i.iterated-marks of the paper), the  fast decreasing function $\omega_{p+q}$ associated to $\dbtilde \mathcal{P}$ depends on the functions $\varphi_{p+q}$ and $\phi $ as well as on  the constants $(C_k)_{k = 1}^{\infty}$ and $\kappa_{p+q}$ related to $\xi$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, respectively. In particular, there exist constants $C<\infty$, $c>0$ which  depend on $p,q$,  such that for all $s > 0$
  
\begin{equation} \omega_{p+q}(s) \leq C \exp(-cs^b) + C\varphi_{p + q}\big( cs^{b(1-a)/2( p + q + d)} \big),
\end{equation}
where $a,b$ are as in~(equation eqn:sum of the paper) and (equation phibd of the paper), respectively. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let X_1, ..., X_n be INDEPENDENT random variables taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces - they need NOT be identically distributed and need not be real-valued - and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with E[Z^2] < infinity. Let X_i' be an independent copy of X_i, independent of everything else, and put Z^{(i)} = f(X_1, ..., X_{i-1}, X_i', X_{i+1}, ..., X_n). Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z^{(i)})^2 ] = sum_{i=1}^n E[ ((Z - Z^{(i)})_+)^2 ]. Equivalently, and often more convenient, Var(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z_i)^2 ] for ANY random variables Z_i that are measurable functions of the n-1 variables other than X_i; taking Z_i = inf over the i-th coordinate of f gives the version used for suprema and for first-passage times. Equality holds if and only if f is a sum of functions of the individual coordinates. Independence is the only structural hypothesis and it is essential; the inequality is FALSE for dependent coordinates. Applied with a bounded-difference function it recovers the variance half of McDiarmid's inequality; applied to first-passage percolation with the geodesic length as the influence bound it produces the linear variance upper bound. [Efron and Stein (1981), Steele (1986); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.1]
X_1, ..., X_n independent (arbitrary measurable state spaces, not necessarily identically distributed)
E[Z^2] < infinity
X_i' an independent copy of X_i

[Prop max_action of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] For any $\beta\in \mathbb R$, the action $A_{\beta}$ has a unique minimizer $(\pi_1^{(\beta)}, \pi_2^{(\beta)})$ in $\mathcal{D}$. For $\beta \leq 0$, we have $\pi_1^{(\beta)}=\pi_2^{(\beta)}=\frac{1}{2}\Leb_{[0,1]}$. 
    For $\beta>0$, the densities of $\pi_1^{(\beta)}$ and $\pi_2^{(\beta)}$ on $[0,1]$ are given by
	\begin{equation}
	    \rho_1^{(\beta)}(x) := \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(\beta(\frac12-x) \right)}, 
        \quad \rho_2^{(\beta)}(x) := \frac{1}{1+\exp\left(\beta(x-\frac12) \right)}.
	\end{equation}
	In particular, both $\pi_1^{(\beta)}$ and $\pi_2^{(\beta)}$ have total mass $\frac{1}{2}$.

[Corollary 20 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $l_0:=0$. For a strictly increasing sequence $l_1<\cdots<l_s$ of positive integers, the following statements are equivalent.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} There exists a cyclic $C_{p^s}$-extension of $k((t))$ whose lower jumps are $l_1<\cdots<l_s$.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} The following conditions hold.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (2.a)} We have $p\nmid l_1$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (2.b)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s-1\rrbracket$ we have $p^j\mid l_{j+1}-l_j$ and
$$l_{j+1}-l_j\ge (p-1)\sum_{i=0}^{j-1} p^{j-i}(l_{i+1}-l_i).$$

\noindent
{\bf (2.c)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s-1\rrbracket$ such that $l_{j+1}-l_j> (p-1)\sum_{i=0}^{j-1} p^{j-i}(l_{i+1}-l_i)$, the positive integer $l_1+\sum_{i=1}^{j}\frac{l_{i+1}-l_i}{p^i}$ is not divisible by $p$.

body:
[Corollary cor:label-configuration-reversal of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For fixed $h\geq2$ and $k\geq3$, as $q\to\infty$ a uniformly random
$A\in\binom{[q]}k$ satisfies
\[
 \mathbb P(A\text{ is not }B_h)
 =\frac{k!K_{h,k}}q+O_{h,k}(q^{-2}),
 \qquad K_{h,k}\asymp_k h^{k-2}.
\]
For each $2\leq r\leq h$,
\[
 \mathbb P(|hA|=M_{h,k}-M_{h-r,k})
 =\frac{k!\kappa_{k,r}}q+O_{h,k}(q^{-2}).
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb P\bigl(r_{h,k}(|hA|)\leq1\bigr)
   &=1-O_{h,k}(q^{-2}),\\
  \mathbb P\bigl(r_h(A)=1\mid A\text{ is not }B_h\bigr)
   &=1-O_{h,k}(q^{-1}).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
By contrast, if $k\geq4$ is fixed and $N_{h,k}$ is uniform in the finite set
$\mathcal R(h,k)$, then, as $h\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P\bigl(r_{h,k}(N_{h,k})\leq1\bigr)
 =\frac{h}{|\mathcal R(h,k)|}
 =h^{-(k-2)+o_k(1)}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Thus principal labels are asymptotically negligible among attainable
cardinalities, although their realizations account for asymptotically almost
every fixed-order configuration in a growing interval.
Here $h$ is fixed before $q\to\infty$;
no joint $(h,q)$ assertion is made.

[Pro Pro_basic_properties of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] Let $I\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a nondegenerate interval.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
 \item If $L_i:I\to\mathbb{R}$ is strongly $\alpha_i$-convex for $i=1,2$, where $\alpha_1,\alpha_2:(I-I)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ are even error functions
       and $c_1,c_2\in\mathbb{R}_+$, then $c_1L_1+c_2L_2$ is strongly $(c_1\alpha_1+c_2\alpha_2)$-convex.
 \item If $\alpha_1,\alpha_2:(I-I)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ are even error functions with $\alpha_1\leqslant\alpha_2$ and $L:I\to\mathbb{R}$ is strongly $\alpha_2$-convex, then $L$ is strongly $\alpha_1$-convex as well.
 \item If, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $L_n:I\to\mathbb{R}$ is strongly $\alpha_n$-convex, where $\alpha_n:(I-I)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ is an even error function,
 and the sequences $(L_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $ (\alpha_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ pointwise converge to $L:I\to\mathbb{R}$ and to $\alpha:(I-I)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ as $n\to\infty$, respectively, then $L$ is strongly $\alpha$-convex.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity. Scarce calibration (P30, 240 of the calibration rows per cell, split B): P30 (a) HELD: at n = 240 the simplex beats least squares by +14.10 on EMIT (full calibration +8.83); (b) REFUTED: t* averages 0.22 on EMIT and the blend reads -2.61 vs the simplex; (c) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells and the simplex reads +2.27 vs least squares (full calibration -0.18); falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT) TRIGGERED. The observable part of the bias shift (P31): adding t^2 (D_ev - D_cal), the shift in the two bases' mean squared disagreement between the evaluation and calibration rows, to the criterion - P31 (a) REFUTED: the R'-blend reads -0.71 vs the simplex on EMIT split B (R-blend +0.08) and +0.71 on split C (R-blend +0.63); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R'-blend is -0.11 vs the R-blend on split B and -0.12 on split C; (c) REFUTED: mean t** 0.39 against t* 0.33 on EMIT, share of the hindsight optimum 0.07 -> -0.62; falsifier (R'-blend worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 on any corpus or split) TRIGGERED.

    \item For any flat $G$ in $L$, we have
    \(
        \rk_M F + \rk_M G = \rk_M (F \vee G) + \rk_M (F \cap G).
    \)
    \item For any flat $G$ of $M$ with $\rk_M F + \rk_M G > \rk M$, we have $\rk_M (F \cap G) > 0$.
    \end{enumerate}
    We say $F$ is \textbf{{modular}} in $M$ if it satisfies these equivalent conditions.
title: {\cite{constructions}*{Theorem 3.3}}

[Theorem 19 of arXiv:2609.01098, 'Gaussian upper bounds for averaged heat semigroups on graphs'] Let $x,y\in X$, $p\in[1,\infty]$, $r_2\geq r_1\geq0$, $t>0$, and $\delta\in(0,1)$. Assume that for $z\in\{x,y\}$ and all $\omega\in\ell^\infty(X)$ there are $\phi_z(h)=\phi_z(p,r_1,r_2,\delta,t,h)>0$, monotone increasing in $h$, such that 
\[
\left(\fint_{t/2-\delta r_1^2}^{t/2+\delta r_1^2}\|{B_z(r_1)}P_\tau^\omega\|_{2,2p}^{2p}\drm \tau\right)^\frac{1}{p}
\leq \phi_z(h(\omega))^2\fint_{t/2-\delta  r_2^2}^{t/2+\delta r_2^2}\| P_\tau^\omega\|_{2,2}^2\drm \tau.
\] 
Then, for $t\geq 2r_1^2$,  we have
\[
\left(
\fint_{t-2\delta r_1^2}^{t+2\delta r_1^2} \|{B_x(r_1)}P_{\tau}{B_y(r_1)}\|_{(2p)',2p}^p\drm \tau
\right)^\frac{1}{p}
\leq 
\phi_x(\sigma)\phi_y(\sigma)\euler^{\sigma(\delta r_2^2-t/2)-\Lambda(t-2\delta r_1^2)-tS^{-2}\zeta(\rho(B_x(r_1),B_y(r_1))S/t)},
\]
where 
\[
\sigma=\sigma(\rho(B_x(r_1),B_y(r_1))S/t),\qquad \sigma(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}-1.
\]
title: Theorem 19 of arXiv:2609.01098

Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear, i.e. H(p)/|p| → +∞ as |p| → ∞. Its Legendre (Fenchel) transform is L(q) := sup_{p ∈ R^n} ( p·q - H(p) ), q ∈ R^n, and L is called the Lagrangian associated with H. Then: (i) the supremum is attained for every q, and L is finite, convex and superlinear; (ii) L* = H, i.e. H(p) = sup_q ( p·q - L(q) ) (duality of H and L); (iii) Fenchel-Young: p·q ≤ H(p) + L(q) for all p,q, with equality iff q ∈ ∂H(p) iff p ∈ ∂L(q); (iv) if in addition H ∈ C^2 with D^2H(p) ≥ θ I for all p and some θ > 0, then DH: R^n → R^n is a bijection, L ∈ C^1, DL = (DH)^{-1}, DL is Lipschitz with constant 1/θ, and consequently L(q+w) + L(q-w) - 2L(q) ≤ |w|^2/θ for all q,w.
H: R^n → R is finite everywhere and convex (hence continuous)
H is superlinear: H(p)/|p| → ∞ as |p| → ∞
for part (iv): H ∈ C^2 and D^2H ≥ θI with θ > 0 (which already implies superlinearity)
title: Legendre Transform of a Convex Superlinear Hamiltonian

 q_{ij}^A\!\left(\frac{\rho_i}{\rho_j}c\right).

$V_{ij}(A^t)=V_{ji}(A)$.

[Theorem 1 ($L_p$ Brunn-Minkowski inequality) of arXiv:2609.00743, '$L_p$ Brunn-Minkowski inequality for the eigenvalue of generalized Monge-Ampère equation'] Suppose $k\ge 0$. Let $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$ be bounded, smooth and strictly convex domains containing the origin as an interior point, and $\Omega_\alpha:=(1-\alpha)\Omega_0+_p \alpha\Omega_1$ be the $L_p$-Minkowski addition of $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$, where $p:=k+1\ge 1$ and $\alpha\in[0,1]$. Then
\begin{equation}
    \lambda(\Omega_\alpha)^{-\frac{p}{2n}}\ge (1-\alpha)\lambda(\Omega_0)^{-\frac{p}{2n}}+\alpha\lambda(\Omega_1)^{-\frac{p}{2n}}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: $L_p$ Brunn-Minkowski inequality

[Corollary Dynamic formulation of $W_p$ of arXiv:2603.14163, '\LARGE \bf Tail Bounds for Queues with Abandonment: Constant, Moderate, Large Deviations, '] Let $\mathcal{L}(X), \mathcal{L}(Z') \in \mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R})$ and suppose there exists a weakly continuous curve $\mu_t:(0,\infty)\to\mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R})$ and a Borel vector field $v_t$ such that
    $\partial_t \mu_t + \partial_x(\mu_t v_t)=0$,
    $\sup_{t\in(0,\infty)} \|x\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}<\infty$. Moreover, suppose
    $\mu_t \Rightarrow \mathcal{L}(X)$ as $t\downarrow 0$, and
    $\mu_t \Rightarrow \mathcal{L}(Z')$ as $t\uparrow \infty$.
    Then
    \[
    W_p(\mathcal{L}(X),\mathcal{L}(Z'))
    \le
    \inf\left\{
    \int_{0}^{\infty}
    \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} |v_t(x)|^p\,d\mu_t(x)\right)^{1/p}\!dt
    :\ \partial_t \mu_t + \partial_x(\mu_t v_t)=0,\ 
    \mu_t \overset{t\downarrow 0}{\Rightarrow} \mathcal{L}(X),\ 
    \mu_t \overset{t\uparrow \infty}{\Rightarrow} \mathcal{L}(Z')
    \right\},
    \]
    where $\Rightarrow$ denotes weak convergence. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Dynamic formulation of $W_p$

[Theorem thm:vonLuxburg of arXiv:2606.14895, 'Effective Resistances and Commute Times in Sparse Random Geometric Graphs'] Let $G_n = (V_n, E_n)$ be an RGG with radius of connection $r_n$ from $n$ uniformly distributed points on $\mathbb{T}^2$ with vertex degrees $D_u$ and graph volume $\mathrm{Vol}(G_n) = \sum_{u\in V_n} D_u$. Suppose that the fixed pair of vertices $u$ and $v$ at positions $X_u$ and $X_v$ are separated by Euclidean distance $d(X_u,X_v) > 8r_n$. Assuming that $n r_n^2 / \ln n \to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$, there exists a constant $c$ such that the commute distance satisfies, with probability converging to $1$, 
\[
nr_n^2\left\vert\frac{1}{\mathrm{Vol}(G_n)}C_{uv} -
\left(\frac{1}{D_u}+\frac{1}{D_v}\right)\right| \leq c/nr_n^3\,.
\]
Therefore, further requiring that $r_n\to 0$ and $nr_n^3\to\infty$ yields
\[
C_{uv} \;\to\; \mathrm{Vol}(G_n)\left(\frac{1}{D_u} + \frac{1}{D_v}\right)\qquad almost\;surely\,.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of von Luxburg et al.\ \cite{vonLuxburg2014} as applied to uniformly distributed points on $\mathbb{T}^2$

Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear, L = H*, g: R^n → R Lipschitz, and let u(x,t) = min_y ( tL((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) be the Hopf-Lax function. (i) If g is semiconcave with constant C, i.e. g(x+z) - 2g(x) + g(x-z) ≤ C|z|^2 for all x,z ∈ R^n, then u(x+z,t) - 2u(x,t) + u(x-z,t) ≤ C|z|^2 for all x,z ∈ R^n and all t > 0. (ii) If instead H ∈ C^2 with D^2H(p) ≥ θ I for all p and some θ > 0 (uniform convexity), and g is merely Lipschitz, then u(x+z,t) - 2u(x,t) + u(x-z,t) ≤ |z|^2 / (θ t) for all x,z and all t > 0. In dimension one, (ii) is equivalent to the one-sided (Oleinik) derivative bound u_x(x+h,t) - u_x(x,t) ≤ h/(θ t) for h > 0 in the distributional sense. This one-sided bound is what distinguishes the Hopf-Lax solution from other Lipschitz almost-everywhere solutions.
H convex and superlinear; L = H*
g Lipschitz (plus, in (i), semiconcave with constant C)
in (ii): H ∈ C^2 with D^2H ≥ θI, θ > 0
t > 0 (the bound in (ii) degenerates as t ↓ 0)

body: For differentiable problems, the KKT conditions at a point are: primal feasibility, dual feasibility (lambda >= 0), complementary slackness (lambda_i g_i(x) = 0 for each i), and stationarity (the gradient of the Lagrangian in x vanishes). Under a constraint qualification they are necessary for optimality; for convex problems they are also sufficient, and with Slater's condition they characterize the optima.
title: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker Conditions

Let X be a nonnegative random variable (or f a nonnegative measurable function on a measure space, integrated against the measure) and a > 0. Then P(X >= a) <= E[X] / a. More generally, if phi: [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) is nondecreasing and phi(a) > 0, then for any real random variable X, P(X >= a) <= E[phi(X^+)] / phi(a), and for any X and a > 0, P(|X| >= a) <= E|X|^p / a^p for every p > 0 (Markov applied to |X|^p). The bound is attained: for X taking the value a with probability m/a and 0 otherwise (0 < m <= a), E X = m and P(X >= a) = m/a.

body:
Let d,m>=1 and x in R^d be deterministic with ||x||_2=sqrt(d). Let w_i be iid N(0,I_d/d), a_i iid N(0,1/m), and suppose all hidden and output weights are independent. Put f(x)=sum_(i=1..m) a_i sigma(w_i^T x). Assume sigma:R->R is continuous and nonconstant, differentiable almost everywhere, has an almost-everywhere continuous derivative, and |sigma_prime(t)|<=C_sigma(1+|t|^(k-1)) almost everywhere for a fixed integer k>=1 and constant C_sigma>0. There is a C>0 depending only on sigma such that, for every delta in (0,1), with probability at least1-delta, ||grad f(x)||_2 <= C(1+log(1/delta)/sqrt(d))(1+1/sqrt(m delta)). Consequently for any deterministic s>0 and x_s=x-sign(f(x))*s*grad f(x), on the same event ||x_s-x||_2/||x||_2 <= (Cs/sqrt(d))(1+log(1/delta)/sqrt(d))(1+1/sqrt(m delta)). This is the size estimate; no sign-reversal success rate is asserted here.
Deterministic input of norm sqrt(d)
Independent hidden Gaussian vectors of variance1/d and Gaussian output weights of variance1/m
Finite m,d; no relative-width restriction
Continuous nonconstant activation with a.e. differentiability and a.e. continuous derivative
Fixed polynomial growth bound on the derivative
delta in (0,1), deterministic positive step s

body: In calculus, Taylor's theorem gives an approximation of a -times differentiable function around a given point by a polynomial of degree , called the -th-order Taylor polynomial. For a smooth function, the Taylor polynomial is the truncation at the order of the Taylor series of the function. The first-order Taylor polynomial is the linear approximation of the function, and the second-order Taylor polynomial is often referred to as the quadratic approximation. There are several versions of Taylor's theorem, some giving explicit estimates of the approximation error of the function by its Taylor polynomial.
title: Taylor's theorem

[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] We consider a cyclic $C_{p^s}$-extension of $k((t))$, its lower jumps $l_1<\cdots <l_s$, and its upper jumps $u_1<\cdots<u_s$. Then the following properties hold. 

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The lower and upper jumps determine uniquely each other by the recursive identities $l_1:=u_1$ and $l_i:=l_{i-1}+p^{i-1}(u_i-u_{i-1})$ for each $i\in\llbracket2,s\rrbracket$. 

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket $ we have $l_j=u_1+\sum_{i=1}^{j-1} p^i(u_{i+1}-u_i)$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ we have identities 
$$\sum_{i=1}^j \frac{l_i}{p^i}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^j p^{i-1}u_i}{p^j}$$
and
$$p^{j-1}u_j:=l_j+(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}l_ip^{j-i-1}.$$

{\bf (4)} For $b\in\llbracket0,p^s-1\rrbracket$, write
\[
b=\delta_{1,b}+\delta_{2,b}p+\cdots+\delta_{s,b}p^{s-1}
\]
with $\delta_{i,b}\in\llbracket0,p-1\rrbracket$ for each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ and define
\[
N_{s,b}:=\sum_{i=1}^s p^{s-i}\bigl[p-1+(p-1-\delta_{i,b})l_i\bigr].
\] Then for each $b\in \llbracket1,p^s-1\rrbracket$, if $j\in\llbracket0,s-1\rrbracket$ is the largest such that $p^j\mid b$, then we have identities 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}&=p^{s-j-1}\Big[l_{j+1}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j p^{j+1-i}l_i\Big]\\
&=p^{s-j-1}[l_1+\sum_{i=1}^j p^i(u_{i+1}-pu_i)].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
In particular, $N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}\ge p^{s-j-1}l_1\ge l_1>0$ and therefore we have $\frac{l_{j+1}}{p^{j+1}}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j\frac{l_i}{p^i}\ge\frac{l_1}{p^{j+1}}>0$.

Then, there exists a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$, which supports two $\llbracket 1, k \rrbracket$-indexed geometric line ensembles $\mathfrak{Q}^t$ and $\mathfrak{Q}^b$ on $\llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket$ such that the law of $\mathfrak{Q}^{t}$ {\big (}resp. $\mathfrak{Q}^b${\big )} under $\mathbb{P}$ is given by $\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{Inter},\operatorname{Geom}}^{T_0, T_1, \vec{x}\,^t, \vec{y}\,^t, \infty, g^t}$ {\big (}resp. $\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{Inter},\operatorname{Geom}}^{T_0, T_1, \vec{x}\,^b, \vec{y}\,^b, \infty, g^b}${\big )} and such that $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $Q_i^t(r) \geq Q^b_i(r)$ for all $i \in \llbracket 1, k \rrbracket$ and $r \in \llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket$. For the minimal spanning forest of a homogeneous Poisson process in R^d, connectivity (a single tree) is proved only for d = 2 (Alexander) and is open for every d >= 3. The Lyons-Peres-Schramm theory (Minimal spanning forests, Ann. Probab. 2006, on transitive graphs; the Poisson case is its continuum analogue) does not settle it: uniqueness of the infinite cluster makes the free and wired minimal spanning forests coincide, and the absence of percolation at criticality makes every tree of the wired forest one-ended, but neither gives a single tree. The same argument would make the minimal spanning forest of Z^d connected for d >= 11, where theta(p_c) = 0 is known from the lace expansion and uniqueness holds by Burton-Keane, and that question is open (Lyons-Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, Question 11.35). The Newman-Stein heuristic predicts infinitely many trees when d > 8.

Assumes: homogeneous Poisson process in R^d, Euclidean edge lengths

[Lemma lem:prefix-postbin-coefficient-estimates-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] There is an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every \(\xi\neq0\), \(d\in\mathfrak D_\xi\), \(\ell\ge0\), and child interval \(J\in\mathcal D_{\ell+1}^\circ\), 
\[
\lvert c_J(\xi,d,\ell)\rvert
\le C2^{\ell-m_{\xi,d}}
\qquad
(0\le\ell<m_{\xi,d}),
\]
and
\[
\lvert c_J(\xi,d,\ell)\rvert\le C
\qquad
(\ell\ge m_{\xi,d}).
\]

[Proposition prop:tight1 of arXiv:2412.02160, 'A functional central limit theorem for weighted occupancy processes of the Karlin model'] Assume $|a_{i+j}-a_i| \le Cj^\beta$ with $\beta\in[0,\alpha/2)$. 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For all 
$p\in[1,\alpha/{2\beta})$,
 we have, for some constant $C$, 
\begin{equation}
{\mathbb E}\abs{\what W_n(t)-\what W_n(s)}^{2p} \le C \pp{\sigma_n^2|t-s|^{\alpha} + \sigma_n^{2p}|t-s|^{\alpha p}}, \mbox{ for all } 0\le s<t\le 1, n\in{\mathbb N}.
\end{equation}
\item For some constant $C>0$, almost surely, 
\begin{equation}
\abs{\what W_n(t)-\what W_n(s)}\le C (N(nt)-N(ns) + n(t-s)), \mbox{ for all } 0\le s\le t\le 1.
\end{equation} 
\end{enumerate}
As a consequence, if in addition 
\[
\beta\in\bigg[0,\frac{\alpha^2}2\bigg) \quad\mbox{ and }\quad p\in\pp{\frac1\alpha,\frac{\alpha}{2\beta}}, 
\]
the process $\sigma_n^{-1}\what W_n$ is tight in $D([0,1])$.

body:
[Lemma lemm_BH of arXiv:2503.24372, 'A criterion on the free energy for log-Sobolev inequalities in mean-field particle systems'] Let $N \geq 1$ and $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\R^N$ satisfying a log-Sobolev inequality with constant $\gamma_{\rm LS}>0$. 
Take $F:\R^N\to\R$ to be smooth and compactly supported and a Lipschitz function $H:\R^N\to\R$.
Then:

\begin{equation} 

\cov_{\mu}(F^2,H)^2
\leq 
\frac{4}{\gamma_{\rm LS}^2}  \sup_{x\in\R^N}|\nabla H (x)|^2 \, 
\E_{\mu}[F^2] \; \E_{\mu}\big[|\nabla F|^2\big],
\end{equation}

with the notation $|\nabla H (x)| = \big( \sum_{i =1}^N (\partial_{x_i}  H (x))^2 \big)^{1/2}$.
The same bound holds for a vector valued function $H(x)\in\R^d$.

Let $H_i:\R\to\R$ be Lipschitz ($1\leq i\leq N$) and let $F:\R^N\to\R$ be smooth and compactly supported. Then:

\begin{equation}

\sum_{i=1}^N\cov_{\mu}(F^2,H_i(x_i))^2
  \leq 
  \frac{4}{\gamma_{\rm LS}^2} \max_{1\leq i\leq N}\|H'_i\|^2_\infty \;  \E_{\mu}[F^2] \;  \E_{\mu}\big[|\nabla F
  |^2\big] 
  .
\end{equation}

The inclusion is strict whenever mu has sets of arbitrarily small positive measure (e.g. Lebesgue measure on [0,1]). (b) Counting measure / atoms bounded below: if every atom has measure at least c > 0 and mu has no nonatomic part (e.g. mu = counting measure on N), then for 0 < p < q <= infinity, L^p is contained in L^q and ||f||_q <= c^{1/q - 1/p} ||f||_p; for c = 1 (counting measure), ||f||_q <= ||f||_p. (c) In general (e.g. Lebesgue measure on R^n) there is no inclusion in either direction between L^p and L^q for p different from q.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps scales as n^{1/(2+theta)} for some theta>0 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate showing R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) grows faster than linearly, of order r^{1+theta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. Combining volume growth and resistance growth via the Nash/heat-kernel machinery, or a direct expected-exit-time computation, gives the subdiffusive exponent. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.
the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph
a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster
a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure
typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales
title: Technique: Kesten's Subdiffusivity Argument

body: [Theorem 5.3 of arXiv:2509.26030, 'Muon Outperforms Adam in Tail-End Associative Memory Learning'] If Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2 hold, with fixed $\alpha,\beta$ such that $\alpha\neq\beta$, and $K$ goes to infinity, we obtain the following results for one-step gd, Muon, and Adam. • For gd, for any $\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satistifying Assumption 5.1, we have $\displaystyle\varrho_{\text{GD}}^{\epsilon}=O(\epsilon^{-r(\alpha,\beta)}K^{r(\alpha,\beta)-1}),\text{ where }r(\alpha,\beta)=\min\bigg\{\frac{\alpha(1-\beta)}{\beta(1-\alpha)},\frac{\beta(1-\alpha)}{\alpha(1-\beta)}\bigg\}<1.$ • For Muon, for any $\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satistifying Assumption 5.1, we have $\displaystyle\varrho_{\text{Muon}}^{\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon\bigg(1+O\bigg(\frac{\log K}{K}\bigg)\bigg),\text{ and }G_{\text{Muon}}(W_{0})=-\widetilde{E}E^{\top}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{K}\widetilde{E}J_{K,K}E^{\top}\bigg),$ where $J_{K,K}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K}$ is the matrix with all elements equal to $1$. The big- $O$ notation for matrices means that for $A=O(B)$, each entry satisfies $A_{ij}=O(B_{ij})$ for all $i,j$. • For Adam, there exist $\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satisfying Assumption 5.1 such that $\varrho_{\text{SignGD}}^{\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon.$ There also exist $\widetilde{E}^{\prime}$ and $E^{\prime}$ satisfying Assumption 5.1 such that $\displaystyle\varrho_{\text{SignGD}}^{\epsilon}=O(\epsilon^{-0.7}K^{-0.3}),\text{ and }\frac{\sigma_{\min}\big(G_{\text{SignGD}}(W_{0})\big)}{\sigma_{\max}\big(G_{\text{SignGD}}(W_{0})\big)}\leq 25\%,$ where $\sigma_{\max}$ and $\sigma_{\min}$ are the largest and smallest singular values, respectively.

[Lemma 154 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Under Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta}, \ref{Assumptions_basic}, \ref{Assumptions_offcrit} and \ref{Assumptions_analyticity}, there exist $\eps>0$, $(2K - 1)$ real deterministic constants $\mathfrak{t}^{\textnormal{b}}_{1},\ldots,\mathfrak{t}^{\textnormal{b}}_K,\mathfrak{t}_{2}^{\textnormal{a}},\ldots,\mathfrak{t}_K^{\textnormal{a}}$ in the above rules, a $\N$-independent constant $C > 0$ depending only on the constants in the assumptions, and an event $\mathcal{A}$ of probability at least $1 - Ce^{-\frac{\N}{C}(\log \N)^2}$, having the following properties in combination with the above rules.
 \begin{itemize}
 \item[(P1)] The segments $[\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k]$ indexed by $k\in[K]$ are disjoint and at distance at least $\eps$ from each other.
 \item[(P2)] $\forall k \in [K] \qquad [\alpha_k-\eps,\beta_k+\eps]\subseteq [\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k]\subseteq [\hat a_{h^k},\hat b_{h^k}]$.
 \item[(P3)] $\forall k \in [K] \qquad \big|N^\circ_k-\N \mu([\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k])\big|< C \N^{\frac{1}{2}} \log \N$.
 \item[(P4)] $\forall k \in [K] \quad N^\circ_k = \# \big\{i \in [N] \quad \big| \quad \ell_i \in [\N \hat{a}_k^{\circ},\N \hat{b}_k^{\circ}]\big\}$.
 \item[(P5)] The complement of $\,\bigcup_{k = 1}^{K} (\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k)$ in $\bigcup_{h = 1}^{H} [\hat a_h,\hat b_h]$ splits into finitely many segments, such that on each segment there are either no particles or no holes in the configuration $\boldsymbol{\ell}$, corresponding to whether the equilibrium measure $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is void or saturated on these segments.
 \item[(P6)] The random $3K$-tuple $(\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}^\circ, \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}^\circ, \boldsymbol{N}^\circ)$ is a deterministic affine function of the random $K$-tuple $\boldsymbol{Q}^\circ$. Furthermore, for any $k \in[K]$, the difference $N^{\circ}_k-\N \mu([\hat a^{\circ\,\prime}_k, \hat b^{\circ\,\prime}_k])$ is a deterministic affine function of $(Q_1^\circ,\ldots,Q_k^\circ)$ and the linear coefficient of $Q_k^\circ$ takes values in $\big\{1,-\frac{1}{\theta_{1,1}},\ldots,-\frac{1}{\theta_{H,H}}\big\}$.
\end{itemize}

[Cor 2 of arXiv:2604.26316, 'Smallest distances between zeros of Gaussian analytic functions'] Let $\sigma_k$ be the $k$-th smallest distance between all pairs of zeros,  
		then its limiting density satisfies 
		$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb P\Big(\big(\frac 18\big)^{1/4}n^{3/4}\sigma_k\in [x,x+ dx]\Big)=\frac{ 4x^{4k-1}}{(k-1)!}e^{-  x^4}dx.$$
		Furthermore, let $\pi_k$ be the location of $\hat z_{ij}$ such that $d_g(z_i,z_j)$ equals $\sigma_k$, then $\pi_k$ is asymptotically independent of $\sigma_k$, and tends to the uniform measure with respect to the volume form, i.e.,  for any $U\subseteq M$,
		$$

body: Noether's theorem states that every continuous symmetry of the action of a physical system with conservative forces has a corresponding conservation law. This is the first of two theorems published by the mathematician Emmy Noether in 1918. The action of a physical system is the integral over time of a Lagrangian function, from which the system's behavior can be determined by the principle of least action. This theorem applies to continuous and smooth symmetries of physical space. Noether's formulation is quite general and has been applied across classical mechanics, high energy physics, and recently statistical mechanics.
title: Noether's theorem

body: The heat equation is the parabolic partial differential equation u_t = k Laplacian(u) for a function u(x, t), with k > 0 the diffusivity. On R^n with initial data u(x, 0) = f(x), the solution is the convolution of f with the heat kernel (4 pi k t)^(-n/2) exp(-|x|^2 / (4 k t)); solutions smooth out instantly and obey the maximum principle.

\[
(W_L(\sigma)f)(x')
=

body:
[Ppn 255 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We have $\chi'(1) \le L^2$.

\begin{proof}
Throughout this proof we abbreviate $\bg\equiv(\bG,\bg^\aux)$.  Consider small positive $\delta$, and define
    \[\begin{aligned}
    \bx&=\cA( (1-\delta)^{1/2}\bg+\delta^{1/2}\bg')\,,\\
    \by &= \E(\bx\,|\, \bg)\,,\\
    \bz &= \bx-\by\,.
    \end{aligned}\]
By iterated expectations, we have
    \[
    \frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\by)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta)\,, 
    \]
as well as $\E(\by,\bz)=0$. It follows that
    \beq
    \chi(1)
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\bx)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}+\frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta) + \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}\,.\eeq
Let us treat $\bz$ as a function of $\bg'$ for fixed $\bg$. Note that $\E(\bz\,|\,\bg)=0$. Since $\cA$ is $L$-Lipschitz, we see that $\bz$ is $(L\delta^{1/2})$-Lipschitz as a function of $\bg'$. It follows (using e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that
    \[
    \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N} \le O(L^2\delta)\,.
    \]
Recalling \eqref{eq:bz}, we see that $\chi(1-\delta) \ge \chi(1)-O(L^2\delta)$, which implies $\chi'(1) \le L^2$ as claimed. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Ppn 255 of arXiv:2608.29416

body: In probability theory, Lindeberg's condition is a sufficient condition for the central limit theorem (CLT) to hold for a sequence of independent random variables. Unlike the classical CLT, which requires that the random variables in question have finite variance and be both independent and identically distributed, Lindeberg's CLT only requires that they have finite variance, satisfy Lindeberg's condition, and be independent. It is named after the Finnish mathematician Jarl Waldemar Lindeberg.
title: Lindeberg's condition

body: Theorem (campaign status: proved): Let the saturated quotient have $m+1-(m-2)=3$ units of class excess; a signed spanning forest of its nontrivial classes has exactly three edges. Restriction is injective on $\widehat R$ when $h\notin\widehat R$, so two old-old edge residuals span the two-dimensional admissible space and one further edge joins $h$ to an old form. An unsigned three-edge forest is, after removing isolated vertices, exactly one of $3K_2$, $P_3+K_2$, $P_4$, $K_{1,3}$ (tag 10), and a signed forest can be switched so all three edges are ordinary differences. With edge evaluations $d_1,d_2,d_3$ satisfying $d_i/2\in\{0,\pm1\}$ on the antipodal atom, a primitive dependence $\alpha$ is the cross product of two rows of $\{0,\pm1\}^3$, giving exactly sixteen normalized triples. Notes: The sixteen: $(1,\pm1,\pm1),(1,\pm1,\pm2),(1,\pm2,\pm1),(2,\pm1,\pm1)$. VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY: cross products of ternary rows with all entries nonzero give exactly 16 canonical lines, matching this list. This proves the coefficient search is EXHAUSTIVE, not a bounded-coefficient heuristic. [Lemma L:location-bd of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ with $x \le n/100$. Take parameters $\alpha, \beta$ satisfying that
$\alpha \ge 1/2 - n^{-1/6}$ and $\beta \in (2(1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0, 1/100)$. Define
$$
y^\pm(\beta) = \argmax_{y\in\llbracket-n, n + x \rrbracket} f^\pm(y, \beta), \quad \text{where }\quad f^\pm(y, \beta) = \frac{|y|}{1/2 \mp \operatorname{sgn}(y)\beta} + \mu[y-\operatorname{sgn}(y), 1; x, n]_\textsf{L}.
$$
Then we have $y^+(\beta)>0$, and
$|y^\pm(\beta) - (x \pm 8 \beta n)|\le 100 \beta^2 n + 1$.
Moreover, there are universal constants $C, c>0$ such that the following statements hold. Let
\[
y^\pm_* = \argmax_{y\in\llbracket-n,n+x \rrbracket} (Z^\pm(y) + X[y-\operatorname{sgn}(y),1; x,n]_\textsf{L}) .
\]
For any $\epsilon > C (1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0$ we have
\[
\mathbb{P}(|y^+_* - y^+(\beta)|\ge \epsilon n),\quad \mathbb{P}(|y^-_* - y^-(\beta)|\ge \epsilon n\;\text{and}\;y^-_*>0)\le 2\exp(- c \epsilon^3 n) + 2 \exp(-c\sqrt{n}).
\]
title: Lemma L:location-bd of arXiv:2604.10020
