ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Compute a_2(d) by the cycle-correction method as a check, and identify why the expansion truncates at d/3. Result: On K_n^d every vertex has degree d(n-1); at p = lambda/(d(n-1)) the exploration is close to a branching process; the first correction to the branching ratio comes from triangles: each vertex lies in d (n-1)(n-2)/2 triangles (all in one coordinate line), so the effective number of NEW vertices reached in two steps is reduced by a relative amount of order 1/d... normalising, the triangle correction is of relative order (n-2)/(d(n-1)) ~ 1/d, not 1/n, so it shifts p_c at relative order 1/d which is absorbed into a_1(d)?? The source states a_1(d) = 1/d exactly and the corrections are in powers of 1/n, so the d-dependence at fixed order is packaged into a_i(d). The triangle correction: the branching process approximation counts each vertex's d(n-1) neighbours; the neighbours along the same coordinate line are mutually adjacent (a clique K_n), so a cluster exploring along a line finds n-1 vertices at once; this is a finite-size correction of relative order 1/n at each step, giving a_2(d) of order 1 in d; the source's Federico et al. result identifies it. The truncation at d/3 comes from the window width: the critical window of the Hamming graph has width V^{-1/3} = n^{-d/3} in p (relative), so terms beyond order n^{-d/3} are inside the window and meaningless as an expansion of a single critical value; this explains the O(n^{-1-d/3}) error and the number of meaningful terms d/3. Beyond this structural explanation and the second-order term, I did not compute a_3(d); it would need the 4-cycle and two-triangle corrections on the Hamming graph, where 4-cycles through a vertex number about d(d-1)(n-1)^2/2 (two coordinates) plus in-line ones. Key identity: Only terms above the critical window width n^{-d/3} are meaningful, which explains the truncation index d/3. Obstruction: Third-order cycle corrections on K_n^d not computed.

No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

[Proposition 13 (Lower bound in the Lipschitz constant-coefficient subclass) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $p=\alpha-1$ and fix $T>0$. In each of the four constant-coefficient families in Proposition~\ref{prop:constant-consistency}, there do not exist constants $C>0$, $q>p$ and $E_0>0$ such that
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^p\le C E^q
\]
for all $0<E<E_0$, where $E$ denotes the corresponding single nonzero error variable among $|x_0-\wt x_0|$, $B$, $A$, and $S$. In particular, the exponent $\alpha-1$ in the Lipschitz case $\wt\eta=1$ is optimal separately for the initial value, drift, Brownian diffusion, and stable jump coefficient errors within this constant-coefficient subclass.

Unreviewed campaign deduction from Gwynne-Pfeffer Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.7. Fix gamma in (0,2), a whole-plane GFF h and a nonempty deterministic planar domain U. Write Q=2/gamma+gamma/2 and xi=gamma/d_gamma for the canonical gamma-LQG metric D_h. The gamma-thick points X in U have Euclidean Hausdorff dimension 2-gamma^2/2 and D_h dimension d_gamma almost surely. Applying the independent-set equality dim_E X=xi Q dim_D X-(xi^2/2)(dim_D X)^2 to this field-dependent X instead gives 2; the residual is gamma^2/2. At gamma=sqrt(8/3), applying that equality to a nonconstant D_h-geodesic of intrinsic dimension 1 would instead give Euclidean dimension 3/4, whereas a connected continuous image with distinct endpoints has Euclidean dimension at least 1 by a Lipschitz distance projection. These are obstructions to deleting independence, not values of the general d_gamma.

Gamma is fixed in (0,2)
Thick points use circle-average limits
Known d_sqrt(8/3)=4 for the geodesic control

body: In a floating-point number system, the machine epsilon eps is the smallest positive representable number such that 1 + eps, computed with that system's rounding rule, is strictly greater than 1; equivalently, eps is the gap between 1 and the next larger representable floating-point number. For IEEE 754 binary double precision (53-bit significand, including one implicit leading bit), eps = 2^(-52). The associated unit roundoff u = eps/2 = 2^(-53) bounds the relative error of rounding a real number x, within the representable range, to the nearest floating-point number fl(x): |fl(x) - x| / |x| <= u. More generally, each basic arithmetic operation (+, -, *, /) computed in IEEE arithmetic satisfies fl(a op b) = (a op b) * (1 + delta) for some |delta| <= u.
title: Floating-Point Machine Epsilon

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending. Let d>=1,N>=2d+1,n>=0,K>=2,1<=r<K and 0<=ell<=r be integers. There are d pairs among N contexts, one arbitrary A and one systematic S per pair, and N-2d known S contexts; each has K candidates. S has all K truths; each A has an independent uniform random r-subset. The target p chooses contexts uniformly then truths uniformly; orientation class has VC dimension d. Observe n iid factual (context,candidate) samples WITHOUT partition tags. A perfect independent post-training verifier certifies a uniform ell-subset of truths in every variable context, including paired S, without orientations; ell=0 means no verifier. Let C_x be the union of distinct observed and certified identities. Any context with |C_x|>r must be S. ERM minimizing violations of these S certificates over the paired class uniquely recovers the true partition on the data-measurable event G that every pair has a certificate. For kappa=1-r/K,p0=kappa/N, uniformly over all fixed worlds P(G fails)<=min(1,d*P[Bin(n,p0)<=r-ell]). For 0<delta<1, n*kappa/N>=max(2*(r-ell+1),8*log(d/delta)) suffices for P(G)>=1-delta. Conditional on G, define D_j as the number of identified A contexts with j=|C_x| distinct known truths,ell<=j<=r; B_j=D_j*(r-j)/(N*r),T_j=sum_{h=j}^r B_h,alpha_j=(K-r)/(K-j). For arbitrary generators and every c in [0,1], the exact conditional worst-world false-mass frontier subject to robust source Mis_infinity(g,p)<=c in all compatible worlds is F_D(c)=alpha_ell*(T_ell-c)_+ +sum_{j=ell+1}^r (alpha_j-alpha_{j-1})*(T_j-c)_+. The source statistic uniformly coarsens p within exact g-probability level sets. This equals the oracle frontier with the partition given but the same factual data and verifier truths, simultaneously for all c on G. The attaining polynomial-representation estimator removes mass from posterior uncertified A groups in decreasing false-risk order and transfers it to the known S reservoir. On failure it outputs the uniform law over all NK candidates, maintaining robust feasibility on every outcome. For every fixed c the unconditional expected minimax value lies between E[O_D(c)] and E[O_D(c)]+(kappa*d/N)*min(1,d*P[Bin(n,p0)<=r-ell]), with O_D the same-data true-partition oracle. Under the displayed sample condition the gap is at most delta*kappa*d/N. The binomial comparison uses an explicit stopped iid-uniform coupling; context recovery events are not assumed independent. No exact frontier before G, intermediate-bin upper bound, or novelty/optimality for support testing is asserted.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:3ffec2716da19c038aaf6407a632799f668c5bf05de522ce0b5a91a7af1da523","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/3f/3ffec2716da19c038aaf6407a632799f668c5bf05de522ce0b5a91a7af1da523.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:681fb91ba97bc3208b9cf7de6506e7aea25f4da254acdee47bcec6ed2d3fe21d","bundle_entry_key":"untagged-certified-frontier","bundle_id":"population.t379-untagged-certified-recovery-frontier-20261020","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; support identification","draft":"w709/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.calibration:untagged-support-certified-vc-calibration-frontier","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Untagged factual training: exact frontier after certified VC recovery

Candidate T379-C012 v2; OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, proof (unaudited).
Targets 1 and 2. This is a high-probability identified-partition regime,
not a theorem for unresolved untagged posteriors. The hardest remaining
piece is the frontier before all pairs admit a support certificate;
C010 shows why the old global posterior-ordering step does not cover it.

## Experiment, entirely without supplied partition tags

Integers d>=1,N>=2d+1,n>=0,K>=2,1<=r<K and 0<=ell<=r.
There are d variable pairs, each with exactly one A and one S context,
and N-2d known S contexts. S has all K truths; A has an independent
uniform random r-subset. The target chooses contexts uniformly, then
true candidates uniformly. The orientation class has VC dimension d.
Observe n iid factual samples (context,candidate), with NO A/S tags.
After training the same perfect verifier as C009 independently draws a
uniform ell-subset of truths in each variable context, including S,
certifying identities but no orientations. At ell=0 there is no verifier.

Let C_x be the union of distinct observed identities and verifier truths
in context x. If |C_x|>r, context x must be S. Label these certified
contexts S and minimize certificate violations over the paired VC class.
This is a finite-class ERM: the true partition has loss zero. Let G be
the DATA-MEASURABLE event that each pair has a certificate. A can never
be certified S, so on G every consistent ERM returns the TRUE partition.
Indeed, it is the only orientation compatible with the factual data and
truth certificates. The conclusion is stronger than an unobservable
event that an estimated partition happens to be correct.

Write kappa=1-r/K and p0=kappa/N. Uniformly over every fixed world,

 P(G fails)<=min(1,d*P[Bin(n,p0)<=r-ell]).                 (1)

In particular, for 0<delta<1, the sufficient condition

 n*kappa/N >= max{2*(r-ell+1),8*log(d/delta)}             (2)

ensures P(G)>=1-delta. Thus the fraction gamma=ell/r of arbitrary
truths changes the recovery threshold from r+1 to r-ell+1. The verifier
also provides ell truths per paired systematic context, explicitly.

## Dependent coupon discoveries: explicit coupling proof

Fix a world and one of its systematic contexts x. Conditional on its
verifier set T_x, start with ell known distinct truths. Training samples
are independent of T_x conditional on this world: the verifier draws
were specified to be independent after training. For probability analysis
one may draw T_x first and then training, without changing their joint
law or giving the learner extra information.

If J_t<=r distinct truths in x are known before a sample, its probability
of discovering another distinct truth there is

 q_t=(K-J_t)/(NK)>=p0.

Use independent uniforms V_t to generate the training categorical draw,
placing all currently fresh facts in context x first in its inverse-CDF
ordering. The fresh-fact indicator is then 1{V_t<=q_t}. Independently
of the past, B_t=1{V_t<=p0} are iid Bernoulli(p0). Until the certificate
has been reached, each fresh indicator dominates B_t. On the event the
certificate is NEVER reached by sample n, this domination holds for all
n draws; hence sum_t B_t<=r-ell. Therefore the marginal failure
probability for x is at most that binomial tail. It is NOT asserted that
different context certificates are independent. Union bound over the d
true systematic contexts proves (1).

If mu=n*p0 satisfies (2), r-ell<mu/2. The multiplicative Chernoff lower
tail for the INDEPENDENT comparison B_t gives failure probability at
most exp(-mu/8) per context. Another union bound gives (2). The
independence used belongs to the constructed B_t, not to the coupon
increments or the context recovery events.

## Exact robust calibration frontier on the recovery event

On G, orientations are forced by logical support compatibility. For each
identified A context, let j=|C_x|, ell<=j<=r, and let D_j count these
contexts. Set B_j=D_j*(r-j)/(N*r), T_j=sum_{h=j}^r B_h, and
alpha_j=(K-r)/(K-j). For every calibration budget c in [0,1], the
exact conditional frontier over ALL generators satisfying source
Mis_infinity<=c in every compatible world is

 F_D(c)=alpha_ell*(T_ell-c)_+
       +sum_{j=ell+1}^r (alpha_j-alpha_{j-1})*(T_j-c)_+.              (3)

It equals the oracle frontier with the partition given and the SAME
factual data and verifier output. Its conditional posterior-average
version under uniform compatible supports has the same value. This
equality holds simultaneously for all c on G.

For completeness: conditional on identified orientation, a factual
sequence has the same likelihood for every r-support containing its
observed A identities; the independent verifier likelihood is also
constant among supports containing its certified identities. Thus the
posterior is uniform on supports containing C_x. Uncertified A atoms
at j have mean factual density (r-j)/(Nr(K-j)) and false risk alpha_j.
Certified A atoms are safe with density 1/(Nr); known S atoms are safe
with density 1/(NK). Density decreases with positive false risk.

For any upper-risk threshold E and ANY coarsening Pi,
mu_Pi(E)>=mu(E), by averaging lower inside densities with higher
outside densities in every cell. For arbitrary g and its score bins,
TV(mu_Pi,g)<=E[TV(p_Pi,g)]. The robust calibration budget therefore
forces g(E)>=(mu(E)-c)_+. Finite layer cake at the risk levels
alpha_ell,...,alpha_r yields exactly (3)'s lower bound, with no
restriction on g or purity assumption for bins.

To attain it, start from mu, remove up to c mass from uncertified A
groups in decreasing j/risk order, uniformly in each group, and add it
uniformly to the fixed S reservoir. Every score bin is a union of entire
certified or uncertified A subgroups and S fibres, each with invariant
p mass across compatible supports. Hence p_Pi=mu_Pi; because g is
constant within exact bins, TV(p_Pi,g)<=TV(mu,g)<=c. The false fraction
in each removed group is alpha_j in every world, so actual H=F_D(c)
worldwise. Merging scores or zero scores do not alter this argument.
The matching upper bound is only for exact-level calibration, not
arbitrary finite coarse bins.

On G's complement use the uniform law on all NK candidates. It has
Mis_infinity=0 in EVERY world and H=kappa*d/N. Consequently this
algorithm is robustly feasible at every budget on every data outcome,
and attains the exact known-partition frontier with probability >=1-delta
under (2). Processing certificates, orienting the paired class and
sorting the at-most-d occupied risk groups is polynomial in the explicit
data/verifier size and bit lengths; group sampling avoids an NK array.

## Unconditional matching bracket

Let O_D(c) be the same-data oracle value (3), formed using the true
partition even off G. Its distribution is world-invariant by renaming
context siblings and truth candidates. An algorithm without orientations
cannot beat the oracle's Bayes lower bound in minimax expectation:
condition on the true orientation in the prior argument, then integrate.
The preceding fallback algorithm is equal to O_D on G and has excess
at most kappa*d/N off G, since 0<=O_D<=kappa*d/N. Thus

 E[O_D(c)] <= minimax E[H(c)]
             <= E[O_D(c)]+(kappa*d/N)*min(1,d*BinCDF(n,p0,r-ell)).   (4)

Under (2) the gap is at most delta*kappa*d/N. This is an oracle
bracket, NOT a matching positive lower bound on the estimation penalty
below the recovery regime. Exact conditional equality (3), rather than
an allegedly novel coupon-testing rate, is the proposed target narrowing.

## Prior work and scope

The definition of calibration is Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3,
Definitions 1--2, printed pp.8--9. The known collision uniformity-testing
substep was checked in Diakonikolas--Gouleakis--Peebles--Price
1611.03579v1, Theorem 1,p.4; no novelty or optimality is claimed here
for testing support size or for the elementary coupon/Chernoff bound.
The certificate here has zero false positives and logically rules out
alternative orientations, which permits the all-compatible-world
calibration lower/upper match. Merely applying a noisy partition test
and conditioning on its correctness would not justify that robust claim.

The explicit independence assumptions in the verifier and iid training
are essential. Before G there may be unresolved posterior asymmetries
as in C010; no exact frontier is supplied there. The source innovation
theorems' global Regular Facts assumption is not invoked. This is a
candidate for independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review.

body:
[Prop 11 of arXiv:2607.22416, 'A multi-player optimal stopping game based on a spider Brownian bridge'] Fix $d>0$.
    Recall the definition of $\Gamma_d$ in \eqref{ExpressionGammap0.5} and define $\Upsilon = \Upsilon_d = \Upsilon_{\alpha,\theta,d}:[0,\infty) \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ by $\Upsilon(z) = \Gamma_d(z) - h_\alpha(z)$.
 Then $\tilde{z}$ is a turning point of $\Gamma_d$ if and only if $\tilde{z}$ is a root of $\Upsilon$.
  
The function $\Gamma_{d}$ admits a maximizer, denoted $z^{*}=z^{*}(\alpha,\theta,d)$. 
Furthermore, there exists $\hat{\Theta}:(0,\infty) \times (0,\infty)$ with $\Theta_*(\alpha,d) \leq \hat{\Theta}(\alpha,d)\leq \Theta^*(\alpha,d)$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\theta < \Theta_*(\alpha,d)$ then
$\Upsilon$ has a unique root $z_1 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$, and that root is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\theta = \Theta_*(\alpha,d)$ then 
$\Upsilon$ has two roots $z_1=0$ and $z_2 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$, and $z_2$ is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\Theta_*(\alpha,d) < \theta < \hat{\Theta}(\alpha,d)$ then $\Upsilon$ has two roots $z_1 \in (0, \frac{\alpha}{2})$ and $z_2 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$ and  $z_2$ is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\theta= \hat{\Theta}(\alpha,d)$ then $\Upsilon$ has two roots $z_{1}\in (0,\frac{\alpha}{2})$ and $z_2 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$. Both $0$ and $z_{2}$ are maximisers of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\hat{\Theta}(\alpha,d) < \theta < \Theta^*(\alpha,d)$ then $\Upsilon$ has two roots $z_{1}\in (0,\frac{\alpha}{2})$ and $z_2 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$. 0 is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\theta = \Theta^*(\alpha,d)$ then $\frac{\alpha}{2}$ is the unique root of $\Upsilon$ and $0$ is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$. 

    
\item If $\theta > \Theta^*(\alpha,d)$ then $\Upsilon$  has no roots and $0$ is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$. 
\end{enumerate}
title: Prop 11 of arXiv:2607.22416

Let N take values in {0, 1, ..., m} on a probability space, mu = E[N] > 0 and beta = E[binom(N, 2)] = E[N(N-1)/2]; put x = 2 beta / mu and r = 1 + floor(x). With theta = x - (r - 1) and C = mu^2/E[N^2] = mu/(1 + x), the optimized bound D satisfies D - C = mu theta (1 - theta)/(r(r+1)(r+theta)) >= 0, so D is strictly larger exactly when 2 beta/mu is not an integer.
N is integer valued with 0 <= N <= m
mu = E[N] > 0

Let $\mathcal E\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ be a centered ellipsoid, choose $P$ and $K$

Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent centered random variables such that |X_i| <= M almost surely for all i. Let sigma^2 = (1/n) * sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i^2]. Then for all t >= 0, P(sum_{i=1}^n X_i >= t) <= exp(- t^2 / (2 * (n * sigma^2 + M * t / 3))).
X_1, ..., X_n are independent and centered
|X_i| <= M almost surely
t >= 0

[Cor 2. cor: embedding of Mdis to sP of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] The map $\mathfrak{p}: \mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{dis}}(S) \to \mathscr{P}(S)$ is a topological embedding,
  i.e.,
  a homeomorphism onto its image.
  If we write $\mathscr{P}^{*}(S)$ for the image,
  then 
  \begin{equation}  
    \mathscr{P}^{*}(S)
    =
    \Bigl\{
      \pi \in \mathscr{P}(S) 
      \mid
      \pi = \sum_{i \in I} \delta_{(x_{i}, w_{i})}\ \text{with}\ x_{i} \neq x_{j}\ \text{if}\ i \neq j
    \Bigr\},
  \end{equation}
  and the inverse map is $\mathfrak{v} |_{\mathscr{P}^{*}(S)}$, i.e., the restriction of the map $\mathfrak{v}$ to $\mathscr{P}^{*}(S)$.

[Lem c1 of arXiv:2606.16237, 'The Backward Stochastic Partial Differential Integral Equations: Solvability and Compariso'] Assume that $v,m,v^{*}$ are three processes defined on $\Omega\times[0,T]$ and valued in $V,H,V^{*}$, respectively. For any $\eta\in V$, $v(t), m(t), \langle\eta, v^{*}(t)\rangle$ are $\mathscr{F}_{t}$-measurable for a.e. $t\in[0,T]$, and $m$ is a strongly c\`{a}dl\`{a}g local martingale. If $\varphi\in L_{\mathscr{F}_{T}}^{2}(\Omega;H)$ and for any $\eta\in V$, $(\omega,t)\in\Omega\times[0,T]$, it holds that
\begin{eqnarray*}
    ( \eta,v(t))_H = ( \eta,\varphi)_H
    + \int_{t}^{T} \langle \eta,v^{*}(s) \rangle ds
    + ( \eta, m(T)-m(t) )_H,
\end{eqnarray*}
then there exists a full-measure set $\Omega'\subset \Omega$ and a process $h$ valued in $H$ such that\\
(i) $h(t)$ is $\mathscr{F}_{t}$-measurable for any $t\in[0,T]$ and strongly c\`{a}dl\`{a}g for any $\omega\in\Omega$;\\
(ii) $h(t)=v(t)$ in the space $H$ for a.s. $\omega\in\Omega$ and a.e. $t\in[0,T]$, and $h(T)=\varphi$ for any $\omega\in\Omega'$;\\
(iii) for any $\omega\in \Omega'$ and $t\in[0,T]$,
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \|h(t)\|_{H}^{2} = \|\varphi\|_{H}^{2} + 2\int_{t}^{T}\langle v^{*}(s), v(s)\rangle ds + 2 \int_{t}^{T}( h(s-), d m(s)) - [m ]_{T} + [m]_{t},
\end{eqnarray*}
where $[m]$ denotes the quadratic variation of the $H$-valued martingale. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem c1 of arXiv:2606.16237

body:
A family \Pi of Borel probability measures on a metric space (S, d) is said to be tight if for every \epsilon > 0, there exists a compact subset K_\epsilon \subseteq S such that \sup_{\mu \in \Pi} \mu(S \setminus K_\epsilon) < \epsilon. On \mathbb{R}^k, this is equivalent to: for every \epsilon > 0, there exists M < \infty such that \sup_{\mu \in \Pi} \mu(\{x \in \mathbb{R}^k : \|x\| > M\}) < \epsilon.
(S, d) is a metric space
\Pi is a family of Borel probability measures on S
title: Tightness of Probability Measures

Let tau_i be independent standard Brownian first hitting times of -1. For a deterministic exceptional-index set let m(N) count its first N indices and S_N=sum_(i=1 to m(N)) tau_i. For m(N)>0 and epsilon>0, P(S_N>epsilon N)=erf(m(N)/sqrt(2 epsilon N)). Thus S_N/N tends to zero in probability if and only if m(N)/sqrt(N) tends to zero. A zero density m(N)/N->0 alone is insufficient. If m(N)=O(N^(1/2-delta)) for some delta>0, then S_N/N->0 almost surely. These are clock statements, not a construction of a backward or two-sided Brownian law after a finite random shift.

\]

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Lower-bound the complexity by the OSSS inequality with the sharp four-arm exponent and compare with the exploration-path algorithm. Result: The exploration algorithm reveals the pivotal-rich interface, of expected size n^{7/4+o(1)}, giving sigma <= 7/4. The lower bound 6/4 in the notes comes from Theorem VIII.6 (revealment times complexity). A better lower bound would follow from the OSSS inequality Var f <= sum_i delta_i I_i if one could bound the revealments delta_i by C(A)/n^2 uniformly, giving C(A) >= n^2 Var f / (sum_i I_i) = n^2 / (n^2 alpha_4(n)) = n^{5/4}, which is WEAKER than 6/4. So OSSS with the 4-arm exponent cannot beat 6/4; the 6/4 bound uses the stronger Theorem VIII.6. Improving the lower bound needs a new inequality between complexity and the spectral measure beyond the second Fourier level; I checked that the third-level analogue of OSSS (via the pivotal-triples) gives at best n^{6/4} again because three-pivotal points have density n^2 alpha_6... which is smaller. No improvement. Obstruction: Both OSSS-type bounds saturate at 6/4; closing the gap to 7/4 needs a genuinely new lower-bound technique.

body: Let A be an m by n matrix and B an n by m matrix with m <= n. Then det(A B) = sum_{S} det(A_S) det(B_S), where the sum is over all m-element subsets S of {1, ..., n}, A_S is the m by m submatrix of A formed by the columns indexed by S, and B_S is the m by m submatrix of B formed by the rows indexed by S. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis]

For epsilon,B>0 and X=(x_1,...,x_n) in R^(d by n), Fan-Wang call X (epsilon,B)-orthonormal when | ||x_alpha||_2^2-1 |<=epsilon for every alpha, |x_alpha^T x_beta|<=epsilon for every alpha!=beta, ||X||_op<=B, and sum_alpha (||x_alpha||_2^2-1)^2<=B^2. Their linear-width spectral theory assumes X_0 is (epsilon_n,B)-orthonormal for a constant B and epsilon_n*n^(1/4)->0. This includes a total squared norm-error requirement as well as pairwise near-orthogonality; bounded column norms and small pairwise inner products alone are not the definition.

Let Omega in R^n be a bounded open set of diameter d, and Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + sum b^i D_i u + c u with a^{ij} = a^{ji} measurable and (a^{ij}(x)) positive definite for a.e. x; set D* = (det(a^{ij}))^{1/n}. Assume c <= 0 a.e. and |b|/D* in L^n(Omega). Let u in C^0(closure of Omega) intersect W^{2,n}_loc(Omega) satisfy Lu >= f almost everywhere, with f/D* in L^n(Omega). Then sup over Omega of u <= sup over the boundary of u^+ + C ||f^-/D*||_{L^n(Omega)}, where f^- = max(-f, 0) and C depends only on n, d and || |b|/D* ||_{L^n(Omega)}; when b = 0 one may take C = d/(n omega_n^{1/n}), omega_n being the volume of the unit ball. The dual statement bounds -inf u for supersolutions. This is the maximum principle that survives merely measurable leading coefficients and an L^n right-hand side; it is the entry point to the Krylov-Safonov theory, and it gives uniqueness of W^{2,n}_loc strong solutions of the Dirichlet problem when c <= 0.

a^{ij} = a^{ji} measurable, (a^{ij}(x)) positive definite a.e.; no continuity assumed
c <= 0 a.e.; |b|/D* in L^n(Omega); f/D* in L^n(Omega)
u in C^0(closure of Omega) intersect W^{2,n}_loc(Omega) with Lu >= f a.e.

OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), no novelty established. In dimension two let the teacher be (1/3)sum_j N(a A u_j,I_2), A=diag(1,3), with unit equilateral vertices u_j. Consider physical Euclidean unit-step population DDPM GD projected onto zero-centroid student means, using the canonical equal-weight identity-covariance mixture score. Write M=a sqrt(2C) R_theta U on one orientation branch, c=(C11,C12,C22), and c_a(theta) for the unique normal critical risk section near C_*=diag(1,9)/2. Let H(theta)=[(61/4)(cos(3theta)-1)^2+(189/4)sin^2(3theta)]/2 and cbar_a=c_a+a^2(0,Hprime/40,0). Put beta=arccos(-61/128), l=beta/3, r=(2pi-beta)/3. For each fixed 0<delta<(r-l)/4 there exist rho>0 and a_0>0, independent of a, such that 0<a<a_0, theta_0 in [l+2delta,r-2delta], and ||c_0-cbar_a(theta_0)||<=rho imply convergence to the nonglobal local minimum in this sector. The covariance tracking error satisfies ||e_k||<=rho exp(-lambda a^2 k)+C a^4. After O(a^(-2)log(1/a)) steps the angle is trapped in [l+delta,r-delta]. This auxiliary centered-planar basin lemma does not establish random entry, free-centroid behavior, annealed learning, or the full T309 target.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:ad45f0dcb993b4170da90e1babdd7e8f0f55c8ef3b65a2591cacacafe8285075","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/ad/ad45f0dcb993b4170da90e1babdd7e8f0f55c8ef3b65a2591cacacafe8285075.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:71277a4e53854eb1e431d4b1d5c973097110bdd94d7a3c6b800f2b8612041ce5","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c15","bundle_id":"population.t309-centered-anisotropic-discrete-trapping-draft","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian mixture learning and diffusion objectives","draft":"w721/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:anisotropic-gaussian-mixture-ddpm-centered-discrete-covariance-tracking-bad-sector","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; T309-w721-C15 v1; proof (unaudited); Target 2 route 12 auxiliary lemma.

# Discrete tracking and a fixed angular trapping sector for the centered planar anisotropic student

This pays the centered planar discrete-tracking step left in C14. It does not pay random entry, a free centroid, additional ambient directions, annealing, or the full K=3 learning target. It is an auxiliary obstruction lemma, not a scored resolution of the target. Its analytic dependencies C06, C13 and C14 remain unaudited; no novelty finding is claimed.

## Statement

Use C06's teacher with A=diag(1,3), equal weights and identity covariance in dimension two. Optimize its population single-time DDPM excess risk by physical Euclidean unit-step GD projected onto the zero-centroid student subspace. In one orientation branch write the student means M=a sqrt(2C) R_theta U, where C is positive definite. Let beta=arccos(-61/128), l=beta/3, r=(2pi-beta)/3, and fix 0<delta<(r-l)/4. There are absolute positive rho,a_0, depending on this fixed delta only, such that for 0<a<a_0,

    theta_0 in [l+2delta,r-2delta],
    ||c_0-cbar_a(theta_0)||<=rho

imply convergence to C06's strict bad minimum in this angular sector. Here c=(C11,C12,C22) with ordinary Euclidean coordinate norm and

    cbar_a(theta)=c_a(theta)+a^2(0,H'(theta)/40,0),

where c_a is the normal critical section. In particular the initial covariance width rho does not shrink with a. During the motion,

    ||e_k||<=rho exp(-lambda a^2 k)+C a^4,
    e_k=c_k-cbar_a(theta_k),                         (1)

for an absolute lambda>0. After O(a^(-2)log(1/a)) steps the angle remains forever in [l+delta,r-delta]. The same assertions hold in the other two sectors by label symmetry. No actual random-initialization probability is asserted.

## 1. Uniform coordinates and analytic inputs

The centered rank-two planar means form a four-dimensional smooth coordinate chart (C,theta) on an orientation branch. At C_*=diag(1,9)/2 the map sqrt(2C) is smooth; compactness of the theta circle supplies uniform derivative bounds on a fixed covariance neighborhood. C06's softmax/Gaussian differentiated expansion applies uniformly on this bounded set. Specifically,

    F_a(c,theta)=a^4[(x-1/2)^2+2y^2+(z-9/2)^2]
                       +a^6 K(c,theta)+O_C^m(a^8),  (2)

with any fixed finite m used below. This is the same expansion as C06's local one; its dominated Taylor estimates hold for all angles because the unit locations and their derivatives stay bounded on the compact circle. The leading normal Hessian D=diag(2,4,2) is constant and invertible. The parameter-dependent implicit function theorem, with uniqueness on a fixed small normal ball, gives a smooth periodic section c_a(theta)=c_*+O_C^m(a^2). Finite patches agree by that uniqueness. The reduced risk is a^6 H(theta)+O_C^m(a^8).

The normalized physical metric G(c) is independent of theta: right multiplication by R_theta preserves Frobenius products, and J commutes with R_theta. It and its inverse are uniformly smooth and positive definite on this neighborhood. C13 gives its value at c_*, and C14 verifies the leading graph correction cbar_a. All these estimates are dimension-two estimates; no assertion about an ambient-dimension constant is needed here.

## 2. The exact mean step and its coordinate remainder

Let J_mean=M/a denote normalized centered means. The physical Euclidean step on means induces

    J_mean,+ = J_mean-a^(-2) grad_J_mean F_a.

Taylor expansion of the inverse mean-coordinate chart shows that its coordinate increment is

    (Delta c,Delta theta)=-a^(-2)G(c)^(-1)dF_a+R,
    ||R||<=C(a^2||e||+a^4)^2,                     (3)

on a slightly smaller fixed covariance neighborhood. Indeed at cbar the gradient in normalized means is O(a^6), and displacement by e changes it by O(a^4||e||); multiplying by a^(-2) gives O(a^4+a^2||e||). The inverse chart has bounded second derivative on the enlarged neighborhood. Its step segment remains there for small a, so (3) is a justified coordinate remainder rather than a flow approximation assumed valid over many steps. The same estimates can be differentiated once for the monotonicity argument below.

C14 cancels the order-a^4 covariance velocity at cbar. Its theta velocity is -a^4 H'/15+O(a^6). At fixed theta the derivative of the covariance velocity in e has leading matrix -a^2 B, where

    B=(G(c_*)^(-1))_cc D=diag(4/3,20/3,12).

The theta derivative of cbar is O(a^2). Subtracting cbar(theta+Delta theta) in the new normal variable therefore changes the normal update by O(a^6+a^4||e||+a^4||e||^2), including the second derivative remainder. From (2),(3) we obtain uniform recurrences

    e_+=(I-a^2 B)e+R_e,
    ||R_e||<=C[a^2||e||^2+a^4||e||+a^6],           (4)
    theta_+=theta-(a^4/15)H'(theta)+R_theta,
    |R_theta|<=C[a^2||e||+a^6].                    (5)

The map in (5), at fixed e and with c=cbar(theta)+e, has theta derivative 1+O(a^4+a^2||e||). This follows by the differentiated versions of (2),(3), with the leading normal covariance penalty independent of theta and cbar'=O(a^2).

## 3. Normal confinement and the fast initial layer

For a^2<=1/12, the Euclidean operator norm of I-a^2 B is 1-(4/3)a^2. Choose a fixed neighborhood size rho_max small enough that C rho_max<=1/3, and then a small enough that C a^2<=1/3. Equation (4) gives, for lambda=2/3 after harmless reductions,

    ||e_+||<=(1-lambda a^2)||e||+C a^6.             (6)

Choose initial rho<rho_max/2 and a so that C a^4/lambda<rho. Induction keeps ||e||<=2rho<rho_max for every step, without restricting theta, since the estimates are periodic and uniform in theta. Solving (6) proves (1), with the constant floor C a^4/lambda absorbed into C.

Choose a small fixed w>0 later. Let N be the first integer at least

    (lambda a^2)^(-1) log_+(2rho/(w a^2)),

where log_+(s)=max(0,log s). For a sufficiently small, the floor is <=w a^2/2 and (1) gives ||e_N||<=w a^2. Since |H'| is uniformly bounded, (5),(1) imply through this initial layer

    sum_{k<N}|theta_{k+1}-theta_k|
        <=C a^4 N+C a^2 sum_{k<N}||e_k||+C a^6 N
        <=C' rho+C'' a^2[1+log(1/a)].              (7)

Choose rho so the first term is <=delta/4, then a so the second is <=delta/4. Thus every initial angle in [l+2delta,r-2delta] remains at least delta/2 inside I=[l+delta,r-delta] through time N. This is a direct displacement estimate on a fast time interval; no long-time Gronwall factor is introduced.

## 4. A fixed trapping interval after the initial layer

At the left endpoint of I, H'<0; at its right endpoint H'>0. Both signs are strict because these endpoints are strictly between the bad minimum and its two maxima. Put m=min(-H'(l+delta),H'(r-delta))>0.

Choose w small enough that Cw<=m/60. Choose a small enough that the remaining C a^2<=m/60. If ||e||<=w a^2, (5) shows that each endpoint's angular image points inward by at least a fixed positive multiple of m a^4. The differentiated estimate after (5) makes the angular map increasing at fixed e on I for small a. Its values on all of I therefore lie between its two endpoint values, which are in I; the small O(a^4) step ensures neither endpoint jumps across the other. Consequently theta_+ is in I whenever theta is in I and ||e||<=w a^2.

Normal confinement (6) simultaneously preserves ||e||<=w a^2, provided C a^4/lambda<=w a^2, already enforced by small a. Starting at time N, both bounds therefore persist forever. This proves the angular trapping claim. The initial layer was needed: setting e merely O(rho) in the endpoint test would introduce an order-a^2 error larger than the order-a^4 angular drift.

## 5. Convergence to the bad minimum

The trapped coordinates lie in a compact positive-definite covariance neighborhood and the compact angular interval I. Centered means and step segments remain in a fixed bounded normalized-mean set. By (2) the physical centered-mean Hessian is bounded by C a^2 there. Hence, for small a, physical unit-step GD satisfies

    F_a(M_+)<=F_a(M)-(1/2)||grad_centered F_a(M)||^2.

The risk is nonnegative, so the gradient tends to zero. Every accumulation point is critical. Normal criticality forces c=c_a(theta) by the uniqueness in Section 1. On I the reduced derivative is a^6[H'+O_C^1(a^2)]. The function H' has only one zero in I, at theta=pi/3, and its derivative there is 603/4>0. On a small neighborhood of this point the reduced derivative is strictly increasing; outside it H' is bounded away from zero. For sufficiently small a there is exactly one reduced critical point in I, the bad minimum from C06. Thus the compact trajectory has exactly one accumulation point and converges to it. Nonzero limiting loss and nonglobality are inherited from C06, not re-proved here.

## Checks, rung, and unpaid steps

C13/C14 exact scripts verify the metric, lag cancellation and B; check_tracking_recurrence.py verifies the scalar contraction-floor and sum identities, including a wrong forcing-scale control. These checks certify finite algebra only. The smooth coordinate estimates, domination in (2), discrete Taylor remainder and trapping argument remain an unaudited analytic proof. No Lean or independent PASS is asserted.

This is a centered, planar projected-GD basin result. A generic unrestricted student has a free centroid, and random initialization is not confined to the plane or to this covariance neighborhood. Neither gap is covered by calling the covariance critical section invariant. Full random-initialized DDPM failure probability, efficient annealed learning, and the full T309 target remain open.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:f22afa8dbc4714698345d222fcaa86db49adc9c307443f1daede1d6e777bb6df","revision_digest":"sha256:b9039c66778e3af025bde199d0edc165da1fa1e71f765b549cd5297ada650e26","source_id":"owner-own-work:T309-w721-C15-v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1-unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: In mathematical analysis, the Kakutani fixed-point theorem is a fixed-point theorem for set-valued functions. It provides sufficient conditions for a set-valued function defined on a convex, compact subset of a Euclidean space to have a fixed point, i.e. a point which is mapped to a set containing it. The Kakutani fixed point theorem is a generalization of the Brouwer fixed point theorem. The Brouwer fixed point theorem is a fundamental result in topology which proves the existence of fixed points for continuous functions defined on compact, convex subsets of Euclidean spaces. Kakutani's theorem extends this to set-valued functions.
title: Kakutani fixed-point theorem

body: In functional analysis, the Hahn–Banach theorem is a central result that allows the extension of bounded linear functionals defined on a vector subspace of some vector space to the whole space. The theorem also shows that there are sufficient continuous linear functionals defined on every normed vector space in order to study the dual space. Another version of the Hahn–Banach theorem is known as the Hahn–Banach separation theorem or the hyperplane separation theorem, and has numerous uses in convex geometry.
title: Hahn–Banach theorem

A point $\bm{x} \in A$ is \textbf{terraced} if $A$ is locally modeled on a standard multiquadrant near $\bm{x}$, i.e., there exist a (box-convex) multiquadrant $Q \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ at $\bm{0}$ and a neighborhood $U$ of $\bm{x}$ such that 
    $$A \cap U = \left( \bm{x} + Q\right) \cap U.$$
    Otherwise, $\bm{x}$ is called \textbf{slippery}.

body: For estimating the mean of a multivariate normal N(mu, I_d) in dimension d >= 3 from one observation X under squared loss, the James-Stein estimator (1 - (d - 2)/||X||^2) X strictly dominates the maximum likelihood estimator X everywhere: shrinking toward the origin reduces total risk uniformly (Stein's paradox). The MLE is admissible in dimensions 1 and 2; the phenomenon opened empirical Bayes and shrinkage estimation.
title: James-Stein Shrinkage

[Proposition prop:layeredmax of arXiv:2609.03081, 'Non-attacking rook placements on crossword grids'] For a positive integer $n$, consider the collection of integers
    \[
    \sum_{i = 0}^{m-1} S(m_1, m - i)S(m_2, m - i)\left((m-i)^{n - m_1 - m_2} \cdot (m-i)!\right)^2
    \]
    over all pairs $m_1, m_2$ of integers with $0 \leq m := \min(m_1, m_2)$ and $m_1 + m_2 \leq n$.  Then the largest of these numbers is achieved when
    \[
    m_1 = m_2 \in [m_*, m^*]
    \]
    where $m_*, m^*$ are respectively the (unique) positive solutions of
    $n = \frac{\ln(m_* + 1)}{\ln(1 + 1/m_*)} + 2m_*$ and $n = \frac{\ln\big((3m^* + 1)(m^* - 1))/4\big)}{2 \ln(1 + 1/m^*)} + 2m^* + 1$.
title: Proposition prop:layeredmax of arXiv:2609.03081

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For an electrical network on a graph with nonnegative edge conductances c_e, the effective resistance R_eff(a,b) between vertices a, b is defined variationally, via Thomson's principle, as the minimum of sum_e (1/c_e) i_e^2 over unit flows i from a to b obeying Kirchhoff's node law, or equivalently via Dirichlet's principle over voltage functions. Rayleigh's monotonicity law states that R_eff(a,b) is monotone nonincreasing as a function of each conductance: increasing any conductance, adding an edge, or short-circuiting (identifying) any pair of vertices can only decrease or preserve R_eff(a,b), while decreasing a conductance, or deleting an edge, can only increase or preserve it. This purely variational fact underlies comparisons between random walks on different graphs via the resistance-recurrence correspondence, that a network is recurrent for its associated random walk if and only if R_eff(a,infinity)=infinity, comparisons of hitting and commute times, and resistance-based bounds on percolation-type crossing quantities. It gives only monotone comparisons, no quantitative rates, and using it for random-walk conclusions requires the standard electrical network-reversible Markov chain correspondence, with conductances proportional to transition rates, to be correctly set up first. Typical failure: Applying Rayleigh monotonicity to compare effective resistances between two networks that differ in more than conductance values on a shared edge set, such as networks on genuinely different vertex sets or after a modification that is not literally a conductance increase/decrease, edge addition/deletion, or vertex identification; the monotonicity is a coupling statement about the same underlying network with modified weights, and applying it across structurally different networks without an explicit embedding produces an unjustified comparison. Canonical reference: Rayleigh, 1871, Philosophical Magazine; Doyle and Snell, Random Walks and Electric Networks, 1984, Mathematical Association of America; Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, 2016, Cambridge University Press.
a well-defined electrical network with nonnegative conductances, on a finite graph or an infinite graph with appropriate limiting or boundary conditions
the comparison is between two networks differing only in conductance values on a common edge set, or related by a clean edge addition, deletion, or vertex identification
finite total energy for the relevant flows or potentials, so the variational characterization is well posed
for random-walk conclusions, the standard correspondence between the electrical network and a reversible Markov chain

body:
[Defn $\partial$-ribbons of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] A \textbf{system of $\bm \partial$-ribbons} adapted to $Z$ is a finite collection of pairwise disjoint smoothly embedded strips $R_m = \sigma_m \times [-1, 1] \subset M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ such that
    \begin{itemize}
        \item The arcs $\sigma_m \times \{\pm1\}$ are tangent to the foliation $\mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$, and each ribbon is transverse to $\mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ and tangent to $Z$,
        
        \item For the initial point $p_m$ of $\sigma_m$, the interval $p_j \times [-1,1]$ lies on $\partial_* M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ away from $N_\partial^\mathrm{win}$, and for the end point $q_m$, the interval $q_m \times [-1,1]$ lies either in the interior of a vertical side of an annular fence, or in the interior of a window. Moreover, $R_m$ intersects $\partial M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ along these intervals only, and transversally. 
        
        We further require that the ribbons are tangent to $\partial_y$ inside of $N_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$.
    \end{itemize}

    This system is \textbf{$\bm \partial$-full} if for each point $p \in \partial_* M_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$, the leaf of $\partial \mathcal{F}_{\mathord{\scalebox{0.45}{$\square$}}}$ passing through $p$ intersects interiors of initial intervals of $\partial$-ribbons, or interiors of windows, on both sides of $p$.
title: $\partial$-ribbons

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:04b7f623c8e0de363dc42d2967a953279ac588e6e59705f29822a9cb4bae81c6","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/04/04b7f623c8e0de363dc42d2967a953279ac588e6e59705f29822a9cb4bae81c6.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:65d11978ec33d8be369af5a745954f6f209062ceba8da95bb586b599673e43ca","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c12","bundle_id":"population.i0005-sink-capacity-and-gradient-obstruction-005","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"parking and killed random walks","draft":"w661/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:permanent-trap-obstruction-to-free-green-gradient-comparison-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C12 v1: a trap prevents a universal free-Green gradient comparison

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN killed Green identity and Green
asymptotics; UNCHECKED prior statement of this particular route obstruction.

Use full-space discrete-time uniform nearest-neighbor SRW on Z^4. Let
G(x)=sum_{n>=0}P_0(X_n=x), g=G(0), a=2/pi^2, v_R=R e_1,
y_R=(R-1)e_1, and w_R=y_R+e_2, for integer R>=3. Thus v_R and w_R
are two possible destinations of a departure from y_R. Define

    q_R(z)=P_z(T_0<T_{v_R}),

where entrance times include time zero: v_R is a permanent absorbing trap
and 0 is the target. Put gamma=G(e_2-e_1). Then

    q_R(v_R)=0,
    q_R(w_R)=a(g-gamma)/g^2 R^(-2)+O(R^(-3)),
    [G(w_R)-G(v_R)]/g=2a/g R^(-3)+O(R^(-4)).

In particular there is no constant C independent of the trap location
such that the difference between these two killed hitting probabilities
is always at most C times the corresponding free hitting-probability
difference. The ratio grows asymptotically like (g-gamma)R/(2g).

## Exact killed Green identity

For any z!=v_R, strong Markov at T_{v_R} gives the expected number of
visits to 0 before the killing time:

    G^{v_R}(z,0)=G(z)-P_z(T_{v_R}<infinity)G(v_R)
                =G(z)-G(z-v_R)G(v_R)/g.

All quantities are finite by transience, so subtracting the expected
post-hitting visits is justified. Apply strong Markov instead at T_0,
on the event T_0<T_{v_R}:

    G^{v_R}(z,0)=q_R(z)G^{v_R}(0,0),
    G^{v_R}(0,0)=g-G(v_R)^2/g.

The denominator is positive (it counts at least the time-zero visit).
Thus

    q_R(z)=[G(z)-G(z-v_R)G(v_R)/g]/[g-G(v_R)^2/g].

For z=w_R, the numerator is G(w_R)-(gamma/g)G(v_R). Also gamma<g,
because gamma/g is the probability of ever hitting 0 from e_2-e_1,
which is strictly less than one for this transient walk. This strictness
also follows from the maximum principle and the decay of G at infinity.

## Constants and errors

Lawler--Limic Theorem 4.3.1 explicitly covers simple random walk including
the bipartite case, and yields G(x)=a|x|_2^(-2)+O(|x|_2^(-4)) in d=4.
Since |v_R|_2^2=R^2 and |w_R|_2^2=R^2-2R+2,

    G(v_R)=a R^(-2)+O(R^(-4)),
    G(w_R)=a R^(-2)+2a R^(-3)+O(R^(-4)).

Substitution into the exact formula, and the expansion of its denominator
as g+O(R^(-4)), give the assertions. Both leading constants are positive,
so their ratio has the stated asymptotic.

## Scope of the refuted route

The parking source, Proposition 8.3 Step 3, bounds instruction covariance
by products of hitting influences. One might hope to recover a single
Green function by replacing every obstacle-conditioned influence difference
with a free-Green gradient. The permanent-trap example shows that such a
uniform replacement is false even for a simple killed-walk influence.
It does not exclude an averaged estimate exploiting the random environment,
nor does it identify these q_R with all the source's conditional influences.
The initial-value contribution in Step 2 would in any event still require
a separate treatment.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:fb8fccc578ac5b2adf0f53a9de6f6cd4ac7f55cbcca4e34b8b2f482f45071155","revision_digest":"sha256:b957320fe2184e13d7ae44b858c0f0243162548c4028cdc2cc8b7ea2d0bdaaef","source_id":"owner-own-work:w661:I0005-C12:v1","source_revision":"v1; 2026-10-14T06:02:25.9473414+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition 2 (Blowdowns under Type-III curvature and diameter control) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be a closed connected orientable three-manifold modeled on
\(\RR^3\), \(\Nil\), or \(\Sol\), and let \(g(t)\) be an immortal Ricci
flow.  Suppose that, for all sufficiently large \(t\),
\begin{equation}
        |\Rm_{g(t)}|\leq C/t,
        \qquad
        \diam(M,g(t))\leq C\sqrt t.
\end{equation}
Then the compact and universal-cover blowdown conclusions of
\cite[Theorem~1.2]{Lott10} hold in the following form.  The compact normalized
metrics converge to a point in the Euclidean and Nil cases.  In the Sol case,
every Gromov--Hausdorff subsequential limit is a metric circle or a compact
interval.  The lifted blowdown flows
converge in the pointed Cheeger--Hamilton sense to the corresponding
homogeneous expanding soliton solutions.  In the Euclidean case, the limit is
the static Euclidean flow \((\RR^3,g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau))\), where
\(g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau)=dx^2+dy^2+dz^2\) for \(\tau>0\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Blowdowns under Type-III curvature and diameter control

Let A be a real D-by-D matrix and 0<=K<=D. Suppose a_1,...,a_K are linearly independent real left eigenvectors with a_i^T A=lambda_i a_i^T, and b_1,...,b_(D-K) are linearly independent real right eigenvectors with A b_j=mu_j b_j. Assume a_i^T b_j=0 for every i,j. Then det(z I-A)=product_(i=1)^K(z-lambda_i) product_(j=1)^(D-K)(z-mu_j). Thus these two lists give all eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity. No orthogonality within either family and no diagonalizability of A are required.
Finite-dimensional real square matrix
Independent left eigenvectors and independent right eigenvectors of complementary cardinalities
Every left eigenvector is orthogonal to every right eigenvector

[Corollary cor:two_sided_current_explicit of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $i\in\{1,2\}$ and adopt the assumptions of Theorem~(thm:explicit_current_1 of the paper)
($i=1$) or Theorem~(thm:explicit_current_2 of the paper) ($i=2$). 
Since $Q$, $\mathrm{Var}_\mu(W)$
and $\|\bar W\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}$ are invariant under sign reversal 
of $\overline{J}_t(U)\mapsto -\overline{J}_t(U)$ (hence $U\mapsto -U$)
the parameters
$\tilde\sigma_{J,i}^2, c_{J,i}$ remain unchanged.
Applying the theorems to 
$-\overline{J}_t(U)$ therefore leads to bounds on the left tail with the same constants.
For all $t>0$, $a>0$,
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\E^\mu[\overline{J}_t] -\overline{J}_t(U)\geq a\right)
\leq
\left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
\exp\left[-t\frac{\tilde\sigma_{J,i}^2}{c_{J,i}^2}
  h\left(\frac{c_{J,i} a}{\tilde\sigma_{J,i}^2}\right)\right].
\end{align}
Correspondingly, a union bound correspondingly gives the two-sided sub-gamma bound, and its simpler Bernstein
form with the additional factor of $2$, i.e.,
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\bigl|\overline{J}_t(U) - \E^\mu[\overline{J}_t]\bigr| \geq a\right)
&\leq
2\left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
\exp\left[-t\frac{\tilde\sigma_{J,i}^2}{c_{J,i}^2}
  h\left(\frac{c_{J,i} a}{\tilde\sigma_{J,i}^2}\right)\right]
\\
&\leq
2\left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
\exp\left[-\frac{ta^2}{2(\tilde\sigma_{J,i}^2 + c_{J,i}a)}\right].
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Left-tail and two-sided bounds for current observables

body:
Let X be a Banach space. A strongly continuous semigroup (C_0-semigroup) on X is a family (T(t))_{t ≥ 0} of bounded linear operators on X with T(0) = I, T(t + s) = T(t)T(s) for all t, s ≥ 0, and t ↦ T(t)x continuous from [0, ∞) to X for every x ∈ X (for a semigroup this is equivalent to T(t)x → x as t ↓ 0 for every x, and also equivalent to weak continuity, i.e. continuity of t ↦ ⟨T(t)x, x*⟩ on [0, ∞) for every x ∈ X and every x* ∈ X*). Every C_0-semigroup is exponentially bounded: there are M ≥ 1 and ω ∈ ℝ with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ M e^{ωt} for all t ≥ 0; the growth bound is ω_0 = inf of such ω. It is a contraction semigroup if ‖T(t)‖ ≤ 1 for all t, and quasi-contractive if ‖T(t)‖ ≤ e^{ωt}. Its (infinitesimal) generator is the operator A with D(A) = {x ∈ X : lim_{t↓0} (T(t)x − x)/t exists} and Ax equal to that limit. One says A generates T and writes T(t) = e^{tA}. Norm continuity of t ↦ T(t) at 0 (a uniformly continuous semigroup) holds if and only if the generator is bounded, in which case T(t) = Σ t^n A^n / n!; the typical generators of PDE semigroups are unbounded and the semigroup is only strongly continuous.
X is a Banach space
each T(t) is bounded and linear
T(0) = I and the semigroup law holds
strong continuity: T(t)x → x as t ↓ 0 for each x
title: Strongly Continuous (C0) Semigroup and Its Generator

[Definition 31 (Ordering of triples) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Consider two triples $\tau=(\alpha,\omega,\eta)$ and $\tau'=(\alpha',\omega',\eta')$.
    We say that the first is smaller than the second,
    and write $\tau\preceq\tau'$,
    whenever all of the following conditions hold:
    \[
    \alpha \leq \alpha', \qquad -\omega \leq -\omega', \qquad \eta \leq \eta',
    \]
    where the inequalities are understood componentwise.
    This defines a partial order on $\Pi_G$.
title: Ordering of triples

body: A topological space X is Hausdorff (T2) if for every pair of distinct points x and y in X there exist disjoint open sets U and V with x in U and y in V. In a Hausdorff space every singleton is closed, every compact subset is closed, and limits are unique: a sequence (more generally, a net or a filter) converges to at most one point. Every metric space is Hausdorff.
title: Hausdorff space

[Theorem Fiberwise estimate theorem of arXiv:2608.27248, 'Optimal Transport and the ABP Method in Higher Codimension'] Assume the hypotheses of Theorem (Inverse transport theorem of the paper) with
$1\leq m\leq4$ and $\mathcal K=\mathcal E$, where $\mathcal E$ is a centered
ellipsoid.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \int_\Sigma w_xp_\infty(x)\,\mathrm d\lambda_u(x)
 \geq\frac{\omega_n}{\omega_{n+m}}.
\end{equation}
The constant is sharp.  If $m=4$ and equality holds, then for $\mu$-almost
every $x$ with $p_\infty(x)>0$,
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_x=\mathbb{B}^4_{R(x)},
 \qquad
 y\longmapsto\det Q_x(y)\text{ is constant on }\mathcal{C}_x.
\end{equation}
Here $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_x$ and $R(x)$ are defined in Section
(section fiberwise estimate of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let n ≥ 2 and let ψ ∈ C_c^∞(R^n) be supported in the annulus {1/2 ≤ |ξ| ≤ 2}. Define Pf = F^{−1}(ψ f̂) and the half-wave propagator e^{±it|∇|}f = F^{−1}(e^{±it|ξ|} f̂). There is C = C(n,ψ) such that for all t ∈ R and all f ∈ L¹ ∩ L², ‖e^{±it|∇|} P f‖_{L^∞(R^n)} ≤ C (1 + |t|)^{−(n−1)/2} ‖f‖_{L¹(R^n)}. By scaling, with P_N f = F^{−1}(ψ(ξ/N) f̂), N > 0, ‖e^{±it|∇|}P_N f‖_{L^∞} ≤ C N^n (1 + N|t|)^{−(n−1)/2}‖f‖_{L¹}. The frequency localization is essential: e^{it|∇|} itself is not bounded from L¹ to L^∞.

[Proposition thm:WindingZero of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $\gamma:\left[0,K\right]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$
be a continuous BV path which is parametrised at unit speed. Suppose that $\log S(\gamma)_{u,v}$ has infinite R.O.C. on all time intervals $[u,v]\subseteq[0,K]$. 
Let $s$ be a given fixed time at which $\gamma$ is differentiable and let  $\varepsilon\in(0,1/6]$. Let $T\in(s,K]$ be chosen such that 
\begin{align}
\left|\gamma_{t}-\gamma_{s}-\gamma_{s}^{\prime}\left(t-s\right)\right| & \leqslant\varepsilon\left(t-s\right),\\
\Big|\Big|\frac{\gamma_{t}-\gamma_{s}}{t-s}\Big|-1\Big| & \leqslant\varepsilon\nonumber 
\end{align}for all $t\in (s,T]$ 
and that
$\left|\gamma_{t}-\gamma_{s}\right|<\left|\gamma_{T}-\gamma_{s}\right|$ for all $s\in(t,T)$.
Then one has
\[
\eta\big(\tilde{{\cal A}}_{s,T}\gamma,(x,y)\big)=0
\]
for all $(x,y)\in(0,1)\times\mathbb{R}\backslash(\tilde{{\cal A}}_{s,T}\gamma)[s,T].$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition thm:WindingZero of arXiv:2506.18207

For $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ open and bounded and $T>0$, the parabolic cylinder is $U_T=U\times(0,T]$ (the top $U\times\{T\}$ is included) and its parabolic boundary is $\Gamma_T=\overline{U_T}\setminus U_T=(\overline U\times\{0\})\cup(\partial U\times[0,T])$, the bottom together with the lateral sides; the top is not part of it. Maximum principles place extrema of subsolutions on $\Gamma_T$, and initial-boundary data are prescribed exactly on $\Gamma_T$. The standard backward cylinder of radius $r$ at $(x_0,t_0)$ is $Q_r(x_0,t_0)=B_r(x_0)\times(t_0-r^2,t_0]$; it respects the parabolic scaling $(x,t)\mapsto(rx,r^2t)$, and the natural distance is $|x-y|+|t-s|^{1/2}$. Interior estimates for parabolic equations hold on sets at positive parabolic distance from the parabolic boundary, including sets reaching up to the top time.
U open and bounded in R^n
T > 0
title: Parabolic Cylinder and Parabolic Boundary

[Theorem thm:defecttwodiameter of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For every $h\geq2$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\qquad \eta_2(h)=1+\binom{h+1}{2}.\qquad}
\end{equation}
More explicitly, if
\[
 D_h=1+\binom{h+1}{2},
\]
then equality is attained by
\[
 \{0,1,D_h-h,D_h\}\qquad(h\ \textup{even})
\]
and by
\[
 \left\{0,\frac{h-1}{2},D_h-\frac{h+1}{2},D_h\right\}
 \qquad(h\ \textup{odd}).
\]

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2608.27569, 'Laplace and Dolbeault operators on Sasakian manifolds'] Let $(M^{2n+1},g,\xi )$ be a compact Sasakian
manifold. Let $m\in\{0,\ldots, n-1\}$. If  $\omega$ is a nonzero eigenform of $\Delta_{\overline\partial}$ restricted to $m$-forms, that is $\Delta_{\overline\partial}\omega=\lambda\omega$ with $\mathcal{L}_\xi\omega=iq\omega$, for some $q\leq 0$, then the following estimate
$$\lambda\geq -q(n-m).$$
holds. Equality is attained if and only if $\lambda=q=0$, that is, $\omega\in \mathcal{H}^m_{\overline\partial}(0)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem T_sub_density of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] Fix $r\geqslant5$. 
Let $p=(\bar\gamma n)^{-1/\lambda}$
for some 
$\bar\gamma > \gamma$, where 
$\gamma$ is as  in (equation E_gamma of the paper) above. Define 
\[
\bar\alpha:= (r-2)!\bar\gamma^{r-2} > \alpha_{{r\choose2}-2}\,, 
\]
and let $1<\rho < 
1+\left(\binom r2-2\right)^{-1}$
be the smallest root of the equation 
\[
\rho^{\binom r2-1}=\bar\alpha(\rho -1)\,.
\]
Then, 
\[
|E(\langle \mathcal G_{n,p}\rangle_{K_r})|\sim \rho\cdot p\binom n2\,,
\]
in probability, as $n\to\infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

	\begin{itemize}

If setup durations B are sampled independently with finite second moment and a time observer samples a stationary setup interval, the residual mean is E[B^2]/(2*E[B]). Deterministic B=beta gives beta/2, while Exp(mean beta) gives beta. But an arrival that initiates a setup samples the original B, not this length-biased residual. Check: Renewal reward integrates the residual triangular area B^2/2 in each interval and divides by E[B]. The initiation observer is an independent endpoint observer, distinguishing its sampling law. Let p and q be probability mass functions on a nonempty finite set S and L = max_x (p(x) + q(x) - 1)_+. Over all couplings (X, Y) of p and q, the agreement probability P(X = Y) takes exactly the values in [L, 1 - d_TV(p, q)], and the disagreement probability exactly those in [d_TV(p, q), 1 - L]. At most one point x* has p(x*) + q(x*) > 1. If L = 0 some coupling has X != Y almost surely; if L > 0 a coupling of least agreement can put mass L on (x*, x*) and nothing elsewhere on the diagonal.

couplings are arbitrary joint laws with marginals p and q

Let (X, mu) be a measure space. If 0 <= f_1 <= f_2 <= ... are measurable and f_n increases pointwise almost everywhere to f, then f is measurable and integral f_n dmu increases to integral f dmu, with values in [0, infinity]. If instead the nonnegative measurable f_n decrease pointwise almost everywhere to f and integral f_1 dmu < infinity, then integral f_n dmu decreases to integral f dmu; without the integrability of f_1 this fails (f_n = 1 on [n, infinity) in R decreases to 0 while every integral is infinite). Separately, every monotone sequence of real numbers converges in the extended reals, and converges in R exactly when it is bounded.

Decreasing case: f_1 is finite almost everywhere, and f_1 - f_n increases to f_1 - f, nonnegative and measurable, so the increasing case gives integral (f_1 - f_n) -> integral (f_1 - f); subtracting from the finite integral f_1 gives integral f_n -> integral f. Real sequences: a nondecreasing sequence converges to its supremum, which is finite exactly when the sequence is bounded above; a nonincreasing one to its infimum, likewise.","provenance":"correction of claim_4ecf42a1906b7833d5ccb1be36fe1b0db3da05c59e2e1798e0ac4ccb0d1aa8a4 (06 Oct 2026): merged with its duplicate in dedup group 204 (group04/B11 20261006T0920Z MERGE_PLAN.jsonl, read again by claude-4a88bc43)","source_id":"proofwiki:Monotone Convergence Theorem (Measure Theory)","supersedes":"claim_4ecf42a1906b7833d5ccb1be36fe1b0db3da05c59e2e1798e0ac4ccb0d1aa8a4","trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem thm:generative of arXiv:2608.30072, 'Learning Representations through Token Prediction: \\ Geometry, Approximation, and Downstr'] Suppose Assumption~(asp:generative of the paper) holds. Then, the generated sequence from both the pre-trained and post-trained generators is likely to stay within the set of plausible continuations
	$$
	\rho_{p}(q^{\rm pre},p)\ge 1-C_{\mathbb{Q}^{\rm pre}}\epsilon_p\qquad {\rm and }\qquad \rho_{p}(q^{\rm post},p)\ge 1-C_{\mathbb{Q}^{\rm post}}\exp\left( {2\epsilon_r\over \lambda}\right)\epsilon_p.
	$$
	In addition, the regret of the post-trained generator can be upper bounded
	$$
	\rho_s(q^{\rm post},r^\ast)\le \min\left\{R, 4 \epsilon_r+2\lambda\left(1+\log \left(2k\right)\right)+4C_{\mathbb{Q}^{\rm post}}k^2\epsilon_p\right\}.
	$$
	There exist instances $(r^\ast, \hat{r}, p_j(X), q^{\rm pre})$ that satisfy Assumption~(asp:generative of the paper) for which
	$$
	\rho_s(q^{\rm post},r^\ast)\ge  {1\over 2}\min\left\{R,2\epsilon_r+\lambda\log(k-1)\right\}.
	$$
	
	As a comparison, we also evaluate the performance of $q^{\hat{r},\pi,\lambda}$ when the reference distribution $\pi$ is a uniform distribution on $\mathcal V$. We show
	$$
	\rho_s(q^{\hat{r},\pi,\lambda},r^\ast)\le \min\{R, 4 \epsilon_r+2\lambda\left(1+\log d\right)\},
	$$
	and there exist instances $(r^\ast, \hat{r})$ for which
	$$
	\rho_s(q^{\hat{r},\pi,\lambda},r^\ast)\ge  {1\over 2}\min\left\{R,2\epsilon_r+\lambda\log(d-1)\right\}.
	$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 28 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Let $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $h\in Z\hat C^{1}(\Delta^3_T;B_\alpha)$. For each $\tau\in[0,T]$, define $\mathfrak r_{\mathrm d, \mathrm {log}}^\tau(h):=[r_{\mathrm d}^\tau(h)]_\tau$, where $r_{\mathrm d}^\tau(h)$ is the dyadic frozen increment from Definition~\ref{def:dyadic-frozen-defect-family}. Then
\[
\mathfrak r_{\mathrm d, \mathrm {log}}(h):=\bigl(\mathfrak r_{\mathrm d, \mathrm {log}}^\tau(h)\bigr)_{\tau\in[0,T]}\in \mathfrak Q_{\mathrm{fr}, \mathrm {log}}^{1,\alpha}.
\]
Moreover, for every $\tau\in[0,T]$ and every representative $r^\tau\in \mathfrak r_{\mathrm d, \mathrm {log}}^\tau(h)$, one has $\delta r^\tau = h^\tau$. Finally,
\begin{equation*}
\|\mathfrak r_{\mathrm d, \mathrm {log}}(h)\|_{\mathfrak Q_{\mathrm{fr}, \mathrm {log}}^{1,\alpha}}\le C_T M_{\alpha,T}\|h\|_{1,\alpha}.
\end{equation*}

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; status: independently checked proof; F0124_C20 version 1. For 0<p<16/17, theta=(1-p)/p>1/16, independent iid fair sign scenery and the exact maximal-cut interval gas, consider constant full words on odd lengths l. Condition on center +1 and every interval variable OTHER than the whole-word interval being vacant. This event has positive finite-volume probability. The whole interval then has conditional occupation probability h_l(theta)/(1+h_l(theta)), since the only remaining sets have weights 1 and h_l. Confined-loop contributions force h_l to infinity through odd l, so this probability tends to one. No summable length-only occupation profile can bound EVERY partial conditional distribution. This rules out extending universal all-history independent interval domination through p<16/17; it does not prove bad configurations. Keeping competing intervals, restricting exploration histories, or controlling rare adverse histories in aggregate may still work. No assertion is made at p=16/17.

In the fixed-n common-Hessian RR model f_i=x^2/2+kappa_T*y^2/2+b_i*x+c_i*y, with n>=2, fixed deterministic x0!=0,y0, fixed zero-sum linear terms of mean squares s1>=0,s2>0, fresh independent uniform epoch permutations and T=nK, assume kappa_T*log(T)/T->c in (4,infinity). Then the globally minimized expected final-epoch function error is asymptotic to A*exp(-4*T/kappa_T), and every sequence of global minimizing constant steps satisfies eta_T=2/kappa_T+o(1/T). {"artifact_digest":"sha256:691a4c750e6ef517bcddbbcef877e4a72ddda8e7f56739c0bedbf39be8a7f57b","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/69/691a4c750e6ef517bcddbbcef877e4a72ddda8e7f56739c0bedbf39be8a7f57b.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:2d54bcb61f0352dd3dbe49d643f6003b09a5032407fee7ca3f568da285d67514","bundle_entry_key":"supercritical-kappa-common-hessian","bundle_id":"population.t362-supercritical-kappa-004","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"optimization; random reshuffling; supercritical condition number; optimal constant step","draft":"w732/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.randomreshuffling:common-hessian-random-reshuffling-supercritical-condition-number-stability-edge-optimizer","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Target 1: supercritical condition number and the stiff stability edge

Status: proof draft (unaudited). No novelty or full-T362 claim.

## Statement

Take the common-Hessian model of C001, with mu=1, fixed n>=2, deterministic x0!=0 and y0, and fixed zero-sum component linear terms of mean squares s1>=0 and s2>0. Epoch permutations are fresh, independent and uniform, shared across coordinates. Set T=nK. Suppose kappa=kappa_T satisfies

    kappa*log(T)/T -> c,   4<c<infinity.

Let P_T(eta) denote expected final-epoch function error and A=x0^2/2. Then

    min_{eta>=0} P_T(eta) ~ A*exp(-4T/kappa).              (1)

Every sequence of global minimizers satisfies

    eta_T = 2/kappa + o(1/T).                            (2)

In particular log(min P_T)/log T -> -4/c. Equation (1), rather than A*T^(-4/c), retains subleading dependence of kappa_T: the ratio assumption alone does not justify replacing the exponential by that power with relative error o(1).

## Exact input, inherited from C001

For q=kappa*eta and W_n(q)=sum_{0<=i<j<n}((1-q)^i-(1-q)^j)^2, the stiff-coordinate variance satisfies

    P_T(eta) >= [s2*q^2*W_n(q)/(2(n-1)*kappa)]
                   *sum_{r=0}^{K-1}(1-q)^(2nr).          (3)

Always W_n(q)>=q^2, by the pair (0,1). The flat deterministic term is exactly A*(1-eta)^(2T). For 0<q<2 the stationary stiff variance is (s2/kappa)*J_n(q), where

    J_n(q)=q^2*W_n(q)/[2(n-1)(1-(1-q)^(2n))].

The actual finite-horizon stiff variance is this stationary quantity times 1-(1-q)^(2T). All objective contributions are nonnegative; correlations of the two coordinate noises introduce no mixed objective term.

## Upper bound

1. Put ell=log T, delta=ell^(-2), and choose q_c=2-delta, eta_c=q_c/kappa. For large T, 0<q_c<2 and eta_c->0. Since n is fixed, W_n stays bounded near 2; expansion of the fixed polynomial denominator at 2 gives J_n(2-delta)=O(delta^-1). Explicitly 1-(1-delta)^(2n)~2n*delta, with a positive leading coefficient. The stiff variance is therefore

    O(1/(kappa*delta))=O(ell^3/T).                       (4)

The stiff deterministic contribution is at most (kappa*y0^2/2)*exp(-2*delta*T).

2. Since T/kappa~ell/c and T/kappa^2->0, the flat deterministic term is

    A*(1-eta_c)^(2T)
      = A*exp(-4T/kappa)
          *exp(2*delta*T/kappa + O(T/kappa^2))
      = A*exp(-4T/kappa)*(1+o(1)).                       (5)

The flat variance is O(eta_c^3)=O(kappa^-3) by the settled fixed-n scalar variance estimate. This is an upper bound on the finite-horizon contribution, because its stable geometric multiplier is bounded by the stationary one.

3. Let B_T=A*exp(-4T/kappa). Its logarithm divided by ell tends to -4/c. Since c>4,

    (ell^3/T)/B_T ->0,   kappa^-3/B_T ->0,
    [kappa*exp(-2T/ell^2)]/B_T ->0.

For example the logarithm of the first ratio divided by ell tends to -1+4/c<0. The third ratio has a dominant negative term -2T/ell^2, while all its other logarithmic terms are O(ell). Thus (4)-(5) prove

    min P_T <= B_T*(1+o(1)) ->0.                        (6)

## Global lower bound and optimizer localization

4. The exact error is a continuous coercive polynomial by (3) and W_n(q)>=q^2; hence global minimizers exist. Fix ANY sequence eta_T of them and write q_T=kappa*eta_T. Eventually q_T<3. Indeed if q_T>=3 along a subsequence, the last summand of (3) gives

    P_T(eta_T) >= [s2*q_T^4/(2(n-1)*kappa)]
                       *(q_T-1)^(2n(K-1))
                >= const * 2^(2(T-n))/kappa ->infinity,

contradicting (6). This uses kappa~cT/ell, and K->infinity; no small-step assumption is made.

5. If 2<q_T<3, let epsilon=q_T-2 in (0,1). The same last-summand bound gives

    P_T(eta_T) >= [8*s2/((n-1)*kappa)]
                         *(1+epsilon)^(2(T-n)).

Since log(1+epsilon)>=epsilon/2 for epsilon in [0,1], and P_T(eta_T)<=1 eventually by (6),

    epsilon*(T-n) <= log kappa + O(1).

Consequently, whether q_T>2 or q_T<=2,

    q_T <= 2 + O(log kappa/T).                          (7)

The implied constant can be chosen uniformly over all global minimizers. This bounds possible unstable overshoot using noise amplification, not an assumed step-size cap.

6. From q_T<3, eta_T=q_T/kappa->0 and uniformly

    log[(1-eta_T)^(2T)] = -2q_T*T/kappa + O(T/kappa^2).

Because T/kappa^2->0 and log kappa/kappa->0, (7) implies

    P_T(eta_T) >= A*(1-eta_T)^(2T)
       >= A*exp(-4T/kappa-o(1))
       = B_T*(1-o(1)).                                 (8)

Combined with (6), this proves (1).

7. The same transient comparison, now using the relative upper bound (6), gives

    exp(2*(2-q_T)*T/kappa+o(1)) <= 1+o(1).

Thus limsup (2-q_T)*T/kappa<=0. Bound (7) also gives liminf (2-q_T)*T/kappa>=0, since its possible negative part is O(log kappa/kappa)->0. Hence (2-q_T)*T/kappa->0, exactly (2). The proof applies to every sequence of global minimizers; it assumes neither uniqueness nor a local optimizer.

## Scope and least-trusted steps

This extends named target 1 to the parameter interval c>4, beyond C004's c in (0,4). The transition c=4 remains unpaid: the logarithmic variance cost in (4) is no longer negligible relative to the candidate transient, so this proof does not cover it. No assertion is made for s2=0, x0=0, growing n, a general finite-sum Hessian, or a full minimax last-iterate RR rate.

Independent audit should focus on steps 5-7 (unrestricted-step overshoot and the relative lower bound). Prior-art context is inherited from the C001 primary sources and the bounded literature query recorded with C004. No priority conclusion is drawn from that search. ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Controlled generators, exact finite-state diagnostic, coupling, renewal reward or capacity comparison Result: For queue-length vector q and a simultaneous unit increment on selected set A of size k, the quadratic potential changes by 2*sum_{i in A}q_i+k. Selecting the k shortest queues minimizes this one-step drift over all distinct-server choices. Uniform selection instead gives mean increment 2*k*sum_i q_i/n+k. This establishes a local balancing property, but the response of the job is the maximum of its task sojourn times, which also depends on residual service and the joint selected-state law. Check: Expand (q_i+1)^2-q_i^2 separately at each selected coordinate. A pairwise exchange replacing a selected larger queue by an unselected smaller queue decreases the drift, proving the minimizer. Obstruction: No stationary maximum-sojourn law or optimality for mean job response follows from the quadratic drift inequality.

[Lemma lem:boundary-construction of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Fix $n \geq 1$, and let $R$ be an $\ell_1 \times \ell_2$ rectangle, where $\ell_1, \ell_2 \gg (\log L)^6$. Let $\Lambda_{9L/10} \subset V \subset \Lambda$, and $0 \leq k \leq H-n$. Suppose that, w.h.p.\ under $\pi_{V}^k$, $R$ is contained in the interior of $\mathfrak{L}_{n-1}$ and that there are two points $A, B$ on the sides of $\partial R$ with the top arc of $\partial R$ from $A$ to $B$ in the interior of $\mathfrak{L}_n$, such that if $d$ is the distance from $\{A, B\}$ to the top or bottom of $R$, then $\sqrt{\ell_1}(\log L)^2 \leq d$. 

        Then there exists a $\pi^k_V$-measurable distribution on connected regions $Q\subset R$ with marked boundary conditions $\xi$ satisfying  (it:Q-simp-conn,it:dist-Q-R-bdy,it:good-boundary-points,it:Q-bc-arc of the paper)
        below, such that the following holds. If $\ensuremath{\mathcal A}_1$ is the area of the interior of $\mathfrak{L}_n$ intersected with~$Q$, and $\ensuremath{\mathcal A}_2$ is the area above the $(H+1-n)$ level line in $Q$ under $\pi^\xi_Q$, then $\ensuremath{\mathcal A}_2 \subset \ensuremath{\mathcal A}_1$ w.h.p.\ under $\pi^k_V$.        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $Q$ is simply connected,

            \item $\dist(\partial Q, \partial R) \leq \log L$,

            \item There exists $A', B' \in \partial Q$ such that ${\ensuremath{\mathscr C}}(\overline{A'B'}) \subset Q$, $\ensuremath{\mathcal Y}^{\blacktriangleleft}(A')$ does not intersect the left side of $Q$, $\ensuremath{\mathcal Y}^{\blacktriangleright}(B')$ does not intersect the right side of $Q$, and $\max\{d(A, A'), \dist(B, B')\} \leq 2(\log L)^5$.

            \item  The boundary conditions $\xi$ assigns height $H+1-n$ on the top arc from $A'$ to $B'$, and $H-n$ on the bottom arc.
        \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\subset\mathbb R\) be bounded pairwise disjoint Borel
sets, set \(A_j:=B_j\times I_a\) and \(A:=\bigcup_{j=1}^m A_j\). Let \(K_A\)
be the integral operator on \(L^2(A,\mathrm dA)\) with kernel
\(K_{\mathbb H}\) restricted to \(A\times A\). Then \(K_A\) is a positive
trace-class contraction, \(0\le K_A\le \operatorname{Id}\). Moreover, for
\(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\in\mathbb C^m\), define
\[
        g_s(z):=\sum_{j=1}^m(s_j-1)\mathbf 1_{A_j}(z),
        \qquad z\in A,
\]
and let \(M_{g_s}\) be multiplication by \(g_s\) on \(L^2(A,\mathrm dA)\).
Then \(M_{g_s}K_A\) is trace class and
\begin{equation}

        \mathbb E\left[\prod_{j=1}^m s_j^{\#(Z\cap A_j)}\right]
        =
        \det\left(\operatorname{Id}+M_{g_s}K_A\right),
\end{equation}
where the determinant is the Fredholm determinant on \(L^2(A,\mathrm dA)\).

body:
Let $\kappa \ge 0$ be a kernel supported in $[-a, a]$ with $\int\kappa = 1$ and moments $m_k = \int t^k \kappa(t)\,dt$, and let $H_\kappa(x) = \pi^{-1}\,\mathrm{PV}\!\int \kappa(t)/(t - x)\,dt$. For $|x| > a$ no principal value is needed and $H_\kappa(x) = -\pi^{-1}\sum_{k \ge 0} m_k\, x^{-(k+1)}$, the series converging absolutely; for a symmetric kernel the odd moments vanish. For the Epanechnikov kernel $\kappa(x) = \tfrac{3}{4\sqrt5}(1 - x^2/5)^+$ ($a = \sqrt5$): $m_2 = 1$, $m_4 = 15/7$, so $H_\kappa(x) = -\pi^{-1}(x^{-1} + x^{-3} + \tfrac{15}{7}x^{-5}) + O(x^{-7})$. Its closed form $-\tfrac{3x}{10\pi} + \tfrac{3}{4\sqrt5\pi}(1 - x^2/5)\log|\tfrac{\sqrt5 - x}{\sqrt5 + x}|$ is the same function, but in floating point its two $O(x)$ terms cancel to leave the $O(1/x)$ value with absolute rounding error of order $\varepsilon |x|$: the error exceeds the value once $|x| \gtrsim \varepsilon^{-1/2}$, and the three-term series is accurate to $10^{-7}$ from $|x| = 30$ on, so a numerically sound evaluation switches to the series there.
kappa nonnegative, integrable, compactly supported in [-a, a]
the moment series is used only for |x| > a (outside the support)

[Theorem MH2p1 of arXiv:2511.15893, 'On a Class of Dynamical Poisson-Voronoi Tessellations'] Suppose there are two types of stations with intensities $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ and speeds $v_1> v_2$. Let $\lambda_1+\lambda_2=\lambda$. Then we have:

\begin{enumerate}[(i).]
\item  The pure handover frequencies are 
\begin{equation}
     \Lambda_l= \frac{4v_l\sqrt{\lambda}}{\pi}\left(\frac{\lambda_l}{\lambda}\right)^2, \text{ for }l=1,2.
\end{equation}
\item   The mixed handover frequencies satisfies the relations $\Lambda^{(1)}_{1,2}=\Lambda^{(2)}_{2,1}$ and $\Lambda^{(2)}_{1,2}=\Lambda^{(1)}_{2,1}$.
\item  For $k=1,2$,
\begin{align}

body: A sunflower (or Delta-system) with r petals is a collection of sets S_1, ..., S_r such that the pairwise intersection S_i intersect S_j is the same set Y (the core) for every pair i not equal to j. The classical sunflower lemma: if F is a family of finite sets, each of size at most k, with |F| > k! (r-1)^k, then F contains a sunflower with r petals. [Erdos and Rado (1960) (1960); see Jukna, Extremal Combinatorics]
title: Sunflower Lemma (Delta-System Lemma, Classical Bound)

$$
N = M_1 + \ldots + M_k,\quad X = Y_1 + \ldots + Y_k
$$
into $k$ independent copies of $M$ and $Y$, respectively. Then $X$ is $N$-stable if and only if $Y$ is $kM$-stable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
