body:
[Corollary cor:critical-window-saturation of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq3$.  For each $h\geq2$, put
\[
 H_{h,k}=(k-1)h^{k-2},\qquad
 \mathcal M_{h,k}
 =\{A\subseteq\{0,\ldots,H_{h,k}\}:0\in A,\ |A|=k\}.
\]
The maps from $\mathcal M_{h,k}$ onto the realized weak types and onto the
realized ordered $h$-addition-table types are surjective.  Moreover, as
$h\to\infty$,
\[
 |\mathcal M_{h,k}|=\binom{H_{h,k}}{k-1}
 =\Theta_k\!\left(h^{(k-1)(k-2)}\right),
\]
and both target sets have the same order of magnitude.  Consequently, the
average fibre of either type map has order $\Theta_k(1)$, and choosing one
representative from each fibre gives a positive-proportion subfamily on which
the map is injective.  For either type map, such a full-order subfamily may
be chosen entirely among representatives of maximal-rank weak types, and
hence inside the exact core $[0,h^{k-2}]$.

body:
[Definition 2 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $m,n\in\Nsf$, $p\in [1,3)$, $x\in C^{p-\mathrm{var}}([S,T],\Rsf^n)$, and let $f_\alpha^i:\Rsf^m\to\Rsf$ (for $i\in\llbracket 1, m \rrbracket$ and $\alpha\in\llbracket 1,n \rrbracket$) be smooth functions. Let also $Y_S\in\Rsf^m$. Consider the system of controlled differential equations
	\begin{equation}
	
		\d{Y}^i  = f_{\alpha}^i(Y)\d{x}^\alpha, 
			\quad 
		Y^i(S) = Y_S^i,
	\end{equation}
for $i\in \llbracket 1, m \rrbracket$. Given a rough path lift $(X^\tau)$ of function $x$ (see \autoref{ex:natural-lift}), we say that a function $Y: [S,T]\to\Rsf^m$ is a \emph{Davie solution} to problem~\eqref{eq:ode} if $Y(S) = Y_S$ and if there exists a constant $C\in (0,\infty)$ such that the inequality
	\begin{equation}
	
		\left|
			Y^i(t) - Y^i(s) 
			- f_\alpha^i(Y(s)) X^{\ta}(s,t) 
			- \left(
				\frac{\partial f_\beta^i}{\partial y^j}f_\alpha^j
			  \right)
			(Y(s)) X^{\tc} (s,t)
		\right| 
		\leq C\omega(s,t)^\frac{3}{p}
	\end{equation}
holds for every $i\in \llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in \Delta [S,T]$.
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2609.01190

[Thm 51 (Erd\"os-Taylor theorem for SRI chains in $d=2$) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Let $d=2$ and assume Assumption \ref{ass:SRI}. If $\x_N$ is any sequence in $I^2$ such that $x^1_N-x^2_N$ remains bounded as $N\to\infty$, then $(\log N)^{-1}\sum_{r=0}^N f_N(   R^1_r-   R^2_r) $ converges in law (viewed under $\Ebbnn$) as $N\to \infty$ to an exponential random variable of rate $2/\big(\int f\dr\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}\big)$. 

    Furthermore, for any $t>\varepsilon>0$ the random variable $\sum_{r=N\varepsilon}^{Nt}f_N(   R^1_r-   R^2_r)$ goes to 0 in probability, thus $(\log N)^{-1}\sum_{r=0}^{Nt} f_N(   R^1_r-   R^2_r), $ viewed as a process in the variable $t$, converges in f.d.d.'s to a constant process equal to the same exponential random variable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Erd\"os-Taylor theorem for SRI chains in $d=2$

[Definition 1 (Cascade system) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] For $v\in V(T)$ and a state $s^{(v)}_t\in\R$,
\[
ds^{(v)}_t=\Big[-\alpha_{d(v)}\,s^{(v)}_t+\sum_{u\sim v}\gamma_{d(u)\to d(v)}\,\sigma\big(s^{(u)}_t-\theta_{uv}\big)\Big]\,dt+b_{d(v)}\,dW^{(v)}_t,
\]
with $\alpha_d\ge\alpha_{\min}>0$, $b_d^2\ge\mu_0>0$, thresholds $\theta_{uv}\ge\theta_{\min}>0$, couplings $\gamma_{d\to d'}\ge0$, $\sigma$ the logistic function, and $\{W^{(v)}\}$ independent Brownian motions. A vertex fails when $s^{(v)}$ crosses a threshold $\theta^{\mathrm{fail}}$ into an absorbing basin $B_{\mathrm{fail}}=[\theta^{\mathrm{fail}},\infty)$ before returning to a safe value $s_{\mathrm{safe}}$.

[Lemma 21 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] The operators \(W_L(r_a)\) and \(\widetilde{W}_{a,L}\) admit a common
Hilbert--Schmidt factorization: there exists
\(V_{a,L}:L^2(0,L)\to L^2(0,\infty)\) such that
\[
        W_L(r_a)=V_{a,L}^{*}V_{a,L},
        \qquad
        \widetilde{W}_{a,L}=V_{a,L}V_{a,L}^{*}.
\]
Consequently, they are positive trace-class operators with the same nonzero
eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, and for every \(t\in\mathbb C\),
\[
        \det(\operatorname{Id}+t\widetilde{W}_{a,L})
        =
        \det(\operatorname{Id}+tW_L(r_a)).
\]
Moreover, with \(\rho_a:=\sup_{\xi>0}r_a(\xi)\in(0,1)\),
\[
        0\leq W_L(r_a)\leq \rho_a\operatorname{Id},
        \qquad
        0\leq \widetilde{W}_{a,L}\leq \rho_a\operatorname{Id}.
\]

[Corollary 6 (Gaussian-noise bulk and full-trace LSS) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let $f$ satisfy \eqref{eq:Gaussian-f-assumptions-main}, let $\lambda\ge0$ be
fixed, and suppose that the deterministic spike obeys
\begin{equation}
 \norm{x}_2=1,
 \qquad
 \norm{x}_\infty=o(N^{-1/4}),
 \qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^N x_i=O(N^{o(1)}).
\end{equation}
Let $\Gamma$ satisfy (G1)--(G4) with $\theta_{f,\nu}$ replaced by $\theta_f$,
and let $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_k$ be analytic on a neighborhood of
$\overline{D_\Gamma}$ and real-valued on its intersection with $\mathbb R$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \left(
 \mathcal L_{M_{N,\gamma}^f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi_\ell)
 -N\int_{-2}^2\varphi_\ell(t)\rho_{\scal}(t)\,\dd t
 -m_{\varphi_\ell,\Gamma}^{\gamma,f}
 \right)_{\ell=1}^k
 \Longrightarrow
 (G_{\varphi_\ell})_{\ell=1}^k,
\end{equation}
where the limiting vector is centered Gaussian with
\begin{equation}
 \Cov(G_\varphi,G_\psi)
 =\mathcal V_{\kappa_f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi,\psi).
\end{equation}
If $|\theta_f|\le1$, then
$\mathcal L_{M_{N,\gamma}^f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi)
=\Tr\varphi(M_{N,\gamma}^f)$ with probability tending to one, so
\eqref{eq:Gaussian-bulk-CLT-main} is the full-trace CLT.  If
$|\theta_f|>1$ and each $\varphi_\ell$ is also analytic and real-valued on the
real axis near
\begin{equation}
 \rho_f:=\theta_f+\theta_f^{-1},
\end{equation}
then the full-trace CLT is obtained from
\eqref{eq:Gaussian-bulk-CLT-main} by replacing the statistic there with
\begin{equation}
 \left(
 \Tr\varphi_\ell(M_{N,\gamma}^f)
 -N\int_{-2}^2\varphi_\ell(t)\rho_{\scal}(t)\,\dd t
 -m_{\varphi_\ell,\Gamma}^{\gamma,f}
 -\varphi_\ell(\rho_f)
 \right)_{\ell=1}^k
 \Longrightarrow
 (G_{\varphi_\ell})_{\ell=1}^k,
\end{equation}
with the covariance \eqref{eq:Gaussian-covariance-main}.
In particular, all these conclusions hold for every centered and
variance-normalized polynomial-growth transform.

[Dfn 187 (approximate quadratic variation processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, define $\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ to be the piecewise linear process with increments
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)
	\equiv
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d,B)
	\equiv
	\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)\Big)
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\tau}(q_d,a)\Big)\,.
	\eeq
For the Ising case, we also define
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}(q_d)
	\equiv \frac{1}{|B||B^{\Ising}|}
	\sum_{a\in B,i\in B^{\Ising}}
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)\Big)
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)\Big)
	=
	\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\sigma(q_d)\Big)
	\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)\Big)
	\eeq
for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$; 
as well as
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\Ising}(q_d)
	\equiv
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\Ising}(q_d,B^\Ising)
	\equiv 
	\frac{1}{|B^{\Ising}|}
	\sum_{i\in B^{\Ising}}
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)\Big)^2\,.
	\eeq
Denote also $E^{\sigma,\tau}\equiv Q^{\sigma,\tau}-\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$. We define likewise $\Delta\tilde{Q}^\frozen$ using increments of $X^\frozen$. Then, 
analogously to \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus},
for all $\sigma , \tau \in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have for $B^\frozen \cap [M] = B \neq \emptyset$
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\frozen,\sigma,\tau}(q_d,B^\frozen)
	=\frac{|B|}{|B^\frozen|}
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d,B)
	\,.\eeq
A similar relation holds between $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}$ and $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\frozen,\sigma,\Ising}$, and likewise between
$\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\frozen,\Ising}$
and $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\Ising}$.

Fitting a stack (or any linear predictor) under the per-sample relative L2 loss, mean over rows of ||y_i - yhat_i||^2 / ||y_i||^2, is weighted least squares with case weights s_i = 1 / ||y_i||^2. By the two-regimes corollary those are Aitken's variance-stabilising weights exactly when the error scale is proportional to the target norm (multiplicative error, elasticity of log ||e_i|| on log ||y_i|| equal to one); then the relative-metric fit is the efficient one and its optimism is 2m/n relative to its own noise level, regardless of how concentrated 1/||y_i||^2 is. If the error carries an additive floor, the rows with the smallest targets - exactly the rows the relative weights concentrate on - have the largest floor relative to their target, the concentration re-enters, and Kish's n_eff of the relative weights measures how far the fit is from balanced. The discriminating measurement is the elasticity of the out-of-fold residual norm to the target norm and the nonnegative fit ||e_i||^2 = a + b ||y_i||^2 (the floor share a / (a + b median ||y||^2)) on the calibration rows; on a pool whose targets vary by orders of magnitude (the EMIT radiance outputs) the question is live, on one whose targets are homogeneous (the OCO-2 retrievals, n_eff within a few percent of n) the two metrics coincide and it is moot.
the per-sample relative L2 loss as used by the EMIT/OCO-2 stacking pools; independent errors across rows
the multiplicative-versus-additive question is empirical and is measured by ens_rmt_elast.py (P21 of the RMT program)
title: Relative-L2 Case Weights Are Aitken's Weights When the Error Norm Scales With the Target Norm

body:
For a finite graph G and a positive integer k let P(G, k) be the number of proper colourings of the vertices of G with k colours (adjacent vertices receive different colours). THEOREM (Birkhoff, Whitney): P(G, k) is a polynomial in k of degree |V|, the chromatic polynomial, determined by the deletion-contraction recurrence P(G, k) = P(G - e, k) - P(G / e, k) for any edge e (G - e deletes the edge, G / e contracts it, merging its endpoints and removing loops and parallel copies), with P(empty graph on n vertices, k) = k^n. Facts: P(K_n, k) = k (k - 1) ... (k - n + 1); P(tree on n vertices, k) = k (k - 1)^{n-1}; P(C_n, k) = (k - 1)^n + (-1)^n (k - 1); P is multiplicative over connected components; its coefficients alternate in sign, the leading coefficient is 1, the coefficient of k^{|V| - 1} is -|E|, and the constant term is 0 for a graph with a vertex; the chromatic number is the least positive integer that is not a root; k = 0, 1, ..., chi(G) - 1 are roots; the chromatic polynomial is a specialisation of the Tutte polynomial, P(G, k) = (-1)^{|V| - c(G)} k^{c(G)} T(G; 1 - k, 0). Computing P is #P-hard in general, and evaluating it at k = 3 is #P-complete; the four colour theorem says P(G, 4) > 0 for every planar G.
finite simple graphs (loops make P identically 0; parallel edges do not change P)
k a nonnegative integer in the counting definition; the polynomial identity then holds for all k

[Definition def:e of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] We say that the semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ satisfies the \emph{$e$-property} if for every 
$F\in \operatorname{Lip}_b(H)$, for every $x\in H$, and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that 
\[
|P_t F(x)-P_t F(y)|<\varepsilon\quad \textrm{ for all }\quad y\in B(x,\delta)\quad \textrm{ and }\quad t\geq 0,
\]
where 
$\operatorname{Lip}_b(H):=\{F:H\to \mathbb{R}:\,F\textrm{ is Lipschitz and bounded}\}$.
title: $e$-property

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02398, '\textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}'] Recent work has shown that sub-Gaussian random variables are dominated in convex order by a sharp multiple of a Gaussian. We study the analogous question for the sub-Gamma class underlying Bernstein's inequality, with the Laplace law as the majorant. Here the moment generating function is controlled by a Bernstein-type bound over a finite range of frequencies, rather than by a purely quadratic bound. We derive a variational formula for the optimal multiple, show that it is strictly larger than the natural scale $σ\vee α$, and prove that this value is sharp, being attained by an asymmetric two-point distribution. We then turn to the sub-exponential class, which has a quadratic bound as in the sub-Gaussian case, but only over a bounded range as in the sub-Gamma case. Interestingly, the sub-exponential class displays a different behavior: the optimal multiple is exactly $σ\vee α$, but is attained only when $α\leq σ$; when $α> σ$, the constant remains sharp, but equality cannot hold for any non-affine convex function. Both results rely on a sharp finite-range variant of the Kearns-Saul inequality, which is of independent interest. (abstract text taken from the arXiv listing metadata; the TeX carried no abstract environment)
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.02398: \textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}

[2 16 of arXiv:2607.12303, 'Marginal Stationary Distributions and Convergence Rates of Higher Order Markov Chains'] Suppose that $\{X_t\}_{t=1}^{\infty}$ is an $(m-1)$th order regular Markov chain  on state space $S$ whose transition tensor $\mathcal{P}$ is positive.  Let $Q=[q_{i_1i_2 \ldots i_{m-1}, j_1 j_2 \ldots j_{m-1}}]$ be the transition matrix of its reduced first order chain. Denote
$Q^k=[q^{(k)}_{i_1i_2 \ldots i_{m-1}, j_1 j_2 \ldots j_{m-1}}]$
 Let 
$$
\alpha = \max _{i_1i_2 \ldots i_{m-1}, j_1 j_2 \ldots j_{m-1}} q^{(m-1)}_{i_1i_2 \ldots i_{m-1}, j_1 j_2 \ldots j_{m-1}}
$$
and
$$
\beta = \min_{i_1i_2 \ldots i_{m-1}, j_1 j_2 \ldots j_{m-1}} q^{(m-1)}_{i_1i_2 \ldots i_{m-1}, j_1 j_2 \ldots j_{m-1}}.
$$  
Then for any eigenvalue of $Q$ other than $\rho(Q)=1$, we have

Little Picard theorem: if f is entire and nonconstant, then the complement of its image, C minus f(C), contains at most one point; i.e. a nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < r and has an essential singularity at a, then for every ε in (0,r) the image of the punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < ε is all of C with at most one point removed, and every value so attained (again with at most one exception) is attained infinitely often. Both exceptional values are genuinely possible and the count is sharp: exp(z) is entire and omits exactly the value 0, and exp(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0 and omits exactly 0 near 0. Meromorphic versions: a nonconstant meromorphic function on C omits at most two values of the Riemann sphere, and near an essential singularity a meromorphic function takes every spherical value with at most two exceptions.
Little: f entire and nonconstant
Great: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a with an isolated essential singularity at a

In the first case the f_{n_k} are uniformly bounded by some M on the circle |z| = 3r/4, i.e. |f| ≤ M on the circles |z| = 3r 2^{-n_k}/4; the maximum modulus principle applied to the annuli between consecutive such circles gives |f| ≤ M on a punctured disk about 0, so the singularity is removable by Riemann's theorem, a contradiction. [Definition 5 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] \begin{enumerate}
\item A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Kato class measure} if it satisfies \( \lim_{\alpha \to \infty}\|U_\alpha \mu\|_{\infty, q} =0.\) Denote by \(\mathcal{K}\) the set of all Kato class measures.
\item  A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Dynkin class measure} if it satisfies \(\|U_1 \mu\|_{\infty, q} < \infty \). Denote by \(\mathcal{D}\) the set of all Dynkin class measures.
\item A Kato class measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Green-tight measure} for \(R_1\) if, for any \(\varepsilon >0\), there exists a compact set \(K\) such that \(\|R_1(1_{K^c}\mu)\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon\). Denote by \(\mathcal{K}_\infty= \mathcal{K}_\infty(R_1)\) the set of all Green-tight measures.

\item A Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}_1(f,f)}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_0\) the set of all Radon measures of finite energy integrals.

\item When $(\form,\dom)$ is transient, a Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it \(0\)-order finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}(f,f)}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_0^{(0)}\) the set of all Radon measures of finite \(0\)-order energy integrals.
\end{enumerate}

[Thm 1.2 of arXiv:2606.16237, 'The Backward Stochastic Partial Differential Integral Equations: Solvability and Compariso'] Assume that Assumption (ass:1.1 of the paper) holds. Then BSEE (equation eq:a2 of the paper) has a unique solution.
Moreover, let $(A, f, g, \varphi)$ and $(A, \bar f, \bar g, \bar{\varphi})$ be two sets of coefficients satisfying Assumption (ass:1.1 of the paper), and $(u, q, r)$ and $(\bar u, \bar q, \bar r)$ be the solutions of BSEE (equation eq:a2 of the paper) with coefficients $(A, f, g, \varphi)$ and $(A, \bar f, \bar g, \bar \varphi)$, respectively, then we have the following estimate
\begin{eqnarray}
&& E \sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} \| u(t) - \bar{u}(t) \|_H^2 + E \int_0^T \| u(t) - \bar{u}(t) \|_V^2 \, dt \nonumber \\
&& + E \int_0^T \| q(t) - \bar{q}(t) \|_H^2 \, dt + E \int_0^T \int_Z \| r(t, e) - \bar{r}(t, e) \|_H^2 \nu(de) \, dt \nonumber \\
&\leq& C \left[ E \| \varphi - \bar{\varphi} \|_H^2 + E \int_0^T \| f(t, \bar{u}(t), \bar{q}(t), \bar{r}(t, \cdot)) - \bar{f}(t, \bar{u}(t), \bar{q}(t), \bar{r}(t, \cdot)) \|_{V^*}^2 \, dt \right. \nonumber \\
&& \left. + E \int_0^T \| g(t, \bar{u}(t), \bar{q}(t), \bar{r}(t, \cdot)) - \bar{g}(t, \bar{u}(t), \bar{q}(t), \bar{r}(t, \cdot)) \|_H^2 \, dt \right].
\end{eqnarray}
Here and in the rest of this paper $C$ is a generic constant depending only on given parameters, and we may indicate the parameters it depends on by a bracket. For example, the above $C= C(l, \lambda, \alpha, \kappa, M, T)$ is a constant depending on the parameters $l, \lambda, \alpha, \kappa, M, T$.

In particular, when $(A, \bar f, \bar g, \bar \varphi) = (A, 0, 0, 0)$, it follows from ((eq:130 of the paper)) that
\begin{eqnarray}
&& E \sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} \| u(t) \|_H^2 + E \int_0^T \| u(t) \|_V^2 \, dt + E \int_0^T \| q(t) \|_H^2 \, dt + E \int_0^T \int_Z \| r(t, e) \|_H^2 \nu(de) \, dt \nonumber \\
&\leq& C\left[ E \| \varphi \|_H^2 + E \int_0^T \| f(t, 0, 0, 0) \|_{V^*}^2 \, dt + E \int_0^T \| g(t, 0, 0, 0) \|_H^2 \, dt \right].

body: Let f be continuous on the closed interval [a,b]. Part 1: the function F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt is differentiable on [a,b] and F'(x) = f(x) for every x in [a,b]. Part 2 (evaluation): if G is any antiderivative of f on [a,b], meaning G'(x) = f(x) for all x in [a,b], then the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals G(b) - G(a). Together the two parts show differentiation and (Riemann) integration are inverse processes: every continuous function has an antiderivative, and definite integrals are computed from any one of them.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check whether the ergodic-environment argument for the two-sided statement (Theorem 2.3/3.2) localises to one side. Result: The two-sided 0-1 law (range infinite or not) follows from stationarity of the environment plus a Borel-Cantelli over the sites visited; the one-sided event {sup X_n = infinity} is not invariant under the natural shifts because the walk started at 0 and the environment to the left matter. Under (SE) and (EL) the source notes (3.4) and (3.5) are equivalent, so the question is the 0-1 property itself. A sufficient condition beyond Theorem 3.10: if the environment is i.i.d. and the walk is 'monotone' in the environment (Proposition 4.2 style coupling, which needs (POS1) or its mirror), then P_0(sup X_n = infinity) is a monotone function of a product measure, and the event {sup X_n = infinity} is a tail event with respect to the environment on the right half-line only if the walk's right excursions are determined by the right environment, which fails because the walk can be pushed back by the left environment. I tried the following route: under (SE) and (WEL), the event {sup X_n = infinity} is invariant under the environment shift restricted to trajectories that reach every site to the right, so conditionally on reaching site k the probability of eventually reaching k+1 is the same functional of the shifted environment; if the walk reaches every site to the right a.s. on the event, an ergodicity argument along the sequence of first-hitting times gives 0-1. The gap is exactly that 'reaching k' depends on the environment left of k through the returns. No general 0-1 law obtained; the reduction to a renewal-type ergodicity along right-hitting times is recorded. Obstruction: Left environment influences right excursions; no shift invariance of the one-sided event.

[Corollary cor:known-learned-gap of arXiv:2608.20295, 'Physical-Support Confidence Sets for Highly Coherent Dictionaries'] Consider a sequence of problems for which
\[
    I_G^{(r)}\rightarrow\infty,
    \qquad
    I_S\rightarrow\infty,
\]
while $I_D=Ns^6$ remains bounded. If the dictionary were known, the
deployment experiment would eventually separate the competing atom supports.
When the dictionary is learned from finite calibration data, however, every
uniformly valid physical-support confidence correspondence has worst-case
expected diameter at least $cs$. Hence a support decision that is precise
conditional on one fitted dictionary can be strictly more precise than the
physical conclusion justified after dictionary uncertainty is taken into
account. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In mathematics, Abelian and Tauberian theorems are theorems giving conditions for two methods of summing divergent series to give the same result, named after Niels Henrik Abel and Alfred Tauber. The original examples are Abel's theorem showing that if a series converges to some limit then its Abel sum is the same limit, and Tauber's theorem showing that if the Abel sum of a series exists and the coefficients are sufficiently small then the series converges to the Abel sum. More general Abelian and Tauberian theorems give similar results for more general summation methods.
title: Abelian and Tauberian theorems

Let $\Sigma$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $M \times M$ matrix (the true, out-of-sample covariance) and $\hat\Sigma$ any symmetric estimate, with entrywise error $\varepsilon := \max_{i,j} |\hat\Sigma_{ij} - \Sigma_{ij}|$. For $c \ge 1$ let $\mathcal{W}_c = \{w : \mathbf{1}^T w = 1,\ \|w\|_1 \le c\}$, let $\hat w \in \arg\min_{w \in \mathcal{W}_c} w^T \hat\Sigma w$ and $w^* \in \arg\min_{w \in \mathcal{W}_c} w^T \Sigma w$. Then (i) $|w^T(\hat\Sigma - \Sigma)w| \le \varepsilon\, c^2$ for every $w \in \mathcal{W}_c$, and (ii) $0 \le \hat w^T \Sigma \hat w - w^{*T}\Sigma w^* \le 2\varepsilon c^2$. The long-only simplex is the case $c = 1$: the out-of-sample risk of the long-only plug-in exceeds the long-only oracle's by at most $2\varepsilon$, whatever the conditioning of $\Sigma$ or $\hat\Sigma$ and whatever the ratio $M/n$. If $\hat\Sigma$ is the sample covariance of $n$ independent cases with sub-Gaussian coordinates, a union bound over the $M(M+1)/2$ entries gives $\varepsilon = O_p(\sqrt{\log M / n})$, so the excess risk is $O_p(\sqrt{\log M/n})$ - against the unconstrained plug-in, whose risk inflation $1/(1 - M/n)$ (Pafka-Kondor, Gaussian, well-conditioned case) grows with $M/n$ and which is unbounded when $\hat\Sigma$ has a near-null direction that $\Sigma$ does not.
Sigma symmetric positive semidefinite; Sigma_hat symmetric (not necessarily PSD)
the tail bound: n independent cases with sub-Gaussian coordinates (bounded errors suffice)
the feasible set W_c is compact and nonempty (it contains every vertex of the simplex)

Result: On the complete graph the MST limit is built from the scaling limit of the critical Erdos-Renyi components (as metric spaces) glued along the multiplicative coalescent; the same construction on the torus would follow from (i) C0071 upgraded to metric-space (Gromov-Hausdorff-Prokhorov) convergence of the window clusters, and (ii) the coalescent dynamics of the clusters as p increases through the window, i.e. that clusters merge at rate proportional to the product of their sizes, which is the mean-field merging rule and requires the merged clusters to be 'spread out' (same mechanism as in C0071: clusters wrap around the torus in d > 6 so their mutual boundary is proportional to the product of sizes). So Open Problem 16.4 is the metric upgrade of C0071 plus the wrapping-based merging rule; both are open, and the constant multiple would be determined by the variance v of the local branching structure. Obstruction: Metric-space convergence of window clusters and the product merging rule are unproved on the torus.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0088-scaling-limit-of-the-minimal-spanning-tree-on-high-dimensional-tori
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved
title: Attempt on Scaling limit of the minimal spanning tree on high-dimensional tori

[Conjecture Comparison between the True system and the Mean-Field approximations of arXiv:2606.13264, 'Interference Queueing Networks: A Replica Mean-Field Approach in the Symmetric Setting'] For $\lambda < \mu^*$, the stationary busy probability of the original system lies between those predicted by the two mean-field models:
\[
\pi_\lambda^{\mathrm{MF2}}(q > 0)
\leq
\pi_\lambda(q > 0)
\leq
\pi_\lambda^{\mathrm{MF1}}(q > 0).
\]
In particular, Mean-Field 1 overestimates the busy probability, whereas Mean-Field 2 underestimates it. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Comparison between the True system and the Mean-Field approximations

[Thm 18 (\Cref{thm: restate of window growing m} in the text) of arXiv:2603.27433, 'The $k$-cycle shuffling with repeated cards'] Let \(n=ml\), such that \(l=\omega(1)\) but \(l=o(\log n)\). Suppose \(2\le k\le n^{c_0+o(1)}\), where \(c_0\in[0,1)\) is an absolute constant, and
$$
t=\frac nk\left(\log n-\frac 12\log l+c\right),
$$
where \(c\in \R\) is an absolute constant. Then, we have
$$
d_{TV}(\sim_l\backslash P_{n,k}^{*t},\sim_l\backslash U_{\S_n})
=
2\Phi(\exp(-c)/2)-1+o(1).
$$
Here, \(\Phi(x):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^x\exp(-y^2/2)\,dy\) denotes the cumulative distribution function of the normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \Cref{thm: restate of window growing m} in the text

[Prop prop exp mixing of arXiv:2411.14350, 'Randomized Geodesic Flow on Hyperbolic Groups'] Let us assume $r=2$, and let $f, g\in L^\infty(\bar\mathbb{P}_o)$ be H\"older continuous functions with exponent $\alpha = \min\{\alpha_f, \alpha_g\}>0$. Then for all $s,t\in \mathbb{Z}$, 
$$
\bigg|\int (f\circ \tau_t) (g\circ \tau_s) {\rm{d}}\bar\mathbb{P}_o - \int f {\rm{d}}\bar\mathbb{P}_o \int g{\rm{d}}\bar\mathbb{P}_o \bigg|  \leq C(f,g) {\rm e} ^{- \delta |t-s|}, \qquad\delta= \alpha/2>0.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop prop exp mixing of arXiv:2411.14350

[Lemma lem:honesty-diameter of arXiv:2608.20295, 'Physical-Support Confidence Sets for Highly Coherent Dictionaries'] Let $\vartheta(\xi_i)=(m_i,A_i)$, $i=0,1$, and set
\[
    d=d_H^{\mathrm{pr}}(A_0,A_1).
\]
If a random compact correspondence $\widehat C$ has coverage at least
$1-\alpha$ at both parameter values, then
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb E_{\xi_0}
    \operatorname{diam}_{\mathrm{pr}}(\widehat C)
    \ge
    d\left[
        1-2\alpha
        -
        \operatorname{TV}
        \left(
            \mathbb P_{\xi_0}^{N,T},
            \mathbb P_{\xi_1}^{N,T}
        \right)
    \right]_+ .
    
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Coverage at two alternatives implies nonzero physical diameter

[Defin 1 (Empirical measure) of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Given a vector $\bs{x}_N \in \mathbb{R}^N$, the associated empirical measure corresponds to

\begin{align}

\op{L}_N^{(\bs{x}_N)} \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^N \delta_{x_i} \, .

\end{align}

Note that the map $\iota : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathcal{M}_1(\mathbb{R})$, $\iota(\bs{x}_N) := \op{L}_N^{(\bs{x}_N)}$ is continuous.
In particular this means that if $E \subset \mathcal{M}_1(\mathbb{R})$ is a Borel set then
$\iota^{-1}(E) = \big\{ \bs{x}_N \in \mathbb{R}^N \, : \, \op{L}_N^{(\bs{x}_N)} \in E \big\}$ is a Borel set.
title: Empirical measure

[Theorem thm:density-bound of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $\eta$ be a translation-invariant point process of
intensity $\rho$. Suppose that, for some $r>0$, the process is
supported on $r$-separated configurations. Then
\[
    \sigma_\eta(\Omega)=0
    \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
    \rho\geq\mathcal D(\Omega)
\]
for every open neighborhood $\Omega$ of the origin. In particular,
if $C\subset\Omega$ is a symmetric convex body, then
\[
    \rho\geq2^{-d}\lambda_d(C).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Density bound

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:2d14dff23ed67bea8ee6e9a336404434b1f65c6c49ba51c5064e551c4fbdff28","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/2d/2d14dff23ed67bea8ee6e9a336404434b1f65c6c49ba51c5064e551c4fbdff28.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:ac94520dd14667574818c4e5bdd7d6df7d8846c54fdf5cf64184077d7f769f36","bundle_entry_key":"even","bundle_id":"population.probability-hole-coefficient-and-forkjoin-partials-008","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-01a07a40/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.geometry:ideal-voronoi-even-positive-series-sixth-coefficient-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Boundary-hole monotonicity and the odd-dimensional polynomial

Status: private author-checked partial candidate. No independent review, no novelty certification, and no claim that the whole source conjecture is solved.

Source: D'Achille, Curien, Enriquez, Lyons and Unel, *Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations on hyperbolic spaces*, archived as `ideal_voronoi_2023`, Proposition 5.1 and equation (5.1), PDF35; Conjecture 7.5, PDF48. The source already computes the dimension-three formula and observes rationality in odd dimensions. Those facts are credited. The claims attempted here are the all-dimensional monotonicity and positive coefficients in every odd dimension. The final addendum gives a candidate counterexample to the even-dimensional positive-power-series clause in its displayed distance variable.

## Exact starting identity

Let $n=d-1\ge1$ and let $H_d(u)$ be the probability that the hyperbolic ball of radius $u\ge0$ about the origin lies inside its ideal Voronoi cell. Write $J_d(u)=1/H_d(u)$. Equation (5.1) and Proposition 5.1 give

$$
J_d(u)=\frac1{c_d}\int_{\mathbb R^n}
\left(\sqrt{\cosh^2u+|x|^2}-\sinh u\right)^{-2n}\,dx,
\qquad
c_d=\frac{\pi^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)}{\Gamma(n)}.
$$

The normalization follows independently by setting $u=0$ and integrating $(1+|x|^2)^{-n}$ in polar coordinates. In particular $J_d(0)=1$.

## Monotonicity in every dimension

Set $q=e^{2u}$ and substitute $x=e^{-u}z$. Then

$$
e^{-nu}J_d(u)=\frac1{c_d}\int_{\mathbb R^n}D_q(z)^{-2n}\,dz,
\qquad
D_q(z)=\sqrt{(q+1)^2/4+|z|^2}-(q-1)/2.
$$

The denominator is positive. For $z\ne0$,

$$
\frac{\partial D_q(z)}{\partial q}
=\frac{q+1}{4\sqrt{(q+1)^2/4+|z|^2}}-\frac12<0.
$$

Thus the integrand strictly increases with $q$ away from a null set. All integrals are finite by the exact source identity. Pointwise comparison of two values of $q$ proves that $e^{-nu}J_d(u)$ is strictly increasing; no interchange of differentiation and integration is needed. Taking reciprocals proves

$$
u\longmapsto e^{(d-1)u}H_d(u)
\quad\hbox{is strictly decreasing on }[0,\infty).
$$

The strictness follows because the difference of the positive finite integrands is strictly positive on a set of positive Lebesgue measure.

## Positive rational polynomial for odd dimensions

Let $d=2m+1$, so $n=2m$, with integer $m\ge1$. Put $a=e^{-u}$ and $s=\sinh u=(a^{-1}-a)/2$. In the radial integral make the substitution

$$
y=\sqrt{\cosh^2u+r^2}-s.
$$

Its lower endpoint is $a$, and

$$
r^2=(y-a)(y+a^{-1}),\qquad r\,dr=(y+s)\,dy.
$$

After setting $y=az$, the exact integral becomes

$$
J_{2m+1}(u)=C_m a^{-4m}
\int_1^\infty (z-1)^{m-1}(a^2z+1)^{m-1}
\bigl[a^2(2z-1)+1\bigr]z^{-4m}\,dz,
\qquad C_m=\frac{\Gamma(2m)}{\Gamma(m)^2}.
$$

Here the factor $C_m$ is half the ratio of the $(2m-1)$-sphere area to $c_d$. Expand the two bracketed factors as a polynomial in $a^2$. Every coefficient is a strictly positive integrable function of $z>1$: the only apparent subtraction is $2z-1$, which is positive on this domain. The degree is exactly $m$. The resulting integrals are rational because expanding $(z-1)^{m-1}$ reduces them to finite sums of powers of $z$ with integer exponents at most $-2$.

For an explicit formula, let $B$ denote the beta function, and interpret binomial coefficients outside $0,\ldots,m-1$ as zero. Define, for $0\le j\le m$,

$$
b_{m,j}=\binom{m-1}{j}B(3m-j,m)
+\binom{m-1}{j-1}\left[2B(3m-j,m)-B(3m-j+1,m)\right].
$$

This follows from $\int_1^\infty(z-1)^{m-1}z^{j-4m}\,dz=B(3m-j,m)$. All beta arguments are positive integers. Moreover $B(A+1,m)<B(A,m)$, so each displayed coefficient is positive. Hence

$$
p_m(q)=C_m\sum_{j=0}^m b_{m,j}q^{m-j}
$$

is a degree-$m$ polynomial with strictly positive rational coefficients, and

$$
H_{2m+1}(u)=\frac{e^{-2mu}}{p_m(e^{2u})}.
$$

The normalization gives $p_m(1)=1$. The first two cases are

$$
p_1(q)=\frac{q+2}{3},\qquad
p_2(q)=\frac{q^2}{7}+\frac{16q}{35}+\frac25.
$$

The first reproduces the already-known dimension-three formula in Remark 5.2. It is a control, not a newly solved special case.

## An additional odd-dimensional consequence

The polynomial representation makes $J_d(u)$ a positive sum of exponentials with rates in $[n,2n]$. Let $L=\log J_d$. Under the exponential weights, $L'$ is the mean rate and $L''$ its variance. Therefore $L'\ge n$ and $L''\le n^2/4$. The density $f=-H_d'=H_dL'$ satisfies

$$
f'=H_d\bigl(L''-(L')^2\bigr)<0.
$$

This proves the source's proposed decreasing-density property in odd dimensions. It also implies that the median is smaller than the mean. For completeness, if $M>0$ is the median and $v=f(M)>0$, convexity of the survival function gives

$$
H_d(x)\ge\max\{1/2-v(x-M),0\},\qquad x\ge0.
$$

Integrating yields $E X\ge(1/2+vM)^2/(2v)\ge M$, since the difference in the last inequality is $(vM-1/2)^2/(2v)$. Strict convexity makes the first inequality strict on a positive-length interval. The mean is finite by the source exponential tail bound.

## Adversarial checks and remaining gap

The load-bearing points to try to break are the factor from the radial Jacobian, the power $a^{-4m}$, and the distinction between polynomial positivity in $q=e^{2u}$ and power-series positivity in $u$. The check script compares the beta coefficients with an independent expansion and exact integration of the radial polynomial. It also compares the resulting formula with the original angular integral in Proposition 5.1, including even dimensions for the separate monotonicity calculation.

The even-dimensional positive-power-series assertion is not implied by monotonicity. The addendum below supplies a candidate counterexample to that clause in dimension two. No independent referee has checked this packet, and the bounded literature search is not a novelty certificate. Other even-dimensional density and median claims remain unproved here, so this grouped entry retains its partial-candidate classification.

## Addendum: a negative sixth coefficient in dimension two

Author-checked candidate counterexample, 2026-09-07. This uses the source's displayed distance variable $u$ and interprets "power series" as a convergent series in nonnegative integer powers of $u$ about zero. It makes no claim about series in a different variable.

The source's Remark 5.2, equation (5.2), credits its dimension-two formula to earlier work. We do not claim that formula as new:

$$H_2(u)=\frac{\pi}{4\arctan(e^u)\cosh^2u+2\sinh u}.$$

Conjecture 7.5 would require $H_2(u)=e^{-u}/f(u)$ with positive power-series coefficients. Thus $f$ is uniquely determined near zero by

$$f(u)=\frac{(e^u+2e^{-u}+e^{-3u})A(u)+1-e^{-2u}}{\pi},\qquad A(u)=\arctan(e^u).$$

Since $A(0)=\pi/4$ and $A'(u)=1/(2\cosh u)$,

$$A(u)=\frac\pi4+\frac u2-\frac{u^3}{12}+\frac{u^5}{48}+O(u^7).$$

Put $E(u)=e^u+2e^{-u}+e^{-3u}$. The coefficients needed for degree six are $[u^6]E=61/60$, $[u^5]E=-61/30$, $[u^3]E=-14/3$, and $[u]E=-4$. Consequently,

$$[u^6]f(u)=\frac{61}{240}+\frac1\pi\left(-\frac{61}{60}+\frac7{18}-\frac1{12}-\frac4{45}\right)=\frac{61\pi-192}{240\pi}<0.$$

The sign is exact: $\pi<22/7$ gives $61\pi-192<-2/7$. Numerically the coefficient is approximately $-0.000481242280365871$. A function analytic at zero has unique power-series coefficients, so no alternative positive-coefficient series in the same variable can represent this $f$ near zero. This contradicts the stated even-dimensional coefficient clause already at $d=2$.

### Checks and strongest alternative explanation

The coefficient was obtained by exact rational convolution using the recurrence for the reciprocal of $\cosh u$, by high-precision differentiation of the closed formula, and by Cauchy coefficient extraction directly from the original angular integral of Proposition 5.1. The last lane avoids the closed arctangent formula. Reproduction: `check_IPVT_even_coefficients.py`; receipt: `IPVT_even_coefficient_checks.json`.

The strongest interpretation risk is that the authors intended a series in another transformed variable or a different normalization. The archived conjecture writes $f(u)$ in the distance variable and specifies no alternative. The calculation refutes that literal Maclaurin-series clause; it does not refute monotonicity, the odd-dimensional formula, or every possible reformulation. A source clarification or corrected conjecture could change the disposition. [Lemma 11 of arXiv:2609.03386, 'Twisted Gradient Flow Approach to Vegetation-Rainfall-Bushfire Interactions Model'] For each $z_0 \in H^1(\Omega)$ and $\tilde{v} \in \mathcal{V}(v_0)$ the initial-boundary value problem $\text{(AP2)}{}_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}}$ has a unique 
strong solution $z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}} (z_0,\tilde{v})$ on $[0,T]$ satisfying 

\begin{gather}

\hspace*{-0.8cm}z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}} (z_0,\tilde{v}) \in W^{1,2}(0,T\,;L^2(\Omega)) \cap L^\infty (0,T\,;H^1(\Omega)) \cap L^2(0,T\,;H^2(\Omega)),\\

(z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}}(z_0,\tilde{v}))'(t)-\varepsilon \Delta_N z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}}(z_0,\tilde{v}\,;t)=\tilde{v}'(t) \quad 
\text{in} \quad L^2(\Omega), \quad \text{a.e.}~t \in (0,T),\\

z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}}(z_0,\tilde{v}\,;0)=z_0 \quad \text{in} \quad L^2(\Omega).
\end{gather}

\indent
Moreover, there exists a constant $C_6>0$, which depends on the following values:

\begin{equation*}
T,\quad \|z_0\|_{H^1(\Omega)},\quad \int_0^T \|\tilde{v}'(t)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2dt,
\end{equation*}

such that the following estimate holds for all $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$:

\begin{align*}
&\left(\max_{0 \le t \le T} \|z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}} (z_0,\tilde{v}\,;t)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\right)^2
+\int_0^T \|z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}}'(z_0,\tilde{v}\,;t)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2dt\\
&\hspace*{1cm}+\varepsilon \left(\sup_{0 \le t \le T} \|\nabla z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}} (z_0,\tilde{v}\,;t)\|_{\bm{L}^2(\Omega)} \right)^2
+\varepsilon^2 \int_0^T \|z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}} (z_0,\tilde{v}\,;t)\|_{H^2(\Omega)}^2dt \le C_6.
\end{align*}

Especially, as a result of this estimate we have the boundedness of the strong solutions $z_{\text{{\tiny $\varepsilon$}}} (z_0,\tilde{v})$ in 
$C([0,T]\,;L^2(\Omega)) \cap W^{1,2}(0,T\,;L^2(\Omega))$ uniformly with respect to $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$.

On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. For rho in [-1, 1], T_rho is the noise operator: T_rho f(x) = E[f(Y)] where the Y_i are independent with P(Y_i = x_i) = (1 + rho)/2, so T_rho chi_S = rho^|S| chi_S. Let H(t) = Stab_{e^{-t}}[f] for t >= 0. For every m >= 0, (-1)^m H^(m)(t) = sum_k k^m W_k e^{-kt} >= 0, so H is completely monotone; H(t) > 0 if f is not 0, H(t) -> W_0 = (E f)^2 as t -> infinity, and for m >= 1 the derivative is strictly signed iff f is not constant. With the tilted degree law nu_t(k) = W_k e^{-kt}/H(t), (log H)'(t) = -E_{nu_t}[K] and (log H)''(t) = Var_{nu_t}(K) >= 0, so H is log-convex, strictly at every t unless all the nonzero mass sits at a single level.

[Corollary 12 of arXiv:2608.18834, 'The Parabolic Anderson Model's Total Mass at Small Times: Geometry, Fluctuations, and Reno'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{Assumption} holds,
and let $\ka>0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\rho>H_0-1$, then
\[\mbf E\big[\msf Q_\ka(t)\big]=o(t^{H_0})
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mbf E[\msf Q_\ka(t)^2]^{1/2}\sim\ka\mf c\,t^{H_0}.\]
\item If $\rho=H_0-1$ and $H_0\neq1$, then
\[\mbf E\big[\msf Q_\ka(t)\big]\sim\frac{\ka^2|D|(2H_0-1)}{(H_0-1)2^{H}}\prod_{j=1}^d\frac{\Ga(2H_j+1)}{\Ga(H_j)}\,t^{H_0}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sqrt{\mbf{Var}[\msf Q_\ka(t)]}\sim\ka\mf c\,t^{H_0}.\]
\item Otherwise:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\rho=H_0-1$ and $H_0=1$, then
\[\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\msf Q_\ka(t)}{t\log(1/t)}=-\frac{\ka^2|D|}{2^{d-1}}\prod_{j=1}^d\frac{\Ga(2H_j+1)}{\Ga(H_j)}\qquad\text{in probability.}\] 
\item If $\rho<H_0-1$, then
\[\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\msf Q_\ka(t)}{t^{1+\rho}}
=\frac{\ka^2|D|H_0(2H_0-1)}{2^H(1+\rho)\rho}\prod_{j=1}^d\frac{\Ga(2H_j+1)}{\Ga(H_j)}\qquad\text{in probability.}\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 30 of arXiv:2511.10814, '\Large \bf \boldmath\ \\ Convergence of the extended Kalman filter with small and state-de'] Let $A, B \in \mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ be symmetric. Let $\lambda_1(A) \leq \ldots \leq \lambda_n(A)$ and $\lambda_1(B) \leq \ldots \leq \lambda_n(B)$ be the ordered eigenvalues of A and B, respectively.
										
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $A \gm  0$ and $B \gm 0$, then $A \geqm B$ if and only if $ B^{-1} \geqm A^{-1}$.
\item If $A \gm  0$, $B \geqm 0$, and $A \geqm  B$ , then $A^{1/2} \geqm  B^{1/2}$.
	\item If $A \geqm B$, then $ \lambda_i(A)\geq \lambda_i(B)$ for each $i = 1, \ldots , n$.
	\item If $A \geqm  B$, then $\trace A \geq  \trace B$ with equality if and only if $A = B$.
	\item If $A \geqm B \geqm 0$, then $\det A \geq  \det B \geq 0$.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let n >= 2k >= 2 and let F be a family of k-element subsets of an n-element set such that every two members of F intersect. Then |F| <= binom(n-1, k-1). When n > 2k, equality holds exactly when F consists of all k-subsets containing one fixed element; when n = 2k every intersecting family of size binom(2k-1, k-1) is obtained by choosing one set from each complementary pair, so the extremal families are not unique.

body:
Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a Lebesgue space and let P be a countable measurable partition of finite entropy. If P is a GENERATOR - that is, the smallest T-invariant sigma-algebra containing P is B modulo null sets (for invertible T one uses the two-sided join over all integers, for non-invertible T the one-sided join over nonnegative integers) - then the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of the system equals the entropy of that one partition: h(T) = h(T, P). There is also an increasing-partitions form: if P_1 is contained in P_2 is contained in ... is an increasing sequence of finite-entropy partitions whose union generates B modulo null sets, then h(T, P_n) increases to h(T).
Finite entropy of the generating partition, and generation modulo null sets.
For an invertible T it suffices that P generate under the two-sided join; h(T, P) itself is always defined with the one-sided joins P v T^{-1}P v ... v T^{-(n-1)}P.
One-sided generation is a stronger hypothesis for an invertible T and forces h(T) = 0: the join of T^{-n}P over n >= 1 is then T^{-1}B = B, so h(T, P) = H(P | that join) = 0.
The Lebesgue-space assumption is the usual standing hypothesis.

r(t)=\prod_{j=1}^{r}(t-a_j)^{-\lfloor e_j/n\rfloor},\qquad u=t,\qquad v=s\,r(t).
\]

Then $v^n=h(u)$ with

\begin{equation}
h(u)=c\prod_{j=1}^{r}(u-a_j)^{\bar e_j},\qquad \bar e_j\equiv e_j\pmod n,\quad 0\le\bar e_j<n,
\end{equation}

so $h\in k[u]$, and $k(u,v)=k(C)$.

body: Sylvester's law of inertia is a theorem in matrix algebra about certain properties of the coefficient matrix of a real quadratic form that remain invariant under a change of basis. Namely, if $S$ is a symmetric matrix, then for any invertible matrix $P$, the numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues of $S'=PSP^{\mathsf {T}}$ are constant (i.e., the inertia of $S'$ is constant). This result is particularly useful when $S'$ is diagonal, as the inertia of a diagonal matrix can easily be obtained by looking at the signs of its diagonal elements.

[Thm zetaM_fourier_An of arXiv:2604.23890, 'The Cutoff Profile for Random Transpositions on Repeated Cards in the Full Range of Parame'] Suppose $0\le M\le n/3$. Then, we have
\[
\widehat{\xi_M}(\lambda)
=
\frac{K_{\lambda,\mu}}{d_\lambda}\,\Id_{d_\lambda},
\]
where
\[
\mu=\mu_M:=(n-M,1,1,\dots,1)\vdash n,
\]
and $K_{\alpha,\mu}$ denotes the Kostka number.

Moreover, if $\lambda_1<n-M$, then $\widehat{\xi_M}(\lambda)=0$. If $\lambda_1\ge n-M$, we have
$$\widehat{\xi_M}(\lambda)=\binom{M}{\,n-\lambda_1\,}\frac{
d_{\lambda^*}}{d_\lambda}\Id_{d_\lambda}.$$

body:
Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with boundary of class C^1 and outward unit normal nu. RELLICH IDENTITY: for every u in C^2(closure of Omega) one has integral_Omega (x . grad u) Laplacian(u) dx = ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx - (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |grad u|^2 dS + integral_{boundary} (x . grad u)(du/dnu) dS. POHOZAEV IDENTITY: if in addition u = 0 on the boundary of Omega and -Laplacian(u) = f(u) in Omega with f continuous and F(t) = integral_0^t f(s) ds, then, since on the boundary grad u = (du/dnu) nu, the two boundary terms collapse and one gets ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx + (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |du/dnu|^2 dS = n integral_Omega F(u) dx. CONSEQUENCE (nonexistence): let n >= 3, let Omega be star-shaped with respect to the origin (x . nu >= 0 on the boundary) with C^1 boundary, and let f(u) = |u|^(p-1) u with p >= (n+2)/(n-2). Multiplying the equation by u gives integral |grad u|^2 = integral |u|^(p+1), while Pohozaev gives ((n-2)/2) integral |u|^(p+1) + (1/2) integral_{boundary}(x . nu)|du/dnu|^2 = (n/(p+1)) integral |u|^(p+1). Since p >= (n+2)/(n-2) is exactly n/(p+1) <= (n-2)/2, the boundary term is <= 0 while star-shapedness makes it >= 0; hence it vanishes and integral |u|^(p+1) = 0 for p > (n+2)/(n-2). In the critical case p = (n+2)/(n-2) the two bulk terms cancel identically and one concludes only that (x . nu)|du/dnu|^2 = 0 on the boundary; if Omega is strictly star-shaped (x . nu > 0) this forces du/dnu = 0 on the whole boundary and then u = 0 by the Hopf lemma or unique continuation. WHERE IT FAILS: star-shapedness is essential, not technical - on an annulus {a < |x| < b} in R^n there exist positive radial solutions of -Laplacian(u) = u^p vanishing on both boundary spheres for EVERY p > 1, including supercritical p (Kazdan-Warner). Regularity is also essential: the identity is proved for u in C^2 up to the boundary (it is valid for H^1_0 weak solutions only after elliptic regularity has upgraded them, which requires growth conditions on f), and the boundary must be regular enough for the divergence theorem. The origin matters: star-shapedness is with respect to the point used in the multiplier x . grad u.
Omega is bounded and open in R^n with C^1 (or piecewise C^1) boundary, so the divergence theorem applies
u is in C^2 up to the closure of Omega
for the Pohozaev form: u = 0 on the boundary, f is continuous, F(t) = integral_0^t f and F(0) = 0
for the nonexistence corollary: n >= 3, Omega star-shaped about the origin, f(u) = |u|^(p-1)u with p >= (n+2)/(n-2), and strict star-shapedness plus Hopf or unique continuation in the critical case

[Thm 15 of arXiv:2609.03054, 'The classes of bivariate Schur and Herglotz matrix-valued rational functions: realizations'] Let $F(z) \in \mathbb{R}^{k\times l}(z)$ be a real rational matrix function that takes on contractive values for $z\in {\mathbb D}=\{ z \in{\mathbb C} : |z|<1\}$. Then $F(z)$ has a real contractive finite dimensional realization; that is, there exists a real contractive block matrix ${\scriptscriptstyle \begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{bmatrix}}\in{\mathbb R}^{(d{+}k)\times(d{+}l)}$ so that 
\begin{equation} F(z) = D +zC (I -zA)^{-1} B   ,\quad z\in {\mathbb D}. \end{equation} This realization can be chosen to be minimal, i.e., $$
\bigcap_{j=0}^\infty \ker CA^{d-1} = \{0\}, \quad \bigvee_{j=0}^{d-1} \operatorname{ Ran} A^jB = {\mathbb R}^d. $$

body: [Prop mean_curvature_flow of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a Reebless $C^{\infty,0}$ foliation of $\mathbb{T}^2$. Equip $\mathbb{T}^2$ with a flat Euclidean metric. Then after a preparatory arbitrarily $C^0$-small isotopy to $\mathcal{G}$, leafwise mean curvature flow on $\mathcal{G}$ converges tangentially to a linear foliation of slope $\slope(\mathcal{G})$. body: Load-bearing hypothesis: in ‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^q_t L^r_x(R×R^n)} ≤ C‖f‖_{L²} the exponents must satisfy 2/q + n/r = n/2 exactly, and q ≥ 2 (and r ≥ 2). None of these can be relaxed, so an argument that 'interpolates' to a pair off the scaling line, or that uses a short-time-looking pair with q < 2, is wrong. Scaling: for f_λ(x) = f(λx) one has (e^{itΔ}f_λ)(x) = (e^{iλ²tΔ}f)(λx), hence ‖e^{itΔ}f_λ‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} = λ^{−2/q − n/r}‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} while ‖f_λ‖_{L²} = λ^{−n/2}‖f‖_{L²}. If 2/q + n/r ≠ n/2 the ratio of the two sides is λ^{n/2 − 2/q − n/r}, which is unbounded as λ → 0 or λ → ∞ for any fixed f ≠ 0. So an estimate off the scaling line fails for every nonzero f. Necessity of q ≥ 2 (the case r > 2; on the scaling line r = 2 forces q = ∞, so there is nothing to prove there): take φ ∈ S(R^n) and f_N = Σ_{k=1}^N e^{−i t_k Δ}φ with t_1 ≪ t_2 ≪ ... ≪ t_N separated enough that Σ_{j≠k}|t_k − t_j|^{−n(1/2−1/r)} is small for every k. Since |⟨e^{isΔ}φ, φ⟩| ≤ (4π|s|)^{−n/2}‖φ‖_{L¹}² → 0, the summands are almost orthogonal in L² and ‖f_N‖_{L²}² ≈ N‖φ‖²_{L²}; and for t within O(1) of t_k the dispersive estimate makes every term but the k-th small in L^r_x, so ‖e^{itΔ}f_N‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} ≳ N^{1/q}‖e^{itΔ}φ‖_{L^q_t([−1,1]) L^r_x}. The ratio is ≳ N^{1/q − 1/2}, unbounded when q < 2. Known excluded endpoints, where the pair is on the scaling line and q = 2 but the estimate is still false: (q,r) = (2,∞) for Schrödinger in n = 2 (Montgomery-Smith), and (q,r) = (2,∞) for the wave equation in n = 3 (Klainerman–Machedon). Also for the wave equation the Lebesgue-space estimate is stated with r < ∞; at r = ∞ one must pass to Besov spaces.
title: Pitfall: A Strichartz Estimate Needs the Scaling Relation and q ≥ 2

[Theorem 256 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Assume $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ is realized by a bipartite gluing graph $\mathsf{G}$, with bipartition $\epsilon : [m] \rightarrow \{\pm 1\}$. Then the vector $\boldsymbol{v} = \epsilon_1\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_1}$ has $\mathfrak{G}$-orbit $\{\epsilon_i\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_i}\,\,|\,\,i\in [m]\}$, this orbit is good (\textit{cf.} Definition~\ref{def:goodor}) and has minimal size $m = \textnormal{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) + 1$. For any $i \in [m]$ and $h \in [H]$ we have
\[
T^{(h)}(\epsilon_i \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_i}) = \left\{\begin{array}{ccc}  \epsilon_i \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_i} && \textnormal{if}\,\,h \notin \mathcal{H}_i, \\[0.6ex] \epsilon_{i'_h}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{i'_h}} && \textnormal{if}\,\,h \in \mathcal{H}_i. \end{array}\right.
\]
The genus of the spectral curve $\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ is $\mathsf{g}_{\boldsymbol{v}} = \textnormal{corank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta})$ and the group $\hat{\mathfrak{G}}$ is the Weyl group of type $A_{m - 1}$ (\textit{i.e.} the symmetric group in $m$ elements).

The bidifferential $\mathcal{B}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{v}}}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:Bcont} is defined on $\Sigma^{[2],\circ}_{\boldsymbol{v}} = \Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}} \times \Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ and can simply be denoted $\mathcal{B}_{\boldsymbol{v}}$. Its matrix of biresidues is \textbf{\foreignlanguage{russian}{B}} = $\textnormal{\textbf{Id}} - \boldsymbol{1}$, and the bidifferential itself is equal to
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{B}_{\boldsymbol{v}} = \mathcal{B}^{\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}},\mathcal{L}} - \frac{\dd z_1\dd z_2}{(z_1 - z_2)^2},
\end{equation}
where $(z_1,z_2) = Z_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{v}}}$, the Lagrangian $\mathcal{L} \subset H_1(\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}},\amsmathbb{Z})$ is spanned by cycles around the components of the gluing locus (\textit{cf.} Definition~\ref{def:spcurv1}), and $\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}},\mathcal{L}}$ is the fundamental bidifferential of Section~\ref{sec:fund02}.

From the analytic continuation of first-kind functions in Proposition~\ref{Lem:Holo1form}, we get a linear isomorphism
\[
\begin{array}{ccc} \textnormal{Ker}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) & \longrightarrow & H^1(\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}},\amsmathbb{C}) \\
\boldsymbol{v}' & \longmapsto & \mathfrak{u}_{\boldsymbol{v};\boldsymbol{v}'} \end{array}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 256 of arXiv:2601.16377

This right-orthogonally invariant event has probability at least 2/5, using the settled Gaussian singular-value estimate of C07. Conditional on E_good and either determinant branch, the angle of the orthogonal polar factor of Lambda^(-1/2)E^T Z(S) is uniform. Thus anisotropic covariance-surrogate entry takes O(log d+log(1/rho)) rescaled time. This is not an entry guarantee or failure probability for exact DDPM GD: finite-step comparison, free centroid and subsequent unrestricted angular tracking remain open.

# Quantitative Gaussian entry for the anisotropic covariance-factor surrogate

This supplies the covariance-surrogate random-entry estimate missing from C12. It uses C07's Gaussian singular-value event as settled input, without re-proving its probability. It does not compare unrestricted exact DDPM GD with this surrogate, release the centroid, or prove a full-GD failure probability. No target resolution or novelty finding is asserted.

## Statement

Let d>=2, E^T E=I_2, Lambda=diag(1,9), D=E Lambda E^T. Let Z(s) solve

    Z_dot=(D-ZZ^T)Z,

from a d-by-2 matrix Z_0 with iid N(0,1/d) entries. Put sigma_0=1/(80 sqrt(d)). Define the event

    E_good={||Z_0||_F<=4, sigma_min(E^T Z_0)>=sigma_0}.

It has probability at least 2/5. For every 0<rho<=1/100, set

    L=100/(sigma_0 rho), S=10 log L.

On E_good the flow exists globally, ||Z(s)||_F<=4, and

    min_{O in O(2)} ||Z(S)-E Lambda^(1/2) O||_F <rho/2.    (1)

Conditional on E_good and either determinant branch, the angle of the orthogonal polar factor of Lambda^(-1/2)E^T Z(S) is uniform. The time S=O(log d+log(1/rho)); all constants here are independent of d. This is an exact deterministic-flow and Gaussian-initialization statement, not a training experiment or a claim that the DDPM trajectory equals this flow.

## 1. Global bounded flow

Set Q=ZZ^T, R=tr Q=||Z||_F^2. Then

    R_dot=2 tr(DQ)-2||Q||_F^2
         <=2||Q||_F(sqrt(82)-||Q||_F).

The rank of Q is at most two, hence ||Q||_F>=R/sqrt(2). At R>=16 this is larger than sqrt(82), since 16^2/2=128>82. Thus the derivative points inward at the norm-4 boundary and beyond it. On ||Z_0||<=4 the solution cannot exit this ball. The polynomial ODE is locally Lipschitz and bounded solutions extend globally. This bound does not use an incorrect isotropic replacement for the largest eigenvalue 9.

## 2. Exact covariance formula

Write A=E^T Z_0, B=(I-EE^T)Z_0. On E_good, A is invertible, ||A||_F,||B||_F<=4 and sigma_min(A)>=sigma_0. Define

    W(s)=E exp(Lambda s) A+B,
    H(s)=I+A^T diag(e^(2s)-1,(e^(18s)-1)/9) A+2s B^T B.

Then H=I+2 integral_0^s W(u)^T W(u) du is positive definite and

    Q(s)=W(s) H(s)^(-1) W(s)^T.                        (2)

Differentiating gives Q_dot=DQ+QD-2Q^2 and Q(0)=Z_0 Z_0^T. The actual covariance has this same Riccati equation, so uniqueness gives (2). No identity Z=W H^(-1/2) for the actual factor trajectory is assumed.

Let Q_pp=E^T Q E. Inverting its planar factor in (2) gives

    Q_pp^(-1)=Lambda^(-1)+T(s),
    T(s)=exp(-Lambda s) A^(-T)
       [I+2s B^T B-A^T Lambda^(-1) A]
          A^(-1) exp(-Lambda s).

Consequently

    ||T(s)||_op<=e^(-2s) sigma_0^(-2)(17+32s).         (3)

All inverses are legitimate: A is invertible on E_good and H is positive definite for every nonnegative time.

## 3. Planar and perpendicular entry errors

At S, (3) and sigma_0^(-2)=L^2 rho^2/10000 give

    ||T(S)||<=rho^2(17+320 log L)/(10000 L^18)
              <=337 rho^2/(10000 L^17)<rho^2/25,       (4)

using L>=1 and log L<=L. Our actual parameters give S>=1. In particular ||T||<1/18. Matrix inversion then yields

    ||Q_pp-Lambda||_op
       <=81||T||/(1-9||T||)<=162||T||.                (5)

Let C=Lambda^(-1/2)E^T Z(S), and O its orthogonal polar factor. Its singular values are positive. The inequality |sqrt(x)-1|<=|x-1| for x>=0 gives

    ||C-O||_F<=||CC^T-I||_F
                  <=||Q_pp-Lambda||_F.

Multiplying by Lambda^(1/2), and using (5), bounds the planar factor error by

    ||E^T Z(S)-Lambda^(1/2)O||_F
          <=486 sqrt(2)||T||<700||T||<=28rho^2.         (6)

For the perpendicular part, (e^(18s)-1)/9 >= e^(2s)-1 for s>=0; this follows by comparing the corresponding integrals of 2e^(18u) and 2e^(2u). Therefore

    H(s)>=(e^(2s)-1) A^T A.

For s>=1 this gives

    ||(I-EE^T)Z(s)||_F^2
       =tr(B H(s)^(-1) B^T)
       <=32 sigma_0^(-2)e^(-2s).

At S the last expression is at most 32rho^2/(10000 L^18)<rho^2/100. Combining with (6) and rho<=1/100 bounds the total factor error by

    28rho^2+rho/10 <=(19/50)rho<rho/2.

This proves (1). Orthogonality of planar and perpendicular errors could give a slightly tighter bound, but is not needed.

## 4. Probability and the correct phase symmetry

C07's settled Gaussian good event has probability at least 2/5 and implies both ||Z_0||<=4 and sigma_min(E^T Z_0)>=sigma_0. It is therefore a subset of E_good, proving the stated probability. We do not condition on C07's particular column-based construction of that event, since that construction need not be invariant under right rotations.

E_good itself IS invariant under Z_0 -> Z_0 O for every O in O(2), because Frobenius norm and singular values are unchanged. The Gaussian law has the same right invariance. The ODE is right equivariant: (ZO)(ZO)^T=ZZ^T, and uniqueness implies Z(s;Z_0 O)=Z(s;Z_0)O. Thus C at time S right-rotates in the same manner. Its left polar decomposition C=S_C O_C is unique because C is invertible; right rotation preserves S_C and rotates O_C. Rotations preserve either determinant branch and act transitively on its circle. The conditional angular law on each nonnull branch is therefore uniform. Reflection interchanges the two branches, and both have positive probability on this invariant event.

This is right-factor symmetry of the covariance surrogate. It is not a physical-plane rotational symmetry of the anisotropic teacher, and it is not a symmetry of the component-identifying DDPM correction. Keeping those distinct is necessary for the eventual probability-transfer argument.

## Remaining transfer

This result supplies a norm-bounded logarithmic-time surrogate entry estimate and the invariant event needed for its uniform phase. To connect it to C15 one must still compare actual finite-step DDPM GD over this entry interval, release centering and planarity, and control their accumulated angular effects. The free-centroid and extra-direction estimates for the equilateral case do not automatically establish those anisotropic statements. No product of independent success probabilities, full-GD basin mass, or annealing obstruction is claimed here.

body:
Let $\Sigma$ be a spacelike hypersurface with timelike unit normal $e_0$ in a spacetime $(\bar{M}, \bar{g})$. For any normal variation with variation vector field $V = \phi e_0$ compactly supported on $\Sigma$, the second variation of the volume functional $\operatorname{Vol}(\Sigma_t)$ at $t=0$ is given by $\left. \frac{d^2}{dt^2} \operatorname{Vol}(\Sigma_t) \right|_{t=0} = - \int_\Sigma \left( |\nabla \phi|^2 - (|h|^2 + \operatorname{Ric}(e_0, e_0)) \phi^2 \right) d\mu_g$. In particular, when $\operatorname{Ric}(e_0, e_0) \ge 0$, any maximal hypersurface ($H=0$) strictly maximizes volume among nearby compact perturbations.
\Sigma is a spacelike hypersurface in Lorentzian spacetime
\phi is a smooth compactly supported function
Ric(e_0, e_0) >= 0 (dominant energy condition)

[Definition def-thin-disk of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $W\in(0, \frac{\gamma^2}{2})$. 
	    Sample $(\mathcal{W}, T) \sim \mathcal{M}^\mathrm{wed}(W) \times (1-\frac{2}{\gamma^2}W)^{-2}\textup{Leb}_{\mathbb{R}_+}$, and write $\mathcal{W} = \{(u, \mathcal{D}_u)\}$. The \emph{weight $W$ quantum disk} is the concatenation of the quantum disks $\{\mathcal{D}_u \: : \: u \leq T\}$ according to the ordering induced by $u$. Its left (resp.\ right) boundary length is the sum of the left (resp.\ right) boundary lengths of its constituent $\mathcal{D}_u$.
	    We define the infinite measure ${\mathcal{M}}^\mathrm{disk}_{0,2}(W)$ to be the law of the weight $W$ quantum disk.
	    For $x\in [0,T]$, the \emph{quantum cut point measure} assigns  mass
	    $x$ to the collection of cut points between the quantum disks $\{\mathcal{D}_u:u\leq x\}$.
title: Definition def-thin-disk of arXiv:2411.19810

Let y_i = x_i' beta + e_i for i = 1..n with independent errors of mean zero and variances sigma_i^2, and let beta_hat = (X'SX)^(-1) X'S y be the weighted least-squares fit with fixed positive weights S = diag(s_i). Write L_tr = sum_i s_i (y_i - yhat_i)^2 for the weighted training loss and L_te = sum_i s_i (y_i* - yhat_i)^2 for the same loss on an independent copy y* of y at the same design. Then E[L_te] - E[L_tr] = 2 sum_i s_i^2 sigma_i^2 x_i'(X'SX)^(-1) x_i = 2 tr( (X'SX)^(-1) X' S^2 Sigma X ), where Sigma = diag(sigma_i^2). No distributional assumption beyond independence and finite second moments is used.
errors independent across rows with mean zero and finite variances sigma_i^2; the design X and the weights S are fixed (or independent of the errors)
the test loss is evaluated at the same design with an independent copy of the responses (in-sample optimism in the sense of Efron and Mallows)

For each row, E(y_i - yhat_i)^2 = E((y_i - mu_i) - (yhat_i - mu_i))^2 = sigma_i^2 + E(yhat_i - mu_i)^2 - 2 Cov(y_i, yhat_i), while for the independent copy E(y_i* - yhat_i)^2 = sigma_i^2 + E(yhat_i - mu_i)^2 because y_i* is independent of yhat_i and has the same mean and variance as y_i. body: A discrete-time Markov chain on a countable state space S with transition matrix P is irreducible if for every pair of states x, y in S there exists n >= 0 with P^n(x,y) > 0 (y is reachable from x). The period of a state x is the greatest common divisor of {n >= 1 : P^n(x,x) > 0}; an irreducible chain has a single common period shared by all states, and the chain is aperiodic if this common period equals 1, equivalently if for some x and all sufficiently large n, P^n(x,x) > 0. [standard, e.g. Levin and Peres, Markov Chains and Mixing Times]
title: Irreducible and Aperiodic Discrete-Time Markov Chain

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(a>1\) and \(r_a(\xi)=e^{-2\xi}-e^{-2a\xi}\), \(\xi>0\). Then
\(0<r_a(\xi)<1\) for every \(\xi>0\), and
\[
        \rho_a:=\sup_{\xi>0}r_a(\xi)
        =
        (a-1)a^{-a/(a-1)}<1.
\]
Moreover, \(r_a\in L^1(0,\infty)\),
\begin{equation}

        \int_0^\infty r_a(\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi
        =
        \frac12\left(1-\frac1a\right),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}

        \int_0^\infty r_a(\xi)(1-r_a(\xi))\,\mathrm d\xi
        =
        \frac{(a-1)(a+3)}{4a(a+1)}.
\end{equation}
Finally, \(r_a(\xi)=2(a-1)\xi+O(\xi^2)\) as \(\xi\downarrow0\), and \(r_a\)
decays exponentially as \(\xi\to\infty\).

A bent sign vector has full Walsh support, so one admissible witness meets every edge of a perfect matching: the weighted batching can be a SINGLE batch with a legal one-row basis exchange. Take K = M = 2 and restrict to the symmetric slice Q_11 = Q_22 = q, Q_12 = c, all R_in = r, which the ODE preserves. For every eta in [2499/5000, 2501/5000], the solution from (q, c, r) = (1, 0, 0) exists for all t >= 0 and converges exponentially to an equilibrium x*(eta). That equilibrium is the unique zero of the slice drift in a certified box where it is physical (q - c > 0, q + c - 4 r^2 > 0) and Hurwitz in the slice. Its antisymmetric block has exactly the plateau's unstable direction (lambda > 0). Hence the spherical start reaches the symmetric saddle along its stable manifold.

body: Localized regime of the bounded-density conjecture for quadratic forms (Proposition 4). Let X_1..X_n be independent with densities <=1 and Q(x)=x^T A x with A symmetric. (a) If some 2x2 PRINCIPAL submatrix B of A (two original coordinates i, j) is definite, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/sqrt(det B). Proof: condition on the other n-2 ORIGINAL coordinates (independent, so Fubini is genuine); given them Q is a quadratic-plus-linear form in (X_i, X_j); complete the square (B invertible), which shifts (X_i, X_j) and keeps their joint density <=1; for definite B each set {s <= y^T B y <= s+h} is an elliptic annulus of area at most pi h/sqrt(det B), so the conditional density is at most pi/sqrt(det B); average. (b) Hence if A has a 3x3 PRINCIPAL submatrix A_[S] all of whose eigenvalues have modulus >= c>0, and A_[S] is definite or diagonal, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/c: for definite A_[S], Cauchy interlacing puts both eigenvalues of every 2x2 principal block of A_[S] at modulus >= c with one sign, so det >= c^2; for diagonal A_[S], two of the three diagonal entries share a sign and form a definite diagonal block with det >= c^2. This contains the separable case. (c) For other well-conditioned blocks the bound K/c is not proved. A block may have no definite 2x2 principal block at all, e.g. [[0,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,0]] (eigenvalues 2, -1, -1), and the rank-3 coarea bound ||p_S||_inf <= K||rho||_inf^{2/3} is false for general bounded densities on R^3: a density rho <= B placed on a thin shell around {S = s} gives p_S of order B s^{1/2}/sqrt(l1 l2 l3) for a definite form, unbounded in s. So the localized regime is settled for forms with a definite 2x2 principal block of determinant >= c^2, in particular when a well-conditioned 3x3 principal block is definite or diagonal; the other localized forms stay open, together with the DELOCALIZED forms (every 3x3 principal block near-singular), which is the CLT regime.

body:
[Proposition 18 (A sufficient condition for proxy-faithfulness) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Let transforms $A,B$ act on the same operand under a common grouping and produce group-RMS profiles with $\sum_g\sigma_g^2=S_A\ge S_B$ and per-group crest factors $M_g=\mathrm{CF}_g\,\sigma_g$ all lying in a band
$\mathrm{CF}_g\in[\underline c,\bar c]$ (necessarily $1\le\underline c\le\bar c\le\sqrt G$
for a group of size $G$). If that band is tight relative to the proxy gap,
$\bar c^2/\underline c^2 < S_A/S_B$, then the $L^2$ proxy $\sum_g\sigma_g^2$ and the
AbsMax step-size surrogate $\sum_g M_g^2$ rank $A$ and $B$ the \emph{same} way. When
the crest-factor profiles differ enough to break this condition, which a
concentrating transform induces, the ranking can \emph{invert}. Note that the aggregate $\sum_g\sigma_g^2$ is the operand's Frobenius energy divided by $G$, hence unchanged by any orthogonal map: between two rotations $S_A=S_B$ and the sufficient condition is unavailable, so this proposition bites only where the transforms change that energy. What a concentrating rotation still changes is the crest-factor band, and that is the route by which the two surrogates come apart.

Let X be real symmetric with ||X||op<=2 and let mu I<=Lambda<=I. For either sign define H_+=I+eta(Lambda-X), H_-=I-eta(Lambda-X). Direct expansion, requiring no commutation between Lambda and X, gives
 H_+ X H_+ = [X/2-2eta X^2+eta^2 X^3] + C_+ X C_+ - eta^2 R,

where

Here ||R||op<=2+4+4=10.
Both identities are independently verified as universal free noncommutative polynomial identities in scripts/check_spectral_splits.py.

For (A), X is positive definite. On [0,2], the scalar polynomial
 h_+(x)=x/2-2eta x^2+eta^2 x^3
is nondecreasing because h_+'(x)>=1/2-8eta>=0 for eta<=1/16. If w=lambda_min(X)>0, spectral calculus therefore gives
 lambda_min(h_+(X))=h_+(w).
Since C_+ is positive definite and lambda_min(C_+)>=1/sqrt(2)+sqrt(2)eta mu,
 lambda_min(C_+ X C_+)>=w(1/2+2eta mu+2eta^2 mu^2).
Adding these bounds and subtracting the remainder gives
 lambda_min(H_+ X H_+)
 >=(1+eta(mu-w))^2 w
     +eta^2(mu^2 w+2mu w^2)-10eta^2
 >=(1+eta(mu-w))^2 w-22eta^2.
This proves (A).

For (B), if p=lambda_min(X)>=0, congruence preserves positive semidefiniteness.
If p<0, the polynomial h_-(x)=x/2+2eta x^2+eta^2 x^3 is nondecreasing on [-2,2], since h_-'(x)>=1/2-8eta>=0. Thus lambda_min(h_-(X))=h_-(p).
The matrix C_- is positive definite for eta<=1/16 and
 ||C_-||op<=1/sqrt(2)-sqrt(2)eta mu.
From X>=pI and p<0,
 C_- X C_->=p C_-^2>=p||C_-||op^2 I.
Consequently,
 lambda_min(H_- X H_-)
 >=(1-eta mu)^2 p
    +2eta p^2+eta^2 p^3+eta^2 mu^2 p-10eta^2.
The first two correction terms combine as eta p^2(2+eta p)>=0, since p>=-2 and eta<=1/16. Also mu^2 p>=-2. The whole correction is therefore >=-12eta^2, which is stronger than the required -22eta^2. This proves (B), including every sign condition in the congruence comparison.

Let $\mu$ and $

u$ possibly signed or complex. $
u$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$, written $
u \ll \mu$, if $
u(A) = 0$ for every $A \in \Sigma$ with $\mu(A) = 0$ (for signed $
u$, equivalently $|
u|(A) = 0$, where $|
u|$ is the total variation). If $
u$ is FINITE (or finite signed/complex), this is equivalent to the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $|
u(A)| < \varepsilon$ whenever $\mu(A) < \delta$; for infinite $
u$ the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition is strictly stronger (e.g. $
u(A) = \int_A |x|^{-1}dx$ on $(0,1)$ has $
u \ll$ Lebesgue but fails $\varepsilon$-$\delta$). Any measure of the form $
u(A) = \int_A f\,d\mu$ with $f \geq 0$ measurable (or $f \in L^1(\mu)$ for signed $
u$) satisfies $
u \ll \mu$; the Radon-Nikodym theorem is the converse under $\sigma$-finiteness. $\mu$ and $
u$ are mutually singular, $\mu \perp 
u$, if there is $A \in \Sigma$ with $\mu(A) = 0$ and $
u(X\setminus A) = 0$. Lebesgue decomposition: for $\sigma$-finite $\mu, 
u$ there is a unique splitting $
u = 
u_{ac} + 
u_s$ with $
u_{ac} \ll \mu$ and $
u_s \perp \mu$. Related but different: a FUNCTION $F: [a,b]	o\mathbb{R}$ is absolutely continuous iff its Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is absolutely continuous w.r.t. Lebesgue measure iff $F(x) = F(a) + \int_a^x F'$ with $F' \in L^1$; the Cantor function is continuous, increasing, but not absolutely continuous (its measure is singular). Sharp edge: $
u \ll \mu$ is not symmetric, and $
u \ll \mu$ with $\mu \ll

[Dfn 232 (truncated Lipschitz algorithm) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Consider an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ with input $(\bG, \bg^\aux)$. Denote its output $\bx\equiv\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. For $a\in [M]$, define the random variable
	\[\fm_a\equiv
		\fm_a(\bG,\bg^\aux;\cA_N)
		\equiv
		\frac{(\bg^a,\bx)}{N^{1/2}}\,,
	\]
where we recall that $\bg^a$ is the $a$-th row of $\bG$.
	For $K > 0$, define
	\[
		S_K(\cA_N) = \bigg\{
			a \in [M] : 
			\Big|\E\fm_a(\bG,\bg^\aux;\cA_N)\Big|
			\ge K
		\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Let $\hbG \in \R^{M\times N}$ be a matrix of i.i.d. gaussians independent of $(\bG, \bg^\aux)$.
	Then define the \textbf{truncated algorithm} $\cA_{N[K]}$ as the function
	\[\cA_{N[K]}\Big(\bG, 
	\bg^{\aux+}
	\equiv(\bg^\aux, \hbG)\Big)
	\equiv
	\cA_N\Big(\tbG(\bG,\hbG;S_K(\cA_N)), \bg^\aux\Big)\,,
	\]
where $\tbG$ is the row-splicing operation from Definition~\ref{d:row.splice}. In words, if $|\E\fm_a| \ge K$, then $\cA_{N[K]}$ ignores the $a$-th row $\bg^a$ of $\bG$ and replaces this input with the independent gaussian vector $\hat\bg$. 	Clearly $\cA_{N[K]}$ is also an $L$-Lipschitz function, with output
	\[\tilde{\bx} \equiv 
		\cA_{N[K]}(\bG, (\bg^\aux, \hbG)) \stackrel{\textit{d}}{=}
		\bx
		= \cA_N(\bG, \bg^\aux)\,.
	\]
It follows that $\cA_{N[K]}$ is also an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}.
title: truncated Lipschitz algorithm

[Lemma 38 (Traces on spacelike hypersurfaces) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Let $\mathbb Q\in L^1_{\rm loc}$ be torus invariant and suppose that
\bel{eq:weak-current-production}
\nabla_\alpha\mathbb Q^\alpha=-\lambda+r\,dV_g,
\qquad
\lambda\in\Meas^+_{\rm loc},
\qquad
r\in L^1_{\rm loc}.
\ee
Then the almost-everywhere function in~\eqref{eq:weak-normal-flux} admits a right-continuous representative of locally bounded variation. For every pair of continuity levels $s_0<s_1$, one has
\bel{eq:weak-Gauss-Green}
\mathfrak H_{\mathbb Q}(s_1)
+\lambda(\mathcal D_{s_0,s_1})
=\mathfrak H_{\mathbb Q}(s_0)
+\int_{\mathcal D_{s_0,s_1}}r\,dV_g.
\ee
In particular, if $r=0$, the normal flux~$\mathfrak H_{\mathbb Q}$ is non-increasing toward the future. The same identity holds between two torus-invariant spacelike Lipschitz hypersurfaces, with the normal fluxes defined by one-sided approximation; these traces do not depend on the Lipschitz time function used between the hypersurfaces.

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, C010 version 2, proof (unaudited); no novelty or independent-audit claim. Fix input dimension d>=1 and finite total mean-field time T>=0, with equal hidden widths m>=36. Let h_i=sigma(w_i dot x), z_j=m^(-1)sum_i B_ji h_i, and f=m^(-1)sum_j a_j sigma(z_j). Assume sigma is globally C2 with absolute values of sigma and its first two derivatives at most one; data satisfy ||X||<=1 and |Y|<=1; loss is population half-squared error. Initialize two independent runs with every coordinate of w_i, every a_j and every B_ji mutually independent standard normal variables. Train all parameters simultaneously using fresh-iid SGD samples or finite minibatch averages, with multiplier m on w,a and m^2 on B, common deterministic nonnegative steps eta_k summing to at most T; the runs may see independent data. Write S2=sum eta_k^2. Explicit constants kappa_T and C_{d,T} from proof section 1 give beta_T=exp(-kappa_T T)>0 and an initialization-selected compatible permutation tuple with expected population loss-chord barrier bounded by C_{d,T}[(sqrt(log m)m^(-1/(d+2))+sqrt(S2))^(beta_T/2)+m^(-1/2)]. Hence eta_max<=m^(-2/(d+2)) gives O_{d,T}(m^(-beta_T/(2(d+2)))(log m)^(beta_T/4)). On an initialization event of failure probability at most 18/m, empirical exponential tails of alpha_j=1+|a_j(0)|+|a'_j(0)| and initial row/weighted-column averages control all trained lower adjoints. Truncating alpha at K yields C_T[K^2 D+384 exp(-K^2/128)] in the boundary-L1/middle-cut norm D; optimizing K gives the concave capped Osgood modulus. The proof uses accumulated Hilbert martingale noise rather than a maximum-based Hilbert gradient Lipschitz constant. All Gaussian arrays are unbounded; no trained-layer independence or teacher model is assumed. This is not a ReLU, fixed independent-data step, low-risk convergence, growing-depth, growing-time or dimension-free theorem, and it does not close the unrestricted permutation conjecture.

Fixed d,T; initialization-selected matching; fresh data and common deterministic step schedule; shrinking steps for the vanishing-rate corollary

Method: Polynomial mixing with plus Ising boundary conditions explicit structural calculation Result: The direct disagreement coupling proves the high-temperature part. Write N=n^2 and c=4*tanh(beta). A single disagreement vanishes if its site is updated, while at most four neighboring updates create disagreement with probability at most tanh(beta). Thus the expected Hamming distance contracts by1-(1-c)/N when c<1. Iteration and the coupling inequality give tmix(1/4)<=N*log(4*N)/(1-c), up to integer rounding. Check: Changing one neighboring spin changes the heat-bath plus probability by at most tanh(beta), since the conditional probability is(1+tanh(h))/2. A path coupling along single-spin differences extends the bound to arbitrary initial pairs. Boundary sites have at most four variable neighbors, so the estimate remains valid with fixed plus boundary. Obstruction: For4*tanh(beta)>=1 the coefficient ceases to contract. This is a failure of the local metric argument, not a lower bound showing slow mixing; the low-temperature interface regime remains unresolved here.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0194-polynomial-mixing-with-plus-ising-boundary-conditions

\lim_{n\to\infty} n^\alpha
 \EE  \big( \exp\big(\nu  
\bff_n^T \bfM_{n}(\alpha,\theta)\big); 
K_n(\alpha,\theta) =\lfloor x n^\alpha\rfloor \big)\cr
&&
=
\exp\Big(\frac{x\alpha}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}

g_\alpha(x),

 \be
f_{Y_x^{(\nu,f)}}(1)  =

  \exp\Big(\frac{\alpha x}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}
  \int_{0}^1
 (e^{ \rmi\tau  y} -1 ) e^{\nu  f(y)} y^{-\alpha-1} \rmd y
 \Big) \rmd \tau.
 \ee
