body:
Tarry (1900) showed by exhaustion that no Latin square of order 6 has an orthogonal mate, so Euler's thirty-six officers problem has no solution; a pair of orthogonal Latin squares exists for every order n except n = 2 and n = 6 (Bose, Shrikhande, Parker 1960, refuting Euler's conjecture for all n congruent to 2 mod 4 beyond 6). A Latin square has an orthogonal mate if and only if it can be decomposed into n disjoint transversals. For the cyclic Latin square of order n (the Cayley table of the integers mod n): when n is odd the diagonals give n disjoint transversals, so it has an orthogonal mate; when n is even it has no transversal at all, because a transversal would be a complete mapping of Z_n and the sum of all elements of Z_n, n/2, is not zero (a parity obstruction), so in particular it has no orthogonal mate. The even-order cyclic result is a statement about the cyclic square only; other Latin squares of the same even order (n = 4, 8, 10, ...) can have transversals and mates.
the transversal obstruction is for the cyclic square (Cayley table of Z_n) with n even; it does not transfer to arbitrary Latin squares of even order
Tarry's result is specific to order 6; orthogonal mates exist for every order other than 2 and 6
a transversal is a set of n cells, one per row, column and symbol
title: Tarry's theorem for order 6 (thirty-six officers) and transversals of cyclic Latin squares

body:
[Lemma L_SB of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] Suppose that $H$ is a strictly balanced graph
and that $K$ is a proper subgraph 
of the graph $H\setminus e$,  
obtained from $H$ by 
removing some $e \in E(H)$. 
Let $x$ denote the number of vertices in 
$K$ that are not in $e$. 
Then we have that $0\leqslant x\leqslant v(H)-2$
and 
\[
e(K) \leqslant \lambda(H)x, 
\]  
with equality if and only if 
either 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x=0$ and so $e(K)=0$; or else
\item $x=v(H)-2$ and $e(K)=e(H)-2$.
\end{enumerate}
In all other cases, in fact, 
\[
e(K) \leqslant \lambda(H) x-\xi(H),
\] 
where $\xi(H)>0$ is as in 
Definition (D_xi of the paper).

[Corollary eq:approx-moment-bound of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[corollary]{cor:approx-matching}
Retain the setup of (thm:bulk-universality of the paper), except that exact matching in (equation eq:array-assumptions of the paper) is not assumed, and set
\[
 \delta_{I,r,N}=\abs{\mathbb E J_{I,N}^r-\mathbb E G^r},
 \qquad 1\le r\le m.
\]
Here
\[
 q_N=L^{p-1}N^{-(p-2)/2}(\log N)^{(p-1)/2},
\]
as in (equation eq:qN-main of the paper).  Then, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\begin{equation}
 \left|\log\frac{\mathbb E\mathcal Z_{N,L}^J(V,\varepsilon,f)}
 {\mathbb E\mathcal Z_{N,L}^G(V,\varepsilon,f)}\right|
 \le C\sum_{I\in[N]^p}
 \left(q_N^{m+1}+\sum_{r=1}^m\delta_{I,r,N}q_N^r\right).
\end{equation}
For an identically distributed triangular array, with errors \(\delta_{N,r}\), the right-hand side is
\[
 CN^p\left(q_N^{m+1}+\sum_{r=1}^m\delta_{N,r}q_N^r\right).
\]
Thus a right-hand side of \(o(1)\) implies the ratio conclusion, and \(o(N)\) implies pressure convergence. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Sequential approximate moment matching

[Theorem divergence RW of arXiv:2411.14350, 'Randomized Geodesic Flow on Hyperbolic Groups'] [Woe93]

A random walk $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ on a non-elementary hyperbolic group $G$ with transition probabilities given by $p(x,y)= \mu(x^{-1}y)$, where $\mu$ is a measure whose support is a finite generating set of $G$, converges to a random point $X_{\infty}\in \partial G$ almost surely. The hitting distribution on $\partial G$ is denoted by 
\begin{equation}
\nu_g(\cdot)= \mathbb P_g[X_\infty \in \cdot].
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$\operatorname{Sym}_0(H)$ by the coordinate circle of plane $i$.  Let
$P_{i,m}$ be the Fourier projections for the same circle acting by
conjugation on $S_2(W)$.  For bounded status scalars $\alpha,\beta$, set
\[
 \mathcal F_{B,i}(Y)=\frac1{\sqrt N}\left(
 \alpha\{[\widehat A_i,X_B],Y\}a_i
 +\beta\{X_B,[\widehat A_i,Y]\}a_i\right)
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12q}$}
\]
and, for
\[
 \mathsf M_i^{\rm C}=|a_i\rangle\langle a_i|-N^{-1}I_W,
 \qquad
 \mathsf M_i^{\rm W}=\mathsf M_i^{\rm C}-X_{B_i},
\]
define the correctly ordered generalized defect
\[
 \mathcal D_{i}^{\bullet}(B,Z)
 =(n-2)\left[
 \mathcal F_{B,i}(P_{\mathcal R}\mathsf M_i^\bullet Z)
 -\mathsf M_i^\bullet\mathcal F_{B,i}(P_{\mathcal R}Z)
 \right].
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12q_1}$}
\]
Then:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item for every own-circle-invariant $C_i$, the
zero-coefficient/zero-active-mode block vanishes,
\[
 \mathcal D_i^\bullet(C_i,P_{i,0}Z)=0;
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12q_2}$}
\]
\item for every $m\ne0$, every own-circle-invariant family
$C_i\in\operatorname{Sym}_0(H)$, and arbitrary ancillary contractions
$S_{i,-m}$,
\[
 \boxed{
 \left\|\frac1N\sum_i
   \bigl(\mathcal D_i^\bullet(C_i)P_{i,m}\bigr)
       \otimes S_{i,-m}\right\|_{\rm op}
 \le \frac CN
       \left(\frac1N\sum_i\|C_i\|_F^2\right)^{1/2};}
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12q_3}$}
\]
In particular $C_i=\mathcal A_iB$ gives the right side
$CN^{-1}\|B\|_F$.  The assertion is stable under passive Hilbert amplification, status,
reflection, adjunction, and full transpose; and
\item in the residual packetless cell
$(g,t_\partial,f_R;u,o,v)=(1,1,2;0,0,1)$, use its unique
$\mathsf V$ supernode.  In its coefficient-zero sector the complete
selected-time tensor is one prescribed bounded gate.  Writing
$\mathcal H_{\rm act}$ for the root-facing active curvature-letter
carrier and $E_{\rm in},E_{\rm out}$ for all other rails declared by the
native chronological matricization, that gate is the typed map
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 G_\Xi(B):\mathcal H_{\rm act}\otimes E_{\rm in}
       \longrightarrow W\otimes E_{\rm out},\\
 G_\Xi(B)=\frac1N\sum_i\sum_{m\ne0}
 \bigl(\mathcal D_i^\bullet(\mathcal A_iB)P_{i,m}\bigr)
 \otimes S_{i,-m},\\
 \|G_\Xi(B)\|_{\rm op}\le \frac CN\|B\|_F.
 \end{gathered}
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12q_4}$}
\]
This is the exact selected-time gate for the low-debit cell
\[
 (g,t_\partial,f_R;u,o,v)=(1,1,2;0,0,1).
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12q_5}$}
\]
The chronological sum and its endpoint energy are not part of this local
statement; they are proved separately in
(lem:packetless-root-time,lem:packetless-endpoint-energy of the paper).
\end{enumerate}

body: In statistics, sufficiency is a property of a statistic computed on a sample dataset in relation to a parametric model of the dataset. A sufficient statistic for a model parameter contains all of the information that the dataset provides about that parameter. It is closely related to the concepts of an ancillary statistic which contains no information about the model parameters, and of a complete statistic which only contains information about the parameters and no ancillary information.
title: Sufficient statistic

    \begin{equation}
    
    \int_0^t f(x) dx \leq \int_0^t g(x)dx
    \end{equation}
    for all $0<t< \infty$.
    Then 
    $$\int_0^{\infty} \Phi(f(x))dx \leq \int_0^{\infty} \Phi(g(x))dx$$
    holds for every increasing convex function $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^{+} \xrightarrow{} \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that $\Phi(0) = 0$.

body:
[Lemma 10 (Product-shell bookkeeping) of arXiv:2609.01570, 'A Proof of Fraenkel's Conjecture'] For distinct \(a,b\in A\), write
\[
 d_{ab}=\normQ{ab^{-1}},\qquad P_{ab}=bd_{ab}.
\]
Then
\[
 P_{ab}\in\{a,Q-a,Q+a,2Q-a,2Q+a,\ldots\},
 \qquad \frac1{d_{ab}}=\frac b{P_{ab}}.
\]
For every \(a\in A\), every subset \(B\subseteq A\setminus\{a\}\),
and all real numbers \(L\ge0\) and \(T>0\), if
\[
 \sum_{b\in B}b\le L
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 P_{ab}\ge T\quad(b\in B),
\]
then
\[
 \sum_{b\in B}\frac1{d_{ab}}\le\frac LT.
\]
Also, \(P_{ab}=a\) implies \(b\mid a\).

In the special case \(s=1\), call \(b\) good when
\(b\mid Q-1\) or \(b\mid Q+1\).  If such a good \(b\) satisfies
\(P_{ab}\in\{Q-a,Q+a\}\), then \(b\mid a-1\) or \(b\mid a+1\).

[Definition of arXiv:2609.03959, 'The combinatorial Hopf algebra of signed graphs'] Given a connected signed graph $\Sigma = (V,E, \sigma)$ and $S\subseteq V$, define $I_\Sigma(S)$ to be the set of edges $e\in E$ satisfying one of the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\sigma(e)=+$ and the endpoints of $e$ are in $S$
\item $\sigma(e) = +$ and the endpoints of $e$ are in $V\backslash S$ 
\item $\sigma(e) = -$ and $e$ has one endpoint in $S$ and the other one in $V\backslash S$.
\end{itemize}
Then define $$\zeta_x(\Sigma) := \sum_{A \subseteq V} x^{rk(I_\Sigma(A))}. $$
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2609.03959, 'The combinatorial Hopf algebra of signed graphs'

[Lemma 3 (weak pullback calculus) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X$ be an orientation-preserving global bi-Lipschitz map as above.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $E_i$ is skew-adjoint on $L^2(\mu)$. In particular
  \[
   \int_{\Real_y^n}(E_if)\phi d\mu=-\int_{\Real_y^n}f(E_i\phi)d\mu
  \]
  whenever $f,\phi,E_if,E_i\phi\in L^2(\mu)$.
\item[(ii)] Let $F=F^i\eframe_i$ be a vector field along $X$ whose Cartesian components belong to $L^1_{\rm loc}(\Real^n_y;\Rn)$. If
  $q,c^{ij}\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mu)$, then
  \[
   \Div_{\gmetric}F=q,
   \qquad
   (\curl_{\gmetric}F)^{ij}=c^{ij}
  \]
  in the conjugated distributional sense if and only if
  \[
   \partial_a(J\Kmat_i^aF^i)=Jq,
   \qquad
   \partial_a\!\left(J\Kmat_i^aF^j-J\Kmat_j^aF^i\right)=Jc^{ij}
   \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real^n_y).
  \]
  Equivalently, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Real^n_y)$,
  \begin{equation}
   \int q\varphi d\mu=-\int F^i\Kmat_i^a\partial_a\varphi d\mu,\qquad
   \int c^{ij}\varphi d\mu=-\int\bigl(F^j\Kmat_i^a-F^i\Kmat_j^a\bigr)
          \partial_a\varphi d\mu.
  \end{equation}
  With the convention in \eqref{eq:metric-tensor-divergence}, the same
  calculation gives, whenever
  $H:=\Div_{\gmetric}T\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mu)$,
  \begin{equation}
   JH^j
   =\partial_a(J\Kmat_i^aT^{ji})
   \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real_y^n)
  \end{equation}
  for every locally integrable tensor $T$.
\item[(iii)] If $\mathcal C_X^{-1}F\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}$ for some
  $1\le p\le\infty$, then 
  \begin{equation}
      \partial_aF^i=A_a^jE_jF^i,
  \end{equation}
  and the conjugated divergence and curl in
  (ii) agree almost everywhere with the pointwise formulas $\Kmat^a_i\partial_aF^i$ and
  $\Kmat^a_i\partial_aF^j-\Kmat^a_j\partial_aF^i$.
\item[(iv)] The conjugated derivatives commute on their common
distributional domain:
  \[
   E_iE_j=E_jE_i.
  \]
\end{enumerate}

Let X be a real random variable with E[X^2] < infinity and G a sub-sigma-field. Among all G-measurable real A with E[A^2] < infinity, m = E[X | G] minimizes E[(X - A)^2], and A attains the minimum if and only if A = m almost surely; uniqueness holds only up to almost-sure equality. Square integrability of X is needed: if E[X^2] = infinity, then E[(X - A)^2] = infinity for every square-integrable A, so the loss does not single out a predictor.

Under the partition convention of Randomstrasse101 Definition 14.2, the shape with one edge uv, U={u} and V={v}, gives a symmetric n by n Rademacher matrix A with zero diagonal. Its expected operator norm is Theta(sqrt(n)), so this shape has exponents f=1/2 and g=0. Deterministically ||A||>=sqrt(n-1) by its Frobenius norm. For each unit real x, P(|x^T A x|>=r)<=2exp(-r^2/4); a 1/4 sphere net of size at most 9^n and integration give the O(sqrt(n)) expectation bound. This does not resolve the existence conjecture for every fixed shape.

[Defi eq: 2.1.3 local conv of arXiv:2605.03151, 'Giants through Higher-Order paths in Random Simplicial Complexes'] We say that a sequence of $d$-dimensional finite random simplicial complexes $(X_n)_{n \geq 1}$ \textit{converges locally weakly in probability} to a $(d-1)$-rooted random simplicial complex $(X, o)$ with (possibly random) law $\mu$, when, for every $r \geq 0$ and $H_* \in \mathcal{S}_{d-1}$,
\[  \tag{2.1.3}
\frac{1}{s_{d-1} \left( X_n \right)} \sum_{\sigma \in S_{d-1}(X_n)} \1 \left\{ B_{X_n}(\sigma; r) \cong H_* \right\} \overset{\mathbb{P}}{\to} \mu \left( B_X(o; r) \cong H_* \right).
\]
title: The local-weak convergence in probability of simplicial complexes

body:
[Lemma L:Xalpha-bd of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take any $\alpha_0 \in (0, 1)$, $\delta_0 > 0$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $j_0, x \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ with $x, j_0 \le n/10$. Take parameter $\alpha \ge \alpha_0$, and set (for $j\in\llbracket1-n, n+x-1 \rrbracket$)
$\bar X(j) = \bar X[j, 1; x, n]_\textsf{L}$.
Then there exists $c > 0$ depending only on $\alpha_0, \delta_0$ such that for all $\epsilon \in (0, n^{-1/3})$ we have
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{j\in\llbracket0,n+x-1 \rrbracket} \bar X(j) - \frac{\delta_0(j-j_0)^2}{n} \ge \Delta_\alpha(n) + \epsilon n\right) \le 2\exp\left(-c \epsilon^{3/2}n \left(1 \wedge \frac{\epsilon^{1/2}}{(1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0}\right) \right).
$$

Method: A nontrivial exact Hausdorff gauge for SLE structural reduction or obstruction Result: Hausdorff dimension alone cannot select the exact gauge. For any set of dimension d, a power exponent s>d gives zero Hausdorff measure, while s<d gives infinite measure; at s=d either zero, finite positive, or infinite behavior can occur. Multiplying r^d by a slowly varying factor can change the critical measure while leaving the dimension unchanged. Check: The two off-critical conclusions are the defining threshold property of Hausdorff dimension. At the critical exponent, a smooth interval has finite positive H^1, while a countable union of disjoint intervals with divergent total length has infinite H^1; critical zero examples exist among dimension-one Cantor sets. Obstruction: One needs fine local occupation estimates, not just dimension or existence of Minkowski content. The predicted logarithmic correction has not been proved here.

Method: Integrator-authored exact restricted calculation or proof-obstruction analysis after primary-source comparison Result: Partitioning a domain gives independent fine measures multiplied by an independent, spatially varying Gaussian binding field. On each compact subdomain, the weighted mass lies between exp(alpha*inf(Phi)) times its fine total mass and exp(alpha*sup(Phi)) times that mass. These inequalities explain a possible smoothing-transform route, but the weights are functions of position rather than single scalar multipliers of identically distributed masses. Replacing each field by one value creates an oscillation error that must be controlled on the critical tail scale. Multiplying the entire family by a deterministic c>0 preserves the four premises, so the best possible conclusion must allow its tail constant to change by c. Check: Apply the elementary integral bound inf(w)*mu(A)<=integral_A w dmu<=sup(w)*mu(A). Under deterministic scaling, E[c*Z(A)*exp(-s*c*Z(D))]/log(1/s) has c times the old limit because log(1/(sc))/log(1/s)->1. Obstruction: No scalar smoothing-transform theorem has been applied without checking these errors. No finite-mean or moment-threshold consequence is asserted from the four axioms alone.

Suppose that $h$ is a GFF on $\BH$ with piecewise constant boundary conditions that change only finitely many times. \begin{enumerate}
\item If $u_2 < u_1$, then $\gamma_{u_2}^{x_2}$ a.s.\ stays to the left of $\gamma_{u_1}^{x_1}$ (possibly touching it).
\item If $u_2 = u_1$, then $\gamma_{u_2}^{x_2}$ may intersect $\gamma_{u_1}^{x_1}$ and, upon intersecting, the two curves merge and never separate.
\item If $u_1 - u_2 \geq 2 \lambda$, then $\gamma_{u_1}^{x_1}$ and $\gamma_{u_2}^{x_2}$ do not intersect each other a.s.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Load-bearing hypotheses: A is densely defined, dissipative, AND Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or at least dense) for some λ_0 > 0. What fails without the range condition: a dissipative operator can be closed and densely defined and still generate nothing. Counterexample: X = L²(0, 1), A f = f' with D(A) = {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(0) = f(1) = 0}. Then A is densely defined and closed, and Re⟨f', f⟩ = (|f(1)|² − |f(0)|²)/2 = 0, so A is dissipative (indeed both A and −A are). But solving λf − f' = g with f(0) = 0 gives f(x) = −∫_0^x e^{λ(x−s)}g(s) ds, and the second boundary condition f(1) = 0 forces the constraint ∫_0^1 e^{−λs} g(s) ds = 0: Ran(λ − A) is a closed subspace of codimension 1, not dense, for every λ > 0. Hence A is not a generator, although dropping one boundary condition (D = {f ∈ H¹ : f(1) = 0}) gives exactly the generator of the left shift semigroup. The range condition is what encodes 'the right number of boundary conditions'. What fails without density: X = C[0,1] with the sup norm, A f = f' on D(A) = {f ∈ C¹[0,1] : f(1) = 0}. Solving λ f − f' = g with f(1) = 0 gives f(x) = ∫_x^1 e^{λ(x−s)}g(s)ds, so ‖f‖ ≤ ‖g‖/λ: A is dissipative and Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0. Yet the closure of D(A) is {f ∈ C[0,1] : f(1) = 0}, a proper closed subspace, so A generates no C_0-semigroup on C[0,1] (generators are densely defined); it generates one on the smaller space. Density is automatic only when X is reflexive, which C[0,1] is not. Related trap: for the norm inequality version, dissipativity means ‖(λ − A)x‖ ≥ λ‖x‖ for all λ > 0 - checking it for a single λ, or checking Re⟨Ax, x⟩ ≤ 0 only on a core without knowing the operator is closed or closable there, proves nothing about the closure being a generator unless the range condition is verified on that same core.
X is a Banach space
A is dissipative
the range condition Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or dense) is the hypothesis at issue
title: Pitfall: Lumer-Phillips Needs the Range Condition (and Density) - Dissipativity Alone Is Not Enough

[Lemma 16 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Let $\tau\in[0,T]$, $\beta\in\mathbb R$, and $\gamma\in(0,1]$. Then there exists a linear map
\[
\mathcal I_\tau^{\mathrm d}: \mathcal A^{\gamma}(\Delta_\tau^2;B_\beta) \to C([0,\tau];B_\beta),
\]
obtained from a dyadic recursion on $\mathcal D^\tau$ and continuous extension to $[0,\tau]$, such that, for every $A\in \mathcal A^{\gamma}(\Delta_\tau^2;B_\beta)$, $\mathcal I_\tau^{\mathrm d}(A)_0=0$. If we define the dyadic remainder $\mathcal R_\tau^{\mathrm d}(A):=A-\delta\mathcal I_\tau^{\mathrm d}(A)$, then
$
\delta \mathcal R_\tau^{\mathrm d}(A)=\delta A.
$
Moreover, if $\gamma\in(0,1)$, then
\begin{equation}

\mathcal R_\tau^{\mathrm d}(A)\in C^{\gamma}(\Delta_\tau^2;B_\beta)\ \text{\, and \, }\ \|\mathcal R_\tau^{\mathrm d}(A)\|_{\gamma,\beta;\tau}\le C_\gamma\|\delta A\|_{\gamma,\beta;\tau};
\end{equation}
if $\gamma=1$, then
\begin{equation}

\mathcal R_\tau^{\mathrm d}(A)\in C_{\log}^{1}(\Delta_\tau^2;B_\beta)\ \text{\, and \, }\ \|\mathcal R_\tau^{\mathrm d}(A)\|_{1,\log;\tau,\beta}\le C_{T}\|\delta A\|_{1,\beta;\tau}.
\end{equation}
while, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $\|\mathcal R_\tau^{\mathrm d}(A)\|_{1-\varepsilon,\beta;\tau}\le C_{\varepsilon,T}\|\delta A\|_{1,\beta;\tau}$. Here the constants can be chosen independently of $\tau\in[0,T]$.

[Thm 135 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\iota > 0$, there exists $\epsilon_0 = \epsilon_0(\alpha,\iota) > 0$ such that for all $\epsilon \in (0,\epsilon_0)$ and $L > 0$, there exists $C(L,\epsilon)$ such that the following holds.

recall from \eqref{e:s.sqrt.fn} that we denote $s(t) = ((tp)'(t))^{1/2}$. Let $B$ and $W$ be standard Brownian motions on the time interval $q_0 \le t\le 1$, and consider the SDEs (cf.\ Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main})   \begin{align}

  \end{align}
with initial values $X(q_0) \sim \zeta$ and $Y(q_0) \sim \zeta^\Ising$ independent of $B,W$. Suppose the controls satisfy the following conditions:

    \item  $b(t,x) : [q_0,1] \times \bbR \to [-L,L]$ and $\sigma(t,x), w(t,x) : [q_0,1] \times \bbR \to [0,L]$ are $L$-Lipschitz in $(t,x)$.
    \item  $|\bbE[(w_t)^2] -1| \le \epsilon$ for all $t\in [q_0,1]$.
    \item  $p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ (see Definition~\ref{d:incr.p}) is a twice differentiable function, with $p(q_0) \in [1/L,\epsilon]$ and $\|p\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L$.
    \item  For all $t\in [q_0,1]$, the controls satisfy the approximate budget constraint:
    \begin{align}\nonumber
      \Cost(t)
      &\equiv
      \bbE\bigg[

        \frac{s(t)^2}{p(t)}

    \item  The endpoint of the $Y$ process satisfies

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Integrator-authored exact special-case argument and failure analysis after checking the incoming source Result: Put J=Q(I-Q)^(-1). Given the occupied set B outside e, the conditional odds of presence are s_B=J_ee-J_eB*(J_BB)^(-1)*J_Be. Schur-complement minimization makes s_B decrease as B increases. Its minimum is s_all=1/(J^(-1))ee=1/[(Q^(-1))ee-1]. The conditional probability, however, is s_all/(1+s_all)=1/(Q^(-1))ee. Equivariance makes (Q^(-1))ee=tr(Q^(-1)), with normalized trace, so this probability is the harmonic mean h of all eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. Sequential sampling with common independent uniforms couples the process above iid Bernoulli(h), since every conditional probability given a partial reveal is also at least h. Applying the same argument to the complement gives the upper density 1-HM(I-Q). AM-GM applied to the reciprocals gives HM(Q)<=FK(Q), exposing the exact remaining gap. Check: For a scalar Q=qI, s_all=q/(1-q) but the conditional probability is q; this catches the odds/probability confusion in the incoming record. In a finite group, equal inverse diagonal entries average to the full matrix trace divided by |Gamma|, irrespective of whether the group is abelian. No sum over one-dimensional characters is substituted for the nonabelian spectrum. Obstruction: No geometric-mean domination theorem or sharpness certificate. Numerical coupling feasibility is not exact proof, and the infinite-group extension of this particular calculation is not asserted.

body: In statistics, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is a class of algorithms used to draw samples from a probability distribution. Given a probability distribution, one can construct a Markov chain whose elements' distribution approximates it, i.e. the Markov chain's equilibrium distribution matches the target distribution. The more steps that are included, the more closely the distribution of the sample matches the actual desired distribution.

[Defn 1 of arXiv:2506.15341, '\bf Superpositions for General Conditional Mckean-Vlasov Stochastic Differential Equations'] We define $\hC_b^2(\sM_1)$ to be the set of all bounded, continuous functions $F: \sM_1\rightarrow \hR$ such that:

{\rm (i)}  There exists a bounded function $\pa_{\m}F:\sM_1(\hR^d)\times\hR^d\rightarrow \hR$ such that 
\beaa

\ss
{\rm (ii)} The function $x\mapsto \pa_{\m}F(\m,x)$ is continuously differentiable for $x\in\hR^d$, and the gradient $\nabla_x \pa_{\m}F(\m,x)$ is uniformly bounded in $(\m,x)$, denoted as $\bD_\m F(\m,x)$.

\ss
{\rm (iii)} The second order spacial derivative is defined as $\bD_{\m}^2 F(\m,x,x')$, and  is bounded and continuous for $x,x'\in\hR^d$.

\ss

Let Omega in R^n be bounded and open, A measurable and uniformly elliptic with constants lambda, Lambda, and b, c in L^infinity(Omega) with no sign condition. For u, v in H^1_0(Omega) put B[u,v] = integral ( A grad u . grad v + (b.grad u) v + c u v ) dx. Then: (i) |B[u,v]| <= alpha ||u||_{H^1} ||v||_{H^1} with alpha = Lambda + ||b||_infinity + ||c||_infinity (boundedness); (ii) B[u,u] >= (lambda/2) ||grad u||_{L^2}^2 - gamma ||u||_{L^2}^2 for all u in H^1_0(Omega), with gamma = ||b||_infinity^2/(2 lambda) + ||c^-||_infinity (the Gaarding inequality); in particular B + mu(.,.)_{L^2} is coercive for every mu >= gamma, so Lu + mu u = f is uniquely solvable in H^1_0 for such mu. (iii) Fredholm alternative: exactly one of the following holds: either for every f in L^2(Omega) there is a unique weak solution u in H^1_0(Omega) of Lu = f, or the homogeneous problem Lu = 0 has a nontrivial weak solution in H^1_0(Omega). In the second case the solution space N and the corresponding space N* for the formal adjoint L* have the same finite dimension, and Lu = f is solvable if and only if integral f v = 0 for every v in N*. (iv) There is an at most countable set Sigma of real numbers, with no finite accumulation point if it is infinite, such that Lu = mu u + f is uniquely solvable for every f exactly when mu is not in Sigma.

$c=c(\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})>0$ and
$t_0=t_0(\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})<\infty$ such that, for every mean-zero i.i.d.\
field $(\zeta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^4}$ satisfying
\[

    \mathbb{E} e^{\theta_{0}|\zeta(0)|}\leq K_{0}\, ,
\]
and every $t\geq t_0$, the planar set
\[
    \{x\in\Pi:u_t(x)>c\log t\}
\]
contains an infinite nearest-neighbor component almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Lemma (campaign status: audited-pass): The projective full dual of A_n is exactly D_n = {A, B_i, C_i : i in Z/nZ} with A=e_0, B_i=e_i, C_i=e_0+e_i+e_{i+1}. Proof: normalize a sign-valued affine form on the positive half to value -1 at the empty independent set; its values on the singletons force every singleton increment to be 0 or 2, so the form is -1+2|S cap K| for a vertex set K; it is sign-valued on every independent set iff K is a clique; for n>=4 the cliques of C_n are the empty clique, the vertices and the edges. body:
[Lemma 56 of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a connected semisimple real Lie group, $X$ be its symmetric space  and $\Gamma\subseteq G$ be a discrete subgroup.
    Then the following holds.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[{\rm(1)}] There is $k\in \mathbb{N}$ such that the restriction $p_\Gamma$ of the projection $p:G\to X$ to $\Gamma$ is $k$-to-$1$.
        Moreover, if $\Gamma$ is torsion-free, then $p_\Gamma$ is injective.
        \item[{\rm(2)}] The set $p_\Gamma(\Gamma)\subset X$ induces a $\Gamma$-equivariant Voronoi diagram $\{V_\gamma\}_{\gamma\in \Gamma}$ as a multi-set.
        Moreover, if $\Gamma$ is co-compact, then there is $R>0$ and $d\in \mathbb{N}$ with the property that $V_\gamma\subseteq \mathcal{B}_R(\gamma o)$ for every $\gamma\in \Gamma$ and every cell intersect $k(d+1)-1$ many other cells (where $k\in \mathbb{N}$ is from {\rm(1)}).
        \item[{\rm(3)}] Let $\mathbf Z=(Z(\gamma))_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ be a collection of iid ${\rm Unif}[0,1]$ random variables and $\lambda>0$ and $p\in(0,1]$.
        Then $\omega_p^{(\lambda)}$ may be realized as a $\Gamma$-equivariant factor of $\mathbf Z$.        
    \end{enumerate}

body: In mathematics, the Cartan–Hadamard theorem is a statement in Riemannian geometry concerning the structure of complete Riemannian manifolds of non-positive sectional curvature. The theorem states that the universal cover of such a manifold is diffeomorphic to a Euclidean space via the exponential map at any point. It was first proved by Hans Carl Friedrich von Mangoldt for surfaces in 1881, and independently by Jacques Hadamard in 1898. Élie Cartan generalized the theorem to Riemannian manifolds in 1928. The theorem was further generalized to a wide class of metric spaces by Mikhail Gromov in 1987; detailed proofs were published by Ballmann (1990) for metric spaces of non-positive curvature and by Alexander & Bishop (1990) for general locally convex metric spaces.

[Lemma 28 of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] Fix $p\in (0,1)$ and let $(Z_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be the Markov chain on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting from $0$ with transition probabilities:
\[
\P(Z_{n+1}=j \mid Z_n=i) = \begin{cases} 
(1-p)\mathbf{1}_{j=1}+p\mathbf{1}_{j=-1} & \text{if } i= 0 \\
(1-p)\mathbf{1}_{j=i-1}+p\mathbf{1}_{j=i+1}  & \text{if } i\neq 0. \end{cases}
\]
Let $U \coloneqq \inf\{n\ge 0 : |Z_n|=3\}$. Then 
\[ \P(Z_U=3) = 1 - \P(Z_U=-3) = p. \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 28 of arXiv:2606.11271

Let (X_n)_{n=1}^\infty be independent random variables with \mathbb{E}[X_n] = 0. Let \phi: [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty) be a strictly increasing, convex function such that \phi(0) = 0, \phi(x)/x \uparrow \infty and \phi(x)/x^2 is nonincreasing on (0, \infty). If \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\mathbb{E}[\phi(|X_n|)]}{\phi(n)} < \infty, then \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n X_k \to 0 almost surely.
(X_n) independent, mean zero
\phi convex, strictly increasing, \phi(x)/x \to \infty
\phi(x)/x^2 nonincreasing on (0, \infty) (without it the law fails: \phi(x) = x^4, X_n = \sqrt{n}\,\varepsilon_n)
\sum \mathbb{E}[\phi(|X_n|)]/\phi(n) < \infty

Let Z be standard normal, g(z)=phi(z)+z Phi(z), a=1/sqrt(pi), and v=1/3+(sqrt(3)-2)/(2*pi). Then E[g(Z)]=a and Var(g(Z))=v. W=(a-g(Z))/sqrt(v) has support (-infinity,a/sqrt(v)] and no atom at its finite endpoint. For w<a/sqrt(v), with z=g^{-1}(a-sqrt(v)w), its CDF is 1-Phi(z) and its density is sqrt(v)*phi(z)/Phi(z). This non-Gaussian law is the standardized-degree limit only conditional on the earlier degree/moment convergence being established in a stated regime.

Let Z be standard normal, phi its density, Phi its distribution function, and g(z)=phi(z)+z*Phi(z). Put a=1/sqrt(pi), v=1/3+(sqrt(3)-2)/(2*pi), and W=(a-g(Z))/sqrt(v). Then E[W]=0, Var(W)=1, W has support (-infinity,a/sqrt(v)], has no atom at the finite endpoint, and is not Gaussian. For w<a/sqrt(v), define z=g^{-1}(a-sqrt(v)*w). Then

    P(W<=w)=1-Phi(z),
    density_W(w)=sqrt(v)*phi(z)/Phi(z).

Proof: differentiation gives g'=Phi>0 and g''=phi. Also g(z)=E[(z-Y)_+] for an independent standard normal Y, so g is positive; it tends to zero as z tends to minus infinity and diverges at plus infinity. Thus it is a continuous increasing bijection onto (0,infinity). The distribution and density follow by reversing its monotone change of variables. No finite Z maps to the upper endpoint, so that endpoint has no mass.

For the constants, normal integration by parts gives E[phi(Z)]=1/(2*sqrt(pi)) and E[Z*Phi(Z)]=E[phi(Z)], hence E[g(Z)]=a. Write A=E[phi(Z)^2]=1/(2*pi*sqrt(3)) and B=E[Z*phi(Z)*Phi(Z)]=A/2, by integrating the derivative of phi^2. Since Phi(Z) is uniform, E[Phi(Z)^2]=1/3. Applying E[Z^2*h(Z)]=E[h(Z)]+E[h''(Z)] to h=Phi^2 gives E[Z^2*Phi(Z)^2]=1/3+2A-2B=1/3+A. Therefore E[g(Z)^2]=A+2B+(1/3+A)=1/3+sqrt(3)/(2*pi). Subtracting a^2 gives v. All integrations have Gaussian tails, so the boundary terms vanish. A nondegenerate Gaussian has no finite upper endpoint; W does.

Conditional application: if the earlier packet proves (k-D)/sqrt(k) converges to g(Z) with convergence of the first two moments in a specified k,n regime, subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation gives (D-E[D])/sqrt(Var(D)) converging to W. This consequence does not extend the packet to other k regimes. The saved attempt's error O(k^2/n+k^5/n^2) tends to zero, for example, when k tends to infinity and k=o(n^(2/5)); that observation alone is not a proof of the whole graph limit.

body: For an integer n >= 2, there is an explicit bijection, the Prufer correspondence, between the set of labeled trees on the vertex set {1, ..., n} and the set {1, ..., n}^{n-2} of sequences of length n-2 with entries from {1, ..., n}, obtained by repeatedly removing the leaf of smallest label and recording the label of its unique neighbor. In particular the number of labeled trees on n vertices equals n^{n-2}. [Prufer (1918); see van Lint and Wilson, A Course in Combinatorics]
title: Prufer Sequence Bijection Lemma (Labeled Trees)

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; status: independently checked proof. For a fixed pair of internally compatible nearest-neighbor path halves under independent iid fair two-color scenery, let V^- and V^+ be their observed spatial sites, and K=|V^- intersect V^+|. Let A mean that the two records prescribe the same color at every shared site. The joint record likelihood equals L^- L^+ 2^K 1_A, where each half likelihood is 2^(-|V^sign|) and is zero for internal incompatibility. Because the two increment halves are independent before color conditioning, their joint two-sided posterior is the product of the separate half-posteriors reweighted by 2^K 1_A and normalized by its positive expectation. Spatial zero is included in K if both halves revisit it; the origin color is not fixed in this identity. Bounding this overlap reweighting uniformly is an unproved input for transferring one-sided escape estimates.

body:
Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a STANDARD Borel (Lebesgue) probability space, and let I be the sub-sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets.

ERGODIC DECOMPOSITION. There is a measurable family x -> mu_x of T-invariant Borel probability measures on X such that (i) mu_x is a version of the conditional measure of mu given I, so mu(A) = integral of mu_x(A) d mu(x) for every A in B and integral of f d mu = integral over x of (integral of f d mu_x) d mu(x) for f in L^1(mu); (ii) mu_x is ERGODIC for mu-a.e. x; (iii) the family is essentially unique. Writing P for the law of the random measure x -> mu_x, one gets mu = integral of nu dP(nu) supported on the ergodic T-invariant measures -- the Choquet representation of mu in the simplex of invariant measures.

AFFINITY OF ENTROPY. Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is affine in the measure, with values in [0, +infinity]:
  for every finite measurable partition Q,   h_mu(T, Q) = integral of h_{mu_x}(T, Q) d mu(x);
  and                                        h_mu(T)    = integral of h_{mu_x}(T) d mu(x).
In particular, for T-invariant mu and nu and t in [0,1],  h_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(T) = t h_mu(T) + (1-t) h_nu(T).

SHARP EDGES. (1) AFFINE IS NOT CONTINUOUS: nu -> h_nu(T) is affine on the simplex of invariant measures but is in general NOT weak-* continuous; for expansive homeomorphisms it is upper semicontinuous, and in general it can fail even that. Do not use affinity to pass to weak-* limits. (2) The decomposition genuinely needs a standard/Lebesgue space; on a pathological measure space conditional measures need not exist and the statement can fail. (3) The convex combination must be of INVARIANT measures -- entropy is undefined for a non-invariant measure, so there is no affinity statement along an arbitrary path in the space of measures. (4) The identity holds in [0, +infinity]; if h_mu(T) = +infinity the integral is +infinity, and no finiteness is assumed anywhere. (5) The affinity is a property of measure-theoretic entropy, not of topological entropy: the variational principle gives h_top(T) = sup over invariant nu of h_nu(T), which is a supremum over the simplex, so it is attained (if at all) at ergodic measures precisely BECAUSE h is affine -- but h_top itself is not an average.
(X, B, mu, T) is measure-preserving on a standard Borel (Lebesgue) probability space
mu is T-invariant; entropies are Kolmogorov-Sinai entropies with values in [0, +infinity]
the ergodic decomposition is taken over the sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets
convex combinations are of T-INVARIANT measures only
no finiteness of entropy and no continuity of the entropy map is assumed or asserted

Affinity, finite convex combinations first. Let phi(s) = -s log s (concave on [0,1]). For any finite partition Q and t in [0,1]:
  lower bound: H_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(Q) >= t H_mu(Q) + (1-t) H_nu(Q) by concavity of phi applied atom by atom;
  upper bound: H_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(Q) <= t H_mu(Q) + (1-t) H_nu(Q) + log 2, obtained by adjoining a Bernoulli(t) label L that records which of the two measures a point is drawn from and using H(X) <= H(X, L) = H(L) + H(X | L), with H(L) <= log 2.

The integral version (Jacobs' theorem) is the same estimate with the two-point mixture replaced by the integral decomposition: the concavity bound integrates directly, and the label term is replaced by the entropy of a finite measurable partition of the index space, whose contribution is again O(1) and is killed after dividing by n; measurability of x -> h_{mu_x}(T, Q) holds because each H_{mu_x}(Q_n) is a measurable function of x.

From partitions to the entropy itself: on a standard space choose an increasing sequence of finite partitions Q_1 < Q_2 < ... generating B modulo mu. Since a mu-null set is mu_x-null for a.e. x and the algebra generated is countable, the same sequence generates modulo mu_x for mu-a.e. x. By the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem h_mu(T) = lim_k h_mu(T, Q_k) and h_{mu_x}(T) = lim_k h_{mu_x}(T, Q_k) for a.e. x, both limits increasing. Apply the partition-wise identity for each k and pass to the limit by monotone convergence. [Proposition 10 (Persistence through reset) of arXiv:2608.16701, 'Order-Sensitive Fast-Synapse Limits in Sparse Excitatory--Inhibitory Threshold--Reset Netw'] Fix $\rho>0$ and $T_P>\rho$.  There are uniformly bounded-degree,
Dale-compatible networks with the same initial data in both orderings such
that, for every $t_*>T_P$ and every $\varepsilon_N\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}
 F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\E}(\rho/2)
 -F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\I}(\rho/2)\longrightarrow\frac14,
 \qquad
 F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\E}(t_*)
 -F_N^{\varepsilon_N,\I}(t_*)\longrightarrow\frac12.
 
\end{equation}
For all sufficiently large $N$ along the stated sequence, every nonisolated
target has fired twice by $t_*$ under E-first and has not fired under
I-first.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Deterministic limits for trace-reinforced ants structural argument Result: If two parallel edges connect N directly to F, an ant crosses exactly one and reinforces it. Starting at weights a,b gives the classical Polya urn: the first normalized weight has Beta(a,b) limit with variance ab/((a+b)^2(a+b+1))>0. Thus the unrestricted multigraph formulation is false, and the underlying no-parallel-food assumption is necessary. Check: The transition probability and one-increment update coincide exactly with the urn. This is a scope counterexample, not a refutation under the original restriction. Obstruction: For simple finite graphs the nonlinear trace-hitting probabilities still require a uniqueness/attraction argument. On Z^2, changing conductances additionally complicate the guarantee that every ant reaches food.

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). After the optimism reading was refuted (P20), the gain was located row by row: the per-evaluation-row relative-score gain of the long-only stack over least squares against the bootstrap variance of the least-squares stack at that row. P22 (a) REFUTED at the pre-registered 0.2: the within-cell median Spearman between a row's gain and the least-squares variance load at that row is 0.13 over the 40 EMIT cells (positive in 36 of 40; 0.37 on Y2, 0.01 on Y1); (b) HELD on Y2, REFUTED as an every-group claim: the top-decile-load rows carry 47 pct of Y2's gain (a uniform spread gives 10) but only 11 pct on Y1 (20 on Y3, 32 on Y4); (c) HELD: across the 40 EMIT cells the gain rank-correlates 0.54 with the variance-load share of least squares' error, and 0.65 with the share the constraint removes (least squares minus nn1) - the between-cell statistic that optimism (P20) failed to be; (d) REFUTED as written: the OCO-2 top-decile share reaches 0.40 on sco2, but as the share of a gain of -0.55 pct it is the ratio of two near-zero numbers and does not test the clause; falsifier (within-cell correlation at or below zero) not triggered. Reading: where the gain is large (Y2, +18) it sits where least squares is uncertain - row-level rank correlation 0.37, 47 pct of the gain on the tenth of rows with the largest variance; where it is modest (+5 to +6) it is spread over the rows; between cells the variance-load share of least squares' error predicts the gain (0.54) and the variance the constraint removes predicts it better (0.65). The calibration and evaluation rows share the same target-norm distribution, so this is not a split shift; the gain leans toward the small-norm evaluation rows the reported metric weights most. Cell level: the variance the constraint removes (least squares' bootstrap variance share minus the long-only stack's) predicts the gain within every output group (Spearman 0.79, 0.87, 0.54, 0.43 on Y1-Y4; 0.69 across 40 cells with the group effect removed), while the L1 norm of the least-squares weights does not survive the group adjustment (0.02): the constraint pays what it saves in estimation variance at the rows it is scored on. Fresh-split replication (split C, SPLIT_SEED 11): P23 (a) REFUTED at the per-group 0.5, HELD in the aggregate: on split C the within-group Spearman between the gain and the variance removed is +0.59, +0.49, +0.64, +0.22 on Y1..Y4 and +0.74 across the 40 cells with the group effect removed (split B: +0.69); (b) REFUTED: the split-B variance-removed share predicts the split-C gain only on Y1 and Y2 (+0.72, +0.47; Y3 +0.09, Y4 -0.24; demeaned +0.17), and the split-B gain itself predicts the split-C gain only weakly (Y1 +0.82, Y4 +0.47, Y2 +0.15, Y3 -0.14); (c) HELD: the long-only stack beats least squares on 35 of 40 split-C cells (mean +9.59 against +8.83 on split B); falsifier (any group at or below 0.2, or the demeaned correlation at or below 0.3) not triggered. Fresh-split check of the calibration-side correlates (P32, the P20 driver on split C): P32 (a) HELD: on split C the between-cell Spearman of the gain with the least-squares L1 is +0.55 and with n_eff -0.44; (b) REFUTED: group-demeaned, L1 +0.29 and members kept +0.21; (c) HELD: the nn0 RMSE gain with the smallest relative eigenvalue +0.29 and with the condition number -0.31; falsifier (L1 above +0.3 after the group adjustment) not triggered. The gain off the tail (P36, the top tenth of evaluation rows by |gain| removed): P36 (a) HELD for the sign, REFUTED for the size: the trimmed gain is positive on 36 and 36 of 40 EMIT cells (splits B, C) but reads +7.67 and +8.30 against untrimmed +8.83 and +9.59 - the body keeps 87 pct of the gain, not less than half; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the trimmed gain is +0.25 against -0.18 untrimmed; (c) REFUTED: the smallest trimmed gain is on Y4, not Y1; falsifier (negative trimmed gain on EMIT) not triggered. Removing the two-sided tail leaves 87 pct of the EMIT gain: the constraint pays broadly across the rows, and the non-transfer between splits comes from the tails' noise, not from where the gain sits. P46: the mechanism on the third family (P46): P46 (a) REFUTED: within-family Spearman(gain, variance removed) = burgers +0.55, darcy +0.80, pkanrtm -0.12 (families with at least ten cells; threshold 0.3); (b) HELD: family-demeaned across 55 cells +0.65 (threshold 0.4); (c) HELD: the family with the most negative gain is pkanrtm, the family with the smallest variance removed is pkanrtm; falsifier (demeaned correlation at or below 0.1) not triggered.

A real-valued random variable X is called sub-Gaussian if there exists a constant sigma^2 >= 0 such that for all lambda in R, E[exp(lambda * (X - E[X]))] <= exp(lambda^2 * sigma^2 / 2). The parameter sigma^2 is called a variance proxy (or sub-Gaussian parameter) for X.

body: Let f : M -> N be a C^k map between smooth manifolds of dimensions m and n respectively, with k >= max(1, m - n + 1). Call x in M a critical point if the differential df_x : T_xM -> T_(f(x))N fails to be surjective, and call f(x) a critical value for such x. Then the set of critical values of f has Lebesgue measure zero in N, measured in any smooth chart, so almost every point of N is a regular value, even though the critical set in M can itself be large, even all of M in degenerate examples.
title: Sard's theorem

[Theorem 39 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] There is a universal constant $C<\infty$ with the following property. Let $Q$ be an $\So{n}$-valued random matrix whose law is $(d_{\mathrm{ph}},L)$-pseudo-Haar in the sense of \eqref{EqJLPseudoHaarDef}. Let $\mathcal X\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ have $N\geq2$ points, and let $0<\varepsilon,\delta<1$. Set
\be 
r=\left\lceil C\log\frac{N}{\delta}\right\rceil.
\ee
Assume
\be 
4r\leq d_{\mathrm{ph}},\qquad
\ell\geq C\varepsilon^{-2}r,
\qquad
L\log n\geq \log\frac{2\binom{N}{2}}{\delta}+2r\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon\ell}.
\ee
Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $Q$,
\be 
(1-\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\leq
\|A_Q(x_i-x_j)\|_2^2
\leq
(1+\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\ee
for every pair $1\leq i<j\leq N$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 39 of arXiv:2608.17374

[Theorem 1 (\cite{efron1981jackknife}, \cite{steele1986efron}) of arXiv:2605.05388, 'The Efron-Stein inequality for identically distributed pairs'] Let \(X_1,\ldots, X_n,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be \(2n\) independent random variables with \(X_i\stackrel{d}{=} Y_i\) for all \(i\). Let \(f\) be a measurable function, and let \(Z_i=f(X_1\ldots X_{i},Y_{i+1},\ldots Y_n)\) for \(i=0,\dots,n\). Then
$$
E(Z_n-Z_0)^2\le \sum_{i=1}^n E(Z_i-Z_{i-1})^2.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let H be a complex Hilbert space and T a compact operator on H. List its nonzero eigenvalues lambda_1, lambda_2, ... with |lambda_1| >= |lambda_2| >= ... , repeated according to algebraic multiplicity and padded with zeros if there are finitely many, and let s_1(T) >= s_2(T) >= ... be the singular values. Then for every n, the product of |lambda_1| ... |lambda_n| is at most the product of s_1(T) ... s_n(T). Consequently, for every p > 0 and every n, sum_{k <= n} |lambda_k|^p <= sum_{k <= n} s_k(T)^p; in particular, if T is Hilbert-Schmidt then sum_k |lambda_k|^2 <= ||T||_2^2 (Schur's inequality), and if T is trace class then sum_k |lambda_k| <= ||T||_1. The inequalities are equalities for normal T.
H is a complex Hilbert space
T is a compact operator on H
eigenvalues are listed with algebraic multiplicity in nonincreasing order of modulus
p > 0

Then the absolute value of det(T|_M) is the product of |lambda_1| ... |lambda_n|. On the other hand, for an n-dimensional subspace the absolute value of the determinant of the compression P_M T|_M equals the product of the n singular values of that compression, and the singular values of a compression are dominated by those of T (s_k(P_M T|_M) <= s_k(T) by the min-max / approximation-number characterisation). Since M is T-invariant, P_M T|_M = T|_M, giving the multiplicative inequality. [Theorem homo multilinear recursion of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Homogeneous Multilinear Recursion]

Let ${\bf x} = \{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequences of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n}$ be a multi-indexed sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a permutation symmetric, homogeneous multilinear polynomial random matrix of degree $d$ as
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $d = a+b+c$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{4t}^{4t} ~\leq~ \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\ a+b+c=d}} (48dt)^{4dt} \cdot L^{4ct} \norm{{\bf F}_{a,b,c}}_{4t}^{4t}.
$$

body: In mathematics, the connective constant is a numerical quantity associated with self-avoiding walks on a lattice. It is studied in connection with the notion of universality in two-dimensional statistical physics models. While the connective constant depends on the choice of lattice so itself is not universal, it is nonetheless an important quantity that appears in conjectures for universal laws. Furthermore, the mathematical techniques used to understand the connective constant, for example in the recent rigorous proof by Duminil-Copin and Smirnov that the connective constant of the hexagonal lattice has the precise value , may provide clues to a possible approach for attacking other important open problems in the study of self-avoiding walks, notably the conjecture that self-avoiding walks converge in the scaling limit to the Schramm–Loewner evolution.
title: Connective constant

For the small-angle chain in C037 additionally killed on U>K, N<=Tn, integer0<=m<N, and a deterministic family of bounded C5 tests with uniform derivative bounds, the sum (1/n)*sum_(k=m)^(N-1) E[|R_(n,k)(U_k)|;alive] is <=C_(K,T)[n^(-3/2)+log(n+1)/n^2+1/(n(m+1))+n exp(-cn)], where R_(n,k)=n(P_n-I)f_(n,k)-Af_(n,k)-Bf_(n,k)/n for the unstopped local kernel and the C036 operators. The bound holds for both exact and regularized chains. It is o(1/n) if m tends to infinity. Assumptions: All C037 hypotheses, angle cutoff epsilon<=C036 theta_star, fixed upper reciprocal cutoff K, uniform test suprema and derivatives through order5; P_n is the local kernel before the additional stopping, evaluated only at alive prestop states. Model: n independent Gaussian/ReLU row pairs x=max(g,0), y=max(cos(theta)g+sin(theta)h,0), g,h independent standard Gaussians, independent across layers; output angle between the resulting n-vectors. Kill at zero norm, zero angle, or exit from the stated interval. The regularized version self-loops outside a fixed small concentration box for sample averages of (x^2+y^2,(x-y)^2/theta^2,(x^2-y^2)/theta) about their population mean. Limit: Depends on unaudited C036/C037. The bound concerns specified local remainders, not a stopped semigroup telescoping identity. Boundary terms and sharp singular occupation matching remain unpaid. The chain starts at theta0 in (0,epsilon], is killed on leaving that interval or U>K, U=1/(n theta), and has E[theta_k^p;alive]<=C_T/(k+1)^p for p=1,2. The differential operators are A=(2u+a)D+u^2 D^2 and B=(10u+6a/5+b/u)D+(11u^2+12au/5+a^2/2)D^2+(4u^3+au^2)D^3+(u^4/2)D^4, a=1/(3pi), b=1/(6pi^2).
All C037 hypotheses, angle cutoff epsilon<=C036 theta_star, fixed upper reciprocal cutoff K, uniform test suprema and derivatives through order5; P_n is the local kernel before the additional stopping, evaluated only at alive prestop states.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:bf1d24fb08e6a498db7489ff7283e7252afce2d52c283423b48ad360c642bc05","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/bf/bf1d24fb08e6a498db7489ff7283e7252afce2d52c283423b48ad360c642bc05.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e5a0b4422f7dc9fa47ee56e6f0b8dd310dc966b446966e66c672db235a60b87d","bundle_entry_key":"relu-accumulated-weak-remainder","bundle_id":"population.t244-stopped-angle-occupation-014","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_014.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-relu-accumulated-weak-remainder","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C037-C038: stopped angle moments and accumulated local remainder

Version 1, 20 October 2026. Target 1, kind moved, proofs (unaudited).
These use the normalized-Gram construction of C032 and C036; neither
claim is a complete network weak-rate theorem.

## C037: inverse occupation is a positive angle-moment problem

For every finite T, there are epsilon>0 and constants C_T,n0 such that the
following holds. Start the Gaussian/ReLU angle chain at any deterministic
theta0 in (0,epsilon], with width n>=n0. Kill it when it leaves that angle
interval or becomes degenerate, and set its killed angle to zero. One may
also kill it when u=1/(n theta) exceeds any fixed K. For p=1,2 and 0<=k<=Tn,

    E[theta_k^p; alive at k] <= C_T/(k+1)^p.                 (1)

This holds both for the normalized-Gram self-loop regularization and for
the exact chain. In particular, with U_k=1/(n theta_k) only on alive states,

    E[U_k^(-p); alive at k] <= C_T n^p/(k+1)^p.             (2)

Here inverse powers at the cemetery are excluded by the alive indicator.
The statement is a small-angle stopped-chain estimate; it does not assign
the initial time of entrance from an arbitrary fixed theta0.

Proof. Write the normalized output multiplier as theta'/theta=1/T_theta
on the C032 good box. For p=1,2 the coordinate test Phi_p=T_theta^(-p)
has uniformly bounded first and second derivatives on that box for all
small theta. Its deterministic value is (F(theta)/theta)^p, where F is
the deterministic ReLU angle map. A second-order sample-average Taylor
bound, uniform normalized row second moments, and exponential deletion
outside the box imply

    E[(theta'/theta)^p]
       <= (F(theta)/theta)^p+C_p/n
       =1-p a theta+O_p(theta^2)+C_p/n,  a=1/(3pi).

To justify the first inequality explicitly, the linear centered-average
term has mean zero before good-box truncation and an exponentially small
deleted mean; the quadratic Taylor remainder is bounded by the coordinate
Hessian bound times E|Zbar-mu_theta|^2=O(1/n). Off the good box the
regularized multiplier is one. No reciprocal-angle moment is used.

Choose epsilon small so the O(theta^2) term is at most p a theta/2. Killing
only decreases positive angle moments. Thus, for p=1,2 and constants c_p>0,

    E[theta_(k+1)^p | theta_k=theta]
       <= theta^p(1+C_p/n)-c_p theta^(p+1).

Let m_k=E theta_k^p, with theta_k=0 after killing. Jensen gives

    m_(k+1) <= rho m_k-c_p m_k^(1+1/p), rho=1+C_p/n.

Put v_k=rho^(-k)m_k. Since rho>=1,

    v_(k+1) <= v_k-(c_p/rho)v_k^(1+1/p).

Decrease the constant if necessary so z=(c_p/rho)v_k^(1/p)<=1/2; this is
possible because v_k<=m_k<=epsilon^p. If v_(k+1)>0, the elementary inequality
(1-z)^(-1/p)>=1+z/p implies

    v_(k+1)^(-1/p) >= v_k^(-1/p)+c_p/(p rho).

If a term becomes zero, the killed nonnegative chain has zero subsequent
moments and the desired bound is immediate. Otherwise summing yields
v_k<=C/(k+1)^p. As rho^k<=exp(C_p T), (1) follows for the regularized chain.

For the exact chain, use the same independent Gaussian rows until a
good-box failure. Its conditional probability is at most C exp(-cn),
uniformly in every alive small angle. A union bound through k<=Tn gives
disagreement probability at most C k exp(-cn). Both killed angles lie in
[0,epsilon], so their pth moments differ by at most
C epsilon^p k exp(-cn). For k<=Tn this is bounded by C_T/(k+1)^p,
uniformly in n>=n0. This proves (1) for the exact chain, and (2) is the
identity U_k^(-p)=n^p theta_k^p on alive states.

## C038: summing the C036 local remainder after a layer cutoff

Use the regularized stopped chain of C037, with the additional upper
cutoff U<=K. Let N<=Tn, 0<=m<N, and let f_(n,k) be deterministic bounded
C^5 tests whose supremum and derivative bounds through order five are
uniform in n,k. Define the *unstopped-kernel* local remainder, evaluated
only at alive prestop states, by

    R_(n,k)(u)=n(P_n f_(n,k)-f_(n,k))(u)
                               -A f_(n,k)(u)-B f_(n,k)(u)/n.

Choose the angle cutoff epsilon at most C036's theta_star. Then

    (1/n) sum_(k=m)^(N-1) E[|R_(n,k)(U_k)|; alive at k]
      <= C_(K,T)[n^(-3/2)+log(n+1)/n^2
                             +1/(n(m+1))+n exp(-cn)].         (3)

The same estimate holds using the exact kernel and its stopped chain.
This is an accumulated estimate for the indicated local remainders. It
does not discard boundary terms or prove a stopped-semigroup comparison.

Proof. C036 applies to every alive state, since 0<U_k<=K and
theta_k=1/(nU_k)<=epsilon. Its (u+sqrt(u))/n^(3/2) term sums after the
outer factor1/n to at most C_(K,T)n^(-3/2). The constant/n^2 term sums to
C_T/n^2. By (2), the other two algebraic terms contribute at most

    C/n^3 sum_(k=m)^(N-1) n/(k+1) <= C_T log(n+1)/n^2,
    C/n^3 sum_(k=m)^(N-1) n^2/(k+1)^2 <= C_T/[n(m+1)].

The exponential term sums to C_T n exp(-cn). This proves (3), separately
for each chain using the C037 moment bounds and C036's exact-kernel bound.

For any m=m_n tending to infinity, the right side is o(1/n). This pays
for the pointwise Taylor-remainder accumulation after a growing cutoff.
The main singular correction B-A^2/2 still needs an asymptotic occupation
calculation matched to the early network chain. An upper bound for its
occupation is not that asymptotic calculation. Neither (1) nor (3) proves
that the network coefficient is D_t/(2pi).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:ef5cf8d24593c8c15d39382f642a60f6bd9f0b66fde78d07f243e32a0c98ecb5","revision_digest":"sha256:c494d6599867161f2613d0eaecee62ddab723d99f1a52cc291e65c8a01331fdf","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C038:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lem 15 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{assump:second_moment} holds with a constant $\SNR_c$. Then, there exists a sequence of events $\Omega_N'$ in $\caX$ with $\p(\Omega_N'^c) = o(1)$ such that for any $\SNR < \SNR_c$,
\beq 
	\E_{\bsx, \bsx' \sim \caX} \left[ \indi(\Omega_N' (\bsx)) \indi(\Omega_N' (\bsx')) \exp \left( \frac{N \SNR \langle \bsx, \bsx' \rangle^2}{2} \right) \right] = (1-\SNR)^{-1/2} + o(1)
\eeq
and
\beq 
	\E_{\bsx, \bsx' \sim \caX} \left[ \indi(\Omega_N' (\bsx)) \indi(\Omega_N' (\bsx')) \exp \left( \frac{N \SNR \langle \bsx, \bsx' \rangle^2}{2 \| \bsx \|^2 \| \bsx' \|^2} \right) \right] = (1-\SNR)^{-1/2} + o(1).
\eeq (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 15 of arXiv:2605.07050

[Lem 4 of arXiv:2604.25725, 'What is The Probability That A Random Graph With A Given Degree Sequence is Connected?'] Suppose  that   $N$  is a  matching on    the half-edges of size at most $\frac{m}{8}$, which is extendable to a full matching giving a simple graph,  and that $h_v$ and $h_w$ are half-edges not matched in $N$ corresponding to distinct vertices $v$ and $w$.  Suppose either that $w$ has degree 
at most $\frac{\sqrt{m}}{10}$ or that $D^* \le \frac{m}{100}$. Then the conditional probability, given $N \subseteq {\mathcal R}$, that $h_vh_w$ is an edge of $R$ and that $D(v)<\frac{m}{100}$, is at most $\frac{4}{3m}$.

body:
[Lem 179 (annealed second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ 
be defined by \eqref{e:barD} and \eqref{e:barD.plus} (see also \eqref{e:drift.error.II}). We have 
the second moment bound 
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}
		{p(q_d)}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS \delta}{N}\,,
	\]
for all $0\le d\le \dmax-1$. The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ in place of $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$.
\begin{proof}
Recalling the notation from
\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.g} and \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y},
we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.II} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)}
		{[\delta_d p(q_d)]^{1/2}}
	= 
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\sum_{a\in B}
	\frac{\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)}{|B|^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1})\bigg)
	\equiv
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)\,.
	\]
Note that $\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)$ is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_d)$. 
It follows by applying Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} that 
	\[
	\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	=\frac{1}{M}\E\bigg[\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)^2
		\bigg]
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}}{M}
	\E\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\frac{\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|^2}{N}\,.
	\]
We then note that if $\ind_B\in\R^M$ is the indicator of the coordinates in $B$, then
	\[
	\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|
	=\bigg\| \bar{\bG}(q_d) \frac{\ind_B}{|B|^{1/2}}\bigg\|
	\le \|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|\,,
	\]
from which it follows that
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	\le
	\frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS 
		\E[\|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|^2]}{MN}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS}{N}\,,
	\]
where the last bound follows from Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}.
This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 16 (From scalar wavelets to vector-valued wavelets) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Let $(\phi,\psi)$ be an orthonormal wavelet basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ associated with an MRA.
Fix $m\ge 2$ and set $D=2^m$. Define $\Phi,\Psi$ by \eqref{eq:Phi-def}--\eqref{eq:Psi-def}.
For $k\in\mathbb Z$ and $j\ge 0$ set
\[
\widetilde\Phi_k=\Phi(\cdot-k),
\qquad
\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}=D^{j/2}\Psi(D^j\cdot-k).
\]

Then the family
\[
\{\widetilde\Phi_k\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}\ \cup\ \{\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\}_{j\ge 0,\ k\in\mathbb Z}
\]

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] is an orthogonal wavelet basis of the Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m)$ (for the usual scalar $L^2$ inner product); moreover $\|\widetilde\Phi_k\|_{L^2}^2=\|\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\|_{L^2}^2=m$,
\item[(b)] is an $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--orthonormal system in the Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module
$\big(L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\big)$, i.e.
\[
\big\langle \widetilde U_\alpha,\widetilde U_\beta\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}
=\delta_{\alpha,\beta}\,I_m
\quad(\alpha,\beta\in\{(0,k)\}\cup\{(j,k):j\ge 0\}),
\]
and it is a Parseval $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module frame with the canonical reconstruction
\[
f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Phi_k\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Phi_k
+\sum_{j\ge 0}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k},
\qquad f\in L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),
\]
with convergence in the module norm.
Moreover, each component inherits compact support, regularity and vanishing moments from $\phi$ and $\psi$.
\end{itemize}

			\[ \sum_{i\in I}i=s \qquad \text{and} \qquad c_ds\leq i\leq s
			\qquad\text{for every }i\in I. \]

[Definition 13 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A weak solution of \eqreftag{eq:cond-Fokker-planck-a} is a measurable map
\[
    \tilde \P:\R_+\times\Xc\longrightarrow \Pc(\R^d),
    \qquad
    (t,x)\longmapsto \tilde\P_{t,x},
\]
together with a Borel vector field
$
    \hat A:\R_+\times\R^d\longrightarrow\R^d,
$
such that the following conditions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item 
    For \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\in\Xc\), the map
    \(t\mapsto \tilde \P_{t,x}\) is weak continuous.

    \item 
    There exists \(p>1\) such that, for every \(T>0\),
    \[
    \int_0^T
    \int_\Xc
    \int_{\R^d}
    \left|
    \hat A(t,y)
    -
    a\bigl(t,x,y,\tilde\P_{t,x}\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(y)
    \right|^p
    \tilde\P_{t,x}(dy)\,\mu(dx)\,dt
    <\infty.
    \]

    \item 
    For every \(h\in C_c^\infty(\R^d; \R)\) and every \(t\ge0\), one has,
    for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\in\Xc\),
    \[
    \E^{\tilde\P_{t,x}}[h]
    =
    \E^{\tilde\P_{0,x}}[h]
    +
    \int_0^t
    \E^{\tilde\P_{s,x}}\!\left[
    \nabla h(Y)\cdot
    \left(
    \hat A(s,Y)
    -
    a\bigl(s,x,Y,\tilde\P_{s,x}\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(Y)
    \right)
    +
    \Delta h(Y)
    \right]ds .
    \]

    \item 
    If
    $
    \P_t(dx,dy)
    :=
    \mu(dx)\,\tilde\P_{t,x}(dy),
$
    then, for a.e. \(t\ge0\),
    \[
    \hat A(t,y)
    =
    \E^{\P_t}\!\left[
        a\bigl(t,X,y,(\P_t)_X\bigr)
        \mid Y=y
    \right],
    \qquad
    \P_t\text{-a.s.}
    \]
\end{enumerate}

The theorem states that each infinite bounded sequence in R^n has a convergent subsequence. An equivalent formulation is that a subset of R^n is sequentially compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. The theorem is sometimes called the sequential compactness theorem.

body: Let V and W be vector spaces over a field F with V finite-dimensional, and let T : V -> W be a linear map. Then dim(V) = dim(ker T) + dim(im T), i.e. dim(V) = nullity(T) + rank(T), where the kernel ker T = {v in V : T(v) = 0} is a subspace of V and the image im T = T(V) is a subspace of W. Equivalently, for any m by n matrix A over F regarded as a linear map F^n -> F^m, rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, the number of columns of A.
title: Rank-nullity theorem

    f(x)=sum_{j>=1} alpha_j f_j(x),

1. The j=1 normalization is C_1=2/pi, since x=sin(theta) gives integral_{-1}^1 x^2/sqrt(1-x^2) dx=integral_{-pi/2}^{pi/2} sin^2(theta) dtheta=pi/2. Therefore f(x)>=alpha_1*(2/pi)*x^2/sqrt(1-x^2) almost everywhere.

Its density h is 4 on each of [1/4,1/3] and [-1/3,-1/4], 1 on each of [1/2,2/3] and [-2/3,-1/2], and zero elsewhere. Indeed each small band receives weight 1/3 and length 1/12; each large band receives weight 1/6 and length 1/6. Its total mass is 2*4*(1/12)+2*1*(1/6)=1.

3. Everywhere on these four bands, x^2>=1/16 and 1/sqrt(1-x^2)>=1, giving f(x)>=alpha_1/(8*pi). Since h(x)<=4, choose p=alpha_1/(32*pi), which lies strictly between zero and one. Then p*h(x)<=alpha_1/(8*pi)<=f(x) on the bands, and domination elsewhere is automatic. The residual density g=(f-ph)/(1-p) is nonnegative, integrates to one and is symmetric. Thus F=pH+(1-p)G satisfies D0007-C002 with m=3.

Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. real random variables with cumulant generating function Lambda(lambda) = log E[ exp(lambda X_1) ] and Legendre transform Lambda^*(x) = sup_{lambda in R} ( lambda x - Lambda(lambda) ). Assume Lambda(lambda) < infinity for every lambda in a neighbourhood of 0. Then the empirical means S_n/n satisfy the LARGE DEVIATION PRINCIPLE with speed n and good convex rate function Lambda^*: for every closed set C, limsup_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in C ) <= - inf_{x in C} Lambda^*(x), and for every open set G, liminf_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in G ) >= - inf_{x in G} Lambda^*(x). In particular, for x > E[X_1], (1/n) log P( S_n/n >= x ) -> - Lambda^*(x), so the Chernoff upper bound is exact at the level of the exponential rate although it can be off by polynomial factors: the sharper Bahadur-Rao asymptotic supplies a factor of order n^{-1/2}. The exponential moment hypothesis is what makes Lambda^* a GOOD rate function, meaning its sublevel sets are compact; on the real line the large deviation principle itself continues to hold without it, but the rate function may fail to be good and the statement must then be handled with care. Heavy-tailed laws with no exponential moments have Lambda^* identically 0 above the mean, and their large deviations are governed by a single big jump rather than by a rate function of this shape. [Cramer (1938); see Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.2.3]

the rate is exponential in n; polynomial prefactors are NOT captured

In particular p_t(t+1)→0 suffices in every dimension. This proves nonuniformity over laws, not a fixed-law counterexample. {"artifact_digest":"sha256:e92649cd01502a4e7930778eebc0e85c8f802d7c7e61e21fc3398b6cdbb256a7","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/e9/e92649cd01502a4e7930778eebc0e85c8f802d7c7e61e21fc3398b6cdbb256a7.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8780c17498b81dc053c1e1cdb56e985244a4d447a54fac0deef20bb1fc05681a","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c6-v3","bundle_id":"population.i0005-sparse-law-nonuniformity-003","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"interacting particle systems","draft":"w661/bundle_003.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:sparse-critical-particle-hole-nonuniform-convergence-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C6 v3: nonuniformity whenever sparse walks rarely encounter a hole

Novelty: UNCHECKED. Elementary free-walk/product-void argument; no earlier separate statement found in the limited I0005 searches. This strengthens v1/v2. It never supplies a fixed-law counterexample.

Fix d≥1 and let R_t be the range through round t of one free nearest-neighbor simple random walk on Z^d. For each observation time t start a new particle–hole process with iid P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p_t, P(η=0)=1−2p_t. Assume

p_t→0 and p_t E_0|R_t|→0.

Then, with synchronous rounds, stationary capacity-one holes, and graph distance,

P_{p_t}(origin strictly nearer an unfilled hole than an active particle at time t)→1/2.

In particular p_t(t+1)→0 suffices in every dimension, because |R_t|≤t+1. This condition is weaker than v2's sufficient condition in d>2. For d=1 one can also use E|R_t|≤C√(t+1), by the maximal-walk moment argument in v2. Each initial law is bounded and mean zero; convergence is not uniform over laws even when d≤3, but no fixed p satisfies these asymptotic assumptions.

## 1. Couple to full free walks

Assign an independent infinite walk to every site, independently of all initial signs. If a site is initially +1, its particle follows this path until it settles; continue the path freely after settlement for comparison. Independent tie-breaking marks select uniformly which arriving particles settle. Let C_t^{free}(B) count initial particles whose completed free endpoints at time t lie in B. The actual active particles are precisely the nonsettled labeled particles in this free configuration at time t.

An initial hole z filled by time t must have been visited by the free path of an initial +1 particle y≠z. Independence of different initial sites and the union bound give

E[number of filled initial holes in B]
≤p_t² sum_{z∈B}sum_y P_y(T_z≤t)
=p_t² |B| E_0|R_t|.

For y=z, the opposite initial signs are impossible; including the nonnegative term in the upper bound is harmless. Translation invariance gives sum_y P_y(T_z≤t)=sum_y P_0(T_{z−y}≤t)=E_0|R_t|.

Every settled particle's free path through t visited an initial hole. The expected number of settled labeled particles with completed free endpoint in B is therefore at most

p_t² sum_y E_y[1_{Z_t∈B}|R_t|]
=p_t² |B| E_0|R_t|.

The last equality follows by fixing a path from zero and summing its translations: exactly |B| translated paths end in B, and translation leaves the range size unchanged. All sums are nonnegative; Tonelli applies. A visit to the particle's own initial site cannot hit a hole and may again be included in the upper bound. The completed prefix includes the path up to actual settlement, so the containment of events is valid even though future free instructions are unused by the actual process.

Put s_t=p_t^{−1/d}. For any fixed M≥0 and B=B_floor(Ms_t), the two discrepancy expectations are at most C_{d,M}p_t E_0|R_t|+o(p_t E_0|R_t|), hence tend to zero. By Markov, within B the surviving holes coincide with initial −1 sites and the actual active-particle counts coincide with the free-endpoint counts, with probability tending to one. Multiplicities at a site are harmless for the nearest-site event.

## 2. Joint initial-hole/free-particle void probabilities

For fixed r,s≥0, let B_H=B_floor(rs_t), B_C=B_floor(ss_t), a_y=1_{y∈B_H}, and b_y=P_y(Z_t∈B_C). At site y, the two mutually exclusive forbidden choices are an initial hole in B_H (probability p_t a_y) and an initial particle whose free endpoint lies in B_C (probability p_t b_y). The signs and free walks are independent across sites. Therefore the exact probability of no initial hole in B_H and no free endpoint in B_C is

product_{y∈Z^d}(1−p_t a_y−p_t b_y).

At fixed t this is a finite product: a_y has finite support and b_y=0 outside B_C+B_t by finite propagation. Moreover sum_y a_y=|B_H| and sum_y b_y=|B_C|, the latter by translation invariance of the transition probabilities. For p_t≤1/4, the logarithm differs from −p_t(|B_H|+|B_C|) by absolute value at most

C p_t² sum_y(a_y+b_y)²≤2C p_t²(|B_H|+|B_C|),

because 0≤a_y,b_y≤1, a_y²=a_y, and b_y²≤b_y. This estimate is uniform in time; no negligible-displacement assumption is needed.

The lattice ℓ1-ball count is |B_R|=v_dR^d+O_d(R^{d−1}+1), v_d=2^d/d!. It follows by counting cubes in the dilated cross-polytope and bounding the boundary layer. Thus p_t|B_H|→v_d r^d and p_t|B_C|→v_d s^d, while the preceding logarithmic error tends to zero. The joint void probability tends to

exp(−v_d(r^d+s^d)).

This is the survival function of two independent identically distributed continuous nearest-distance variables with marginal tail exp(−v_d u^d).

## 3. Transfer to actual surviving holes and active particles

For each fixed pair r,s, Step 1 shows that the actual joint void probability differs from Step 2 by a quantity tending to zero. Therefore the scaled actual nearest-hole and nearest-active distances converge jointly to the same independent continuous pair. The continuous limiting marginals ensure tightness, and the joint survival function determines the joint law. The set {first distance = second distance} has zero limiting probability. Portmanteau applied to the strict comparison now gives the desired limit 1/2.

## Quantifier limitation

The density p_t is reselected for every observation time. With fixed p>0, the expected range tends to infinity and p E|R_t| does not tend to zero, so this proof cannot refute the fixed-law d4 statement. It is a nonuniformity result and a warning against replacing one counterexample law by a triangular sequence of laws.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:b394da5a021e81781262336433ce1e8ecbf743c4f8739229e9eef1fc2ec412d2","revision_digest":"sha256:c4e8b72f1b0d0ab945ba13b7e5b3a479c5bc9576aa578eac31b196b463af51a2","source_id":"owner-own-work:w661:I0005-C6:v3","source_revision":"v3; 2026-10-14T05:34:54.9593620+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem 31 of arXiv:2511.10814, '\Large \bf \boldmath\ \\ Convergence of the extended Kalman filter with small and state-de'] Let $A \in \mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ be positive semi-definite and let $B \in  \mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ be symmetric.
The following four statements are equivalent:
											
\begin{enumerate}
\item  $x^\top Ax \geq  \vert x^\top Bx \vert$  for all $x \in \mathbb{C}^n$.
\item $x^\top Ax + y^\top Ay \geq  2\vert x^\top By\vert$ for all $x, y \in  \mathbb{C}^n$.
\item $H =\left[ \begin{array}{cc} 
A&B\\
	B&A
\end{array} \right]$  is positive semi-definite.
	\item There is a symmetric contraction $X \in \mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ such that $B = A^{1/2} X A^{1/2}$.

    If A is positive definite, then the following statement is equivalent to \ref{prop1}:
	\item $\rho (A^{-1} B) \leq  1$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\begin{equation}
 D_h^{\max}\leq\nu(h,4)\leq\max\{h^2,D_h^{\max}\}.
\end{equation}
Consequently
\[
 \nu(2,4)=6,\qquad \nu(3,4)=11,
\]
while for every $h\geq4$,
\[
 \binom{h+2}{2}+\mathbf 1_{\{2\nmid h\}}
 \leq\nu(h,4)\leq h^2.
\]
In particular, $\nu(h,4)=\Theta(h^2)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Kalikow's zero-one law (1981; Zerner-Merkl 2001 for the sharp form): for random walk in an i.i.d. elliptic random environment on Z^d and a direction l, let A_l = {X_n . l -> +infinity}. Then P_0(A_l union A_{-l}) is 0 or 1. It does NOT say that P_0(A_l) itself is 0 or 1: the directional zero-one law P_0(A_l) in {0,1} is a theorem in d = 1 (Solomon) and d = 2 (Zerner-Merkl, using planarity: two walks in the same environment must intersect), and is an OPEN PROBLEM for d >= 3 (Drewitz-Ramirez Open Question 3.2; Kalikow's law is often misquoted as the directional one). Kalikow's proof: the event A_l union A_{-l} is invariant under a coupling of walks started at different points that follow the same environment after they meet in a slab, and its probability is a function of the environment's tail sigma-field, hence 0 or 1 by Kolmogorov. Consequences: under transience in some direction the regeneration structure of Sznitman-Zerner applies to the union event; Zerner's law of large numbers then gives X_n/n -> v or -c v. Typical failure: Treating Kalikow's zero-one law as if it determines transience, mistaking the statement that the probability is 0 or 1 for a claim that it equals 1; the theorem only rules out intermediate probabilities and leaves open, often genuinely unresolved, which side of the dichotomy holds for a specific environment law, which is precisely the content of the still largely open general ballisticity conjecture for random walk in random environment in dimension d>=2. Canonical reference: Kalikow, 1981, Annals of Probability; Zeitouni, 2004, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.
i.i.d. (or stationary ergodic with care) elliptic environment on Z^d
The statement concerns the UNION of the two directional events
Directional 0-1 law is open for d >= 3

[Definition of arXiv:2605.15066, 'The critical activation density in graph bootstrap percolation'] For each $e$ in $A^*$, put ${\mathcal R}_e^*=\emptyset$
and recall that $W_e^*=e$.  
For edges $e$ activated at time $t\geqslant1$, 
we put 
\[
{\mathcal R}_e^*=\{e\}\cup\bigcup_{f\in E(H_e^*\setminus e)}{\mathcal R}_f^*. 
\]
We call the edges in ${\mathcal R}_e^*$ the {\it red edges}
of $W_e^*$. 
The edges in $W_e^*$ itself are its {\it black edges}. 
Note that if the black edges of $W_e^*$ are
initially active then the $H$-dynamics will 
activate each red edge of $W_e^*$, towards
eventually activating $e$ itself. We let ${\mathcal R}^*={\mathcal R}^*_{e^*}$
denote the set of red edges of $W^*$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded and open, $T>0$, $a^{ij}=a^{ji}$, $a^{ij},b^i,c\in L^\infty(U_T)$, uniformly parabolic with constant $\theta>0$, $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(U))$, $g\in L^2(U)$. Then there exists exactly one weak solution $u\in L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U))$ with $u'\in L^2(0,T;H^{-1}(U))$ of $u_t+Lu=f$ in $U_T$, $u=0$ on $\partial U\times[0,T]$, $u(0)=g$. It satisfies $u\in C([0,T];L^2(U))$ and the energy estimate. No boundary regularity and no compatibility condition are needed for this basic existence statement. Improved regularity: if moreover $g\in H^1_0(U)$ and the coefficients are time independent and smooth enough, then $u\in L^\infty(0,T;H^1_0(U))$ with $u'\in L^2(0,T;L^2(U))$; if in addition $\partial U$ is of class $C^2$ (or $U$ is convex), then also $u\in L^2(0,T;H^2(U))$. The $H^2$ conclusion is elliptic regularity applied at a.e. time and genuinely needs that boundary hypothesis -- on a domain with a reentrant corner the solution need not lie in $H^2(U)$ -- whereas the $L^\infty_tH^1_0$ and $u'\in L^2_tL^2$ bounds do not.
