body:
[Thm 21 of arXiv:2607.06242, 'Exponential mixing and Freidlin--Wentzell large deviation principle for Markov cocycles'] Assume
  \[
     \|F\|^2\in L^1(\Sigma,m),\qquad
     \|Q\|_{\mathcal L_2(\Rb^{ \mathbf{d}},H^1)}^2\in L^1(\Sigma,m),\qquad
     Q_\infty:=\operatorname*{sup}_{\sigma\in\Sigma}
     \|Q(\sigma)\|_{\mathcal L(\Rb^{ \mathbf{d}},H)}<\infty .
  \]
  Suppose that there exist an integer
  $N_0\geq 1$ and a measurable family of linear maps
  $R_0(\sigma):P_{N_0}H\to \Rb^{ \mathbf{d}}$ such that
  \[
      Q(\sigma)R_0(\sigma)P_{N_0}=P_{N_0},\qquad
      \|R_0\|_{\mathcal L(P_{N_0}H,\Rb^{ \mathbf{d}})}^2\in L^1(\Sigma,m),
  \]
  and $N_0$ is chosen large enough to satisfy the determining mode gap
  \begin{align}
    \nu\lambda_{N_0+1}>
    C_*\int_\Sigma \left(\|F(\sigma)\|^2+\|Q(\sigma)\|_{\mathcal L_2(\Rb^{ \mathbf{d}},H)}^2\right)\,m(d\sigma),
  \end{align}
  where $C_*>0$ 
  is an embedding constant 
  depending  only on $\nu$, $\lambda_1$, and the domain $D$.

  Then the Navier--Stokes system \eqref{e.072601} has a unique stationary measure $\mu_{\s}^{\varepsilon}$ that attracts transition probabilities exponentially under the Wasserstein metric $\mathbb{W}_{\|\cdot\|\wedge 1}$. Moreover, for $m$-a.e. $\s\in \Sigma$, the family $\{\mu_{\s}^{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon\in(0,1]}$ obeys an upper bound Freidlin--Wentzell LDP with a good rate function, which also gives a lower bound, and hence the full Freidlin--Wentzell LDP, in the case when the random attractor of the limiting system consists of a single random point. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 21 of arXiv:2607.06242

[Theorem 201 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] If $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ is a diagonal matrix with positive diagonal elements, then the solution operator is
\begin{equation}

\Upsilon_h[\boldsymbol{E}\,;\,\boldsymbol{\kappa}](z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(z - \alpha_h)(z - \beta_h)}}\left(\kappa_h + \oint_{\gamma_h} \frac{\dd\zeta}{2\ii\pi}\,\frac{E_h(\zeta)}{\theta_{h,h}(\zeta - z)} \right),
\end{equation}
where $\gamma_h\subset \amsmathbb{M}_h$ encloses $\amsmathbb{A}_h^{\mathfrak{m}}$, but not $z$.

If $\theta_{g,h} = \theta > 0$ is independent of $g,h \in [H]$, then the solution operator is uniquely determined by the identity
\[
\sum_{h = 1}^{H} \Op_h[\boldsymbol{E}\,;\,\boldsymbol{\kappa}](z) = \frac{1}{\sigma(z)}\Pi^{-1}\left[\boldsymbol{\kappa} - \bigg(\oint_{\gamma_g^+} \frac{\dd \zeta}{2\ii\pi}\,\mathcal{K}[\boldsymbol{E}](\zeta)\bigg)_{g = 1}^{H}\right](z) + \mathcal{K}[\boldsymbol{E}](z),
\]
where
\[
\mathcal{K}[\boldsymbol{E}](z) = \sum_{h = 1}^{H} \frac{1}{\sigma(z)} \oint_{\gamma_h^-} \frac{\dd\zeta}{2\ii\pi}\,\frac{\sigma(\zeta)}{\zeta - z}\,\frac{E_h(\zeta)}{\theta \sqrt{(\zeta - \alpha_h)(\zeta - \beta_h)}}
\]
and $\Pi^{-1}$ term is a polynomial in $z$ of degree at most $H-1$, defined through the hyperelliptic period map $\Pi$, whose more detailed definition is in \eqref{periodmap}. Contours $\gamma_h^-\subset\amsmathbb{M}_h$ enclose $\amsmathbb{A}_h^{\mathfrak{m}}$, but not $z$. Contours $\gamma_h^+\subset \amsmathbb{M}_h$ enclose the respective $\gamma_h^-$, as Figure~\ref{Fig:Kdomain}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: (1) One omitted value is not enough. The family {exp(nz) : n ≥ 1} on the unit disk omits the value 0 everywhere, but it is not normal, not even in the extended sense: on the left half of the disk exp(nz) → 0 while on the right half |exp(nz)| → ∞, and a locally uniform limit on the connected set D would have to be holomorphic throughout or identically ∞. Montel's fundamental normality test needs two distinct omitted values, and that is sharp. (2) When two values are omitted, the conclusion is normality in the extended sense: the constant functions f_n = n omit 0 and 1 and converge to ∞, so a proof that assumes the limit is a finite holomorphic function must first exclude the ∞ branch (typically by a bound at one point or by the maximum principle). (3) Pointwise bounds are not local bounds. Montel's first theorem needs a bound uniform on each compact set; pointwise boundedness of the family is genuinely weaker (Runge's theorem produces sequences of polynomials converging pointwise on C to a discontinuous function, so such a sequence is pointwise bounded and not normal). (4) Normality is not convergence: it only yields subsequences, and the limit may leave the class one is working in — the injective maps z/n converge to a constant, and the limit of a normal family of functions in some prescribed family need not satisfy the same constraint unless Hurwitz-type arguments are added.
title: Pitfall: normality needs two omitted values (or local boundedness), and the limit may be ∞

[Theorem thm:rankone-multiplicity of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $h\geq2$, $k\geq3$, and let $A\subset\mathbb Z$ be an ordered
$k$-set with $r_h(A)=1$.  Let $z$, chosen up to sign, be the primitive
generator of the rank-one lattice
\[
 L_h(A)\cap\mathbb Z^k=\mathbb Zz,
\]
and put $r=\rho(z)$.  Then $2\leq r\leq h$, and, for every $j\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 H_j(A;h)
 =
 M_{h-(j-1)r,k}
 -2M_{h-jr,k}
 +M_{h-(j+1)r,k}.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
Here and below $M_{s,k}=0$ when $s<0$.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \max_{n\in hA}r_{A,h}(n)
 =1+\left\lfloor\frac hr\right\rfloor
\end{equation}
and
\[
 |hA|=M_{h,k}-M_{h-r,k}.
\]
The collision counts satisfy
\begin{align}
 C_2(A;h)
 &=M_{h-r,k}-2M_{h-2r,k}+M_{h-3r,k},
 \\
 C_{\geq3}(A;h)
 &=M_{h-2r,k}-M_{h-3r,k}.
 
\end{align}

[Theorem thm:equivtwist of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] The twist correlation function 
$\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,v}(z_1,z_2)$ for the field with constant boundary condition $v \in \mathbb{R}$ can also be equivalently expressed as the following renormalised probabilities:
\begin{itemize}
\item Let $E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{v,\rm{holes}}$ 
be the event that no cluster of  
$\mathcal{L}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}
\cup
\Xi^{v^2/2}_{D, D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}$
disconnects $\mathbb{D}(z_1, \varepsilon_1)$ from $\mathbb{D}(z_2, \varepsilon_2)$. 
Then we have  
$$\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,v}(z_1,z_2) 
= \lim_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2 \to 0} 
\dfrac{\pi}{2} 
(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{-1/8}|\log \varepsilon_1|^{-1/2}|\log \varepsilon_2|^{-1/2}
\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{v,\rm{holes}}).$$

\item Let $E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{v}$ be the event that 
$\text{no cluster of }
\mathcal{L}_{D}
\cup
\Xi^{v^2/2}_{D}
\text{ disconnects } \mathbb{D}(z_1,\varepsilon_1) 
\text{ from } \mathbb{D}(z_2,\varepsilon_2)$.
Then 
$$\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,v}(z_1,z_2) 
= \lim_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2 \to 0} (\mathbf{C}_{\rm{SLE}4}^{\rm loop})^{-2}(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{-1/8}\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{v}).$$

\item Let $E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{v,\rm{exc}}$ be the event that no sign excursion cluster of the GFF in $D$ with constant boundary condition $v \in \mathbb{R}$ disconnects 
$\mathbb{D}(z_1,\varepsilon_1)$ from $\mathbb{D}(z_2, \varepsilon_2)$. Then we have  
$$\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,v}(z_1,z_2) 
= \lim_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2 \to 0} (\mathbf{C}_{\rm{SLE}4}^{\rm loop})^{-2} (\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{-1/8}\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{v,\rm{exc}}).$$

\item Let $E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{v,\rm{CLE}}$ 
be the event that a $0$-height CLE$_4$ gasket in the nested CLE$_4$ coupling with $\Phi_D^{(v)}$
intersects both $\mathbb{D}(z_1,\varepsilon_1)$ and $\mathbb{D}(z_2, \varepsilon_2)$. 
Then we have  
$$\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,v}(z_1,z_2) 
= \lim_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2 \to 0} (\mathbf{C}_{\rm{SLE}4}^{\rm loop})^{-2} (\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{-1/8}
\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{v,\rm{CLE}}).$$
\end{itemize}
The constant $\mathbf{C}_{\rm{SLE}4}^{\rm loop}$ above is given by 
Proposition (Prop asymp 1 pt ED Ver 2 of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Lemma (campaign status: proved): After fixing all parameters outside a selected active set of size u, the event is sum_{i=1}^u c_i*eps_i in {b-1, b+1} with all c_i nonzero and b arbitrary (tag 12). For any two active coordinates, condition on the other u-2 signs: the four sums +-c_1 +- c_2 cannot all lie in a fixed two-point set when c_1,c_2 are nonzero. They have fewer than three distinct elements only if c_1 = +-c_2, in which case they are 0, 2c_1, -2c_1 up to translation - still three distinct values over R and over F_p with odd p > 2. Hence at most three of the four assignments work and the probability is <= 3/4 (13). Notes: Target-uniform and valid in every odd characteristic. This is the u = 2 branch of psi and the only branch that survives when u is small.

body:
[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.13273, 'Asymptotics of transition densities for L\'evy processes with stochastic resetting'] Let $\boldsymbol{Y}$ be the Brownian motion in $\Rd.$ Then
    for all $\lambda>0, t>0$ the density $p_\lambda$ of the
    corresponding process $\boldsymbol{X}$ with resetting exists and, for any $x\in\Rd$,
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For every $M>\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\lambda}}$ we have
        \begin{equation}
          p_\lambda(t,x,y) \sim \frac{\lambda^{\frac{d+1}{4}}}{2^{\frac{d+1}{4}}\pi^{\frac{d-1}{2}}} \frac{e^{-\sqrt{2\lambda}|y|}}{|y|^{\frac{d-1}{2}}}, \quad \text{ on } \quad \frac{t}{|y|}\geq M.
        \end{equation}
        \item For every $0<  M <\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\lambda}}$ we have
        \begin{equation}
            p_\lambda(t,x,y) \sim e^{-\lambda t}p(t,y) \left(\frac{2\lambda}{(|y|/t)^2-2\lambda}+e^{\frac{-|x|^2+2\langle x,y
            \rangle}{2t}}\right) 
            , \quad \text{ on } \quad 0< \frac{t}{|y|} \leq M.
        \end{equation}
        \item For $\frac{t}{|y|}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\lambda}}$ we get
        \[
             p_\lambda(t,x,y) \sim \frac{\lambda^{\frac{d+1}{4}}}{2\cdot 2^{\frac{d+1}{4}}\pi^{\frac{d-1}{2}}} \frac{e^{-\sqrt{2\lambda}|y|}}{|y|^{\frac{d-1}{2}}}.
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma main of arXiv:2609.02871, 'Estimating the number of real zeros of linear combinations of radicals of polynomials'] Let $\beta>-1/2$ and $\lambda=-\beta(\beta+1)< \frac{1}{4}$. Let $u$ be a solution to
\[
\Delta_{\mathbb{D}} u + \lambda u=\sum_{k=1}^{n}c_{k}\delta_{p_{k}} \quad \text{ in Poincare's disc } \quad \mathbb{D},
\]
where $c_{k} \in \mathbb{R}\setminus{0}$ and $p_k$ are distinct points on $D$. Assume that $u(z) = o(1-|z|^2)^{-\beta}$ as $z \to \partial \mathbb{D}$. Then $u$ has at most $n$ nodal domains in $D$.

body:
[Lemma lem:heterogeneous-packet of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a circuit state $\tau$, including a maximizing smoothing, all
pair-support groups and prime tags, every declared port, and one base on
each original $p\vee r$ circuit.  For an occurrence $v$, let
$\mathscr R_{\tau,v}$ be the finite set of typed nonfront roles in which
that occurrence appears in the root, pass, fold, and signed-transport
daughters.  If $D$ is a four-index curvature tensor, put
\[
 \mathfrak k_{\tau,v}(D)
 :=\max_{M\in\mathscr R_{\tau,v}}\|M(D)\|_{\rm op}.
\]
The maximum over an empty role set is defined to be zero.
Here the raw cups, caps, and circuit bases stay in the declared circuit
wiring and are not absorbed into $M$.  Every map which is absorbed into
$M$ is a wedge inclusion or projection, a normalized Brauer map, a signed
permutation, a full transpose, or one of the finitely many Bianchi
transfers.  The first four kinds are contractions or isometries in the
normalized coordinate Hilbert structures.  Each normalized Bianchi
transfer is a signed sum of at most a numerical number of coordinate-index
isometries.  Hence its operator norm is at most a numerical multiple of
the four-index Hilbert--Schmidt norm, and consequently
\[
 \boxed{\mathfrak k_{\tau,v}(D)\le C\|D\|_2,}
\tag{3.4.1x$_{7a}$}
\]
where the norm on the right is the invariant four-index
Hilbert--Schmidt norm and $C$ is numerical.

Let $P$ be a nonzero connected coefficient packet with $s\ge2$
occurrences and $c=c^{\!*}(P)$.  Give its vertices possibly different
self-adjoint algebraic-curvature tensors $D_v$; they need not be Ricci
flat.  Leave every declared gap and joint context as its formal
multilinear slot, or equivalently factor out its prescribed
operator/projective cost.  Then $c\ge2$, and there are two front
occurrences $r_P,s_P$ and a finite circuit-anchored presentation such that
\[
 \boxed{
 \|\zeta_{P,\tau}(\{D_v\})\|_{\mathscr P_\tau}
 \le C^s n^{c-2}
 \|D_{r_P}\|_2\|D_{s_P}\|_2
 \prod_{v\notin\{r_P,s_P\}}\mathfrak k_{\tau,v}(D_v).}
\tag{3.4.1x$_{7b}$}
\]
Every coefficient occurrence, named gap, joint context, retained
interface, and original circuit base occurs once.  The root creates one
two-front atom; every later prime transports that atom and creates no
new front or base.

body: For a real parameter delta >= 0 the SQUARED BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta started at y >= 0, written BESQ^delta, is the unique strong solution of dY_t = 2 sqrt( |Y_t| ) dW_t + delta dt with Y_0 = y; the solution is nonnegative, and pathwise uniqueness holds despite the non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficient by the Yamada-Watanabe criterion, which requires only Holder continuity of exponent 1/2. The BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta, BES^delta, is X_t = sqrt(Y_t); for X > 0 it solves dX_t = dW_t + ((delta - 1)/(2 X_t)) dt. When delta = d is a positive INTEGER, BES^d started at |x| has the law of the radial part |B_t| of a d-dimensional Brownian motion started at x - a fact that makes the family the natural interpolation of radial Brownian motion to non-integer dimension. ADDITIVITY: BESQ^delta started at y and an independent BESQ^{delta'} started at y' add to a BESQ^{delta + delta'} started at y + y'; this holds for the SQUARED process and is false for the Bessel process itself. The index nu = delta/2 - 1 is the other common parameterisation and is the one that appears in the modified Bessel functions of the transition density; delta and nu must not be confused. For 0 <= delta < 2 the point 0 is reached from y > 0, and the BESQ^delta equation itself fixes what happens there: 0 is absorbing for delta = 0 and instantaneously reflecting for 0 < delta < 2, so the squared process needs no extra boundary convention (the equation for X = sqrt(Y) holds only while X_t > 0). For delta >= 2 the point 0 is never reached from y > 0. [standard; e.g. Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Chapter XI]

Unproved sufficient input, not a theorem. For iid Uniform[1,2] undirected Z^2 FPP with endpoints 0,n e1, put U_e=tau_e-1 and a_e=clamp(A_e-B_e-1,0,1), where A_e is the cheapest avoiding path and B_e the cheapest containing path with e's weight omitted. Let U_-e^(1-s) independently refresh each other coordinate with probability s. For K(a,b)=Cov(min(U,a),min(U,b)), U Uniform[0,1], define J_n(rho)=sum_e E K(a_e(U_-e),a_e(U_-e^rho)) and R_n=J_n-J_n(0). The exact finite-product identity gives Var(T_n)=J_n(0)+integral_0^1 R_n(rho)d rho. A sufficient missing lemma would, for each 0<epsilon<1/3, give n-independent c,C>0, eta>0,p>1 with R_n(1-s)<=Cn(1+s n^(1/3-epsilon))^(-p) for all s in [0,1], and sum_e P(a_e>=eta,a_e^(1-s)>=eta)>=cn for s<=n^(-1/3-epsilon), for all large n. Together with the checked first-order floor bound these inputs imply Var(T_n)=n^(2/3+o(1)). Only zero-noise robust margins and a window of order n^(-2) have been proved in this packet.

Let ell be a nonzero continuous linear functional on a real or complex normed space X. For every x in X, dist(x, ker ell) = |ell(x)| / ||ell||, and for x outside ker ell the infimum is attained exactly when ell attains its norm on the unit sphere. If X = H is a Hilbert space and ell(x) = <x, y> for its Riesz vector y (inner product linear in the first argument), then ker ell = {y}^perp is a closed hyperplane, H = ker ell (+) span{y} as an orthogonal sum, the orthogonal projection onto ker ell is P x = x - (ell(x)/||y||^2) y, and dist(x, ker ell) = ||x - P x|| = |ell(x)| / ||y||, with ||ell|| = ||y||.
X is a real or complex normed space; for the second part H is a Hilbert space

[Prop 10 (Derivations and $p$-Powers) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$. Let $x\in K$. Let $D,E$ be derivations on $K$.

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The $p$-times composition 
        $D^{\circ p}=D^p$
        is a derivation on $K$.
        \item Derivations kill $p$-powers: 
        $$D(x^p)=0.$$
        In particular, all derivations are derivations over $k$.
        \item (Jacobson's formula) There exists a universal Lie polynomial $s$ such that 
        $$\left(D+E\right)^p=D^p+E^p+s(D,E).$$
        \item (Hochschild's formula) We have 
        $$\left(xD\right)^p=x^pD^p+\left(xD\right)^{\circ (p-1)}(x)D.$$
        \item We have
        \[
        [D,xE]=D(x)E+x[D,E].
        \]
    \end{enumerate}
title: Derivations and $p$-Powers

[Proposition 14 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(a>1\). For every \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\lim_{L\to\infty}
\frac{1}{L}
\log\mathbb{E}\exp(\theta N_a(L))
=
\Lambda_a(\theta),
\]
where
\[
\Lambda_a(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}
\int_0^{\infty}
\log\left(1+(e^{\theta}-1)r_a(\xi)\right)
\,\mathrm{d}\xi.
\]
The convergence is locally uniform for \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\).

body:
[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $(\mathcal{L}_t)_{t=0}^{T}$ be a nonnegative process adapted to a filtration $(\mathscr F_t)_{t=0}^{T}$. Let $\mathcal G\subseteq \mathscr F_0$ be an initial sigma-field, and let $B$ be a nonnegative $\mathcal G$-measurable random variable such that $\mathcal{L}_0\leq B$. Fix $\kappa\in(0,1]$, and let $G_0,\ldots,G_{T-1}$ be events with $G_t\in\mathscr F_t$.

Assume that, for every $t=0,\ldots,T-1$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (\textbf{Deterministic non-expansion}) $\mathcal{L}_{t+1}\leq \mathcal{L}_t$ almost surely.
\item (\textbf{Good-step contraction}) On $G_t$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{t+1}\mid \mathscr F_t]\leq (1-\kappa)\mathcal{L}_t.
\]
\item (\textbf{Conditional bad-event control}) For deterministic numbers $\delta_t\geq0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(G_t^c\mid \mathcal G)\leq \delta_t.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then
\be
\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_T\mid\mathcal G]
\leq \left((1-\kappa)^T+\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\delta_t\right)B.
\ee

[Definition def:first-order-occupation-solution of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Given an integer $m\geq1$,
$F\in L_w^2(I;\mathbb R^m)$, and $\eta\in L^2(\mu_{r_1};\mathbb R^m)$, a field
$u\in H_{x,w}^1(I;\mathbb R^m)$ is a \emph{first-order occupation-energy solution}
with data $(F,\eta)$ if
\begin{equation*}
 -(\partial_t+\mathcal L_t)u=F\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(I\times\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^m),
 \qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{r_1}^Xu=\eta(X_{r_1}).
\end{equation*}
Here and below, the second-order part is read in divergence form:
$
 \mathcal L_tu
 =\frac12\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_ju)
  +(D_xu)\left(b-\frac12\operatorname{div}a\right).
$

body: [Proposition prop-resample-inside of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] For $(\phi, \eta) \sim M_W$, the conditional law of $\eta$ given $\phi$ is radial $\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa}(W-2)$ in $\mathbb{H}$ from $\infty$ to $i$ with force point infinitesimally counterclockwise of $\infty$.  Furthermore, consider a bounded neighborhood $A\subset \mathbb{H}$ of $i$ such that $\overline A \cap \partial \mathbb{H} = \emptyset$, and let $\alpha = Q - \frac W{2\gamma}$. Conditioned on $\phi |_{\mathbb{H} \backslash A}$, we have $\phi|_A \stackrel d= h + \mathfrak h + \alpha G_A(\cdot, i)$, where $\mathfrak h$ is the harmonic extension of $\phi|_{\mathbb{H} \backslash A}$ to $A$, $h$ is a zero boundary GFF on $A$ and $G_A$ is the Green function of $h$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let f : T -> [0,1] be a symbol of the form f(theta) = g(k theta) for an integer k >= 2 and a symbol g, and let P_f be the stationary determinantal process on Z with kernel K(x,y) = f-hat(x - y). Then the restrictions of P_f to the residue classes kZ + j, j = 0..k-1, are independent, and each is (after reindexing the class by Z) the stationary determinantal process P_g. Consequence for Lyons's Question 5.4 (ICM 2014): if g is a trigonometric polynomial of degree m/k and P_g is an (m/k + 1)-block factor of an i.i.d. process, then P_f is an (m+1)-block factor of an i.i.d. process on Z; in particular for m = 2, k = 2 the question has a positive answer because the m = 1 case is known.

body: [Definition 8 of arXiv:2606.01742, 'Large deviation principles for SPDEs with locally Lipschitz coefficients'] (Rate function) A function $I(\cdot):\mathcal E^{\beta}([0,T]\times K, \mathbb R)\to [0,\infty]$ is called a rate function if for every constant $M<\infty$, $\{z\in \mathcal E^{\beta}([0,T]\times K, \mathbb R):I(z)\le M\}$ is a compact subset of $\mathcal E^{\beta}([0,T]\times K, \mathbb R)$.

body: [Lem transversalizing of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a $C^0$-foliation on $\mathbb{T}^2$ and $\gamma$ a positively (resp.~negatively) monotone with respect to $\mathcal{G}$. body:
[Cor 226 (\textbf{algorithmic threshold for perceptron model}) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\phi\in C_b(\bbR;\bbR)$, recall the perceptron Hamiltonian $H_N$ from in \eqref{e:hamiltonian}. We have the following:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item  
        For any $\iota> 0$, there exists $L$ large enough and $c$ small enough such that the following holds.
        For sufficiently large $N$, there exists a $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ such that for $\bx = \cA_N(\bG,\bg^{\aux})$,
        \[
            \bbP\bigg(\bx \in \Sigma_N(\iota), H_N(\bx) \ge M(\ALG-\iota)\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
        \]
        \item 
        For any $\iotaval > 0$, there exists sufficiently small $\iotasol > 0$ such that the following holds.
        For any $L$, there exists $c$ small enough that for any $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$, and $\bx = \cA_N(\bG,\bg^{\aux})$,
        \[
            \bbP\bigg(\bx \in \Sigma_N(\iotasol), H_N(\bx) \ge M(\ALG+\iotaval)\bigg) \le e^{-cN}\,.
        \]
    \end{enumerate}
In the above, $\ALG=\ALG^{\Ising}(\phi,\alpha)$ is defined by \eqref{eq:def-ALG-Ising} in the Ising setting, and analogously in the spherical setting
by replacing
$\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)$ with $\ocM^{\sph}(\alpha)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textbf{algorithmic threshold for perceptron model}

[Theorem thm:chronological-renewal of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a reflected two-replica monomer--dimer word with
$r\le L\log n$ nonconstant slots and one rooted spatial ribbon map
$\Gamma$.  Keep every same-time packet as one fused physical supernode,
every packet token once, the coupled pure-Weyl root, and the complete
finite-gap and weak chronological sums.  Remove the
scalar Jacobi child $-\gamma N^{-1}I$ before forming residual components.
Fix a reduced temporal record $\omega$ which records
all data listed in (thm:root-fused-allocation of the paper) except the
ordered root anchors $\mathbf t$ and the root-fusion map $\phi$.  Put
\[
 \mathcal X_{\Gamma,\omega}(\mathbf t)
 :=\sum_{\phi\in\Phi_{\Gamma,\omega}(\mathbf t)}
 \mathcal A_{\Gamma,\omega}(\mathbf t,\phi).
\]
Then
\[
 \boxed{
 \sum_{\mathbf t\in\Delta_{q(\omega)}(m)}
 |\mathcal X_{\Gamma,\omega}(\mathbf t)|
 \le A_L^r(r+1)^B\mathfrak a_\Gamma D_\omega
 \prod_{\rho\in R(\omega)}(m\mathfrak e_\rho).}
\tag{3.4.1x$_9$}
\]
Here $\mathfrak a_\Gamma$ retains the positive, already normalized
fixed-ribbon projective majorant and all unspent packet weights; the
phrase ``unspent'' excludes the mobile all-Weyl and mixed debits already
used in (thm:root-fused-allocation of the paper).  Summing
the reduced records is
paid by (lem:rooted-component-allocation of the paper) and the exponential
local state count.  Crucially, the absolute value is outside the complete
$\phi$-sum.  No extra $n$,
$\log n$, short-gap scale, Bell factor, matching factorial, or component
multinomial occurs.

body:
[Definition 133 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Let $L$ be a positive integer. If $\boldsymbol{\chi}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{\chi}^{(2)}$ are two random $L$-dimensional vectors depending on a large parameter $\N$ and having moments of all orders, we say that $\boldsymbol{\chi}^{(1)}$ approximates $\boldsymbol{\chi}^{(2)}$ in the sense of moments if
\[
\forall k \in \amsmathbb{Z}_{> 0} \quad \forall l_1,\ldots,l_k \in [M]\qquad \lim_{\N \rightarrow \infty} \bigg|\amsmathbb{E}\bigg[\prod_{j = 1}^{k} \chi_{l_j}^{(1)}\bigg] - \amsmathbb{E}\bigg[\prod_{j = 1}^{k} \chi_{l_j}^{(2)}\bigg]\bigg| = 0.
\]
In this case we write $\boldsymbol{\chi}^{(1)} \mathop{\sim}^{\text{mom}} \boldsymbol{\chi}^{(2)}$. In this definition, we do not require the convergence to be uniform in $k,l_1,\ldots,l_k$.
title: Definition 133 of arXiv:2601.16377

Own-work C010 v1, proof (unaudited); novelty unestablished. Fix n>=2, m>=1, rank{z_i}>=2, z_i=y_i*x_i with labels +/-1, ||x_i||<=1, and z_i dot z_l>=kappa>0 for every pair. Let unit u satisfy u dot z_i>=gamma>0. Use literal leaky ReLU phi(v)=max(v,lambda*v), 0<lambda<1, and f_i=m^-1 sum_j a_j phi(w_j dot x_i), average logistic loss L, g_i=(1+exp(y_i*f_i))^-1 and G=average g_i. Train BOTH layers simultaneously at actual step m*eta, any eta>0; hidden derivatives at zero may be selected in [lambda,1]. All initial a_j and w_j coordinates are independent N(0,sigma^2), sigma>0. Define b=(gamma/sqrt(2*pi*d))^d*exp(-(1+gamma/2)^2/2) and C^2=lambda^2*sigma^2*gamma^2*b/8. With probability at least 1-exp(-b*m/8), simultaneously for every finite time and every eta>0, m*||grad_a L||^2>=C^2*G^2>=C^2*L^2/(1+n*L)^2. The output-coordinate gradient always exists, even at hidden kinks; every selected full GD gradient has at least this squared norm. The Gaussian event counts neurons with a>0 and w/sigma in B(u,gamma/2), or the simultaneous negative. Each such neuron remains aligned with all signed sample projections at any step, regardless of arbitrary other neurons. With r=sigma*gamma/2, each survivor has |partial L/partial a_j|>=lambda*r*G/m. Summing squared coordinates avoids cancellation; independent initial indicators give at least b*m/2 survivors except with probability exp(-b*m/8). The event is defined at initialization, not through independent trajectory events. The loss-to-gradient comparison uses g_i=1-exp(-ell_i)>=ell_i/(1+n*L), valid at negative margins too. This is a surviving-gradient lemma, NOT a convergence or burn-in theorem: trained-output curvature or a discrete descent potential at arbitrary eta remains missing. Dimension and separation can make b very small. 15753 finite exact rational checks support selected update, normalization, cancellation and binomial-tail algebra only. Formal attempt returned RUNTIME_UNVERIFIED; independent analytic/probability audit and novelty comparison remain pending.
Strict positive signed-Gram rank>=2 bounded separable data; literal leakage in (0,1).
All output and hidden coordinates iid centered Gaussian with common nonzero variance; no restrictions on nonsurviving neurons.
Simultaneous both-layer GD with actual step m*eta on average logistic loss.
Proof (unaudited), no convergence or sharp Cai burn-in conclusion; no formal certificate or novelty claim.
title: T368 leaky-ReLU both-layer GD: Gaussian survivors give a time-uniform gradient lower bound (unaudited)

[Prop 6 of arXiv:2603.27433, 'The $k$-cycle shuffling with repeated cards'] Suppose $r:=n-\l_1\in[1, \log n]$, and $2\le k\le o(n/\log n)$. Moreover, suppose that $t':=t-\frac{n\log n}{k}$ satisfies $|t'|\le \frac{n(\log\log n-\omega(1))}{2k}$. Then, we have
$$s_\l(k)^t=\exp\left(-\frac{rkt}{n}-\frac{r(k+r)\log n}{2n}(1+o(1)+O(1/k))\right).$$
title: Prop 6 of arXiv:2603.27433

body: An algorithm computing an approximation y_hat to y = f(x), for an input x in floating-point arithmetic with unit roundoff u, is backward stable if for every admissible input x the computed output equals the exact result of the same problem applied to a slightly perturbed input: y_hat = f(x_hat) for some x_hat with ||x_hat - x|| = O(u) * ||x||. Informally, a backward stable algorithm gives an exactly correct answer to a slightly wrong question. Backward stability of the algorithm, combined with a bound on the conditioning of the problem f at x (its sensitivity to perturbations of the input), yields a bound on the forward error ||y_hat - y|| / ||y||, since the forward error is controlled, to first order, by the backward error multiplied by the condition number of the problem.
title: Backward Stability

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2607.23401, 'Limit Theorems for the Pitman-Yor Frequency Spectrum'] Let $J,k,n, (m_i)_{1\le i\le n}$ be integers
  with $0\le J< n$, $1\le k\le n$, and 
  $0\le m_i\le n$, $1\le i\le n$.
Let $m_{+}^{(J)}= \sum_{j=1}^Jm_j$ and
$m_{++}^{(J)}= \sum_{j=1}^Jjm_j$, with
$m_{+}^{(0)}=m_{++}^{(0)}=0$, 
$m_{+}=m_{+}^{(n)}=k$, $m_{++}=m_{++}^{(n)}=n$,
$k^{(J)}=k-m_{+}^{(J)}$ and 
$n^{(J)}=n-m_{++}^{(J)}$.
Let  $\mu_j$, $J+1\le j\le n$,  be positive constants with
$\mu_+^{(J)}=\sum_{j=J+1}^n \mu_j$.
Let $\bfm^{(J)}= (m_{J+1},\ldots,m_n)$ and 
  \ben
  A_{kn}^{(J)}=\Big\{m_j\ge 0, J+1\le j\le n: \,
 \sum_{j=J+1}^nm_j= k^{(J)},\, 
\sum_{j=J+1}^n jm_j=n- m_{++}^{(J)}\Big\},
\een
and let 
 $\big(X_{in}^{(J)}\big)_{1\le i\le  k^{(J)}}$ be i.i.d. with
\be
\PP\big(X_{1n}^{(J)}=j\big) =
\frac{\mu_j}{\mu_+^{(J)}},\ J+1\le j\le n.
\ee
Then 
\be
\sum_{\bfm^{(J)}\in A_{kn}^{(J)}}
\prod_{j=J+1}^n \frac{ \mu_j^{m_j}}{m_j!}
=
\frac{\big(\mu_+^{(J)} \big)^{ k^{(J)}}}
{k^{(J)}!}
 \PP\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{ k^{(J)}} X_{in}^{(J)}= n^{(J)}\Big).
\ee (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 9 of arXiv:2607.23401

DRAFT proof (unaudited), T318-C7 v2. For random features x_j(g)=[f_j dot g/sqrt(d)+10]/sqrt(p), independent f_j uniform on the radius-sqrt(d) sphere, independent Gaussian inputs, p/d->1/4 and n/p->gamma in (0,1/1000], let y=Xw_*+epsilon with independent w_*~N(0,4I_p), epsilon~N(0,I_n), prior N(0,I_p). Temper only the training likelihood by 1/T; retain original unit test noise. Conditional on input design/features and averaged over teacher/training noise/test input, the excess predictive log risk is L_p(T)=0.5 E_g[log(1+x Sigma_T x)+(1+x K_T x)/(1+x Sigma_T x)-1], Sigma_T=T(B+TI)^(-1), K_T=4T^2(B+TI)^(-2)+B(B+TI)^(-2), B=Xprime X; quadratic forms use xprime on the left. For each fixed M>0, inf_{0<T<=M} L_p(T)>=(log 2)/2+13/20-o_P(1). The predetermined T_n=(300/97)n has limiting risk (log 5)/2+9/250. Their strict gap exceeds 57/500 since log(5/2)<1. Thus every measurable o_P(1)-approximate global minimizer diverges in probability. The bounded-temperature lower bound uses K_T>=4P_ker(X), a uniform noncentral-Gaussian quadratic-form variance bound, and the sample-centering estimate 100 eprime Sigma_T e<=2T/n+2||zbar||^2. Growing T retains mean-direction predictive variance discarded at fixed T. This counterexample concerns teacher-averaged risk and optimization/limit exchange; it does not assert a realized-teacher result, the optimal escape rate, or failure of the fixed-T formulas. No novelty or independent-audit claim.

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] Let $\Zc$ be a complete metric space, and let $(\pi_n)_n\subset\Pc(\Zc)$.
Assume that there exists a Borel measure $\lambda$ on $\Zc$ such that, for every
$n\ge1$, the measure $\pi_n$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\lambda$,
with density
\[
f_n:=\frac{d \pi_n}{d \lambda}.
\]
Assume moreover that there exists $p>1$ such that, for every compact set
$K\subset\Zc$, there exists a constant $C_K>0$ satisfying
\vspace{-2mm}
\[
\|f_n\mathbf{1}_K\|_{\L^p(\lambda)} \le C_K,
\qquad
\text{for all }n\ge1.
\vspace{-2mm}
\]
If $\pi_n\to\pi$ weakly, then, for every bounded Borel-measurable function $g:\Zc\to\R$, 
\vspace{-2mm}
\[
\int_{\Zc} g(z)\,\pi_n(dz)
\longrightarrow
\int_{\Zc} g(z)\,\pi(dz).
\vspace{-2mm}
\]

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2606.29512, '2606.29512'] Let Assumptions \ref{assumption1a}, \ref{assumption2a} 
and \ref{assumption3a} hold. Then there is a constant $N=N(d,r,\kappa)$ 
such that if $u$ is an admissible solution to \eqref{NS3}--\eqref{bin3} 
satisfying 
$$
\tilde u+L<\delta/N,\quad \tilde u=\hat u+\esssup_{t\in[0,T]} \bar u_t,  
$$
then we have 
$$
\int_0^T|u_t-v_t|^2_{\cV}\leq \tfrac{1}{2\gamma}|u_0-v_0|^2_{\cH}
\quad\text{with} \quad \gamma:=\delta-N(\tilde u+L), 
$$
and 
$$
|u_t-v_t|_{\cH}\leq |u_0-v_0|_{\cH}e^{-\frc^{-2}\gamma t}
\quad 
\text{for $t\in[0,T]$}
$$
for any admissible solution $v$ to \eqref{NS} with zero boundary condition 
and initial condition $v_t|_{t=0}=v_0\in\cH$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A topological space is a pair (X, T) where X is a set and T is a collection of subsets of X, called the open sets, such that: (i) the empty set and X itself are open; (ii) the union of any family of open sets is open; (iii) the intersection of any finite family of open sets is open. A subset C of X is called closed when its complement in X is open. An open set containing a point x is called an open neighborhood of x.

$(q_*,v_*)\in\mathcal D$.  There are unique $s_{*,i}\in\mathbb R$ such that
\[
  H(s_{*,i})=q_*+\alpha\ip{x_i}{v_*}.
\]
Define
\[
  a_{*, i}=r(s_{*,i}),
  \qquad
  b_{*,i}=H(s_{*,i})=s_{*,i}+a_{*,i}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  b_{*}-R a_{*}=c\mathbf 1
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  \sum_{i=1}^m\log\Phi(s_{*,i})
  +\frac12a_{*}^{\mathsf T}(I_m-R)a_{*}
  \geq m\log\Phi(c).
\end{equation}

OWNER OWN WORK, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C007 v1. Fix C>sqrt(2), c>0, and any fixed C_out>0. For every sufficiently large fixed alpha depending on C, m=ceil(alpha*d), iid real a_i~N(0,I_d), deterministic unit signal x_*, eta=c/log d, and loss f(x)=(1/(4m)) sum_i ((a_i^T x)^2-(a_i^T x_*)^2)^2, with probability tending to one there exists a sample-dependent x0 at distance d^-10 from x_* with max_i |a_i^T(x0-x_*)|<=C sqrt(log d)||x0-x_*||, yet after one unmodified GD step |a_1^T(x1-x_*)|>C_out sqrt(log d)||x1-x_*||. The first iterate still has error O(d^-10), inside the local ball. Write a_i=g_i e1+b_i for e1=x_*, v=b_1/||b_1||, b_j=t_j v+c_j for j>=2, and z=(2/m)sum_{j>=2}g_j^2 1_{|g_j|<=1} t_j c_j. Take x0=e1+d^-10 z/||z||. Row-removal Gaussian tails prove initial incoherence; selected rows make v^T Hess f(e1) z/||z|| tend to 2sqrt(mu/alpha)>0, mu=E[G^4 1_{|G|<=1}]. Thus the Hessian produces a row-1 projection of order sqrt(d) although the original direction is exactly orthogonal to row 1. The nonlinear remainder is negligible at this radius. This refutes uniform preservation from initial relative incoherence for C>sqrt(2), not contraction assuming all-time incoherence, random-start convergence, or preservation for C<=sqrt(2). No novelty claim; independent review pending.

Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. with E[X_1] = 0, E[X_1^2] = sigma^2 in (0, infinity), and rho = E|X_1|^3 < infinity. Let S_n = X_1 + ... + X_n and let Phi be the standard normal distribution function. Then there is an ABSOLUTE constant C, not depending on the law of X_1 or on n, with sup_{x in R} | P( S_n / (sigma sqrt(n)) <= x ) - Phi(x) | <= C rho / ( sigma^3 sqrt(n) ). The rate n^{-1/2} is optimal in general: for a symmetric two-point law the Kolmogorov distance really is of order n^{-1/2} along a subsequence, because of the lattice jumps. Concerning the constant, successive work has pushed the best known value for the i.i.d. case below 0.5, while Esseen's own example gives the lower bound (3 + sqrt(10))/(6 sqrt(2 pi)), about 0.4097, so the optimal constant lies in a narrow window; NO specific numerical value should be quoted from this node. A non-identically-distributed version holds with rho replaced by sum_i E|X_i|^3 and sigma^3 sqrt(n) by (sum_i E X_i^2)^{3/2}. The third absolute moment is a real hypothesis: with only two moments the CLT still holds but no rate of this form does. [Berry (1941), Esseen (1942); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.4.17]

body: The axiom of choice (AC) states: for every family (A_i)_{i in I} of nonempty sets, indexed by a set I, there exists a function c on I with c(i) in A_i for every i. Equivalently, every family of nonempty sets admits a choice function selecting one member of each set; every Cartesian product of nonempty sets is nonempty; every surjection has a right inverse; and every set of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets has a transversal selecting exactly one element from each. Over Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory ZF, AC is equivalent to Zorn's lemma, the well-ordering theorem, and Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary compact spaces. AC asserts existence, not a specified construction; Zermelo formulated it in 1904 in order to prove the well-ordering theorem. AC is independent of ZF, assuming ZF is consistent: Godel (1938) established relative consistency of ZF+AC using the constructible universe, and Cohen (1963) established relative consistency of ZF+not-AC by forcing. Choice for every finite index set is a theorem of ZF. Choice for arbitrary countable families of nonempty sets is not provable in ZF in general.

The empty family has the empty choice function. Given a choice function on k indices and one further nonempty set A, there exists a in A; adjoining that one pair to the function gives a choice function on k+1 indices. This finite induction is not a simultaneous selection from infinitely many sets. The indexed and unindexed formulations are equivalent: a choice function on the set of members gives c(i) by evaluation at A_i; conversely apply the indexed form to a family indexed by its own members. A Cartesian-product element is exactly such a choice function. For a surjection, choose an element from each nonempty fiber to obtain a right inverse; conversely the projection from the disjoint union {(i,a):a in A_i} onto I has nonempty fibers, and a right inverse yields c(i). The same tagged disjoint union proves the transversal formulation. The deep Zorn/well-ordering/Tychonoff equivalences and independence results are retained standard results, not proved anew here.","provenance":"correction of claim_f0d630daf2b020660e71ada6912cbc65cadaabb956acfe1ff58ddf76f6278e47 (06 Oct 2026): merged with its duplicate in dedup group 63 (group04/B04 20261006T142000Z MERGE_PLAN.jsonl, second reading by w09, read again by claude-4a88bc43)","source_id":"wikipedia:Axiom_of_choice","supersedes":"claim_f0d630daf2b020660e71ada6912cbc65cadaabb956acfe1ff58ddf76f6278e47","trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: In the study of graph algorithms, Courcelle's theorem is the statement that every graph property definable in the monadic second-order logic of graphs can be decided in linear time on graphs of bounded treewidth. The result was first proved by Bruno Courcelle in 1990 and independently rediscovered by Borie, Parker & Tovey (1992). It is considered the archetype of algorithmic meta-theorems.

Status: proof draft (unaudited). No independent reviewer PASS, no established novelty/priority. This is a restricted square-2x2 statement, not a general T232 solution. The constituent analytic proofs must be audited; passing their finite algebra checks is insufficient.

## Exact proposed theorem
Let M be an invertible real 2x2 matrix, Sigma a real symmetric positive-definite 2x2 matrix, and suppose the singular values of M Sigma satisfy s1>s2>0. Fix a finite hidden width w>=2. Let B0 in R^(2xw), A0 in R^(wx2) have mutually independent standard Gaussian entries, fix that seed once, and for alpha->0 start the asymmetric factor flow
  B'=-G A^T, A'=-B^T G, G=(BA-M)Sigma
at (alpha B0,alpha A0). This is negative gradient flow for C(BA)=tr((BA-M)Sigma(BA-M)^T)/2, with the ordinary Euclidean factor metric.

For almost every fixed seed there are a balanced nonzero rank-one critical factor zstar=(bstar;astar), physical arrival times T_alpha>=0, positive numbers p_alpha->0, and fixed-in-time hidden orthogonal rotations Q_alpha such that, on every fixed compact shifted interval,
  [B_alpha(T_alpha+log(1/p_alpha)/s+t); A_alpha(T_alpha+log(1/p_alpha)/s+t)^T] Q_alpha
       -> Ustar(t).
Here s is the unique positive singular value of Gstar=(bstar astar^T-M)Sigma, and the canonical limit Ustar has only two nonzero columns. It is a complete nonconstant factor-flow connection from [zstar,0,...] at t->minus infinity to a finite global-minimizing factor at t->infinity with product M.

The actual arrival Grams satisfy Z_alpha(T_alpha)->Z1=zstar zstar^T and
  liminf [v^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)v / ||Z_alpha(T_alpha)-Z1||F]>0,
where v is the unit positive-growth residual vector. More precisely the chosen rotations give active parameter error O(p_alpha^2), dormant norm O(p_alpha), and dormant projected row norm p_alpha. Consequently a_alpha=v^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)v=p_alpha^2+O(p_alpha^4), so the Gram clock log(1/a_alpha)/(2s) is asymptotically equivalent to the displayed parameter clock.

No hypothesis of arrival alignment is imposed on the Gaussian seed. Sigma need not be a scalar matrix or commute with any target covariance. No gap assumption is imposed on the singular values of M Sigma^(1/2). The exclusion is the repeated origin singular value s1=s2, together with rank-deficient M or covariance. The first rank-one endpoint is allowed to be a saddle even within rank-one factors; the theorem does not incorrectly call every such endpoint a best rank-one product.

For ordinary data X in R^(2xN), Y in R^(2xN), this applies when XX^T is positive definite, M=YX^T(XX^T)^(-1) invertible, and the two singular values of YX^T/N are distinct, taking Sigma=XX^T/N. The irreducible least-squares residual adds a constant to the loss and leaves all gradients and strict energy comparisons unchanged.

## 1. First path and normalized inactive remnant
By C006 v2, the fixed seed can be rotated once so the positive top origin row occupies only the active hidden column. The first-escape shifted time is tau_alpha=log(1/alpha)/s1. On every fixed shifted compact interval,
  z_alpha(t)->zbar(t),
  X_alpha(t)/epsilon_alpha->chi(t)c2,
  epsilon_alpha=alpha^(1-s2/s1).
The top row is nonzero and c2, the projected second positive row, is nonzero almost surely: two orthogonal positive-origin eigenrows of an iid Gaussian matrix are independent Gaussian rows, and conditional projection onto the (w-1)-dimensional hidden complement is nondegenerate. This is a statement at initialization only. No independence of later evolving modes is used.

C008 v2 sharpens the active conclusion to z_alpha-zbar=O(epsilon_alpha) on these fixed compact intervals. Its proof cancels the exact active top coefficient and retains the O(alpha^3) canonical initial mismatch; this bound is needed below and is stronger than unquantified first-phase convergence.

## 2. The first path has a nonzero critical endpoint without assuming it is best
The rank-one path is balanced because its conserved scalar difference ||bbar||^2-||abar||^2 tends to zero backwards. Its product is bounded by decreasing loss and positive-definite Sigma, and the balance identity bounds both factors. Thus it is a bounded polynomial negative-gradient trajectory, hence converges to a stationary factor. The analytic finite-length argument is recalled below; no assumption of a discrete critical set is required.

The backward leading term is c1 exp(s1 t)v1 with c1>0, so the path is nonconstant. A gradient orbit cannot become stationary at a finite time without being constant by uniqueness. Therefore its loss at every finite time is strictly below its backward limit C(0). At its forward limit the loss remains below C(0), by choosing one fixed finite time first. The balanced zero product would force both rank-one factors to vanish, which would have loss C(0). Thus the limiting factor zstar is nonzero. The residual has rank exactly one: Gstar astar=0, Gstar^T bstar=0, and invertible M prevents Gstar=0. This proves s>0 and the simple positive residual direction.

This argument intentionally does not identify the endpoint as a best rank-one solution. The explicit diagonal example in C006 disproves that identification for all covariances. Exponential reference convergence is not needed, because C009 includes its convergence-only diagonal construction.

## 3. Local unstable cone entrance and strong actual arrival alignment
The ideal vectors zbar and chi meet C003's J-null geometry and graph determinant sign det M, as proved in C006 from their two distinct positive backward origin modes. C003 therefore gives chi/||chi|| tending to the positive residual eigendirection up to sign at this nonzero critical endpoint.

Choose a fixed late first-path time T0 so zbar remains in the required saddle neighborhood and chi(T0)c2 is strictly inside the C009 unstable cone. The fixed-compact conclusions of C006 and C008 give, at physical time tau_alpha+T0, dormant cone amplitude comparable to epsilon_alpha and active-reference error O(epsilon_alpha). C009 v2 then applies. Its spectral comparison is the strict inequality
  largest eigenvalue(Jact)<s,
not an assumption of active stability. The exact identity Jact=Lstar-T^*Sigma*T and the nonzero product response of the simple top frozen residual vector prove it even at a nonminimal rank-one endpoint.

The convergence-only diagonal thresholds in C009 provide later physical times T_alpha and dormant projected norms p_alpha->0 such that
  ||z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar||=O(p_alpha^2),
  ||X_alpha(T_alpha)||F=O(p_alpha),
  ||v^T X_alpha(T_alpha)||F=p_alpha.
They give both strong Gram alignment and the sharper parameter entrance estimates. All constants are uniform along the chosen threshold family for the fixed seed. No fixed-compact convergence is extrapolated to a growing interval: the actual local cone and active-error inequalities control that interval.

## 4. Parameter escape applies despite the multiple dormant top eigenvalue
At theta1=[zstar,0,...], the full factor Jacobian is symmetric and block diagonal with active Jact and w-1 copies of the frozen residual operator Lstar. Its full top eigenvalue is s, possibly of multiplicity w-1, because the active maximum is strictly below s. Rotate only the dormant hidden columns at T_alpha so the row v^T X becomes (p_alpha,0,...,0). This does not move theta1, and the rotation is fixed for the subsequent flow.

The complete top spectral projection is now EXACTLY p_alpha times a fixed unit vector u; all lower parameter components are O(p_alpha). C011 v2 proves weighted Volterra escape with arbitrary top multiplicity under precisely these hypotheses. Hence the shifted factors converge to a canonical Ustar(t) after log(1/p_alpha)/s. A published simple-top theorem is not used as if the multiplicity were one. The original seed rotation and this later dormant rotation compose to the Q_alpha stated in the theorem.

The canonical Volterra solution has only the active and first dormant columns nonzero, since that zero-extra-column subspace is invariant. Its backward form is
  z(t)=zstar+O(exp(2st)),
  x(t)=exp(st)v+O(exp(2st)).
The input/output parts of v are nonzero and perpendicular to astar/bstar. Therefore both square two-column factors have a nonzero determinant leading term of order exp(st); the canonical rank-two mode does not disappear in the limit. Exact conserved factor balance tends to its value zero at theta1, and the graph determinant is sign det M by the critical determinant identity. Nonconstant gradient descent gives loss below the first critical value, which itself is below C(0).

## 5. The canonical forward endpoint is global
C010 v2 now applies to the actual canonical width-two factor path at a sufficiently negative but finite time: both square factors are invertible, balanced, correctly oriented, and their loss is below C(0). That theorem gives boundedness and analytic factor convergence, excludes zero by energy, and excludes every rank-one stationary endpoint by positive asymptotic growth of the input determinant. Its remaining full-rank stationary product is M.

Thus the canonical second step is a complete saddle-to-global-minimum connection for this square-2x2 data class. Its incoming parameter limit is theta1 by the canonical backward expansion; its outgoing parameter limit is finite by C010. The clock equivalence and compact Gram convergence follow from the arrival estimates and continuous multiplication of factors.

## Analytic convergence ingredient used above
For a bounded analytic negative-gradient trajectory, the loss decreases to a limit ell. Bounded Hessian on its compact range makes the gradient norm uniformly continuous; its squared norm is integrable by energy dissipation, so the gradient tends to zero. Any cluster point is stationary and has loss ell. At one such point the local analytic gradient inequality has the form ||grad f||>=c|f-ell|^(1-theta), 0<theta<=1/2. Along a trajectory remaining in that neighborhood,
  -d/dt (f-ell)^theta >=c theta ||grad f||.
Take a sufficiently late cluster-near time for which the right-side integral length bound (f-ell)^theta/(c theta) is smaller than the distance to the neighborhood boundary. The trajectory cannot then exit; its finite-length tail is Cauchy and converges. This proof needs analyticity and boundedness, not merely existence of critical points. The local analytic gradient inequality is the standard ingredient also used in the cited Li-Luo-Lyu analytic-convergence discussion and explicitly in C002; a queued generic analytic-convergence card was found and not duplicated.

Let X be a real n by d matrix with ||X||_2<=R, let y=X*w_star, and let lambda>0. Put L(w)=||X*w-y||^2/2, B_lambda=(I_n+X*X^T/lambda)^(-1), and g_lambda(w)=(X*w-y)^T*B_lambda*(X*w-y)/2. Then g_lambda(w)=min_u {L(u)+(lambda/2)*||u-w||^2}, grad g_lambda(w)=X^T*B_lambda*(X*w-y), and argmin_u {L(u)+(lambda/2)*||u-w||^2}=w-(1/lambda)*grad g_lambda(w). The surrogate is convex, has minimum0 at w_star, and has gradient Lipschitz constant at most lambda*R^2/(lambda+R^2). For every w, g_lambda(w)<=L(w)<=(1+R^2/lambda)*g_lambda(w). These conclusions hold separately for every task and every positive time-dependent lambda_t; a common realizable w_star minimizes all the resulting surrogates.

LoRA-One (Zhang, Liu, Chen, arXiv:2502.01235) distinguishes alignment of vanilla zero/Gaussian LoRA from convergence under a changed initializer. Assumptions 2.1-2.3 use an exact low-rank shift, noiseless labels, isotropic sub-Gaussian linear-regression inputs and N>d. Theorem 3.1/C.10 gives the known zero-factor right-subspace invariant; Theorem 3.2/C.9 gives a small-Gaussian principal-angle alignment statement for the other factor, including an exact-ranked case. Appendix C.2 then assumes Spectral-init, with factors constructed from square roots of singular values and singular vectors of the full first gradient G=C Delta, so their initial product is G rather than zero. Theorem C.17, printed p.37, gives its linear fitting guarantee under that spectral initializer and explicit covariance/step restrictions. Theorem C.21 additionally requires Prec-GD. A Gaussian/zero fitting-time theorem cannot inherit these conclusions without verifying the changed initialization or optimizer. In positive-noise regression G is a generally full-rank sample cross matrix, so the source's exact rank(Delta)-dimensional noiseless invariant is not a noise-robust training theorem. The alignment results and fitting theorem have different conclusions and hypotheses; no literature-absence or whole-target-resolution claim is made.

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2606.25501, 'An RDT based approach to large deviations of Wishart and Wigner matrices spectral edges'] (\cite{Gordon85})
 Let $X_{ij}$ and $Y_{ij}$, $1\leq i\leq n$, $1\leq j\leq m$, be two centered Gaussian processes which satisfy the following inequalities for all choices of indices
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mE(X_{ii}^2)=\mE(Y_{ii}^2)$
\item $\mE(X_{ij}X_{il})\geq \mE(Y_{ij}Y_{il})$
\item $\mE(X_{ij}X_{lk})\leq \mE(Y_{ij}Y_{lk})$, $i\neq l$.
\end{enumerate}
 Then
\begin{equation*}
\mE(\min_{i} \max_{j} X_{ij})\leq \mE(\min_i \max_{j} Y_{ij}) \quad  \Longleftrightarrow \quad \mE(\max_{i}\min_{j} X_{ij})\geq \mE(\max_i \min_{j} Y_{ij}).
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

OWNER OWN WORK method record, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C015 v1. Standard Gaussian-conditioning technique; no specialist novelty asserted. For real A with iid N(0,1) entries, deterministic unit x_*, independent x_0, fixed eta>0 and quartic phase-retrieval GD x_(t+1)=x_t-(eta/m)A^T r_t, r_t=((Ax_t)^2-(Ax_*)^2) elementwise times Ax_t, let Q_t=[x_*,x_0,...,x_t], Y_t=AQ_t, M_t=[r_0,...,r_(t-1)], e_t=P_(M_t)^perp r_t and k_t=d-rank Q_t. Conditional on the chronological transcript through Ax_t, A^T r_t=(Q_t^dagger)^T Y_t^T r_t+||e_t||P_(Q_t)^perp z_t for fresh standard Gaussian z_t. When e_t!=0, K_t=||P_(Q_t)^perp A^T r_t||^2/||e_t||^2 is conditionally chi-square_(k_t). After revealing A^T r_t, with q=x_(t+1), the next forward query equals in conditional law Y_t Q_t^dagger q-(eta/m)K_t e_t+||P_(Q_t)^perp q||P_[M_t,r_t]^perp u_t, with fresh standard Gaussian u_t. If e_t=0 the next query is already known and the reaction term is zero. For deterministic finite T and delta in (0,1), L=log(2T/delta), all nondegenerate t<T satisfy |K_t-k_t|<=2sqrt(k_t L)+2L simultaneously with probability at least 1-delta. For m=ceil(alpha*d), the scalar reaction coefficient obeys |eta*K_t/m-eta/alpha|<=(eta/m)(2sqrt(d L)+2L+T+2+1/alpha). The history projection and cubic residuals are retained, not controlled; no escape or convergence theorem is proved. Proof idea: conditional Gaussian matrices are their minimum-norm constrained mean plus P_M^perp G P_Q^perp. Every earlier backward image belongs to span Q through the GD update, so the backward mean simplifies. After the next backward query, the minimum-norm dual of the new residual direction is e_t/||e_t||^2. Its projection onto the next GD query gives the displayed reaction term. Gaussian chi-square tails are conditioned on each chronological transcript and union-bounded over the deterministic horizon; no independence of adaptive K_t is assumed. No stopped Gaussian list is called iid. The full-history projection and residual-correlation bounds needed for escape remain unproved.
real standard Gaussian matrix; deterministic unit signal; x_0 independent of A
fixed positive GD step and the stated quartic normalization by 1/(4m)
chronological forward/backward linear-query transcript, enlarged by the signed Ax_* only for analysis; no conditioning on future events
orthogonal projectors and Moore-Penrose inverses; dependent query columns allowed; deterministic finite horizon cap

body: Ross's second conjecture (the mean workload of an M/G/1 queue in a Markov-modulated random environment is non-increasing in the environment's speed c) is false. With a 64-state cyclic environment (rates d = tan(pi/m) + eta, m = 64, covariance 4 + (1/2) e^{-dt} cos t), arrival modulation g injective over 64 values in (1,3) with mean 2, and service law U[0.99, 1.01], the second-order coefficient satisfies Delta = I_d(3 pi) - I_d(2 pi) = +0.0044 > 0 (2.64 times the required 1/600), so the mean workload increases between speeds 2 pi and 3 pi for arrival intensity eps below about 3.3e-4; the effect is about 1e-11 in absolute workload. The expansion E[V] = eps a b2/2 + eps^2 b1 (Int k_B) a^2 + R with R <= eps^3 M^3 b1^2 b2 / (2 (1 - eps M b1)) reproduces Pollaczek-Khinchine exactly in a constant environment with the remainder bound attained, and an exact QBD (exponential service) confirms it uniformly in c. The construction escapes Bauerle-Rolski (not reversible: detailed balance violated by 0.159) and Chang-Chao-Pinedo (row rates take two distinct values). Service criterion: a reversal needs H_B(s) = E[1 - cos(sB)]/s^2 non-monotone (Erlang-20 gives none; U[0.99, 1.01] does).

body:
[Thm optimali of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] {\bf (P-2)}
Consider the secretary problem
with the  Mallows distribution with $q=q_n\in(0,1)$ in the case that the largest number is  of highest rank..

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
n-M_n^*\sim\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
\noindent iii. Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*=n-L, \ \text{where}\ L \ \text{satisfies}\ \frac q{1-q}\le L<\frac 1{1-q}.
$$
The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=(1-q)q^{L-1}L>\frac1e.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defn def:smc of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] Let $(Y_{\ell})_{\ell\ge0}$ be a Markov
jump process on $(0,\infty)$ with the following dynamics. When $Y_{\ell}=y$,
the process waits an exponential time $r(y)=y$ before jumping,
at which time the process takes on
the new value $Y'=Uy+Z$, where $U\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ is the
recombination time on the current tree expressed as a fraction of
the tree height, and $Z\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ is the additional coalescence
time after the recombination event. 

Equivalently, one may construct $(Y_{\ell})$ from its embedded jump
chain and holding times as follows. Let $(X_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be the
jump chain and let $(E_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$,
independent of the chain. Given $X_{n}$, define the holding time
\[
\Delta\ell_{n}:=\frac{E_{n}}{X_{n}}\ \sim\ \mathrm{Exp}(X_{n}),
\]
and jump locations $\ell_{0}:=0$, $\ell_{n+1}:=\ell_{n}+\Delta\ell_{n}$.
Then define 
\begin{align}
Y_{\ell} & :=X_{n}\quad\text{for }\ell\in[\ell_{n},\ell_{n+1}),\nonumber \\
X_{n+1} & :=U_{n}X_{n}+Z_{n},
\end{align}
where $(U_{n},Z_{n})$ are i.i.d.\ with $U_{n}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$
and $Z_{n}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$. In particular, $(Y_{\ell})$ is almost surely
piecewise constant.
title: Sequentially Markov coalescent process

$\gamma$-avalanches may be coupled so that
\[
        r_N^\gamma(t)=r_\infty^\gamma(t)\wedge N.
\]
Consequently,
\[
        R_N^\gamma(t)
        =\mathbb{E}[r_\infty^\gamma(t)\wedge N]
        \uparrow R_\infty^\gamma(t),

        P_N^\gamma(t)
        =\mathbb{P}(r_\infty^\gamma(t)\geq N)
        \downarrow P_\infty^\gamma(t).
\]
On $\{r_\infty^\gamma(t)<N\}$ the two avalanches have the same duration.

Given an outer measure mu* on X, call a set E measurable (in Caratheodory's sense) if it splits every test set additively: mu*(A) = mu*(A ∩ E) + mu*(A ∩ E^c) for all A subset X. The collection of measurable sets is a sigma-algebra, and mu* restricted to it is a complete (countably additive) measure. Consequently a premeasure on an algebra extends to a measure on the generated sigma-algebra (used to build Lebesgue measure).

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:06bdf48cee34086f60bc0c9383563e692549d4b18552ade27d28fc71c00ee29c","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/06/06bdf48cee34086f60bc0c9383563e692549d4b18552ade27d28fc71c00ee29c.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:48287783b52d19f42a15e24da3ee41b38593d085dc0ad02fc5fe89c55f0315bf","bundle_entry_key":"full-column","bundle_id":"population.t419-lora-all-scale-square-input-and-expected-risk-scope-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"LoRA factor gradient descent","draft":"w705/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-full-column-population-gd-all-gaussian-scales","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C012 v1: population GD at every scale for full-column-rank targets

Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim.
This covers an entire dimension family and initialization interval, but it is the full-input-rank subfamily; the low-rank case r<d_in at moderate/large scale remains open in this work. The techniques are elementary imbalance and descent estimates. Related primary initialization results were consulted; the Springer 2024 source was inaccessible beyond its landing response, so literature coverage and novelty are unresolved. The result must not be advertised as a new published theorem or a solution of the whole row.

## Statement

Let Delta be an m-by-r real matrix, m>=r>=1, of exact rank r and ||Delta||op=1. Let 0<rho<1, c=10r/rho, and let s>0 be arbitrary. Initialize B0=0 of size m-by-r and A0 of size r-by-r with iid N(0,s^2) entries. Define

 h=s^2/(c^2 r), H=4c^2 r^2 s^2,
 K=2 sqrt(r) H+4r,
 0<eta<=min{h/(4r), 1/(6K+1)}.

For simultaneous constant-step GD on f(B,A)=(1/2)||BA-Delta||F^2, with probability at least 1-rho over A0, for every integer t>=0,

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F <=sqrt(r) exp(-eta h t/4).

Thus for 0<eps<1 it suffices to take

 t>=ceil[(4/(eta h)) log(sqrt(r)/eps)].

Unlike C003 this statement places no upper or lower restriction on s. It requires d_in=r, so it does not address learning a proper input-side rank-r subspace. The bound has no dependence on sigma_r(Delta) after normalization; fitting a full-column-rank product with an invertible square input factor does not require resolving an unobserved input subspace. For an unnormalized target with lambda=||Delta||op, use s_bar=s/sqrt(lambda), eta_bar=eta lambda, and error eps_bar=eps/lambda in the normalized statement.

## Initial event

Use only the square-Gaussian part of C004, not its optional small-scale Loewner comparison. With probability at least 1-rho,

 sigma_min(A0)>=2s/(c sqrt(r)),
 ||A0||F<=2crs.

Consequently, with D0=A0 A0^T,

 D0>=h I, ||D0||F<=||A0||F^2<=H.

These inequalities hold for every s>0. The Gaussian density/column-distance and Markov argument in C004 is scale-independent. Fix this event for the rest of the proof.

## Exact imbalance identity and a factor-size bound

Put E=BA-Delta, G_B=E A^T and G_A=B^T E. Simultaneous GD gives the exact cancellation

 D_next-D=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 D=A A^T-B^T B.

Hence ||D_next-D||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

For arbitrary factors let P=B^TB and Q=AA^T, both r-by-r positive semidefinite. The trace Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and direct expansion give

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 =tr(P+Q)^2 <= r tr((P+Q)^2)
 =r [||P-Q||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

Here tr(P+Q)^2 means the square of the scalar trace, whereas tr((P+Q)^2) is the trace of the squared matrix. This identity does not require P and Q to commute.

Whenever f<=f0 and ||D-D0||F<=h/4, one has ||BA||F<=||Delta||F+sqrt(2f0)<=2sqrt(r), and

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2
 <=sqrt(r) sqrt[(H+h/4)^2+16r]
 <=2 sqrt(r) H+4r=K.

The last inequality uses h<=H and sqrt(x^2+y^2)<=x+y for nonnegative x,y. The initialization satisfies this factor bound as well.

## Descent without a circular boundedness assumption

Inductively suppose the factor-pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have the descent inequality. At the current point,

 ||grad f||F<=||E||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(K/2+1)sqrt(K).

Therefore eta<=1/(6K+1) makes the proposed next point have pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The entire connecting segment lies in that ball. Throughout that ball,

 ||B||op^2+||A||op^2<=4K,
 ||BA-Delta||op<=2K+1,

so the factor Hessian has norm at most 6K+1. This follows by expanding its quadratic form as ||dB A+B dA||F^2+2<E,dB dA>. Thus ordinary smooth descent along this segment yields

 f_next<=f-(eta/2)||grad f||F^2.

Summing the valid descent inequalities, including this proposed step, gives

 sum_(j<=t) eta^2||grad f_j||F^2<=2eta f0<=eta r<=h/4.

The exact imbalance identity then gives ||D_next-D0||F<=h/4. The next point also has f_next<=f0, so the preceding factor-size bound shows its pair norm is actually at most sqrt(K), closing the induction. This argument justifies the required segment bound before using the resulting factor bound at its endpoint.

## Uniform gradient domination and rate

For every iterate,

 D>=D0-(h/4)I >=(3h/4)I,
 AA^T=D+B^TB >=(3h/4)I.

Since A is square, right multiplication by A^T is bounded below on every residual matrix:

 ||grad f||F^2>=||E A^T||F^2
               >=(h/2)||E||F^2.

Combining this with descent gives

 ||E_next||F^2 <=(1-eta h/2)||E||F^2.

The factor is nonnegative because h<=H<=K and eta<=1/(6K+1). Since ||E0||F^2=||Delta||F^2<=r, iteration and 1-x<=exp(-x) prove the statement.

## Essential scope and boundaries

For a rectangular A of size r-by-p with p>r, AA^T positive definite does not imply ||E A^T||F>=sqrt(h/2)||E||F for arbitrary m-by-p residual E. Residual directions orthogonal to A's row space can be annihilated. This is the precise point where this proof fails for genuinely low-rank input adaptation, so the argument must not be extended to that case silently.

The scale s=0 is excluded: both factors would remain zero. The result includes r=1, m=r, all positive scales, and every full-column-rank target condition number. No finite precision, asymptotic random-matrix formula, probability multiplication or independence among iterates is used. Only the original Gaussian initial event is probabilistic; everything after it is deterministic. Independent audit and prior-work novelty checks remain pending.

body: A probability distribution \mu on \mathbb{R} (or random variable X) is said to be infinitely divisible if for every integer n \ge 1, there exist i.i.d. random variables Y_{n, 1}, \dots, Y_{n, n} such that \sum_{k=1}^n Y_{n, k} has distribution \mu. Equivalently, the characteristic function \phi(t) of \mu has an nth root \phi_n(t) for every n \ge 1 that is itself a valid characteristic function.

For any metric D on X and 0<a<1, D^a is a metric with the same topology and dim_H(X,D^a)=dim_H(X,D)/a. If D_{h+c}=exp(xi*c)D_h for constant c, then D_{h+c}^a=exp(a*xi*c)D_h^a, so the product xi*dim_H is unchanged. This shows that constant-shift covariance alone cannot determine metric dimension. It is not a second LQG metric: every continuous path from 0 to 1 in the snowflaked Euclidean interval has infinite D^a-length, by the first hitting times of levels k/n and partition sums n^(1-a). Thus the LQG length-space and pathwise Weyl axioms are outside this countermodel.
D is a metric
0<a<1
only reduced constant-shift covariance is tested, not full strong-LQG axioms
title: Snowflaking preserves reduced scaling while changing dimension

body: In complex dynamics, the Julia set and the Fatou set are two complementary sets defined from a function. Informally, the Fatou set of the function consists of values with the property that all nearby values behave similarly under repeated iteration of the function, and the Julia set consists of values such that an arbitrarily small perturbation can cause drastic changes in the sequence of iterated function values. Thus the behavior of the function on the Fatou set is "regular", while on the Julia set its behavior is "chaotic".
title: Julia set

The Random Connection Model (RCM) simplicial complex $\Delta$ is constructed inductively: (0) The vertex set is the set of points of $\Phi$; (1) For each pair of points $x, y \in \Phi$, the edge $\{x, y\}$ is added independently with probability $\varphi_1(x, y)$; (k) For $j \in \{2, \dots, \alpha\}$ and any $(j+1)$-tuple $\{x_0, \dots, x_j\} \subset \Phi$ all of whose proper subsimplices have been added to $\Delta$, the $j$-simplex $\{x_0, \dots, x_j\}$ is added independently with probability $\varphi_j(x_0, \dots, x_j)$.

[Corollary t:cltspindisag1 of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] (CLT for sum of spins on Poisson-Boolean model)
Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a stationary Poisson process on $\mathbb{R}^d$ of intensity \(\rho\) and $K$ be a compact set containing the origin and with a non-empty interior. Let  \(\Psi = \Psi(\cdot)\) be the Poisson-Boolean graph induced by the Poisson-Boolean model on \(\mathcal{P}\), as described above. Consider a spin configuration model with the Gibbs distribution given by (equation eqn:gibbs of the paper), defined on the graph~\(\Psi\) and with finite spin space $\mathbb{K}$.
Assume that for some \(\epsilon > 0\), the maximum influence (equation defq of the paper) satisfies
\[
q(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n)) < \min \{1, \rho_c / \rho\} - \epsilon
\]
almost surely for all $\mathcal{P}_n$, for all large enough $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and where $\rho_c$ is the critical intensity for percolation of the Poisson-Boolean model.
Under these conditions, the spin model \(\{V_x(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n))\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}_n}\) satisfies the central limit theorem as stated in Theorem~(spinmain of the paper), provided that the moment and variance conditions specified in the theorem are also met. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary t:cltspindisag1 of arXiv:2605.28430

body: Without hub diagonal, 2 X_h (L + beta) + 2 eps L P = 2 (L + beta)(X_h + eps P) - 2 eps beta P, so Y = X_h + eps P is a hub whose conditional density given the light coordinates is at most 1 and depends on them only through P. For Q = 2 Y (L + beta) + lambda (V - v_c(L, P))^2 + F(L, P) with such a hub, L, V, P orthonormal projections of independent coordinates with densities at most 1, t = l + beta, c = 2 sqrt 2 |lambda|^{-1/2} and a(l, p) = sup_v rho_{L,V,P}(l, v, p): ||p_Q||_inf <= 1/2 + int int_{|t| <= 1} min(rho_{L,P}(l, p), c a(l, p) |t|^{1/2}) dl dp/(2|t|). Proof: given X' the form is affine in Y; for fixed (l, p) the bathtub step of Proposition S bounds int f(y|p) dv/(2|t|) by sqrt 2 (|lambda| |t|)^{-1/2}; |t| > 1 contributes at most 1/2. Windowed corollary: 1/2 + int r(p)(2 + 2 log_+(c a(p)/r(p))) dp with r, a the suprema over |l + beta| <= 1. This covers the single hub with no hub or light diagonal and linear terms in span(w, v, q^), uniformly in eps. The windowed form is NOT bounded under the (0.1) leverage condition alone: w = (e1+e2)/sqrt2, q^ = (e1-e2)/sqrt2, v = (e3+e4)/sqrt2 and two combs with incommensurate spacings of order N^{-1/2} give int r = 3.9, 7.5, 22.6, 83.7 at N = 64..4096, while the sharp form stays bounded (V independent of (L, P)) and Proposition 3.15 covers that configuration. Open: is the sharp form bounded uniformly under w_i^2 + v_i^2 + q^_i^2 <= 1/2? A yes settles the no-diagonal single hub for every eps.

[Lemma prob0 pure of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Assume that $\xi$ is pure $p$-spin. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Let $u\in(0,1)$, $q\in(0,1)$, $f\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $\zeta\in \mathrm{Prefix}_2(u,q)$ where $\mathrm{Prefix}_2$ is as in Definition (def:nprefix of the paper).
		
		Let $\delta\in[\varepsilon,1)$ and $\mathbf{m}\in[-1+\delta,1-\delta]^N$. Suppose moreover that $q_\mathbf{m}\in (q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon)$ and
		$\mathrm{dist}\!\bigl(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\,\zeta|_{(q,1]}+\zeta([0,q])\,\delta_q\bigr)<\varepsilon$.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item  The gradient $\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})$ is a non-degenerate Gaussian vector in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Its log-density at $0$, tilted by
			\[
			u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right),
			\]
			satisfies
			\begin{multline}
				\log \varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				+u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right)
				\\
				=
				\frac{1}{2}N\xi(q)u^2
				-\frac{1}{2}N\xi''(q)\!\left(\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t\right)^{\!2}
				-\frac{1}{2\xi'(q)}
				\Vert \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})-u\xi'(q)\mathbf{m}\Vert^2
				\\
				-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi \xi'(q))
				+\frac{N(p-1)}{2p\,\xi'(q)\,q}
				\!\left(
				\frac{1}{N}\langle \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m}),\mathbf{m}\rangle
				-\xi'(q)\int_0^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				\right)^{\!2}
				\\
				-u\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)+N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)+Nf\right)
				+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right).
			\end{multline}
			
			\item  Suppose moreover that
			\begin{equation}
				\langle \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m}),\mathbf{m}\rangle
				=
				N\xi'(q)\int_0^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t+O(N\varepsilon)
			\end{equation}
			and
			\begin{equation}
				\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(h_\zeta(q,m_i)-\partial_m h_\zeta(q,m_i)m_i\bigr)
				+N\int_0^q t\xi''(t)\zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				+\frac{N}{2}\int_q^1 t\xi''(t)\zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				=
				-Nf+O(N\varepsilon).
			\end{equation}
			Then the squared term in (equation eq:pure-prob0-main of the paper) is $O(N\varepsilon)$, so that 
			\begin{multline}
				\log \varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				+u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right)
				\\
				=
				\frac{1}{2}N\xi(q)u^2
				-\frac{1}{2}N\xi''(q)\!\left(\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t\right)^{\!2}
				-\frac{1}{2\xi'(q)}
				\Vert \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})-u\xi'(q)\mathbf{m}\Vert^2
				\\
				-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi \xi'(q))
				-u\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)+N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)+Nf\right)
				+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right),
			\end{multline}
			and, on the event $\{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0\}$,
			\begin{equation}
				F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right).
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate}

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked; reduction plus asserted conditional, not a solution] Svante Janson's Problem 18.39 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510, asks whether Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability is possible in the condensation regime 0 < nu < lambda. Janson conjectures that it is not possible for the full sequence and, more strongly, that there are always epsilon > 0 and a subsequence along which Y_(1) >= epsilon n w.h.p. (Example 18.36 gives Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability along a subsequence.) Setting: let w_k >= 0 with w_0 > 0, let Phi(z) = sum_k w_k z^k have radius rho in (0,infinity) with Phi(rho) < infinity, and put pi_k = w_k rho^k/Phi(rho), a law with generating-function radius one and finite mean nu > 0. Let m_n/n -> lambda > nu. (Y_1,...,Y_n) is n i.i.d. pi variables conditioned on sum m_n, Y_(1) = max_i Y_i, and M = (lambda-nu)n. Heuristic rate: carrying M in r = M/a boxes of size a has class weight binomial(n,r) pi_a^r up to the bulk's fluctuation, giving log P = M Lambda(a) + o(M) with Lambda(a) = [log pi_a + log(a/(lambda-nu)) + 1]/a. For pi_k ~ c k^(-beta) and for pi_a = exp(-a^gamma), 0<gamma<1, Lambda increases on large a, so the optimum is a = M (one box), matching the known condensation picture. Since limsup_a Lambda(a) = 0 and Lambda < 0 for large a, Lambda has infinitely many upper records a_1 < a_2 < ... (Lambda(a_j) > Lambda(a) for all a < a_j). The record asserts, as author-checked and with no proof given beyond reference to an analogous step for Problem 18.40 in a companion memo, the following Proposition: if for some epsilon > 0 and every C, along infinitely many records, Lambda(a_j) - max_{a <= epsilon a_j} Lambda(a) > C a_j^(-1/2), then along n_j = a_j/(lambda-nu), P(Y_(1) >= ((lambda-nu)/2) n_j) -> 1, so the conjecture holds. Caveat: the only derivation offered is the heuristic rate with an o(M) error, which is coarser than the order sqrt(a_j) resolution this hypothesis requires, so the record does not establish the Proposition. The record poses the open Question whether, for every law pi on Z_{>=0} with radius one and finite mean, [log pi_a + log a]/a has infinitely many records with gap exceeding a_j^(-1/2) below max_{a <= epsilon a_j} for some fixed epsilon > 0. This is not a proved equivalence with the conjecture. A negative answer would only give a candidate counterexample, still requiring proof that the allocation spreads. The Question's normalisation and fixed threshold also differ from the Proposition's hypothesis. The problem remains open. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The allocations are defined along sizes with positive conditioning probability.
0 < nu < lambda and the boundary-tilted law pi has generating-function radius one.

[Corollary 18 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] Assume that $\mu\in{\cal S}$ and its $\alpha$-potential $R_\alpha\mu$ belongs to $L^\infty(E;m)$ for  all $\alpha>0$. 
Then for any compact set $K\subset E$, the restricted measure $1_K\mu$ is of finite energy integral; that is, $1_K\mu \in \mathcal{S}_0$.

In particular, if $\mu(E) < \infty$, then $\mu$ itself belongs to $\mathcal{S}_0$, which further implies that $\mu \in \mathcal{S}_{00}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 3 (Regeneration at a level) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] Suppose that the $t$-avalanche has finite range $I$. Conditionally on
$\mathcal H_t$, its terminal fitnesses are independent and have the form
\[
        F_x=t+E_x,\qquad x\in I,
\]
where the $E_x$ are independent $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ variables,
independent of $\mathcal H_t$. Consequently, when the threshold is raised
above $t$, the next triggering level occurs at rate $|I|$, its location is
uniform on $I$, and the subavalanche attached there is independent of
$\mathcal H_t$ and has the law of an avalanche at the triggering level.
