Let K be a compact topological space and f_n : K -> R continuous. Suppose the sequence is monotone in n at every point (f_n(x) <= f_{n+1}(x) for all n and all x, or the reverse for all n and all x), that f_n -> f pointwise, and that the limit f is continuous. Then f_n -> f UNIFORMLY on K. All four hypotheses carry weight: (a) compactness - on the non-compact [0,1) the sequence f_n(x) = x^n decreases continuously to the continuous limit 0 but not uniformly; (b) continuity of the limit - on the compact [0,1] the same f_n(x) = x^n is monotone and continuous with a discontinuous limit and the convergence is not uniform; (c) monotonicity - the moving bump f_n which is the piecewise-linear tent of height 1 on [1/(n+1), 1/n] and 0 elsewhere on [0,1] converges pointwise to 0 with all data continuous and compact, but sup |f_n| = 1; (d) continuity of each f_n - on [0,1] the indicators of the OPEN intervals, f_n = 1_{(0, 1/n)}, decrease pointwise to the identically zero function, which is continuous, on a compact space, so every hypothesis except the continuity of the f_n holds, yet sup |f_n| = 1 for every n. Monotonicity is required POINTWISE IN THE SAME DIRECTION for all x, not merely that each f_n is a monotone function of x. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.13]
K compact
each f_n continuous
for each x the sequence f_n(x) is monotone in n, in the same direction for every x
the pointwise limit f is continuous

body: Implicit function theorem (planar case): Let F be a real-valued function that is continuously differentiable on an open subset of R^2 containing a point (a, b), with F(a, b) = 0 and F_y(a, b) = (partial F / partial y)(a, b) nonzero. Then there are open intervals I containing a and J containing b and a unique continuously differentiable function g : I -> J such that g(a) = b and, within the rectangle I x J, the solution set of F(x, y) = 0 is exactly the graph {(x, g(x)) : x in I}; moreover g'(x) = -F_x(x, g(x)) / F_y(x, g(x)). Example: for F(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 1 (the unit circle) at (a, b) = (0, 1) one gets g(x) = sqrt(1 - x^2), the upper semicircle; no such g exists near (1, 0), where F_y = 0. General version: if F : R^{n+m} -> R^m is C^1 near (a, b), F(a, b) = 0, and the m x m Jacobian of F with respect to the y-variables at (a, b) is invertible, then near (a, b) the equation F(x, y) = 0 determines a unique C^1 map y = g(x) with g(a) = b and F(x, g(x)) = 0.

[Theorem thm:zero-terminal-bochner of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Suppose Assumptions~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper) and
(ass:bochner-regularity of the paper) hold.  Let $w$ be a regular weight and let
$I=(r_0,r_1)$.  If $q\in\mathfrak C_{\rm B}(I,w)$ and $F=\mathcal Pq$, put
$
 E_q(t):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|\nabla^{g_t}q(t)|_{g_t}^2\,\mathrm d\mu_t.
$
For every $s\in(r_0,r_1)$ preceding the terminal gap,
\begin{equation}
 4\left\lVert F\right\rVert_{w;(s,r_1)}^2
 =4\left\lVert D_t^cq\right\rVert_{w;(s,r_1)}^2
  +\norm{\operatorname{Hess}_gq}_{w,g;(s,r_1)}^2
  +\int_{(s,r_1)\times\mathbb R^d}
     \mathscr R_{w,t}(\nabla^gq,\nabla^gq)\,\mathrm d\mathfrak m
  +2w(s)E_q(s).
 
\end{equation}
Consequently, suppose that for some $0\leq\theta<1$ every
$q\in\mathfrak C_{\rm B}(I,w)$ satisfies, on each
$I_s=(s,r_1)$,
\begin{equation}
 \int_{I_s\times\mathbb R^d}\mathscr R_{w,t}(\nabla^gq,\nabla^gq)\,\mathrm d\mathfrak m
 \geq-\theta\norm{\operatorname{Hess}_gq}_{w,g;I_s}^2,
 
\end{equation}
Then the Hessian constant satisfies
\begin{equation}
 C_{w,I}(X)\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-\theta}}.
 
\end{equation}

[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2609.01166, 'Nonparametric inference for density-dependent McKean--Vlasov diffusions'] Assume that Assumptions~\ref{ass:potential} and~\ref{ass:coefficient} and the conditions of
Lemma~\ref{lem:dnn} hold, and
let $\widehat\Xi_n$ be the full MLE over the graded ReQU sieve \(\cX_m\) defined in \eqref{eq:smooth-dnn-sieve}. Fix \(c_a<\kappa\) and choose \(\ve>0\) such that \(\Xi_0(0)-\ve>c_a\). Finally, let \(M_n=v_\star+C_{tr}\log n\) with some \(C_{tr}>0\) such that \(C_{tr}c_a>1\).
Then with probability at least 
\(
(1-\delta)(1-\tau_0(M_n))^n

\)
it holds that
\begin{multline}
 \KL(\pi_0\Vert\pi_{\widehat\Xi_n})\\
 \leq C_\mathrm{or}
 \left( 
 m^{-2(\beta+1)} +\frac{b_n(m\log n+\log(1/\delta))}{n} +d_m(M_n)+\bar R_m(M_n) 
 \right),
\end{multline}
where
\(C_\mathrm{or}
=C(C_\mathrm{KL},
C_\mathrm{ent}, 
C_\mathrm{st},c_\infty,
C_\mathrm{tr})\) 
is a fixed constant, and
\(b_n=O(1)\) in the compact case and \(b_n\leq O(\log n)\) in the non-compact one.
Choosing \(m\asymp\left(n/(b_n\log n)\right)^{1/(2\beta+3)}\) yields
\begin{equation}
 \KL(\pi_0\Vert\pi_{\widehat\Xi_n}) = O_{\Prob}\left( (b_n\log n/n)^{2(\beta+1)/(2\beta+3)} \right).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem 1.1 of arXiv:2607.29403, 'Strong invariants and Tverberg numbers in convexity spaces'] Let $(X,\mathcal{C})$ be a convexity space and let $d\geq 1$. body: Let X be a square-integrable function of independent coordinates and let X^L denote X with the coordinates in a block L replaced by an independent copy. Then (X, X^L) is an exchangeable pair, and E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 Var(X) - 2 Cov(X, X^L). Consequently E[(X - X^L)^2] <= 4 Var(X) always, and E[(X - X^L)^2] <= 2 Var(X) whenever Cov(X, X^L) >= 0. The identity requires no independence beyond that of the resampled block and no structure on X beyond square-integrability.

body:
[Proposition 14 (Simplicity, positivity, monotonicity, analyticity) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Let $M(\theta)$ have entries $M_{d,d'}(\theta)=m_*q(d')p_{d,d'}(\theta)$, with $\theta\mapsto p_{d,d'}(\theta)$ real-analytic (it is a ratio of analytic Wald integrals \eqref{eq:wald}).
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Krein--Rutman is unnecessary.) $\rho(M)$ is a simple, isolated eigenvalue with a strictly positive right eigenvector $\psi$ and left eigenvector $\phi$, by the Perron--Frobenius theorem for irreducible nonnegative matrices.
\item (Monotonicity.) $\rho(M)$ is nondecreasing in each entry of $M$, strictly so under irreducibility, since $\rho(M)=\lim_n\|M^n\|^{1/n}$ and $M^n$ is entrywise monotone.
\item (Analyticity and the gradient.) $\theta\mapsto\rho(M(\theta))$ is real-analytic on the region where $M$ is irreducible (a simple eigenvalue of an analytic matrix family is analytic, Kato \cite{Kato66}, finite-dimensional case, with no eigenvalue crossing at the top because the Perron root is simple and isolated), and
\[
\partial_{\theta_i}\rho(M)=\frac{\phi^\top(\partial_{\theta_i}M)\psi}{\phi^\top\psi}\qquad(\ne0\text{ generically, since }\partial_{\theta_i}M\ge0\text{ with a positive entry}).
\]
\item (Operator van den Driessche--Watmough lift is unnecessary.) Writing $M=FV^{-1}$ with $V=\diag(\alpha_d)$ and $F$ the $m\times m$ fertility block, the finite-dimensional next-generation theorem \cite{vdDW02} gives directly: $s(J)<0\Leftrightarrow\rho(M)<1$ and $s(J)>0\Leftrightarrow\rho(M)>1$, where $J=F-V$ is the linearised drift and $s(\cdot)$ its spectral abscissa.
\end{enumerate}

# Third conditional cumulant: an exact source countercheck

Claim T244-w691-C054 v1. Kind: moved. Target: 3. Status: proof (unaudited).
The source correction requires the reviewer's independent audit. It does not
reopen the audited diffusion law or certify C053's uniform expansion.

## Statement and source locator

Hanin, arXiv:2204.01058, Corollary 3.4, equation (3.16), prints the
nonlinear contribution to the normalized sixth output cumulant as
`-(3/8) T_{4,1} (chi_parallel kappa_4)^2`.
With the source's definitions (3.12), (3.14), the correct contribution is
`+(3/4) T_{4,1} (chi_parallel kappa_4)^2` to leading order at fixed depth.
This is a sign and factor error, not an ordinary-versus-normalized
cumulant convention. An exact two-layer polynomial example below
contradicts the printed formula at order n^-2.

Worker source-reading claim, worker visually checked PDFp45; EXCLUDED from reviewer PASS; allocation count is worker-derived: the missing contribution can be located inside the source's own expansion:
equation (9.4) includes `3 kappa_4^2/(2^4 4!)` times the fourth power
of the sum of coordinate Laplacians. In its application to X1 X2 X3
at the end of Section 9, the three allocations (2,1,1) of those four
Laplacians have total multinomial multiplicity 36. They contribute

    (3*36)/(16*24) kappa_4^2 C_W^3
                      <partial^4 X> <partial^2 X>^2
      = (9/8) T_{4,1} (chi_parallel kappa_4)^2.

That order-n^-2 term is absent from the displayed evaluation of
C_W^3 E[X1 X2 X3] immediately before the end of Section 9.
Adding it to the retained -3/8 term gives +3/4. Thus (9.4) itself
already contains the correction; it is dropped when that formula is used.

For the critical tanh scalar chain, the corrected recurrence gives

    lim_{ell -> infinity} ell^-2 lim_{n -> infinity}
      n^2 kappa_3(K_ell) / q_ell^3 = 16/15,
    q_ell = lim_{n -> infinity} E K_ell.

The limits are in this order: width first at every fixed depth, then depth.
This independently agrees with the Brownian functional's small-t coefficient;
no interchange of these two limits is asserted. Worker source-reading claim, visually checked PDFp19 and EXCLUDED from reviewer PASS: the printed C6=28/15 in
Corollary 4.1, (4.12), is instead reproduced by the printed erroneous term.
No claim concerning the printed eighth-cumulant coefficient is made here.

## Conditional calculation

Let K' = n^-1 sum_i X_i(K), where conditional on K the samples are iid.
Write f(q)=E X(q), s(q)=Var X(q), r(q)=kappa_3(X(q)). The exact law of
total cumulance is

    kappa_3(K') = kappa_3(f(K))
                  + (3/n) Cov(f(K),s(K)) + (1/n^2) E r(K).

At a fixed layer put q=lim E K, a=lim n Var K, c=lim n^2 kappa_3(K).
Then the leading coefficients obey

    q' = f(q),
    a' = f'(q)^2 a + s(q),
    c' = f'(q)^3 c + 3 f'(q)^2 f''(q) a^2
                           + 3 f'(q) s'(q) a + r(q).                 (1)

To check the nonlinear coefficient directly, center Delta=K-E K.
The quadratic part of f(K)-E f(K) is
`f''(q)(Delta^2-E Delta^2)/2`. Its contribution to the third centered
moment is
`(3/2) f'(q)^2 f''(q) [E Delta^4-(E Delta^2)^2]`.
At this order E Delta^4=3a^2/n^2+o(n^-2), giving the coefficient +3.
In Gaussian activation notation, differentiation under the Gaussian integral
gives chi_parallel=f', T_{4,1}=4f'', and T_{2,2}=2s'. Thus (1) gives
`+(3/4) T_{4,1} (chi_parallel a)^2`, whereas (3.16) gives -3/8.

For tanh all the required fixed-layer expansions are justified without a
depth-uniform claim. Start with deterministic K0>0; induction over a fixed
finite number of layers gives centered moments of order p bounded by
O(n^-p/2) for even p, and the usual paired leading fourth moment.
Conditional sample-mean moment identities and Taylor expansion around each
strictly positive deterministic q establish the induction. Tanh is bounded;
on the complement of a fixed neighborhood of q, use an arbitrarily high
even moment and boundedness to make the contribution o(n^-2). Inside it,
derivatives of f,s,r are bounded. The leading Gaussian fourth-moment
identity is preserved by the linear conditional innovation and follows by
the conditional fourth-moment identity. Terms of degree five or higher
are o(n^-2). This proves existence of a,c and (1), without assuming a
uniform-in-depth expansion or exchanging width and depth limits.

## Exact finite-n counterexample

Take sigma(z)=z^2, zero bias, Gaussian weights of variance 1/n and
initial preactivation variance one. This activation is smooth with
polynomially bounded derivatives, as required in the source. If
S_i=n^-1 sum_j Z_{ij}^4, the exact scalar chain is

    K1=S1,    K2=S1^2 S2,

with S1,S2 independent. Here q1=3, a1=96, c1=9504;
f(q)=3q^2, s(q)=96q^4, r(q)=9504q^6.
Exact iid Gaussian moment enumeration gives

    kappa_3(K2) = 169851168/n^2 + 16456504320/n^3
      +812822169600/n^4 +24773968723968/n^5
      +399858181668864/n^6 +2861591250862080/n^7.

Equation (1) gives 169851168 for the first coefficient. The printed
recurrence gives 89229600, a difference of 80621568 at order n^-2,
which cannot be absorbed by its fixed-depth O(n^-3) remainder.
This is deterministic exact rational arithmetic, not Monte Carlo.
The script also checks n=1 against the direct product Z1^8 Z2^4 law.

## Critical tanh large-depth coefficient

For X(q)=tanh(sqrt(q) Z)^2, Gaussian Taylor integration gives

    f(q)=q-2q^2+O(q^3), f'=1-4q+O(q^2), f''=-4+O(q),
    s(q)=2q^2+O(q^3), s'=4q+O(q^2), r(q)=8q^3+O(q^4).

These differentiated expansions follow either from the Gaussian heat
identity or Taylor's theorem with Gaussian-integrable remainders. Since
0<f(q)<q for q>0, q_ell decreases to zero. Reciprocation yields
1/q_(ell+1)-1/q_ell=2+O(q_ell), hence ell q_ell -> 1/2.

Consequently the variance recursion in (1) becomes

    a_(ell+1)=(1-4/ell+o(1/ell)) a_ell
                       +(1/2+o(1))/ell^2,

so ell a_ell -> 1/6. Substituting this in the third recursion gives

    c_(ell+1)=(1-6/ell+o(1/ell)) c_ell
                       +(2/3+o(1))/ell^2,

because the nonlinear and covariance forcings are respectively
`-12/(36 ell^2)` and `1/ell^2`; the conditional third cumulant is O(ell^-3).
Thus ell c_ell -> 2/15, and c_ell/(ell^2 q_ell^3) -> 16/15.

For completeness, the scalar recurrence fact used twice is: if
x_(ell+1)=(1-b/ell+o(1/ell))x_ell+(d+o(1))/ell^2, b>1,
then ell x_ell -> d/(b-1), for any fixed initial value. Set y_ell=ell x_ell;
subtract d/(b-1), and bound the absolute deviation eventually by
`(1-(b-1-epsilon)/ell)` times itself plus epsilon/ell.
Iterating gives limsup deviation <= epsilon/(b-1-epsilon), then let
epsilon decrease to zero. The multipliers are positive eventually;
no sign assumption on x is needed.

Using the printed coefficient instead changes the nonlinear forcing from
-1/3 to +1/6, hence d becomes 7/6, ell c_ell becomes 7/30, and the
normalized coefficient becomes 28/15. This identifies precisely how the
source discrepancy propagates into (4.12).

## Verification and remaining audit

`scripts/third_cumulant_source_check.py` computes the entire finite-n
polynomial using partial Bell polynomials and exact Fraction arithmetic.
Its log is `logs/third_cumulant_source_check.json`. It checks the
conditional-recursion coefficient, disagreement with the printed source,
the n=1 identity, and independently enumerated raw moments at n=1,2,3
through degree six. The asymptotic recurrence argument above is a
mathematical proof draft; the algebra script does not certify it. No Lean
certificate is claimed. Reviewer audit is required before promoting the

OWNER OWN WORK method record, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C017 v1; no specialist novelty asserted. Let nested H_t support A_(t+1)=A_t-eta b_t-eta D_t with predictable A_t,b_t, H_(t+1)-measurable conditionally mean-zero D_t, and a predictable budget B_t on which E[D_t^2|H_t]<=eta^2 C/m. Fix positive eta,gamma,a,epsilon, m>=1, C>=0 and finite deterministic T. Before reaching |A_t|>=epsilon, an update is valid when B_t holds, A_t!=0 and beta_t=1-eta b_t/A_t>=rho=1+gamma eta. Let F be the event of an invalid update before the hit and before T. If T>=max(0,ceil(log(2epsilon/a)/log rho)), then P(max_(0<=t<=T)|A_t|<epsilon)<=P(|A_0|<a)+P(F)+2eta^3 C/(gamma m a^2). Predictably stopping at invalid updates or a hit, extending multipliers by rho after stopping, and defining P_(t+1) as their product yields a normalized-noise martingale with E[M_T^2]<=eta^4 C/[m(rho^2-1)]. No independence of growth multipliers and earlier noise is required. For m=ceil(alpha*d), eta=c/log d, a=1/(sqrt(d)log d), fixed positive constants and fixed target epsilon, T=O(log^2 d) suffices and the displayed noise-probability term is O(1/log d). Actual-path budget survival, positive drift and initial-small-signal probabilities are not bounded. In the C016 GD specialization, A_0=x_*^T x_1, not x_*^T x_0. No unconditional escape theorem follows. Proof: divide the stopped signal update by the predictable positive product P_(t+1). Normalized increments have conditional variance at most eta^4 C/(m rho^(2t+2)); summing the geometric series and applying the squared-martingale maximal inequality bounds the chance that normalized noise cancels half the initial signal. Until stopping, A_n/P_n=A_0+M_n, so the remaining signal grows by at least rho each step. No future product is pulled through conditional expectation. No probability bound for actual-path budget failure or initial-small-signal events is supplied.

Let mu be a positive measure (sigma-finiteness is not needed), f in L^1(mu) complex-valued, g >= 0 in L^1(mu), nu = f mu and lambda = g mu. Then nu << lambda if and only if f = 0 mu-almost everywhere on Z = {g = 0}. When this holds, q = (f/g) 1_{g > 0} is in L^1(lambda), d nu = q d lambda, |nu| << lambda and d|nu|/d lambda = |q|. On a measurable set E, the restrictions satisfy nu_E << lambda_E if and only if f = 0 mu-almost everywhere on E n Z, with density q 1_E. For nonnegative a, b in L^1(mu), the measures a mu and b mu are mutually absolutely continuous if and only if {a > 0} and {b > 0} agree up to mu-null sets. A common dominating measure is not enough: with mu Lebesgue measure on [0, 1], lambda = 1_[0,1/2] mu and nu = 1_(1/2,1] mu are both << mu, but lambda((1/2, 1]) = 0 while nu((1/2, 1]) = 1/2. Example: g = 2 on [0, 1/2] and 1 on (1/2, 1], f = 3 + 4i then -5 + 12i give d nu/d lambda = (3 + 4i)/2 then -5 + 12i, d|nu|/d lambda = 5/2 then 13, and ||nu|| = 9.
mu is a positive measure
f in L^1(mu) is complex-valued and g in L^1(mu) is nonnegative

Let each f(.;z):R^d->R be convex and beta-smooth, beta>0, and let a common x_star minimize f(.;z) over R^d for every z. Let F(x)=E_z f(x;z) be well-defined. For an iid sequence z_1,...,z_T and fixed x_1, run x_(t+1)=x_t-eta*grad f(x_t;z_t), with constant 0<eta<2/beta. For every integer T>=2, E[F(x_T)-F(x_star)] <= 3*||x_1-x_star||^2/[eta*(2-beta*eta)*T^(1-beta*eta/2)]. In particular eta=1/beta gives 3*beta*||x_1-x_star||^2/sqrt(T). The output is x_T in this indexing. This is an upper bound, not a matching lower bound, and does not claim the same rate for sampling without replacement or for non-interpolating losses.

[Theorem thm:explicit_density of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be an ergodic diffusion with invariant measure $\mu$ whose
symmetric part $\mathcal{L}_S$ satisfies the Poincar\'e inequality~(equation eq:poincare of the paper)
with spectral gap $\lambda_\mathrm{gap}>0$ (by Assumptions~(ass:dynamics of the paper)). 
Let $\overline{\rho}_t(V)$ denote the empirical density according to Definition~(def:empirical_density of the paper)
with ergodic mean $\E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t(V)]=\E^\mu[V]$,
and let $\nu\ll\mu$ with $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu\in L^2(\mu)$.
Then for all $t > 0$ and $a > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{\rho}_t(V) - \E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t] \geq a\right)
  \leq
  \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
  \exp\left[-t \frac{\tilde\sigma_\rho^2}{c_\rho^2} h\left(\frac{c_\rho a}{\tilde\sigma_\rho^2}\right)  \right],
  
\end{align}
where $h(u) \equiv 1 + u - \sqrt{1 + 2u}$ and we define 
\begin{align}
  \tilde\sigma_\rho^2 \equiv \frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(V)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}},
  \qquad
  c_\rho \equiv \frac{\|V - \E^\mu[V]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}.
\end{align}

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Let X in R^d be centered, Cov(X)=b I_d with b>0, E||X||^10<infinity, and let G be independent standard Gaussian. For s>=0, I(X;sqrt(s)X+G)=dbs/2-db^2s^2/4+(db^3/6-||cum3(X)||_F^2/12)s^3+(-db^4/8+b||cum3(X)||_F^2/4-||cum4(X)||_F^2/48)s^4+R(s), where |R(s)|<=2688 E||X||^10 s^5. Cumulants use ordered indices. This is a finite-dimensional expansion with an explicit remainder, not a size-uniform expansion of the extensive-rank limit. The derivative coefficients are known from Nguyen (arXiv:2303.02500); the draft derives a crude explicit remainder by posterior replica streaming.
Finite dimension d>=1
Centered input, isotropic covariance b I with b>0
Finite absolute tenth moment
Independent standard Gaussian noise

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:de904624f38253ac48750f202fbbab5e2b734d0668f97125393d0e49e788b8aa","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/de/de904624f38253ac48750f202fbbab5e2b734d0668f97125393d0e49e788b8aa.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:2f3275b96176775d8eb5dc40419f498be81655f87995faf6f4fc0f29ccdd72c9","bundle_entry_key":"finite-tenth-moment-mi-cumulant-remainder-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-finite-moment-and-orbit-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:finite-tenth-moment-mi-cumulant-remainder-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Gaussian-channel fourth-cumulant expansion with a tenth-moment remainder

Target 1. Proof draft, unaudited; novelty not established. This is a
finite-dimensional result. The bound below does not justify exchanging
the small-SNR limit and the extensive-rank limit.

Let X take values in R^d, have mean zero and covariance b I_d with b>0,
and satisfy E||X||^10<infinity. Let G be independent standard Gaussian.
Write K3 and K4 for its third and fourth joint cumulant tensors, with
ordered indices and Euclidean tensor norms. Then, for s>=0,

 I(X;sqrt(s)X+G)
  = db s/2 - db^2 s^2/4
    + (db^3/6-||K3||^2/12)s^3
    + (-db^4/8+b||K3||^2/4-||K4||^2/48)s^4 + R(s),       (1)

    |R(s)| <= 2688 E||X||^10 s^5.                         (2)

The cumulant definition is
K3_ijk=E Xi Xj Xk and
K4_ijkl=E Xi Xj Xk Xl-b^2(delta_ij delta_kl+
delta_ik delta_jl+delta_il delta_jk).

## A. Posterior streaming for bounded signals

First suppose X is bounded. Use the Brownian observation process
Y_t=tX+B_t, where B is a standard Brownian motion independent of X.
For t>0, Y_t/sqrt(t) has the Gaussian-channel distribution in (1).
The observation path has sufficient statistic Y_t: its posterior is

 pi_t(dx)=exp(x.Y_t-t||x||^2/2) mu(dx)/Z_t(Y_t).

Here mu is the law of X. Put m_t=pi_t(x). Applying Ito's formula to
this ratio gives, for every bounded function h,

 d pi_t(h) = [pi_t(hx)-pi_t(h)m_t].dW_t,
 dW_t=dY_t-m_t dt.                                      (3)

The innovation W is Brownian in the observation filtration: its
conditional drift vanishes and its quadratic variation is t I_d.
Bounded X makes the integrands bounded, so the martingales used below
are true martingales and expectations of their stochastic integrals
vanish.

Write <f>_t for integration of f(x^1,...,x^n) under pi_t^tensor n.
In the equations below the outer expectation over observations is
written explicitly as E<...>.
Let R_ab=x^a.x^b. The Ito product rule applied to the n posterior
measures gives

 d/dt E<f> = E<f A_n>,

 A_n = sum_{1<=a<b<=n} R_ab
       -(n-1) sum_{a=1}^n R_{a,n+1}
       + n(n-1) R_{n+1,n+2}/2.                           (4)

For clarity, the pair (a,b) in the product rule contributes
(x^a-m_t).(x^b-m_t). The first term gives R_ab; across all
pairs each x^a.m_t occurs n-1 times; each ||m_t||^2 is
represented by two additional posterior replicas. Thus (4) follows
without assuming that posterior replicas are unconditionally independent.
Polynomial f on bounded support is a finite sum of products of
one-replica functions, so the product rule applies directly to every
polynomial used here.

Define F(t)=E||m_t||^2=E<R_12>. Starting with P_0=R_12, define

    P_{k+1}=P_k A_{2k+2},

using two fresh replica labels at every step. Equation (4) implies
F^(k)(t)=E<P_k>. When differentiating a polynomial using at most
2k+2 labels it is legitimate to include any unused labels: their
posterior integrals are one.

The sum of absolute coefficients of A_n is

    n(n-1)/2+n(n-1)+n(n-1)/2=2n(n-1).

Therefore the sum of absolute coefficients of P_k is at most

    product_{j=1}^k [2(2j)(2j-1)]=2^k (2k)!.             (5)

Every monomial of P_k is a product of k+1 inner products. Its absolute
value is at most a product of replica norms of total degree 2k+2.
Each replica has marginal law mu after averaging the observations:
E pi_t(h)=E h(X). Generalized Holder, without independence, gives

    |F^(k)(t)| <= 2^k (2k)! E||X||^(2k+2).               (6)

This is uniform in t>=0 but not in dimension through the moment.

## B. I-MMSE and the exact finite polynomial at t=0

For completeness the required I-MMSE identity follows within the
same Brownian model. The density of Y_t relative to N(0,t I_d) is
Z_t(Y_t). Hence

    I(t)=t E||X||^2/2-E log Z_t(Y_t).

Ito gives d log Z_t=m_t.dY_t-||m_t||^2 dt/2. Since
E[m_t.X]=E||m_t||^2 by conditional expectation,

    I'(t)=[E||X||^2-F(t)]/2.                            (7)

In particular (6), with k=4, bounds

    |I^(5)(t)| <= 2^3 8! E||X||^10 = 322560 E||X||^10.  (8)

At t=0 all replicas are independent with law mu. A monomial having a
replica vertex of degree one vanishes by centering. The remaining
multigraphs of P_1,P_2,P_3 are listed below; coefficients include every
labeling, with cancellation. The complete recursion is implemented
using integer arithmetic in scripts/replica_coefficients.py and its
output is logs/replica_coefficients.json. The recursion generates every
term of A_2,A_4,A_6,A_8; none is sampled or discarded except by exact
coefficient cancellation. Degree-one graphs are discarded only for
evaluation at t=0.

 P_1: double edge, coefficient 1, value tr(C^2)=db^2.

 P_2: triangle, coefficient -2, value tr(C^3)=db^3;
      three parallel edges, coefficient 1, value ||K3||^2.

 P_3: four parallel edges, coefficient 1, value ||M4||^2;
      doubled star on three vertices, coefficient -6,
          value b^2 E||X||^4;
      two disjoint doubled edges, coefficient 3, value d^2 b^4;
      four-cycle, coefficient 12, value d b^4;
      triangle with one doubled edge, coefficient -12,
          value b||K3||^2.

Here C=b I_d and M4=E X^tensor 4. Each contraction is obtained by
writing R_ab=sum_i x_i^a x_i^b and integrating the independent replicas.
For example, the doubled triangle contracts its degree-two vertex
using b delta_ij and leaves b times the squared norm of the third
moment tensor. The doubled star contracts its two degree-two leaves
and leaves b^2 E||X||^4. This checks where isotropic covariance is used.

To convert the raw fourth moment to the fourth cumulant, let
W_ijkl=delta_ij delta_kl+delta_ik delta_jl+delta_il delta_jk.
Then <M4,W>=3 E||X||^4 and ||W||^2=3d(d+2). Consequently

    F(0)=0,
    F'(0)=db^2,
    F''(0)=-2db^3+||K3||^2,
    F'''(0)=6db^4-12b||K3||^2+||K4||^2.                (9)

Equation (7) gives all coefficients in (1). Taylor's integral remainder
and (8) give 322560/5!=2688 in (2). No infinite power series is assumed.

## C. Passage to finite tenth moment

The same argument first proves the expansion for bounded signals
with arbitrary positive-definite covariance C: equations (4)-(8)
are unchanged, and the coefficients at zero are finite polynomials in
joint moments of order at most eight. This observation permits a
truncation passage without differentiating an unbounded posterior.

Alternatively retain exact isotropy as follows. For B sufficiently
large set

 T_B=X 1_{||X||<=B},
 Z_B=T_B-E T_B,
 C_B=E Z_B Z_B^T,
 X_B=sqrt(b) C_B^(-1/2) Z_B.

C_B tends in operator norm to b I_d, so it is positive definite for
all sufficiently large B. Functional calculus gives
sqrt(b)C_B^(-1/2) -> I_d. Thus X_B is bounded, centered and has
covariance b I_d; also X_B -> X in L^10. In particular its joint
moments through order ten converge to those of X. This construction
does not require symmetry.

For each fixed t>=0 the mutual informations also converge. Indeed
Y_B=sqrt(t)X_B+G -> Y=sqrt(t)X+G in L^10 under the same G, and
the convolution densities p_B(y) converge pointwise to p(y), since
the Gaussian kernel is bounded and continuous. A fixed ball contains
at least half the probability mass of every X_B, by their common
second moment db. Hence, uniformly in sufficiently large B,

    p_B(y)>=c exp(-C(1+||y||^2)),
    p_B(y)<=(2pi)^(-d/2)<1.

Thus -p_B log p_B <= C'(1+||y||^2)p_B. The fourth moments of Y_B
are uniformly bounded (indeed the tenth moments converge), so the
integrals of this upper bound outside a large ball tend uniformly to
zero. On each ball dominated convergence applies. It follows that
h(Y_B)->h(Y), hence I(X_B;sqrt(t)X_B+G)->I(X;sqrt(t)X+G).

Passing to the limit in the bounded-signal inequality proves (1)-(2)
under E||X||^10<infinity. This passage is at fixed finite d and fixed t;
there is no unproved exchange with the extensive-rank limit.

## D. Matrix product and the first appearance of prior fourth moments

Let X_ij=N^(-1/2) sum_{r=1}^M U_ir V_jr, with independent factor
arrays, centered iid entries of variance one, and finite absolute
tenth moments. Here d=NP and b=M/N. No symmetry assumption is needed.
Finite dimensionality and finite factor tenth moments imply the
tenth-moment hypothesis in (1).

The third cumulant is nonzero only when all three entry indices
coincide. Thus

    ||K3||^2 = NP M^2/N^3 (E U^3 E V^3)^2.                (10)

The fourth-cumulant norm is formula (7) in bounded_prior_expansion.md,
valid here with q_U=E U^4, q_V=E V^4; its derivation uses moments only.
Substituting these expressions in (1) and dividing by NP supplies
the requested explicit finite-size expansion through the first order
where prior fourth moments enter, including nonzero third moments.
The remainder is at most 2688 E||X||_F^10 s^5/(NP).

A wholly explicit factor-moment bound is available without evaluating
the whole vector moment. Let mu_10,U=E|U|^10 and similarly for V.
Convexity gives

    E||X||_F^10 <= (NP)^5 M^10 N^(-5) mu_10,U mu_10,V.    (11)

Indeed (sum_{ij}X_ij^2)^5 <= (NP)^4 sum_{ij}|X_ij|^10,
and |sum_{r=1}^M U_ir V_jr|^10 <= M^9 sum_r |U_ir V_jr|^10.
All denominators in (10)-(11) are positive since N,P,M>=1.

Under fixed aspect ratios the prior-dependent terms displayed in
(1)/(NP) vanish as N->infinity. The remainder bound (11) grows with
size; it therefore leaves the principal frontier question unpaid:
does a prior-dependent coefficient survive at some higher fixed order,
or is there a low-SNR universal interval? This result does not answer
that question and does not prove Gaussian-factor extremality.

Checks that can fail: the Brownian posterior drift in (4), the full
finite replica enumeration, the K3 correction when symmetry is absent,
the factorial in the integral remainder, and the unbounded-prior
entropy continuity argument. Exact finite algebra is certified by the
saved script; the analytic arguments require independent review.

## Prior literature

The vector derivative formulas themselves are known: Minh-Toan Nguyen,
"Beyond the I-MMSE relation: Derivatives of mutual information in
Gaussian channels", arXiv:2303.02500v3 (25 August 2024), Theorem 1,
PDF pp.5-6, gives an all-order conditional-moment formula. Its Examples
2-5 include the second through fourth derivatives. Dongning Guo,
Yihong Wu, Shlomo Shamai, Sergio Verdu, arXiv:1004.3332, Section IV,
equation (61), PDF p.10, already gives the scalar third-order MMSE
expansion in the dossier. No novelty is claimed for these coefficients.
The purpose of the derivation above is an explicit finite-tenth-moment
remainder and its application to the joint matrix-product cumulants.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:8f63ff0321a76b62e9dac113608ece73cd7dca48d071ce1c705e60d4b4dbfd27","revision_digest":"sha256:ca2e07b31ea4080c48eb31f1bdc9f06d087b85647bda98a4eedb375143c2749b","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:finite-tenth-moment-mi-cumulant-remainder-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

holds for all $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$:

\begin{align*}
&\sup_{\nu \in (0,1)} \left\{ \max_{0 \le t \le T^*} \|z_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\varepsilon,\!\nu$}}}(t)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2
+\varepsilon \left( \sup_{0 \le t \le T^*} \|\nabla z_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\varepsilon,\!\nu$}}}(t)\|_{\bm{L}^2(\Omega)}\right)^2\right.\\
&\hspace*{2cm}\left.+\varepsilon^2 \int_0^{T^*} \|z_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\varepsilon,\!\nu$}}}(t)\|_{H^2(\Omega)}^2
+\int_0^{T^*} \|z_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\varepsilon,\!\nu$}}}'(t)\|_{L^2 (\Omega)}^2dt \right\} \le C_{16}.
\end{align*}

[Theorem 17 (Distribution of RSK shape) of arXiv:2606.18047, 'Analysis of the asymmetric shelf shuffle'] Let $\pi\sim\nu^{(p)}_{n,m}$. If $Q$ is a standard Young tableau of shape $\lambda\vdash n$, then
\[
\Pbb\{Q(\pi^{-1})=Q\}=S_{\lambda}^{(m,p)}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\Pbb\{\operatorname{sh}(\pi)=\lambda\}=f^{\lambda}S_{\lambda}^{(m,p)},
\]
where $f^{\lambda}$ is the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$.

[Cor probability of exploration processes of arXiv:2605.03151, 'Giants through Higher-Order paths in Random Simplicial Complexes'] Let $X_n \sim \MRSC_d(n; \bm{p})$ with the assumptions ((eq: 1.3.1 assumption 1 of the paper)) and ((eq: 1.3.2 assumption 2 of the paper)). Then, conditional on $\mathcal{X}_{k-1}$, the number of new forward $(d-1)$-simplices at each step $k$, denoted by $F_k$, satisfies
\[  \tag{3.2.27}
F_k \geq_{\mathrm{st}} d \mathsf{Bin} \left( n - s_0(\mathcal{X}_{k-1}), p_k^F \right),
\]
and the number of new backward $(d-1)$-simplices at each step $k$, denoted by $B_k$, satisfies
\[  \tag{3.2.28}
B_k \geq_{\mathrm{st}} d \mathsf{Bin} \left( s_0(\mathcal{X}_{k-1}) - C \sum_{\ell = 1}^{d-1} \max_{\rho \in S_{\ell -1}(\mathcal{X}_{k-1}} \deg_{\ell -1, d-1}^{\mathcal{X}_{k-1}}(\rho), p_k^B \right),
\]
where the constant $C > 0$ only depends on $d$. Furthermore, conditional on $\mathcal{X}_{k-1}$, $F_k$ and $B_k$ are independent, and it holds that
\[  \tag{3.2.29}
F_k + B_k \geq_{\mathrm{st}} d  \mathsf{Bin} \left( n - C \sum_{\ell = 1}^{d-1} \max_{\rho \in S_{\ell - 1}(\mathcal{X}_{k-1})} \deg_{\ell - 1, d-1}^{\mathcal{X}_{k-1}}(\rho), \min\{p_k^F, p_k^B\} \right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is the proved elementary covering-code reduction for Afonso S. Bandeira's Open Problem 11, How many deviations are needed afterall?, in Did just a couple of deviations suffice all along? (problems 10-14), Randomstrasse 101 (19 December 2024; https://randomstrasse101.math.ethz.ch/posts/HowManyDeviations/). For an n-by-n matrix A with entries in {+1,-1}, define disc(A)=min_{x in {+1,-1}^n} ||Ax||_infinity, where ||y||_infinity=max_i |y_i|, and let D_n=max_{A in {+1,-1}^{n-by-n}} disc(A). For r,x in {+1,-1}^n let d_H(r,x) be the number of differing coordinates and let the complement of r be -r. For an integer v in [0,n] with the same parity as n, |r dot x|>=v exactly when d_H(r,x)<=(n-v)/2 or d_H(-r,x)<=(n-v)/2. Thus disc(A)>=v exactly when the rows of A and their complements cover the sign cube within radius (n-v)/2. For a complement-closed nonempty code C contained in {+1,-1}^n, define its covering radius rad(C)=max_x min_{c in C} d_H(x,c), and define rho_n as the minimum of rad(C) over such C with at most 2n codewords. Then D_n=n-2rho_n. If K(n,R) is the least number of unrestricted binary codewords of length n covering the cube within an integer radius R, K(n,R)<=n certifies D_n>=n-2R, while K(n,R)>2n rules out D_n>=n-2R. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
Integer n>=1; the threshold v has the same parity as n.
Codes may have at most 2n distinct codewords; repeated matrix rows are allowed.

body: [Lemma distribution:hitting0 of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] Let $(S_x,x\ge 0)$ be a ${\rm BESQ}(\delta_1\, |_r\, \delta_2)$ process starting at $0$ with $\delta_1>0$, $\delta_2<2$ and $r>0$. Let $T:=\inf\{x\ge r: S_x=0\}$. Then $\frac{r}{T}$ has the beta distribution $\mathcal{B}(\frac{2-\delta_2}{2},\frac{\delta_1}{2})$. In particular, the distribution of $\frac{r}{T}$ does not depend on $r$.

F_k(r) denotes P(||Z||<=r) for Z standard Gaussian in R^k; chi_k is this radius law.

T358-C2 v1 [independently checked proof]: For G_y(z)=y(b+a|z|), a,b>0, the exact robust Bayes accuracy is 1 for epsilon<=b and 1/2+Q(2(epsilon-b)/a) for epsilon>b. Nearest-image accuracy is 2Q((epsilon-b)/a), strictly smaller for every epsilon>b. For injective bent generators G_y(z)=(s z,y(b+a|z|)), s>0, nearest-image remains sign(x_2), and the same strictly better shifted-threshold accuracy is attained. For b<epsilon<=2b both classifiers have perfect clean accuracy. Scope: Exact-version independent PASS received. Original scope restrictions remain; no priority claim. For T358-C9 the exact excluded-region optimum remains open.

T358-C12 v1 [proof (unaudited)]: For equal-prior scalar radial Gaussian maps G_y(z)=y(b+a||z||), a>0,b>=0,z standard Gaussian in R^k, robust Bayes accuracy at e>b is 1-1/2 min_{p in [0,2t]}[F_k(p)+F_k(2t-p)], t=(e-b)/a. For k>=2 nearest-image is exactly optimal iff e<=b+a sqrt(k-1). Above that phase boundary the two shifted thresholds with d in (0,t) satisfying (k-1)log((t+d)/(t-d))=2td attain strictly better accuracy. This is the scalar zero-horizontal-embedding case of reviewer route c, not a solution of the full injective family. Scope: Independent review required; no novelty or scored frontier move claimed. Nonzero horizontal embedding and excluded asymmetric V exact transport remain open.

T358-C16 v1 [proof (unaudited)]: For every k>=2, equal-prior radial Gaussian generators G_y(z)=(s z,y(b+a||z||)), a>0,0<s<=a,b>=0, have exact robust Bayes accuracy 1 for e<=b. For every e>b, define D(r,q)=s^2(r-q)^2+(2b+a(r+q))^2, R0 by D(R0,0)=4e^2, psi(r) by D(r,psi(r))=4e^2, and m=min_{0<=r<=R0}[F_k(r)+F_k(psi(r))]. Then maximum close coupling mass is m and robust Bayes accuracy is 1-m/2. A partial radial CDF reflection and a closed tube around a truncated positive image attain the two optima. Nearest-image is optimal iff m=2F_k((e-b)/a). For t=(e-b)/a>sqrt(k-1) a shifted vertical hyperplane strictly improves on nearest-image for every s>0. Scope: Independent audit and literature priority remain open. Exact one-dimensional minimum, not elementary minimizer classification. Does not settle s>a or general two-piece-linear generators; no scored move claimed.

T358-C17 v1 [proof (unaudited)]: For every integer k>=2, equal-prior homogeneous Gaussian radial cones G_y(z)=(a z,y a||z||), a>0,z~N(0,I_k), have exact robust Bayes and coupling phase as follows. For k=2 and t=e/a>0, A*=(1+exp(-t^2))/2 and c*=1-exp(-t^2); nearest-image is strictly suboptimal. For k>=3 nearest-image is optimal exactly when t^2<=k-2, with A*=1-F_k(t),c*=2F_k(t). Above that threshold, the unique d in (0,t^2) solving (k-2)log((t^2+d)/(t^2-d))=2d gives c*=F_k(sqrt(t^2-d))+F_k(sqrt(t^2+d)) and A*=1-c*/2>1-F_k(t). At e=0 A*=1. Scope: Independent audit and literature priority remain open. Exact homogeneous equal-slope radial family, not arbitrary two-piece-linear generators; positive-offset or unequal-slope minimizer classification remains open. No scored move claimed.
T358-C18 v1 [proof (unaudited), equal-prior radial extension]: Let k>=2, Z|Y=y~N(0,I_k), P(Y=+1)=P(Y=-1)=1/2, G_y(z)=(s z,y(b+a||z||)), a,s>0,b>=0. Use closed Euclidean adversarial balls of radius e>=0 and measurable classifiers with measurable robust-correct indicators. For e<=b, A*=1 and c*=0. For e>b put t=(e-b)/a and let F be the chi_k CDF. Define D(r,q)=s^2(r-q)^2+(2b+a(r+q))^2; N(q)={r in [0,t]:D(r,q)<=4e^2}, C(q)=P(||Z|| in N(q)). There is a unique R*>t with min_{0<=r<=t}D(r,R*)=4e^2. Set x*=min_{t<=q<=R*}(F(q)-F(t)+C(q)). Then maximal close coupling mass c*=F(t)+x*, and robust Bayes accuracy A*=1-(F(t)+x*)/2. The proof constructs both coupling marginals explicitly by capacity quantiles; an attaining classifier is a closed e-tube about the positive image whose radii lie in the relative closure of the complement of N(q*) for a minimizing q*. Nearest-image is optimal iff x*=F(t). This extends the earlier C16 slope restriction; C16 and C17 remain retained in the linked compendium. C18 has no independent PASS, no novelty claim, and does not solve anisotropic horizontal maps, unequal priors or arbitrary two-piece generators.
T358-C19 v1 [proof (unaudited)]: In the same radial Gaussian family with arbitrary prior p in [0,1], the centered nearest-image classifier is strictly suboptimal whenever e>b and p!=1/2; e<=b gives accuracy 1. For 1/2<p<1 put t=(e-b)/a,m=1-p,M=2(k-1)/t+3t/2 and delta=min(t/2,log(p/m)/(4M)). The threshold c=-a delta on the last ambient coordinate improves accuracy by at least (sqrt(pm)-m)(F_k(t+delta)-F_k(t))>0. Reflect for a negative majority; endpoint priors use constant classifiers. This gives an explicit improvement, not the exact weighted optimum; independent review and priority remain open.
T358-C20 v1 [proof (unaudited)]: For integer k>=2, conditional standard Gaussian latent, arbitrary prior p in [0,1], a>0,0<s<=a,b>=0 and G_y(z)=(s z,y(b+a||z||)), exact robust Bayes accuracy is 1 for closed Euclidean radius e<=b. For e>b let D(r,q)=s^2(r-q)^2+(2b+a(r+q))^2, let D(R0,0)=4e^2 and D(r,psi(r))=4e^2. Then A*=1-min_{0<=r<=R0}[p F_k(r)+(1-p)F_k(psi(r))]. A weighted prefix anti-quantile partial measure has both marginals dominated by the required weighted class laws, and a closed positive-tail tube attains the bound. [Lemma lem:cut_graft of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Let $\mathcal E$ be an event on finite plane trees, and let
$(\mathcal Q_m)_{m\in I}$ be a finite family of events with
$\P(\mathcal T\in\mathcal Q_m)>0$. Assume that there exist a set
$\mathscr R\subseteq\mathscr A_\ell$ and a map
$\tau:\mathscr R\to I$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] for every $A\in\mathscr R$ and every
$S'\in\mathcal Q_{\tau(A)}$, one has $A[S']\in\mathcal E$;
\item[(b)] whenever $|T|\ge\ell+1$, $T\in\mathcal E$, and
$T_{u_{\ell+1}(T)}\in\mathcal E$, one has
$
\operatorname{Cut}_\ell(T)\in\mathscr R$
and
$T_{u_{\ell+1}(T)}
\in
\mathcal Q_{\tau(\operatorname{Cut}_\ell(T))}$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
$$\P\bigl(
|\mathcal T|\ge\ell+1,\
\mathcal T\in\mathcal E,\
\mathcal T_{u_{\ell+1}(\mathcal T)}\in\mathcal E
\bigr)
\leq 
\P(\mathcal T\in\mathcal E)
\max_{m\in I}
\P\bigl(
\mathcal T\in\mathcal E
\mid
\mathcal T\in\mathcal Q_m
\bigr).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cut-and-graft bound

body:
The estimate $\|u(t)\|_{L^2}\le e^{-\lambda_1t}\|u(0)\|_{L^2}$ comes from the Poincare inequality $\|\nabla v\|^2\ge\lambda_1\|v\|^2$ on $H^1_0(U)$, i.e. from a positive spectral gap; it is not a property of the heat equation as such. (1) Unbounded domains: on $U=\mathbb R^n$ the Dirichlet spectrum is $[0,\infty)$, $\lambda_1=0$, and $\|e^{t\Delta}\|_{L^2\to L^2}=1$ for every $t$, so no rate is uniform over the unit ball of $L^2$; individual solutions do decay, but only algebraically in general -- for $g=\Phi(\cdot,1)$ one has $\|u(t)\|_{L^2}=(8\pi(t+1))^{-n/4}$. Half-spaces and cones behave the same way. (2) Neumann boundary conditions: constants solve the Neumann heat equation, $u\equiv1$ does not decay at all. The correct statement is decay to the mean: for $U$ bounded, connected and Lipschitz (so that $H^1(U)\hookrightarrow L^2(U)$ is compact and the Neumann spectrum is discrete), $\|u(t)-\bar g\|_{L^2}\le e^{-\mu_2t}\|g-\bar g\|_{L^2}$, where $\bar g$ is the mean of $g$ and $\mu_2>0$ is the first nonzero Neumann eigenvalue. (3) Zeroth-order terms: for $u_t=\Delta u+cu$ the decay rate becomes $\lambda_1-\sup c$, which is a growth rate as soon as $\sup c>\lambda_1$. Auditor's check: whenever an exponential-decay claim appears, identify the eigenvalue being used, verify it is positive on the stated function space, and verify that the domain's geometry (boundedness in at least one direction for Dirichlet, connectedness and mean-zero for Neumann) actually supplies the gap.
Dirichlet case: U bounded in at least one direction gives lambda_1 > 0
Neumann case: U bounded, connected, Lipschitz, and the datum must be measured against its mean
Reaction terms shift the rate by sup c
title: Pitfall: Exponential decay of the heat flow needs a spectral gap

A surface is a topological 2-manifold: a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space in which every point has an open neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open subset of R^2. A surface with boundary allows neighbourhoods homeomorphic to open subsets of the closed half-plane {(x, y) : y >= 0}. Classification theorem: every compact connected surface without boundary is homeomorphic to exactly one of the sphere, a connected sum of g >= 1 tori (the orientable surface of genus g, Euler characteristic 2 - 2g), or a connected sum of k >= 1 real projective planes (the non-orientable surface of genus k, Euler characteristic 2 - k).
Hausdorff and second countable are part of the definition; the line with two origins is locally Euclidean but not a manifold
the classification is for compact connected surfaces without boundary; with boundary one also records the number of boundary circles
title: Surface (topology)

 \pi_*\mu_t\rightharpoonup\delta_{q_\pi(\xi)},

 \le C_0(T-t).
\]

\(T-t\) satisfies
\[
 z_t\in\pi^{-1}\!\left(
 B_\eta\bigl(q_\pi(\xi),C_0\sqrt{T-t}\bigr)\right),
 \qquad t<T.
\]
\item In either of the preceding settings, put
\[
 (\lambda_t,t_{\rm pole},q_{\rm pole})
 =\begin{cases}
 (\nu_{x_0,t_0;t},t_0,\pi(x_0)),&\text{in \textup{(i)}},\\
 (\mu_t,T,q_\pi(\xi)),&\text{in \textup{(ii)}}.
 \end{cases}
\]
If, for a fixed finite \(A\ge0\), a point \(z_t\) satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \int_Xd_{g(t)}(z_t,x)^2\,d\lambda_t(x)
 \le A(t_{\rm pole}-t),
\end{equation}
then
\[
 d_\eta(\pi(z_t),q_{\rm pole})
 \le C_0(A)\sqrt{t_{\rm pole}-t}.
\]
Thus the center conclusions in \textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)} are the
special case \(A=H_{2n}\).
\end{enumerate}

In contrast Q/r has stationary exponential limit of rate beta. Consequently a positive linear state-space collapse W/c_r=c*Q/r cannot hold in this regime. Check: The normalization c_r^(1-alpha)*L(c_r)=1/r makes the transform coefficient a/(m*beta). The limiting workload transform has infinite derivative at zero, whereas every scaled exponential has finite mean; the two laws cannot coincide. It neither identifies the temporal law nor proves tightness; even a nonlinear relation is not excluded by this marginal calculation.

[Lem prop:strict-limit of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Let $(\Gamma_N,\omega_N)$ be finite planar networks whose weight matrices converge to $A$, and suppose the networks $(\Gamma_N,\lvert \omega_N\rvert )$ have weight matrices converging to $A_0$.  Fix $I,J$ with $|I|=|J|$.  Assume that every $\Gamma_N$ contains two distinguished $I$-to-$J$ path families with weights $u,v\in\mathbb C^*$ independent of $N$, such that $u/v\notin\mathbb R_{>0}$.  There exists \(0<q<1\), which isindependent of \(N\), such that
\[
 |\Delta_{I,J}(A_N)|\le q\,\Delta_{I,J}(A_{0,N})
\]
for every \(N \geq 1\); consequently the same inequality holds in the limit.

[Lemma diamond of arXiv:2608.28505, 'Quagmires and large Suslin forests'] Given an infinite cardinal $\kappa$ with $\kappa^{<\kappa} = \kappa$ and a stationary $S \subseteq E^{\kappa^+}_\kappa$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label={\upshape (\arabic*)}]
\item $\diamondsuit(S)$,
\item There exists a sequence $\langle \Omega_\alpha : \alpha < \kappa^{+}\rangle$ such that for every cardinal $\mu > \kappa^+$, parameter $p \in H(\mu)$, and subset $\Omega \subseteq H(\kappa^{+})$, there exists an elementary submodel $N \prec H(\mu)$ satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}[label={\upshape (\alph*)}]
\item ${}^{<\kappa} N \subseteq N$,
\item $p \in N$,
\item $\kappa^+ \cap N \in S$,
\item $\Omega_{\kappa^+ \cap N} = \Omega \cap N$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Suppose that there exists $\delta>0$ such that for every $t\in (-\delta,\delta)$,  $$\E \left(e^{tX_N}\Big |Y_N\right) \xrightarrow{P} \E e^{tV}$$ for some random variable $V$. Then,
   \begin{enumerate}
       \item $X_N \xrightarrow{d} V$,
       \item For every $p\ge 1$, $\E (X_N^p|Y_N) \xrightarrow{P} \E V^p$. 
   \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

## Hardest step: actual-world bin reduction in the mixed case

Resolved pairs may still have partially unknown A support. Thus blindly
extending C023's all-unresolved formula is invalid. The source-bin lattice
forces invariant bin masses for c<1/(2NrK). Apply C022's known-false
removal first: saturated resolved A outside atoms can be assigned zero
without increasing risk or robust calibration. The zero-score lattice
argument ensures their bin has no possible true source mass.

Known-A unsaturated support swaps force its outside-known set into one
score bin. For unresolved pairs, C019's coprime reduction forgets surplus
known truths to h_i without changing any source bin mass or actual false-
count vector. These facts hold while other resolved/unresolved blocks
are held fixed, since the compatible world family is a product.

Fix an actual world. In each invariant bin, unresolved components are
common residual objects peeling k_i<=h_i, whole contexts in separate
bins, or balanced saturated split objects, exactly as in C023.
Identified-A residuals are indivisible objects if a_i<r. Every other
remaining component is safe.

Native residual objects and their data-dependent types are:

 U_h: m=2(K-h), f=F, p=m*b_h (unresolved pair);
 A_j: m=K-j, f=F, p=(r-j)/(Nr), j<r (resolved arbitrary context).

At h=r a balanced split can be represented by f=v,m=2v,p=v/(NK)
for integer 1<=v<=F; equivalently it is v unit U_r objects. Their
target density and risk equal the unsplit U_r object's.

Write lambda=1/(NK) and sigma=(1/(Nr)+lambda)/2. Every residual object
has mean source density <=lambda; all safe components have density
>=lambda in the fair compatible orientation mean used to compute COMMON
source masses. Analytically removing safe components weakly lowers a
bin's false cost. This is not a new generator.

A common unresolved residual at k_i<h_i can be reduced to its native
U_hi object by removing 2(h_i-k_i) known atoms at density sigma>=lambda.
For a whole actual-A context m=K,p=1/N,f=F, replace it analytically
by its native U_hi. Since h_i>=ell>=K/2, Delta_m=K-2(K-h_i)>=0, and

 Delta_p-lambda*Delta_m
     =2(K-h_i)*(lambda-b_hi)>=0.

Thus the removed mass has density >=lambda (or positive mass with zero
size when Delta_m=0). Remaining native objects have density <=lambda,
so this replacement weakly lowers the bin's baseline false cost.
The whole actual-S context is safe and can be removed analytically.
Replacing objects here may depend on the actual orientation SOLELY in

## Native object ordering

For each native object put q=m/f, t=p/m. Within each type,

 U_h: t=sigma-1/(Nr*q), q=2(K-h)/F>=2;
 A_j: t=1/(Nr)-1/(Nr*q), q=(K-j)/F.

The verifier threshold ell>=Kr/(2K-r) gives
 a_ell<=lambda/2, and also ell>r-F, hence q_A<= (K-ell)/F<2.
All A_j densities are <=a_ell<=lambda/2, and every U_h density is
>=b_r=lambda/2. Thus q and t are jointly nondecreasing across ALL
native objects, including saturated unit splits.

For any bin of native objects (f_i,q_i,t_i), the baseline false mass
minus the sum of their singleton false masses is

 [sum_{i<j} f_i*f_j*(q_i-q_j)*(t_i-t_j)]/(sum_i f_i*q_i)>=0.

This is the elementary weighted Chebyshev identity. Together with the
analytic native replacements it gives H_theta(p0)>=B(D) for the common
coarsened source p0, POINTWISE in every actual world.

Every actual risk-bearing component in the original reduced bins has
false fraction <=R(D): common k_i objects have risk<=tau_hi, whole A

separate at its native source density. Use paired selected known truths
at sigma, resolved A known truths at1/(Nr), and known S at lambda.

f/m and add c to fixed S. If no native object remains, emit the known
true source and attain zero. Every positive native group has source

mergers preserve calibration<=c. Actual false mass is B-cR worldwise.

(a,b) union sizes to U_min(a,b) when b<=r; to A_a when b>r,a<r;

All polynomials are truncated after degree n, and sum_t Q_t=exp(2z).
Type baseline beta_t and risk xi_t are (F*b_h,tau_h) for U_h,

The oracle expectation is C023 Eq(6), which needs no sample-size

Outside the new threshold, native singleton groups need not be optimal.
Take K=20,r=19,F=1,ell=10,N>=5. One unresolved pair has h=15, with
native size10, source mass35/(76N), density7/(152N). One resolved A has

enough actual samples (e.g.21 suitably chosen samples). This is a real
source-invariant pooling improvement, not a floating-point estimate.
Thus ell>=K/2 alone does not justify the all-n singleton formula.

body:
[Lemma xxphi of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([0,1])$ and fix $q\in[0,1]$.
		Let $(X_t)_{t\in[q,1]}$ solve the Auffinger--Chen SDE 
		\[
		\mathrm{d} X_t=\xi''(t)\,\zeta([0,t])\,\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,X_t)\mathrm{d} t+\sqrt{\xi''(t)}\,\mathrm{d} B_t.
		\]
		Write $u(t,y):=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,y)$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
		\begin{equation}
			\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,x)
			=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,u(q,x)^2
			-\int_{[q,1]}\mathbb{E}\!\left[u(t,X_t)^2\,\middle|\,X_q=x\right]\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\end{equation}
		Consequently,
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\big[\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,X_q)\big]
		=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,\mathbb{E}\big[u(q,X_q)^2\big]
		-\int_{[q,1]}\mathbb{E}\big[u(t,X_t)^2\big]\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\]
		Moreover, if $\mathbb{E}[u(t,X_t)^2]=t$ for $\zeta$-a.e.\ $t\in[q,1]$
		and also $\mathbb{E}[u(q,X_q)^2]=q$,
		then
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\big[\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,X_q)\big]
		=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,q-\int_{[q,1]}t\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t)
		=\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\mathrm{d} t.
		\]

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Degree fluctuations in bilateral preference random graphs (October 2026). In the graph LK(n,k) of La and Kabkab, independent uniform scores sit on the edges of K_n, each vertex prefers its k incident edges of smallest score, and an edge is kept when both endpoints prefer it. Dabirian and Subramanian (J. Appl. Probab. 63 (2026), Section 1.1) asked for the limiting distribution of the standardized degree (D - ED)/sqrt(Var D). With s_n^2 = k(n-k)/n, H = k - D and g(z) = phi(z) + z Phi(z): if k -> infinity and n - k -> infinity, H/s_n converges to g(Z) with Z standard normal, ED = k - s_n/sqrt(pi) + o(s_n), Var D = v s_n^2 + o(s_n^2) with v = 1/3 + (sqrt 3 - 2)/(2 pi), and the standardized degree converges to a non-normal law L_inf bounded above by 1.04643... For fixed r = n - 1 - k the limit is a Poisson mixture over a Gamma(r,1) variable, L_r, with L_r => L_inf as r -> infinity; for fixed k the limit comes from the Erlang weighted tree. L_1 and L_2 differ, so when n - 1 - k alternates between 1 and 2 there is no limit. E(k - D) takes the same value at budgets k and n - 1 - k. Exact rational checks and a Lean 4 file accompany the paper. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/bilateral-preference-degree-limits (commit 14c1e8bc386e). Not refereed.
title: Degree fluctuations in bilateral preference random graphs LK(n,k): every subsequential limit of the standardized degree, answering Dabirian-Subramanian (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/bilateral-preference-degree-limits)

[Theorem 3 (\textsf{Four-moment criterion on Rademacher chaos}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $d\in\N$ and $\lambda\in(0,\infty)$.  
Let $F_n\in\cC_d^{\mathsf{R}} \cap L^4(\PP)$ satisfy
 the lattice condition \eqref{cond_La} with shift $\theta_n$.
Suppose that

\noi
\begin{align}
 \cM(F_n)\to0.
 
\end{align}
Then the following assertions are equivalent.

\smallskip
\noi
{\rm (i)}
The first four   moments of $F_n+ \theta_n$ converge to the four numbers in
\eqref{4M}.

\smallskip
\noi
{\rm (ii)}
One has
$\big(\theta_n, m_2(F_n),   \cR(F_n) \big) \to (\lambda,  \lambda,  0)$

 

\smallskip
\noi
{\rm (iii)}
One has
$\dTV\bigl(\cL(F_n + \theta_n), P_\lambda\bigr) \to0$
and the family $ \{ (F_n + \theta_n)^4\}_{n\geq1}$ is uniformly integrable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textsf{Four-moment criterion on Rademacher chaos}

  \begin{equation*}
  M_0\in\CC_\tau(R,\alpha),
  \qquad
  |A|^2\leq R^{-2}\quad\text{on }M_0.
  \end{equation*}
 For every $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, the dimensionless surgery parameters and the
  upper bound for the ratio of the surgery radius to $R$ may be chosen,
  depending only on   $n$, $\tau$, $\alpha$, $\varepsilon$, and $\eta$, so that every   surgically modified flow satisfies
  \begin{align}
    \lambda_1
    &\geq
    -\varepsilon H-C_\varepsilon R^{-1},
    \\
    |A|^2-\frac1{n-1}H^2
    &\leq
    \eta H^2+C_\eta R^{-2}.
    
  \end{align}
  Here
  \begin{equation*}
  C_\varepsilon
  =C_\varepsilon(n,\tau,\alpha,\varepsilon),
  \qquad
  C_\eta
  =C_\eta(n,\tau,\alpha,\eta),
  \end{equation*}
  and neither constant depends on the number or the times of the surgeries.

For each n, let X_{n,k}, 1<=k<=k_n, be a finite square-integrable real martingale-difference row adapted to F_{n,k}. Write

    v_{n,k} = E[X_{n,k}^2 | F_{n,k-1}],
    V_n = sum_k v_{n,k},
    L_n(epsilon) = sum_k E[X_{n,k}^2 1{|X_{n,k}|>epsilon} | F_{n,k-1}].

Assume V_n -> sigma^2 in probability for a deterministic sigma^2>0, and L_n(epsilon)->0 in probability for every epsilon>0. Then sum_k X_{n,k} converges in distribution to N(0,sigma^2). No nesting of filtrations across different rows is assumed, and no stable-convergence conclusion is asserted.

Divide the increments by sigma, so it suffices to prove the case V_n->1.

## 1. A diagonal threshold and predictable localization

Choose increasing integers N_m tending to infinity such that, for every n>=N_m,

    P(L_n(1/m)>m^(-4)) < 1/m.

This is possible by the assumed convergence in probability for each fixed threshold. Let m(n) tend to infinity slowly enough that n>=N_{m(n)}, and put epsilon_n=1/m(n), delta_n=epsilon_n^4. The finitely many initial rows may use any positive values. Then

    P(L_n(epsilon_n)>delta_n)->0,
    delta_n/epsilon_n^2 -> 0,
    delta_n/epsilon_n -> 0.

Suppress n within a row. Set l_k=E[X_k^2 1{|X_k|>epsilon}|F_{k-1}] and define

    A_k = 1{sum_{j<=k} v_j <= 2 and sum_{j<=k} l_j <= delta}.

This indicator is F_{k-1}-measurable: even the kth conditional moment is known before the kth increment. The cumulative sums are nondecreasing, so accepted indices form an initial segment, and

    sum_k A_k v_k <= 2,       sum_k A_k l_k <= delta

pathwise, including the row where the next increment would overshoot. On the event V_n<=2 and L_n(epsilon_n)<=delta_n, every A_k is one. The probability of the complementary event tends to zero.

## 2. Truncate, recenter, and compare sums and variances

Let

    m_k = E[X_k 1{|X_k|<=epsilon} | F_{k-1}],
    Y_k = A_k (X_k 1{|X_k|<=epsilon} - m_k).

The Y_k are martingale differences and |Y_k|<=2epsilon. Because E[X_k|F_{k-1}]=0, m_k=-E[X_k 1{|X_k|>epsilon}|F_{k-1}], giving

    sum_k A_k |m_k| <= delta/epsilon.

The probability that any accepted increment exceeds epsilon is at most

    sum_k E[A_k P(|X_k|>epsilon | F_{k-1})]
    <= epsilon^(-2) E sum_k A_k l_k
    <= delta/epsilon^2.

On the complementary event, sum A_k X_k - sum Y_k = sum A_k m_k, whose absolute value is at most delta/epsilon. Combined with the event where all A_k equal one, this proves

    sum X_k - sum Y_k -> 0 in probability.

For w_k=E[Y_k^2|F_{k-1}], conditional centering gives

    A_k v_k - w_k = A_k (l_k + m_k^2).

Conditional Cauchy-Schwarz gives m_k^2 <= l_k (in fact it gives l_k times a probability at most one). Consequently

    0 <= sum A_k v_k - sum w_k <= 2delta.

Writing W_n=sum w_k, we therefore have W_n->1 in probability, 0<=W_n<=2 pathwise, and each |Y_k|<=b_n=2epsilon_n->0. This establishes every hypothesis needed in the next step without assuming convergence of the original unconditional variance sums.

## 3. A compensated exponential, conditioned one increment at a time

Fix t in R and put a=t^2/2. Write T_k=sum_{j<=k}Y_j and W_k=sum_{j<=k}w_j. Define

    Z_k = exp(it T_k + a W_k),       Z_0=1.

All Z_k are integrable since |Z_k|=exp(a W_k)<=exp(2a). Also 0<=w_k<=b_n^2. The real-variable Taylor remainder for exp(it y) gives

    E[exp(itY_k)|F_{k-1}] = 1-a w_k+r_k,
    |r_k| <= |t|^3 E[|Y_k|^3|F_{k-1}]/6
            <= |t|^3 b_n w_k/6.

For x>=0, the identity 1-exp(x)(1-x)=integral_0^x u exp(u)du implies

    |exp(x)(1-x)-1| <= x^2 exp(x)/2.

Since w_k is F_{k-1}-measurable, these estimates yield

    |E[exp(itY_k+a w_k)|F_{k-1}]-1|
    <= exp(a b_n^2) [a^2 b_n^2/2 + |t|^3 b_n/6] w_k.

Apply the tower property to Z_k-Z_{k-1}, with Z_{k-1} measurable at time k-1, and telescope its EXPECTATION. There is no factorization of dependent conditional characteristic functions. Using E W_n<=2 gives

    |E Z_{k_n}-1|
    <= 2 exp(2a+a b_n^2) [a^2 b_n^2/2 + |t|^3 b_n/6]
    -> 0.

This is a bound on the absolute value of the expectation difference; it is not a claim that E|Z_{k_n}-1| tends to zero.

Finally,

    E exp(it T_{k_n}) = E[Z_{k_n} exp(-a W_n)].

Because W_n->1 in probability, W_n is bounded, and |Z_{k_n}|<=exp(2a),

    |E[Z_{k_n} exp(-a W_n)] - exp(-a) E Z_{k_n}|
    <= exp(2a) E|exp(-a W_n)-exp(-a)|
    ->0.

Here convergence in probability plus boundedness implies convergence in L1. Thus the characteristic functions converge to exp(-t^2/2). Levy's continuity theorem and the negligible difference between the original and truncated sums prove the stated weak convergence. Rescaling restores sigma.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:3d98775b15e063ab5412171ff78b20512070def0754220a3225c1c8341903839","revision_digest":"sha256:cad77494db1a3fced403dcd6efd0faea8e070987fb43d8eb2e194eab81eb9ff5","source_id":"owner-original:martingale-proof-repair-brown-clt-20260909","source_revision":"aa0993714f6348156147b91cec8bdd862e3efaa5fc92558b9cf20f27058bfbdf","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":["claim_93496985eb04487f804e73c18222e3e96a5692e1ef9149cfd6521dda21fa38dd"],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Definition 240 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] If $\boldsymbol{v} \in \amsmathbb{R}^H$ is non-zero, we set $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{v}} = (\boldsymbol{v} \otimes \boldsymbol{v},0)\in (\amsmathbb{R}^{H} \otimes \amsmathbb{R}^{H}) \oplus \amsmathbb{R}$ and construct the complex surface
\[
\Sigma^{[2]}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{v}}} = \left( \bigsqcup_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}} \in \mathfrak{G}^{[2]}.\widetilde{\boldsymbol{v}}} (\widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^{+} \sqcup \widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^-) \times (\widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^+ \sqcup \widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^-) \right)\Big/\sim.
\]
The equivalence relation identifies for each $h \in [H]$, $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon_1',\epsilon_2' \in \{\pm 1\}$ and $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}} \in \mathfrak{G}^{[2]}.\boldsymbol{v}$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\prod_{i = 1}^2 (\widehat{\amsmathbb{R}}^{\epsilon_i} \setminus \amsmathbb{B}^{\epsilon_i})$ with $\prod_{i = 1}^{2} (\widehat{\amsmathbb{R}}^{\epsilon_i'} \setminus \amsmathbb{B}^{\epsilon_i'})$ both in the $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}$-th copy;
\item $\overline{\amsmathbb{B}}_{h}^{+} \times \widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^{\epsilon}$ in the $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}$-th copy with $\overline{\amsmathbb{B}}_{h}^- \times \widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^{\epsilon}$ in the $T_1^{(h)}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}})$-th copy;
\item $\widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^{\epsilon} \times \overline{\amsmathbb{B}}_h^+$ in the $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}$-th copy with $\widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^{\epsilon} \times \overline{\amsmathbb{B}}_h^-$ in the $T_2^{(h)}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}})$-th copy.
\end{itemize}

Let us denote for $\textnormal{supp}_i(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}) = \big\{h \in [H] \quad \big|\quad T_i^{(h)}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}) \neq \widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}\big\}$ for $i = 1,2$. The image in $\Sigma^{[2]}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{v}}}$ of the $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}$-th copy of
\[
\bigcup_{ \epsilon,\epsilon' \in \{\pm 1\}} \bigg(\widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^{\epsilon} \setminus \bigcup_{g \in \textnormal{supp}_1(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}})} \overline{\amsmathbb{B}}_g^{\epsilon}\bigg) \times \bigg(\widehat{\amsmathbb{H}}^{\epsilon'} \setminus \bigcup_{g \in \textnormal{supp}_2(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}})} \overline{\amsmathbb{B}}_g^{\epsilon'}\bigg)
\]
is denoted $\Sigma^{[2]}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{v}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}}$ and called the $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}$-th sheet. The $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{v}}$-th sheet is called the principal sheet.

body: [Defn 11 ($k$-point motion) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] We define the path measure $\mathbf P_{RW^{(k)}}$ on the canonical space $(I^k)^{\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}}$ to be the \textit{annealed} law of $k$ independent walks (all started from the origin) sampled from kernels $K_n$ satisfying Assumption \ref{a1}. The Markov chain whose law is given by the canonical process $\mathbf R= (\mathbf R_r)_{r\ge 0}$ on $I^{\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}}$ under the measure $\mathbf P_{RW^{(k)}}$ is called the \textbf{$k$-point motion}.

[Theorem prop:super_4 of arXiv:2508.17838, '\bf Edge Universality for Inhomogeneous Random Matrices'] Given fixed integers $s \geq 1$ and $k_i \geq 1$ for $1 \leq i \leq s$, if  
\begin{equation}
    t_N \ll n_{i,j} \leq \tau N^{\frac{1}{3}}, \quad \forall  1 \leq i \leq s, \quad 1 \leq j \leq k_i,
\end{equation} for any fixed constant $\tau > 0$, and $ 
    \|A_N\|_{\mathrm{op}} \leq 1 + O(N^{-\frac{1}{3}}),
$ 
then  
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}\bigg[\prod_{i=1}^s \mathrm{Tr} \Big(\prod_{j=1}^{k_i} \frac{1}{n_{i,j}+1} U_{n_{i,j}}\big(\frac{X}{2}\big)\Big)\bigg]
    =  \mathbb{E}\bigg[\prod_{i=1}^s \mathrm{Tr} \Big(\prod_{j=1}^{k_i} \frac{1}{n_{i,j}+1} U_{n_{i,j}}\big(\frac{\widetilde{X}}{2}\big)\Big)\bigg] + o(1).

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Identify which estimate needs d > 6 and whether it is an artefact. Result: The source's proof of the Alexander-Orbach behaviour for the oriented IIC uses a zigzag-path count converging like sum_m m^{(4-d)/2}, which needs d > 6, while the oriented IIC's mean-field structure (Hofstad-den Hollander-Slade) holds for d > 4. The zigzag count controls the resistance between the origin and level n via the number of paths that go up, come back down and go up again; in d = 5, 6 these counts diverge, meaning the crude flow bound fails, but the true resistance may still be of order n (mean-field, tree-like) because the divergent terms are overcounting: paths in the oriented IIC cannot return to earlier times, so a zigzag in the bound corresponds to two disjoint upward paths connected through the IIC's backbone, whose number is controlled by the two-point function squared, giving a convergent sum for d > 4 if the backbone is used correctly. So I expect the Alexander-Orbach value d_s = 4/3 to hold for the oriented IIC in d = 5, 6 as well, and the obstruction to be technical (the resistance lower bound of Kumagai-Misumi type needs a better flow construction using the backbone). This is a prediction with a proposed route (flow along the oriented backbone with branching at the pivotal levels), not a proof. Key identity: Oriented paths cannot return to earlier times, so the zigzag overcount should be replaceable by a backbone-branching flow with convergence for d > 4. Obstruction: The improved flow construction is not carried out.

Let N,d be positive integers, B_x,B_w>0, B_y>=0, lambda>=0 and 0<=alpha<=beta with alpha+lambda>0. Suppose 0<epsilon<B_x B_w/2. Put kappa=(beta+lambda)/(alpha+lambda), R=max{B_x B_w,B_y,1}, and L=ceil(2 kappa log(B_x B_w/(2 epsilon)))+1. There exists one fixed L-layer attention-only transformer, depending on these bounds and not on the dataset, with token dimension D=2d+3 and at most three heads per layer, with the following property. For every training dataset (x_i,y_i) for 1<=i<=N and query x_(N+1) such that ||x_i||_2<=B_x for all 1<=i<=N+1, |y_i|<=B_y, alpha I <= X^T X/N <= beta I, and ||w_ridge||_2<=B_w/2, where X has rows x_i^T and w_ridge minimizes (1/(2N)) sum_i (<w,x_i>-y_i)^2+(lambda/2)||w||_2^2, its output prediction differs from <w_ridge,x_(N+1)> by at most epsilon. Its second-to-last-layer tokens all contain an estimate of w_ridge with Euclidean error at most epsilon/B_x. The architecture uses normalized ReLU attention: on S tokens h_i, each layer sends h_i to h_i+(1/S) sum_m sum_j ReLU(<Q_m h_i,K_m h_j>) V_m h_j, with no MLP. Initially h_i=[x_i;y'_i;0_d;1;t_i], where y'_i=y_i and t_i=1 for training tokens, and y'_(N+1)=t_(N+1)=0. The prediction is coordinate d+1 of the last query token; the weight estimate is coordinates d+2 through 2d+1 of each penultimate token. The parameter norm max_layer(max_m{||Q_m||op,||K_m||op}+sum_m ||V_m||op) is at most 4R+8/(beta+lambda). Source: arXiv:2306.04637, Theorem 4, equations (3)–(6), PDF pages 5–7; proof Appendix D.1, PDF pages 41–42. This is the paper's normalized-ReLU-attention architecture.

0<epsilon<B_x B_w/2
Training and query features have Euclidean norm at most B_x; training labels have absolute value at most B_y

For two independent collections of n independent uniform unit-square points sharing n labels, the maximum same-label induced subposet agreement C_n satisfies liminf E C_n/n^(1/3)>=exp(-2). The construction retains isolated matches in an m by m grid with m=floor(n^(1/3)). It does not establish the optimal constant or its existence.

Coordinatewise partial order

Partition each square into m-by-m cells, m=floor(n^(1/3)). Keep a label when its two points occupy the same cell, and retain it only if no other kept label shares that row or column. The retained labels have identical comparisons in both posets. For a fixed label the match probability is1/m^2; conditional on its cell, another label is a conflicting match with probability(2m-1)/m^4. Therefore the expected retained number is n/m^2*[1-(2m-1)/m^4]^(n-1), asymptotic to exp(-2)*n^(1/3).

Second check. Two retained labels have distinct row and column indices, so each of their coordinate orderings is determined by cell indices in both independent samples. Independence over labels gives the exact no-conflict probability. The bound is liminf E C_n/n^(1/3)>=exp(-2).

Limits. The isolated-cell matching discards many usable labels and supplies no matching upper constant. Optimizing a local grid construction does not establish existence of the global optimal limit.

[Definition 6 of arXiv:2606.31287, '\bf Heat kernel lower bound estimates for symmetric pure jump processes via averaged jump '] \rm 
 Let $(\sX,d,m,\sE, \sF)$ be an MMD space.
\begin{enumerate}  
\item[\rm (i)] We say that the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ is conservative if its associated Hunt process is conservative. 

\item[\rm (ii)] We say that the transition density upper bound estimate ${\rm UHK}(\phi)$ holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$  has a jointly continuous density function
 $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty )\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there is a positive constant $c_{\ref{e:2.6}} >0 $ so that 
\begin{equation}
 p(t, x, y) \leq c_{\ref{e:2.6}}\left( \frac{1}{V(x, \phi^{-1}(t))} \wedge
\frac{t}{V(x, d(x,y))\phi (d(x, y))} \right)
\end{equation}
for any $t > 0$ and $x, y \in \sX$.  
Here $\phi^{-1}$ denotes the inverse function of $\phi$.
 
\item[\rm (iii)] We say that the near diagonal lower bound estimate ${\rm NLHK}(\phi)$
 holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$  has a jointly continuous density function $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty)\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there exist constants $\e_{\ref{e:1.9}} \in (0,1)$ and $c_{\ref{e:1.9}} > 0$ such that  
\be 
p(t, x ,y )\ge \frac{c_{\ref{e:1.9}}}{V(x , \phi^{-1}(t))} \quad \hbox{for any } x ,y \in \sX
\hbox{ with }  d(x, y) < \e_{\ref{e:1.9}}\phi^{-1}(t)  .
\ee

 \item[\rm (iv)]  We say that the transition density lower bound estimate for the Dirichlet transition density, ${\rm NDL}(\phi)$ for short, holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$   has a jointly continuous density function $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty)\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there exist  $\e_{\ref{e:2.15}} \in (0, 1)$ and $c_{\ref{e:2.15}} > 0$ so that for every $x_0 \in \sX$, $r > 0$, $t\in (0, \phi (\e_{\ref{e:2.15}}r))$ and 
 $B = B(x_0, r)$, 
 \begin{equation}
 p^B(t, x, y) \geq   \frac{c_{\ref{e:2.15}}}{V(x_0, \phi^{-1}(t))}  \quad \hbox{for } x, y \in B(x_0, \e_{\ref{e:2.15}} \phi^{-1}(t)).
 \end{equation}
 Here $p^B(t, x, y)$ is the transition density function of the part process $X^B$ of $X$ killed upon leaving the ball $B$. 
\end{enumerate}

[Lem 184 (quenched second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\Ising}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] In addition to Lemma~\ref{l:barD.Ising.second} we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[\max\bigg\{
	\bE\Big[\Delta\bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)^2\Big]
	: 0\le d\le\dmax-1
	\bigg\}
	\le \frac{\SMAX_N(\Ising)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{N}\]
where $\SMAX_N(\Ising)$ is a random variable satisfying the bound
	\[\P\Big(\SMAX^N(\Ising) \ge \log N\Big)
	\le \exp
	\bigg(
	-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}
	\bigg)
	\,.\]
The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$ in place of
$\bar{D}^{\Ising}$.

\begin{proof}
Recall that we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.Ising} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)}{(\delta_d)^{1/2}}
	=\frac{1}{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\sum_{i\in B}
	\frac{\be_i}{|B|^{1/2}},
	\by\bigg)
	\equiv \frac{(\be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))}{|B|^{1/2}}\,,
	\]
where we abbreviate $B\equiv B^\Ising$.
If we define the random variable
	\[
	\SMAX_N(\Ising)
	\equiv\max
	\bigg\{
	\Big|( \be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: 
	0\le d\le \dmax-1, B\in \mathcal{B}^\Ising(q_d)
	\bigg\}\,,
	\]
then we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[
	\bE[\Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)^2]
	= \frac{\delta_d}{N}
	\sum_{B\in \mathcal{B}^\Ising(q_d)}
	(\be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))^2
	\le  \frac{\SMAX_N(\Ising)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{N}\,.
	\]
The bound on $\SMAX_N(\Ising)$ follows by a similar argument as the bound for $\SMAX_N(\RomII)$ from Lemma~\ref{l:barD.II.second.quenched}, with the simplification that $\|\be_B\|=1$ is trivially bounded. 
This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\Ising}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof}

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2609.02017, 'Optimal girth-dependent bounds for the Bethe approximation of the permanent'] For $\bs{q}=(q_1,\ldots,q_d)\in\Delta_d$, let
\[
  H(\bs{q}):=-\sum_{i=1}^d q_i\log q_i
\]
denote the usual Shannon entropy, and define the complementary entropy functional
\[
  H_{\mr c}(\bs{q}):=-\sum_{i=1}^d(1-q_i)\log(1-q_i).
\]
We call the difference
\[
  S(\bs{q}):=H(\bs{q})-H_{\mr c}(\bs{q})
\]
the local Bethe entropy functional.
If $\mu$ is a
probability distribution on a finite set, we write $H(\mu)$ for the
entropy of its probability vector; for a finite random variable $U$, we write $\mc{L}(U)$ for its law and set $H(U):=H(\mc{L}(U))$.
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2609.02017

[Ppn 127 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take independent random variables $\sss\sim\tphi$ and $\xxx\sim\sphi$.
Let $\vY^\frozen$ be a subsequential limit of the $\vY^{\frozen,N}$ processes, and let $\hvY^\frozen(t)\equiv \vY^\frozen(t-\sss)+\xxx$. Take the coordinate sum
	\beq
	\iY^\frozen\equiv
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomI,
		\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\iY^{\frozen,\sigma}\,.\eeq
Let $\iX^\frozen$ and $\iX^{\frozen,\Ising}$ be the unique solutions of the SDEs \eqref{e:iX.sde} such that  $\iX^\frozen(q_*)$ is equidistributed as $\iY^\frozen(q_*)$, and 
$\iX^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_*)$ is equidistributed as $\iY^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_*)$. Then the (one-dimensional) processes 
$\iX^\frozen$ and $\iY^\frozen$
satisfy the same Fokker--Planck equations on the time interval $[q_*,1]$.
As a consequence, for each fixed $t$ the marginal law of $\iX^\frozen(t)$ agrees with the marginal law of $\iY^\frozen(t)$.
The same statements hold for $\iX^{\frozen,\Ising}$ and $\iY^{\frozen,\Ising}$.

\begin{proof}
This follows from Lemma~\ref{l:projected.fokker.planck},  using the regularity estimates from Corollary~\ref{c:reg.in.limit}. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 45 of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] For every $d\ge1$ and all $i,j$,
\begin{equation}
 x_i-x_j=(z_i-z_j)\bigl(1-(z_iz_j)^{-1}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Consequently, in the residue field of $\widehat\cO_d$,
\begin{equation}
 \bar x_i=\bar x_j
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \bar z_i=\bar z_j
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \bar z_i=\bar z_j^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Thus the full inverse image of an $x$-residue class consists of either
one inversion-stable $z$-disk or two $z$-disks exchanged by inversion; a
finite node cluster may meet one or both disks.

Equivalently, the incidence graph of (X, F) contains the bipartite complement of a matching of size m as an induced subgraph. Observation 3.3. ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Counterexample to the usual pathwise lifetime monotonicity coupling Result: Consider a deterministic contact schedule with A initially infected: A-C at time .1, A-B at 1, C-B at 9, B-D at 10, and no other contacts. Baseline infectious lifetimes are L_A=.5, L_C=12, L_B=2. Then B is infected at 9 and infects D at 10. Multiply every lifetime by 3: A now infects B at 1; B is removed at 7, cannot be reinfected at 9, and D is never infected. Check: Check both timelines: C remains infectious at 9 in each case; A has already died at 1 only in the baseline. The example refutes infection-set inclusion under scaled lifetimes on a fixed contact schedule. Obstruction: This is not a counterexample to survival monotonicity or to the Brownian epidemic conjecture. It blocks a direct attractiveness proof; a Brownian contact-support realization was not proved.

point process $\eta$ is \emph{stealthy on $\Omega$} if

Let (X, mu) and (Y, nu) be sigma-finite measure spaces, 1 <= p <= infinity, and f : X x Y -> [0, infinity] product-measurable. Then the L^p(mu) norm of the y-average dominates in the direction: || integral_Y f(., y) dnu(y) ||_{L^p(dmu)} <= integral_Y || f(., y) ||_{L^p(dmu)} dnu(y). For signed or complex f the same holds provided the right-hand side is finite, and then the inner integral converges absolutely for mu-a.e. x. The inequality is the continuous form of the triangle inequality for the L^p norm and reduces to it when nu is counting measure on two points. The reverse inequality is false for p > 1 and TRUE for 0 < p <= 1 with the roles of the two sides exchanged. Special case worth naming: taking nu counting measure on the integers gives || sum_n f_n ||_p <= sum_n || f_n ||_p. [standard; e.g. Stein, Singular Integrals and Differentiability Properties of Functions, Appendix A.1]
both measure spaces sigma-finite (needed for Tonelli and for L^p-L^q duality)
f product-measurable and nonnegative, or with a finite right-hand side
1 <= p <= infinity
