[Proposition AS of arXiv:2609.00324, 'Quantitative Stability for Fractional Yamabe minimizers'] Let $(M,[\hat{h}])$ be the conformal infinity of an asymptotically hyperbolic manifold $(X^{n+1},g^+)$, and $p\geq 3$. Let $u_0$ be a non-integrable minimizer of the fractional Yamabe energy and suppose that it satisfies the $\text{AS}_p$ condition. Then, there exists a sequence $(u_k)_{k\in \mathbb{N}} \subset H^\gamma (M)$ with $u_k \to u_0$ in $H^\gamma (M)$ such that 
\begin{align*}
    \lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{I_\gamma [u_k,\hat{h}] -\Lambda_\gamma (M,[\hat{h}])}{\|u_k - u_0\|_{H^\gamma (M)}^{p-\alpha} } = 0 \quad \forall \alpha>0.
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: $\text{AS}_p$ implies $\theta>0$

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2607.13273, 'Asymptotics of transition densities for L\'evy processes with stochastic resetting'] Assume that for every $t>0$ there exists a transition density $p(t,y)$ of the L\'evy process $\boldsymbol{Y}$  and let $\theta\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1},$ $\lambda>0$, and $x\in\Rd$. If there exist Borel functions $f,A,\tilde{A}:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}_+$, and $r_0>0$ such that
	\[
        \lim_{r\to\infty} \frac{p(t,r\theta)}{f(r)}= A(t), \, t>0,
        \quad\text{ and } \quad
        \frac{p(t,r\theta-z)}{f(r)}\leq \tilde{A}(t),\, t>0, r>r_0, z\in \{0,x\}, 
	\]
	\[
        \lim\limits_{t\to\infty} e^{-\lambda t} \tilde A(t)=0
        \quad \text{ and } \quad
        \int\limits_{0}^\infty e^{-\lambda t} \tilde A(t)\, \dx[t]<\infty,
	\]
	then the density $p_\lambda$ of the corresponding process with resetting $\boldsymbol{X}$ satisfies
	\[
		\lim\limits_{\substack{r\to\infty\\t\to\infty}}\frac{p_\lambda(t,x,r\theta)}{f(r)}=\int\limits_0^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda s}A(s)\, \dx[s].
	\]

body:
Little Picard theorem: if f is entire and nonconstant, then the complement of its image, C minus f(C), contains at most one point; i.e. a nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < r and has an essential singularity at a, then for every ε in (0,r) the image of the punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < ε is all of C with at most one point removed, and every value so attained (again with at most one exception) is attained infinitely often. Both exceptional values are genuinely possible and the count is sharp: exp(z) is entire and omits exactly the value 0, and exp(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0 and omits exactly 0 near 0. Meromorphic versions: a nonconstant meromorphic function on C omits at most two values of the Riemann sphere, and near an essential singularity a meromorphic function takes every spherical value with at most two exceptions. If f is entire and transcendental (not a polynomial), then f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often.
Little: f entire and nonconstant
Great: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a with an isolated essential singularity at a

[Defn 11 of arXiv:2608.12804, 'Scaling Limits for Ising Models on Inhomogeneous Random Graphs and Applications'] A function $f: [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$ is absolutely continuous if for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that for any finite collection of pairwise disjoint subintervals $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ of $[0,1]$ satisfying
\(
\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i) < \delta
\),
we have
\(
\sum_{i=1}^n |f(y_i) - f(x_i)| < \varepsilon
\).

[Thm 16 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] For each $p \in \N$, let $\mathbf x^{(1)}_p,\dotsc,\mathbf x^{(m)}_p$ be $m = m(p)$ i.i.d.\ random vectors in $\R^p$, with $\Sigma_p = \E \mathbf x\mathbf x^\trp$ satisfying $\tr \Sigma_p^2= o(p^2)$, and also \begin{equation} 
    \frac{\mathbf x_p^\trp A_p \mathbf x_p - \tr(\Sigma_pA_p)}{p} \to 0\quad\text{in probability}\end{equation} for any sequence of PSD matrices $A_p \in \R^{p\times p}$ with $\opnm{A_p} \leq 1$. Assume $\ESD(\Sigma_p) \wkconv \rho$ for some deterministic measure $\rho$. Assume in addition for each $p$ and $m = m(p)$, we have a diagonal matrix $T_p = \diag\{R_1,\dotsc,R_{m}\}$, with nonnegative entries and independent of $\bigl\{\mathbf x_p^{(k)}\bigr\}_{k=1}^m$, and $\ESD(T_p) \wkconv \tau$ for some deterministic measure $\tau$ with probability $1$. Then, assuming $p / m \to c$ for some fixed $c > 0$, the weighted sample covariance matrix $\widetilde K_{p} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{k=1}^m R_k \mathbf{x}_p^{(k)} {\mathbf{x}_p^{(k)}}^\trp$ converges weakly with probability $1$ to some deterministic measure $\mu$, which is uniquely determined by its Stieltjes transform \[
        s_\mu(z) = \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{\lambda \int_0^\infty \frac{x}{1 + c x \tilde s(z)}\,d\tau(x) - z }\,d\rho(\lambda)\quad \text{for }z\in \C^+,
    \] where $\tilde s$ is defined by \[
        \tilde s(z) = \int_0^\infty \frac{\lambda}{\lambda \int_0^\infty \frac{x}{1 + c x \tilde s(z)}\,d\tau(x) - z }\,d\rho(\lambda) \quad \text{for }z\in \C^+.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Known-source analytic consequence, proof unaudited: for every compactly supported probability law mu on R, positive semicircular heat mu_t=mu free-plus semicircle_t has finite logarithmic energy E(t)=Sigma(mu_t), and E is C1 for all t>0 with E_prime(t)=Phi(mu_t)/2=(2*pi^2/3) integral p_t^3. Phi is continuous at every positive time. Biane's density-cube Lipschitz estimate, uniform support and weak time continuity give uniform density-cube continuity by Arzela-Ascoli; Voiculescu's one-variable chi*=chi heat-integral definition then pays differentiation. The free Fisher constant is checked by an explicit Cauchy-cubic contour identity. No density or finite initial energy is required of mu. This closes the scalar positive-noise regularity input, but the real matrix observation-law and calibration-transfer steps remain separate. This is a consequence of known results, not a novelty claim.
mu is a compactly supported probability on R; t>0.
Centered semicircular convolution has variance parameter t.
Natural logarithmic energy; free Fisher is squared L2 norm of the scalar conjugate variable.

Target 2 analytic input. Proof draft, unaudited. This is an explicit
consequence of known Biane and Voiculescu results, not a novelty claim.
It does not by itself establish the observation law for the real matrix
model or prove the T287 MMSE comparison.

Let mu be a compactly supported probability law on R. Write
mu_t=mu free-plus sigma_t, where sigma_t is the centered semicircle law
of variance t>0, p_t its density, and

    E(t)=Sigma(mu_t)=double integral log|x-y| mu_t(dx)mu_t(dy).

Then E is C1 on (0,infinity), with

    Phi(t)=(4*pi^2/3) integral p_t(x)^3 dx,
    E'(t)=Phi(t)/2.                                  (1)

No density, non-atomicity or finite initial logarithmic energy of mu is
assumed. In particular finite-rank/zero-atom input laws are allowed.

## Primary inputs and normalization

1. Biane, *On the free convolution with a semi-circular distribution*,
   Indiana Univ. Math. J.46 (1997),705-718, DOI10.1512/iumj.1997.46.1467.
   Lemma2, journal p709, defines v_t and gives its positive-level equation.
   Corollaries1-3, journal p711, give the continuous Cauchy boundary,
   a continuous density, and p_t(psi_t(u))=v_t(u)/(pi*t).
   Proposition4, journal p714, gives
   |p_t(x)^2 p_t'(x)|<=1/(4*pi^3*t^2) where p_t>0.
2. Voiculescu, *Free Entropy*, arXiv:math/0103168, chi.4 (one variable),
   and Section3.5 definition and chi*.1. In one variable
   chi(mu)=Sigma(mu)+3/4+(1/2)log(2*pi)=chi*(mu), and

   chi*(mu_t)=(1/2)integral_0^infinity
                  [1/(1+u)-Phi*(mu_(t+u))]du+(1/2)log(2*pi*e).

   Section3.3, J.1 and J.3 identify the scalar conjugate variable and
   the score under a positive semicircular perturbation. The Phi*
   convention is its squared L2 norm, Section3.4. We verify the scalar
   density constant explicitly below rather than borrow a classical
   Fisher-information convention.

All source artifacts and SHA256 values are recorded in SOURCES.jsonl.
The hypotheses quoted here were checked in the original journal PDF
and the author's arXiv survey, not inferred from an unrelated classical
de Bruijn card.

## Uniform spatial regularity and continuity in heat time

The v_t equation gives v_t<=sqrt(t): if v_t>0,
1/t=integral[(u-x)^2+v_t^2]^-1 mu(dx)<=1/v_t^2.
At v_t=0 the bound is immediate. Therefore

    0<=p_t(x)<=1/(pi*sqrt(t)).                       (2)

Set q_t=p_t^3. Proposition4 gives |q_t'|<=3/(4*pi^3*t^2) on the open
positivity set. Since q_t is continuous and zero on its complement,
this is a global Lipschitz bound on R. To see the extension across zeros,
integrate within each positive component; if two points lie in different
components, the values at their adjacent boundary zeros bound the
absolute difference by the same constant times the distance.

Fix 0<a<b<infinity. Realize mu as the law of a bounded selfadjoint X,
free from a variance-one semicircular S. The norms of X+sqrt(t)S for
t in [a,b] are bounded by ||X||+2sqrt(b). Thus all p_t have a common
compact support. Norm continuity of X+sqrt(t)S gives weak continuity
of its laws (first for polynomials, then for continuous functions on
the common compact interval).

For any t_k->t in [a,b], the q_(t_k) are uniformly bounded by (2),
uniformly Lipschitz and have common compact support. Every subsequence
has an Arzela-Ascoli uniformly convergent further subsequence, say to q.
Taking cube roots gives uniform convergence p_(t_k)->q^(1/3). The
weak-continuity statement forces q^(1/3)=p_t, since continuous densities
of the same law agree everywhere. Every possible subsequential uniform
limit is therefore q_t. Hence q_(t_k)->q_t uniformly, and

    t -> integral p_t^3                             (3)

is continuous on [a,b]. This argument does not assume joint parameter
regularity beyond Biane's actual spatial estimates.

## The exact scalar Fisher constant

Fix t>0, abbreviate p=p_t and define
G(z)=integral(z-x)^-1 p(x)dx. By Biane Corollary1 its upper boundary is
continuous, with G(x+i0)=h(x)-i*pi*p(x), h=PV integral p(y)/(x-y)dy.
It is bounded on compact subsets of the closed upper half-plane and
decays as O(1/|x|) off the compact support. In particular the boundary
function lies in L3(R).

For epsilon>0, the contour integral of G(z+i*epsilon)^3 around an upper
half-disk vanishes: it is analytic there and its large arc is O(R^-2).
Thus integral_R G(x+i*epsilon)^3 dx=0. Let epsilon decrease to zero.
Continuous boundary values give a uniform compact bound; outside a
fixed interval |G(x+i*epsilon)|<=2/|x| for 0<epsilon<=1. Dominated
convergence justifies passing the cubic integral to the boundary.
Taking imaginary parts gives

    integral p(x) h(x)^2 dx=(pi^2/3) integral p(x)^3 dx.                (4)

The scalar conjugate variable is 2h(X_t). This is Voiculescu J.1 with
the Hilbert-transform normalization removed; it can also be checked
directly from its defining polynomial identity:

    double integral [f(x)-f(y)]/(x-y) p(x)p(y)dxdy
                           =2 integral f(x)h(x)p(x)dx.

The principal-value passage is valid here: q_t is Lipschitz, so p_t is
Holder1/3, compactly supported, and its symmetric principal-value
integrals converge; the subtracted polynomial numerator is nonsingular.
Polynomial uniqueness in L2 on compact support identifies the score.
Therefore Phi*(mu_t)=4 integral p h^2=(4*pi^2/3)integral p^3, as asserted.
By (3), Phi*(mu_t) is continuous at every positive time.

## From the defining heat integral to the derivative

J.3 writes the score as t^(-1/2) E[S|X+sqrt(t)S]. The conditional
expectation is an L2 contraction and E S^2=1, hence

    0<=Phi*(mu_t)<=1/t.                              (5)

The bounded continuous compact density at positive t gives finite
logarithmic energy; thus the one-variable chi*=chi identity is finite
there. Apply Section3.5 at times 0<t1<t2 and subtract its two defining
improper heat integrals with the same upper cutoff T. The reference
1/(1+u) terms cancel. The result is

    chi(mu_t2)-chi(mu_t1)
      =(1/2)integral_t1^t2 Phi*(mu_v)dv
         -(1/2)lim_(T->infinity) integral_(T+t1)^(T+t2) Phi*(mu_v)dv.

The last term vanishes by (5), bounded by
(1/2)log((T+t2)/(T+t1)). Subtracting the constant between chi and Sigma
therefore gives the integral identity for E. The continuity already
proved gives E'(t)=Phi*(mu_t)/2 at every t>0, proving (1).

## Consequence once the matrix spectral identity is attached

For a compact symmetric input law mu, suppose a square matrix channel
has limiting normalized MI

 i(s)=Sigma(dilation_sqrt(s)(mu) free-plus sigma_1)-Sigma(sigma_1).

Dilation and the heat semigroup give
i(s)=E(1/s)+(1/2)log(s)-Sigma(sigma_1). Consequently i is C1 for s>0 and

    i'(s)=1/(2s)-Phi*(mu_(1/s))/(2s^2).              (6)

This is a conditional matrix consequence. The real Gaussian-reference
spectral identification and transfer assumptions remain to be paid in

For a real continuous local martingale M starting at zero, quadratic variation [M] is characterized by: [M] starts at zero, is adapted, continuous and increasing, and M^2 - [M] is a continuous LOCAL martingale. Uniqueness is up to indistinguishability. For each finite T, squared-increment sums along deterministic partitions of [0,T] with mesh tending to zero converge in probability to [M]_T. If E([M]_T) is finite at every finite T, the compensated square is a true martingale; this condition is equivalent to M being a true martingale with E(M_T^2) finite at every finite T. Brownian motion has [B]_t=t. Merely assuming M is a true continuous martingale does not justify the compensated-square integrability upgrade.

[Theorem quadratic of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Quadratic Recursion]

Let $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequence of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{i,j}\}_{(i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n}$ be a double sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define 
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) = \sum_{(i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n} {\bf A}_{i,j} x_{i}x_{j}.
$$
Suppose that ${\bf F}({\bf x})$ is also permutation symmetric, i.e.,\xspace ${\bf A}_{i,j} = {\bf A}_{j,i}$, $\forall (i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n$. Then for $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $2 \leq t < \infty$,
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{4t} ~ \leq ~ 2 (32t)^{2} \cdot \left( \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\a+b+c=2 }} L^c \cdot \norm{ {\bf F}_{a,b,c}}_{4t} \right).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem quadratic of arXiv:2412.07936

body: Mordell-Weil theorem: Let A be an abelian variety over a number field K. Then A(K), the group of K-rational points of A, is a finitely generated abelian group, called the Mordell-Weil group; equivalently A(K) is isomorphic to Z^r x T, where r >= 0 is the rank and T is the finite torsion subgroup. The special case in which A = E is an elliptic curve and K = Q is Mordell's theorem, which answers a question apparently posed by Henri Poincare around 1901 and was proved by Louis Mordell in 1922; the general case is due to Andre Weil (1928). It is a foundational theorem of Diophantine geometry and of the arithmetic of abelian varieties.

Convention $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$ (Plancherel transform on $L^2$). For every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ and all $x_0,\xi_0\in\mathbb R$, $$\Big(\int_{\mathbb R}(x-x_0)^2|f(x)|^2dx\Big)\Big(\int_{\mathbb R}(\xi-\xi_0)^2|\hat f(\xi)|^2d\xi\Big)\;\ge\;\frac{\|f\|_2^4}{16\pi^2},$$ where for $f\ne0$ both factors are strictly positive (possibly $+\infty$). Equality holds if and only if $f(x)=Ce^{2\pi i\xi_0x}e^{-a(x-x_0)^2}$ for some $a>0$ and $C\in\mathbb C$, i.e. exactly for modulated translated Gaussians. In $\mathbb R^d$: $\big(\int|x-x_0|^2|f|^2\big)\big(\int|\xi-\xi_0|^2|\hat f|^2\big)\ge d^2\|f\|_2^4/(16\pi^2)$. With the convention $\hat f(\xi)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int fe^{-ix\xi}dx$ the constant on the right is $\|f\|_2^4/4$ (the physics form $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$).

body: Method for the bounded-density quadratic-form conjecture. ||p_Q||_inf <= (1/2 pi) int |phi_Q|, so a bounded density follows from |phi_Q(t)| <= C min(1, |t|^{-1-kappa}). The decay per large eigen-direction is NOT uniform over amplitudes: for every t and lambda there is a density f <= 1 with Re int f(x) e^{i t lambda x^2} dx >= 1/2 (f the indicator of a unit-measure subset of {cos(t lambda x^2) >= 1/2}), so van der Corput, which needs an amplitude of bounded variation, does not apply to one rough coordinate. What is uniform over all laws is the decay along spread directions: for orthonormal v_1..v_k with sum_j v_ji^2 <= 1/2 for every coordinate i, the Fresnel identity e^{i eta lambda V^2} = (4 pi i eta lambda)^{-1/2} int e^{-i xi^2/(4 eta lambda) + i xi V} d xi and the geometric Brascamp-Lieb inequality (Hoelder with p_i >= 2 and int |psi_i|^p <= 4 pi/sqrt p) give |E e^{i eta (sum_j lambda_j V_j^2 + diagonal + linear)}| <= (4 pi)^{k/2} prod_j |eta lambda_j|^{-1/2} for every diagonal and every linear term, and three spread large directions give a bounded density. The conjecture is hard exactly where a coordinate carries a large part of an eigenvector (a pivot or a hub), where the one-coordinate obstruction returns.

Let T be an arbitrary index set and suppose that for every finite subset {t_1, ..., t_n} of T a probability measure mu_{t_1, ..., t_n} on R^n (or on S^n for a Polish space S with its Borel sigma-algebra) is given. Suppose the family is CONSISTENT: (i) permuting the indices permutes the measure correspondingly, and (ii) the marginal of mu_{t_1, ..., t_n, t_{n+1}} on the first n coordinates is mu_{t_1, ..., t_n}. Then there is a probability measure P on the product space S^T equipped with the PRODUCT sigma-algebra whose finite-dimensional marginals are exactly the given family, and P is unique. TWO LIMITATIONS, both routinely forgotten. FIRST, the topological hypothesis is essential: for general measurable spaces the theorem is FALSE, and there are consistent families with no extension (Andersen and Jessen); what is really needed is that the marginals be inner regular in a suitable sense, which Polish spaces provide. SECOND, the resulting measure lives on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra, every member of which is determined by countably many coordinates. When T is uncountable, sets such as {the path is continuous}, {sup_t X_t <= c}, or {the path is bounded} are therefore NOT measurable for that sigma-algebra, so the theorem does not by itself construct Brownian motion as a continuous process; it constructs a process with the right finite-dimensional laws, and a separate regularity theorem - Kolmogorov's continuity criterion - is needed to produce a modification with continuous paths. [Kolmogorov (1933); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 2.1.21, and Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 36]

Consistency makes this well defined, since a given cylinder has many representations differing by adding dummy coordinates or permuting them, and the two consistency conditions say exactly that all representations give the same value. Finite additivity on the algebra follows from finite additivity of each mu. The whole content is COUNTABLE additivity on the algebra, equivalently continuity at the empty set: if cylinders A_1 containing A_2 containing ... have empty intersection then P_0(A_n) -> 0. Suppose instead P_0(A_n) >= eps > 0 for every n. Then P_0(K_n) >= eps/2 > 0, so each K_n is nonempty; picking a point from each and using compactness of the bases coordinate by coordinate, a diagonal argument produces a point lying in every K_n, hence in every A_n, contradicting that the intersection is empty. So P_0 is countably additive on the algebra, and Caratheodory's extension theorem extends it uniquely to the generated product sigma-algebra. Let (S, d) be a metric space. A sequence of Borel probability measures (\mu_n)_{n=1}^\infty on S converges weakly to a probability measure \mu (denoted \mu_n \Rightarrow \mu) if for every bounded continuous function f: S \to \mathbb{R}, \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_S f d\mu_n = \int_S f d\mu.
(S, d) is a metric space
(\mu_n)_{n=1}^\infty, \mu are Borel probability measures on S
title: Weak Convergence of Probability Measures

Let X_1, \dots, X_n be independent real-valued random variables with characteristic functions \phi_{X_1}, \dots, \phi_{X_n}. [Proposition 5 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Let $\resexp$ be the exponent in Theorem~\ref{thm:unique_metric}. Almost surely, the heat kernel of the \clekp{} Brownian motion satisfies
 \[
 p(t,x,x) = t^{-\dcle/(\dcle+\resexp)+o(1)}
 \quad\text{for each } x \in \Upsilon_\Gamma \quad\text{as } t \searrow 0 .
 \]
 That is, the spectral dimension of the \clekp{} Brownian motion is $2\dcle/(\dcle+\resexp)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 1 of arXiv:2512.03884, '2512.03884'] Assume $\mathbb{E} (X_1) =0$ and $0<\mathbb{E} (X_1^2) < \infty$, and $\alpha$ is a quadratic irrational. Then
\[ \mathbb{E} \left( W_{\mathbb{T},2}^2 (\mu_N, \lambda) \right) \sim \frac{L^2 c_1(L \alpha)}{\sigma^2} \cdot \frac{\log N}{N} \quad \textrm{and} \quad \mathrm{Var} \left( W_{\mathbb{T},2}^2 (\mu_N, \lambda) \right) \sim \frac{L^4 c_2(L \alpha)}{\sigma^4} \cdot \frac{\log N}{N^2} \]
with $L = \mathrm{gcd} (\mathrm{supp} (X_1))$, $\sigma^2 = \mathbb{E} (X_1^2)$ and explicit positive constants $c_1(L \alpha)$, $c_2(L \alpha)$. If in addition $\mathbb{E} (|X_1|^p) <\infty$ with some real constant $p>2$, then
\[ \begin{split} \mathbb{E} \left( W_{\mathbb{T},2}^2 (\mu_N, \lambda) \right) &= \frac{L^2 c_1(L \alpha)}{\sigma^2} \cdot \frac{\log N}{N} + O \left( \frac{1}{N} \right) , \\ \mathrm{Var} \left( W_{\mathbb{T},2}^2 (\mu_N, \lambda) \right) &= \frac{L^4 c_2(L \alpha)}{\sigma^4} \cdot \frac{\log N}{N^2} + O \left( \frac{(\log \log N)^2}{N^2} \right) \end{split} \]
with implied constants depending only on $\alpha$ and the distribution of $X_1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: For two probability measures mu and nu on a measurable space (S, A), the total variation distance is d_TV(mu, nu) = sup over A in A of |mu(A) - nu(A)|, a number in [0, 1]. If mu and nu have densities f and g with respect to a common reference measure lambda (which always exists, for instance lambda = mu + nu), then d_TV(mu, nu) = (1/2) integral |f - g| d lambda = 1 - integral min(f, g) d lambda, and the supremum is attained at A = { f > g }. Equivalent characterisations: d_TV is half the supremum of |integral h d mu - integral h d nu| over measurable h with |h| <= 1; and by the coupling characterisation, d_TV(mu, nu) = min P(X not equal to Y) over all couplings (X, Y) with X distributed as mu and Y as nu, the minimum being attained by the maximal coupling. Convergence in total variation is strictly stronger than weak convergence (point masses at 1/n converge weakly to the point mass at 0 but stay at total variation distance 1). The normalisation matters: some texts use the un-halved integral |f - g| d lambda, which lies in [0, 2].

body:
Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with C^1 boundary (or any bounded extension domain, for instance a bounded Lipschitz domain), let 1 <= p < n and let p* = np/(n-p) be the Sobolev conjugate exponent. Then the embedding of W^{1,p}(Omega) into L^q(Omega) is COMPACT for every q strictly less than p*. At the endpoint q = p* the embedding is continuous but NOT compact. For p = n the embedding into L^q is compact for every finite q, and for p > n the embedding into C^{0,gamma}(closure of Omega) is compact for gamma < 1 - n/p. For the space W_0^{1,p}(Omega) no boundary regularity is needed: boundedness of Omega suffices.
Boundedness of Omega is essential (the embedding is never compact on R^n, by translating a fixed bump), and for W^{1,p} rather than W_0^{1,p} some boundary regularity is needed so that an extension operator exists.
Compactness FAILS at the critical exponent q = p*, which is exactly the loss of compactness behind concentration phenomena in critical problems.

[Proposition pr:tracking of arXiv:2504.11107, 'An Invariance Principle for some\\% Reaction-Diffusion Equations with a Multiplicative Ran'] For every $T>0$ let $u=u^{(T)}$ denote the solution to the parabolic Anderson model,
	\begin{equation*}\left[\begin{split}
		&\partial_t u = \partial^2_x u + \mu u  + \sigma u\dot{W}
			\hskip.95in\text{on $(T\,,\infty)\times\mathbb{T}$},\\
		&\text{subject to }u(0)=w(T)\hskip.9in\text{on $\mathbb{T}$}.
	\end{split}\right.\end{equation*}
	Then, for every $k \in (6\,,\infty)$ there exist non-random numbers
	$L=L(k\,,f\,,g)>0$ and 
	$\Delta_0=\Delta_0(k\,,f\,,g)\in(0\,,1)$ such that, independently of
	the value of $T$ and uniformly for all $\Delta(T)\in(0\,,\Delta_0)$,
	\[
		\mathrm{E}_{\mathscr{F}(T)}\left(\|w_T-u_T\|_{C([T,T+\Delta(T)]\times\mathbb{T})}^k
		\right)
		\leqslant L \left[\mathscr{E}\left({\rm e}^{-\gamma T}\right)\right]^k\|w(T)\|_{C(\mathbb{T})}^k,
	\]
	almost surely on the event $\{\tau(T)>T\}$, where
	$\mathscr{E}$ was defined in (equation R:star of the paper), and
	\[
		w_T(t\,,x) = w(t\wedge\tau(T)\,,x),\
		u_T(t\,,x) = u(t\wedge\tau(T)\,,x)\quad\forall t\geqslant T,\ x\in\mathbb{T}.
	\]
title: Proposition pr:tracking of arXiv:2504.11107

Own-work target-partial result C008 v1, proof (unaudited); novelty unestablished. Let n>=2, m,d>=1, labels y_i in {-1,1}, z_i=y_i*x_i, ||x_i||<=1, rank{z_i}>=2, z_i dot z_l>=kappa>0 for all pairs, and a unit u satisfy u dot z_i>=gamma>0. With literal leaky ReLU phi(v)=max(v,lambda*v), 0<lambda<1, f_i=m^-1 sum_j a_j phi(w_j dot x_i), train both layers simultaneously by step m*eta on average logistic loss, any eta>0. Assume for each neuron a_j(0) and every w_j(0) dot z_i have the same strict sign. Put r_j=min_i|w_j(0) dot z_i|, H=eta*lambda^2*m^-1 sum_j r_j^2, c=H/(4+2H). This open cone is invariant: all sample branches stay fixed, neuron products increase, and every margin grows by at least H*G_t, G_t the average logistic weight. Consequently L_t<=1/(1/L_0+c*t). With epsilon_s=min(log(2)/2,1/H) and s=ceil(max(0,1/epsilon_s-1/L_0)/c), one has L_t<=8/[H*(t-s)] for every integer t>s. Under independent Gaussian initialization a_j~N(0,sigma^2), w_j~N(0,sigma^2 I_d), sigma>0, consider for each neuron the union of {a_j>0,w_j/sigma in B(u,gamma/2)} and its simultaneous negative. Independence across initial neurons gives event probability at least b^m, where b=(gamma/sqrt(2*pi*d))^d*exp(-(1+gamma/2)^2/2). On this event H>=H0=eta*lambda^2*sigma^2*gamma^2/4. Set c0=H0/(4+2H0), epsilon0=min(log(2)/2,1/H0), s0=ceil(max(0,1/epsilon0-1/log(2))/c0). Then simultaneously L_t<=1/(1/log(2)+c0*t) for t>=0 and L_t<=32/[eta*lambda^2*sigma^2*gamma^2*(t-s0)] for t>s0. The Gaussian lower bound is positive mass and decays with width: no high-probability or almost-sure generic cone-entry conclusion is claimed. Sharp Cai-type burn-in and the full target remain open. 25965 finite rational checks support selected algebra only; independent mathematical audit, analytic certification and novelty comparison remain pending.
Strictly positive signed Gram entries, rank>=2, bounded separable data and positive leakage.
Aligned initial neuron cone for deterministic theorem; explicitly specified Gaussian ball/sign event for the probability corollary.
Both layers trained simultaneously with actual step m*eta; no output-layer freezing.
Proof (unaudited), C008 v1; Gaussian positive-mass statement only, no general Gaussian entry or novelty claim.

body:
[Definition def:qRacah_tilings of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] We put a probability measure on the set of all
	nonintersecting path ensembles. The measure depends on the
	geometry of the hexagon (parametrized by $(T,S,N)$), and
	on two parameters $q>0$ and $\kappa\in
	\mathbf{i}\mathbb{R}$.
	The
	probability weight of a nonintersecting path ensemble is
	proportional to
	\begin{equation}
		
		\prod_{\textnormal{holes in the path ensemble}} \mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}\bigl( x-\tfrac t2+1\bigr),
		\qquad
		\mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}(j) \coloneqq \kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}-\frac{1}{\kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}}.
	\end{equation}
	Here the holes are points $(t,x)$ such that $x\notin X(t)$,
	but $x$ satisfies the inequalities
	(equation eq:hexagon_constraints of the paper). In other words,
	holes are lozenges of the type
	\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline = (current bounding box.south),scale=.25]
		\draw[thick] (0,0)--++(1,1)--++(1,0)--++(-1,-1)--cycle;
	\end{tikzpicture}.
	For example, in (fig:tiling_and_path_picture of the paper), right, the holes are $(1,2),(2,1),(2,4),(3,0),(3,2),(3,5),(4,2),(4,3),(5,3)$.
	The probability weights are normalized so that the total probability of all path ensembles is $1$.
	We call the resulting probability measure the \emph{$q$-Racah measure} on nonintersecting path ensembles
	(equivalently, on lozenge tilings of the hexagon).
title: $q$-Racah measure on nonintersecting path ensembles

|\Sha(E_n)|_{\mathrm{an}}
 =\left(\frac{\Delta_Q(n)}{2\sigma_Q(n)}\right)^2.

If $L(E_n,1)=0$, then $\Delta_Q(n)=0$.
\item If $m$ is odd and $m\equiv1\pmod8$, then
\[
r_f(m)+r_g(m)=4h(-m),
\qquad
\frac{r_f(m)-r_g(m)}2=r_a(m)-h(-m).
\]
\item If $m$ is odd and $m\equiv1\pmod4$, then
\[
r_s(m)+r_t(m)=2h(-2m).
\]
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Lemma lem2 of arXiv:2608.30848, '\huge \bf Limit Laws of the Iterated Logarithm Under Sub-linear Expectations'] Let $X\in \mathscr{H}$.
\begin{description}
  \item[\rm (i)]
 For any $\delta>0$, we have
$$ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbb V\big(|X|\ge \delta \sqrt{n\log\log n} \big)<\infty \;\; \Longleftrightarrow C_{\mathbb V}\bigg[\frac{X^2}{\log\log|X|}\bigg]<\infty.
$$
 \item[\rm (ii)]
   If $C_{\mathbb V}\bigg[\frac{X^2}{\log\log|X|}\bigg]<\infty$, then for any $\delta>0$ and $p>2$, we have
$$ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\widehat{\mathbb E}\big[\big(|X|\wedge (\delta \sqrt{n\log\log n})\big)^p\big]}{(n\log\log n)^{p/2}}<\infty. $$
 \item[\rm (iii)] If $C_{\mathbb V}\bigg[\frac{X^2}{\log\log|X|}\bigg]<\infty$, then for any $\delta>0$, we have
 $$ \widehat{\mathbb E}[X^2\wedge (2\delta n\log\log n)]=o(\log \log n), $$
  $$ \breve{\mathbb E}[(|X|-\delta \sqrt{2 n\log\log n})^+]=o(\sqrt{\log\log n/n}). $$
\end{description} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem2 of arXiv:2608.30848

THE ROUTE: write P(Y_1 = k) = w_k Z(m - k, n - 1)/Z(m, n) and union bound over the n boxes. WHERE IT BREAKS: Lemma 13.1, the local limit theorem that (18.14) rests on, is proved for FIXED lambda in (0, nu). When lambda_n = m/n -> 0 the tilted laws degenerate - the mass at 0 tends to 1 and the variance to 0 - so the Gaussian local limit theorem has to be replaced by a Poisson-regime one and glued to the Gaussian regime when m is comparable to n. That uniform statement does not appear to exist in the literature, and without it the union bound has no input at all. CONDITION OF FAILURE: m/n -> 0, which is exactly the regime the conjecture is about. The heuristic the route does give is still useful as a target: P(Y_1 >= k) is about w_k tau_n^k / Phi(tau_n) with tau_n = tau(m/n) -> 0, so n P(Y_1 >= k) -> 0 once k >= (1 + eps) log n / log(1/tau_n), and that threshold is o(log n) precisely because tau_n -> 0.

body:
In the binomial random graph G(n,p) with p = (log n + c)/n for a fixed real c, the number of isolated vertices converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable with mean e^{-c} (the method of moments: the factorial moments of the count converge to those of the Poisson law), and the probability that G(n,p) is connected tends to exp(-e^{-c}) (Erdos and Renyi 1959, 1960). The obstruction to connectivity in this window is isolated vertices alone: P(G connected) - P(G has no isolated vertex) tends to 0. Consequently p = log n / n is a sharp threshold: for p = (1 - epsilon) log n / n the graph is disconnected with probability tending to 1 (with a growing number of isolated vertices), and for p = (1 + epsilon) log n / n it is connected with probability tending to 1. Below the threshold at p = c'/n with c' > 1 the graph already has a unique giant component but is disconnected.
edges are present independently with the same probability p (the binomial model; the uniform model G(n,m) has the analogous statement with m = (n/2)(log n + c))
the statement is about the window p = (log n + c)/n with c fixed as n grows
the Poisson approximation is for the count of isolated vertices; other small components are negligible in this window
title: Erdos-Renyi connectivity threshold of G(n,p) and the Poisson paradigm for isolated vertices

[Definition of arXiv:2608.28505, 'Quagmires and large Suslin forests'] Given two cardinals $\kappa < \lambda$, a $(\kappa, \lambda)$-forest\footnote{In Eskew's more general notation, this is a $(\kappa, \lambda, 2)$-forest [MR3326048].} is a collection $F$ of functions satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for every $f \in F$, $\mathrm{ran}(f) \subseteq \{0,1\}$,
\item $\{\mathrm{dom}(f) : f \in F\} = [\lambda]^{< \kappa}$,
\item for every $x,y \in [\lambda]^{< \kappa}$ with $x \subseteq y$,
\[
\{f \in F : \mathrm{dom}(f) = x\} = \{f \upharpoonright x : f \in F \text{ and } \mathrm{dom}(f) = y\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 7 (cf.~\cite{Kobayashi96}) of arXiv:2608.25785, 'Proper Actions on Homogeneous Spaces of the Upper Triangular Matrix Group via Coarse Geome'] Let $G$ be a locally compact Hausdorff group, $L$ and $H$ closed subgroups of $G$.
    The following six conditions are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The natural $L$-action on the homogeneous space $G/H$ is proper.
        \item The natural $H$-action on the homogeneous space $G/L$ is proper.
        \item The diagonal $G$-action on the space $G/H\times G/L$ is proper.
        \item The intersection $L\cap CHC^{-1}$ is relatively compact in $G$ for any compact subset $C$ of $G$.
        \item The intersection $CLC^{-1}\cap H$ is relatively compact in $G$ for any compact subset $C$ of $G$.
        \item The intersection $CHC^{-1}\cap CLC^{-1}$ is relatively compact in $G$ for any compact subset $C$ of $G$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

such that if $u$ is an admissible solution 
to \eqref{SNS2}--\eqref{bin2} satisfying

$$
\E e^{-\phi_{t}}|u_t-v_t|^2_{\cH}
\leq \E |u_0-v_0|_{\cH}^2\quad\text{for $t\in[0,T]$}

for any admissible solution $v$ to \eqref{SNS2}--\eqref{bin2} 
on $[0,T]$ with an $\cH$-valued initial condition

\quad 
\beta_s=\hat u^2+\bar u_s^2+\lambda^2_s+\vartheta^2+\chi^2_s+\kappa_s
$$
and $N=N(d,r,\delta)$ is a constant. In particular, if $u_0=v_0$ 
then almost surely $u_t=v_t$ for all $t\in[0,T]$ for the $H$-valued c\`adl\`ag  
version of the solutions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Owner draft: independently checked proof (C007 v1). Let 1<=d<=m. A spherical R^m law whose first d-coordinate projection is Unif(B_d) must have m<=d+2. Its coordinate second and fourth moments are 1/(d+2) and 3/((d+2)(d+4)), so E||Y||^2=m/(d+2) and E||Y||^4=m(m+2)/((d+2)(d+4)). Nonnegative variance of ||Y||^2 implies the ceiling. At m=d+2 the radius is one almost surely. This is a restriction on spherical extensions, not on arbitrary nonspherical constant-sum couplings. It warns against assuming the matrix-generator extension in Yin's elliptical theorem without checking it.
Integers 1<=d<=m
Spherical invariance of full R^m law
First d-coordinate projection exactly uniform on unit ball

$${\cal A}^1={\cal A}, ~{\cal A}^{k+1}={\cal A}^k \boxtimes {\cal A}, ~k=1, 2, \ldots.$$
By convention, ${\cal A}^0$ is the identity tensor ${\cal I}=[\delta_{i_1i_2\ldots i_m}] \in \mathbb R^{u \times u \times n \times \cdots \times n}$, where for any $1 \le i_1, i_2 \le u$ and $1\le i_3, \ldots, i_m \le n$,
$$\delta_{i_1i_2\ldots i_m}=\delta_{i_1i_2}=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
1, & i_1=i_2;\\
0, & {\rm otherwise}.
\end{array}\right.$$

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a connected compact abelian group, let $\mu$ be its 
Haar probability measure and $Y$ be a random variable on $G$ with 
density $f_Y$. Let $S$ be a set of positive Haar measure 
and $g_S = \frac{1}{\mu(S)}\mathbb{I}_S$ be the density of a uniform 
random variable $U_S$ on $S$. For $t>0$, also define
    \begin{equation*} 
    g^t(y) = \frac{t+f_Y(y)}{1+t}, \quad y \in G.
    \end{equation*}
    Then, for all $t > 0 $
\begin{equation*} 
    \chi^2(f_Y \ast g_S \| g^t  \ast g_S) \leq \eta_S\frac{t+\|f_Y\|_{\infty}}{t}\chi^2(f_Y\|g^t),
\end{equation*}
where
$$\eta_S = \left(\frac{\sin(\pi \mu(S))}{\pi \mu(S)}\right)^2.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.22534

Let $S$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $M \times M$ matrix (a sample covariance) and consider the long-only minimum-variance problem $\min_w w^T S w$ subject to $\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$ and $w \ge 0$. Let $w^+$ be a solution and $\delta \in \mathbb{R}^M$, $\delta \ge 0$, the Lagrange multipliers of the nonnegativity constraints ($\delta_m > 0$ only where $w^+_m = 0$). THEOREM (Jagannathan and Ma, 2003). $w^+$ is also the UNCONSTRAINED minimum-variance solution (subject only to $\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$) for the modified covariance $$\tilde S = S - \delta \mathbf{1}^T - \mathbf{1}\delta^T,$$ which is symmetric, positive semidefinite on the relevant set, and differs from $S$ by lowering the covariances of the constrained (excluded) assets with every other asset by $\delta_m$ and their variances by $2\delta_m$. Imposing the no-short constraint is therefore equivalent to shrinking the large entries of the sample covariance toward zero by data-determined amounts - which is why the constraint improves out-of-sample risk even when the true covariance would not call for it ("why imposing the wrong constraints helps"): it acts as a covariance-shrinkage estimator whose amount is chosen implicitly by the optimisation, without cross-validation.
S symmetric positive semidefinite
the feasible set is nonempty (it always is: the simplex)

body: A random variable X is sub-Gaussian with proxy sigma^2 if E exp(t(X - EX)) <= exp(sigma^2 t^2 / 2) for all real t. Equivalently, its tails satisfy P(|X - EX| > s) <= 2 exp(-s^2 / (2 sigma^2)) up to constants; bounded random variables are sub-Gaussian by Hoeffding's lemma with sigma = (b - a)/2.

\[
p^\star=\mathbb P(q^{p^\star}>0),
\]
where \(q^p\) denotes the stationary random-environment queue defined above.

For each \(i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\), let \(D_i^p\) be a Poisson random measure on
\[
\mathbb R_+\times \mathbb R_+\times \{0,1\}^{N-1}
\]
with intensity
\[
\mathrm du\,\mathrm dz\,\nu_{
p}(\mathrm d\theta),
\]
where \(\nu_{p}\) is the product measure of \(N-1\) independent Bernoulli random
variables with parameter \(p\).

For \(\theta=(\theta_m)_{m\neq i}\in\{0,1\}^{N-1}\), define
\[
\mu_i^{\mathrm{MF2}}(\theta)
=
B\log_2\left(
1+
\frac{1}{1+\sum_{m\neq i}\theta_m l(d(i,m))}
\right).
\]
The McKean--Vlasov approximation of type 2 is defined by
\begin{equation}
q_i^{\mathrm{MF2}}(t)
=
q_i^{\mathrm{MF2}}(0)
+
A_i[0,t]
-
\int_{\{0,1\}^{N-1}}\int_{\mathbb R_+}\int_0^t

[Theorem teoScaleFnBV of arXiv:2604.08889, 'Matrix Representations for Scale Functions of Spectrally Negative Lévy Processes with Rati'] Let $X$ be a L\'evy process as in (equation eqnXTrajectories of the paper), with $\sigma=0$ and $d>0$. Then, for any $x\geq 0$ and $q\geq 0$ such that $\psi'(\Phi_q)>0$ we have
\begin{equation}
W^{(q)}(x) = \frac{1}{\psi'(\Phi_q)} \Big( \mathrm{e}^{\Phi_q x} - \bm{\Psi}\, e^{\bm{G}x}\,\bm{\nu} \Big), \qquad x \ge 0,
\end{equation}where $\bm{G}: = \bm{T} + \bm{t}\,\bm{\Psi}$, $\bm{\nu}:=(\Phi_q \bm I - \bm{T})^{-1}\bm{t}$ with $\bm I$ the identity matrix.
The matrix $\bm{\Psi}$ is a solution to 
\begin{equation}
\bm{\Psi} \big( (\lambda + q)\bm{I} - d\bm{T} - d\,\bm{t}\,\bm{\Psi} \big) = \lambda\, \bm{\alpha}.
\end{equation}Finally, $\bm{\Psi}$ can be obtained as the limit of the recursive equation
\begin{equation}
\bm{\Psi}_n
:=
\Big(\frac{\lambda}{d}\bm{\alpha} + (\bm{\Psi}_{n-1}\bm{t})\bm{\Psi}_{n-1}\Big)
\left(\frac{\lambda + q}{d}\bm I - \bm{T}\right)^{-1},
\end{equation}with  $\bm{\Psi}_0=\bm{0}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Thm summary of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $\gamma_L=(L-1)/\ell$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label={\normalfont(\arabic*)}]
\item The discrete in space processes DITP (resp. DFTP) converge, with quantitative control,  when $L$ tends to infinity, in Skorohod topology towards the continuous-space piecewise deterministic Markov process CITP (resp. CFTP).
\item The processes DITP and DFTP are exponentially ergodic with invariant measures converging as $L$ tends to infinity to the unique invariant measures of the CITP and CFTP.
\item The invariant measures of CITP and CFTP have a positive mass at $\{0\}\times \{-1,0,1\}$ and  $\{\ell\}\times \{-1,0,1\}$.
\item Let us define for a Markov process with semigroup $P_t$ and invariant measure $\pi$ its mixing time as
$t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)=\inf\left\{t\ge0\,;\, sup_\mu\|\mu P_t-\pi\|_{TV}\le \epsilon\right\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\normalfont (a)] The mixing time $t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)$ of CITP is of the order $C'(\epsilon)\frac 1\omega(1+\omega^2l^2)$ for some $C'(\epsilon)$.
\item[\normalfont (b)] The mixing time $t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)$ of CFTP is of the order $C'(\epsilon)(\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta)(1+\alpha^2l^2)$ for some $C'(\epsilon)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm summary of arXiv:2411.13964

body: In computational complexity theory, a branch of computer science, bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time (BPP) is the class of decision problems solvable by a probabilistic Turing machine in polynomial time with an error probability bounded by 1/3 for all instances. BPP is one of the largest practical classes of problems, meaning most problems of interest in BPP have efficient probabilistic algorithms that can be run quickly on real modern machines. BPP also contains P, the class of problems solvable in polynomial time with a deterministic machine, since a deterministic algorithm is a special case of a probabilistic algorithm.

For a measure space (X, mu) and measurable sets A, B, d_mu(A, B) = mu(A symmetric difference B), possibly infinite. For an increasing sequence E_1 in E_2 in ... with increments D_k = E_{k+1} minus E_k and union E, d_mu(E_m, E_n) = sum_{k=m}^{n-1} mu(D_k) for m <= n and d_mu(E_m, E) = sum_{k >= m} mu(D_k). Hence the following are equivalent: the sequence is d_mu-Cauchy; sum_{k >= m} mu(D_k) < infinity for some m; d_mu(E_m, E) < infinity for some m; d_mu(E_n, E) -> 0. Consecutive distances tending to zero are not enough: under the measure with weight 1/k at the point k, the chain E_n = {1, ..., n} has d(E_n, E_{n+1}) = 1/(n+1) -> 0 but is not Cauchy.

body: Let M be a compact, oriented, boundaryless smooth surface with Gaussian curvature K and area element dA. The Gauss-Bonnet theorem states that the integral over M of K dA equals 2 pi chi(M), where chi(M) is the Euler characteristic of M; for instance a topological sphere always has total curvature 4 pi, whatever its metric. If M has a piecewise-smooth boundary with geodesic curvature k_g and exterior angles theta_i at its corners, the formula generalizes to: integral of K dA over M, plus integral of k_g ds over the boundary, plus the sum of the theta_i, equals 2 pi chi(M). Due to Carl Friedrich Gauss and Pierre Ossian Bonnet.
title: Gauss-Bonnet theorem

[Proposition prop:complexZero of arXiv:2608.18320, 'Asymptotics for Beta-Splitting Trees via Homogeneous Fragmentations and Meromorphic Potent'] Let $\beta>0$ be noninteger and let $      \beta=n_\beta+\theta_\beta$ with $       n_\beta=\lfloor\beta\rfloor$.

If $n_\beta$ is even, then $f_\beta$ has exactly $n_\beta$
nonreal zeros, counted with multiplicity. They occur in conjugate pairs.

Suppose that $n_\beta$ is odd. Let $q_\beta$ be the number of zeros
of $f_\beta$ in the upper half-plane, counted with multiplicity, and,
for $0\leq k\leq n_\beta+1$, let $M_k(\beta)$ be the total
multiplicity of the real zeros of $f_\beta$ in $\mathcal I_k$. Then
each $M_k(\beta)$ is odd and
\begin{equation}
        2q_\beta
        +
        \sum_{k=0}^{n_\beta+1}
        \left[M_k(\beta)-1\right]
        =
        n_\beta+1.
\end{equation}
In particular, $f_\beta$ has at most $n_\beta+1$ nonreal zeros,
counted with multiplicity.

Consequently, for every noninteger $\beta>0$, only finitely many zeros
of $f_\beta$ are nonreal or multiple. All the remaining zeros are real
and simple.

[Theorem 1 ($J$-stable criterion, see Theorem 1.1 of Song~\cite{Song}) of arXiv:2608.29736, '2608.29736'] Let $(M^n,\omega)$ be a compact K\"ahler manifold of complex
 dimension $n\geq 2$. Let $\chi$ be another K\"ahler form. Suppose that the pair $(\chi,\omega)$ is $J$-stable, that is,
  $\displaystyle\int_M \left(\chi^n-n\chi^{n-1}\wedge\omega\right)\geq 0,$ and for any $p$-dimensional subvarieties $V\subset M$ with $1\leq p\leq n-1$, \(
    \displaystyle\int_V \left(\chi^p-p\chi^{p-1}\wedge\omega\right)>0.\)
    Then there exists a smooth function $u$ such that  $\chi_u$ is a K\"ahler form and satisfies the cone condition $$\chi_u^{n-1}-(n-1)\chi_u^{n-2}\wedge\omega>0.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 251 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If $\bX:\R^{N'}\to\R^N$ is $L$-Lipschitz, and $\bg$ is a standard gaussian in $\R^{N'}$, then $\bX(\bg)-\E[\bX(\bg)]$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $2L^2$.
(As a result, Lemma~\ref{l:sg.norm.bound} applies with $\sigma^2=2L^2$.)

\begin{proof}
Recall from \cite[Thm.~1.3.4]{MR2731561} that if the function $F: \R^N\to\R$ is $L$-Lipschitz, and $\bg$ is a standard gaussian in $\R^N$, then
    \[
    \E \exp\bigg\{
     s\Big( F(\bg)-\E f(\bg)\Big)\bigg\}
    \le \exp(s^2 L^2)
    \]
for all $s\in\R$, i.e., the random variable $F(g)-\E F(g)$ is subgaussian
with variance proxy $2L^2$. As a consequence we have the subgaussian tail bound
    \beq
    \P\bigg(
    \Big|  F(\bg)-\E f(\bg) \Big| \ge t
    \bigg)
    \le 2 \exp\bigg\{ -\frac{t^2}{4L^2}
    \bigg\}
    \eeq
for all $t\ge0$. Now suppose $\bX:\R^{N'}\to\R^N$ is $L$-Lipschitz. If $\theta$ is a unit vector in $\R^N$, then it is easily seen that $\bg\mapsto (\theta,\bX(\bg))$ is $L$-Lipschitz. It follows from \eqref{e:lip.subgaus} that the scalar random variable $(\theta,X(\bg)-\E[X(\bg)])$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $2L^2$, as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:topo of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $z_1, \dots, z_n$ be distinct points in $D$. Let $A \subseteq D$ be a closed connected set not containing any of the $z_j$, such that $D \setminus A$ has countably many connected components,  the boundary of each connected component is a Jordan curve, and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ only finitely many of these curves have diameter more than 
$\varepsilon$. 

Let $\widehat A$ be the set obtained as follows: we take the connected components $O_j$ of $z_j$ in $D \setminus A$, the connected component $O_0$ whose boundary is $\partial D$ and set 
$\widehat A := \overline{D \setminus \bigcup_{j=0}^n O_j}$.

Then there exists a closed path $\gamma \subseteq A$ with $\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\indx_{\gamma}(z_j) \text{ odd}$ if and only if there exists a closed path $\widehat \gamma \subseteq \widehat A$ with $\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\indx_{\widehat \gamma}(z_j) \text{ odd}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:topo of arXiv:2604.15146

On Z^4 let p_n be the full-space discrete-time nearest-neighbor SRW kernel, g_T(x)=sum_{n=0}^T p_n(x), sigma_T^2=sum_x g_T(x)^2, and let xi_z be independent standard Gaussians. Define Y_T(x)=sum_z g_T(x-z)xi_z/sigma_T and H_T(x)=1{Y_T(x)>=sqrt(2 log T)}, h_T=E H_T(0). For every fixed a>0, with graph radius R_T=floor(a h_T^(-1/4)), liminf_{T->infinity} log[sum_{0<|x|<=R_T} E(H_T(0)H_T(x))/h_T]/log T >= 2/3. Thus this comparison field violates bounded Palm clustering at mean spacing. It is not a parking process and has no active-particle field. Novelty: UNCHECKED exact comparison statement; KNOWN Gaussian tail method. Status: independently checked proof.

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: UNCHECKED exact comparison statement;
KNOWN Gaussian density method and SRW kernel estimates. This is not a
claim about the actual parking field.

Let p_n be the full-space, discrete-time, uniform nearest-neighbor SRW
kernel on Z^4. For integer T>=2 put g_T(x)=sum_{n=0}^T p_n(x). Let
(xi_z) be independent standard real Gaussian variables, and define

    Y_T(x) = sum_z g_T(x-z) xi_z / sigma_T,
    sigma_T^2 = sum_z g_T(z)^2.

The sums are finite. Each Y_T(x) is standard normal, and the field is
stationary. Define H_T(x)=1{Y_T(x)>=sqrt(2 log T)}, h_T=E H_T(0), and
R_T=floor(a h_T^(-1/4)) for a fixed a>0. Then

    liminf_{T->infinity} log[ sum_{0<|x|_1<=R_T}
                  E(H_T(0)H_T(x))/h_T ] / log T >= 2/3.

In particular this field violates C9's bounded Palm clustering hypothesis
for every a>0. There is no active-particle field or parking dynamics in
this construction; it does not refute any claim concerning that dynamics.

## Covariance and the graph-ball scale

By symmetry and the semigroup property,

    C_T(x):=sum_z g_T(z)g_T(z-x)
           =sum_{n=0}^{2T} w_{T,n} p_n(x),

where w_{T,n}=n+1 for n<=T and w_{T,n}=2T-n+1 for T<n<=2T.
The uniform heat-kernel bound p_n(x)<=C n^(-2) shows that the tail
T<n<=2T contributes O(1), uniformly in x. The first part is exactly
the kernel of I0005-C1 v1. Consequently, with c=4/pi^2,

    C_T(x)=c log_+(T/(1+|x|_2^2))+O(1),
    sigma_T^2=c log T+O(1).

All constants are independent of x and T. The positive covariance kernel
here is the convolution square of g_T; no assertion of positive
definiteness for an arbitrary truncated semigroup polynomial is needed.

Mills' estimate follows directly by integrating the normal density: for
v>0, phi(v) v/(v^2+1)<=P(Z>=v)<=phi(v)/v. Thus

    h_T=(1+o(1))/(2 sqrt(pi log T) T).

It follows that R_T=T^(1/4+o(1)). In the annulus
R_T/2<=|x|_1<=R_T, norm equivalence gives |x|_2=T^(1/4+o(1)), uniformly.
Therefore

    rho_T(x):=E[Y_T(0)Y_T(x)]=1/2+o(1)

uniformly on this annulus. In particular rho lies in [1/3,2/3] eventually.

## Uniform bivariate tail estimate

Let (Z,W) be standard jointly Gaussian with correlation rho in [1/3,2/3]
and put v=sqrt(2 log T). The implication Z,W>=v => Z+W>=2v and the
Gaussian exponential-moment bound give

    P(Z,W>=v)<=exp(-v^2/(1+rho)).

For a matching logarithmic lower bound, integrate the joint density over
[v,v+1/v]^2. Its area is 1/v^2. On that rectangle the density exponent is

    (z^2-2rho zw+w^2)/(2(1-rho^2))
                  <=v^2/(1+rho)+C,

with one uniform C because rho stays in the stated compact interval.
The density prefactor is uniformly bounded below by a positive constant.
Hence

    P(Z,W>=v)>=c v^(-2) exp(-v^2/(1+rho)).

For rho_T(x)=1/2+o(1), these bounds imply

    E[H_T(0)H_T(x)]=T^(-4/3+o(1))

uniformly throughout the annulus.

## Palm summation

The number of annulus sites is a positive constant times R_T^4,
up to a lower-order boundary error, hence T^(1+o(1)). Also
h_T^(-1)=T^(1+o(1)). Keeping only this annulus in the nonnegative sum
gives

    sum_{0<|x|_1<=R_T} E[H_T(0)H_T(x)]/h_T
                    >=T^(1+1-4/3+o(1))=T^(2/3+o(1)).

This proves the claimed liminf and divergence.

## What the comparison excludes

The full-space G*G obstruction in the parking source resembles the
logarithmic covariance used here. By contrast the interlacement benchmark
C10 uses a single Green function and has bounded Palm counts. Neither
comparison identifies the actual parking field. They show that decay of
the one-hole intensity and a reference to random-walk Green functions do
not, by themselves, imply C9's Palm bound. The stopping dynamics must be
used in any valid transfer theorem.

I0005-C1 periodic local-CLT expansion also supplies the uniform heat-kernel bound.

aperiodicity hypothesis excludes this SRW. The elementary

For a d-regular Cayley graph, if rho is the normalized simple-random-walk spectral radius, the Benjamini-Schramm sufficient criterion is d*rho*p_c<1. The earlier C0047 attempt's p_c<1/rho drops d; when 0<rho<1 this inequality is automatic because p_c<=1<1/rho, so it cannot certify p_c<p_u. The corrected criterion is only sufficient: on the four-regular tree p_c=1/3, rho=sqrt(3)/2 and d*rho*p_c=2sqrt(3)/3>1 although p_u=1.

For B in R^(m x w), A in R^(w x n), and differentiable convex loss C on m-by-n matrices, set U=[B;A^T], Z=UU^T and F(Z)=C(Z12)+C(Z21^T) on (m+n)-square matrices. Then F(UU^T)/2=C(BA). At symmetric Z, with G=grad C(Z12), grad F(Z)=[[0,G],[G^T,0]]. Thus Uprime=-grad F(UU^T)U is exactly the asymmetric gradient flow Bprime=-GA^T, Aprime=-B^T G; the Gram matrix solves Zprime=-Z grad F(Z)-grad F(Z)Z. No whitening, data commutation, or initial balance is required. With a simple positive top residual singular value s, the conditional Gram escape theorem uses rate 2s and requires (v^T Zalpha v)/||Zalpha-Zbar||_F to have a strictly positive liminf; nonzero projection alone is insufficient. Section 3 of arXiv:2012.09839, PDF p.3 explicitly gives the square asymmetric-to-symmetric reduction; these formulas spell out arbitrary rectangular block sizes and the exact gradient-flow normalization. Applying Theorem G.2 requires all its hypotheses; for quadratic regression its all-real-time convention requires a local complete extension, since quadratic flow need not be backward complete. This is an existing reduction and conditional local theorem, not an unconditional Gaussian second-step result.

[Cor 190 (quenched first moment bounds on $Q^\sigma$ and $Q^{\sigma,\frozen}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $Q$ as in Definition~\ref{d:Q}, we have
	$\bE[\Delta Q^\RomI(q_d)]
	\le L^{O(1)}(\MAX_N)^2\delta^2$
with $\MAX_N$ as in Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}. We also have
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
	\bE\Delta Q^\sigma(q_d)
	\le L^{O(1)}\bigg\{
	(\MAX_N)^2
	+ \frac{(\SMAX_N)^2 \BUCKETS}{N}
	\bigg\} \delta
	\]
with $\SMAX_N$ as in Proposition~\ref{p:drift.quenched}. The same bound holds for the $Q^{\frozen,\sigma}$ processes.
	
\begin{proof}
Recall that $Q^\sigma=E^\sigma+\tilde{Q}^\sigma$. It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:qv.simplification} that
	\[
	\Big|\Delta E^\sigma(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O\bigg(
	\eta^2
	+\eta\Big(\Delta\tilde{Q}^\sigma(q_d)\Big)^{1/2}
	+\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\sigma(q_d)\Big)^2\bigg)\,.
	\]
For $\sigma=\RomI$, it follows by combining Lemma~\ref{l:barD.I.second.quenched} with Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched} that
	\[
	\bE\Delta Q^\RomI(q_d)
	\le \bE\Delta \tilde{Q}^\RomI(q_d)
		+\bE\Big|\Delta E^\RomI(q_d)\Big|
	\le
	L^{O(1)} \bigg\{
	\eta^2 + (\MAX_N)^2\delta^2 \bigg\}\,.
	\]
For $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$,
it follows by combining Lemmas~\ref{l:barD.II.second.quenched}--\ref{l:barD.Ising.second.quenched} with Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched} that
	\[
	\bE\Delta Q^\sigma(q_d)
	\le\bE\Delta \tilde{Q}^\sigma(q_d)+ \bE\Big|\Delta E^\sigma(q_d)\Big| 
	\le L^{O(1)}\bigg\{
	\eta^2
	+(\MAX_N)^2\delta
	+ \frac{(\SMAX_N)^2 \BUCKETS\delta}{N}
	\bigg\}\,.\]
This proves the claim for the $Q^\sigma$ processes,
using that $\MAX_N\ge1$ and $\eta\ll\delta$. The analogous bound for the $Q^{\frozen,\sigma}$ processes follows by the same argument.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$$p_n(\theta)\, =\, {\mathbb{E}}\left[ X_\theta^n\right]\qquad \mbox{and}\qquad p_n(1/\theta)\, =\, {\mathbb{E}}[X_{1/\theta}^n]$$
for all $n\ge 0.$

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is the computed finite table in the campaign partial answer to Afonso S. Bandeira's Open Problem 11, How many deviations are needed afterall?, in Did just a couple of deviations suffice all along? (problems 10-14), Randomstrasse 101 (19 December 2024; https://randomstrasse101.math.ethz.ch/posts/HowManyDeviations/). For an n-by-n matrix A with entries in {+1,-1}, define disc(A)=min_{x in {+1,-1}^n} ||Ax||_infinity, where ||y||_infinity=max_i |y_i|, and let D_n=max_{A in {+1,-1}^{n-by-n}} disc(A). The record reports (n,D_n)=(2,2),(3,1),(4,2),(5,3),(6,4),(7,3),(8,4),(9,5),(10,4),(11,5). Achievability was checked by exhaustive sign-colouring enumeration of computed witness matrices; for each next possible level the sign-cube covering count is insufficient, except at n=10 and level six. At that exception the record invokes both a solver's proved infeasibility and the published binary covering-code minimum K(10,2)=30>20, where K(n,R) is the least number of binary codewords covering all binary vectors of length n within Hamming radius R. Only the size-six and size-nine matrices are written out in the listed record and retained as explicit proved entries here; the rest of this table remains a reported exact computation without all its witness certificates in this bundle. The record leaves n=12 and the unrestricted supremum undecided. This is an unrefereed campaign result.

[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2607.04193, 'Onsager--Machlup Functionals for Generalized Newtonian Equations of Motion with Time-Varyi'] Let $\frac14<H<\frac12$ and set $\alpha=\frac12-H\in(0,\frac14)$. Let
$f\in C^{1+\beta}_0([0,1];\mathbb R^d)$ with
\[
    0<\beta<H-\frac14 .
\]
Then the mapping
\[
    s\mapsto s^{-2\alpha}I_{0^+}^{\alpha}(s^\alpha f_s)
\]
belongs to $C^1([0,1];\mathbb R^d)$. Moreover, there exists a constant $C>0$
such that
\begin{equation}
    \left\|
        s^{-2\alpha}I_{0^+}^{\alpha}(s^\alpha f_s)
    \right\|_{C^1([0,1];\mathbb R^d)}
    \le C\|f\|_{1+\beta}.
\end{equation}

body: In mathematics, the axiom of choice, abbreviated AC or AoC, is an axiom of set theory. Informally put, the axiom of choice says that given any collection of non-empty sets, one can identify another set containing one element chosen from each set, even if the collection is infinite. Formally, the axiom establishes existence rather than a construction; it states that for every set and every -indexed family of nonempty sets, there exists an -indexed set of elements of such that for every . The axiom of choice was formulated in 1904 by Ernst Zermelo in order to formalize his proof of the well-ordering theorem.
title: Axiom of choice

    Assume that Assumption \ref{ass:affine-coeff} holds, that $a^0(t)$ is continuously differentiable and that the pair $(a^1,X)$ is semimartingale differentiable as in \eqref{cond:for-diffusion-part} with coefficients $(\Gamma, \Pi)$, where $\Gamma$ is by assumption affine with representation $\Gamma(t,x) = \Gamma^0(t) + \Gamma^1(t) \cdot x_{[0,t]}$ for $(t,x) \in \ccC_T^1$.

    \begin{align}

        \Pi(t)(b^1(t) \cdot x_{[0,t]}) - \Gamma^1(t) \cdot x_{[0,t]} & = \lambda(t)\bigl( a^1(t) \cdot x_{[0,t]} \bigr), \quad \forall (t,x) \in \ccC_T^1. 
    \end{align}
    Then $a(t,X_{[0,t]})$ is non-decreasing on the zero set for all $t \in [0,T]$.

body:
Ren-Nichani-Wu-Lee population MSE identity. Let X~N(0,I_d), let v_star,1,...,v_star,P be orthonormal, and let a_p>=0 with sum_p a_p^2=1. Let sigma be a real even link with sigma=sum_{i>=I} c_2i h_2i in L2(N(0,1)), I>=1, and sum_i c_2i^2=1, in the normalized probabilists Hermite basis. Let all student vectors v_k be nonzero and finite in number, and set f_v(x)=sum_k b_k sigma(u_k dot x), u_k=v_k/||v_k||_2, b_k=||v_k||_2^2, and f_star(x)=sum_p a_p sigma(v_star,p dot x). Define C(r)=sum_{i>=I} c_2i^2*r^(2i), -1<=r<=1. Then L=(1/2)E[(f_star(X)-f_v(X))^2]=(1/2)sum_p a_p^2-sum_{p,k}a_p*b_k*C(v_star,p dot u_k)+(1/2)sum_{k,l}b_k*b_l*C(u_k dot u_l). Equivalently, L=(1/2)sum_{i>=I}c_2i^2*||sum_p a_p*v_star,p^(tensor 2i)-sum_k b_k*u_k^(tensor 2i)||_F^2. Both series are finite-valued and converge absolutely. This deterministic identity is the source equation4; it needs no SGD convergence, sample independence across training steps, or neuron-initialization assumption. It is valid under the weaker link hypotheses displayed here, in particular without the differentiability assumptions needed to run SGD.
Finite orthonormal teacher family and finitely many nonzero student vectors.

[Lemma 13 (Uniform boundary decay) of arXiv:2608.30211, '2608.30211'] Let $G_j$ be domains whose boundaries in $B_{2r}(p_j)$ are given by
uniformly $C^{1,1}$ graphs, and let
$h_j\in L^\infty(G_j\cap B_{2r}(p_j))$.  Suppose that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 w_j\in H^1(G_j\cap B_{2r}(p_j))
 \cap C(\overline{G_j\cap B_{2r}(p_j)}),\\
 -\Delta w_j=h_j\quad\hbox{in }G_j\cap B_{2r}(p_j),\\
 \|w_j\|_\infty\leq M,\qquad \|h_j\|_\infty\leq M_1.
 \end{gathered}
\]
There are $\eta\in(0,1)$ and $C>0$, depending only on the dimension and
the uniform graph bounds, such that, for $0<\delta<r/8$,
\begin{align}
 \sup_{\substack{x\in G_j\cap B_{r/2}(p_j)\\
                  \dist(x,\partial G_j)\leq\delta}}
 |w_j(x)|
 &\leq \sup_{\partial G_j\cap B_r(p_j)}|w_j|
 \notag\\
 &\quad+C(M+M_1r^2)\left(\frac{\delta}{r}\right)^\eta .
 
\end{align}
The constants are uniform over the family $G_j$.

body: The Fourier entropy-influence conjecture is equivalent to its restriction to Boolean functions all of whose influences are below any fixed tau: a coordinate of influence at least tau has restriction drop Delta_i <= (2/ln 2 + log2(e/tau)) Inf_i, so a violation localizes to a subcube on which every influence is small and the restriction step fails at every coordinate. On self-compositions of Numaro's record function the restriction-step constant rho_0 = min_i Delta_i/Inf_i is 6.3290, 6.8901 and 7.0519 at 324, 5832 and 104976 variables (limit about 7.1116), so no potential-free coordinate induction can give a constant below 7.05. The XOR gate inequality is certified, so read-once formulas over AND, OR, XOR and NOT satisfy H <= 6.4573 I; a prime monotone 7-input gate breaks the read-once potential behind that bound; the five prime 3-input classes (one-hot, MAJ3, EQ3, MUX, Q3) are proved, while fan-in 3 at 6.4573 in general is numerical only. Per-coordinate erasure bounds fail even for monotone functions (majority with one flipped point gives ratio at least (n - 3 log2 n)/2). The full conjecture remains open.

[Definition 6 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $U : \T^d \to \R^d$ with $U \in C^0(\T^d)$ and $y \in \T^d$. Define
    \[R_t(y) := \sup_{X^1,\ X^2 \text{ solutions to~\eqref{eq:main ODE autonomous data}}}  d_{\T^d}(X^1_t, X^2_t).\]
    If, for some $t_0 >0,$ $R_t(y) = 0$ for all $t \in [0,t_0]$, then we say that $U$ is \textit{effectively regular at $y$}.
    Otherwise, we define
    \[E(y) := 1-\limsup_{t \to 0^+} \frac{\log t}{\log R_t(y)}.\]
    We then say that $U$ has \textit{effective Lagrangian regularity} $E(y)$ at $y$.

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2606.31287, '\bf Heat kernel lower bound estimates for symmetric pure jump processes via averaged jump '] \begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm (i)]  We say that ${\rm J}_{\phi, \leq}$ holds if there is some constant $c_{\ref{e:1.2}} > 0$ so that 
\be 
  J(x, y) \le \frac{c_{\ref{e:1.2}}}{V(x,d(x, y)) \phi (d(x, y))}
\ee 
for any $x, y \in \sX$.
 

 \item[\rm (ii)]\,\,Let $D$ be an open subset of $\sX$. Define
\[
\sF_D := \{ u : u \in \sF, u = 0 \,\,\text{for $\sE$-quasi everywhere on $D^c$}\}
\]
and
\[
\lambda_1(D) = \inf \left\{ \sE(f,f):  \,  f \in \sF_D \hbox{ with }  \|f\|_2 =1 \right\},
\]
where $\| u\|_2$ is the $L^2$-norm of $u \in L^2(K, \mu)$. Note that $\lambda_1(D)$ is the bottom of the Dirichlet spectrum for the generator of the subprocess $X^D$ of $X$ killed upon leaving $D$.

\item[\rm (iii)]\,\,
 We say that an MMD space $(\sX,d,m,\sE, \sF)$  satisfies the {\em Faber-Krahn
inequality} ${\rm FK}(\phi)$, if there exist constants $c_{\ref{e:fki}} > 0$, $\sigma_{\ref{e:fki}} \in (0, 1/2)$ and
$\theta > 0$ such that for any $r \in (0, {\sigma_{\ref{e:fki}}}\,\diam{\sX})$, any ball $B(x, r)$ and any open set $D \subseteq B(x, r)$, 
\be 
 \lambda_1(D) \ge \frac{c_{\ref{e:fki}}}{\phi(r)} \Big(\frac{V(x,r)}{m(D)}\Big)^{\theta}.
\ee

 \item[\rm (iv)]\,\, Let $\sF_b = \sF\cap L^\infty(\sX, m)$. We say that an MMD space $(\sX,d,m,\sE, \sF)$   satisfies the 
 {\em weak Poincar\'e inequality}
(${\rm PI} (\phi)$)
  if there exist constants $c_{\ref{eq:PIn}} > 0 $, $\sigma_{\ref{eq:PIn}} \in (0, 1/2)$ and $\delta \ge 1$ such that
for any $r \in (0, \sigma_{\ref{eq:PIn}}\,\diam{\sX})$, any $x \in \sX$ and $f \in \sF_b$,
\begin{equation}
\int_{B_r} (f(x) - \bar{f}_{B_r})^2m(dx) \le c_{\ref{eq:PIn}}\phi(r)\int_{{B_{\delta r}}\times {B_{\delta r}}} (f(y)-f(x))^2\,J(dx,dy),
\end{equation}
 where $B_r = B(x, r)$ and $\bar{f}_{B_r}= \frac{1}{m({B_r})}\int_{B_r} f(x)m(dx)$ is the average value of $f$ on $B_r$.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:four-point-prime-energy-stability of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] The four-point seed is a shift-stable $3$-chart of depth $\gamma_0h$.
For every fixed $t\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ and every fixed system of prime
windows satisfying (equation eq:prime-window-constants of the paper),
the suspended four-point chart satisfies, uniformly in the prime tuple,
\begin{equation}
 N_h\gg_t h^4,
 \qquad
 E_h\leq h^5\exp\!\left(O_t\!\left(
  \frac{\log h}{\log\log h}\right)\right).
\end{equation}
In particular it is prime-energy stable with exponents $(a,\mu)=(4,5)$.

body:
[Lemma lem:invariant-selected-column of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $V$ be a real orthogonal space of dimension $d$, with
\[
 \Omega_V=d^{-1/2}\sum_{\mu=1}^d e_\mu\otimes e_\mu.
\]
Let $R_i:L\to M_i$ and orthogonal projections $P_{i,m}$ satisfy
\[
 \sum_iR_i^*R_i\preceq I_L,
 \qquad [P_{i,m},R_i^*R_i]=0.
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12p_7}$}
\]
Let $T:V\to L\otimes E$ be fixed, let $S_{i,\theta}$ be contractions
on the passive factors, and let $\rho_i(\theta)$ be orthogonal on $V$.
Then
\[
 \boxed{
 \sum_i\int
 \|(R_iP_{i,m}\otimes S_{i,\theta})
       (T\rho_i(\theta)\otimes I)\Omega_V\|^2
 \frac{d\theta}{2\pi}
 \le \frac1d\|T\|_2^2
 \le\|T\|_{\rm op}^2.}
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12p_8}$}
\]
The same assertion holds if an own-circle output rotation is placed
between $T$ and $R_iP_{i,m}$, provided the latter intertwines that
rotation.  It is stable under passive Hilbert amplification, adjunction,
full transpose, and orthogonal rail permutation.

Fix depth l+1 and a fully connected scalar-output ReLU network with input dimension d and hidden widths d_1,...,d_l. All weight matrices are independent with independent Gaussian entries of variance 1/d_previous. Put b=min(d,d_1,...,d_l) and D=max(d,d_1,...,d_l); the scalar output width is not included. There are positive constants c_1,c_2,c_3 depending only on l such that, for D sufficiently large and 0<delta<=1/2, b>=c_1*(log D)^c_2*log(1/delta) implies: for each fixed deterministic x!=0, with probability at least 1-delta there is a scalar eta, allowed to depend on the sampled network and x, for which f(x+eta*grad f(x)) has the opposite sign from f(x), and ||eta*grad f(x)||/||x||<=c_3*sqrt(log(1/delta)/d). No hidden layer is required to be comparable to the input dimension. For l=2, w=floor(d^c), 0<c<1, and w<=m<=d^A for fixed A>=c, delta=w^(-p), p>0 fixed, satisfies the condition for all sufficiently large d. At ||x||=sqrt(d), the radius is then O(sqrt(log w)).
Fixed depth l+1
Independent Gaussian entries with inverse incoming-width variance
ReLU activation
Fixed deterministic nonzero input
D sufficiently large, 0<delta<=1/2, and the stated quantitative minimum-width condition
Adaptive scalar eta along the initial gradient is permitted

body: Kuratowski's theorem: A finite graph G is planar if and only if G contains no subgraph that is a subdivision of K_5 (the complete graph on 5 vertices) and no subgraph that is a subdivision of K_{3,3} (the complete bipartite graph with parts of size 3 and 3). Here a subdivision of a graph H is any graph obtained from H by replacing its edges with internally disjoint paths.

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent review pending. # Positive-budget global risk differs from expected conditional minimax risk

T379-C014 v2: proof (unaudited), exact rational checks PASS. Target 2;
route-failure of a tempting extension, not a new exact global frontier.

Use the full-verifier, untagged experiment of C013 with d=3,K=2,r=1,
n=1,N>=7. Write lambda=1/(2N), kappa=1/2 and choose robust calibration
budget c=2lambda=1/N. The three pairs are numbered 0,1,2. Conditional
on the verifier output, relabel each certified candidate as 0. Each A
therefore has only candidate 0 true; S has both candidates true. This
relabeling preserves all factual probabilities. Fixed S contexts are
6,...,N-1. The verifier supplies no orientation labels.

One factual sample outside the certified sets resolves exactly one
pair; otherwise all three are unresolved. Thus P(U=3)=1-3lambda and
P(U=2)=3lambda, uniformly in every fixed world and verifier output.
C013's conditional worst-world frontier is zero at U=2 and lambda/2
at U=3. Its expectation is

 E V(c,U)=lambda/2-3lambda^2/2.                         (1)

## Feasible asymmetric algorithm

On U=2, use C013's attainer, removing all posterior mass 2lambda from
the unresolved outside-certificate atoms and adding it to fixed S.
This has zero false mass in every compatible world and Mis<=2lambda.

On U=3, leave pair 0 balanced. For each of pairs 1 and 2, if the factual
sample is a certified candidate in that pair, predict that its context
is A. Otherwise predict either orientation by an independent fair coin.
This is a rule using observed data only. Form two sets of outside-
certificate atoms:

* B1: both atoms of pair 0 and the predicted-S atom of pairs 1 and 2;
* B2: the predicted-A atom of pairs 1 and 2.

Assign g=lambda/4 to each of B1's four atoms, g=0 to B2's two atoms,
g=3lambda/2 to each of the six certified atoms, and
g=lambda+lambda/(N-6) to each of the 2(N-6) fixed S atoms.
These masses sum to lambda+9lambda+2(N-6)lambda+2lambda=1.

For ANY compatible orientation let t be the number of true S atoms
in B1 from pairs 1 and 2. The source mass of B1 is lambda(1+t),
that of B2 is lambda(2-t), and that of the six certified atoms is
9lambda, all with the latter group assigned equal g. The fixed S
group receives exactly 2lambda extra g mass. Uniformly coarsening p
within these four groups gives TV to g equal to

 [t lambda+(2-t)lambda+2lambda]/2=2lambda.

Each group has constant g; the exact score partition can only merge
groups. Uniform averaging is TV-contractive and fixes g, so actual
source Mis_infinity<=2lambda even at N=8 where two scores coincide.
This verifies robust feasibility for every orientation and every coin
realization, without assuming that the orientation predictions are right.

Let E be the number of wrong orientation predictions in pairs 1 and 2.
Exactly one atom of pair 0 is false. Therefore on U=3 the ACTUAL false
mass is

 H=(lambda/4)(1+E).                                   (2)

For example, if both predictions happen to be right, H=lambda/4 is
strictly below the conditional minimax value lambda/2. For the opposite
orientations the same generator has H=3lambda/4. Thus a conditional
worst-world lower bound is not a lower bound in each actual world.

## Expectation in each fixed world

The one-sample categories below are disjoint. Each expected H averages
only the algorithm's independent fair tie coins; their probabilities
are factual sampling probabilities in a fixed actual world.

| Observation | Probability | Expected H |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outside certificate in any S of the three pairs | 3lambda | 0 |
| Certified atom in pair 0 | 3lambda | lambda/2 |
| Certified atom in true A of pair 1 or 2 | 4lambda | 3lambda/8 |
| Certified atom in true S of pair 1 or 2 | 2lambda | 5lambda/8 |
| Fixed S context | 1-12lambda | lambda/2 |

Multiplying and summing gives, in EVERY fixed world and conditional
on EVERY verifier realization,

 E H=lambda/2-7lambda^2/4
     < lambda/2-3lambda^2/2=E V(c,U),                  (3)

with strict gap lambda^2/4=1/(16N^2). Thus the global minimax expected
value is at most the left expression and is strictly below the expected
conditional worst-world value. For N=7 these values are 3/112 versus
11/392, separated by 1/784. No optimality of this algorithm is asserted.

This does not contradict C013, whose exact GLOBAL value was asserted
only at c=0; its positive-budget conditional statement and global bracket
remain intact. This auxiliary-route counterexample is not claimed to
score as a target narrowing. Source calibration definition: Kalai--
Vempala 2311.14648v3, Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9. All other work here is
an owner-own-work unaudited draft. Priority and independent audit pending.

Exact verification: logs/positive_budget_separation_check.json records
13824 compatible-world feasibility checks, 1920 sample/coin outcomes,
32 fixed-world expectation checks and 384 pointwise negative controls.
The runs include N=7,8,9,12; N=8 checks the merged-score case directly.
The construction and expectation derivation above cover every N>=7.
Full-support verification in every variable context including paired S, without orientations
Independent fair algorithmic orientation tie coins; robust source Mis_infinity<=c on every data/coin outcome
All other hypotheses and sample protocol exactly as C013, specialized as stated

[Lem MainSeriesKeyLem of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $L_{1},\cdots,L_{r}$ be given vectors
of positive integers and let $n_{0}\geqslant1$. Suppose that $|L_{1}|+\cdots+|L_{r}|+n_{0}=k\leqslant N.$
Then one has 
\begin{align}
 & \sum_{\xi_{0}+\xi_{1}+\cdots+\xi_{r}=l-r}{\rm ad}_{A}^{\xi_{r}}\circ{\rm ad}_{\hat{F}_{w}(H_{L_{r}})}\circ\cdots\circ{\rm ad}_{A}^{\xi_{1}}\circ{\rm ad}_{\hat{F}_{w}(H_{L_{1}})}\circ{\rm ad}_{A}^{\xi_{0}}\big(\hat{F}_{w}(D_{n_{0}}\tilde{L})\big)\nonumber \\
 & =\sum_{i}\sum_{\mu=1}^{r+1}\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}\cdot(b_{i}^{i+n_{0}^{\mu-1}-1})^{l+1-\mu}\nonumber \\
 & \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \sum_{I\in{\cal W}_{\mu,r}}\frac{(-1)^{\varepsilon(I)}\Psi_{I,n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf L}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}\cdot}{b_{(i_{\mu}),n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf n}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}b_{(i_{\mu},i_{\mu+1}),n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf n}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}\cdots b_{I,n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf n}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}}E_{i-|{\bf n}_{{\bf p}}^{\mu,r}|,i+n_{0}^{\mu-1}+|{\bf n}_{{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}|}.
\end{align}
Here \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{W}_{\mu,r}$} denotes the set of words $I=(i_{\mu},i_{\mu+1},\cdots,i_{r})\in\{\pm1\}^{r-\mu+1}$. Given such a word $I$, the vector $\mathbf{p}$
denotes the subword of $(\mu,\cdots,r)$ which records the locations
of $-1$'s in $I$ and ${\bf q}\triangleq(\mu,\cdots,r)\backslash{\bf p}$.
The quantity $\varepsilon(I)$ denotes the length of ${\bf p}$ (i.e.
number of $-1$'s in $I$). The function $\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}$
is defined by 
\[
\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}\triangleq\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0},i}(b_{i},b_{i+1},\cdots,b_{i+k-1}),
\]
where $\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0},i}$ is a suitable meromorphic
function in $m$ complex variables ($m\triangleq n_{0}+|L_{1}|+\cdots+|L_{\mu-1}|$)
whose shape depends on $(L_{1},\cdots,L_{\mu-1}),n_{0}$ and $i$.
The family $\{\Theta_{L_{1},\cdots,L_{\mu-1},n_{0}}^{i}\}$ of functions
satisfy the following property: for any integer $i$, $1\leqslant\nu\leqslant r$
and any sequence of vectors ${\bf V}=(V_{1},\cdots,V_{r})$, under
the one-dimensional reduction $b_{j}\triangleq b_{j}^{*}+w$ the function
\begin{equation}
w\mapsto\sum_{\sigma\in{\cal S}_{\nu}}\Theta_{V_{\sigma(\nu)},\cdots,V_{\sigma(1)},n_{0}}^{i}
\end{equation}
is analytic near $w=0$ and vanishes at $w=0$. When $\mu=1,$ the
function $\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}$ depends only
on $n_{0}$ and $i$. As a convention, if $\mu=r+1$ the summation
$\sum_{I\in{\cal W}(\mu,r)}$ in ((lem:MainSeriesKeyLem of the paper)) is
set to be one and $|{\bf n}_{{\bf p}}^{\mu,r}|=|{\bf n}_{{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}|\triangleq0$
. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Rouché's theorem, named after Eugène Rouché, states that for any two complex-valued functions f and g holomorphic inside some region K with closed contour partial K (the boundary of K), if |g(z)| < |f(z)| on partial K, then f and f + g have the same number of zeros inside K, where each zero is counted as many times as its multiplicity. This theorem assumes that the contour is simple, that is, without self-intersections. Rouché's theorem is an easy consequence of a stronger symmetric form of Rouché's theorem, in which the strict inequality |f(z) - g(z)| < |f(z)| + |g(z)| on the contour implies that f and g have the same number of zeros inside.

body:
Let (P_t) be the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup on L^p of the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. For 1 < p <= q < infinity, || P_t f ||_q <= || f ||_p for every f, PROVIDED e^{-t} <= sqrt( (p-1)/(q-1) ). The constant is exactly 1 - the semigroup is a contraction from L^p to the strictly larger L^q, not merely bounded - and the condition on t is sharp. Two consequences used constantly: taking p = 2 gives || P_t f ||_q <= || f ||_2 for e^{-t} = 1/sqrt(q-1); and restricting to the n-th Wiener chaos, where P_t acts as multiplication by e^{-nt}, gives the MOMENT COMPARISON || F ||_q <= (q-1)^{n/2} || F ||_2 for every F in the n-th chaos and every q >= 2. That comparison is dimension-free and is the reason all L^q norms on a fixed chaos are equivalent, with a constant depending only on the chaos order and q. GROSS'S THEOREM: hypercontractivity of (P_t) with these exponents is EQUIVALENT to the logarithmic Sobolev inequality Ent(f^2) <= 2 E|grad f|^2 for the same measure; each implies the other by differentiating or integrating the relation at q = q(t). The discrete-cube analogue with the noise operator is the Bonami-Beckner inequality, and the Gaussian case follows from it by the central limit theorem. [Nelson (1966, 1973); Gross (1975); see Bakry, Gentil and Ledoux, Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators, Chapter 5]
