{"artifact_digest":"sha256:3d0face865ebb1a496c1c5b8aa5a366d01d218fc34c2a57768d81c094b1ab539","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/3d/3d0face865ebb1a496c1c5b8aa5a366d01d218fc34c2a57768d81c094b1ab539.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e2356ce156c7945a3833a0fff0886654b697fc6276b740bf16563605885cacad","bundle_entry_key":"tanh-next-reciprocal-drift","bundle_id":"population.t244-critical-tanh-reciprocal-mean-rate-016","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_016.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-tanh-next-reciprocal-drift","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C044-C045: exact critical tanh inverse moments and next reciprocal drift

Version 1, 20 October 2026. Target3, kind moved. Proofs (unaudited).
Prior-work distinctions are C025: variance1/n, zero bias, unshaped tanh;
no shaped-activation variance multiplier. No literature novelty is asserted.

Write Y_q=tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2/q for q>0 and Z standard Gaussian, and
S_(n,q)=n^(-1)sum_(i=1)^n Y_q(Z_i), with iid rows.

## C044: uniform inverse sample moments and deleted tails

For every fixed Q<infinity and positive integer p, there is a finite
C_(Q,p) such that

    sup_(0<q<=Q, n>=4p) E[S_(n,q)^(-p)] <= C_(Q,p).            (1)

For any fixed sufficiently small eta>0, with m(q)=E Y_q and
G_(n,q)={|S_(n,q)-m(q)|<=eta},

    P(G_(n,q)^c)<=C_Q exp(-c_Q n),
    E[S_(n,q)^(-p);G_(n,q)^c]<=C_(Q,p)exp(-c_Q n/2), n>=8p.   (2)

Constants can be made explicit from the Gaussian expectations in the
proof. The sample mean is strictly positive almost surely. These are
exact-chain inverse moment estimates, in contrast with the ReLU atom and
near-collinearity obstruction.

Proof. tanh(x)/x decreases for x>0: tanh(x)-x sech(x)^2 has derivative
2x sech(x)^2 tanh(x)>0 and value0 at zero. Therefore Y_q>=Y_Q for q<=Q,
and Y_q<=Z^2. Let H=Y_Q>0 and phi(s)=E exp(-sH). For small y>0,

    P(H<=y)=P(|Z|<=arctanh(sqrt(Qy))/sqrt(Q))<=C sqrt(y),

using arctanh(w)<=2w for w<=1/2 and the bounded Gaussian density.
Increasing C_Q extends P(H<=y)<=C_Q sqrt(y) to every y>0.
Integration by parts gives phi(s)<=C'_Q s^(-1/2). Also for0<=s<=1,

    phi(s)<=1-c_Q s<=exp(-c_Q s), c_Q=E[H exp(-H)]>0,

and rho_Q=phi(1)<1. The Gamma identity and independence yield

    E[(n^(-1)sum_i H_i)^(-p)]
       =n^p/Gamma(p) integral_0^infinity s^(p-1)phi(s)^n ds.    (3)

Choose s0>=max(1,(2C'_Q)^2). On [0,1], (3) is bounded by c_Q^(-p).
On [1,s0], use rho_Q^n, giving at most
n^p s0^p rho_Q^n/(p Gamma(p)), uniformly bounded in n. On [s0,infinity),
for n>=4p,

    integral_(s0)^infinity s^(p-1)(C'_Q/sqrt(s))^n ds
      <= s0^p 2^(-n)/(n/2-p).

After multiplication by n^p/Gamma(p), this is uniformly bounded too.
This proves (1), since S_(n,q)>=n^(-1)sum H_i under the common-row coupling.

Uniform exponential integrability follows from0<=Y_q<=Z^2; m(q)>=E H>0.
Centered exponential-moment bounds and Chernoff give the first part of(2),
uniformly in q. Choose eta< E H/2 so G also stays uniformly away from zero.
Cauchy-Schwarz, (1) at order2p and the first bound in(2) prove its second
bound. All integrations use nonnegative integrands, so Tonelli applies.

## C045: full next drift of the exact reciprocal

Consider the exact scalar critical chain K_next=q S_(n,q) and
v=1/(nq), V_next=1/(n K_next). There are epsilon>0,C,c,n0 such that for
0<q<=epsilon and n>=n0,

    E(V_next-v)
      =(2v+2)/n + [4v-4-5/(3v)]/n^2+r_n(v),
    |r_n(v)|<=C[v/n^(5/2)+(1+1/v+1/v^2)/n^3+v exp(-cn)].     (4)

The exact inverse moments in C044 justify this unbounded observable.
In particular the singular next correction is negative. On any fixed
0<q<=Q, the following coarser estimates hold uniformly for sufficiently
large n (depending on Q and the indicated moment orders):

    E[(V_next/v)^j]<=1+C_(Q,j)(q+1/n), j=1,2,
    E[(V_next-v)^2]<=C_Q(v^2/n+1/n^2),                        (5)
    |E(V_next-v)-(2v+2)/n|
                         <=C_Q[q/n+1/n^2+v/n^(3/2)].         (6)

Proof of(4). Global Taylor inequalities for tanh, using boundedness on
|x|<=1 and polynomial domination on |x|>=1, imply

    m(q)=1-2q+(17/3)q^2+O(q^3),
    Var(Y_q)=2-16q+O(q^2),
    kappa_3(Y_q)=8+O(q).

For example tanh(x)^2=x^2-(2/3)x^4+(17/45)x^6+O(x^8), with a global
remainder bound C|x|^8. Similarly E Y_q^2=3-20q+O(q^2). Every fixed
positive row moment is bounded; its first variation is O(q) since
|Y_q-Z^2|<=Cq Z^4.

Taylor expand 1/S about m(q) through order four on G. The fifth absolute
sample-average moment is O(n^(-5/2)); it follows, for instance, from the
sixth moment bound for centered iid sample sums and Holder. The exact
sample-mean third moment is kappa_3(Y_q)/n^2, and its fourth moment is
3 Var(Y_q)^2/n^2+O(n^-3). Deleted inverse tails are exponentially small
by C044. Therefore uniformly on0<q<=epsilon,

    E S^(-1)=m^(-1)+Var(Y_q)/(n m^3)
              +[-kappa_3(Y_q)/m^4+3 Var(Y_q)^2/m^5]/n^2
              +O(n^(-5/2))+O(exp(-cn))
      =1+2q-(5/3)q^2+(2-4q)/n+4/n^2
              +O(q^3+q^2/n+q/n^2+n^(-5/2)+exp(-cn)).         (7)

Multiply by v, subtract v, and use vq=1/n. This gives(4).

For(5), the same good-event Taylor expansion through order two applied
to S^(-j), with C044 for the deleted tails, gives
E S^(-j)=m(q)^(-j)+O_(Q,j)(1/n). The function
[m(q)^(-j)-1]/q stays bounded on0<q<=Q, so its first assertion follows.
The Lipschitz estimate for1/S on G, and C044 off G, give
E(S^(-1)-m(q)^(-1))^2<=C_Q/n. Since m(q)^(-1)-1=O_Q(q), the second
assertion follows by v^2 q^2=1/n^2.

For(6), the second-order centered Taylor expansion has remainder
O(n^(-3/2)), and Var(Y_q)/m(q)^3=2+O(q). This yields
E S^(-1)=1+2q+2/n+O(q^2+q/n+n^(-3/2)) for small q, which gives(6).
On epsilon<=q<=Q, v<=1/(n epsilon); the error is O_Q(1/n), absorbable
in C_Q q/n. This completes the global extension.

The constants are analytic bounds; no floating-point integration is part
of this proof. C045's next coefficients are checked separately by exact
symbolic algebra, which does not certify the remainder proof.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:33310ec7d7ee9992c8f2862dbcd7608afde5016da91276ffa01336685b6b5ff6","revision_digest":"sha256:d3be762dc251fdbb7947015d26af2f0c44e93160274e953a2389f4c3dd5586d1","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C045:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition 45 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in S_X$ be a homogeneous regular sequence, and set
\[
A \defeq S_X/(f_1,\ldots,f_r).
\]
Let
\[
\widehat Z
 \defeq 
V(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\cap U_X
\subset
\operatorname{Spec}(A)
\]
and $Z\defeq\widehat Z/G_X\subseteq X$.

Then \(Z\) is HT-split.
In particular, if \(Z\) is smooth, then there is an isomorphism
\[
F_{*}\Omega^\bullet_{Z/k}
\simeq
\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\dim Z}
\Omega^i_{Z/k}[-i]
\]
in \(\mcalD_{\qcoh}(Z)\).
Consequently, the Hodge-to-de Rham spectral sequence of \(Z\)
degenerates at \(E_1\), and \(Z\) satisfies the
Akizuki--Nakano-type vanishing theorem.

[Lemma lem:remove0s of arXiv:2509.16541, 'Two-stage Bootstrap Percolation'] Consider two dynamics with the same initial configurations of $1$s and $2$s on ${\mathbb Z}^2$. 
    The first dynamics is the standard one on the full ${\mathbb Z}^2$, and denote by $A_f\subset {\mathbb Z}^2$ the set of vertices that are eventually occupied by $2$s in these dynamics. 
    For the second dynamics, we remove from ${\mathbb Z}^2$ all the vertices that are initially $0$s, then run the standard dynamics on the induced subset of ${\mathbb Z}^2$ and obtain the set $A_r$ of vertices that are eventually in state $2$. 
    Then $A_r\subset A_f$.

body:
Let (T(t)) be a C_0-semigroup on a Banach space X satisfying the growth bound ||T(t)|| <= M exp(omega t). Then there is an EQUIVALENT norm on X, namely |||x||| = sup over t >= 0 of exp(-omega t) ||T(t) x||, in which the semigroup satisfies |||T(t) x||| <= exp(omega t) |||x||| - that is, the constant M is normalised away and the semigroup becomes a quasi-contraction. The new norm satisfies ||x|| <= |||x||| <= M ||x||, so it is equivalent and the generator, its domain and its spectrum are unchanged; only the operator NORMS and the numerical range move. This is the standard reduction that lets one prove results for contraction semigroups and transfer them to general ones.
The uniform growth bound with constants M and omega, which every C_0-semigroup has by the uniform boundedness principle.
The renorming changes the geometry of the space - the new norm need not be, for instance, a Hilbert norm even if the original was, so any argument relying on inner-product structure must be checked rather than assumed to survive.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.26490, 'Bayesian methods and Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms for curve reconstruction and poin'] For a fixed $n=1,\dots,N$, let $r_n$ be a random position generated according to the sampling scheme in \cref{eq:un,eq:sn,eq:pi,eq:L}. Then \cref{eq:rn} follows.
\begin{proof}
Given a geometry $G$, the position $r_n$ specifies and is specified by a global coordinate $v_n$ that equals the arc-length from $h^1$ along the curve $\mathcal{G}$ encoded by $G$. Consequently, it suffices to show that $v_n$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,L^G]$ where $L^G=\sum_{k=1}^K L_k^G$ is the total arc-length of $\mathcal{G}$.

Conditional on $s_n$ and $u_n$, such global coordinate $r_n$ is obtained deterministically by
\begin{align*}
v_n|s_n,u_n
&\sim\delta_{C^G_{s_n-1}+u_nL_{s_n}^G},
\end{align*}
where the cumulative segment lengths are defined by
\begin{align*}
C^G_0&=0,
\\
C^G_k&=\sum_{k'=1}^K L^G_{k'},
&
k&=1,\dots,K.
\end{align*}
According to the law of total probability, we obtain the marginal
\begin{align*}
p(v_n)
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
p(v_n|s_n,u_n)p(s_n,u_n),
\end{align*}
and, because of independence in \cref{eq:sn,eq:un}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
p(v_n)
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
p(v_n|s_n,u_n)p(s_n)p(u_n)
\\
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{C^G_{s_n-1}+u_nL_{s_n}^G}(v_n)\pi_{s_n}^G
\\
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\frac{1}{L_{s_n}^G}\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)\frac{L_{s_n}^G}{L^G}
\\
&=\frac{1}{L^G}
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)
\\
&=\frac{1}{L^G}
\end{align*}
indicating that, indeed, $v_n$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,L^G]$ which completes our proof. Here, the last equality holds because, from the $K$ different summands $\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)$, only one integrates over the singularity.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.26490

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:1ae190435e7b657c945d3a052b349474d8561c45b1e0a73355ca4689c9eb58a9","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/1a/1ae190435e7b657c945d3a052b349474d8561c45b1e0a73355ca4689c9eb58a9.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8ffd51d76159978854be883eb7fce596c987ccd0352be4aef57cba9cf5aab7fe","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c19","bundle_id":"population.t309-random-anisotropic-fixed-noise-bad-basin-draft","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian mixture learning and diffusion objectives","draft":"w721/bundle_012.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:gaussian-mixture-ddpm-random-anisotropic-fixed-noise-bad-basin","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; T309-w721-C19 v1; proof (unaudited); Target 2 route 12 auxiliary composition lemma.

# A constant random-initialization bad-basin probability at fixed high noise

This composes the unaudited C17 entry and C18 unrestricted local trapping lemmas. It is a fixed-noise population result for a particular anisotropic three-component teacher. It neither refutes annealed learning nor settles the well-separated K=3 target. No novelty finding is asserted.

## Statement

Let d>=2, E^T E=I_2, A=diag(1,3), and use the teacher (1/3)sum_j N(a E A u_j,I_d), where u_j are unit equilateral vertices. Optimize the canonical equal-weight identity-covariance mixture score by physical Euclidean unit-step GD on the single-time population DDPM excess risk, with all entries of the d-by-3 initial mean matrix iid N(0,3a^2/(2d)). There is a fixed positive constant c_* such that taking a^2=c_* d^(-420) gives probability greater than 79/600 that the unrestricted trajectory converges to a strict non-global local minimum. Entry into its trapping neighborhood takes O(d^420 log d) steps. The convergence assertion is asymptotic; no finite-time identification rate is claimed here.

The statement depends on C06, C17 and C18 as analytic proof drafts, not independently checked theorems. In particular the original well-separated means need not resemble the small noisy means displayed here, and the statement is not a result about changing noise levels, empirical gradients, bit complexity or every random initialization.

## 1. Fix angular margins before the noise level

Set beta=acos(-61/128) and p=1-beta/pi. Since -61/128>-1/2 and acos is strictly decreasing on (-1,1), beta<2pi/3, hence p>1/3. Also beta>pi/2, so p<1/2. Set

    g=p-1/3>0, delta=pi*g/18.

C18's three bad sectors in each determinant branch have endpoints

    l_j=beta/3+2pi*j/3,
    r_j=(2pi-beta)/3+2pi*j/3, j=0,1,2.

Each width is 2pi*p/3. The chosen delta is less than one fourth of this width, so it is allowed in C18. Erode each sector by 3delta at each endpoint. Their total uniform angular measure, divided by 2pi, is

    3[(2pi*p/3)-6delta]/(2pi)
       =p-9delta/pi=(p+1/3)/2>1/3.              (1)

The intervals are disjoint modulo 2pi. Thus this measure calculation neither double-counts labels nor treats the three sectors as independent events.

## 2. Match all entry hypotheses simultaneously

Choose K in C18 large enough for C17's bound ||b_N||<=C_0 a^4. With this K and the fixed delta above, C18 supplies a fixed normal radius rho_T and smallness threshold a_T. The constants are independent of d.

Near the compact orbit {E A O:O in O(2)}, the polar chart is uniformly Lipschitz in Frobenius norm, independent of d: its planar part is a two-by-two positive-definite polar map, and its perpendicular part is a projection followed by a two-by-two rotation. Therefore factor distance at most rho implies

    ||c-c_*||+||Y||<=C_chart rho.               (2)

C17 also gives actual-to-surrogate polar angle distance at most C_phase rho at time N, with the same determinant branch. Choose a fixed entry tolerance 0<rho<=1/100 so that C_chart rho<rho_T/4 and C_phase rho<delta. Shrink rho further if necessary to stay within the uniform chart. Since cbar_a(theta)-c_*=O(a^2) uniformly in theta, sufficiently small a makes

    ||(c_N-cbar_a(theta_N),Y_N)||<rho_T.         (3)

The O(a^2) section displacement is explicitly included here; covariance-orbit distance alone is not the normal hypothesis in C18.

For this fixed rho, choose the absolute constant c in C17's prescription a^2=c rho exp(-84(S+1)), S=10log(8000 sqrt(d)/rho), small enough to enforce a<a_T, (3) and all its own assumptions for every d>=2. This prescription is exactly a^2=c_* d^(-420) with a fixed positive c_*. Consequently the constants and tolerances are chosen before d, and the polynomial exponent does not hide dimension dependence.

## 3. Conditional uniform phase, not independence

Let G be C17's joint good event: its right-invariant shape event together with ||b_0||<=10. It satisfies P(G)>=79/200. Conditional on G and either determinant branch, the C16 surrogate phase at the deterministic terminal time N gamma is uniform. The terminal time depends on d and fixed constants only, not on the random trajectory. Both determinant branches have positive conditional mass by the reflection symmetry of the Gaussian initialization and G.

Let A_good be the event that this surrogate phase lies in one of the three eroded sectors in Section 1. Formula (1) gives

    P(A_good | G, branch)=(p+1/3)/2>1/3.

Summing over the two branches gives exactly the same conditional probability given G. There is no factor one half: in the negative branch C18 uses a fixed reflection J that permutes the equilateral vertices, so R_theta J U=R_theta U Pi, and the same angular sectors apply by label symmetry. Nor is A_good asserted independent of G; its conditional probability is supplied by right-rotation invariance.

On G intersect A_good, the actual phase differs from the surrogate by less than delta. Its distance from each bad-sector endpoint is therefore greater than 2delta. Equations (3) and the centroid bound meet the remaining C18 hypotheses. C18 then gives convergence to that sector's strict bad minimum. Thus

    P(converges to a strict non-global minimum)
       >=P(G) P(A_good|G)
       >=(79/200)*(p+1/3)/2
       >79/600>1/8.                            (4)

This multiplication is the conditional-probability identity with an established conditional measure, not a product of unproved independent bounds. Component-label sectors and determinant branches have both been accounted for.

## Scope, checks and the unpaid target

Exact rational checks certify -61/128>-1/2 and 79/600>1/8; elementary algebra certifies the erosion formula (1). They do not validate C17's phase coupling or C18's analytic normal contraction. All those inputs and the present composition remain proof (unaudited), with no independent reviewer PASS.

The result explains a fixed-noise obstruction to the intermediate-noise route for this teacher. The noisy teacher here is not itself well separated when a is small. General Target 2 concerns efficient learning of well-separated components and may use a schedule; nothing here excludes that. The next unpaid step toward that target is to determine whether lowering the noise after this bad basin destabilizes it before one can claim either a scheduled failure or a successful escape route. {"artifact_digest":"sha256:2fb14c31740fa511acca049d47e110dfe0c184ccddfd618b8a81e7a016204d80","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/2f/2fb14c31740fa511acca049d47e110dfe0c184ccddfd618b8a81e7a016204d80.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:18499b33ae9f1f2876a26450ea86e2fe3aa56587c81b023705ca8745c76822a9","bundle_entry_key":"random-comb-exit-scale-collision-count-lower-bound","bundle_id":"population.w664-i0012-conditional-extensions-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"w664/bundle_003.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.random.walks:random-comb-exit-scale-collision-count-lower-bound","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0012-Q2 v1: almost-sure lower collision counts along geometric exit scales

NOVELTY: UNCHECKED (direct adapted-tail consequence of the conditional one-scale bound; no priority claim).
Status: proof (unaudited).

## Statement and scope

Assume the critical analytic inputs and nonempty window of notes/boundary_comb.tex. Let b>=2 be the integer scale multiplier and c>0 its deterministic one-scale constant. For two independent walks started at the backbone origin, let sigma_m be the first time either exits R_{b^m}((b^m)^(3/2)). Let C_T count backbone collision times from time 1 through T. Then in almost every environment,

    liminf_{m->infinity} C_{sigma_m}/log m >= c/log b, almost surely.

In particular the count is at least a positive multiple of log m along exit scales. This is a log log N lower bound when N=b^m. No almost-sure order log T, deterministic-time rate, or limiting coefficient is claimed. The inputs remain conditional, with the upstream caveats in UPSTREAM_CHECK.md.

## Adapted indicators

Fix an environment where Lemma B of the note holds. Beyond a finite deterministic index in this fixed environment, define I_m as the indicator of a backbone collision in [sigma_m,sigma_{m+1}). Let F_m be the pair filtration at sigma_m. Then I_m is F_{m+1}-measurable and

    E[I_m | F_m] >= a_m := c/(1+m log b).

The interval count includes the endpoint sigma_m, whereas C_T excludes time zero. Discard finitely many initial blocks so sigma_m>=1, and all remaining successful blocks yield distinct collision times counted by C_{sigma_{M+1}}.

## Lower-tail product

Fix a starting index M0 beyond that threshold. For lambda>0,

    E[exp(-lambda I_m) | F_m]
        =1-(1-exp(-lambda)) E[I_m | F_m]
        <=1-(1-exp(-lambda))a_m.

Iterated conditioning, using measurability of earlier indicators at F_m, gives for S_M=sum_{m=M0}^{M-1} I_m,

    E exp(-lambda S_M)
        <= product_{m=M0}^{M-1}[1-(1-exp(-lambda))a_m]
        <= exp(-(1-exp(-lambda)) H_M),

where H_M=sum_{m=M0}^{M-1}a_m. Markov's inequality therefore gives, for 0<theta<1,

    P(S_M <= theta H_M)
        <= exp(-[1-exp(-lambda)-lambda theta]H_M).

Choose lambda small enough that d:=1-exp(-lambda)-lambda theta>0; this is possible because (1-exp(-lambda))/lambda tends to one as lambda decreases to zero.

The harmonic sum satisfies H_M=(c/log b)log M+O(1), by comparison with the integral of c/(1+x log b). Hence the lower-tail probability is at most D M^(-d c/log b) for a fixed finite D in this fixed environment.

## Sparse subsequence and interpolation

Take M_j=ceil(exp(j)). The probabilities P(S_{M_j}<=theta H_{M_j}) are summable in j. The first Borel-Cantelli lemma, which needs no independence, implies that almost surely, eventually

    S_{M_j} > theta H_{M_j}.

For M_j<=M<M_{j+1}, monotonicity gives S_M>=S_{M_j}. Since log M<=log M_{j+1}=j+1+o(1) and H_{M_j}=(c/log b)(j+o(j)), it follows that

    liminf_{M->infinity} S_M/log M >= theta c/log b

almost surely. Intersect the probability-one events for a countable sequence of theta tending to one to obtain liminf S_M/log M>=c/log b.

Finally C_{sigma_M}>=S_M because each counted successful block is disjoint and ends by sigma_M. This proves the assertion.

## Limits

The finite-bounded-interval upper time for each successful collision does not itself give an upper bound on all exit times sigma_m. Thus replacing sigma_m by a deterministic power of b^m would require a separate quenched exit-time upper bound. Likewise a logarithmic expectation from Q1 does not imply concentration or an almost-sure logarithmic growth rate.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:2475b91ab27b6b8f749e21ccda38cde2a2d4e3e843fd0c376ab39677344d6132","revision_digest":"sha256:d3f6d5c434cc97d3f8a8304b8d7f4c51729782f8b317949de1e4112ab9638128","source_id":"owner-own-work:w664:I0012-Q2:v1","source_revision":"v1; w667 and w668 PASS; upstream qualifications persist","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Shmalo, Non-normal orbit quotients that are not normal quotients (October 2026), addresses Question 4.5 of Grimmett and Li, Self-avoiding walks and connective constants (arXiv:1704.05884): can a non-normal subgroup A of a transitive automorphism group of an infinite transitive graph G give a transitive orbit quotient G_A not isomorphic to G_N for any normal subgroup N of any transitive automorphism group, and does a free action of A matter? For every m >= 3 there is an infinite, connected, locally finite Cayley graph X whose automorphism group acts regularly, with a non-normal subgroup B acting freely, such that X_B is the complete graph K_m while no normal quotient of X is K_m. X is a graphical regular representation (Leemann and de la Salle) of F * F, with F = S_3 for m = 3 and F = A_m for m >= 4; B is the preimage of a point stabiliser under the projection onto the first factor. The quotient is finite; the infinite-quotient version and Question 4.6 are not addressed. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/nonnormal-orbit-quotients (commit b11def36f965). Not refereed.

body: A function holomorphic on an annulus 0 <= r < |z - c| < R has a Laurent series f(z) = sum over all integers n of a_n (z - c)^n, converging there; the coefficient a_{-1} is the residue of f at c. At an isolated singularity c the principal part (negative-index terms) classifies it: none => removable; finitely many, lowest index -m => pole of order m; infinitely many => essential singularity (near which f comes arbitrarily close to every value, Casorati-Weierstrass / Picard). The residue a_{-1} is what contour integrals of f pick up.
title: Laurent Series and Classification of Singularities

[Thm DL-infty of arXiv:2411.16376, 'Higher order approximations in arcsine laws for subordinators'] Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Let $X=(X_t)_{t\geq0}$ be a killed subordinator which is not identically zero. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label={\upshape (\arabic*)}]

\item The killing rate $a$ is zero, and the tail $\Pi((x,+\infty))$ of the L\'evy measure  is regularly varying at $+\infty$ with index $-\alpha$.

\item The Laplace exponent $\Phi:(0,+\infty)\to(0,+\infty)$ (restricted over $(0,+\infty)$) is regularly varying at $0+$ with index $\alpha$. 

\item	
$\displaystyle \lim_{s\to+\infty}\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}\bigg(\frac{X_{T(s)-}}{s} \leq t\bigg)=\frac{\sin(\pi\alpha)}{\pi}\int_0^t x^{-1+\alpha}(1-x)^{-\alpha}\,dx$ for any $0\leq t\leq 1$.

\item 
$\displaystyle \lim_{s\to+\infty} s^{-1}\ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}[X_{T(s)-}]=\alpha$.

\item The law of $tX_{1/\Phi(t)}$ converges weakly to a stable law with index $\alpha$, as $t\to0+$. 

\item The distribution function $U([0,x])$ of the potential measure  is regularly varying at $+\infty$ with index $\alpha$.  
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'] Let $G$ be non-deterministic and $B>t_{0}(G)$. For any edge $e$ of the lattice, we define the \emph{detour height} as the distance to an edge with small passage time:
\[
k_B(e):=\min\left (k\ge 1 | \,  \min( \tau(e+(0,k)),\tau(e-(0,k)))< B\right).
\]
The \emph{detour} of $e$ is the path that starts at one edge of $e$, goes $k_B(e)$ edges upwards or downwards, passes the horizontal edge with weight less than $B$ and goes $k_B(e)$ edges down back to the other endpoint of $e$. The \emph{detour time} $dt_B(e)$ is the passage time of the detour.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'

For probability measures P and Q on one space, TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) - Q(A)| and D = D(P || Q) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence in nats (+infinity unless P << Q). Then TV(P, Q) <= sqrt(1 - exp(-D)), and consequently 1 - TV(P, Q) >= 1 - sqrt(1 - exp(-D)) >= (1/2) exp(-D). Unlike Pinsker's bound sqrt(D/2), this never exceeds 1. In base-b units, exp(-D) = b^(-D_b). (J. Bretagnolle and C. Huber, 1979.)
P and Q are probability measures on one measurable space

body:
[Corollary 2.9 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] Let f : Ω → R be c-Lipschitz and let the Ω-valued random vector X = (X_1, ..., X_n) be m-dependent for some m ≥ 1. Split [n] into consecutive blocks B_j := {k : (j−1)m + 1 ≤ k ≤ jm} for j ∈ [⌊n/m⌋] and, when m does not divide n, a last block B_{⌈n/m⌉} := [n] \ ∪_{j≤⌊n/m⌋} B_j. Then for every t > 0, P(f(X) − E[f(X)] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t² / (Σ_{i=1}^{⌈n/m⌉−1} (Σ_{j∈B_i∪B_{i+1}} c_j)² + min_{i∈[⌈n/m⌉]} (Σ_{j∈B_i} c_j)²)). The blocks form a path on ⌈n/m⌉ vertices, and Theorem 2.1 is applied to it with block coefficients Σ_{j∈B_i} c_j. The paper prints the first sum over i ∈ [⌊n/m⌋]: the same range when m does not divide n; when m divides n the path has n/m − 1 edges, as the paper's own Remark 2.10 uses. With all c_i = c the denominator is at most 4mnc², so P(f(X) − E[f(X)] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−t²/(2mnc²)) (Remark 2.10).
c-Lipschitz (Definition 1.1 of the paper): Ω = Ω_1 × ... × Ω_n is a product of Polish spaces, c = (c_1, ..., c_n) ∈ R_+^n, and f : Ω → R is c-Lipschitz when |f(x) − f(x')| ≤ Σ_{i=1}^n c_i 1{x_i ≠ x'_i} for all x, x' ∈ Ω (Lipschitz for the c-weighted Hamming distance).
m-dependence (Definition 2.8 of the paper): (X_j)_{j=1}^i and (X_j)_{j=i+m+1}^n are independent for every i.

Let U be an open subset of C, f holomorphic on U, and let the closed disc {|z - z_0| <= r} lie in U. Then for every a with |a - z_0| < r, f(a) = (1 / (2 pi i)) integral over the positively oriented circle |z - z_0| = r of f(z) / (z - a) dz, and for every n >= 0, f^{(n)}(a) = (n! / (2 pi i)) integral of f(z) / (z - a)^{n+1} dz. In particular a holomorphic function is infinitely differentiable and analytic. General form: for a closed piecewise smooth curve gamma in U that is null-homotopic in U and a point a in U not on gamma, n(gamma, a) f(a) = (1 / (2 pi i)) integral over gamma of f(z) / (z - a) dz, where n(gamma, a) is the winding number.

  B\times\mathbb R^d\) be a \(C^s\) rank-\(m\) subbundle, \(0\leqslant m \leqslant d\). Assume that

body: In mathematics, the Banach fixed-point theorem is an important tool in the theory of metric spaces; it guarantees the existence and uniqueness of fixed points of certain self-maps of metric spaces and provides a constructive method to find those fixed points. It can be understood as an abstract formulation of Picard's method of successive approximations. The theorem is named after Stefan Banach (1892–1945) who first stated it in 1922.
title: Banach fixed-point theorem

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be any locally compact abelian group. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on $G$ that are absolutely continuous with respect to Haar measure, 
and such that $D(P\|Q)<\infty.$ For any $t\geq 0$, 
write $Q^t$ for the probability measure
    $$
    Q^t:= \frac{tQ+P}{1+t}.
    $$
    Then for any $T>0$:
    $$
    \int_0^T \chi^2(P\|Q^t)\,\frac{dt}{t(1+t)} = D(P\|Q) - \int\log{\Biggl(\frac{\frac{dP}{dQ} + T}{1+T}\Biggr)}\, dP. 
    $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:degeneracy of arXiv:2608.16915, 'Exact mean--covariance dynamics of the Weber field in the stochastic Lagrangian representa'] In centre and separation variables $c=\tfrac{x+y}{2}$, $r=x-y$,
\[
  (\nabla_x+\nabla_y)^2=\Delta_c,\qquad
  u(x)\cdot\nabla_x+u(y)\cdot\nabla_y
  =\frac{u_++u_-}{2}\cdot\nabla_c+(u_+-u_-)\cdot\nabla_r,
\]
with $u_\pm=u(t,c\pm r/2)$. The diffusion therefore acts on the centre variable only;
there is no $\Delta_r$. In particular the model equation
$\partial_tH-\nu(\nabla_x+\nabla_y)^2H=0$ admits every bounded profile
$H(t,x,y)=h(x-y)$ as a stationary solution, so no estimate can extract regularity in
$x-y$ from the common-noise diffusion alone.

body: Godel's completeness theorem for first-order logic: for any first-order language L, any set T of L-sentences, and any L-sentence phi, T semantically entails phi (every model of T satisfies phi) if and only if phi is derivable from T in a standard proof calculus for first-order logic (Hilbert-style, natural deduction, or sequent calculus - all such standard calculi are both sound and complete). Equivalent model-existence form: every syntactically consistent first-order theory (one from which no contradiction is derivable) has a model; by the Henkin construction the model can be taken of cardinality at most the maximum of the cardinality of L and aleph_0. Soundness (derivable implies entailed) is the elementary converse direction. This theorem concerns first-order logic itself and does not conflict with Godel's incompleteness theorems, which concern the incompleteness of specific arithmetical theories, not of the logic.
title: Godel completeness theorem (statement)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Numerical test on random pairs of positive contractions, plus the diagonal and one-element cases in closed form. Result: Exact facts: for |E| = 1 the measure is Bernoulli(q) and Ent = h(q) is concave, so the conjecture holds; for commuting diagonal kernels the measure is a product and Ent = sum h(q_i), concave; for Q_2 = I - Q_1 the midpoint is I/2, whose entropy |E| log 2 is the maximum possible, so the inequality holds trivially. Numerical check (raw/C_lyons_conj26_entropy_check.json): 1440 random pairs of symmetric positive contractions in dimensions 2..6 with spectra in (0.02, 0.98), entropy computed exactly from P(A) = det(I-Q) det(J_A) with J = Q(I-Q)^{-1}; the concavity gap Ent(mid) - average was positive in every trial, minimum gap 8.5e-4 (dimension 2). No counterexample; the minimum gap being attained in dimension 2 suggests that a proof for 2x2 kernels, where the measure has four atoms with explicit determinants, would be the first non-trivial case to attempt analytically. Key identity: P_Q(A) = det(I-Q) det(J_A), J = Q(I-Q)^{-1}, gives an exact finite formula for the entropy. Check: Probabilities summed to 1 within 1e-8 in every trial and were non-negative. Obstruction: No analytic argument beyond diagonal kernels; the 2x2 case is the natural next target.

[Definition 28 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Visibility, relaying scheme.}

Let $\landsc$ be a landscape.

Let $(a_1, b_1)$ and $(a_2, b_2)$ be two buildings of $\landsc$. We say that $(a_2, b_2)$ is visible from $(a_1, b_1)$ if it is in range and there are no buildings above the segment from $(a_1, b_1)$ to $(a_2, b_2)$. In other words, if the following conjunction of events holds true:
\[\{(a_2, b_2)\text{ is in range from } (a_1, b_1)\} \cap \below{[a_1, a_2]}{(a_1, b_1)}{\frac{b_2-b_1}{a_2-a_1}}.\]

Thanks to this, we can define the relaying scheme $\tau$ as
\[\tau_{\mathrm{R}} (x, y, \landsc) = (x_b, y_b) := \underset{\substack{(a, b) \in \landsc\cap \mathrm{R}+(x, y) \\(a, b) \text{ visible from }(x, y)}}{\text{argmax}} \frac{b-y}{a-x}.\]
When this is well defined, and $\tau (x, y, \landsc) = (-\infty, -\infty)$ otherwise.

The blockage angle and its tangent are defined as usual in this context

body: [Lem smoothingfol of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\Phi$ be a smooth nonsingular flow on $M$, and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a topological foliation on $M$ which is topologically transverse to $\Phi$. Then $\mathcal{F}$ is topologically isotopic to a $C^0$-foliation with smooth leaves, which is genuinely transverse to $\Phi$. Moreover, the isotopy can be made arbitrarily small, and along the flow lines of $\Phi$.

body: [Definition 11 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Suppose $b,y>0$. Let $\{\vec{W}_t\}_{t\ge 0}$ be a standard three-dimensional Brownian motion. The \textit{3D Bessel bridge} on $[0,b]$ to $y$ is the stochastic process $\{V_t = \lVert \vec{W}_t\rVert_2 : t\in[0,b]\}$ conditioned on $V_b = y$. (For a formal definition of this conditioning, see \cite[Section XI.3]{RY}.)

[Theorem 27 (Reduction lemma: reduced-group and path conjugacy) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous tree-reduced bounded-variation path, translated so that $\gamma_0=0$. Set
\[
g=S(\gamma),\qquad v=S_1(\gamma)=\gamma_T\neq0.
\]
The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item There is $a\in\Sl(V)$ such that $g=a\e^v a^{-1}$.
\item There is $t_0\in[0,T]$ such that, for $\beta=\gamma|_{[0,t_0]}$,
\[
\gamma\sim_{\mathrm{rep}}
\beta*\lambda_v*\overleftarrow{\beta}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Under \textup{(a)}, let $p$ be the gate from $1$ to the axis in \cref{prop:axis-gate-decomposition}. One may choose $S(\beta)=p$, and this prefix signature is independent of the auxiliary Euclidean norm.

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity. Scarce calibration (P30, 240 of the calibration rows per cell, split B): P30 (a) HELD: at n = 240 the simplex beats least squares by +14.10 on EMIT (full calibration +8.83); (b) REFUTED: t* averages 0.22 on EMIT and the blend reads -2.61 vs the simplex; (c) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells and the simplex reads +2.27 vs least squares (full calibration -0.18); falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT) TRIGGERED. The observable part of the bias shift (P31): adding t^2 (D_ev - D_cal), the shift in the two bases' mean squared disagreement between the evaluation and calibration rows, to the criterion - P31 (a) REFUTED: the R'-blend reads -0.71 vs the simplex on EMIT split B (R-blend +0.08) and +0.71 on split C (R-blend +0.63); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R'-blend is -0.11 vs the R-blend on split B and -0.12 on split C; (c) REFUTED: mean t** 0.39 against t* 0.33 on EMIT, share of the hindsight optimum 0.07 -> -0.62; falsifier (R'-blend worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 on any corpus or split) TRIGGERED. Per-output mixing weights (P34, the criterion decoupled across outputs): P34 (a) REFUTED: the per-output blend reads -0.41 vs the per-cell blend on EMIT split B and -0.53 on split C; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 -0.02 and -0.08 on split C; (c) REFUTED: on Y2 the share of outputs at t_d = 0 is 0.20 and at t_d >= 0.5 is 0.34; falsifier (per-output worse than per-cell by more than 0.3 anywhere) TRIGGERED. A nearest-neighbour proxy for the bias shift (P35, the simplex's out-of-fold residuals at the nearest calibration rows standing in for its bias at the scored rows): P35 (a) REFUTED: the full-shift blend reads -0.69 vs the R-blend on EMIT split B and -0.12 on split C; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 -0.08 and -0.14 on split C; (c) REFUTED: cross-only vs full on EMIT -0.05 vs -0.62 (split B); falsifier (either variant worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 anywhere) TRIGGERED. Scarce calibration, the ratio-metric criterion (P41, 240 calibration rows, split B, three-vertex form, registered and R_1 choices side by side): P41 (a) HELD: at n_cal = 240 the R_1 blend reads +1.17 vs the simplex on EMIT (within 1.0; the registered three-vertex blend reads -1.83); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R_1 blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells (at least 25); (c) HELD: R_1 vs the registered blend on EMIT +1.38 (at least +1.0); falsifier (R_1 worse than the simplex by more than 2.0 on EMIT) not triggered. So the P30 caveat is confined to the squared-loss criterion; the criterion in the score's own metric keeps the simplex where it should at scarce calibration. P44: the shipped tool against the driver (P44): P44 (a) REFUTED: the tool's mixing weight is within 0.2 of the driver's on 14 (squared) and 11 (ratio) of 14 cells; (b) HELD: the tool's blend scores within 1 pct of the driver's on 12 / 12 of 14; (c) HELD by the clause's wording (worse than both endpoints by more than 1 pct while the driver beats one: none); under the stricter test the analyzer was first written with (worse than the better endpoint by more than 1 pct): one cell, emit s102 Y3 (ratio); falsifier not triggered by the clause's wording, TRIGGERED under the stricter test.

body: Let X and Y be real-valued random variables. Then X is stochastically dominated by Y, meaning P(X > t) <= P(Y > t) for every real t, if and only if there exists a coupling of X and Y, that is, random variables X' and Y' defined on a common probability space with X' having the same distribution as X and Y' having the same distribution as Y, such that X' <= Y' almost surely. [Strassen (1965); Lindvall, Lectures on the Coupling Method]
title: Strassen's Theorem (Coupling Characterization of Stochastic Order)

body:
The Mitchison-Durbin decoder-independent first-moment bound: for a tree sign network with N=Kn total weights and P fair independent labels, Pr(storage)<=min(1,2^{-P} C(P,n)^K), where C(P,n)=2 sum_{j=0}^{min(n-1,P-1)} binom(P-1,j). For fixed K and a=P/N, the exponent on aK>2 is F_K(a)=aK log(aK)-(aK-1)log(aK-1)-a log 2. Its upper-envelope root b_K has b_1=2 and K h(1/(K b_K))=log 2 for K>1, with b_K~log(K)/log(2). This is prior work, not a sharp threshold or a new result.
K,n,P positive integers; N=Kn; K disjoint n-dimensional groups
Each hidden unit is homogeneous sign with nonzero spherical weights; Gaussian input samples, hence general position almost surely
Uniform independent labels independent of the inputs; fixed Boolean decoder and tie rules
First take N to infinity with K fixed; entropy-branch statement uses aK>2

[Lemma 37 (Symmetric feedback closes the primitive criterion) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $q\ge2$, $x\in H^{\odot q}$ and
$F=I_q(x/\sqrt{q!})$.  Put
$\kappa_4(F)=\E[F^4]-3\E[F^2]^2$.  Then
\begin{align}
 \kappa_4(F)
 &=\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}\binom qs^2\norm{x\otimes_sx}^2
 \notag\\
 &\quad+\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}\frac{q^2}{s^2}\,
 b_{q,q,s}\norm{x\wtensor_sx}^2.
 
\end{align}
If $\norm x\le R$, then
\begin{equation}
 |\kappa_4(F)|
 \le 3^{q+1}R^2
 \left(\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}
 b_{q,q,s}\norm{x\wtensor_sx}^2\right)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}
In fact the carré-du-champ defect and the fourth cumulant satisfy the
exact expansion and comparison
\begin{align}
 \kappa_4(F)
 &=3q\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}\frac{b_{q,q,s}}s
   \norm{x\wtensor_sx}^2,
 \\
 \frac1{3q}\kappa_4(F)
 &\le
 \Var\bigl(\Gamma(F,F)\bigr)
 \le\frac{q-1}{3q}\kappa_4(F).
 
\end{align}
Consequently, for a bounded family, vanishing of the symmetric feedback
on the right of \eqref{bridge:eq:kappa-from-symmetric-feedback} forces every
proper unsymmetrized self-contraction to vanish.

body:
[Theorem NEW-t:sysID of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] For $d,d'\in\mathbb{N}$, $t_0\in(0,\infty)$, let $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}:=\{\delta_{(x, M(x),Z_x)}\}_{x\in\mathcal{P}}$ be a 
marked point process 
on $\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^{d'}\times\mathbb {M} $
such that   $Z_x\in\mathbb {M} ={\cal C}([0,t_0],\mathbb{R}^{d'})$ are i.i.d. standard Brownian motions on the interval $[0,t_0]$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d'}$, independent given the  marked point process $\{\delta_{(x, M(x))}\}_{x\in\mathcal{P}}$ of sites with initial conditions. We assume that  the initial conditions $M(x)$, $x\in\mathcal{P}$, are almost surely deterministically, uniformly bounded, i.e.,  $\sup_{x\in\mathcal{P}}|M(x)| \le L<\infty$.  
Moreover, we assume that the marked point process $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ has summable exponential $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations as in Definition (def.A2 of the paper) and has bounded reduced  Palm intensity function as in~(equation bdedreduced of the paper).
Consider a graph $\Psi(\mathcal{P})$ constructed deterministically on $\mathcal{P}$ 
which is fast stabilizing  with the interaction range 
satisfying ~(equation sdecayspin-infty of the paper).
Given Lipschitz diffusion coefficients $(b,\sigma)$ as in  Definition (NEW-d:lip_assum of the paper) consider the strong solution to the interacting diffusions system (equation NEW-e:sys_ID_V of the paper) on $\Psi(\mathcal{P})$, with initial conditions $M(x)$, realized by  individual paths $M^{\Psi(\mathcal{P})}[x]\in\mathbb {M} $ for points  $x\in\mathcal{P}$. Finally,
define the measures
\begin{equation}

\hat{\mu}_n^{\xi} := \sum_{x \in \mathcal{P} \cap W_n} \xi (\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})  \delta_{n^{-1/d}x},
\end{equation}
where $\xi =\xi^{(h, \Psi(\mathcal{P}))}$ are real-valued scores of the  individual paths $M^{\Psi(\mathcal{P})}[x]\in\mathbb {M} $  given by~(equation NEW-xisysID of the paper) with  a Lipschitz function $h : \mathbb {M}  \to \mathbb{R}$.

\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),  labelindent=0pt]
\item  If 
the  score $\xi$ in (equation NEW-xisysID of the paper) satisfies the $p$-moment condition~(equation NEW-momh1 of the paper) for all  $p \in (1, \infty)$, then the random measures $(\hat{\mu}_n^{ \xi})_{ n \in \mathbb{N}}$  at (equation NEW-SysID of the paper) satisfy the central limit theorem,  i.e., for  $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$ such that ${\rm Var}{\hat{\mu}_{n}^{\xi}(f)} = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$, we have

\[ ({\rm Var}{\hat{\mu}_{n}^{\xi}(f)})^{-1/2}(\hat{\mu}_{n}^{\xi}(f) - \mathbb {E} \hat{\mu}_{n}^{\xi}(f)) \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z. \]

\item  If the input process $\{\delta_{(x,M(x))}\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}}$ is stationary and the graph construction $\Psi(\mathcal{P})$ is translation invariant, then the mean asymptotics can be expressed for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$ as:
\begin{align}
 \Big| n^{-1} \mathbb{E}  \hat{\mu}_n^{\xi}(f) -  \rho \mathbb{E} _{\0} \xi(\tilde\0, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}) \int_{W_1}f(x)\,\mathrm{d} x\Big| = O(n^{-1/d}), 
\end{align}
whereas under an extra $p=(2+\epsilon)$-moment condition, for some $\epsilon>0$,  the variance asymptotics  can be expressed as
 \begin{align}
 & \lim_{n \to \infty} n^{-1} {\rm Var} \,\hat{\mu}_n^{\xi}(f) =  \sigma^2(\xi) \int_{W_1} f(x)^2 \,\mathrm{d} x \in [0,\infty),
\end{align}
where 
\begin{align}
 \sigma^2(\xi) & :=
\rho\mathbb {E} _{\0}\xi^2(\tilde{\0},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})   \\
 &+ \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left( \mathbb {E} _{\0,x}(\xi(\tilde{\0}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}) \xi(\tilde{x}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}})) \rho^{(2)}(\0,x) - \rho^2\mathbb {E} _{\0}(\xi(\tilde{\0},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})) \mathbb {E} _{x}(\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))  \right) \mathrm{d} x \in [0, \infty). \nonumber 
\end{align}
 \end{enumerate}

[Theorem 30 (Compact-group variance inequality) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, let $\mu$ be Haar probability measure on $G$, and let
$U$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Let
\[
\rho:G\to \End(U_\C)
\]
be the complexification of an orthogonal representation of $G$ on $U$.
For $T\in \End(U_\C)$ define
\[
\Phi(T)(g):=\langle T,\rho(g)\rangle_{\HS},
\qquad
\Psi(T):=\Phi(T)-\int_G \Phi(T)(h)\,d\mu(h).
\]
Let
\[
\mathcal C:=\{T\in \End(U_\C): \Phi(T)\text{ is constant on }G\}.
\]
Then
\[
\|\Psi(T)\|_{L^2(G,\mu)}^2
\ge
\frac{1}{\dim U}\,\| \mathrm{Proj}_{\mathcal C^\perp}T\|_{\HS}^2.
\]

        where $$\pi^*(f):=\int_{V_r(\bb R^d)\times \bb R^r} f(u,y)\,\pi^*(\rrm du,\rrm dy)$$ and $$\pi^*\big( f(U_t,Y_t)\big):=\bb E[f(U_t,Y_t)],$$ with $\scr L_{(U_0,Y_0)}=\pi^*$.

body: [Proposition 13 (Rotation flattens \citep{suresh2017dme,chee2023quip,tseng2024quipsharp}) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Let $R$ be either Haar-distributed on the orthogonal group or a randomized Hadamard $R=HD$ with $D$ a diagonal of random signs (a \emph{deterministic} Hadamard does not give the guarantee for an arbitrary $w$; nor does an arbitrary random orthogonal $R$, for instance a random signed permutation, which leaves the crest factor untouched). Then for fixed $w$, the entries of $Rw$ are identically distributed and individually sub-Gaussian with proxy variance $\|w\|_2^2/d$ (dependent, not independent; the union bound needs only the marginals), so by \Cref{lem:subg} the expected crest factor of $Rw$ is at most $\sqrt{2\ln(2d)}=O(\sqrt{\log d})$ regardless of the outlier structure of $w$. A worst-case coherent $w$ (mass on one coordinate, $\mathrm{CF}=\sqrt d$) is thereby reduced to $\mathrm{CF}=O(\sqrt{\log d})$: a reduction by a factor of at least $\sqrt{d/(2\ln 2d)}$ in expectation.

[Lemma 5 (Monotonicity of the isoperimetric ratio) of arXiv:2608.26619, 'Uniqueness of Positively Curved Ancient Ricci Flows on Surfaces with Boundary'] Given a metric $(\old,\partial\bD ,g)$, define the isoperimetric ratio
    $$I(g) := \frac{L(\partial \bD,g)^2}{A(\old,g)}.$$
    Let $\{g(t) = u(\psi,t)g_0\}_{t\in [t_0,t_1]}$ be a positively curved rotationally symmetric solution to (\ref{2DRF}) with the initial condition $\partial_\psi u(\cdot,t_0),\; \partial_\psi R(\cdot,t_0) \geq 0$. Then we have
    $$\frac{d}{dt}I(g(t)) \leq 0,\; \forall t\in (t_0,t_1).$$
title: Monotonicity of the isoperimetric ratio

body: In mathematics, Farkas' lemma is a solvability theorem for a finite system of linear inequalities. It was originally proven by the Hungarian mathematician Gyula Farkas. Farkas' lemma is the key result underpinning the linear programming duality and has played a central role in the development of mathematical optimization. Remarkably, in the area of the foundations of quantum theory, the lemma also underlies the complete set of Bell inequalities in the form of necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a local hidden-variable theory, given data from any specific set of measurements.
title: Farkas' lemma

[Theorem 1 (Number of visited points) of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] Let $d \geq 1$ and suppose that Assumption (BS) is satisfied. Then there exist two constants $C_1, C_2 \in (0,+\infty)$ depending\footnote{In fact we obtain constants depending more precisely on $d$, $M$ and $\mu (\{M\})$.} on the dimension $d$ and on the probability distribution $\mu$ such that, for any integer $k \geq 1$,
$$
\P \big[ |\V| \geq k \big] \leq C_1 e^{-C_2 k} ~.
$$
In particular, the following equivalence holds for any $d \geq 1$: $Assumption \,\,(BS) \iff \V \mbox{ is a.s. finite}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

	\qquad\text{for every }x\in G.

If $\lambda>0$, assume additionally that
$\|u_\lambda\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}<\delta_{\lambda,q_0}$.

For $x_0\in G$, set
\[

and therefore

\subset

[Lemma 24 (Discrete local sewing) of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $\theta\in (0,1)$ and let $\Pcal=\{S = U_0<U_1<\ldots<U_N = T\}$ (with $N\in\Nsf$, $N\geq 2$) be a partition of the interval $[S,T]$ satisfying the following condition:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=($P_\theta$)]
	\item
		Whenever $s,t\in\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket$ satisfy $\llbracket s+1,t-1\rrbracket\neq \emptyset$, there exists $u\in\llbracket s+1,t-1\rrbracket$ such that 
            \[
                \omega_{s,u}\leq \theta \omega_{s,t}.
            \]
	\end{enumerate}
Let $K:\Delta\Pcal\to\Rsf^m$ be a function and denote 
	\[
		K_{s,t}:=K(U_s,U_t), \quad (s,t)\in\Delta\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket.
	\]
Assume that the following condition is satisfied:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=($K$)]
	\item
		It holds that $K_{s,s}=0$ for all $s\in\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket$ and $K_{s,s+1}=0$ for all $s\in \llbracket 0,N-1\rrbracket$. Additionally, there exist $C,M\in (0,\infty)$ such that the estimate
	\[
		| K_{s,t} - K_{s,u} - K_{u,t}| \leq C |K_{s,u}|\,\omega_{u,t}^\frac{1}{p} + M\omega_{s,t}^\frac{3}{p}
	\]
holds for every $(s,u,t)\in\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket^3$ satisfying $s\leq u\leq t$ and $\omega_{s,t}\leq 1$.
	\end{enumerate}
Then there exist $\delta \in (0,1)$ and $L\in (0,\infty)$ such that the estimate
	\[
		|K_{s,t}| \leq L M \omega_{s,t}^\frac{3}{p}
	\]
holds for every $s,t\in\Delta\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket$ satisfying $\omega_{s,t}<\delta$. Constant $\delta$ depends only on $p$, $\theta$, and $C$ while constant $L$ depends only on $\theta$ and $p$.
title: Discrete local sewing

[Proposition prop:stealthiness-criterion of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $(P_z)_{z\in Z}$ be a Borel $\Gamma$-equivariant uniformly
Delone family, and let $Y_P$ be the associated cross-section.
Suppose that there are $\rho>0$ and an open neighborhood
$\Omega$ of the origin such that
\[
    \widehat{\delta}_{P_z}
    =
    \rho\delta_0
    \qquad\text{on }\Omega
\]
for $\nu$-almost every $z$, in the sense of tempered
distributions. Then the associated cross-section system has intensity $\rho$.
Moreover, for every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfying
\[
    \operatorname{supp}\widehat f\subset\Omega,
\]
one has
\[
    N_f^{Y_P}(x)
    =
    \rho\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d
\]
for $\mu_{\Gamma,Z}$-almost every $x$. Consequently,
\[
    \sigma_{Y_P,\mu_{\Gamma,Z}}(\Omega)=0.
\]
In particular, the cross-section system is stealthy.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the criterion reproduces the source's worked example, and every algebraic step was confirmed symbolically] Problem 3.3 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240), asks for the optimal universal C>0 such that mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for every t>=C D_mu^2 and every compactly supported probability measure mu. Here D_mu=sup{|x-y|: x,y in supp(mu)}, S(0,t) is the centered semicircle law of variance t, and boxplus is additive free convolution. The source proves C<=4. The record answers C=1. Sufficiency is the proved bound that mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for all t>=D_mu^2. Optimality is the source's Example 2.1: mu=(delta_{-1}+delta_1)/2, with D_mu=2, is not unimodal for any t<4=D_mu^2. Let t*(mu) be the least t_0 such that mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for every t>=t_0. Then t*(mu)<=D_mu^2, and equality holds for every symmetric two-point law (equal weights at two points) by Example 2.1 and scaling. The record further claims (Corollary) that equality holds only for symmetric two-point laws. That direction rests on the record's unproved assertion that t*(mu)=D_mu^2 requires a separating local minimum of value exactly 1/D_mu^2, a limiting step not written out. It is retained here as a claim, not certified. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
D_mu>0.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Reduce to the stabilisability threshold and examine the known bounds. Result: By Fey-Meester-Redig, an i.i.d. sandpile on Z^d stabilises (finitely many topplings per site) if the mean density is below a threshold rho_s and explodes if above rho_c... the known facts: density < 1 (in units where the threshold height is 2d = 4) is not sufficient... on Z^2 the results are: if E s < 2d - 1 = 3?? I recall: on Z^d, i.i.d. sandpiles with density rho < d stabilise? and with rho > 2d - 1 explode; the exact threshold for i.i.d. Bernoulli-type laws is unknown and is believed to depend on the whole law, not only on the mean (Fey-Levine-Peres 'Growth rates and explosions'). The decidability question is whether the 0-1 value is a computable function of the five probabilities; since the event is a tail-type event of an i.i.d. field decided by an infinite dynamics, computability is not automatic (the source's remark). An approach: the event 'every site topples infinitely often' is equivalent to the divisible-sandpile-type criterion of the odometer being infinite, and for i.i.d. initial data with density rho the least-action principle gives that stabilisation holds iff there exists a stabilising toppling function, which is a monotone property; monotonicity in the law (stochastic order) gives a threshold structure along stochastically ordered families, but the threshold depends on more than the mean. I could not produce an algorithm; a natural decidable sufficient condition is: if s is a.s. a stable configuration plus a finite perturbation the answer is 0, and if E s > 2d - 1 the answer is 1 (explosion) by the FLP growth-rate results; the undecided region is between. Recorded with the two rigorous outer bounds. Key identity: Explosion if E s > 2d - 1 (FLP growth rates); no explosion for laws supported on {0,...,2d-1} minus finite perturbations; the middle region is the question. Obstruction: Dependence of the stabilisability threshold on the full law, not a computable functional so far.

Let g:R^d->R be convex and continuously differentiable, and suppose its gradient is globally L-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm for some L>0. Define B_g(x,y)=g(x)-g(y)-<grad g(y),x-y>. For all x,y, ||grad g(x)-grad g(y)||^2/(2L)<=B_g(x,y)<=L||x-y||^2/2. Adding the lower inequality in the two orders gives the Baillon--Haddad cocoercivity inequality <grad g(x)-grad g(y),x-y> >=||grad g(x)-grad g(y)||^2/L. No strong convexity is assumed. Source: Liu--Zhou, Lemma 3.6, which attributes the Bregman bounds to Nesterov.

body:
For events A, B with positive probability, P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A) / P(B). With a partition {A_i}, P(A_i | B) = P(B | A_i) P(A_i) / sum_j P(B | A_j) P(A_j). It inverts conditioning: posterior proportional to likelihood times prior.

Diagnostic corollary: let D be the disease event and T a positive-test event, with 0 < pi = P(D) < 1. Set s = P(T|D), q = P(T|D^c), and assume s*pi + q*(1-pi) > 0. Then P(T) = s*pi + q*(1-pi) and P(D|T) = s*pi/[s*pi + q*(1-pi)]. Thus sensitivity s alone does not determine the posterior in general: for s=9/10 and q=1/10, prevalence pi=1/2 gives posterior 9/10, whereas pi=1/100 gives posterior 1/12.

[Lemma 22 of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] There exists a constant $\kappa_8(d) > 0$ such that the following holds.
Let $S$ be an infinite and locally finite subset of $\R^d$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For all $x_0 \in \R^d$ such that $x_0 \not \in S$,
\[
\big|\{x \in S : x_0 \in B(x,r_M(x,S))\}| \le M\kappa_8(d).
\]
\item 
Let $S_f$ be a finite subset of $S$.
Let $(r(x))_{x \in S_f}$ be a family of non-negative real numbers such that, for all $x \in S_f$, $r(x) \le r_M(x,S)$.
Then 
\[
\cL^d\left(\bigcup_{x \in S_f} B(x,r(x))\right) \ge \frac 1 {M\kappa_8(d)} \sum_{x \in S_f} \cL^d(B(x,r(x))).
\]
\end{enumerate}

[Cor 12 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon\ge0$, 
and for $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, 
the mapping
$(\lambda,\mu)\mapsto S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)[\epsilon]$,
is continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric $d_H$.

\begin{proof}
Fix $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon\ge0$ and $\delta'>0$. By Lemma~\ref{l:S.star.cts.dH}, there exists $\delta>0$ such that if 
$(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda$ and 
$(\lambda',\mu')\in B_\delta(\lambda,\mu)$, then the sets
\begin{align*}
K&\equiv S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\,,\\
K'&\equiv S_\star(\lambda',\mu';\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)
\end{align*}
lie within Hausdorff distance $\delta'$ of one another.
For any $\hat{\YY}\in K[\epsilon]$, there exists $\YY\in K$ with
$\|\hat{\YY}-\YY\|_2\le\epsilon$, and then there exists $\YY'\in K'$ with
$\|\YY-\YY'\|_2\le\delta'$. By Lemma~\ref{l:D.mu.continuity.w}, 
since $\hat{\YY}\in\cD_\mu$,
there exists $\tilde{\YY}\in\cD_{\mu'}$
with $\|\hat{\YY}-\tilde{\YY}\|_1\le\delta/\iota^2$. Then
	\[
	\|\tilde{\YY}-\YY'\|_2
	\le\|\tilde{\YY}-\hat{\YY}\|_2
	+ \|\hat{\YY} - \YY\|_2
	+ \|\YY - \YY'\|_2
	\le \epsilon + \delta' + \frac{\delta}{\iota^2}
	\le \epsilon + 2\delta'\,,
	\]
where the last inequality can be arranged by taking $\delta$ small enough (depending on $\delta'$).
Since $\YY'$ and $\tilde{\YY}$ both lie in $\cD_{\mu'}$, it follows by convexity of $\cD_{\mu'}$ that $\tilde{\YY}$ lies within distance
$2\delta'$ of a vector $\hat{\YY}' \in K'[\epsilon]$. We then finally have
	\[
	\|\hat{\YY}-\hat{\YY}'\|_2
	\le \|\hat{\YY}-\tilde{\YY}\|_2
		+ \|\tilde{\YY}-\hat{\YY}'\|_2
	\le\frac{\delta}{\iota^2} + 2\delta'
	\le 3\delta'\,.
	\]
This implies that $K[\epsilon]$ and $K'[\epsilon]$ lie within Hausdorff distance $3\delta'$ of one another, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

we have
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{P} \mleft[ \max_{s \in [-S,S]} X^1(s) > C \log(S) +  y \mright]
    \leqslant C S e^{- c y^{3/2}}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thmIPS of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let  the input process to the interacting particle system be 

\begin{equation}
\tilde{\mathcal{P}} = \left\{(x, M(x),  \tilde{\tau}_x)\in\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb {M}  \times \hat{\mathcal{N}}_{[0,t_0] \times \mathbb{L}}\right\}, 
\end{equation}

where $ \tilde{\tau}_x$ are i.i.d. and independently marked Poisson clocks, which are also independent of sites and initial states, i.e., independent of $\sum_x \delta_{(x,M(x))}$.
Assume that:
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item 
$\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ has {\em summable exponential $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations}, as in Definition~(def.A2 of the paper), and has  uniformly bounded correlation functions under reduced Palm distributions, i.e., for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a constant $\hat{\kappa}_p$ such that for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$,
\begin{equation}

\sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in \mathbb{R}^d} \sup_{y_1,\ldots,y_m \in \mathbb{R}^d} \rho^{(m)}_{\bk x1p}(\bk y1m) \leq (\hat{\kappa}_p)^m,
\end{equation}
where $\rho^{(m)}_{\bk x1p}$ denotes the $m$-th order correlation function of $\mathcal{P}$ under its reduced Palm distribution $\mathbb{P}^!_{\bk x1p}$.

\item  {\em An admissible update rule} given by a measurable function $\Phi$ as in~(equation e:updaterulef of the paper) acts on a {\em stabilizing interaction graph} $\Psi$ (on finite windows) with respect to $\mathcal{P}$, such that the interaction range satisfies the decay assumption~(equation e:ddecay of the paper).
\item  A {\em score function} $\xi = \xi^{(h, \Phi, \Psi)}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n) := h(M_n[x])$ defined in~(equation xiU of the paper), satisfies the {\em $p$-moment condition}~(equation momh of the paper) for all $p \in [1, \infty)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then the sequence of random measures $(\mu_n^{\xi})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ defined in~(equation IPS of the paper) satisfies the central limit theorem. That is, for every  $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$ such that
$
{\rm Var}[\mu_n^{\xi}(f)] = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$,
we have
$$
({\rm Var}[\mu_n^{\xi}(f)])^{-1/2} \big(\mu_n^{\xi}(f) - \mathbb {E} [\mu_n^{\xi}(f)]\big)  \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z,$$
where $Z$ is a standard Gaussian random variable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:heat of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] Assume that $B\in L_2(U,W_0^{1,2}({\mathcal O}))$. Denote by $c_0$ the inverse Poincar\'e constant of ${\mathcal O}$, and assume that for some $\lambda\in (0,1)$,
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le \lambda\nu c_0^2.\]
Then the Markovian Feller semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ of the stochastic heat equation~(equation eq:heat of the paper) with degenerate additive Wiener noise is exponentially ergodic and exponentially mixing and possesses a unique invariant measure $\mu_\ast$ with finite second moments in the stronger space $V$ in all spatial dimensions. We have the following upper bound for the $\varepsilon$-mixing time 
\[
\tau^x_{\textup{\textsf{mix}}}(\varepsilon)\leq 
\frac{1}{\nu c_0^2}\left[\log\left(\|x\|_H+\frac{\|B\|_{L_2(U,H)}}{\sqrt{2(1-\lambda)\nu}c_0}\right)+\log\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\right].
\]

[Lem 5 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\YY = (\vBBb,\vvvv,\vUUu,\vwww)$ be the random vector defined in \eqref{e:freeprob.random.YY}, and $\mu(\bG,\omega)$ be defined in \eqref{e:lambda-mu-random}.
    For any $\epsilon'' > 0$ there exists $c = c(\alpha,\iota,\epsilon'') > 0$ such that
    \[
        \P\bigg(
            \inf\big\{
                \|\tilde \YY - \YY\|_2 : \tilde \YY \in \cD_{\mu(\bG,\omega)}
            \big\} \le \epsilon''
        \bigg)
        \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
    \]
\begin{proof}
Throughout the proof, we abbreviate $(\lambda,\mu) = (\lambda(\bG,\omega),\mu(\bG,\omega))$, although we keep in mind that they are permitted to depend on $(\bG,\omega)$. We will construct $\tilde\YY = (\tilde\vBBb,\tilde\vvvv,\tilde\vUUu,\tilde\vwww) \in \cD_\mu$ such that $\|\tilde \YY - \YY\|_2 \le \epsilon''$ on an event with probability $1-e^{-cN}$.
    We set $(\tilde\vBBb,\tilde\vUUu) = (\vBBb,\vUUu)$, and $\tilde\vvvv = \max(\vvvv,\vUUu)$ where the maximum is taken entrywise.
    Note that for all $j\in [r]$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives

        &\le

            \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N}
        \bigg)
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N} - 1
        \bigg)\,,
    \ealn
from which it follows that

    \]
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc} and \eqref{e:wishart.bound.repeated}, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$,
    \[

    \]
Set $\delta > 0$ small enough that
    \[
        [(1-\delta)^2,(1+\delta)^2] \subseteq \bigg[
            1 - \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2},

        \bigg]\,.
    \]
    Since $(\bmeta^a : 1\le a\le M)$ are standard gaussians in $\bbR^N$ independent of $\bar{\bx}$ and $B_j$, we have
    \[
        \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N}

        \frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} \cdot \frac{\|\bz\|^2}{|B_j|}
    \]
    where $\bz$ is a standard gaussian in $\bbR^{|B_j|}$.
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc} and a standard gaussian tail bound,
    \[

It follows from the assumption on $\delta$ that

Let f be holomorphic on the open strip {z : 0 < Re z < 1}, continuous and bounded on the closed strip {z : 0 ≤ Re z ≤ 1}. For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 put M(x) = sup over y real of |f(x + iy)|. Then log M(x) is a convex function of x on [0,1]; in particular M(x) ≤ M(0)^{1-x} M(1)^x for all x in [0,1]. If M(0) = 0 or M(1) = 0 then f is identically zero. Boundedness on the closed strip is essential (see the pitfall entry). This is the analytic engine behind the Riesz–Thorin interpolation theorem.

body: In mathematics, Minkowski's theorem is the statement that every convex set in $\mathbb {R} ^{n}$ which is symmetric with respect to the origin and which has volume greater than $2^{n}$ contains a non-zero integer point (meaning a point in $\mathbb {Z} ^{n}$ that is not the origin). The theorem was proved by Hermann Minkowski in 1889 and became the foundation of the branch of number theory called the geometry of numbers. It can be extended from the integers to any lattice $L$ and to any symmetric convex set with volume greater than $2^{n}d(L)$, where $d(L)$ denotes the covolume of the lattice (the absolute value of the determinant of any of its bases).

body:
[Lemma rosenthal of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Non-Hermitian Matrix Rosenthal Inequality]

Suppose that $t=1$ or $t \geq 1.5$. Consider a finite sequence $\{{\bf Y}_k\}_{k\geq 1}$ of centered, independent, random matrices, and assume that ${\mathbb E} \ensuremath{\left\lVert {\bf Y}_k \right\rVert}_{4t}^{4t} < \infty$. Then
$$
    {\mathbb E} \norm{\sum_{k}{\bf Y}_k}_{4t}^{4t} \leq (16t)^{3t} \cdot \left\{ \norm{\left(\sum_k{\mathbb E}  {\bf Y}_k {{\bf Y}}^{\mathsf{T}}_k \right)^{1/2}}_{4t}^{4t} + \norm{ \left(\sum_k{\mathbb E} {{\bf Y}}^{\mathsf{T}}_k{\bf Y}_k \right)^{1/2} }_{4t}^{4t} \right\} + (8t)^{4t}\cdot \left(\sum_k {\mathbb E} \ensuremath{\left\lVert {\bf Y}_k \right\rVert}_{4t}^{4t} \right).
$$
title: Lemma rosenthal of arXiv:2412.07936

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, proof (unaudited). There are rho0,delta>0 such that for uncorrected scalar Adam at beta1=.9,beta2=.999, epsilon outside sqrt, and 0<epsilon/(eta lambda)<=rho0, all but countably many standard initial x0 satisfy limsup_t |eta C_t-38|>=delta. For p>1 and any countable eta_n->0, an absolutely continuous initial x0 almost surely obeys this for all sufficiently large n. The same holds on an exactly dormant-coordinate 2D invariant family; corrected Adam and full-dimensional diagonal random initialization are not covered. Additionally, for H=diag(lambda,0), any absolutely continuous full-dimensional random initial position inherits this active-curvature obstruction; finite exact-zero first-coordinate iterates form another countable exceptional set.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:ebe4bd36ade091b992520698d91281b9388a07f6d144ef589a2db55d847fb656","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/eb/ebe4bd36ade091b992520698d91281b9388a07f6d144ef589a2db55d847fb656.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:0baac2cb0f39a1f87ae57c605114bc7776b2a544391d27cf3c62fa1b89a84984","bundle_entry_key":"claim-013","bundle_id":"population.adam-global-critical-cap-and-uncorrected-tracking-obstruction-005","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"deterministic adaptive optimization","draft":"w706/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.adam:adam-uncorrected-small-epsilon-uniform-curvature-tracking-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-013 v2; target1; kind special; proof (unaudited).

Statement. There exist rho0>0 and delta>0 depending only on b=.9,d=.999
such that for every uncorrected scalar Adam run, epsilon outside sqrt,
standard m0=v0=0, with 0<rho=epsilon/(eta lambda)<=rho0, all but countably
many x0 satisfy
 limsup_(t->infinity) |eta C_t-38| >=delta.                    (1)
Here C_t=lambda/(sqrt(v_(t+1))+epsilon). The constants are existential,
not numerical bounds. For every p>1, fixed lambda>0, and any countable
eta_n->0, absolutely continuous random initialization almost surely
satisfies (1) for all sufficiently large n with epsilon_n=eta_n^p.
No choice of finite burn-in can give eventual o(1/eta) tracking along
this sequence for uncorrected scalar Adam.

In a positive two-eigenvalue diagonal quadratic, the same conclusion
holds for ACTIVE curvature on the invariant standard-initialization
family (x1,0), with x1 absolutely continuous. The second coordinate is
exactly dormant. This is not a full-dimensional random initialization
theorem, and does not cover ordinary time0 bias correction. Those are
explicit remaining gaps for the full dossier target. The result records
a rigorous tracking obstruction in a stated variant; it is not a generic
two-dimensional solution or a claim that every Adam convention fails.

Hardest remaining step: exclude capture in the higher-dimensional
clock-augmented stable set from standard starts under bias correction,
and control genuine two-coordinate averaging.

Proof. Work in claim009's normalized variables X,M,V with map
 M'=bM+(1-b)X, V'=dV+(1-d)X^2,
 X'=X-M'/(sqrt(V')+rho).
Choose, for definiteness, rho0=1/1000, which is strictly below
rho_*=358811/13673160. At rho in [0,rho0] the nonzero cycle has
 a(rho)=1/38-rho>=1/38-1/1000>0,
 p_s(rho)=(s a,-s a/19,a^2), s in {+1,-1}.
By claims003 and009 its two-step derivative has one simple real stable
eigenvalue and two unstable eigenvalues, uniformly separated from the
unit circle on this compact interval. At rho=0 the count follows from
the exact negative discriminant and real-root bounds in claim009; the
no-unit-root argument of claim003 excludes crossings throughout.

UNIFORM LOCAL STABLE CAPTURE
Claim009 constructs the analytic stable curve of each phase directly
by the power-series coefficient equation
 w_n=(mu(rho)^n I-A(rho))^(-1)[N_rho(v_rho s+w)]_n.
That proof can be made uniform on [0,rho0]. The simple stable spectral
projection and its complement vary continuously; choose continuous
local bases and norms, or use finitely many such choices on this compact
parameter interval. The stable eigenvalue has a uniform upper bound<1,
all unstable eigenvalues have a uniform lower modulus>1, and the linear
operators are invertible. Thus the inverses in the coefficient equation
are uniformly bounded for all n>=2 and all rho: large n are handled by
mu(rho)^n->0 uniformly, and finitely many small n by compactness.
The nonlinear maps are analytic on a fixed complex neighborhood of the
cycle branches, since their variances are bounded below by a(rho0)^2.
Their Taylor majorants are therefore uniformly bounded. One contraction
radius works on each of a finite cover and their minimum is positive.
Graph-relative unstable expansion also has a uniform factor>1 in the
chosen norms after shrinking. Since all these finitely many norms are
uniformly equivalent to the Euclidean norm, there is a single radius
r>0 with this property: an orbit of F_rho^2 staying within the Euclidean
r-neighborhood of a phase forever lies on its local stable curve and
converges to that phase. Smaller r may be chosen so neighborhoods of the
two phases are disjoint, uniformly in rho.

AN EVENTUAL CURVATURE BAND FORCES SUCH CAPTURE
Put k_t=eta C_t=1/(sqrt(V_(t+1))+rho). Suppose that eventually
 |k_t-38|<delta, where delta will be chosen sufficiently small below.
For delta<=1, the map k->1/k is uniformly Lipschitz on [37,39], so
 sqrt(V_(t+1))=a(rho)+O(delta),
 V_(t+1)=a(rho)^2+O(delta).
Every O(delta) here and below has a constant uniform for rho in
[0,rho0]. Subtracting dV_t in the exact variance update gives
 X_t^2=a(rho)^2+O(delta)/(1-d).
Since 1-d is a fixed positive number and a(rho) is uniformly positive,
 |X_t|=a(rho)+O(delta).                                    (2)
In particular X_t is nonzero for all sufficiently large t if delta
is small. Let s_t=sign(X_t).

Eliminate momentum exactly:
 X_(t+1)=[1+b k_t/k_(t-1)-(1-b)k_t]X_t
              -b k_t/k_(t-1)X_(t-1).
Using k_t=38+O(delta), (2), and b=.9, this yields
 s_(t+1)=-(1+b)s_t-b s_(t-1)+O(delta).                      (3)
For a sign triple that is not alternating, the absolute residual of
the exact relation in (3) is at least 2b=1.8: if the two preceding
signs coincide, the residual is at least1.8; if they differ, the wrong
next sign has residual2. Thus delta can be chosen uniformly so that
the error in (3) is smaller than0.9, forcing sign alternation at every
sufficiently late step. The exact preceding update also gives
 M_t=(X_(t-1)-X_t)/k_(t-1)=-s_t a(rho)/19+O(delta).
Together with (2) and the variance estimate, this puts every sufficiently
late state within C delta of p_(s_t)(rho), with uniform C. Choose delta
smaller still so C delta<r. Alternating signs then ensure each parity
subsequence remains in one local stable neighborhood forever. By uniform
local capture it converges to the alternating cycle.

COUNTABLE EXCEPTIONS AND THE SMALL-ETA CONSEQUENCE
For each fixed rho>0, claim009 proves that only countably many standard
initial X0 can converge to this cycle. The previous paragraph shows that
every orbit with limsup|k_t-38|<delta belongs to that countable set.
Scaling X0=x0/eta preserves countability. Therefore all other starts
satisfy (1). For p>1 and eta_n->0,
rho_n=eta_n^(p-1)/lambda eventually lies in (0,rho0]. For each such n
the exceptional x0 set is countable, and their countable union is null
for any absolutely continuous initialization law. Thus (1) holds almost
surely simultaneously along the specified sequence. This order of
quantifiers does NOT claim one null set for an uncountable eta family.

For the diagonal invariant-coordinate family, g2=m2=v2=0 at all times,
and the active quotient equals the scalar channel's curvature whenever
g1!=0. The eventual-band assumption itself forces g1!=0, so no undefined
quotient enters the capture implication. One may state the scalar bound
using the always-defined scalar C_t to avoid isolated zero-gradient times.

Scope/novelty: this strengthens claim009's noncap-limit obstruction to
a positive, eta-uniform limsup gap. It is a consequence of the local
analytic cycle argument, not a numerical attractor calculation. The
literature already observes default-beta cycle instability; instability
alone is not the argument. Bias-corrected and full-dimensional diagonal
claims remain open. No bound on a time average or invariant distribution
is asserted. Independent audit of uniform local capture is required.


VERSION2: FULL-DIMENSIONAL RANDOM INITIALIZATION FOR RANK ONE
Consider H=diag(lambda,0), lambda>0, with ordinary coordinatewise
uncorrected Adam and standard zero moments. The flat coordinate has
zero gradient and stays fixed for arbitrary x2,0. Thus active curvature
equals the scalar first-channel curvature whenever x1,t!=0. For an
absolutely continuous law on R^2, its first-coordinate marginal is
absolutely continuous, so the scalar exceptional set is null.

We also exclude exact zero iterates without an added assumption. For
fixed rho>0 and n>=1, the finite-time function X_n(X0) is real analytic
on each of (0,infinity),(-infinity,0), since V_1>0 and all later V stay
positive. It is not identically zero on either branch: the moment bound
gives |X_n-X0|<=nK, so X_n is unbounded as X0 tends to either infinity.
The real-analytic identity theorem makes its zeros isolated on each
branch and therefore countable. Union over n is countable. Outside
this extra null set all active quotients are defined, and the scalar
limsup bound transfers literally. The same countable-eta argument
already given proves the result simultaneously along any chosen
eta_n->0 for absolutely continuous random initial positions in R^2.

This is a full-dimensional random-initialization obstruction for the
RANK-ONE uncorrected quadratic, which is in the repaired row statement.
It is not a full-rank two-positive-eigenvalue result and is recorded
as special for target1. [Proposition prop:lcp-centered-green-inverse of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] For every $f\in L_0^2(M_x^\partial)$, the function
$u:=G_xf$ belongs to $V_x$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E(u,v)=\int_{\mathbb T}f\widetilde v\,dM_x^\partial,
 \qquad v\inV_x.
\end{equation}
It is the unique solution of (equation eq:lcp-green-form-inverse of the paper) with zero
$M_x^\partial$-mean.  Moreover,
\[
 G_x:L_0^2(M_x^\partial)\longrightarrow L_0^2(M_x^\partial)
\]
is positive and injective, and
\[
 G_x
 =\left(A_x\big|_{L_0^2(M_x^\partial)}\right)^{-1}.
\]
Consequently, the positive spectrum of $A_x$ is discrete.
