# Target 1: actual fixed-step GD, straddling two-token family

Unaudited proof, version 1. This supplements rather than discretizes the exact invariant in proofs 001-002.

Theorem. Fix b,k>0, |a|<b, and 0<eta<=1/(bk). Write h(p)=a+b tanh(kp), f(v,p)=v h(p), and L=log(1+exp(-f)). For Euclidean gradient descent on (v,p), every finite initialization either converges to the unique saddle (0,p_*), p_*=atanh(-a/b)/k, or escapes with (v,p)->(+infinity,+infinity) or (-infinity,-infinity). The set converging to the saddle has planar Lebesgue measure zero. Both escaping basins are nonempty open sets. In each escaping basin, p/v->0, L->0, and the normalized parameter limit is respectively (+1,0) or (-1,0). When 0<|a|<b, the basin selecting the smaller absolute endpoint has limiting normalized margin b-|a|, strictly below the attainable b+|a|. Therefore the open suboptimal basin obstruction persists for actual GD at every step in the displayed interval.

Proof.

1. Write q=eta/(1+exp(vh(p)))>0 and u=p-p_*. The update is
   v_+=v+q h(p), u_+=u+q v h'(p).
   Put M=bk. Then 0<h'<=M, sign h=sign u, and |h|<=M|u|. Also qM<1, including when eta M=1, because the logistic factor is strictly below one at every finite point.

2. The two open good quadrants {v>0,u>0} and {v<0,u<0} are forward invariant. A point on one coordinate axis, except the origin, enters a good quadrant after one step. A point in a bad quadrant cannot cross both axes in one step. Indeed for v>0,u<0, such a crossing would require v<=q|h| and |u|<=q v h'. Combining gives |u|<=q^2 |h|h'<=q^2 M^2|u|<|u|, contradiction. The other bad quadrant is identical after reversing signs. Thus a bad-quadrant orbit either enters a good quadrant in finitely many steps, or remains in its original bad quadrant forever. In the latter case |v_n| and |u_n| decrease monotonically. Their finite limits must make both increments zero; since the logistic factor has a positive finite limit, h=0 and vh'=0. Consequently (v_n,u_n)->(0,0).

3. A good-quadrant orbit escapes in both coordinates. Consider v,u>0. They increase strictly, and let c=h(p_N)>0 for the first point in this quadrant. If v were bounded, then |f|<=v(|a|+b) would be bounded, so q would be bounded below; the increment Delta v=q h>=q c would contradict boundedness. Thus v->infinity. If p were bounded, h' would have a positive lower bound d on its compact monotone range, and h<=H=|a|+b, giving
   Delta p / Delta v = v h'/h >= d v/H.
   Summing v_n Delta v_n diverges whenever v_n increases without bound: for n after v>=1, the sum dominates sum Delta v_n. Hence p cannot stay bounded. Thus p->+infinity. Reverse signs, replacing a by -a, for the negative good quadrant. Both yield f->+infinity.

4. The exceptional set is null. The GD map T is real analytic on the plane. At the saddle its eigenvalues are 1+-eta h'(p_*)/2; one lies in (0,1), the other in (1,infinity). In particular det DT at the saddle is positive, so the analytic function D=det DT is not identically zero. Its zero set Z has planar measure zero: the one-variable analytic function D(v,p_*) is nonzero at v=0, so its zero set of v-values is countable. For every other v, the analytic function p->D(v,p) is nonzero at p_*, so has a countable zero set. Fubini on bounded rectangles, followed by a countable union, proves the assertion. The local stable-manifold theorem provides a one-dimensional local stable manifold W, a null set, containing the tail of every orbit converging to the saddle. Any null set A has null preimage under T: outside Z, cover the plane by countably many neighborhoods on which T is a diffeomorphism; the local inverse is locally Lipschitz and therefore preserves null sets. Add Z. Induction gives that every T^{-n}(W) is null. The entire converging set is contained in their countable union and is null. This reasoning does not assume a globally bounded Hessian or a globally invertible GD map.

5. Every escaping orbit eventually enters one of the good quadrants, by step 2. Its basin is therefore the union of the iterated preimages of that open quadrant, so is open by continuity. Each contains its good quadrant. Thus both basins have positive measure and positive probability under any everywhere-positive density.

6. Directional normalization. Along a positive good orbit, h>=c>0, q<=eta exp(-cv), and Delta p=q v h'<=M eta v exp(-cv)->0. For late n, p_n>=0 and Delta p<=1. Since h'(p)<=4bk exp(-2kp), the mean-value theorem gives
   exp(2kp_{n+1})-exp(2kp_n)
   <=2k exp(2kp_n) exp(2k Delta p_n) Delta p_n
   <=8bk^2 exp(2k) q_n v_n
   <=[8bk^2 exp(2k)/c] v_n Delta v_n.
   Summing and using 2v_n Delta v_n <= v_{n+1}^2-v_n^2 yields exp(2kp_n)<=C(1+v_n^2). Hence 0<=p_n<=log(v_n)/k+O(1), so p_n/v_n->0. Reverse signs for the negative orbit. The normalized margin and its global supremum follow exactly as in proof 002.

Audit concerns explicitly checked: the flow's exact stable graph is NOT asserted invariant under GD; eta is fixed and positive; the strict qM<1 still holds at eta M=1; the stable-set argument accounts for noninvertible points through the analytic determinant zero set; only straddling tokens |a|<b are covered by this discrete theorem. No numerical experiment is used as proof.

[Dfn 139 (IAMP mimicking BOGP SDE) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall from Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} 
  the initial conditions $X(q_0)\sim\zeta$ and $Y(q_0)\sim\zeta^\Ising$. Now let
  \[
  \breve{X}(q_0)\equiv0\,,\quad
  \breve{Y}(q_0)\equiv
    \frac{Y(q_0) \sqrt{q_0}}{(\bbE[Y(q_0)^2])^{1/2}}\,.\]
If $Y(q_0)\equiv0$ then we (somewhat arbitrarily) set $\breve{Y}(q_0)\sim\cN(0,q_0)$.
Then $\E[\breve{Y}(q_0)^2]=q_0$ in either case,
and it follows from
assumption~(\ref{i:IAMP-main-init}) of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} 
that
  \beq
    \bbE\bigg[
      \Big(
  Y(q_0)-\breve{Y}(q_0)
  \Big)^2\bigg]
  =\Big(
   \E[Y(q_0)^2]^{1/2}
   -  (q_0)^{1/2}\Big)^2
    \leq \Big|
    \bbE[Y(q_0)^2]-q_0\Big|
    \leq \epsilon\,.
    \eeq
We initialize vectors $\bx^0,\prxbx^0\in\R^M$ and 
$\by^0,\prxby^0\in\R^N$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item The coordinates of $\prxby^0$ are sampled i.i.d.\ from $\Law(Y(q_0))=\zeta^\Ising$. If $\bbE[Y(q_0)^2]>0$, then we set 
	\[\by^0 = \bigg(
	\frac{q_0}{\bbE[Y(q_0)^2]}
	\bigg)^{1/2} \prxby^0\,.\]
If $\bbE[Y(q_0)^2]=0$, then we let $\by^0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_0 I_N)$. 

\item the coordinates of $\prxbx^0$ are sampled i.i.d.\ from $\Law(X(q_0))=\zeta$, and we set $\bx^0 = \bzero \in \R^M$.
\end{itemize}
For fixed $\delta$ we abbreviate $ b^\ell(x)\equiv b_{q_0+\ell\delta}(x) \equiv b(q_0+\ell\delta,x)$, etc. We then introduce the vectors
\beq
\begin{aligned}
\bb^{\ell}
&\equiv
b^\ell(\prxbx^{\ell})
\equiv
b_{q_0+\ell\delta}(\prxbx^{\ell}) \in \bbR^M\,,\\
\bsig^{\ell}
&=
\sigma^\ell(\prxbx^{\ell})
\equiv
\sigma_{q_0+\ell\delta}(\prxbx^{\ell}) \in \bbR^M,
\\
\bw^{\ell}
&\equiv
w^\ell(\prxby^{\ell})
\equiv w_{q_0+\ell\delta}(\prxby^{\ell})
 \in \bbR^N, 
\end{aligned}\eeq
where the functions $b^\ell,\sigma^\ell,w^\ell$ are applied coordinate-wise. Let 
  \beqc_\ell(\epsilon)
  \equiv
  \bigg[\alpha\delta
  \Big( \budget(q_0+\ell\delta)+\epsilon-\Cost(q_0+\ell\delta) \Big)
    \bigg]^{1/2}\,.
  \eeq
As in \eqref{eq:IAMP-fully-general-fixed}, each $\bar{\bg}^\ell$ is an independent standard gaussian vector in $\R^N$. We let $\gamma(\ell,\delta)$ and $\prxgamma(\ell,\delta)$ be certain positive scalars, defined in \eqref{eq:proxy-C-ell-delta-def} below.  The IAMP iterates are as follows, with $\bu^0=\bzero \in \R^N$ and $\bm^{-1} = \bm^0=\bzero\in\R^M$: 
\begin{align}

  \prxby^{\ell+1}
  -
  \prxby^{\ell}
  &=
  \prxgamma(\ell,\delta)^{-1}
  \bw^{\ell}\odot(\bu^{\ell+1}-\bu^{\ell})
  \in\bbR^N,
  \\

  \by^{\ell+1}
  -
  \by^{\ell}
  &=
  \gamma(\ell,\delta)^{-1}
  \bw^{\ell}\odot(\bu^{\ell+1}-\bu^{\ell})\in\bbR^N\,,
  \\

  \bu^{\ell+1}
  -
  \bu^{\ell}
  &\equiv
  (\bA_\ell)^{\top}
  \big(
    \bm^{\ell}
    -
    \bm^{\ell-1}
  \big)
  + \delta^{1/2}
  (\bJ_{\ell+1})^\top\bb^\ell
  + c_\ell(\epsilon)
  \bar{\bg}^{\ell}
  -
  \ons_{\bu,\ell}
  \in\R^N\,,\\

  \bv^{\ell}&=\bA_{\ell}\by^{\ell}-\ons_{\bv,\ell-1}\in\bbR^M\,,
  \\

  \bm^{\ell+1}-\bm^{\ell}
  &=p(q_0+\ell\delta)^{-1}
  \big(\bsig^{\ell}
  -
  1
  \big)
  \odot
  \big(\bv^{\ell+1}-\bv^{\ell}\big)
  \in \bbR^M\,,
  \\

  \prxbx^{\ell+1}
  -
  \prxbx^{\ell}
  =
  \bx^{\ell+1}
  -
  \bx^{\ell}
  &=
  \bsig^{\ell}\odot
  \big(\bv^{\ell+1}-\bv^{\ell}\big)
  +
  \delta
  p'(q_0+\ell\delta)^{1/2}
  \,
  \bb^{\ell}
  \in 
  \bbR^M
  \,.
\end{align}
The Onsager terms $\ons_{\bu,\ell}$ and $\ons_{\bv,\ell-1}$ will be defined in \eqref{e:u.combined.ons} and \eqref{e:v.combined.ons} below. 
\textbf{We denote the above iteration by $\IAMP_N(\sigma,b,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising,\delta)$.} 
In the notation of Remark~\ref{rmk:omega-general-seed}, 
this algorithm will have random seed given by
	\beq
	\omega= \Big(
	\bG_\circ,
	(\bar\bg^\ell)_{1\le\ell\le\ubl},
	\bx[0], \by[0]\Big)\,.
	\eeq
For a fixed realization of $\omega$, this IAMP iteration will be a $C(L,\epsilon)$-Lipschitz function of the random matrix $\bG$ on an event with probability $1-e^{-cN}$, and the algorithm witnessing Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main} is its globally Lipschitz extension.
title: IAMP mimicking BOGP SDE

[Proposition 110 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] In the setting of Lemma~\ref{Checkzw}, uniformly in any compact subset of $\mathcal{D}$, we have the asymptotic expansion as $\N \rightarrow \infty$
\[
\log \Z^{\textnormal{ref}}_{\N} = \N^2 \F^{[0],\textnormal{ref}} + \theta \hat{n}\,\N \log \N + \N\F^{[1],\textnormal{ref}} + \frac{1}{12}\bigg(\theta + \frac{1}{\theta} - 3\bigg)\log \N + \F^{[2],\textnormal{ref}} + O\bigg(\frac{1}{\N}\bigg).
\]
The coefficients $(\F^{[p],\textnormal{ref}})_{p = 0}^{2}$ are given using the notation \eqref{Ddefzw} by the following expressions
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\F^{[0],\textnormal{ref}} & = \frac{1}{\theta}\bigg[\mathrm{LLlog}(\theta\hat{n}) + \mathrm{LLlog}(\hat{D}' + \theta\hat{n}) - \mathrm{LLlog}(\hat{D}')  - \!\! \sum_{k,\ell = 1}^{2} \big(\mathrm{LLlog}(\hat{D}'_{k,\ell} + \theta\hat{n}) - \mathrm{LLlog}(\hat{D}_{k,\ell}')\big)\bigg] \\
\F^{[1],\textnormal{ref}} & = -  \hat{n}\log\big(2\pi \Gamma(\theta)\big) + \frac{\theta -1}{2\theta}\bigg[\mathrm{Llog}(\theta\hat{n}) - 5\big(\mathrm{Llog}(\hat{D}' + \theta\hat{n}) - \mathrm{Llog}(\hat{D}')\big) \\
& \qquad + \sum_{k,\ell = 1}^{2}  3 \big(\mathrm{Llog}(\hat{D}'_{k,\ell} + \theta\hat{n}) - \mathrm{Llog}(\hat{D}'_{k,\ell})\big)\bigg] \\
\F^{[2],\textnormal{ref}} & = \frac{37(\theta - 1)^2 - \theta}{12\theta} \log \bigg|\frac{\hat{D}' + \theta\hat{n}}{\hat{D}'}\bigg| - \sum_{k,\ell = 1}^{2} \frac{13(\theta - 1)^2 - \theta}{12\theta} \log\bigg|\frac{\hat{D}'_{k,\ell} + \theta \hat{n}}{\hat{D}'_{k,\ell}}\bigg| \\
& \quad + \frac{1}{12}\bigg(\theta + \frac{1}{\theta} - 3\bigg)\log\hat{n} + \chi_2'(0|\theta^{-1},1).
\end{split}
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

The martingale method decomposes any function f(X_1, ..., X_n) of independent random variables into a sum of martingale differences D_k = E[f | X_1, ..., X_k] - E[f | X_1, ..., X_{k-1}], transforming the study of arbitrary functions into the study of martingales with bounded increments. This framework yields Azuma-Hoeffding, McDiarmid, and various dependent concentration bounds.
Independent random variables and filtered martingales

[Ppn 23 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall $F^{\riii}$ from \eqref{e:F.iii}
    and $F^{\riv}$ from \eqref{e:F.iv}.
    Fix any $\cB \in \scB(\lambda,\mu)$ (independent of $\bG$).
    For sufficiently large $N$, we have for all $t\in \R$
    \[
        \P\Big(F^{\riii}(k,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)) \ge t\Big)
        \le \P\bigg(F^{\riv}(\cB) + \frac{\epsilon'}{5} \ge t\bigg)
         + e^{-cN} \,.
    \]
That is, $F^{\riv}(\cB)$ approximately stochastically dominates $F^{\riii}(k,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Bound log R_eff by the field along an annulus decomposition; compare upper and lower bounds. Result: Rayleigh monotonicity gives R_eff(x, D_N^c) <= sum over dyadic annuli around x of the resistance across the annulus, each bounded by the maximum of e^{beta h} over the annulus times a constant, so log R_eff <= beta max_{annuli} (h max over annulus) summed... more precisely log R_eff <= log sum_k e^{beta M_k} where M_k is the field maximum over annulus k; by the concentric decomposition M_k is the walk value at scale k plus a bounded extremal term, so log R_eff is bounded above by beta times the maximum over k of the concentric walk, which after dividing by (log N)^{1/2} converges to beta sqrt g times the maximum of a Brownian motion on [0,1]. The lower bound via cutsets gives the same functional with the minimum over annuli of the field minimum, i.e. a different functional. The two bounds do not match: the upper bound is a maximum of a Brownian motion and the lower bound is a minimum, so the limit distribution is sandwiched between beta sqrt g times max and min of a Brownian motion but not identified. The notes' guess of a CGFF limit for the field x -> log R_eff is consistent with this sandwich only if the resistance is dominated by the coarse scale. Key identity: beta sqrt g min_{[0,1]} B <= liminf (log N)^{-1/2} log R_eff <= beta sqrt g max_{[0,1]} B in distribution (heuristic sandwich). Obstruction: Upper (flow) and lower (cutset) bounds converge to different functionals of the concentric walk.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0014-limit-of-the-normalised-log-effective-resistance-of-the-dgff-electric

AUTHOR-CHECKED PARTIAL LEMMA, NOT INDEPENDENTLY REVIEWED. For the unit-square Aldous-Huang city model with influence c0*N^alpha*r^(-beta),0<alpha<1 and beta>2*alpha, set theta=(1-alpha)/(1+beta/2-alpha). There exist kappa,c>0 such that P(M_t<floor(kappa*t^theta))<=exp(-c*floor(kappa*t^theta)) for all sufficiently large integer t. This does not prove the conjectured matching upper bound or population balance.
Uniform independent unit-square arrival locations
Founding probability 1/(1+maximum influence)
Total population equals integer arrival count t

Thus the conditional founding probability is at least1/[2*(1+K*t^alpha*M_t^d)], K=(2pi)^(beta/2)*c0. Put theta=(1-alpha)/(1+d) and m=floor(kappa*t^theta). Until M reaches m, each of the last floor(t/2) arrivals has founding chance at least p=1/[2*(1+K*t^alpha*m^d)]. Choose kappa small so this Bernoulli count has mean at least2m. [Lem 66 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have 
$\sM^{\siii}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\siv}(\alpha,q_0)$.

\begin{proof}
We repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} for this proof:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
	\MSRheader\\
	\hline
	\TMPTWOdefn\\
	\GOODdefn
	\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
We see that the $\siii$ and $\siv$ classes 
differ only in the conditions on the $L^2$ norms of the initializations $X(q_*)$ and $Y(q_*)$:
the $\siii$ class satisfies  condition~\ref{it:6.1}, while the $\siv$ class satisfies condition~\ref{it:6.2}. 

Therefore, let us suppose we have controls $({{q_*=q_0}},b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the $(\alpha,q_0,L,\epsilon)$-$\siii$ conditions, which drive processes $X,Y$ as in \eqref{e:formal.sde.main}, \eqref{e:formal.sde.ising}. We will construct controls $(\tilde q_*=q_0,\tilde b,\tilde \sigma,\tilde w,\tilde p,\tilde \zeta,\tilde \zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the $(\alpha,q_0,L,\tilde \epsilon)$-$\siv$ conditions, for $\tilde{\epsilon}$ tending to zero as $\epsilon\to0$. The latter controls will drive processes $\tilde X, \tilde Y$ that will approximate $X,Y$. 

We take $\tilde p = p$ and $\tilde{X}(q_0)=0\sim\tilde \zeta = \delta_0$. We will define a measure $\tilde{\zeta}^\Ising$ such that $\tilde{Y}(q_0)\sim\tilde{\zeta}^\Ising$ satisfies the required condition~\ref{it:6.2}. We will then define $(\tilde{b},\tilde{\sigma},\tilde{w})$ to simulate the original controls $(b,\sigma,w)$: from the definition \eqref{e:filt.X.Y} of $\cF_X$ and $\cF_Y$, we can write
    \begin{align*}
        \sigma_t &= \sigma_t( (B(s))_{s\in[q_0,t]},U,X(q_0))
        \,, \\
        b_t &= b_t( (B(s))_{s\in[q_0,t]},U,X(q_0))
        \,, \\
        w_t &= w_t( (W(s))_{s\in[q_0,t]},U',Y(q_0))\,,
    \end{align*}
where the $\sigma_t,b_t,w_t$ on the right-hand sides are measurable functions. Then sample independent random variables $\hat{X}(q_0)\sim\zeta$ and $\tilde{U}\sim\unif([0,1])$. 
The laws of $\tilde{U}$ and $(U,\hat{X}(q_0))$ are atom-free Borel measures on Polish spaces, so by Maharam's theorem \cite[Chapter 33]{fremlin2000measure}, there exists a measure-preserving bijection $\rho$ such that $\rho(\tilde{U}) = (U,\hat{X}(q_0))$. We use this to define
     \begin{align*}
        \tilde\sigma_t( (B(s))_{s\in[q_0,t]},\tilde U, \tilde X(q_0))
        &= \sigma_t( (B(s))_{s\in[q_0,t]} ,U,\hat X(q_0))\,, \\
        \tilde b_t(
            (B(s))_{s\in[q_0,t]},\tilde U, \tilde X(q_0))
        &= b_t(
        (B(s))_{s\in[q_0,t]},U,\hat X(q_0))\,,
    \end{align*}

Since we take $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ in the definition of $\cM^\star(\alpha,q_0)$ (see Definition~\ref{d:measure.classes}), we may assume $\epsilon$ to be small relative to $q_0$, so that condition~\ref{it:6.1} for $Y(q_0)$ implies

Then $L\ge l$.

The nondimensionalized Rosenzweig-MacArthur ODE system has at most three equilibria in the nonnegative quadrant: K_1 = (0, 0) (total extinction), K_2 = (k, 0) (predator extinction), and K_3 = (N*, P*) = (c/(m - c), [k*(m - c) - c] / [k*(m - c)^2]) (coexistence). The coexistence equilibrium K_3 lies in the open interior D if and only if m > c and k*(m - c) > c. If m <= c or k*(m - c) <= c, the predator population converges to 0 as t -> infinity.
Model parameters k, m, c > 0
Coexistence requires m > c and k*(m - c) > c

Let X and Y be topological spaces and give X x Y the product topology. Write B(Z) for the Borel sigma-algebra of a space Z and B(X) tensor B(Y) for the product sigma-algebra, i.e. the sigma-algebra on X x Y generated by the measurable rectangles A x B with A in B(X) and B in B(Y). Then: (i) ALWAYS B(X) tensor B(Y) is contained in B(X x Y), because the two coordinate projections are continuous, hence Borel measurable. (ii) If X and Y are both SECOND COUNTABLE (each has a countable base of open sets), then equality holds: B(X x Y) = B(X) tensor B(Y). In particular this applies to separable metric spaces, so B(R^(m+n)) = B(R^m) tensor B(R^n), and to Polish spaces and to countable products of second countable spaces. Practical consequence: for second countable targets, a map into X x Y is Borel measurable exactly when both components are, and Borel functions of two variables are jointly measurable in the product sense - which is what lets Fubini-Tonelli be applied to Borel functions. WHERE IT FAILS: second countability is not a technicality. Let X be a set of cardinality strictly greater than the continuum equipped with the discrete topology, so that B(X) is the full power set and X x X is discrete. The diagonal {(x,x)} is closed, hence Borel in X x X, but by a classical theorem (B. V. Rao) the diagonal of X belongs to P(X) tensor P(X) if and only if the cardinality of X is at most the continuum. So B(X x X) strictly contains B(X) tensor B(X). The underlying reason is structural: every set in a product sigma-algebra is already measurable with respect to a countably generated pair of sub-sigma-algebras, so a product sigma-algebra can only see countably many 'coordinates' at a time, while the product topology of a non-second-countable space produces open sets that need uncountably many. A second warning of the same kind: for Lebesgue sigma-algebras the analogous equality is FALSE - the Lebesgue sigma-algebra of R^(m+n) is strictly larger than the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras of R^m and R^n; it is its completion.
X and Y are topological spaces and X x Y carries the product topology
for the equality: both X and Y are second countable (a countable base of open sets); separable metric suffices
B(X) tensor B(Y) denotes the sigma-algebra generated by measurable rectangles, not its completion
the inclusion B(X) tensor B(Y) inside B(X x Y) needs no countability hypothesis

body:
Dayi and Chen, Gradient dynamics for low-rank fine-tuning beyond kernels (arXiv:2411.15385v1), analyze a specific frozen-factor spherical online algorithm, not simultaneous ordinary factor GD. The two-layer teacher has f_star(x)=lambda^T sigma((W+xi c u^T)x), known xi>0, unit u orthogonal to the pretrained row span of W, and c uniform in {+/-1/sqrt(k)}^k. The student draws c_hat uniformly from this quantized set and keeps c_hat frozen, initializing u_0 uniformly on the unit sphere of the orthogonal complement of the pretrained row span. If P is the orthogonal projector onto that complement and L(u;x)=(f_star(x)-lambda^T sigma((W+xi c_hat u^T)x))^2, define g_sph=(I-u u^T)P grad_u L. Equation (4) uses u_next=(u-eta g_sph)/||u-eta g_sph|| with a fresh x~N(0,I) each step. The unit-norm and subspace restrictions, frozen factor and fresh-sample spherical update distinguish this from zero/iid-Gaussian simultaneous empirical LoRA GD. Section 1.2.2 explicitly leaves joint training of c and u for future work. The paper's convergence theorems require additional activation and pretrained-feature hypotheses and are not restated here. Locators: section 1.1 equations (2)-(3), printed p.2; section 1.2.2 equation (4), p.3; section 2.2 Theorems 4-6, pp.7-9.
Known pretrained W, fixed output weights lambda, known scale xi; a nonempty pretrained-span orthogonal-complement sphere
Statement defines the source algorithm and its scope; it does not claim a convergence rate under only these assumptions
title: Dayi-Chen low-rank fine-tuning: frozen factor and spherical online SGD scope

The following expression will be referred to as the \emph{polymer partition function} with activities $\mathsf{w}$:
\[
\Xi(\mathsf{w}) \coloneqq  \sum_{\{\gamma\} \in \mathfrak{I}} \prod_{\gamma\in\{\gamma\}} \mathsf{w}(\gamma).
\]
Observe that due to the non-intersection constraint, $\Xi(\mathsf{w})$ is always a finite sum.

PRIVATE AUTHOR-CHECKED DRAFT, no independent review. Let f_k be the iterated majority-of-three function on n = 3^k bits. The greedy recursive algorithm (evaluate two random children, the third only if they disagree) has revealment (5/6)^k = n^{-log(6/5)/log 3} = n^{-0.1660}, so the optimal revealment delta(f_k) is at most that. Every leaf has influence 2^{-k} = n^{-log 2/log 3}, and the inequality delta(f) >= Var(f)/(n max_i I_i) (Garban-Steif notes, Theorem VIII.7) gives delta(f_k) >= (2/3)^k = n^{-(1 - log 2/log 3)} = n^{-0.3691}. So the exponent sigma asked for in Exercise VIII.5 of the Garban-Steif notes lies in [0.1660, 0.3691]; the exact value is open.

body: Curved marginal of a product law. Let u, v in R^m be orthonormal with u_i^2 + v_i^2 <= 1/2 for every i, let X have independent coordinates with densities at most 1, U = <u, X>, V = <v, X>, and c != 0. (a) The density of U + cV^2 is at most 1/pi + 4 pi^{1/2} |c|^{-1/2} (Fresnel identity in V and the two-dimensional geometric Brascamp-Lieb bound). (b) For every pair of coordinates i != j it is at most 4 (|v_i| + |v_j|)/|u_i v_j - u_j v_i|, uniformly in c and in all laws: condition on the other coordinates; along the parabola the two remaining coordinates are quadratic in the value b of B = v_i X_i + v_j X_j + b_0, with critical points |D|/(2|c v_i v_j|) apart, so near either critical point the other coordinate is monotone with slope at least 1/(2|v|). (a) is uniform in the frame and blows up as c -> 0 (at c = 0 the density is at most sqrt 2); (b) is uniform in c and grows like sqrt(m) for frames spread over m coordinates. Whether one absolute constant works for all c and all frames is open; it is the unsliced form of the curved-slice statements (CS) and (VD) that the single hub of the bounded-density quadratic-form conjecture needs.

body: In physics, Liouville's theorem, named after the French mathematician Joseph Liouville, is a key theorem in classical statistical and Hamiltonian mechanics. It asserts that the phase-space distribution function is constant along the trajectories of the system—that is that the density of system points in the vicinity of a given system point traveling through phase-space is constant with time. This time-independent density is in statistical mechanics known as the classical a priori probability.

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; T419-C013 v1, proof (unaudited), no novelty claimed; counterexample only to a specified formulation. Fix arbitrary m,p>=2, nonzero rank-one Delta in R^(m by p), s>0, sigma>0 and integer n>p+1. Let x_i iid N(0,I_p), z_i=Delta x_i+e_i with e_i iid N(0,sigma^2 I_m), and independent rank-one initialization b_0=0, a_0~N(0,s^2 I_p). Run simultaneous factor GD on sum_i ||b a^T x_i-z_i||^2/(2n), with any finite positive step eta chosen independently of initialization (it may be a measurable function of the data), held fixed in time. Then liminf_(t->infinity) E ||b_t a_t^T-Delta||F^2=infinity, whereas rank-one reduced-rank regression has finite expected population excess risk. This holds for arbitrarily large n and target condition number 1. The lower-limit risk is infinite on a positive-probability escape event. Deterministically, for C=XX^T/n positive definite, D=ZX^T/n nonzero, lambda=lambda_min(C), L=||D||op, the region ||a||^2,||b||^2>=6/(eta lambda), ||a||||b||>=2L/lambda is invariant and each factor norm grows by at least 2 per update. A Gaussian a_0 reaches its strict interior at iteration 1 on a nonempty open set. Fatou's lemma gives the expected-risk conclusion. This does not rule out high-probability results, initialization-dependent or adaptive steps, or finite statistical stopping; it does not settle the whole target.
Rank-one target and rank-one factors; arbitrary m,p>=2; n>p+1
Independent standard Gaussian inputs, positive-variance isotropic Gaussian label noise and nondegenerate Gaussian input-factor initialization
Finite positive constant step chosen independently of initialization; expectation includes initialization

Kind: route-failure (counterexample to a specified interpretation of Target 2). Target: 2.
Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim. This concerns the fixed-positive-step, unconditional expected-limit-risk version, not all possible GD algorithms or the whole written target.

## Deterministic escape lemma, arbitrary input and output dimensions

Let X be a p-by-n full-row-rank design and Z an m-by-n residual-label matrix. Write C=XX^T/n, D=ZX^T/n and assume D is nonzero. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, L=||D||op>0. For rank-one factors b in R^m and a in R^p, simultaneous GD with any fixed eta>0 on

 f(b,a)=(1/(2n))||b a^T X-Z||F^2

has the updates

 b_next=(1-eta a^T C a)b+eta D a,
 a_next=(I-eta ||b||^2 C)a+eta D^T b.

Define alpha=||a||, beta=||b|| and the closed escape region

 alpha^2>=6/(eta lambda), beta^2>=6/(eta lambda),
 alpha beta>=2L/lambda.

If an iterate is in this region, the next iterate satisfies

 ||a_next||>=2alpha, ||b_next||>=2beta.

To prove the b bound, eta a^TCa>=6 and the reverse triangle inequality give

 ||b_next|| >= (eta lambda alpha^2-1)beta-eta L alpha
             >= (eta lambda alpha^2/2-1)beta>=2beta,

where L alpha <= lambda alpha^2 beta/2 follows from alpha beta>=2L/lambda. For the a bound, every eigenvalue of I-eta beta^2 C is negative, and its least singular value is at least eta beta^2 lambda-1. Therefore

 ||a_next|| >= (eta lambda beta^2-1)alpha-eta L beta
             >= (eta lambda beta^2/2-1)alpha>=2alpha.

The escape region is invariant, so both norms grow at least by 2 per step. Since the product is rank one,

 ||b_t a_t^T||F=||a_t||||b_t||

grows at least by 4 per step. This argument does not require the factor directions to remain aligned, C to be diagonal or near identity, or a relation between the input and output dimensions.

## Positive-probability entry from the prescribed initialization

Initialize b0=0 and a0~N(0,s^2 I_p), s>0, independently of the data. Then

 a1=a0, b1=eta D a0.

Because D is nonzero, choose a unit vector w with ||Dw||>0. Taking a0=t w with t sufficiently large makes all three escape-region inequalities strict at iteration 1. By continuity they remain strict on a nonempty open ball around t w. A nondegenerate Gaussian law gives that ball positive probability. Thus for every fixed dataset with C positive definite and D nonzero, and every fixed eta>0, the prescribed initialization has strictly positive probability of entering the invariant escape region at its very first update.

The same argument permits eta to be any finite positive measurable function of the training dataset, provided it is chosen independently of a0 and then held constant throughout the iterations. It does not cover initialization-dependent or iteration-dependent step rules.

## Consequence for the named statistical target

Fix any dimensions m,p>=2, any nonzero rank-one signal Delta, any s>0, and Gaussian regression data

 x_i iid N(0,I_p), z_i=Delta x_i+e_i,
 e_i iid N(0,sigma^2 I_m), sigma>0,

with all inputs, label noises and initialization independent. Choose any n>p+1. The design has full row rank almost surely. Conditional on X, the sample cross matrix D has a nondegenerate Gaussian perturbation, so D is nonzero almost surely. Conditional escape probability is strictly positive almost surely, hence its joint probability is positive; no multiplication of unrelated probability bounds is involved.

On the escape event,

 R_t=||b_t a_t^T-Delta||F^2 -> infinity,

because R_t^(1/2)>=||a_t||||b_t||-||Delta||F. Isotropic population excess prediction risk equals R_t. Fatou's lemma for the nonnegative R_t gives

 liminf_(t->infinity) E R_t >= E[liminf_(t->infinity) R_t] = infinity.

In contrast, the global rank-one reduced-rank regression estimator has finite expected population risk at every n>p+1, by C002's exact-rank Gaussian-design specialization of Zindari-Mulayoff-Stich Theorem 2. Its inverse-covariance expectation is finite in this sample-size regime. Therefore no finite constant factor compares the limiting expected risk of this fixed-step GD to the reduced-rank estimator under these conditions.

This holds for arbitrarily large n, including n>=C0(m+p) for every proposed universal sample-size constant C0. The nonzero signal has condition number 1 because it has rank one. Hence the sample-size and target-condition-number requirements alone cannot rescue this version of Target 2. This is an infinite family with arbitrary input/output dimensions, not a scalar-only example or a zero-noise finite-time technicality.

## Exact limitation and relation to earlier claims

This does not rule out a high-probability guarantee, conditioning on a bounded initialization event, initialization-dependent steps, adaptive steps, clipping/restarts, or statistically chosen finite stopping. It does not claim that any of those alternatives achieves the target. It identifies assumptions that an unconditional fixed-step expected-limit-risk theorem must address.

C003 and C012 only assert high-probability convergence on explicit Gaussian initial events. Their positive-probability complements cannot be discarded when computing an unconditional expectation. The present escape result is compatible with both high-probability bounds.

Mu-Klabjan's norm-dependent step restriction in equation (8) is relevant prior context, but this escape proof is elementary and does not invoke their theorem or any unverified random-matrix limit. Existing-literature novelty is unresolved; a discovery search is recorded, not treated as evidence of absence. # Joint low-noise central-window bifurcation

T267 / Target 2 / C012 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is a local, rescaled noise-onset result in C010's restricted model.
It is not an exact global two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Precise scaling and result

Use C010's four-point stratified design, centered unit-norm ReLU teacher,
paired nonzero initialization with fixed nu in (0,1], both-layer GD with
step 1/2, and label-noise-averaged clean risk Q. Let alpha=alpha_e and
let b_h denote C009's full-kernel rates. Set

eta_e=(b2+b12)/b1 ~ e,
rho_e=kappa sqrt(eta_e), kappa>0 fixed,
sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e),
t0_e=log(1/sqrt(eta_e)).

Here sigma_e is the amplitude of independent symmetric label noise.
It is asymptotic to sqrt(kappa) e^(9/4). The network step size remains
1/2; eta_e in this proof is a spectral ratio, not that step size.

Let F_e(z) be the continuously interpolated frozen risk divided by
alpha^2. Define its central-time version
G_e(s)=F_e((t0_e+s)/b1). Then, uniformly on compact real s intervals,

G_e'(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa(s)
       =kappa exp(-s)-exp(-2s)-1,
G_e''(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa'(s)
       =-kappa exp(-s)+2exp(-2s).

Equivalently, the normalized value differences converge locally uniformly:

[G_e(s)-G_e(0)]/(2 eta_e) -> V_kappa(s)-V_kappa(0),
V_kappa(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(1/2)exp(-2s)-s.

If kappa>2, define z_+=(kappa+sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2 and
z_-=(kappa-sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2. The frozen curve has a central strict local
minimum at scaled time tending to s_min=-log z_+, and a subsequent strict
local maximum at scaled time tending to s_max=-log z_-.
In small fixed neighborhoods of those two points there is exactly one
frozen stationary point of the indicated type for sufficiently small e.
The actual nonlinear discrete-GD risk has strict descent-rise-descent
witnesses near these points, with probability tending to one in the
iterated even-width-then-feature-scale limit. Its interval minimizers and
maximizers on these separate neighborhoods have the same scaled limits.
Its resulting central local peak obeys

b1 k_peak-t0_e -> s_max,
k_peak ~ (2pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e),

in that iterated probabilistic sense. The first assertion refers to every
maximizer in a chosen sufficiently small neighborhood of s_max; it does
not assert that all actual extrema are unique.

For 0<kappa<2, the FROZEN interpolated risk is strictly decreasing on any
fixed compact central s window for sufficiently small e. No monotonicity
of actual finite-width risk is asserted. At kappa=2 the leading derivative
has a degenerate zero; this proof does not resolve its finite-e unfolding.
Thus 2 is a threshold for this limiting central-window shape, not a proved
global critical noise level or a global absence theorem.

## 2. Uniform derivative limit

The exact frozen curve is
F_e(z)=rho_e(1-exp(-b0 z))^2
      +sum_(h=1,2,12)[exp(-2b_h z)+rho_e(1-exp(-b_h z))^2].
Its nonconstant h derivative with respect to z is
2 b_h q_h [rho_e-(1+rho_e)q_h], q_h=exp(-b_h z).
At z=(t0_e+s)/b1, q1=sqrt(eta_e)exp(-s). Therefore its contribution to
G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) is exactly
kappa exp(-s)-(1+kappa sqrt(eta_e))exp(-2s).

For h=2,12, b_h/b1=O(eta_e) and
q_h=1+O(eta_e log(1/eta_e)), uniformly on compact s sets. Their combined
contribution to G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) tends to -1, since their b_h/b1 weights
sum to eta_e. Differentiating with respect to s makes their contribution
tend to zero: the extra b_h/b1 factor is O(eta_e).
The constant-mode term and its s derivatives tend to zero after division
by eta_e. Indeed b0/b1 is of order 1/e, t0_e is of order log(1/e), and
exp[-(b0/b1)(t0_e+s)] decays faster than every power of e on compact s
sets. These exact formulas prove both uniform derivative limits.
Integration from zero proves the uniform value-difference limit.

## 3. Limiting stationary points and risk witnesses

Writing z=exp(-s)>0, H_kappa=kappa z-z^2-1.
For kappa>2 its roots are z_+>1 and z_-<1 with product one.
At s_min=-log z_+, H_kappa'=z_+ sqrt(kappa^2-4)>0;
at s_max=-log z_-, H_kappa'=-z_- sqrt(kappa^2-4)<0.
Thus V has a strict minimum then a strict maximum. Compact uniform
convergence of H and H' gives a unique frozen critical point near each,
of the same type; the derivative is bounded away from zero outside small
root neighborhoods inside a fixed central compact window.

Choose delta>0 sufficiently small. The four scaled times
s_min-delta, s_min, s_max, s_max+delta are increasing and have strict
limiting value inequalities descent-rise-descent. Rounded integer times
floor((t0_e+s)/b1) have scaled grid error at most b1, which tends to zero.
The associated frozen risk differences therefore have strictly positive
margins of order alpha^2 eta_e. The same value convergence provides a
strict gap away from the unique minimum or maximum in each separate
small neighborhood.

For 0<kappa<2, completion of the square gives
H_kappa=-(z-kappa/2)^2+kappa^2/4-1<0 for every z>0.
Its maximum is strictly negative, so compact uniform derivative
convergence implies the stated frozen decrease on each fixed compact
s window. This does not control scaled times escaping all compacts.

## 4. Actual nonlinear GD and order of limits

For each fixed e, rho_e, alpha_e and all interval endpoints are fixed
numbers, and all involved integer times lie below T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2))
for sufficiently small e. Labels remain bounded. C010's independent-pair
finite-horizon comparison therefore controls every involved actual risk
uniformly through T_e as width grows, including all sixteen noise
patterns. Multiplication of the error by the fixed positive factor
1/(alpha_e^2 eta_e) preserves convergence to zero for this FIXED e.
It follows, first taking width to infinity then e to zero, that the
actual risk value differences converge to the same V differences and
inherit the strict four witnesses. The positive local value gaps transfer
the interval minimizers and maximizers to s_min and s_max. No derivative
comparison for the actual nonlinear network is needed or claimed.

Finally eta_e~e, b1~nu^2 e/(4pi), so t0_e~(1/2)log(1/e) and the displayed
peak time follows. This theorem concerns a different joint-noise regime
from C011's fixed-rho phase comparison; neither proof exchanges limits.

## 5. Exact concrete witness certificate, kappa=5/2

Here z_+=2, z_-=1/2. Use z values 3,2,1/2,1/4 in decreasing order,
so the corresponding s=-log z and integer times increase. The primitive
values are respectively

-3+log 3, -3+log 2, -9/8-log 2, -19/32-2log 2.

Their required margins are
log(3/2), 15/8-2log 2, log 2-17/32, all strictly positive.
For fully checkable bounds, log(3/2)>1/3 and
7/12<log 2<3/4 follow from integrals of 1/t: the lower bound splits
[1,2] into [1,3/2] and [3/2,2] and uses right-endpoint rectangles.
For the upper bound write t=1+x and use
1/(1+x)<=1-x/2 on [0,1], strict in the interior, since the difference
has numerator x(1-x)/2. The margins exceed 1/3,3/8,5/96 respectively.
This certifies a specific joint-noise witness choice by exact rational
bounds, not a floating-point estimate of a bifurcation.

## Remaining scope

The exact finite-e global onset, the degenerate kappa=2 case, interaction
with the initial constant-mode transient, iid sampling, fixed-positive
noise and all-time nonlinear dynamics remain open. These restrictions
matter: a central-window derivative result cannot imply that no other
double-descent pattern occurs elsewhere in time. Pairing and finite
support remain as in C010. Dependencies C009/C010 and this argument
await independent mathematical review; specialist novelty is unestablished.
All restricted four-point, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher and paired nonzero initialization assumptions of C010
Independent label noise amplitude sigma_e=c_e sqrt(kappa) eta_e^(1/4)~sqrt(kappa)e^(9/4)
Noise-averaged clean risk; simultaneous both-layer GD step 1/2; fixed nu in (0,1]
Even width limit precedes feature-scale limit; local windows only; eta_e is spectral ratio, not GD step size

DETERMINISTIC STATEMENT. Fix a unit v in R^d and measurement vectors a_i,
with z_i=a_i.v nonzero for every i. Put
 L(x)=mean_i((a_i.x)^2-z_i^2)^2,
 M=mean_i z_i^2 a_i a_i^T,
 K={v+h: |a_i.h|<=|z_i|/4 for every i}.
For x in K,

 Hess L(x) >= (11/4) M.                                (1)

Indeed Hess L(x)=mean_i[12(a_i.x)^2-4z_i^2]a_i a_i^T.
The defining inequalities give |a_i.x|>=3|z_i|/4. Hence each coefficient
is at least [12(3/4)^2-4]z_i^2=(11/4)z_i^2. Summing positive-semidefinite
rank-one forms preserves the order. This is a lower bound only; it does
not use any uniform empirical fourth-moment upper bound or matrix RIP.
K is convex, contains v in its interior and, if M>0, is bounded: its
defining inequalities imply h^T M h<=mean_i z_i^4/16. The inradius bound
min_i |z_i|/(4 max_i||a_i||)>0 is valid but can be very small.

GAUSSIAN STATEMENT. Let d>=2, v fixed before the sample, and a_i iid N(0,I_d).
Let q=P(1<=|Z|<=2)>0 for Z~N(0,1). If m>=512d/q, then, except on an event
of probability at most 5 exp(-qm/256),

 M >= (3q/32) I, and Hess L(x)>=(33q/128)I for all x in K. (2)

All z_i are nonzero almost surely, so K has nonempty interior. The assertion
is about the single sample event in (2), uniformly in x in K and beta>0;
it is not a product of rowwise conditional probabilities.

Proof of (2). Select I={i:1<=|z_i|<=2} and n=|I|. The indicators are iid
Bernoulli(q). For completeness, Markov applied to 2^{-n} gives
 P(n<=qm/2)<=exp(qm log(2)/2)(1-q/2)^m<=exp(-qm/8),
using 1-t<=exp(-t) and log(2)<=3/4. The latter follows by integrating
1/t on [1,2] and using its trapezoidal upper bound. On n>=qm/2 we have
n>=256d>=512.

Write a_i=z_i v+w_i. Conditional on all z_i, the selected w_i are iid
standard Gaussian on v-perp. Assemble the n-by-d selected-row matrix
D=[z W] in an orthonormal basis beginning with v. Choose a row-orthogonal
matrix Q taking z to ||z||e_1. Since Q depends only on z, conditional on z
the matrix QW is still iid Gaussian. Write its first row as w_0 and its
remaining (n-1)-by-(d-1) matrix as W_perp. We use the Gaussian singular

for an N-by-k iid standard Gaussian matrix; the second bound is used
with N>=k. No conditional independence of the two estimates is required.

Applied to the (d-1)-by-1 column w_0 with t=sqrt(n)/8, the first estimate
gives ||w_0||<=sqrt(d-1)+1+sqrt(n)/8<=sqrt(n)/4,
except with probability 2exp(-n/128). Here sqrt(d-1)<=sqrt(n)/16 and
1<=sqrt(n)/16 follow from n>=256d and d>=2.
Applied to W_perp with t=sqrt(n)/4, the second estimate gives
sigma_min(W_perp)>=sqrt(n-1)-sqrt(d-1)-sqrt(n)/4>=sqrt(n)/2,
except with probability 2exp(-n/32). For the last inequality one may use
sqrt(n-1)>=7sqrt(n)/8 and sqrt(d-1)<=sqrt(n)/8; both follow from the
displayed dimension conditions. Thus the conditional failure probability
for these two events is at most 4exp(-n/128), by a union bound.

For a scalar a and b in R^(d-1), on those events,
 ||D(a,b)||^2=(||z||a+w_0.b)^2+||W_perp b||^2
 >= (n/2)a^2-(n/16)||b||^2+(n/4)||b||^2

The estimate is simultaneous in (a,b) because it follows from operator

[Theorem 44 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Fix an admissible scale-dependent selection rule $\mathsf s$ on a domain $\D^{\mathsf s}_{\gamma}(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)$.  Let $p\in[1,\infty)$.
If $0<\gamma<1$ and $H\in L^p\big(\Omega; \D^{\mathsf s}_{\gamma}(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)\big)$, then $R^{\mathsf s}:=\hat\Lambda^{\mathsf s}_{S,\gamma,\alpha}H$ satisfies
\begin{equation}

\mathbb E\left[\norm{R^{\mathsf s}}_{\gamma,\alpha}^p\right]\le C^p \mathbb E\left[\norm{H}_{\gamma,\alpha}^p\right]
\end{equation}
and $\hdd R^{\mathsf s}=H$ almost surely.  For a family of individual random defects not lying in one fixed linear domain, the same estimate holds with the right-hand side replaced by
\[
C^p\mathbb E\left[\bigl(\norm{H}_{\gamma,\alpha}+C_H(\omega)\bigr)^p\right].
\]
If $H\in L^p\big(\Omega;\D^{\mathsf s}_{1}(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)\big)$, then $R^{\mathsf s}:=\hat\Lambda^{\mathsf s}_{S,1,\alpha}H$ satisfies
\begin{equation}

\mathbb E\left[\norm{R^{\mathsf s}}_{1,\log;\alpha}^p\right]\le C^p\mathbb E\left[\norm{H}_{1,\alpha}^p\right]
\end{equation}
and $\hdd R^{\mathsf s}=H$ almost surely.  Again, for individual defects one may replace $\norm{H}_{1,\alpha}$ by $\norm{H}_{1,\alpha}+C_H(\omega)$.

body:
[Definition def:initialization-coupling of arXiv:2605.08052, 'Rapid phase ordering of Ising dynamics on $\mathbb Z^2$'] [Time-zero monotone coupling] Assign each vertex in $\mathbb Z^d$ at time $0$ two $\text{Unif}[0,1]$ random variables $(\mathcal U_{v,0}^\pi)_{v\in \mathbb Z^d}$ and $(\mathcal U^Q_{v,0})_{v\in \mathbb Z^d}$ independently. Start with an arbitrary enumeration $v_1,v_2,...$ of the vertices of $\mathbb Z^d$. 
    
    For any distribution $\pi_{\Lambda}^{\eta}$ where $\Lambda \subset \mathbb Z^d$ finite, and $\eta \in \{\pm 1\}^{\Lambda^c}$ is a boundary condition, draw a sample $\sigma \sim \pi_{\Lambda}^{\eta}$  and $Q\sim \bigotimes_{v\in \Lambda} \text{Rad}(p)$ as follows: iteratively, for $i\ge 1$, 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item let $\sigma_{v_i}$ be $+1$ if $$\mathcal U_{v_i,0}^\pi \le \pi_{\Lambda}^{\eta} ( \sigma_{v_i} =+1 \mid (\sigma_{v_j})_{j<i:v_j\in \Lambda})$$
        and $-1$ else. 
        \item let $Q_{v_i}$ be $+1$ if $\mathcal U_{v_i,0}^Q \le p$ and $-1$ else. . 
    \end{itemize}
    Once all vertices in $\Lambda$ have been processed, terminate.
title: Definition def:initialization-coupling of arXiv:2605.08052

Let p and q be probability mass functions on a finite set, d = d_TV(p, q), A an event, u = sum over x in A of (p_x - q_x)_+ and v = sum over x in A of (q_x - p_x)_+. Over all maximal couplings (X, Y) of p and q (those with P(X != Y) = d), P(1_A(X) != 1_A(Y)) takes exactly the values from |p(A) - q(A)| to min(u + v, 2d - u - v) = d - |d - (u + v)|. Since |p(A) - q(A)| is the total variation distance between the laws of the two indicators, for every event A some maximal coupling of p and q is at the same time a maximal coupling of 1_A(X) and 1_A(Y).

[Lem 5 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] Let $u\in H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})$
be a nonnegative function, and $\chi$ be the kinetic function of $u$.
Then, for every $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty))$,
\[
\int_{x,\xi}\nabla_{x}\phi(x,\xi)\chi(x,\xi)=-\int_{x}\phi(x,u(x))\nabla_{x}u(x).
\]
In particular, if $(u,\nu)$ is a stochastic kinetic solution in the
sense of Definition \ref{def:def of stochastic kinetic solution}, then almost surely for every $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T])$,
\[
\int_{x,\xi,s}\nabla_{x}\phi(x,\xi,s)\chi(x,\xi,s)=-\int_{x,s}\phi(x,u(x,s),s)\nabla_{x}u(x,s).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Attributed source theorem, not independently audited here. Let x -> P_x be any channel. A simulator uses common randomness Z independent of the input, a transcript T with at most 2^Q possible values, and an output determined by (T,Z). Suppose its output has TV distance at most delta from P_x for every x. If the original channel has a one-shot code for 2^k equiprobable messages with average decoding error r and delta+r<1, then Q>=k-log2(1/(1-delta-r)). This bounds total transcript bits; real-valued score-query counts require a separate answer-information bound.
Uniform per-input TV bound delta
Common randomness independent of input
At most 2^Q transcript symbols
One-shot code with uniform 2^k messages, average error r, delta+r<1

body: Lemma (campaign status: audited-pass): Let beta = log2(4/3). (a) If every selected witness meets at most D remaining matching pairs, then kappa <= D/beta. (b) If every private row support has size at most s, then kappa <= (s-1)/beta. (c) A maximum-degree bound on the two-shadow graph implies the same conclusion, because every row support spans a clique in the two-shadow graph. Large support is not automatically fatal: what matters is support relative to the entropy loss it certifies. Notes: (b) reconstructed from flattened 'kappa <= s-1 beta' as (s-1)/beta; confirmed by the absolute coefficient 1+2(s-1)/log2(4/3) on p.39. Uses c_s >= beta from the atom bound (p.31).

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Distinct invariant ergodic laws are mutually singular Result: For a fixed countable group action, two distinct invariant ergodic probability measures are mutually singular. In the Lebesgue decomposition of one relative to the other, the absolutely continuous part is invariant. Its density is invariant and hence constant under the second ergodic law; ergodicity of the first forces its absolutely continuous mass to be either zero or one. Nonzero overlap therefore forces equality. Check: The singular and absolutely continuous parts are preserved by the action by uniqueness of Lebesgue decomposition; this is the load-bearing invariance step. Obstruction: This handles forest laws admitting such an ergodic common action. Arbitrary networks may lack it; two distinct probability laws need not be singular in general.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0050-singularity-of-distinct-free-and-wired-forest-measures

\alpha \in (0, 2]
\beta \in [-1, 1]
\gamma > 0
\delta \in \mathbb{R}

    \item $(S_x,x\ge -a)$ is a ${\rm BESQ}(\delta_1\, |_0 \, 0 \, |_{b}\, \delta_2)$ process starting at $0$.
\end{enumerate}
In both cases, let $T_{a,b}:=\inf\{y\ge b: S_x=0\}$. The conditional distribution of $T_{a,b}$ given $\{S_{b}>0\}$ converges as $a\to 0$ to the distribution of $\frac{b}{A}$, where $A$ has the beta distribution $\mathcal{B}(\frac{2-\delta_2}{2},1)$.

Owner draft: independently checked proof (C010 v1). Let C be a compact full-dimensional convex body and p an interior point. If Unif(C) is a probability mixture of Unif(K_alpha), where every component is an inscribed compact full-dimensional convex body and p lies in its interior almost surely, then K_alpha=C almost surely. Averaging normalized mass of shrinking balls around p and applying Fatou yields E[1/vol(K_alpha)]<=1/vol(C); containment gives the reverse pointwise inequality, forcing equal volumes and equal bodies. Thus a nonsimplex C cannot be a mixture of inscribed uniform simplices sharing its centroid, even with overlap or an uncountable mixture. Singular atomic/vertex components are excluded from this obstruction.

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: the Christ–Kiselev lemma passes from an untruncated space-time bound L^p_t → L^q_t to its causal truncation ∫_{s<t} only when p < q strictly. At p = q the truncation can be unbounded even when the full operator is bounded. Concrete counterexample on L²(R): let K(t,s) = sin(t−s)/(t−s) (continuous, locally bounded). The full operator is convolution with the sinc kernel, whose Fourier multiplier is π·1_{[−1,1]}(ξ) (up to normalization), so it is bounded on L² with norm ≈ π. Its causal truncation is convolution with k(u) = 1_{u>0} sin(u)/u, whose multiplier is m(ξ) = ∫_0^∞ e^{−iuξ} sin(u)/u du; using ∫_0^∞ sin(u) sin(uξ)/u du = (1/2) log |(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, the imaginary part of m is −(1/2) log|(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, which is unbounded as ξ → ±1. A convolution operator on L²(R) is bounded if and only if its multiplier is in L^∞, so the truncated operator is unbounded on L²: p = q = 2 fails. Consequence for PDE: the retarded (Duhamel) Strichartz estimate at the double endpoint q = q̃ = 2 cannot be obtained from the untruncated estimate by Christ–Kiselev; it is exactly the case Keel–Tao had to prove directly. Any proof that claims the double-endpoint inhomogeneous estimate 'by Christ–Kiselev' is misapplying the lemma.
title: Pitfall: Christ–Kiselev Needs p < q Strictly

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2604.00642, 'Quantitative central limit theorem for an integrated periodogram via the fourth moment the'] Let $f,g\in L^{1}(-\pi,\pi)$ such that
\begin{align}
\begin{split}
f(\lambda) &= |\lambda|^{-\alpha} L_f(\lambda),\\
g(\lambda) &= |\lambda|^{-\beta} L_g(\lambda), 
\end{split}
\end{align}
where $L_f$ and $L_g$ are slowly varying functions at $0$. Assume that
\[
-1<\alpha, \beta<1,
\qquad
d:=\alpha+\beta < \frac12 .
\]
Then we get
\[
d_W(F_n,Z)\longrightarrow 0 \qquad \text{as } n\to\infty .
\]
Assume moreover that there exists $C>0$ such that, for all $\lambda,\omega$ satisfying
$|\lambda-\omega|<\tfrac{|\lambda|}{2}$,
\begin{align}
\begin{split}
|f(\omega)-f(\lambda)|
&\le C\, f(\lambda)\,|\lambda|^{-1}|\lambda-\omega|,\\
|g(\omega)-g(\lambda)|
&\le C\, g(\lambda)\,|\lambda|^{-1}|\lambda-\omega|.
\end{split}
\end{align}
Then, for every $\eta>0$, there exists a constant $C_\eta<\infty$ such that, for all $n$ large enough,
\[
d_W(F_n,Z)\le C_\eta\, n^{\,d-\frac12+\eta}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In the localized FPP problem on a finite region of Z^2 (weights restricted to a finite edge set), define G as the set of edges lying in EVERY geodesic between two fixed points. Then membership is Borel outright: e belongs to G if and only if the passage time computed with e forbidden strictly exceeds the unrestricted passage time, and both are continuous functions of finitely many weights. No measurable selection of a geodesic is needed for any argument consuming G, and geodesic non-uniqueness only SHRINKS G (more geodesics means more constraints), so uniqueness assumptions are unnecessary for upper bounds on |G|. Confirmed in independent review (2026-08-10) of an entropy-method derivation that had carried a measurable-selection caveat it turned out not to need.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The smoothing transform concerns fixed points of the distributional equation W =_d sum_i T_i W_i, where (T_i) is a given, typically random, sequence of nonnegative weights and (W_i) are i.i.d. copies of W independent of (T_i); such fixed points arise as limits of branching random walk martingales, including derivative martingale limits, or of Mandelbrot multiplicative cascades, and their tail behavior, characterized by a power-law index alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 or a related equation, governs the limit's regular variation. Durrett and Liggett characterized the solution set of the smoothing transform equation, establishing existence, uniqueness up to a scaling constant, and the precise tail index under moment conditions on (T_i), a result foundational for analyzing branching random walk boundary and derivative martingale limits and related models such as the random energy model. Separately, Poisson-Dirichlet distributions PD(alpha,theta) arise as the limiting law of ranked, normalized jump sizes of a subordinator, of ranked cycle lengths in random permutations, or of ranked masses in fragmentation and coalescent processes, characterized via the stick-breaking (GEM) construction or via a Poisson process of jumps of a stable subordinator normalized by its total mass. Neither result gives an explicit closed-form density for the general fixed point or limit; the smoothing transform's fixed point is typically characterized only implicitly, through its tail index and functional equation, and both results require specific moment or regular-variation conditions on the input weights or subordinator to hold. Typical failure: Assuming the smoothing transform has a unique nontrivial fixed point up to scale without checking that the characteristic equation E[sum T_i^alpha]=1 actually has a solution in the admissible range, or without the Durrett-Liggett/Biggins regularity conditions, particularly in boundary cases such as the critical branching random walk where the derivative martingale, rather than the ordinary martingale, is the relevant object; applying the generic smoothing-transform tail behavior in a boundary or degenerate parameter regime without re-deriving it is a common source of incorrect tail-index claims. Canonical reference: Durrett and Liggett, 1983, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Biggins and Kyprianou, 2005, Electronic Journal of Probability; Pitman and Yor, 1997, Annals of Probability.
for the smoothing transform: existence of alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 in the admissible range, plus regularity conditions such as E[sum_i T_i^alpha log^+ T_i]<infinity from Durrett-Liggett/Biggins theory
for Poisson-Dirichlet: a well-defined subordinator, or fragmentation/coalescent structure, whose ranked, normalized jump sizes are being studied
independence of (T_i) from the i.i.d. copies (W_i) in the smoothing transform equation
non-degeneracy conditions ruling out the trivial Dirac-mass-at-0 solution
title: Technique: Poisson-Dirichlet Limits and the Durrett-Liggett Smoothing Transform

body: In mathematics, the connective constant is a numerical quantity associated with self-avoiding walks on a lattice. It is studied in connection with the notion of universality in two-dimensional statistical physics models. While the connective constant depends on the choice of lattice so itself is not universal (similarly to other lattice-dependent quantities such as the critical probability threshold for percolation), it is nonetheless an important quantity that appears in conjectures for universal laws. Furthermore, the mathematical techniques used to understand the connective constant, for example in the recent rigorous proof by Duminil-Copin and Smirnov that the connective constant of the hexagonal lattice has the precise value ${\sqrt {2+{\sqrt {2}}}}$, may provide clues to a possible approach for attacking other important open problems in the study of self-avoiding walks, notably the conjecture that self-avoiding walks converge in the scaling limit to the Schramm–Loewner evolution.

For an integer n>=1, let X=(X_1,...,X_n) be a random vector on one probability space, with each coordinate taking values in a finite discrete alphabet. Let S_1,...,S_m be subsets of [n], repetitions allowed, and let k be a positive integer such that every i in [n] belongs to at least k of the selected subsets. With Shannon entropy computed consistently with any base b>1, define X_S=(X_i)_{i in S}. Then
k H(X_1,...,X_n) <= sum_{j=1}^m H(X_{S_j}).
The empty-projection entropy is zero. Independence of coordinates is not required. The stated finite-alphabet domain guarantees nonnegative finite Shannon entropies and valid chain rule.
n is a positive integer
the random vector is discrete; finite coordinate alphabets are a safe sufficient restriction
the cover multiplicity k is a positive integer
every coordinate occurs in at least k selected subsets
all entropy terms use one logarithm base greater than 1

Let an infinite connected locally finite unit-conductance graph C contain a subdivision of a locally finite graph H, replacing each edge e by an internally vertex-disjoint path of length ell_e. If H has a unit flow f from a root to infinity with sum_e ell_e f(e)^2 finite, then C is transient. Lift the constant current along each replacement path; its energy is exactly that sum and its divergence is inherited at branch vertices. Uniformly bounded corridor lengths suffice whenever H is transient. A percolation argument must establish this quantitative energy condition, not only branching topology.

|f(y)- f(x) |\leq C_d\left(\int_Q \frac {|\nabla f(z)|} {|x- z|^{d-1}} dz\,+\, \int_Q \frac {|\nabla f(z)|} {|y- z|^{d-1}} dz\right).

Similarly for $f\in W^{2, 1}(\Rr^d)$, and $x, y\in Q$ with $|f(y)|, |f(x)|, |\nabla f(x)| <+\infty$

|f(y)- f(x) - \nabla f(x) (y-x)|\leq C_d\left(\int_Q \frac {|\nabla^2 f(z)|} {|x- z|^{d-2}} dz\,+\, \int_Q \frac {|\nabla^2 f(z)|} {|y- z|^{d-2}} dz\right).

Let d>=1, sigma>0, and let f be a measurable deterministic classifier or a measurable input-dependent distribution on a finite label set Y of size K>=2. Its internal randomness is averaged together with independent Gaussian noise epsilon~N(0,sigma^2 I_d). Define g(z) as a class maximizing P(f(z+epsilon)=c), using any fixed rule to resolve ties. Fix x in R^d and cA in Y. Suppose 0<pB<pA<1 and P(f(x+epsilon)=cA)>=pA, while max_(c!=cA) P(f(x+epsilon)=c)<=pB. With Phi the standard normal CDF, set R=(sigma/2)*(Phi^(-1)(pA)-Phi^(-1)(pB)). Then simultaneously for all delta with ||delta||_2<R, cA is the unique most probable class at x+delta and g(x+delta)=cA. In the binary case, taking pB=1-pA for pA>1/2 gives R=sigma*Phi^(-1)(pA). The inequalities are bounds on smoothed probabilities; the certificate does not require them to be exact or the base classifier to be continuous.

Gaussian noise variance sigma^2 I with sigma>0, independent of classifier randomness
Bounds at one fixed x: top-class probability at least pA and every competitor at most pB
Interior nontrivial case 0<pB<pA<1; strict open perturbation ball
No assumption on input distribution or base network architecture

body: In calculus and real analysis, absolute continuity is a regularity property of functions that is stronger than uniform continuity, and hence continuity. The notion of absolute continuity allows one to obtain generalizations of the relationship between the two central operations of calculus—differentiation and integration. This relationship is commonly characterized in the framework of Riemann integration, but with absolute continuity it may be formulated in terms of Lebesgue integration. For real-valued functions on the real line, two interrelated notions appear: absolute continuity of functions and absolute continuity of measures. These two notions are generalized in different directions. The usual derivative of a function is related to the Radon–Nikodym derivative, or density, of a measure. We have the following chains of inclusions for functions over an interval:Lipschitz continuous ⊆ absolutely continuous ⊆ uniformly continuous ⊆ continuous

body:
Let alpha be irrational and let R_alpha(x) = x + alpha modulo 1 on the circle. Then R_alpha is UNIQUELY ERGODIC: Lebesgue measure is its only invariant Borel probability measure. Equivalently (Weyl), for every continuous f the Birkhoff averages (1/N) sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f(x + n alpha) converge to the integral of f UNIFORMLY in x, and for every arc I the orbit spends asymptotically |I| of its time in I, for EVERY starting point with no exceptional set. For rational alpha the rotation is periodic and has many invariant measures, so irrationality is exactly what is used.
alpha irrational.
The conclusion for every point (not merely almost every point) is the force of unique ergodicity;
Birkhoff's theorem alone would give an almost-everywhere statement.
Uniform convergence is asserted for CONTINUOUS f - for an indicator it follows by approximating the arc from inside and outside, since the boundary has measure zero.

PROOF (UNAUDITED); novelty unverified. Consider the exact critical tanh two-input Gram chain: initialize a deterministic positive semidefinite Gram with marginal variances q0,r0 in (0,1]; conditional on the completed past F_j, draw n iid centered Gaussian pairs (Ai,Bi) with covariance the current Gram, and set Qnew=mean tanh(Ai)^2, Rnew=mean tanh(Bi)^2, Cnew=mean tanh(Ai)tanh(Bi). Write D_j=1-C_j/sqrt(Q_j R_j), F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2, delta_j=1-E[tanh(Ai)tanh(Bi)|F_j]/sqrt(F(Q_j)F(R_j)), and eta_(j+1)=D_(j+1)-E[D_(j+1)|F_j]. Let K,Lambda be uniform constants with E[eta^2|F_j]<=K delta_j^2/n and E[eta^4|F_j]<=16Lambda^4 delta_j^4/n^2, as supplied by unaudited C010/C015. For positive F_j-measurable a_j<=1+8(Q_j^2+R_j^2), put P0=1, P_(j+1)=P_j a_j. For deterministic B>=0 let tau=inf{j>=0:delta_j/P_(j+1)>B}. For n>=27648 and every finite L>=1, ||P_L sum_(j=0)^(L-1)1_{j<tau} eta_(j+1)/P_(j+1)||_2 <= exp(96(q0+r0))*(4K^2+48Lambda^4)^(1/4)*B*sqrt(L/n). Norms are probability Lp norms. The terminal product may depend on the same innovations. The proof uses unaudited C005 fourth product moments and elementary conditional fourth-power expansion plus Holder. This is a stopped centered-noise component; removal of stopping, predictable forcing, and the full Tensor Programs rate remain open. The general martingale inequality itself is not claimed new.
Exact critical tanh chain with fresh Gaussian rows; deterministic positive initial variances <=1; n>=27648
Positive predictable multipliers bounded by 1+8(Q_j^2+R_j^2); stopping test uses delta_j/P_(j+1)
C005 product moments and C010/C015 noise moment estimates remain unaudited dependencies
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:3a411f05eda0fdfbb5633adc08a89c030fb69044d7101fe7b146a82db2463e36","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/3a/3a411f05eda0fdfbb5633adc08a89c030fb69044d7101fe7b146a82db2463e36.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e5033f91821cae0cfe4115230e16628858654832246d8c30bb9a7fc4b0fd51f0","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_stopped_angular_martingale","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c016-stopped-angular-martingale","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Tensor Programs and martingale propagation","draft":"w712/bundle_012.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:critical-tanh-stopped-angular-martingale-dependent-terminal-product","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C016 v1: stopped angular martingale with a dependent terminal multiplier

Kind: moved. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified.
The general martingale estimate is elementary; no novelty is claimed for
that inequality. The application handles a specific dependence obstruction
in the two-input critical tanh architecture. Stopping removal is not proved.

## Statement

Consider the exact fresh-row critical tanh Gram chain of C015, starting
from deterministic marginal variances q0,r0 in (0,1]. Let F_j be its
completed layer-j past. Let delta_j be the population angular gap at that
current state, and let

    eta_(j+1)=D_(j+1)-E[D_(j+1)|F_j].

C010 v1 and C015 v1 give universal finite K,Lambda such that

    E[eta_(j+1)|F_j]=0,
    E[eta_(j+1)^2|F_j]<=K delta_j^2/n,
    E[eta_(j+1)^4|F_j]<=16Lambda^4 delta_j^4/n^2.     (1)

These two dependencies are unaudited. C005 v1, also unaudited, is the
occupation/stability-product input below. All new conclusions inherit
these explicitly stated dependencies.

Let a_j be finite, positive, F_j-measurable multipliers with

    a_j<=1+8(Q_j^2+R_j^2),
    P_0=1, P_(j+1)=P_j a_j.

The multipliers may depend on all previous innovations. Fix deterministic
B>=0 and define the F_j-stopping time

    tau_B=inf{j>=0: delta_j/P_(j+1)>B},

with inf empty=infinity. The quantity tested at j is F_j-measurable:
P_(j+1) uses a_j but no layer-(j+1) noise. Define

    M_L=sum_(j=0)^(L-1) 1_{j<tau_B} eta_(j+1)/P_(j+1),
    Z_L=P_L M_L.

For n>=27648 and every finite integer L>=1,

    ||Z_L||_2
      <=exp[96(q0+r0)] (4K^2+48Lambda^4)^(1/4)
                                      B sqrt(L/n).  (2)

The assertion includes arbitrary dependence between P_L and M_L.
For L=0, Z_0=0. No bound on the probability of tau_B<=L is asserted.

## 1. Elementary fourth moment under deterministic conditional envelopes

Let xi_(j+1) be martingale differences and assume
E[xi_(j+1)^2|F_j]<=v_j, E[xi_(j+1)^4|F_j]<=w_j,
where v_j,w_j are deterministic nonnegative finite numbers.
Put S_0=0 and S_l=sum_(j<l)xi_(j+1). We prove

    E S_L^4 <=4(sum_(j<L)v_j)^2+3sum_(j<L)w_j.       (3)

All finite sums have finite fourth moments by the triangle inequality.
The martingale-difference property gives, by expanding the square,

    E S_j^2=sum_(i<j) E xi_(i+1)^2<=sum_(i<j)v_i.

Conditionally on F_j, expand the fourth power of S_j+xi_(j+1).
The term linear in xi vanishes. Conditional Cauchy-Schwarz gives
|E[xi_(j+1)^3|F_j]|<=sqrt(v_j w_j). Thus

    E[S_(j+1)^4|F_j]
      <=S_j^4+6v_j S_j^2+4|S_j|sqrt(v_j w_j)+w_j
      <=S_j^4+8v_j S_j^2+3w_j,

using 4xy<=2x^2+2y^2 with x=sqrt(v_j)|S_j|, y=sqrt(w_j).
This also holds when either envelope is zero. Take expectations and sum:

    E S_L^4 <=8sum_(j<L) v_j sum_(i<j)v_i+3sum_(j<L)w_j
       =4[(sum_(j<L)v_j)^2-sum_(j<L)v_j^2]+3sum_(j<L)w_j
       <=4(sum_(j<L)v_j)^2+3sum_(j<L)w_j.

This proves (3). No independence between different increments is assumed.
The negative term was dropped, not declared equal to zero.

## 2. Predictable stopping supplies the envelopes

For xi_(j+1)=1_{j<tau_B}eta_(j+1)/P_(j+1), the weight is
F_j-measurable. Since j<tau_B implies delta_j/P_(j+1)<=B,
(1) gives

    E[xi_(j+1)|F_j]=0,
    E[xi_(j+1)^2|F_j]<=K B^2/n=:v,
    E[xi_(j+1)^4|F_j]<=16Lambda^4 B^4/n^2=:w.

These bounds also prove integrability of the weighted increments; no
uncontrolled inverse moment of P_(j+1) has been hidden. In the zero-gap
case (1) forces eta_(j+1)=0 conditionally, so B=0 is harmless.
Apply (3) to the L increments to get

    E M_L^4 <=4K^2 B^4 L^2/n^2+48Lambda^4 B^4 L/n^2
             <=(4K^2+48Lambda^4) B^4 L^2/n^2,       (4)

where the last inequality uses L>=1. This is a deterministic-time terminal
estimate; no unproved maximal-martingale inequality is needed.

## 3. The terminal product stays dependent

Pointwise, positivity and the bound on a_j give

    0<P_L<=product_(j<L)[1+8(Q_j^2+R_j^2)].

C005 v1, final stability-product assertion at r=4, requires
n>=6912*4=27648 and gives

    E P_L^4 <=exp[384(q0+r0)],
    ||P_L||_4<=exp[96(q0+r0)].                       (5)

The variances Q_j and R_j may be dependent; C005 already uses Holder
across the two marginal chains. We do not replace the fourth moment in
(5) by the smaller number exp[96(q0+r0)]; the latter bounds its fourth root.

Holder applied to the two possibly dependent factors now yields

    ||P_L M_L||_2<=||P_L||_4 ||M_L||_4.

Combine (4)-(5) to prove (2). A terminal product never leaves a conditional
expectation by an independence assertion.

## 4. Application and the exact unpaid step

The positive secant slopes of the normalized tanh covariance map in the
angular variable are admissible multipliers a_j: the upper bound follows
from C004 and positivity from C012. At equal comparison arguments take
the derivative. The resulting P is the homogeneous product in the
angular error's variation-of-constants formula, with population radial
and finite-width bias terms kept as forcing terms. Claims C004 and C012
are contextual inputs for this particular choice; the theorem above
assumes the multiplier bounds explicitly and does not re-prove them.

Taking B=b D0 with fixed b>0 and deterministic initial gap D0 therefore
gives a stopped stochastic-convolution term of order D0 sqrt(L/n).
It does not show that tau_B is late. The missing implication is a
uniform-in-depth bound on delta_j/P_(j+1) relative to D0, or a replacement
localized estimate plus a tail bound strong enough for unstopping.
C014 controls radial mixed moments, but those estimates alone do not
bound this inverse-product-normalized angular quantity or its maximum.
One cannot remove the indicator in M_L without that further argument.

The estimate treats the centered noise component only. Predictable bias,
radial forcing, removal of stopping, and the final readout coupling still
need a joint proof before the full two-input rate can be asserted.

## 5. Load-bearing hypotheses and boundaries

Predictability is essential to the generic noise-envelope argument. Fix
any n>=27648, independent symmetric signs eps_i, eta_i=eps_i/sqrt(n),
delta=1 and terminal multiplier P=1. All conditional noise bounds in (1)
hold with K=Lambda=1. Use nonnegative weights
w_(i-1)=1_{eps_i=1}, not measurable with respect to the previous past.
Although |w|delta<=1, the weighted sum has expectation L/(2sqrt(n)),
and therefore its L2 norm is at least that number. At L=64 it exceeds
52^(1/4)sqrt(L/n), since 32^4>52*8^4. Thus bounded future-dependent
weights cannot replace predictable ones in the generic argument.
This is a counterexample for the abstract noise-envelope inference, not
a claim that these Rademacher innovations are an exact tanh Gram chain.

Terminal dependence is allowed and handled by Holder, not excluded by
hypothesis. Positive multipliers make the normalization and stopping
test defined. The width threshold comes solely from the cited product
moment bound and also implies n>=64 for C010/C015. Zero initial angular
gap in the identical-input case gives zero innovations exactly.

Author check: the finite algebra and dependence handling re-derive.

C010 v1 equation (1); C015 v1 equations (2) and (12).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:36fafb1fe5b5b0174563524fa7eb99587a35ee6d3602d1e54ff0da8c6df94fdb","revision_digest":"sha256:d98ce27b23ea2784744b82161eacec003e52e6a2e02befd6eccd955a783b20d6","source_id":"owner-own-work:T250-w712-C016-v1","source_revision":"C016-v1-2026-10-21","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 20 (SDE for the second Malliavin derivative) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Assume that Assumptions \ref{ass:smooth},
and \ref{ass:second-malliavin-uniform} hold. Fix
$ 0 \le r \le s \le t $, $ u \in [s,t] $,
$ i,j,k \in \left\{ 1,\dots,N \right\} $, and
$ \alpha,\beta \in \left\{ 1,\dots,m \right\} $.
Then, the process $\left(
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
\right)_{u \in [s,t]}$ solves the SDE
\begin{align}

D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
&=
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
d\rho
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
dB_\rho^i ,
\end{align}
where $\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}$ denotes the initial
condition given by
\begin{align*}
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
&=
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{i,N}
e_\alpha
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{i,N}e_\beta
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}} \frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\alpha
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\beta ,
\end{align*}
with $ e_\alpha $ denoting the $ \alpha $-th vector of the canonical basis of $ \R^m $,
\begin{align}

G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N},
\end{align}
and $H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho) $ is defined by the same formula, with
$ b $ replaced by $ \sigma $, while
\begin{align}

R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\partial_{xx}^2 b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu\left[ \partial_x b \right]
\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_x\left[
\partial_\mu b\left( \cdot,\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\right]\left( X_\rho^{i,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_v\left[
\partial_\mu b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\right]\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1{N^2}\sum_{\ell=1}^N \sum_{q=1}^N
\partial_{\mu\mu}^2 b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N}, X_\rho^{q,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{q,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right],
\end{align}
and $ S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho) $ is defined by the same formula, with
$ b $ replaced by $ \sigma $. Finally, there exists a constant $ C > 0 $, independent of
$ r,s,t,\rho,N,i,j,k,\alpha,\beta $, such that, for every $ \rho \in [s,t] $,
\begin{align}

\norm{R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)}
+
\norm{S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)}
&\le
C \Bigg(
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}}
+
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}
title: SDE for the second Malliavin derivative

body: Publication record. A. E. Holroyd, L. Levine, K. Mészáros, Y. Peres, J. Propp and D. B. Wilson (Chip-firing and rotor-routing on directed graphs, 2008, Question 6.2) asked whether the limiting shape of the sandpile aggregate S_{n,H} on a background of height H is a regular (4H+12)-gon. Y. Shmalo, Corner angles of sandpile aggregates on a background of holes (October 2026) shows that for H >= -1 no limit of the rescaled S_{n,H} is a regular (4H+12)-gon: a corner of opening alpha has alpha > pi/2 and sin(alpha) <= 1/(H+3), and a convex polygonal limit has m >= 2 pi / arcsin(1/(H+3)) vertices with 4 | m (Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2). Existence and polygonality of the limit are not shown. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/sandpile-holes-corner-angles (commit db3b70c1c0ca). Not refereed; an outside audit is owed.
title: Holroyd-Levine-Meszaros-Peres-Propp-Wilson Question 6.2 answered negatively for H >= -1: limiting shapes of sandpile aggregates S_{n,H} are not regular (4H+12)-gons (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/sandpile-holes-corner-angles)

[Proposition Prop:WM of arXiv:2609.02213, 'Invariant subspaces for free linearizations of Lipschitz maps'] Let $M$ be an infinite metric space, let $f:M\to M$ be Lipschitz, and let $e\in M$.
		\begin{enumerate}[$(i)$]
			\item If $f$ is weakly mixing, then $T_{f,e}$ is weakly mixing.
			\item If $f$ is mixing, then $T_{f,e}$ is mixing.
			\item If $f$ is weakly mixing and chaotic, then $T_{f,e}$ is weakly mixing and chaotic.
		\end{enumerate}

For every0<l<=L and0<rho_max<358811/13673160 there is delta(l,L,rho_max)>0 such that ordinary separately bias-corrected Adam at beta1=.9,beta2=.999,epsilon outside sqrt,standard zero moments,lambda1,lambda2 in[l,L],eta>0 and0<epsilon/eta<=rho_max*min(lambda1,lambda2) has limsup_t |eta C_active-38|>=delta for almost every full-dimensional initialization. Hence p>1 fails eventual o(1/eta) tracking generically at small eta for every fixed positive eigenvalue pair; at p=1 generic nontracking holds whenever BOTH eigenvalues exceed13673160/358811. Conclusions hold simultaneously along any specified countable eta sequence under any absolutely continuous joint initialization law, without coordinate independence. All dependencies and this exact version require independent reviewer audit; constants are existential.
