Let G be a finite group of order p^a m, where p is prime, a>=1, and p does not divide m. Then G has a subgroup of order p^a; any two subgroups of order p^a are conjugate in G; and the number n_p of such subgroups divides m and satisfies n_p congruent to 1 modulo p.

For k>=2 labeled points in R^3, a differentiable map on an open subset of R^(3k) whose output is only a common translation of one fixed labeled k-point template has derivative rank at most 3, hence zero determinant. Its image is contained in a 3-dimensional affine subspace and has zero 3k-dimensional Lebesgue measure. A finite union over label permutations is also null. Such a map on a positive-volume bad set cannot meet the positive-Jacobian premise of the Gibbs repair-area-formula bound; repairs retaining full-dimensional displacement freedom are not ruled out.

[Lemma 44 (Reflection-invariant formal descent) of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] Let $\cO$ be a complete DVR with $2\in\cO^\times$, let
$a\in\cO^\times$, and set $x_a=a+a^{-1}$.  Let $F_a$ and
$F_{a^{-1}}$ be integral germs on the residue disks of $a$ and $a^{-1}$,
compatible under $z\mapsto z^{-1}$.  If the two disks coincide, assume
that the germs also agree after recentering.

Then the two germs descend uniquely through $X=z+z^{-1}$.  If
$\bar a^2\ne1$, the descended germ lies in $\cO[[X-x_a]]$.  If
$\bar a=\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$, it lies in
$\cO[[X-2\varepsilon]]$.

[Dfn 123 (L\'evy--Prohorov convergence of derivatives) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The function $(p^N)'$ is nonincreasing, so there exists a nonnegative measure $\nu_N$ on $[q_0,1]$ with
	\[
	\nu_N( (s,t]) = -\Big[(p^N)'(t)-(p^N)'(s)\Big]
	\]
for all $q_0 \le s\le t\le1$, and with $\nu_N(\{0\})=0$. By passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $\nu_N$ converges in the L\'evy--Prohorov metric to a limiting measure $\nu$. Since $(p^N)'$ converges to $p'$ almost everywhere, we immediately conclude that 
	\[\nu((s,t])
	=-\Big[ p'(t)-p'(s)\Big]
	\]
for almost all $s,t$. Now recall that $p'$ denotes the derivative of $p$ from the right, so in particular $p'$ is right-continuous: this implies that the above equality holds for all $s,t\in[0,1]$. For this form of convergence, we hereafter say for short that \textbf{$(p^N)'$ converges to $p'$ in the L\'evy--Prohorov metric.}
title: L\'evy--Prohorov convergence of derivatives

R_A is homogeneous of degree 0 (R_A(c x) = R_A(x) for any nonzero scalar c), so it is determined by the direction of x alone, and its range over all nonzero x is contained in the interval between the smallest and largest eigenvalues of A. [Cor 25 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k,\cB)$ be the function from Lemma~\ref{l:F.iii.sqrtk.Lip}. As stated therein, $\E\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k,\cB)$ does not depend on the choice of $\cB \in \scB(\lambda,\mu)$, so we denote this quantity simply $\E\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k)$. We then have
        \[\P\bigg(
    \Big|F^{\riii}(k,\cB) - \E\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k)\Big|
    \ge \frac{\epsilon'}{10}
    ;\cE_{\gd}
    \bigg) \le e^{-ckN}\]
for any fixed partition $\cB \in \scB(\lambda,\mu)$.

\begin{proof}
From Lemma~\ref{l:F.iii.sqrtk.Lip},
the function $\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k,\cB)$ is $O((kN)^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz, and therefore concentrates around its mean $\E\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k)$ with failure probability $e^{-ckN}$ (by Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}). On the event $\cE_\gd$, the functions
$\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k,\cB)$
and $F^{\riii}(k,\cB)$ coincide,
so the claim follows.
\end{proof}

[Definition 30 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $m\ge 2$ and $X\rightarrow X/G$ is an HKG cover. For a subset $A$ of $\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket$, we consider the restriction
$$\mu_{X;A}:=\mu_X|C_m\times A:C_m\times A\rightarrow\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$$
of $\mu_X$ to $C_m\times A$; so $\mu_X=\mu_{X;\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket}$. If $A=\{b\}$, let $\mu_{X;b}:=\mu_{X,\{b\}}$.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} For $m\ge 2$ (resp.\ $m\ge 3$) we say that $\mu_{X;A}$ has exceptional $+1$ (resp.\ $-1$) jumps or that $\mu_{X;A}$ has jump type $1$ (resp.\ $-1$) if there exists $b\in A\cap\llbracket 1,p^s-1\rrbracket$ such that the function $\mu_{X;b}$ is non-constant and for each such $b$, $\mu_{X;b}$ attains its maximum (resp.\ minimum) at precisely one element of the source.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} We say that $\mu_{X;A}$ has jump type $0$ if either $m=2$ and it does not have jump type $ 1$ or $m\ge 3$ and it does not have jump types $-1$ or $1$. 

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} We say that $\mu_{X;A}$ has regular $\pm 1$ jumps if for each $b\in A$ the function $\mu_{X;b}$ is non-constant, attains its maximum at two or more elements of the source, and attains its minimum at two or more elements of the source.

\smallskip
{\bf (4)} For $m=2$ (resp.\ $m\ge 3$), we fix an $s$-tuple $(\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{s-1})\in\{0,1\}^s$ (resp. $(\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{s-1})\in\{-1,0,1\}^s$). We say the multiplicity function $\mu_X$ has jump type $(\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{s-1})$ if for each $j\in\llbracket0,s-1\rrbracket$, $\mu_{X;A_{s,j}}$ has jump type $\epsilon_j$.

\smallskip
{\bf (5)} We call the $2s$-tuple 
$$(\l_{0,0},|\mathbb J_{X;0}|,\l_{1,0},|\mathbb J_{X;1}|,\ldots,\l_{s-1,0},|\mathbb J_{X;s-1}|)\in(\mathbb N\cup\{0\})^{2s} $$
 as the multiplicity type of $\mu_X$.

CANDIDATE FULL PROOF, AUTHOR CHECKED; NOVELTY UNVERIFIED. The proposed threshold for unimodality of mu freely convolved with a semicircle of variance t is t>=D^2, D the diameter of compact support. A centered tilted-measure fourth-moment argument controls critical points. The source printed lower bound is inconsistent with its Bernoulli normalization and is explicitly discussed. A separate parent-agent analytic review found no gap in the recorded steps; that scoped review is not a full certification or novelty check.
Compactly supported real probability measure; D=support diameter
Semicircle parameter t is variance
Source Hasebe-Ueda2018 Problem3.3; equality case must retain quartic argument
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:64d7702983cc0d0d2c0e8f244152601416355517afb8a186b700b46858f51b61","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/64/64d7702983cc0d0d2c0e8f244152601416355517afb8a186b700b46858f51b61.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:782e3ef5bbb0faf01a685eb529732c0d77bfa3843ab0c5c3cb1c854a588ec117","bundle_entry_key":"free-brownian-threshold","bundle_id":"population.probability-candidate-obstructions-and-spatial-lemmas-005","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-1000-20h-20260906/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.free:candidate-optimal-diameter-free-brownian-unimodality","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# P0174: candidate sharp diameter threshold for free Brownian unimodality

Status: complete candidate proof, author-checked in two analytic formulations; no independent review and no claim of established novelty. Current-literature search is incomplete. Do not count as a promoted original solution.

Source: Hasebe and Ueda, *Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions*, ALEA 15 (2018), 353–374, Problem 3.3; archived arXiv1710.08240v2, PDF p.6. The PDF carries the arXiv revision date14 September2018 and a manuscript header4 November2021; retain that discrepancy. Primary links: https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.08240 and https://alea.math.cnrs.fr/articles/v15/15-15.pdf . The source defines S(0,t) to have variance t, and D_mu to be support diameter.

The source proves the sufficient constant4 and asks for the optimal universal C in t>=C D_mu^2. Its paragraph says the symmetric Bernoulli law on{-1,1} has threshold t=4 and diameter2, then prints2<=C<=4. Those preceding numbers imply the lower bound C>=1. The candidate upper bound below is a separate argument, not a conclusion drawn from that arithmetic inconsistency.

## Candidate theorem

If mu is a compactly supported probability measure on R with support diameter D, then mu free-convolved with the centered semicircle law of variance t is unimodal whenever t>=D^2. The optimal universal constant in the source's normalization is therefore C=1.

When D=0 the measure is a point mass and the assertion is immediate. Henceforth D>0. No symmetry, density, or non-atomicity of mu is assumed.

## An elementary moment inequality

Let Q be a probability law of a centered real variable X supported in an interval of length D. Write a=E_Q X^2 and b=E_Q X^4. Then

\[
 a\le D^2/4,\qquad b+3a^2\le D^2a.
\]

For the first inequality, if the supporting interval is[l,h], then E[(X-l)(h-X)]>=0 gives a<=-lh, and -lh<=D^2/4 because l+h has a real square. For the second, let X' be an independent copy. Pointwise, (X-X')^4<=D^2(X-X')^2. Taking expectations and using E X=0 gives2b+6a^2<=2D^2a. This derivation checks both the coefficient3 and the use of the diameter rather than radius.

Equality a=D^2/4 forces l=-D/2,h=D/2 and Q to put equal mass on the two endpoints: equality in E[(X-l)(h-X)]>=0 forces endpoint support, and centering fixes the weights.

## Cauchy-profile lemma

For R>0 define

\[
 F_R(u)=\int\frac{d\mu(x)}{(x-u)^2+R^2}.
\]

Claim: F_R has no local minimum with value at most1/D^2.

Take any stationary point u of F_R with F_R''(u)>=0. Put y=R^2>0 and

\[
 Z=\int ((x-u)^2+y)^{-2}\,d\mu(x),\qquad
 dQ(x)=Z^{-1}((x-u)^2+y)^{-2}\,d\mu(x).
\]

Differentiation under the integral is justified by R>0 and compact support. Stationarity says E_Q(X-u)=0. With a=E_Q(X-u)^2 and b=E_Q(X-u)^4, the preceding moment inequalities apply. The second derivative is

\[
 \frac{F_R''(u)}{2Z}
 =E_Q\frac{3(X-u)^2-y}{(X-u)^2+y}
 =3-4y E_Q\frac1{(X-u)^2+y}.
\]

Jensen's inequality and F_R''(u)>=0 imply

\[
 \frac1{a+y}\le E_Q\frac1{(X-u)^2+y}\le\frac3{4y},
 \qquad y\le3a.
\]

The normalization of Q gives an exact reciprocal-profile identity:

\[
 \frac1{F_R(u)}
 =\frac{E_Q[((X-u)^2+y)^2]}{E_Q[(X-u)^2+y]}
 =\frac{b+2ay+y^2}{a+y}.
\]

Consequently

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \frac1{F_R(u)}-D^2
 &\le\frac{y^2+2ay-3a^2-D^2y}{a+y}\\
 &=\frac{(y-3a)(y+a)+(4a-D^2)y}{a+y}\le0.
 \end{aligned}
\]

The first inequality uses b<=D^2a-3a^2; the final two summands are nonpositive because y<=3a and4a<=D^2. In particular, F_R(u)>=1/D^2.

The equality case matters for the endpoint t=D^2. If F_R(u)=1/D^2 and F_R''(u)>=0, then the two final nonpositive terms both vanish: y=3a and4a=D^2, since y>0. Equality in the variance bound forces Q to be symmetric Bernoulli on u plus/minus D/2. On these two points the reweighting denominator is equal, so mu is the same symmetric Bernoulli law. Writing c=D/2 and s for displacement from its midpoint, with R^2=3c^2, gives

\[
 F_R(u+s)=\frac{s^2+4c^2}{s^4+4c^2s^2+16c^4},
 \qquad
 F_R(u+s)-\frac1{4c^2}
 =-\frac{s^4}{4c^2(s^4+4c^2s^2+16c^4)}<0\quad(s\ne0).
\]

Thus the only possible equality point is a strict maximum, not a local minimum. Every local minimum therefore has value strictly greater than1/D^2, proving the claim including equality.

## Unimodality via Biane's density parametrization

For fixed t>=D^2 and fixed R>0, the equation F_R(u)=1/t has at most two solutions. Indeed, if there were three solutions u1<u2<u3, then either F_R dips below1/t somewhere in[u1,u3], producing an interior local minimum below that level, or F_R>=1/t throughout that interval, making u2 a local minimum at that level. Both alternatives contradict the Cauchy-profile lemma because1/t<=1/D^2. The analytic function cannot be identically constant on an interval, since F_R tends to0 at infinity.

Now use exactly the density framework stated in source Section2.2 and Lemma3.1. Define v_t(u)>=0 by

\[
 \int\frac{d\mu(x)}{(x-u)^2+v_t(u)^2}=\frac1t
\]

where its positive solution exists, setting v_t=0 elsewhere. Biane's real homeomorphism psi_t satisfies

\[
 p_t(\psi_t(u))=\frac{v_t(u)}{\pi t},
\]

where p_t is the continuous density of mu free-convolved with S(0,t), analytic wherever positive. Each positive density level p_t=a corresponds to F_(pi*a*t)(u)=1/t, and therefore has at most two points. Source Lemma2.2, equivalently Lemma3.1, now gives unimodality. All source assumptions match: mu is compactly supported, t>0, and the semicircle parameter is variance.

## Sharpness

Let mu be symmetric Bernoulli on{-c,c}, c>0, so D=2c. For c^2<t<4c^2, the positive solution at the symmetry center has v_t(0)^2=t-c^2. Implicit differentiation at0 yields

\[
 v_t''(0)=\frac{3c^2-v_t(0)^2}{v_t(0)(c^2+v_t(0)^2)}
 =\frac{4c^2-t}{t\sqrt{t-c^2}}>0.
\]

Thus v_t has a positive strict local minimum at0, and the density under the homeomorphism psi_t does as well. It is not unimodal. For any proposed C<1, choose t strictly between max(C,1/4)D^2 and D^2. Then t>=CD^2 but unimodality fails. This proves the lower bound C>=1 independently of the source's printed inequality.

## Second analytic check and remaining review obligations

The same moment computation can be applied directly at critical points of v_t. At such a point, the profile's first derivative vanishes and the sign of v_t'' equals the sign of F_v-fixed''. The calculation above says a nonnegative second derivative would force t<=D^2. Hence for t>D^2 every critical point of v_t is a strict maximum, giving the same threshold. The equality analysis in the Cauchy-profile proof closes the boundary without appealing to weak closure of unimodal laws.

The load-bearing points to challenge are the Q-normalization identity, the centered fourth-moment inequality, the direction of Jensen, and the equality case at t=D^2. Each is written explicitly; neither a numerical validator nor brain retrieval supplies independent mathematical review. Later literature might already contain this sharp threshold or the same argument. DRAFT AUTHOR PROOF; independent review pending; no novelty claim. Let G be the simple undirected Cayley graph of <a,b | a^2=b^3=1> with the symmetric generating set {a,b,b^-1}. Each unordered a-edge appears once. In iid Bernoulli bond percolation, p_c=q, the unique root in (0,1) of 2q^2+2q^3-2q^4=1, with 0.63<q<0.64, and p_u=1. No infinite cluster exists at p<=q; for each fixed q<p<1 there are almost surely infinitely many; at p=1 there is one. The edge Cheeger constant is 1/3. For rho=||A||/3, the triangle Rayleigh bound gives 3*rho*p_c>=2q>1.26. This refutes universal satisfaction of the sufficient spectral criterion while proving this special case of nonuniqueness.

CANDIDATE APPLICATION, NOT INDEPENDENTLY REVIEWED; PRIOR-LITERATURE STATUS UNVERIFIED. Lyons-Peres Question 17.18 asks whether a flow with stationary measure equivalent to GW must be ergodic. For p2=3/5,p3=2/5 use the measurable AND/OR color and choose uniformly among same-color children. The preceding two lemmas give stationary measure exactly GW, while each color class has probability 1/2 and is invariant. The source definition in Section 17.5 permits zero child weights and requires equivariance and consistency only on positive-flow descendants; products of the local weights satisfy this definition. If all scope and literature checks stand, this answers the question negatively. Exercise 17.22 only gives a merely absolutely continuous stationary measure and does not by itself settle equivalence. Do not label this new or independently reviewed from successful ingestion.

body:
[Lem 164 ($\bar{\bx}$ is Lipschitz) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take $\bar{\bx}\equiv \bar{\bx}(q_d)$
 as in \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.x}, so it is measurable with respect to
 $\cG(q_d)$. Then
		\[
		\|\E\bar{\bx}\|^2
		\le \frac{Nq_0}{q_d} \le N\,.\]
and the centered random vector $\bar{\bx}  -\E\bar{\bx}$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $L^{O(1)}$.

\begin{proof} 
Recall $\chi(p)=\E R(p)$ with $R(p)$ as in \eqref{e:p.corr.overlap}, and $q_d=\chi(p_d)$. Note that
	\[
	\frac{\|\E\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N}
	= \frac{\|\E\cA(\bG)\|^2}{Nq_d}
	= \frac{\chi(0)}{q_d} 
	\le \frac{\chi(p_0)}{q_d} = \frac{q_0}{q_d}\le1\,,
	\]
which proves the first claim. Next note that we can write
	\[
	\sqrt{q_d}\bar{\bx}
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.x}}{=}
	\E\bigg( \cA
	\Big(\sqrt{p_d}\bar{\bG} +\sqrt{1-p_d}\bG'\Big)
	\,\bigg|\,\bar{\bG}\bigg)\,,
	\]
where $\bar{\bG} = \bG(q_d)/\sqrt{p_d}$ and $\bG'$ are independent $M\times N$ matrices, each with i.i.d.\ standard gaussian entries. Since $\cA$ is $L$-Lipschitz, and $p_d/q_d \le L^{O(1)}$ by \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound}, it follows that $\bar{\bx}$ is $L^{O(1)}$-Lipschitz with respect to $\bar{\bG}$. The claim then follows using Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: $\bar{\bx}$ is Lipschitz

body:
[Theorem thm:correlation of arXiv:2608.05089, 'Correlation decay in area-tilted line ensembles'] There are some $\lambda_0 > 1$ and $C, \gamma > 0$ such that for all $\lambda \geqslant \lambda_0$
    and all $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$,
    if $\mathbf{X}$ denotes the $\lambda$-tilted stationary line ensemble
    then for all $t > 0$, we have
    \begin{equation}
        
        0 \leqslant \operatorname{Cov}[X^i(0), X^j(t)] \leqslant C e^{-\gamma t} \lambda^{-(i+j-2)/3}.
    \end{equation}
    The same bound holds if $\mathbf{X}$ is replaced by the stationary
    $n$-line $\lambda$-tilted ensemble $\mathbf{X}_n \sim \mathcal{L}_n^\lambda$, for any $n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Exponential decay of correlations

[Proposition prop:normal_domain_comonotonic of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{Z}$ be $\alpha$-stable with $\alpha \in (0,2)$ and $\bm{X}$ be in its domain of normal attraction. Let Assumption~(\nameref{asm:C}) (with constant $H\equiv G$ and $Q\equiv 1$) hold for some $p\in(0,\infty)\setminus\{\alpha-1\}$. Then, for any $q\in(0,1]\cap(0,\alpha)$ with $\mathds{E}[|\bm{X}_1|^q]<\infty$, we have, as $t \downarrow 0$, 
\[
\mathcal{W}_q\big(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z}\big)
=\begin{dcases}
\mathcal{O}\big(t^{\min\{pq/\alpha,1-q/\alpha\}}\big),&\alpha\in(0,1),\\
\mathcal{O}\big(t^{q\min\{p/\alpha,1-1/\alpha\}}\big),&\alpha\in(1,2).
\end{dcases}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem th:mom-cum-high of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $\Psi_0, \ldots, \Psi_n$ be infinitely differentiable functions at $0$
  and consider the sequences $(c_m^{(0)})_{m \in \mathbb{N}}$, $\ldots$,
  $(c^{(n)}_m)_{m \in \mathbb{N}}$, where for every $i = 0, \ldots, n$,
  \[ c_m^{(i)} := \frac{i! \Psi_i^{(m)} (0)}{(m - 1) !}, \text{\quad for
     every } m \in \mathbb{N}. \]
  Then, for the sequence $(\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k^{(n)})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ defined
  in ((tavradiamouleipis of the paper)) we have, for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the equality
  \begin{equation}
    \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k^{(n)} = \sum_{\underset{\pi = \{V_1, \ldots, V_l \}}{\pi
    \in \ensuremath{\operatorname{NC}} (k)}} \sum_{\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_l = n}
    \frac{1}{\lambda_1 ! \ldots \lambda_l !} c_{|V_1 |}^{(\lambda_1)} \ldots
    c_{|V_l |}^{(\lambda_l)}. 
  \end{equation}
title: Theorem th:mom-cum-high of arXiv:2412.09290

\[
\inf_{\Gamma} P_{z}\bigl(S[0,\tau(\partial B(z,br))]\cap \Gamma\neq\varnothing\bigr)\geq \frac{c}{\log r},
\]

For each N let theta_N be a unit vector in R^N, Y_t iid with law P_N, and L_N(x;Y) a loss on the unit sphere S^(N-1). Let its population loss be Phi_N(x)=E L_N(x;Y)=phi(m_N(x)), where m_N(x)=x.theta_N and the same function phi:[-1,1]->R is used for every N. The spherical stochastic gradients exist almost surely; assume explicitly that E grad_S L_N(x;Y)=grad_S Phi_N(x). Let H_N(x;Y)=L_N(x;Y)-Phi_N(x). For constants C_1,iota>0 independent of N, assume sup_x E[(grad_S H_N(x;Y).theta_N)^2]<=C_1 and sup_x E||grad_S H_N(x;Y)||^(4+iota)<=C_1 N^((4+iota)/2). For a fixed integer k>=1, suppose phi is C^(k+1) on [-1,1], phi_prime(m)<0 for 0<m<1, phi^(ell)(0)=0 for 1<=ell<k, phi^(k)(0)<0, and sup_[-1,1]|phi^(k+1)|<infinity. Starting independently of the samples, use online spherical SGD X_tilde_t=X_(t-1)-(delta_N/N) grad_S L_N(X_(t-1);Y_t), X_t=X_tilde_t/||X_tilde_t||. Here alpha_N>0 and delta_N>0, and there are M_N=alpha_N*N fresh-sample updates (M_N integer). The initial law mu_N is uniform on the hemisphere {x in S^(N-1):x.theta_N>=0}. If k=1 assume alpha_N->0 and delta_N=O(1); if k=2 assume alpha_N/log N->0 and delta_N=O(1); if k>=3 assume alpha_N/N^(k-2)->0 and delta_N=O(alpha_N^(-1/2)). Then max_(0<=t<=M_N)|m_N(X_t)|->0 in probability and in L^p for every finite p>=1. Thus these subcritical fresh-sample online updates cannot weakly recover the teacher. For k>=3 the sample threshold is N^(k-1), while the matched known upper guarantee in this source has extra logarithms. The lower bound is for the stated algorithm and step regime; it is not an information-theoretic lower bound for all estimators or for data reuse.

body:
Let zeta(s) = sum_{n >= 1} n^{-s} for Re s > 1, continued meromorphically to the whole complex plane with a single simple pole at s = 1. Its zeros at the negative even integers are called trivial; all other zeros lie in the strip 0 < Re s < 1. The Riemann hypothesis asserts that every non-trivial zero has real part exactly 1/2. It is open (Riemann 1859). Equivalent forms: pi(x) = Li(x) + O(sqrt(x) log x) for the prime-counting function; and |sum_{n <= x} mu(n)| = O(x^{1/2 + epsilon}) for every epsilon > 0. The zeros have been verified numerically to lie on the critical line up to height 3 x 10^12 (Platt and Trudgian, 2021).
the hypothesis itself is a conjecture; the meromorphic continuation, the pole at s = 1, the trivial zeros, the location of the other zeros in the critical strip, the stated equivalences, and the numerical verification are theorems

body:
[Theorem 2 (The Cauchy stability of finite-energy  Einstein areal flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Consider one of the three Einstein--matter models in \autoref{theo-main-results} with $\Tbb^2$ symmetry on~$\Tbb^3$.
In the Einstein--Navier--Stokes case, assume that the model is admissible and torus-adapted, and that its matter stress tensor~$T_\chi$ obeys the coercive stress condition in \autoref{def-Tchi-coercive}.
In the Einstein--Euler case, we use the conventions $T_\chi=T_{\rm E}$, $\vNumb_\chi=\vNumb_\Jbb$, and $\zeta=0$.
Prescribe\footnote{Equivalently, prescribe a signed areal time~$t_0$ and initial data $(\mathring\Phi,\mathring\Psi,\mathring\zeta)$ for the \JKL{} formulation of the areal flow, together with the conformal modulus of one symmetry orbit.}
 an initial data set $(\mathring g,\mathring k,\mathring\Jbb,\mathring\zeta)$, consisting of a Riemannian metric, second fundamental form, fluid momentum, and relaxation field (absent for the Einstein--Euler model) satisfying Einstein's constraint equations and invariant under two commuting Killing fields $Y,Z$ with closed orbits, and assume that the orbit area constant and equal to $|t_0|\neq 0$.

Consider a regular Cauchy development $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ on $\Tbb^3\times[t_0,t_1]$ of these initial data for the chosen Einstein--Euler or Einstein--Navier--Stokes model in the areal foliation, with an areal time interval $I = [t_0,t_1] \subset \RR\setminus\{0\}$.
\bei
\item Assume that the initial spatial volume, the initial energy norm~$\mathcal E(t_0)$, and the bounded-variation norm of $\mathring\Psi=(\mathring\ell,\log\mathring\Omega,\mathring\Kpar)$ on~$\Tbb^3$ are bounded by a constant~$\mathcal I_0$.

\item In the future-contracting regime, assume that the conformal length has a positive lower bound $\mathcal L_{\min}$ on $I$; in the future-expanding regime, this lower bound is $\mathcal L_{\min}=\mathcal L(t_0)>0$, which is part of the initial data controlled by~$\mathcal I_0$.

\item Assume either that the fluid velocity is orthogonal to the symmetry orbits or, more generally, that the parallel momentum per particle is uniformly bounded in the sense that~\eqref{intro-parall-perpart-bounded} holds at $t=t_0$ for some constant $C^\parallel>0$.
\eei
Then the following Cauchy stability properties hold.

\begin{enumerate}

\item The parallel momentum per particle remains uniformly bounded at all times by~$C^\parallel$ in the sense that~\eqref{intro-parall-perpart-bounded} holds on $[t_0,t_1]\times\Tbb^3$.

\item There exists a constant
\be
C=C\bigl(\mathcal I_0,t_0,t_1,\mathcal L_{\min}^{-1},C^\parallel\bigr)
\ee
such that the $L^2$ norms of~$\Phi$ and bounded-variation norms of~$\Psi$ on areal time slices (constant~$t$) and on timelike slices orthogonal to the areal foliation (constant~$x$ in the \JKL{} formulation) are controlled as
\bel{equajKD93}
\aligned
& \sup_{t\in I}\bigl(
\|\Phi\|_{L^2(\Tbb^3,\dVtrois)}
+ \|\Psi\|_{\BV(\Tbb^3)}
\bigr)
\\
& + \sup_{x\in\Sbb^1}\bigl(
\|\Phi\|_{L^2(\Interval\times\Tbb^2,\dVundeux)}
+ \|\Psi\|_{\BV(\Interval\times\Tbb^2)}
\bigr)
+\int_{I\times\Tbb^3}\!\!\mathfrak d_*\,\dVuntrois
\leq C.
\endaligned
\ee
Here, $\dVuntrois,\dVtrois,\dVundeux$ are volume forms of the (Lorentzian) metric~$g$ and of (Riemannian) induced metrics on spatial and temporal slices.

\item The last term in \eqref{equajKD93} represents the total non-negative production measure and vanishes for the Einstein--Euler system.  For the particle-production Einstein--Navier--Stokes system it is the produced particle number density $\mathfrak d_*=\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}$, while for the dissipated-energy Einstein--Navier--Stokes system it is the dissipated mass-energy density $\mathfrak d_*=\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}/(-n_\alpha\beta^\alpha)$.

\item Moreover, these conclusions allow vacuum, arbitrarily large mass-energy density, and arbitrary finite rapidity. For the two Einstein--Navier--Stokes systems, the constant $C$ is independent of the relaxation rate map~$\mathscr B$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The Cauchy stability of finite-energy  Einstein areal flows

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let (X_{m,n})_{0<=m<n} be a doubly indexed family of random variables satisfying subadditivity X_{m,n} <= X_{m,k} + X_{k,n} for m<k<n, stationarity, that the joint law of (X_{m+1,n+1})_{m<n} equals that of (X_{m,n})_{m<n} under a measure-preserving shift, and integrability, E[X_{0,1}^+] < infinity together with a lower bound such as E[X_{0,n}] >= -cn preventing a trivially degenerate -infinity limit. Then X_{0,n}/n converges almost surely and in L^1 to a random variable X, equal to lim_n E[X_{0,n}]/n = inf_n E[X_{0,n}]/n, and X is almost surely constant if the underlying shift is ergodic rather than merely measure-preserving. This is the random, non-i.i.d. generalization of Fekete's lemma, which is its deterministic special case, and of the classical ergodic theorem, which is its additive special case, and it is the fundamental tool establishing existence of limiting growth rates in first-passage percolation (the time constant), longest increasing subsequence problems, and last-passage percolation, with the closely related Furstenberg-Kesten theorem giving Lyapunov exponents for random matrix products via an analogous but distinct subadditive argument. It does not give the value of the limit X, only its existence as an abstract limit or infimum, and does not by itself give a rate of convergence or determine whether X is almost surely constant unless ergodicity, not merely stationarity, of the shift has been separately established. Typical failure: Invoking Kingman's theorem to conclude the limiting growth rate is deterministic without separately verifying ergodicity of the underlying probability-preserving transformation, checking only stationarity; stationarity alone gives convergence to a possibly random limit X that can be a genuine mixture over ergodic components, so asserting a single deterministic time constant or growth rate without checking ergodicity is a common gap, especially in models built from a mixture of environments. Canonical reference: Kingman, 1968, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B; Kingman, 1973, Annals of Probability; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM.

Let n,m be positive integers with m<=n, and [n]={1,...,n}. For b in {0,1}^n define S0={i:b_i=1}. Independently sample Y1 uniformly from [n]^m, and put S1=Unique(Y1), A=S0\S1 and B=S1\S0. If |A|>=|B|, choose a uniform random injection sigma:B->A and replace each occurrence of a in B by sigma(a). Otherwise choose a uniform random injection tau:A->B and replace each occurrence of tau(a) by a. Call the resulting string Y. All injection choices use fresh private randomness conditional on b,Y1. If b is uniform on {0,1}^n, then Y is exactly uniform on [n]^m. For every b,Y1 and every permitted injection, |S0 symmetric_difference Unique(Y)|=abs(|S0|-|S1|). Thus the coupling has a uniform binary-vector marginal and a uniform length-m string marginal; independence of these two marginals is not asserted.
Positive integers1<=m<=n. Uniform binary b and independent uniform Y1 for the uniformity conclusion.

Let A_1, ..., A_m be events, N the number that occur, 1 <= k <= m, and S_r = sum over r-element I of P(intersection of A_i, i in I), with S_r = 0 for r > m. If S_k > 0, then P(N >= k) >= S_k^2 / sum_{j=0}^k c(k, j) S_{2k - j}, with c(k, j) = (2k - j)!/(j! ((k - j)!)^2). The denominator is also the sum, over ordered pairs (I, J) of k-element sets, of P(intersection of A_i, i in I or J). For k = 1 this is the Chung-Erdős inequality. No independence is assumed.

Initially every neuron is positive-output A (x1-only), positive-output C (both-active), or strictly dead with arbitrary output. At least one A and one C are present, and no B (x2-only) is present. Then a global absolutely continuous flow exists, and every such flow enters strict B at a finite time and subsequently reaches the global normalized margin sqrt17/16 with convergent normalized parameter direction. The reflected statement exchanges x1 and x2 and reverses u. These are scale-invariant sufficient subcones, not entire activation-pattern labels.

## 1. Continuation and the invariant until B appears
Claim017 section1 constructs global absolutely continuous flows for positive-live networks, without requiring both permanent seeds for that construction. Its bounded-norm-on-bounded-time argument and its null-boundary-level-set argument apply here unchanged. Claim019 gives E>0 and u<=0 up to the first strict B entry; positive A stays A, dead neurons stay dead, and C cannot enter A. All live outputs increase. The invariant v^2-||w||^2 is constant, so each C retains v>=||w||. These statements hold along every global absolutely continuous continuation; uniqueness at grazing contacts is not required.

We prove finite B entry by contradiction. Suppose no strict B entry ever occurs. Then all original C neurons remain in the closed C cone forever, their boundary contacts have measure zero, and the C equations hold almost everywhere. In particular v(t)>=v(0)>0. Put a=||x1||=sqrt17/4, c=x1.x2=-15/16, ai=-ell_prime(fi)>0, Ii(t)=integral_0^t ai(s) ds, and T=I1+I2. Since E>0, a1<=a2 and I1<=I2.

For total parameter squared norm N, Ndot<=2a(a1+a2)N. If T were bounded on infinite physical time, N and both predictions would be bounded; exponential and logistic ai would then remain bounded below by a positive constant. This contradicts bounded T. Hence T tends to infinity and I2>=T/2 tends to infinity.

## 2. A dissipative weighted variable for C
For one C neuron set q1=(w.x1)/a>=0 and s=v+q1. Then v<=s<=2v because 0<=q1<=||w||<=v. The C cone estimate from claim016 gives z2=w.x2<=2||w||/sqrt17<=2v/sqrt17. Almost everywhere the exact C equations yield

 sdot=a*a1*s+a2*(z2+(c/a)*v)
      <=a*a1*s-(7/(4sqrt17))*a2*v
      <=(a*a1-b*a2)*s,  b=7/(8sqrt17)>0.

Here c/a=-15/(4sqrt17); no approximation enters these constants. Gronwall implies

Since n=v^2+||w||^2<=2v^2<=2s^2, summing over C gives

## 3. The clock contradiction
For the permanent A sector, its exact hyperbolic solution gives

Consequently H_A>=H_A(0) exp(2a I1), so

If I1 were bounded, the bound for N_C would force N_C->0, contradicting v_j(t)>=v_j(0)>0 for any C neuron. Thus I1->infinity and H_A->infinity. Only C contributes to point2, and its cone estimate gives f2<=N_C/sqrt17. Since f1>=H_A, this implies

For exponential loss a1/a2=exp(-E)->0. For logistic loss, f2>=0 implies a1/a2<=2exp(-E)->0. For every epsilon>0 there is t_epsilon after which a1<=epsilon*a2; integrating and using I2->infinity gives limsup I1/I2<=epsilon. Hence I1/I2->0. It follows that a I1-b I2->-infinity. The bound in section2 now forces every C s_j(t)->0, again contradicting s_j>=v_j>=v_j(0)>0. Therefore the assumption of no finite strict B entry is impossible.

## 4. Global-margin consequence and limits
Take a finite time after the first strict B entry, away from the null boundary contact sets. There is a permanent positive A seed and a permanent positive B seed; all other live outputs are positive. Apply claim017 from that state. Its conclusion is normalized margin sqrt17/16 and convergence of the normalized parameter direction along every global absolutely continuous continuation. Reflection proves the symmetric theorem. Common rescaling of every initial parameter by any sigma>0 preserves all hypotheses, including E>0; thus the result applies at sigma=1e-6.

This is a subcone result and does not classify every initial A/C pattern. It changes no whole-orbit labels: the remaining unknown count stays2713. ## 5. Exact Gaussian mass of the sufficient subcone
Assume all coordinates are independent N(0,sigma^2). Put p=atan(1/4)/pi, q=1/4-p/2. A+ has probability q; strict dead with arbitrary output has probability p. For C require the strict version u<0 and v>||w||. The proofs decompose the sphere into compressible vectors (close to sparse - handled by nets and tensorization) and incompressible vectors (reduced to distance-to-subspace and small-ball estimates via the Berry-Esseen or Littlewood-Offord theory of anti-concentration).

body:
Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT stacking pool (23 members, 285 outputs, the per-sample relative metric; PLACEHOLDER_CELLS). The error covariance of the members is rank-deficient in practice: $\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$ of $10^{6}$ to $10^{17}$, three to five eigenvalues below $0.05\,\sigma^2$ (members that are near-linear combinations of one another). Inside the long-only minimum-variance stack, eight cleaners of that covariance were compared on the same cells, the same split and the same small-calibration draws: the raw sample covariance, the $\eta$-regularised rotationally invariant estimator with floors $0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0\,\sigma^2$, Ledoit-Wolf 2004 linear shrinkage, Ledoit-Wolf 2020 analytical nonlinear shrinkage and Lam's NERCOME. Result: raw, RIE without floor, LW2020 and NERCOME tie - PLACEHOLDER_TIE - at full calibration ($n = 932$) and in the $n = 60/120/240$ arms; the floor $0.05\,\sigma^2$ is marginally negative, floors $0.2$ and $1.0$ lose PLACEHOLDER_FLOORS, linear shrinkage loses PLACEHOLDER_LW2004, and the sum-to-one (unconstrained-sign) forms of the same cleaners lose PLACEHOLDER_S1. Mechanism (seed 101, medians over outputs): the constraint keeps 7-11 of 23 members; the condition number falls from $10^{6}$-$10^{17}$ on the full covariance to $4\times10^{2}$-$3\times10^{4}$ on the active principal submatrix; eigenvalues under the floor fall from 3-5 to 0-1; the active sets of raw, RIE and LW2020 overlap at Jaccard 0.86-0.90 (0.80-0.83 at $n = 60$). By the active-set lemma the weights depend on the covariance only through $S_{AA}$, which is well conditioned, and there every consistent cleaner is close to the identity; a floor or a linear shrinkage lifts the small eigenvalues of the full matrix before the constraint acts and distorts $w_A$. The reading of the whole program: random-matrix theory identifies what to clean (the error covariance, in the reported metric, with an intercept) and why the plug-in fails (the near-null directions of a collinear ensemble); the fix that survives the population is the long-only constraint, itself a data-determined covariance shrinkage, and the spectral cleaners are interchangeable inside it. The pre-registered contrary hypothesis - that the floor was a kernel-bandwidth artefact which LW2020's theory-fixed bandwidth would remove - was refuted on its first cell: consistent estimators correctly keep the tiny eigenvalues, because in the population they are tiny.
the pool protocol: members fitted on training data, the test rows split 40/60 into calibration and evaluation with a fixed permutation, metric = mean per-sample relative L2
the small-calibration arms subsample the calibration rows only; evaluation rows are never touched

\end{enumerate}

Let f be 2pi-periodic and let sigma_N(f) denote the Cesaro mean (1/(N+1)) sum_{n=0}^{N} S_n(f) of the partial sums of its Fourier series. (i) If f is continuous then sigma_N(f) converges to f UNIFORMLY. (ii) If f is in L^p for some p in [1, infinity) then sigma_N(f) converges to f in L^p norm. (iii) (Fejer-Lebesgue) If f is in L^1 then sigma_N(f)(x) converges to f(x) at every Lebesgue point of f, hence almost everywhere. This is the classical repair of the fact that the partial sums S_N themselves need NOT converge pointwise for a merely continuous f.
Periodicity;
the Cesaro means, not the partial sums.
Nonnegativity of the Fejer kernel is the property the Dirichlet kernel lacks and is exactly what makes all three conclusions work.

body: [Theorem 3 of arXiv:2511.18562, 'Ensuring Calibration Robustness in Split Conformal Prediction Under Adversarial Attacks'] Assume that the predictive distribution $f$ assigns probability mass uniformly across all incorrect classes, while allocating the remaining probability to the true class. Let $P_{y,\text{true}}$ be the predictive probability for the true label. Split CP gives the prediction set by $C(x_{n+1})=\{y\in\{1,2,\dots,K\}:f_{y}(x_{n+1})\geq Q\}$ as mentioned in Section 3.1. The event stands for the number of classes contained in the prediction set given by the cardinality of $C(x_{n+1})$ given by: $\displaystyle|C(x_{test})|=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbbm{1}\left(f_{y}(x_{test})\geq 1-Q\right).$ The expectation of the prediction set size can be bounded by: $\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(|C(x_{test})|)\leq 1-\alpha\pm h(\epsilon_{cal},\epsilon_{test})$ $\displaystyle+(K-1)\left(1-\frac{1-Q}{1-P_{y,true}}\right)^{K-2}.$ As in the supporting evidence in Example 1, when adversarial training increases the prediction accuracy in the presence of $\ell_{\infty}$ test-time attacks, the following holds $\frac{1-Q^{\mathrm{adv}}}{\,1-P_{y,\mathrm{true}}^{\mathrm{adv}}\,}\;<\;\frac{1-Q^{\mathrm{clean}}}{\,1-P_{y,\mathrm{true}}^{\mathrm{clean}}\,},$ where $Q^{\mathrm{adv}}$ and $Q^{\mathrm{clean}}$ are the $(1-\alpha)$ -quantiles of the HPS score on the calibration set for adversarially trained and cleanly trained models, respectively, and $P_{y,\mathrm{true}}^{\mathrm{adv}}$ and $P_{y,\mathrm{true}}^{\mathrm{clean}}$ denote the corresponding true-label probabilities. Since the upper bound on the expected set size, $(K-1)\!\left(1-\frac{1-Q}{1-P_{y,\mathrm{true}}}\right)^{K-2}$, is increasing in $\frac{1-Q}{1-P_{y,\mathrm{true}}}$, the adversarially trained model yields a smaller expected prediction-set size than the cleanly trained model.

[Lemma lem:unif_par_comp_strat of arXiv:2607.04514, 'Boundary-layer asymptotics for Gaussian-smoothed singular measures'] Assume (ass:standing of the paper)~(ass:standing:chart of the paper). There are an open set \(\Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\subset\mathbb
  R^{m-c}\) and numbers \(R>0\), \(\delta_0>0\) such that
  \begin{equation*}
    \Theta_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}}\subset \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} \Subset\Theta_{\mathrm{out}},
    \qquad \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} + \mathbb B_{4R}^{m-c} \subset \Theta_{\rm out}
  \end{equation*}
  and the mapping
  \begin{equation*}
    M: \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} \times (\mathbb H_c^m\cap \mathbb B_{4R}^m)
    \to \mathcal{M},\qquad (\theta,\xi)\mapsto \Phi(\theta+\xi_{\mathcal S},\xi_{\mathcal C})
  \end{equation*}
  is well defined and of class \(C^{r+1}\). In addition, if we set
  \begin{equation*}
    \varphi(\theta)=\Phi(\theta,0), \qquad \mathbf{Q}(\theta)=\mathbf{Q}(\varphi(\theta)),
    \qquad \mathbf{L}(\theta)=\mathbf{L}(\varphi(\theta)),
  \end{equation*}
  and define \(\Delta: \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} \times (\mathbb H_c^m\cap \mathbb B_{4R}^m) \to
  \mathbb R^d = \mathbb R^{m-c}\times\mathbb R^c\times\mathbb R^k\) by
  \begin{equation}
    \Delta(\theta,\xi) = \mathbf{Q}(\theta)^\top\bigl(M(\theta,\xi)-\varphi(\theta) \bigr)
  \end{equation}
  then the following properties hold.

  \begin{enumerate}
    \item 
    The map
    \[
      \Delta:\Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\times
      (\mathbb H_c^m\cap\mathbb B_{4R}^m)\to\mathbb R^d
    \]
    is \(C^r\). Moreover, all mixed derivatives
    \[
      \partial_\theta^\beta\partial_\xi^\gamma M(\theta,\xi)
    \]
    with \(|\beta|+|\gamma|\leqslant r+1\), and all mixed derivatives
    \[
      \partial_\theta^\beta\partial_\xi^\gamma \Delta(\theta,\xi)
    \]
    with \(|\beta|+|\gamma|\leqslant r\), are uniformly bounded on
    \[
      \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\times
      (\mathbb H_c^m\cap\mathbb B_{4R}^m).
    \]
    In addition, \(\Delta\) has the following anisotropic regularity: whenever
    \(|\gamma|\geqslant1\) and \(|\beta|+|\gamma|\leqslant r+1\), the derivative
    \[
      \partial_\theta^\beta\partial_\xi^\gamma\Delta(\theta,\xi)
    \]
    exists and is uniformly bounded on the same set.

    \item  At \(\xi=0\), one has
    \begin{equation*}
      M(\theta,0_m)=\varphi(\theta), \qquad \Delta(\theta,0_m) = 0_d,
      \qquad \mathrm{D}_\xi \Delta(\theta, 0)=[\,\mathbf{L}(\theta);\ \mathbf 0_{k\times m}\,].
    \end{equation*}

    \item  For each \(\theta\in\Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\), the map \( M(\theta,\cdot): \mathbb
    H_c^m\cap\mathbb B_{4R}^m \to\mathcal{M}\) is a \(C^{r+1}\) corner chart onto a relatively open
    neighborhood of \(\varphi(\theta)\) in \(\mathcal{M}\).

    \item  For \(\theta\in\Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}}\), define \(J(\theta,\xi) = \det
    \bigl(\mathrm{D}_\xi \Delta (\theta,\xi)^\top \mathrm{D}_\xi\Delta(\theta,\xi) \bigr)^{1/2}\). Then \(J\)
    is jointly \(C^{r}\) in \((\theta,\xi)\), all mixed derivatives
    \begin{equation*}
      \partial_\theta^\beta\partial_\xi^\gamma J(\theta,\xi), \qquad |\beta|+|\gamma|\leqslant r,
    \end{equation*}
    are uniformly bounded on \( \Theta^\circ_{\mathrm{out}} \times (\mathbb H_c^m\cap\mathbb
    B_{4R}^m)\), and \( J(\theta, 0)=|\det\mathbf{L}(\theta)|\).

    \item  For every \(x=\varphi(\theta)\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}\), \(\mathcal{M}\cap \mathbb
    B_{2\delta_0}(x)\subset M\bigl(\theta, \mathbb H_c^m\cap \mathbb B_{R}^m\bigr)\).
  \end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition 9 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The language $G$ admits a well-defined decomposition into primitive languages:
\begin{align*}
  G = \Big[\Big(\C_1^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_1^{\geqslant 1}\Big).\C_1
    \cup \C_1^{\geqslant0} \Big]
  \circ \cdots \circ
  \Big[
    \Big(\C_m^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_m^{\geqslant 1}\Big).\C_m
    \cup \C_m^{\geqslant0} \Big].
\end{align*}
Its exponential generating function is hence
\[
  \hat\phi_G(z) = \left[ (1-p) \left( e^{z/m} - 1 \right) + 1 \right]^m.
\]
\begin{proof}
  It holds for all $i$ that
  \begin{align*}
    \hat\phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}}(z)
    
    &= e^{z/m} - e^{(1-p)z/m}\\
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty
        \frac{(z/m)^n - ((1-p)z/m)^n}{n!},\\
    \phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}}(z)
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty 
        (z/m)^n - ((1-p)z/m)^n.
  \end{align*}
  Then we multiply by $\phi_{\C_i}(z) = \left(1-p\right)z\,m^{-1}$,
  \begin{align*}
    \phi_{\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}\right).\C_i}(z)
    &= \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left[
      \left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^n - \left(\frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m}\right)^n
      \right]\\
    &= (1-p)\sum_{n=1}^\infty
        (z/m)^{n}
      - \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      ((1-p)\,z/m)^{n},\\
    \hat\phi_{\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}\right).\C_i}(z)
    &= (1-p)\sum_{n=1}^\infty
        \frac{(z/m)^{n}}{n!}
      - \sum_{n=1}^\infty
        \frac{((1-p)z/m)^{n}}{n!}\\
    &= (1-p)\left(e^{z/m} - 1\right)
    - e^{(1-p)z/m} + 1.
  \end{align*}
  Finally add $\hat\phi_{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z)
  = e^{(1-p)z/m}$ to achieve
  \begin{align*}
    \hat\phi_{
      {\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}\right).\C_i}
      \cup {\C_i}
    }(z)
    &= (1-p) \left( e^{z/m} - 1 \right) + 1,\\
    \hat\phi_G(z)
    &= \left[(1-p) \left( e^{z/m} - 1 \right) + 1\right]^m. \qedhere
  \end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] Let $ G$ be a finitely generated group with a finite generating set $S$. Then $ G$ is $ \delta$-\textbf{hyperbolic} with respect to $S$, if for any geodesic triangle in the Cayley graph of $G$, any side is contained in the union of the $ \delta$-neighborhoods of the other two sides. We say that $ G$ is \textbf{hyperbolic} if $G$ is $\delta$-hyperbolic with respect to a finite generating set $S$, for some $ \delta\geq 0$.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:ccbef96bfb7a85e6c317e46ffd3c62de6d3b2616fb7a25e8aa9f192a62260b43","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/cc/ccbef96bfb7a85e6c317e46ffd3c62de6d3b2616fb7a25e8aa9f192a62260b43.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:91acd56335975a932539f4073e0edfa8458a1eb6dee249a431112ed253e3e53b","bundle_entry_key":"antisymmetric-variance-trace","bundle_id":"population.probability-critical-moments-two-end-kernels-and-dependence-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-1000-20h-20260906/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.markov:known-antisymmetric-perturbation-reversibilization-trace-monotonicity","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# P0249: reversibilization trace inequality ? known-result consequence

Status: author-checked complete argument for a historical conjecture. A later primary theorem implies the result, so this entry is excluded from the current-open target and original-solution count. The direct matrix proof is not independently reviewed here.

Source question: Aldous?Fill, Conjecture 9.22, PDF pages 327?329, asks whether $\operatorname{tr}[Z^2(P^*-P)]\ge0$. Here $P$ is an irreducible finite-state transition matrix, $P^*$ its adjoint in $L^2(\pi)$, and $Z$ the centered fundamental matrix. The centered convention is $Z1=0$ and $Z=(I-P)^{-1}$ on $L^2_0(\pi)$. Adding the constant projection to $Z$ would not change the displayed product.

## Direct matrix proof

Restrict all operators to the finite-dimensional real Hilbert space $L^2_0(\pi)$. Put

$$A=I-P=H+K,\quad H=\frac{A+A^*}{2},\quad K=\frac{A-A^*}{2}.$$

The reversible Dirichlet form shows $H$ is positive definite: its only zero-energy functions on the full space are constants, because the underlying undirected chain is connected. Also $K^*=-K$ and $P^*-P=2K$.

Let $Q=H^{-1/2}KH^{-1/2}$, $B=-Q^2=Q^*Q\succeq0$, and define $F(t)=\operatorname{tr}(H+tK)^{-1}$ for real $t$. All these inverses exist since their symmetric part is positive definite. Using transpose invariance of trace and averaging the inverses with $t$ and $-t$ gives

$$F(t)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H^{-1}(I+t^2B)^{-1}\right].$$

Indeed $(I+tQ)^{-1}+(I-tQ)^{-1}=2(I-t^2Q^2)^{-1}$. Differentiate the last trace formula:

$$F'(t)=-2t\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H^{-1}B(I+t^2B)^{-2}\right]\le0\qquad(t\ge0).$$

The product inside the trace need not be symmetric. Its trace is nonnegative because $C=B(I+t^2B)^{-2}$ is positive semidefinite and $\operatorname{tr}(H^{-1}C)=\operatorname{tr}(C^{1/2}H^{-1}C^{1/2})\ge0$. This explicitly avoids an invalid commuting assumption.

Differentiating the original inverse instead gives $F'(1)=-\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}KA^{-1})=-\operatorname{tr}(A^{-2}K)$. Consequently

$$\operatorname{tr}[Z^2(P^*-P)]=-2F'(1)=4\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H^{-1}B(I+B)^{-2}\right]\ge0.$$

In fact equality holds if and only if $B=0$, equivalently $K=0$, equivalently the original chain is reversible. This follows from positive definiteness of $H^{-1}$ and the fact that the positive eigenvalues of $B$ remain positive under $b\mapsto b/(1+b)^2$.

## Independent route through established literature

Huang and Mao, *Variational formulas of asymptotic variance for general discrete-time Markov chains*, arXiv:2012.13895 (December 27, 2020), Theorem 4.3 on PDF page 14, proves that the asymptotic variance for a reversible kernel plus an antisymmetric perturbation is even in the perturbation parameter and decreases with its absolute value. Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.13895 . This is a stronger observable-by-observable statement than the required trace monotonicity.

For finite irreducible chains, first add one-half holding: $R=(I+P)/2$. Every convex mixture of $R$ and $R^*$ is irreducible and aperiodic, so the theorem's spectral-radius assumption on the mean-zero space is satisfied. Apply it to $R_t=(R+R^*)/2+t(R-R^*)/2$, for $-1\le t\le1$.

For an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ of $L^2_0(\pi)$, the Poisson-equation formula reads

$$\sum_j\widetilde\sigma^2(R_t,e_j)=2\operatorname{tr}(I-R_t)^{-1}-(n-1).$$

Theorem 4.3 therefore gives the same trace monotonicity. Differentiate from the left at $t=1$; analyticity identifies this with the full derivative and yields the conjectured inequality for $R$. Since $Z_R=2Z_P$ and $R^*-R=(P^*-P)/2$, its trace expression is twice that for $P$. The conclusion follows even if $P$ is periodic. The original series definition of $Z$ in the periodic case is interpreted through the centered inverse or Abel limit.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The conjectured dominating pair for DP-SGD with shuffled batches is not dominating (2026), gives a counterexample to Conjecture 3.2 of Chua, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar, Manurangsi, Sinha and Zhang, How private are DP-SGD implementations? (ICML 2024, arXiv:2403.17673), which says that the Gaussian mixtures P_S = (1/T) sum_t N(2 e_t, sigma^2 I) and Q_S = (1/T) sum_t N(e_t, sigma^2 I) tightly dominate the adaptive batch linear query mechanism with shuffled batches for every adaptive query method. The conjecture fails for every number of steps T >= 2 and every batch size: a query method that answers like the conjectured worst case at every step but the last, and changes the last query when the earlier outputs suggest that the differing record sat in an early batch, has a larger hockey-stick divergence. At T = 2, sigma = 1, eps = 1/2 it reaches 0.22323 against 0.22127 for the pair, and an Arb interval certificate bounds the excess below by 1.04e-4; the same switch also beats the pair in KL divergence and in Renyi divergence of every order tested, from 1/4 to 5. Exact accounting for shuffled batches remains open. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/shuffled-ablq-dominating-pair (commit 7ac96a5055fb). Not refereed.
title: The conjectured dominating pair for DP-SGD with shuffled batches is not dominating, refuting Conjecture 3.2 of Chua et al. (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/shuffled-ablq-dominating-pair)

[Theorem Calderon's theorem of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] [Calderón's interpolation theorem c.f. [Calderon1964]] 
    Let $(E_0, E_1)$ and $(F_0, F_1)$ be Banach couples. Consider a linear map
    $T: E_0 + E_1 \to F_0 + F_1$ such that
    \[
    \|T\|_{E_0 \to F_0} \leq M_0, \qquad \|T\|_{E_1 \to F_1} \leq M_1.
    \]
    Then for every $0 \leq \theta \leq 1$, $T:[E_0, E_1]_\theta \to [F_0, F_1]_\theta$ is bounded with
    \[
    \|T\|_{[E_0, E_1]_\theta \to [F_0, F_1]_\theta} \leq M_0^{1-\theta} M_1^\theta.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let L>=1 be an integer, A a real d_L by d_0 matrix of rank r, and let the prescribed intermediate dimensions d_1,...,d_(L-1) all be at least r. Among real compatible factors A=W_L ... W_1, the minimum of sum_(ell=1)^L ||W_ell||_F^2 equals L sum_(i=1)^r s_i(A)^(2/L). Empty sums are zero. If an intermediate dimension is smaller than r, no such factorization exists. In particular, for every compatible collection of real matrices, L sum_i s_i(W_L ... W_1)^(2/L)<=sum_ell ||W_ell||_F^2. For L>2 the exponent 2/L is below one: this is a Schatten quasi-norm power, not an application restricted to norm exponents >=1. Biases and nonlinear activations are absent from this matrix identity.

Let A be a positive self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H, with form domain Q(A) = D(A^{1/2}) and form q_A(x, y) = ⟨A^{1/2}x, A^{1/2}y⟩. Let β be a Hermitian sesquilinear form with D(β) ⊃ Q(A) satisfying |β(x, x)| ≤ a q_A(x, x) + b‖x‖² for all x ∈ Q(A), with 0 ≤ a < 1 and b ≥ 0. Then there is a unique self-adjoint operator C, written C = A ∔ β (the form sum), with form domain Q(C) = Q(A) and ⟨Cx, y⟩ = q_A(x, y) + β(x, y) for x ∈ D(C), y ∈ Q(A). C is bounded below by −b, and any subspace that is a form core for A (dense in Q(A) in the form norm) is a form core for C. The same holds with A bounded below instead of positive, after shifting. Typical use: −Δ + V on ℝ³ with V = V_+ − V_- where V_- is only form-bounded (e.g. V ∈ L^{3/2}(ℝ³) + L^∞(ℝ³) is −Δ-form-bounded with bound 0 by the Sobolev inequality), defining a self-adjoint Hamiltonian although V need not be operator-bounded and D(C) need not contain or be contained in D(−Δ).

body: [Definition 1 (Function-preserving transform) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] An invertible $T\in GL(d_{\mathrm{in}})$ is \emph{function-preserving} for the layer $Y=XW^\top$ if replacing $(W,X)\mapsto(WT^{-1},\,XT^\top)$ leaves the output unchanged: $(XT^\top)(WT^{-1})^\top=XW^\top$. The weight side $WT^{-1}$ is computed offline; the activation side $XT^\top$ must be produced at inference unless it can be \emph{absorbed} (\Cref{sec:live}).  More generally we call a map function-preserving when its action on one operand is undone exactly by a compensating offline change to the adjacent static weights or bias, by an invariance of the following operation, or by an inverse applied downstream; the linear input-axis case above is the one \Cref{sec:inversion} is stated for, and the other variants are named as such where they appear.
title: Function-preserving transform

[Definition 28 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Given a configuration $\boldsymbol{\ell} \in \W_\N$ in a discrete ensemble of Section~\ref{Section_general_model}, the \emph{empirical measure} is the $H$-tuple of nonnegative atomic measures $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\N} = (\mu_{\N,h})_{h = 1}^{H}$ given by
\[
\forall h \in [H] \qquad \mu_{\N,h} = \frac{1}{\N} \sum_{i = 1}^{N_h} \delta_{\N^{-1}\ell_i^h}.
\]
This tuple $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\N}$ is equivalently specified by the measure $\mu_{\N} = \sum_{h = 1}^{H} \mu_{\N,h} = \frac{1}{\N} \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \delta_{\N^{-1}\ell_i}$. The empirical resolvent is the tuple $\boldsymbol{G}(z) = (G_h(z))_{h = 1}^{H}$ defined for any $h \in [H]$ and $z \in\amsmathbb{C} \setminus [\hat{a}_h,\hat{b}_h]$ by
\begin{equation}
 G_h(z) = \sum_{i = 1}^{N_h} \frac{1}{z - \frac{\ell_i^h}{\N}} = \N \int_{\hat{a}_h}^{\hat{b}_h} \frac{\dd \mu_{\N,h}(x)}{z - x} = \N \Gm_{\mu_{\N,h}}(z).
\end{equation}
It is a holomorphic function of $z$ in this domain, such that for any $h \in [H]$, we have $G_h(z) \sim \frac{N_h}{z}$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$.

We sometimes recenter the empirical measure by subtracting the equilibrium measure $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and introduce $\Delta \boldsymbol{G}(z) = \boldsymbol{G}(z) - \N \Gm_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(z)$. In other words, for any $h \in [H]$ and $z \in \amsmathbb{C} \setminus \amsmathbb{A}_h^{\mathfrak{m}}]$ we have
\[
\Delta G_h(z) = G_h(z) - \N\Gm_{\mu_h}(z).
\]

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, then the $\delta$-càdlàg modulus of continuity of any function $f \in \mathbb{D}([0,T],(X,d))$ is

[Proposition prop:comparison of arXiv:2503.21737, 'High-intensity Voronoi percolation on manifolds'] Assume that all sectional curvatures of \(M\) lie in \([-K,K]\) for some \(K>0\) and that \(r_\text{inj}(M) > 0\).
    Then for all $\delta>0$, there exists an $r_0=r_0(\delta)$ such that for all $r\geq r_0$ there exists a $\lambda_0 = \lambda_0(r,\delta)$ such that for all $\lambda\geq \lambda_0$ and $x_0\in M$ we can find a coupling \((\xi, \eta)\) of Poisson point processes
    \begin{equation}
        \xi\sim \mathrm{PPP}(\lambda\cdot dx, \mathbb R^d) \quad \text{and} \quad \eta \sim \mathrm{PPP}(\lambda\cdot \mu_M, M),
    \end{equation}
    and a chart \(\varphi \in \pazocal{E} (x_0,r\lambda^{-1/d})\) so that the following holds with probability at least \(1-\delta\):
    \begin{enumerate}[(1)]
        \item  $ \pazocal G_{\mathbb R^d}(\xi)|_S = \varphi_*\pazocal G_{M}(\eta), \quad \text{where } S=B_{\mathbb R^d}\big(0, r\lambda^{-1/d}\big)$,
        \item  if a cell \(C(x;\xi)\), \(x\in\xi\), intersects \(S\), then \(\diam_{\mathbb R^d}(C(x;\xi)) \leq r\lambda^{-1/d}/100\),
        \item  if a cell \(C(x;\eta)\), \(x\in\eta\), intersects \(\varphi^{-1}(S) = B_M\big(x_0,r\lambda^{-1/d}\big)\), then \(\diam_{M}(C(x;\eta)) \leq r\lambda^{-1/d}/100\).
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

The teacher is sigma(u dot X), the student is integral sigma(w dot X)rho(dw) on the unit sphere, and all outer coefficients are fixed at +1. The initial law and entropy reference are uniform. R is the squared population risk without factor 1/2, and MFLD is partial_t rho=div_S(rho grad_S(delta R/delta rho))+lambda(t)Delta_S rho. For a single unit teacher on Gaussian population inputs, fixed positive outer coefficients, and uniform sphere initialization in every d>=2, population MFLD reaches risk <=8eps/9. Owner draft: independently checked proof (C012 v1). Let S be a nondegenerate d-simplex, d>=1, m=d+1. Unif(S) is n-CM exactly for every n>=d+1. For n>=m, vectors v_i in C^m with components m^(-1/2)exp(2*pi*i*k*i_index/n), k=0,...,m-1 and i_index=0,...,n-1, satisfy sum_i v_i v_i^*=(n/m)I. For one Haar unitary U, Haar-unitary squared moduli are Dirichlet(1,...,1). The barycentric vectors lambda_(i,j)=|(Uv_i)_j|^2 are therefore uniform on the simplex and obey sum_i lambda_(i,j)=n/m exactly. Mapping to the simplex vertices gives identical uniform marginals and sum n*centroid. For n<=d, a barycentric coordinate near one exceeds the required sum n/(d+1), proving impossibility. This handles nonmultiple orders missed by ordinary cyclic barycentric coupling. Novelty UNKNOWN.

[Lemma 162 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider a uniformly random tiling of $A\times B\times C$ hexagon. Using the notations \eqref{eq_N_hexagon} and \eqref{eq_L_hexagon}, the $N$ horizontal lozenges on the vertical section at distance $\mathfrak{t}$ from the left border with coordinates $1\leq \ell_1<\ell_2<\dots<\ell_N\leq L$ have probability distribution
\begin{equation}

 \amsmathbb P_N(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_N)=\frac{1}{\mathscr{Z}_N} \cdot \prod_{1 \leq i<j \leq N} (\ell_j-\ell_i)^2 \cdot \prod_{i=1}^N w(\ell_i),
\end{equation}
with the weight
\begin{equation}

w(\ell)=
 \left\{\begin{array}{lll}
  (\ell)_{C-\mathfrak{t}}\cdot (A+\mathfrak{t}+1-\ell)_{B-\mathfrak{t}}&& \textnormal{if}\,\,0 < \mathfrak{t}\leq \min(B,C),\\
  (\ell)_{C-\mathfrak{t}}\cdot (A+B+1-\ell)_{\mathfrak{t}-B} && \textnormal{if}\,\,B\leq \mathfrak{t}\leq C,\\
  (\ell)_{\mathfrak{t}-C}\cdot (A+C+1-\ell)_{B-\mathfrak{t}}&& \textnormal{if}\,\,C\leq \mathfrak{t}\leq B,\\
  (\ell)_{t-C}\cdot (A+B+C+1-\mathfrak{t}-\ell)_{\mathfrak{t}-B} && \textnormal{if}\,\, \max(B,C)\leq \mathfrak{t} < B+C,\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
where $(a)_n$ is the Pochhammer symbol,
\[
(a)_n=a(a+1)\cdots (a+n-1)=\frac{\Gamma(a+n)}{\Gamma(a)},
\]
and $\mathscr{Z}_N$ is a normalizing
constant.

body:
Let X and Y be normed spaces over R or C. A linear map T: X -> Y is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball B_X = {x : ||x|| <= 1} is relatively compact in Y, i.e. its closure in Y is compact. Equivalent forms: (i) for every bounded sequence (x_n) in X the sequence (T x_n) has a subsequence that converges in Y; (ii) when Y is a Banach space, T(B_X) is totally bounded. Every compact operator is bounded, and every bounded operator of finite rank is compact. The set of compact operators X -> Y is written K(X,Y), and K(X) = K(X,X). The identity operator of X is compact if and only if X is finite-dimensional (Riesz's lemma). Terminology warning: older texts say 'completely continuous' for compact; in current usage 'completely continuous' means 'maps weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent sequences', which is implied by compactness but is weaker in general (it is equivalent to compactness when X is reflexive).

body: For coprime integers a and q there are infinitely many primes congruent to a mod q; the primes are equidistributed among the phi(q) admissible residue classes in the sense of Dirichlet density and, by the Siegel-Walfisz refinement, in natural density. The proof works with log L(s, chi) for all characters mod q, using orthogonality of characters to isolate the progression and nonvanishing of L(1, chi) to force divergence.
title: Dirichlet's Theorem on Primes in Arithmetic Progressions

body:
[Theorem T:half-space-full-tails of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For $n, m\in \mathbb{N}$ and any $\alpha>0$, let
$$
\Delta_\alpha(n) = \mu_\alpha(n) - \mu(n)
$$
be the gap in the limit shape on the diagonal, and
$$
\nu_\alpha(n, m) = \mu(n, m) +  \Delta_\alpha(m).
$$
Fix $\alpha_0>0$, and take any $\alpha \ge \alpha_0$.
Then there exists a constant $c> 0$ depending only on $\alpha_0$, such that for all $v + (1, 1), v + (n, m) \in \mathbb{Z}^2_\ge$ with $n/m \in [\alpha_0, \alpha_0^{-1}]$ and all $\epsilon \in (0, m^{-1/3}]$ we have
\begin{align}

	\mathbb{P}\Big(X_\alpha(v + (1, 1); v + (n, m)) \ge \nu_\alpha(n, m) + \epsilon n\Big) &\le 2\exp\left(-c \epsilon^{3/2}n \left(1 \wedge \frac{\epsilon^{1/2}}{(1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0}\right) \right).
    \end{align}
Moreover, for all $v + (1, 1), v + (n, m) \in \mathbb{Z}^2_\ge$ with $n/m \in [\alpha_0, \alpha_0^{-1}]$ and all $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$ we have
    \begin{align}
	
	\mathbb{P}\Big(X_\alpha(v + (1, 1); v + (n, m)) \le \mu(n, m) - \epsilon n\Big) &\le 2 \exp\left( - c\epsilon^3 n^2 \right).
\end{align}
title: Theorem T:half-space-full-tails of arXiv:2604.10020

Let H be a Hilbert space, X a Banach space, and T : H → X a bounded linear operator. Let T* : X* → H be its adjoint with respect to the pairing of X with X* (identifying H* with H by the Riesz map). Then ‖T‖_{H→X}² = ‖T*‖_{X*→H}² = ‖T T*‖_{X*→X}. In particular, T is bounded with norm A if and only if T T* is bounded with norm A². In practice one verifies the hypotheses on a dense subspace (e.g. Schwartz functions) and extends by density; this is the standard route from a dispersive kernel bound on TT* to a space-time estimate for T.

[Dfn 3. dfn: topological subfunctor of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Topological subfunctor}] 
  Let $\tilde{\tau}$ and $\tau$ be functors.
  We say that $\tau$ is a \textit{topological subfunctor} of $\tilde{\tau}$ 
  if and only if the following conditions are satisfied.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (T\arabic*)]
    \item 
      For every $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}$,
      there exists a topological embedding of $\tau(S)$ into $\tilde{\tau}(S)$,
      that is,
      there exists a homeomorphism from $\tau(S)$ to a subset of $\tilde{\tau}(S)$.
      Using this map, we always regard $\tau(S)$ as a subspace of $\tilde{\tau}(S)$.
    \item  
      For every $(S_{i}, d^{S_{i}}, \rho_{S_{i}}),\, i=1,2$ 
      and root-and-distance-preserving map $f: S_{1} \to S_{2}$, 
      it holds that $\tau_{f} = \tilde{\tau}_{f}|_{\tau(S_{1})}$.
  \end{enumerate}
title: Dfn 3. dfn: topological subfunctor of arXiv:2412.08236

[Defn d.moment of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] \ 
The real-valued marks of \\
$(\tilde\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}=\bigl(\{(x_i,\xi_{i,n})\}_{x_i \in \mathcal{P}_n}\bigr)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$,
namely $\xi_{i,n}\in\mathbb{R}$, satisfy a $p$-moment condition, $p \in [1, \infty)$, if there are constants $M_p^{\xi} < \infty$
 such that 
 
\begin{equation}

\sup_{1 \leq n< \infty} \sup_{1 \leq q \leq p} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,
  x_{q} \in W_n} \mathbb {E} _{\bk x1{q}}[ \max(1,|\xi_{1,n}|^p)]
\leq M_p^{\xi} < \infty,
\end{equation}
where $\xi_{1,n}$ is the score  of $x_1$ under the Palm distribution of  $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n$ given the ground points $x_1,\ldots,x_q$. Here and elsewhere, we adopt the convention that the sup with respect to $\bk x1p$ is to be understood as $\text{ess}\sup$ with respect to the factorial moment  measures $\rho^{(p)}(\bk x1p) \mathrm{d} \bk x1p$ of the common ground process~$\mathcal{P}$, where  $\rho^{(p)}$ is tacitly assumed to be uniformly bounded by $\kappa_p$. Without loss of generality we assume that $M_p^{\xi}$
  is increasing in $p$ whenever (equation e:xinpmom of the paper) holds.
title: Moment conditions of scores

[Definition 150 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Let $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(2)}$ be two families (indexed by a large parameter $\N$) of discrete random $d$-dimensional real vectors. We say that the distribution of $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(1)}$ is asymptotically equal to the distribution of $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(2)}$ if
\begin{equation}

 \lim_{\N\rightarrow\infty} \sup_{f \in \textnormal{Lip}_1} \big|\E\big[f(\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(1)})\big]-\E\big[f(\boldsymbol{\chi}_{\N}^{(2)})\big]\big| =0,
\end{equation}
where $\textnormal{Lip}_1$ is the set of $1$-bounded $1$-Lipschitz functions
\[
 \textnormal{Lip}_1=\big\{f:\amsmathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \amsmathbb{R} \quad \big|\quad \forall \boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y} \in \amsmathbb{R}^d \quad |f(\x)-f(\y)| \leq |\!|\x-\y|\!|_{\infty}\,\,\textnormal{ and }\, |f(\x)|\leq 1\big\}.
\]
If \eqref{eq_asymptotic_equivalence} holds, we write $\chi_{\N}^{(1)} \stackrel{\textnormal{d}}{\sim} \chi_{\N}^{(2)}$.
title: Definition 150 of arXiv:2601.16377

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Source-specific calculation, conditional implication or exact obstruction Result: Finite-volume derivatives of log Z are energy cumulants: the second is a variance and the kth derivative is the kth centered cumulant up to sign. Analyticity in a beta neighborhood requires control at all orders, typically |cumulant_k|/volume bounded by C^k*k!, not merely a two-point decay estimate. Even real-analytic finite-volume functions can converge to a nonanalytic limit: f_n(beta)=sqrt((beta-beta0)^2+1/n) tends to |beta-beta0| for any fixed positive beta0. Check: Each f_n has a positive radicand on the real axis and is real analytic there, while the limit has different one-sided derivatives at beta0. Its complex singularities approach beta0 at distance1/sqrt(n), showing the missing uniform analytic radius. Obstruction: Uniform higher-order cumulant estimates or a convergent expansion are needed throughout the desired temperature range. The existing two-point control does not by itself provide them. No full analyticity theorem is established here.

A scaling limit for critical length-weighted honeycomb self-avoiding paths between prescribed domain boundary points does not by itself establish a scaling limit for uniformly sampled n-step honeycomb self-avoiding walks from the origin. The former randomizes length and fixes both endpoints; the latter fixes length and leaves the endpoint random. An application to the fixed-length question needs an additional theorem controlling the length disintegration, endpoint law, spatial rescaling, and curve topology. No such theorem is supplied by the cited conjectures or this draft.

[Theorem thm:berkowitz-devlin-one-step-clt of arXiv:2608.06159, 'Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi Graphs:\\[0.5ex] Gaussian Winner '] Let \(\gR_0,\gB_0\) be a deterministic partition of \([N]\). Independently
sample \(\gG\sim\mathbb{G}(N,p)\) and perform one synchronous majority update with
ties retaining their current colors. Define
\[
\sigma_N\coloneqq\sqrt{Np(1-p)}.
\]
For independent random variables
\[
W_R\sim\Bin(|\gR_0|,p),
\qquad
W_B\sim\Bin(|\gB_0|,p),
\]
set
\[
\chi_N
\coloneqq
\P(W_R\ge W_B)\P(W_R\le W_B).
\]
Then the following conclusions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For arbitrary parameter choices,
\begin{align}
\Var(|\gR_1|)
=
N\chi_N
+O\left(
|\Delta_0|+\frac{N}{\sigma_N}
\right).

\end{align}
\item Suppose that
\[
\sigma_N\longrightarrow\infty,
\qquad
\log(1/\chi_N)=o(\log\sigma_N).
\]
Then
\[
\Var(|\gR_1|)\sim N\chi_N,
\]
and, for every fixed \(a<c\),
\begin{align}
\P\left(
a\le
\frac{|\gR_1|-\E|\gR_1|}{\sqrt{N\chi_N}}
\le c
\right)
\longrightarrow
\Phi(c)-\Phi(a).

\end{align}
\end{enumerate}
In particular, the assumptions and conclusions in \textup{(ii)} hold if
\(\sigma_N\to\infty\) and
\[
|\Delta_0|p=O(\sigma_N).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Assuming one-way functions, the GPX posterior-hard family admits positive smooth polynomial-LSI regularizations with bounded covariance, polynomial-time generative descriptions and polynomially accurate computable forward-score networks. Their actual LSI constants lie between D^100/96 and O(D^206(log D)^2); norm-one selector observations with noise Theta((log D)^-2) put their ratios between Omega(D^100(log D)^4) and O(D^206(log D)^6). A polynomial-time posterior sampler achieving TV 10^-6 for at least 1-10^-6 of observations would contradict GPX hardness. The computational interface is polynomial-accuracy score networks, not a unit-cost exact-score oracle. No novelty or independent-check claim. No independent audit or novelty claim. Source Lemmas C.15/C.20 and Theorem C.21 inspected. Thirty-one exact supporting checks pass; no Lean certification.
