[Lem 109 (regularity for spatially smoothed coefficients) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth} are continuously differentiable in the space coordinate, and satisfy the bounds
	\[
	\Big(
	\|\sB^N\|_\infty
    +
    \|\partial_y\sB^N\|_\infty\Big)^2
	+ \max\bigg\{
    \|\tilde{A}\|_\infty
    +\|\partial_y\tilde{A}\|_\infty
    : \tilde{A}\in\{ \sV,\sU,\srrr,\swww\}^N
    \bigg\}
	\le 
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2\,,
	\]
with $\MAX_N$ as in \eqref{e:MAX.N} and Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}.

\begin{proof}
We continue to use the abbreviations introduced above. To simplify notation, we mostly suppress the dependence on $N$ inside the proof. Consider
	\[
	\sB(t,y)
	=\frac{\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)}
	\equiv \frac{\Num(t,y)}{\Den(t,y)}\,.
	\]
We first aim to lower bound the denominator $\Den$.
Recall from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth} that $\sphi$ has support $[-\sep,\sep]^3$, and is $\ge \Omega(1)/\sep^3$ on $[-\sep/2,\sep/2]^3$. 
From the construction of $\vX^\frozen$ and $\vY^\frozen$
(Definitions \ref{d:trunc}--\ref{d:rerand.Ising}), we see that $\varrho_t$ gives measure at least $\Omega( \sep^3 /\trK^{O(1)} )$ to any box of side length $\sep$ contained in $[-2\trK,2\trK]^3$. It follows that, for all $\vy\in[-2\trK+1,2\trK-1]^3$,
	\[
	\varrho_t*\sphi(\vy)
	\ge \int_{[-\sep/2,\sep/2]^3}
		\sphi(\vy-\vx)\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\ge \frac{1}{\trK^{O(1)}}\,.
	\]
Integrating over $\vy\in H(y)$ (as defined by \eqref{e:hspace.y}) gives
	\beq
	\Den(t,y)
	= \overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)
	\ge \frac{1}{\trK^{O(1)}}
	\eeq
for all $y\in[-5\trK,5\trK]$. Next note that since particles outside $[-\trK,\trK]^3$ are frozen (see Definition~\ref{d:trunc}), the numerator $\Num(t,y)$ must be zero for $y\notin[-3\trK-1,3\trK+1]$. For $y\in[-3\trK-1,3\trK+1]$, we bound
	\begin{align*}
	|\Num(t,y)|
	&=\Big|\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)\Big|
	=\bigg| \int_{H(y)}
	\int_{\R^3} \sphi(\vy-\vx)B(t,\vx)\,\varrho_t(d\vx) \,d\vy\bigg|\\
	&=\bigg| \int_{\R^3}
	B(t,\vx) \overline{\sphi}(y-(\underline{1},\vx))\,\varrho_t(d\vx)\bigg|
	\le \|\overline{\sphi}\|_\infty \cdot \int_{\R^3}
	|B(t,\vx)|\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le  \bigg(\frac{L}
		{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)}
		\MAX_N\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last step uses the quenched moment bound on $\bbb$ from Lemma~\ref{l:barD.I.second.quenched}, together with the bound $(p^N)' \le  L^2$ from \eqref{e:sdelimits.pprime}. Combining with \eqref{e:denominator.lbd} gives
	\[\|\sB\|_\infty 
	\le \bigg(\frac{\trK L}
		{\sep}
		\bigg)^{O(1)}
		\MAX_N\,.
	\]
We can also apply \eqref{e:denominator.lbd} to obtain
	\beq
	\Big|\partial_y \tilde{B}(t,y)\Big|
	\le \trK^{O(1)}
	\bigg|
	\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Num(t,y)
	- \tilde{B}(t,y)
	\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Den(t,y)
	\bigg|\,.\eeq
The first term on the right-hand side of \eqref{e:sB.quotient.rule} can be bounded by
	\begin{align*}
	\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Num(t,y)\bigg|
	&=\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
	\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)\bigg|
	=\bigg| 
	\int_{\R^3} B(t,\vx)
	\overline{\sphi}' (y-(\vec{1},\vx))
	\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\bigg|\\
	&\le
	\|\overline{\sphi}' \|_\infty
	\int_{\R^3} | B(t,\vx) | \,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le \bigg(\frac{L}
		{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \MAX_N\,.
	\end{align*}
The second term on the right-hand side of \eqref{e:sB.quotient.rule} can be controlled using the preceding bound on $\tilde{B}$, together with a similar  calculation as above:
	\[
	\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
		\Den(t,y) \bigg|
	=\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\bigg|
	\le  \| \overline{\sphi}' \|_\infty \cdot
	\int_{\R^3} \varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le \frac{1}{\sep^{O(1)} }\,.
	\]
Combining the above gives the claimed bound on $\partial_y \sB$.
The bounds on $\sV$, $\sU$, $\srrr$, and $\swww$ follow by the same argument, using the quenched moment bounds from Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: regularity for spatially smoothed coefficients

[Prop 10 of arXiv:2606.14812, 'Joint convergence in Wiener chaos via transport hierarchy and Malliavin covariances'] Consider two integers $p, q\geq 2$ and let
		\[
		X_N = I_p(f_N), \qquad Y_N = I_q(g_N),
		\]
		where $f_N\in H^{\odot p}$, $g_N\in H^{\odot q}$, and assume that $X_N$ 
		satisfies \eqref{c1} and $Y_N$ is bounded in $L^2(\Omega)$. Write 
		$q = ap + r'$ with $a\geq 1$ and $0\leq r' < p$. For $r\geq 1$, let 
		$Y_{r,N}$ be given by \eqref{yr}. Then the following hold.
		
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item For every integer $r\geq 1$ with $rp\leq q$,
			\begin{equation}
				Y_{r,N} = C_{r,p,q}\,
				I_{q-rp}\!\left(f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r)} g_N\right)
				+ R_{r,N},
			\end{equation}
			where $f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r)} g_N$ denotes the 
			$r$-fold iterated contraction of $f_N$ with $g_N$, 
			defined recursively by $f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(1)} g_N 
			= f_N\widetilde\otimes_p g_N\in H^{\odot(q-p)}$ and
			\begin{equation*}
				f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r)} g_N 
				:= f_N\widetilde\otimes_p 
				\left(f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r-1)} g_N\right)
				\in H^{\odot(q-rp)},
				\quad r=2,\ldots,a,
			\end{equation*}
			i.e.\ at each step the $p$ variables of $f_N$ are 
			fully contracted with $p$ of the remaining variables 
			of the kernel from the previous step. Also,  $C_{r,p,q} = (p!)^r\frac{q!}{(q-rp)!}$ and 
			$R_{r,N}\to 0$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ as $N\to\infty$.
			
			\item \textbf{Non-critical case} $ap < q < (a+1)p$: 
			\begin{equation}
				Y_{a+1,N} \to _{N \to \infty}0 \quad \text{in } L^2(\Omega).
			\end{equation}
			
			\item \textbf{Critical case} $q = ap$: taking $r=a$ in \eqref{14m-2b} gives
			\begin{equation*}
				Y_{a,N} - \mathbf{E}[Y_{a,N}] \to  _{N \to \infty}0 \quad \text{in } L^2(\Omega).
			\end{equation*}
			In particular, if $\mathbf{E}[Y_{a,N}]\to _{N \to \infty}\rho_a$ for some $\rho_a\in\mathbb{R}$, 
			then $Y_{a,N}\to _{N \to \infty}\rho_a$ in $L^2(\Omega)$. Moreover,
			\begin{equation}
				Y_{a+1,N} \to_{N \to \infty}  0 \quad \text{in } L^2(\Omega).
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 10 of arXiv:2606.14812

[Corollary 33 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] There exists a universal constant such that for any martingale difference sequence $D_i$ adapted to a filtration $\mathcal{F}_i$---so $D_i$ is $\mathcal{F}_i$ measurable and $\E[D_i \mid \mathcal{F}_{i-1}] =0$---we have for all $p \geq 2, n \geq 1$, the bounds
    \begin{equation}
        
        \Big\|\sum_{i=1}^n D_i\Big\|_{L^p_\omega} \leq C \sup_{ 2  \lor \frac{p}{n} \leq q \leq p} \frac{p}{q} \Big(\frac{n}{p}\Big)^{1/q} \max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \big\|\E[|D_i|^q \mid \mathcal{F}_{i-1}]^{1/q}\big\|_{L^\infty_\omega}.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 33 of arXiv:2608.05931

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2608.31008, 'Stability of gravitational instantons with a bounded Killing vector field'] Let $(M^4,g)$ be oriented Einstein with scalar curvature $s$.  If
$\alpha^+\in\Omega^2_+(M)$ and $\beta^-\in\Omega^2_-(M)$ are harmonic,
then $h=\alpha^+\circ\beta^-$ is TT, and
\begin{equation}
    \cE_g h=-\frac{s}{2}h-2\sum_a(\nabla_a\alpha^+)\circ(\nabla_a\beta^-),
 
\end{equation}
which implies from $\big\langle(\nabla_a\alpha^+)\circ(\nabla_a\beta^-),
 \alpha^+\circ\beta^-\big\rangle
 =\langle\nabla_a\alpha^+,\alpha^+\rangle
  \langle\nabla_a\beta^-,\beta^-\rangle,$ that
\begin{equation}
    \langle\cE_g h,h\rangle=-\frac{s}{2}|h|^2-\frac12\langle d|\alpha^+|^2,d|\beta^-|^2\rangle.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 7 of arXiv:2608.31008

body:
DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T411-w740-C004 v1. For n>=128, D=n+n^2, a smooth prior with LSI at most 21 and a linear Gaussian observation ratio at most 420000 has posterior Poincare and LSI constants at least n*exp(n/16)/128 with probability at least 1-5*exp(-n/16) over observations. Thus prior LSI and the proposed small-ratio condition cannot alone supply a polynomial posterior-LSI bound, even for typical observations. This does not establish sampling hardness. No novelty or independent-check claim. No independent review or novelty claim; no efficient-score representation is asserted for this family. Twenty-four exact checks pass. Target 1 computational sampling remains open.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:933c1414c688812f0168e6dd597a45252591c27120045874f479e9d03cbd1738","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/93/933c1414c688812f0168e6dd597a45252591c27120045874f479e9d03cbd1738.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:dd45cc5a37eb2bdf6ee694037d47cb625d9da2c201909daabff05ac8adbb64c5","bundle_entry_key":"draft-typical-observation-posterior-lsi-obstruction","bundle_id":"population.w740-t411-polynomial-lsi-hardness-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"posterior sampling and functional inequalities","draft":"w740/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.sampling:draft-typical-observation-posterior-lsi-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Typical observations can destroy a constant prior LSI

Status: proof draft, unaudited. Pending: frontier-check output, source comparison, and exact arithmetic checks. This is a functional-inequality obstruction, not a computational sampling lower bound. No novelty claim is made.

## Statement

For each integer n>=128, put D=n+n^2 and eta^2=sigma^2=1/20000. There is an explicitly samplable, everywhere positive smooth prior mu_n on R^D with C_LS(mu_n)<=21, and a norm-one linear observation selector A:R^D->R^(n^2), such that for Y=AX+sigma E, X~mu_n and E standard Gaussian, with probability at least

1-5 exp(-n/16)

over Y, the posterior satisfies

C_P(mu_n(.|Y)) >= (n/128) exp(n/16),
C_LS(mu_n(.|Y)) >= (n/128) exp(n/16).

The LSI convention is Ent(f^2)<=2 C_LS E||grad f||^2. The observation ratio is at most 420000, independent of n. In particular it is <=c log D for every fixed c>0 and all sufficiently large n, while the typical posterior constants grow faster than every polynomial in D.

The conclusion rules out the proposed high-probability polynomial posterior-LSI inheritance route based only on prior LSI and the observation ratio. It does not rule out a polynomial sampler, an annealing method that handles the two modes, or a method using their exact sign symmetry. It does not supply an efficient neural-network representation of every forward score. All prior scores exist and exact score oracles may be considered abstractly.

## 1. A Gaussian Lipschitz prior

Identify R^D with a vector block R^n and a matrix block R^(n by n), using the Frobenius norm on matrices. For z in R^n let

u(z)=2 projection_{closed ball of radius sqrt(n)/2}(z).

This map is 2-Lipschitz and ||u(z)||<=sqrt(n). Euclidean projection onto a ball is nonexpansive: inside it is the identity, outside its derivative has radial eigenvalue 0 and tangential eigenvalue r/||z||<=1; integrating along line segments, or using the convex projection inequality, gives the global bound.

For ||u||<=sqrt(n) define F(u)=(u,uu^T/sqrt(n)). For two such vectors u,v,

||uu^T-vv^T||_F <= (||u||+||v||)||u-v|| <=2 sqrt(n)||u-v||.

Therefore F is sqrt(5)-Lipschitz. If Z is a standard Gaussian vector in R^n and W an independent standard Gaussian vector in R^D, set

X=F(u(Z))+eta W.

The map (Z,W)->X is sqrt(20+eta^2)-Lipschitz, by Cauchy--Schwarz applied to sqrt(20)||Delta Z||+eta||Delta W||. Gaussian LSI and composition with test functions give C_LS(mu_n)<=20+eta^2<21. Gaussian convolution gives an everywhere positive C-infinity density. Also ||F(u)||^2<=2n, so E||X||^2<=2n+eta^2 D. All the construction's inputs and operations are explicit; unconditional sampling costs polynomial time in D.

Let A select the matrix block. Then ||A||=1 and ||A||^2 C_LS/sigma^2<=21*20000=420000.

## 2. A spherical reference and a rigorous coupling

Define U_s=sqrt(n) Z/||Z|| (the value at Z=0 is immaterial). It is uniform on the sphere of radius sqrt(n). Define a reference prior S_n as the law of X_s=F(U_s)+eta W, using the same Z,W as above. If ||Z||>=sqrt(n)/2, then u(Z)=U_s, so X=X_s.

Write delta=Pr(||Z||<sqrt(n)/2). Gaussian integration gives E exp(-||Z||^2/2)=2^(-n/2). Markov's inequality gives

delta <= exp(n/8)2^(-n/2) <= exp(-n/8),

where log 2>=1/2 follows from integrating 1/x on [1,2]. Thus TV(mu_n,S_n)<=delta. The same coupling, with the same observation noise, bounds by delta both the joint laws of (X,Y) and the Y marginals.

This reference prior is used only to compute the posterior; no LSI assertion for the sphere is needed.

## 3. The Gaussian matrix event

Under S_n, the observed matrix has the form

Y=U_s U_s^T/sqrt(n)+(1/100)G,

where G has independent standard Gaussian entries, since eta^2+sigma^2=1/10000.

A 1/4-net N of the unit sphere can be chosen with |N|<=9^n. To see the bound, take a maximal separated set and compare volumes of disjoint radius-1/8 balls with the containing radius-9/8 ball; maximality supplies the covering property. For every real matrix G,

||G||op <=2 max_{a,b in N}|a^T G b|,

because approximating both unit vectors in a bilinear form produces error at most (1/2)||G||op. Each fixed a^T G b is standard Gaussian. A union bound therefore gives

Pr(||G||op>8 sqrt(n)) <=2*9^(2n) exp(-8n) <=2 exp(-3n),

using log 9<5/2. The latter inequality follows, for example, because the fourth-degree Taylor lower bound for exp(5/2) exceeds 9.

Put H=(Y+Y^T)/2. On the displayed matrix event, its eigenvalues satisfy

lambda_1>= (23/25)sqrt(n),
lambda_2<= (2/25)sqrt(n),
lambda_n>=-(2/25)sqrt(n).

Indeed the noiseless matrix has one eigenvalue sqrt(n) and the rest zero; the symmetric noise has norm at most (2/25)sqrt(n). The first and last bounds follow directly from Rayleigh quotients. For the second, any two-dimensional subspace contains a nonzero vector perpendicular to U_s, whose signal Rayleigh quotient is zero; the eigenvector span for the two largest eigenvalues then proves the bound. In particular the top eigenvalue is simple. Choose a measurable top unit eigenvector v(H); its sign will not matter.

Let E be the event that these three eigenvalue inequalities hold. They depend only on the observation and S_n(Y in E)>=1-2 exp(-3n).

## 4. The reference posterior has an exponentially small equatorial belt

Conditional on U_s=u, Y has independent Gaussian entries with means uu^T/sqrt(n) and variance 1/10000. Since ||u||=sqrt(n), the squared Frobenius norm of uu^T/sqrt(n) is the constant n. Bayes' formula therefore gives the reference latent posterior density, relative to uniform spherical measure, proportional to

exp(theta u^T H u),  theta=10000/sqrt(n).

This is the standard Bingham form. The identity follows by expanding the Gaussian likelihood; the antisymmetric part of Y has zero inner product with uu^T.

Fix Y in E. Let B={|u.v|<=sqrt(n)/2} and C={|u.v|>=sqrt(3n)/2}. On B, the energy theta u^T H u is at most

theta n(lambda_1/4+3 lambda_2/4).

On C it is at least

theta n(3 lambda_1/4+lambda_n/4).

The second minus the first is at least

theta n(lambda_1/2+lambda_n/4-3 lambda_2/4) >=3800 n.

The spherical measure of C is at least exp(-3n). For completeness, use polar angle around v: the two caps of angle pi/6 have measure

2 integral_0^(pi/6) sin(t)^(n-2) dt / integral_0^pi sin(t)^(n-2) dt.

Restrict the numerator integral to [pi/12,pi/6], where sin(t)>1/4, and bound the denominator by pi. The result is at least (1/6)4^(-(n-2)), which is greater than exp(-3n) for n>=2 (use log 6<2 and log 4<2). Consequently

Pr_{S_n}(|U_s.v|<=sqrt(n)/2 |Y) <=exp(-3797 n).

The vector block X_s,vec=U_s+eta W_vec contains Gaussian noise independent of Y and U_s. Even though v depends on Y, conditional on Y its projection of W_vec is still a standard Gaussian independent of U_s. Hence

Pr_{S_n}(|X_s,vec.v|<sqrt(n)/4 |Y)
 <=exp(-3797n)+2 exp(-n/(32 eta^2))
 <=3 exp(-625n).

All probabilities here concern the actual noisy vector block, not a latent variable to which the posterior sampler has no access.

## 5. Transfer to the constant-LSI prior under its own observation law

For any two priors P,Q and a common observation channel, the elementary triangle inequality for their joint and marginal densities gives

E_{Y~Q_Y} TV(P(.|Y),Q(.|Y)) <=2 TV(P,Q).

The proof is included in C002: add and subtract Q_Y(y)P(dx|y), integrate, and use contraction of TV under marginalization. Positive Gaussian observation densities ensure these conditional densities are well-defined throughout.

Apply this with P=mu_n, Q=S_n and epsilon=exp(-n/16). Markov's inequality gives a set J of observations on which the conditional TV distance is at most epsilon, with

S_n(Y notin J) <=2 delta/epsilon <=2 exp(-n/16).

The observation marginals differ in TV by at most delta. Therefore, under the actual prior mu_n,

Pr(Y in E intersect J)
 >=1-2 exp(-3n)-2 exp(-n/16)-exp(-n/8)
 >=1-5 exp(-n/16).

For every Y in this set, its actual posterior belt probability satisfies

Pr_{mu_n}(|X_vec.v|<sqrt(n)/4 |Y) <=3 exp(-625n)+epsilon <=4 epsilon.

The reference measure in the conditional-TV averaging inequality is important: the final extra delta is what changes the observation law from S_n to mu_n.

## 6. A posterior Poincare test

The actual prior is invariant under the transformation that negates the vector block and leaves the matrix block fixed: send Z->-Z, W_vec->-W_vec, and leave W_matrix fixed. The observation depends only on the matrix block, so every posterior has the same symmetry. Thus, for each good observation, the posterior masses of X_vec.v<=-sqrt(n)/4 and X_vec.v>=sqrt(n)/4 are equal and at least (1-4epsilon)/2.

For n>=128, epsilon<=exp(-8)<1/20; the quadratic Taylor lower bound for exp(8) is 41>20. Both masses are therefore at least 2/5.

For this fixed Y choose f_Y(X) that is 0 when X_vec.v<=-sqrt(n)/4, 1 when X_vec.v>=sqrt(n)/4, and linear between them. Its Euclidean gradient has squared norm 4/n in the belt and 0 elsewhere. Therefore

E[||grad f_Y||^2 |Y] <=16 epsilon/n.

Two independent posterior copies show Var(f_Y|Y) is at least the product of the two plateau masses, hence at least 4/25>1/8. The Poincare variational inequality gives

C_P(mu_n(.|Y)) >= (n/128)exp(n/16).

The test function may depend on the fixed observation: C_P of each conditional law is a supremum over its test functions. This dependence is permitted by the quantifiers. Linearizing LSI at a constant gives C_P<=C_LS, proving the same posterior LSI lower bound.

## What this does and does not settle

The ambient dimension is D=n+n^2, so exp(n/16) is superpolynomial in D. The prior LSI and dimensionless observation ratio are bounded by absolute constants. The failure of posterior-LSI inheritance occurs with probability tending to one under the actual observations, rather than on a rare tail event.

This eliminates a proposed proof architecture for Target 1; it does not eliminate all posterior samplers. In particular exact sign symmetry can allow a sampler to assign the two modes correct masses without crossing a low-density belt. Let G = PSL(2,R) and let Gamma be a LATTICE in G: a discrete subgroup such that the quotient M = Gamma\G carries a G-invariant Borel probability measure m (finite covolume, normalised). Gamma is not assumed torsion free, cocompact, or arithmetic. For real t let u_t denote the image in G of the unipotent matrix with rows (1, t) and (0, 1), and define the horocycle flow on M by h_t(Gamma g) = Gamma g u_t. Then: (1) each h_t preserves m; (2) HEDLUND: the flow is ergodic with respect to m; (3) PARRY: the flow is strongly mixing, that is for all F1, F2 in L^2(M, m) the inner product of F1 composed with h_t against F2 converges, as |t| -> infinity, to the product of the integral of F1 and the conjugate of the integral of F2; equivalently m(A intersect h_{-t}B) -> m(A) m(B) for all Borel A, B. Moreover the flow is mixing of all orders. WHERE THE HYPOTHESES BITE: (i) finite covolume is essential. Mixing as stated is a statement about a probability measure; for a discrete subgroup of infinite covolume the correct statements concern Burger-Roblin and Patterson-Sullivan measures and carry extra hypotheses (for instance on the critical exponent), so (3) must not be quoted there. (ii) Ergodicity and mixing hold for EVERY lattice, but MINIMALITY (every orbit dense), Hedlund's other theorem, needs Gamma cocompact: a noncompact finite-volume quotient has closed horocycle orbits encircling each cusp, so the flow there is mixing yet neither minimal nor uniquely ergodic. Confusing the two Hedlund statements is the usual error. (iii) The result concerns the unipotent direction. The geodesic flow a_s is also mixing but has positive entropy and a huge simplex of invariant measures, whereas the horocycle flow has zero entropy and (in the cocompact case) is uniquely ergodic; rigidity statements do not transfer between them. (iv) Nothing here gives a RATE; quantitative mixing needs a spectral gap input and the rate depends on the lattice.
G = PSL(2,R) and Gamma < G is discrete with finite covolume (a lattice)
m is the G-invariant probability measure on Gamma\G
the flow is right translation by the one-parameter unipotent subgroup u_t
no cocompactness, torsion freeness or arithmeticity is assumed for (1)-(3); cocompactness is needed only for minimality and unique ergodicity, which are NOT claimed here
mixing is understood with respect to the normalised invariant probability measure

The Howe-Moore theorem (for G simple with finite centre and pi a unitary representation with no nonzero invariant vectors, all matrix coefficients of pi tend to 0 as the group element leaves every compact subset of G) then applies; since u_t leaves every compact set as |t| -> infinity, the correlation of F1 composed with h_t against F2 tends to 0 for mean-zero F1, F2, which is exactly mixing, and ergodicity follows a fortiori. An elementary route avoiding Howe-Moore is Parry's, based on the commutation relation a_s u_t a_s^{-1} = u_{t e^s} where a_s is the diagonal (geodesic) flow diag(e^{s/2}, e^{-s/2}): conjugating by a_s stretches horocycle arcs, so ergodicity of the flow plus the contraction of the transverse directions upgrades to decay of correlations; the same relation is the source of the Mautner phenomenon, which says that a vector invariant under the unipotent subgroup is invariant under all of G. ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Integrator-authored exact restricted calculation or proof-obstruction analysis after primary-source comparison Result: A commute-time identity controls the sum of opposite hitting times, not a lower bound of comparable size for each direction. A unit-conductance star with n vertices gives a concrete check: from a leaf a to its center b the hitting time is1, while the reverse mean is2*n-3; their sum is2*n-2=2*|E|*R(a,b). Thus a large commute time cannot be assigned to the outward hitting time. Even a genuine large expectation need not give a lower-tail bound: a nonnegative variable equal to n^2 with probability1/n and zero otherwise has mean n but is zero with probability tending to one. A displacement upper bound therefore needs a genuine lower-tail control on exit times or a suitable heat-kernel estimate, beyond these expectation identities. Check: First-step conditioning at the star center gives m=(1/(n-1))*1+((n-2)/(n-1))*(2+m), hence m=2*n-3. The one-way/commute discrepancy is exact. Obstruction: No claim that exit-time concentration fails in the DGFF model. The examples invalidate proposed proof implications, not the requested estimate.

body:
[Theorem thm:abstract-radial of arXiv:2608.18293, 'Critical tensor covariance at the Marchenko--Pastur threshold'] Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$ and $p_n\to\infty$. For each $n$, let
$x_n^{(1)},\ldots,x_n^{(N_n)}$ be independent copies of a random vector
$x_n\in\mathbb F^{p_n}$, set
\[
 R_n=\frac{\|x_n\|^2}{p_n},
 \qquad
 T_n=\frac1{N_n}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{N_n}
 x_n^{(\alpha)}{x_n^{(\alpha)}}^*,
\]
where $*$ denotes transpose or conjugate transpose according to the field,
and suppose $p_n/N_n\to c\in(0,\infty)$. Assume that $R_n\Rightarrow\nu$,
that $\{R_n\}$ is uniformly integrable, and that for some $\varepsilon_n\to0$,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathbb{C}^{p_n\times p_n}\\\|A\|_\mathrm{op}\le1}}
 \mathbb{E}\left|p_n^{-1}x_n^*Ax_n
 -R_np_n^{-1}\operatorname{Tr} A\right|^2\le\varepsilon_n.
 
\end{equation}
Then $\operatorname{ESD}(T_n)$ converges weakly in probability to the unique probability
measure $\mu_{c,\nu}$ whose Stieltjes transform satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \frac1{m(z)}+z=\int_0^\infty\frac{r}{1+crm(z)}\,\nu(\,\mathrm{d} r).
 
\end{equation}
If $\sum_n e^{-ap_n}<\infty$ for every $a>0$, the convergence is almost sure.
No independence between $R_n$ and $x_n/\|x_n\|$ is assumed, and no
mean-one normalization of $\nu$ is needed. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Endogenous radial covariance principle

body: Let X_1, X_2, ... be iid real random variables with finite logarithmic moment generating function Lambda(t) = log E[exp(t X_1)] for every real t, and let S_n = (X_1+...+X_n)/n. Let Lambda*(x) = sup_t (t x - Lambda(t)) be its Legendre-Fenchel transform. Cramer's theorem states that S_n obeys a large deviation principle with rate function Lambda*: for every Borel set A, -inf_{interior of A} Lambda* <= liminf_n (1/n) log P(S_n in A) <= limsup_n (1/n) log P(S_n in A) <= -inf_{closure of A} Lambda*. In particular P(S_n in F) decays like exp(-n inf_F Lambda*) for closed F. Due to Harald Cramer.
title: Cramer's theorem (large deviations)

body:
Let X and Y be Banach spaces and let T from X to Y be a linear map (defined on all of X). If the graph of T, the set of pairs (x, T(x)), is closed in the product space X x Y (equivalently: whenever x_n converges to x in X and T(x_n) converges to some y in Y, it follows that y = T(x)), then T is bounded (continuous). The converse is immediate, so for everywhere-defined linear maps between Banach spaces, closed graph and continuity coincide. The hypothesis that T is defined on all of X and both spaces are complete is essential (densely defined closed unbounded operators exist).
X and Y are Banach spaces
T : X -> Y is linear and defined on all of X
the graph of T is closed in X x Y

body: [Cor complete-k0 of arXiv:2609.00672, 'Deciding superellipticity and computing the Weierstrass normal form'] Let $C$ have genus $g\ge 2$ and let $n\in\Lev(C)$ be realised by a cyclic cover $\pi$ with a separable model $y^n=h(x)$ defined over $k_0$. Then (alg:main of the paper), run over $k_0$, outputs $n$; for $\deg h\ge 3$ the candidate arising from the branch divisor of $\pi$ yields a normal form of $\pi$, and for $\deg h=2$ step 5 yields one. The constant field is extended at most once, by degree at most $\deg h$, and only when $3\le\deg h$, no root of $h$ is $k_0$-rational, and either $\deg h$ divides $n$ or $\deg h=n+\gcd(n,\deg h)$ with $\gcd(n,\deg h)>1$.

[Defn conditions of arXiv:2608.06500, 'Free energy of Ising models under a spectral condition'] Let $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ be a closed interval and $C>0$ be a constant. We
    define $\mathcal{G}_{I,C}$ to be the set of finite weighted graphs
    $G=(\text{\boldmath $A$},\text{\boldmath $h$})$ satisfying the following conditions:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(SW), ref=(SW)]
        \item
        All eigenvalues of $\text{\boldmath $A$}$ lie in $I$. If additionally the
        length of $I$ is strictly less than $1$, we refer to this as
        the \emph{spectral width condition}.
    \end{enumerate}
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(SG), ref=(SG)]
        \item
        The operator norm bound $\|\text{\boldmath $A$}\|_{\infty\rightarrow\infty}\le
        C$ holds, i.e. the $\ell^1$ norm of any row of $\text{\boldmath $A$}$ is at
        most $C$. We refer to this as the \emph{sparse graph
        condition}.
    \end{enumerate}
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(BF), ref=(BF)]
        \item
        The entrywise bound $\|\text{\boldmath $h$}\|_\infty\le C$ holds, i.e. the
        magnitude of the external field $h_i$ on each spin $i\in[N]$
        is at most $C$. We refer to this as the \emph{bounded field
        condition}.
    \end{enumerate}
title: Defn conditions of arXiv:2608.06500

body: Conjecture 13 of the Randomstrasse 2024 problem list asks whether the Sylvester Hadamard matrix H_k of order 2^k has discrepancy disc(H_k) = sqrt(2) sqrt(2^k) for odd k, where disc(A) = min over sign vectors x of the sup-norm of Ax. In plain terms: take the 2^k x 2^k matrix of plus and minus ones whose entry in row a and column u is (-1) to the mod-2 dot product of the k-bit strings a and u, and ask for the smallest possible largest absolute entry of the product Hx over sign vectors x. Indexing H_k by (-1)^{a.u} and reading x as the +-1 truth table of a Boolean function f on k variables, H_k x is the Walsh transform W_f, so disc(H_k) = min_f max_a |W_f(a)| = 2^k - 2 NL_max(k), where NL_max(k) is the largest nonlinearity of a Boolean function on k variables (the covering radius of the Reed-Muller code RM(1, k)). The conjectured value is exactly the bent-concatenation bound NL = 2^{k-1} - 2^{(k-1)/2}, which is beaten for odd k = 15 (Patterson and Wiedemann, 1983) and for every odd k > 7 (Kavut, Maitra and Yucel, 2006), and is optimal for k <= 7. So the conjecture holds exactly for k in {1, 3, 5, 7} and fails for every odd k >= 9. The numbers: for k <= 7 the maximum nonlinearity equals the bent-concatenation value (the covering radius of RM(1,5) is 12, Berlekamp and Welch 1972; of RM(1,7) is 56, Mykkeltveit 1980; k = 1, 3 by hand); for k = 9 functions of nonlinearity 242 exist (Kavut, Maitra and Yucel 2006), so disc(H_9) <= 512 - 484 = 28 < 32; for every odd k = 9 + 2j the direct sum of such a function with a bent function on 2j variables has largest Walsh coefficient 28 * 2^j, below 32 * 2^j, since the Walsh spectrum of a direct sum is the product; and Patterson and Wiedemann's nonlinearity 16276 on 15 variables gives disc(H_15) <= 216 < 256.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a determinantal point process with correlation kernel K, Hermitian and satisfying 0<=K<=I in the discrete finite-space setting, the conditional law of the process restricted to a subset given the exact configuration on the complementary subset is again determinantal, with a kernel given by a Schur-complement formula. Partitioning the index set into A, the observed subset, and B, the remaining subset, and writing K in block form with entries K_AA, K_AB, K_BA, K_BB, the conditional kernel on B given the exact points observed in A is expressed via a Schur-complement expression such as K_BB - K_BA (K_AA - I)^{-1} K_AB, with the precise form depending on the convention used (correlation kernel versus L-ensemble) and on whether one conditions on points being present or absent in A. This identity is the fundamental tool for analyzing conditioning, dynamics, and Gibbs-type properties of determinantal processes, including eigenvalues of random matrices, non-intersecting paths, discrete orthogonal polynomial ensembles, and, via the transfer-current theorem, uniform spanning trees, reducing conditional analysis to linear algebra on the kernel matrix. It does not apply outside the determinantal class of point processes, or its Pfaffian analogue for orthogonal and symplectic ensembles, which has a related but distinct formula, and the exact form of the Schur complement depends sensitively on the specific conditioning event and on invertibility of the relevant block, which can fail or require a pseudo-inverse or limiting argument at special parameter values. Typical failure: Applying a Schur-complement conditional-kernel formula derived under one convention, such as conditioning an L-ensemble on a fixed exact sample, to a different conditioning question, such as conditioning on a sub-event like at least one point in a region, or mixing up the correlation-kernel and L-ensemble conventions, without re-deriving the correct formula; determinantal-process conditioning identities are convention-sensitive, and mixing them up produces a kernel that still looks plausible, expressed via some Schur complement, but does not correctly describe the actual conditional process. Canonical reference: Shirai and Takahashi, 2003, Journal of Functional Analysis; Borodin and Rains, 2005, Journal of Statistical Physics; Lyons, 2003, Annals of Probability.

the conditioning event is of the specific form covered by the Schur-complement formula, i.e. an exact configuration on a subset, or the corresponding L-ensemble conditioning
invertibility, or a well-defined limiting or pseudo-inverse procedure, for the relevant diagonal block appearing in the formula, e.g. K_AA - I
the block partition A, B is taken with respect to the same index set on which K is originally defined

(LATIN 2018, arXiv:1903.11635). Ranking coordinates by |w_i|, the derivative D_i f is the indicator of a slab of width 2|w_i|, and the Erdos-Littlewood-Offord inequality applied to noise on the heavier coordinates gives E_S sum_{i in S} ln+(r(i)/|S|) <= 4.151 I, so the spectral sample lives on the top O(|S|) coordinates by weight; entropy against a rank-weighted reference measure, plus O'Donnell-Wright-Zhou's level-entropy bound (at most 3I), gives the constant (optimum exponent a = 1.2006, 14.2142). For f = G(w.x) with G changing sign t times, H(f) <= C_t I(f) with C_t = O(log t) (16.57 at t = 2). The supremum of H/I over threshold functions appears numerically to be about 4. The rank criterion is sufficient, not necessary: it fails for recursive ternary majority.

Pick q in omega(gamma^+); by invariance, the whole orbit through q lies in omega(gamma^+). Construct a short line segment Sigma through a non-equilibrium point of that orbit, transverse to the vector field (possible since omega(gamma^+) has no equilibria); the flow is then transverse to Sigma nearby, and successive intersections of the orbit through q with Sigma are monotonic along Sigma, a planar fact following from the Jordan curve theorem applied to the closed curve formed by an arc of the orbit between two consecutive intersections together with the segment of Sigma joining them, which separates the plane so the rest of the trajectory cannot cross it. A monotone bounded sequence of intersection points on Sigma converges; if the limit were not the starting intersection point itself, one derives a contradiction using that gamma^+ accumulates on all of omega(gamma^+), so the orbit through q must return exactly to its starting point on Sigma, i.e. be periodic. Finally gamma^+ itself is shown to spiral onto this periodic orbit, so omega(gamma^+) equals it.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:c1fd189475f9669f6e1d375b115cb02df9ccf19cb173abf439ef25d92982d191","revision_digest":"sha256:fb1609461b7906c99582736e3ca7a8a5bfbedf98ec25a1255057b3c85d071ea1","source_id":"wikipedia:Poincare-Bendixson theorem","source_revision":"as-read-2026-08-02","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:a6723bcdde0e3a400ceed939d5e5b320475951c52f9e7ffb42a5f62c93a80bff","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/a6/a6723bcdde0e3a400ceed939d5e5b320475951c52f9e7ffb42a5f62c93a80bff.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:eea7b56f6d534a3fb9ffe2ae8cebd9697697adad861140d4d084e21f5b7966f5","bundle_entry_key":"rank-one-fixed","bundle_id":"population.t419-rank-one-fixed-step-margin-and-noiseless-risk-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"LoRA rank-one convergence and deficiency margins","draft":"w705/bundle_010.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-rank-one-all-scale-gaussian-fixed-step-margin-rate","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C020 v1: one fixed-step rank-one population rate at every Gaussian scale

Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This strengthens the step/accuracy quantifiers in C015: one fixed step works simultaneously for all target accuracies on one high-probability event. The method is the published positive-deficiency-margin idea (Min-Tarmoun-Vidal-Mallada, arXiv:2105.06351, Corollary 5, p.10), applied after the first strict discrete descent, together with C014's explicit boundedness argument. The zero-output invariant subspace is already in Zhang-Liu-Chen, arXiv:2502.01235, Theorem 3.1/C.10. No specialist-level novelty has been established.

## Statement

Let Delta=u v^T with unit u in R^m and unit v in R^p, arbitrary m,p>=1. Initialize b0=0, a0~N(0,s^2 I_p), any s>0, independently of everything else. Fix 0<rho<1 and set

 D_bar=2ps^2/rho, K_bar=D_bar+5.

For simultaneous ordinary GD on ||b a^T-Delta||F^2/2 choose any one constant step

 0<eta<=1/(6K_bar+1).

With probability at least 1-rho, for every integer t>=1,

 ||b_t a_t^T-Delta||F
 <=exp[-eta^3 s^4 rho^4 (t-1)/(128K_bar)].

In particular, for every 0<eps<1, the same run reaches eps by

 t>=1+ceil[(128K_bar/(eta^3 s^4 rho^4))log(1/eps)].

The step does not depend on eps. This includes a proper input and output rank-one bottleneck when m,p>=2 at every Gaussian scale. Rank-one signal condition number is 1; target singular value lambda>0 is handled by s_bar=s/sqrt(lambda), eta_bar=eta lambda and eps_bar=eps/lambda. The constants are deliberately conservative. This is a high-probability statement, not an unconditional expected-risk theorem for an initialization-independent fixed step.

## One initial event and the boundedness component

Let d=||a0||^2 and x0=v^T a0. As in C015, Markov and the standard normal density give the simultaneous event

 d<=D_bar, |x0|>=s rho/2

with probability at least 1-rho, using a union bound. Fix this event.

For the normalized population loss, C014 applies with r=1, C=I_p, D=Delta, q0=1/2, J=d+1, R=2 and K=d+5<=K_bar. Its safe-step conditions are eta<=min{1/2,1/(6K+1)}. The chosen bound meets both. Thus every iterate has

 q_(t+1)<=q_t-(eta/2)||grad q_t||F^2,
 ||b_t||^2+||a_t||^2<=K_bar.

C014 proves these facts through the exact simultaneous Gram-drift identity, a trace factor bound and a descent-segment induction; it does not assume boundedness. No Gaussian event for future iterates is multiplied into the initial probability.

## A positive deficiency margin after the very first step

Because b0=0, the first gradient in a is zero and the first gradient in b is -u x0. Its squared norm is x0^2>0. Descent gives

 q1<=1/2-(eta/2)x0^2,
 e1:=sqrt(2q1)<=sqrt(1-eta x0^2)<1.

The radical is real; explicitly eta x0^2<=eta d<=K_bar/(6K_bar+1)<1. The elementary inequality 1-sqrt(1-z)>=z/2 for 0<=z<=1 now gives

 1-e1>=eta x0^2/2.

This is the rank-one special feature: the initial residual norm is exactly the sole target singular value, so any strict decrease creates positive margin. At higher rank, reducing ||Delta||F slightly need not cross its smallest singular value, and this argument is not a general-rank warm-up proof.

## The margin keeps the output factor away from zero

The known invariant subspace gives b_t=beta_t u at every step. Descent implies e_t=sqrt(2q_t)<=e1 for all t>=1. The reverse triangle inequality therefore gives

 |beta_t|||a_t||=||b_t a_t^T||F>=1-e_t>=eta x0^2/2.

Since ||a_t||^2<=K_bar, it follows uniformly that

 beta_t^2>=eta^2 x0^4/(4K_bar)
             >=eta^2 s^4 rho^4/(64K_bar)=:b_lower^2>0.

This conclusion concerns the scalar factor coefficient in a known rank-one output subspace; it does not assume that the wide input factor is invertible or aligned.

## Gradient domination and the fixed-step rate

In this output subspace, grad_a q=beta_t(beta_t a_t-v). Hence

 ||grad q_t||F^2>=2 beta_t^2 q_t>=2 b_lower^2 q_t,
 q_(t+1)<=(1-eta b_lower^2)q_t, t>=1.

The multiplier is nonnegative. In fact b_lower^2<=beta_t^2<=K_bar and eta K_bar<1/6. Iterating and using e1<=1 yields

 e_t<=exp[-eta b_lower^2(t-1)/2],

which is exactly the displayed rate and hitting time. This is an analytic proof; no floating-point trajectory is used as evidence of convergence. Independent audit remains required.

## Boundaries

C015 remains a valid but more conservative finite-horizon route; the present proof replaces its accuracy-dependent step with a fixed-step margin argument at rank one. It does not claim the known margin technique or invariant reduction as new. It does not extend the all-scale guarantee to ranks greater than one, whose first step need not establish positive deficiency margin. The Gaussian failure event still exists, so C013's unconditional fixed-step expected-limit-risk obstruction remains compatible with this theorem.


Full deterministic C014 component:
# T419-C014 v1: empirical GD boundedness with an initialization-dependent step

Kind: bound. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This is an explicit anisotropic version of the published Gram-imbalance/descent method, not a solution of Target 2. It proves a trajectory component without assuming the iterates are bounded. The prior source is Du-Hu-Lee, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 2.2 and Appendix B, Claim B.1; its full convergence theorems have different initialization/step hypotheses. C009 already identifies the exact covariance metric and C010 the positive-noise empirical landscape.

## Statement

Let C be any real positive definite p-by-p matrix, D any real m-by-p matrix, and r>=1. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op, ell=||D||op, W=D C^(-1), and

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.

## Exact identities and product/factor bounds

Let G=BA C-D. The two factor gradients are G_B=G A^T and G_A=B^T G. With E_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t the first-order cross terms cancel exactly, giving

 E_(t+1)-E_t=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 ||E_(t+1)-E_t||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

This cancellation only uses dependence on BA and does not require isotropic C. Also

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 <=r [||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

To verify it, write P=B^TB,Q=AA^T. Scalar trace Cauchy-Schwarz gives (tr(P+Q))^2<=r tr((P+Q)^2), and cyclicity of trace gives tr((P+Q)^2)=||P-Q||F^2+4 tr(PQ), tr(PQ)=||BA||F^2. No commutation is assumed.

When q<=q0, positivity of C gives ||BA-W||F<=sqrt(2q0/lambda), hence ||BA||F<=R. If additionally ||E-E0||F<=1, then ||E||F<=J, so the preceding trace bound implies

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=sqrt(r) sqrt(J^2+4R^2)<=K.

The initialization meets these conditions and therefore has pair norm at most sqrt(K).

## Descent established before closing the boundedness induction

Suppose at the current iterate the pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have valid descent inequalities. Then

 ||grad q||F<=||BA C-D||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(Kc/2+ell)sqrt(K).

Because eta<=1/(6Kc+ell), the proposed next point has pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The connecting segment also lies in that ball. On that ball the Hessian quadratic form in a perturbation (dB,dA) is

 ||(dB A+B dA) C^(1/2)||F^2+2<BA C-D,dB dA>.

Its absolute value is at most

 [c(||A||op^2+||B||op^2)+||BA C-D||op]
 times (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2)
 <=[4Kc+(2Kc+ell)] (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2).

Here the first summand uses Cauchy-Schwarz on dB A+B dA; the cross term uses |<G,dB dA>|<=||G||op||dB||F||dA||F. Thus the Hessian operator norm on the segment is at most L. Taylor's theorem along that segment proves

 q_next<=q-eta||grad q||F^2+(L eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2
        <=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2.

In particular q_next<=q0. Telescoping the descent inequalities, including the proposed step, and using q>=0 yields

 sum_(j=0)^t eta^2||grad q_j||F^2<=2eta q0
 <=2q0/(1+2q0)<1.

Summing the imbalance increments now proves ||E_next-E0||F<=2eta q0<1. The product/factor bound therefore puts the endpoint back in the smaller ball of pair radius sqrt(K). This closes the induction without assuming a bound before proving descent on the required larger segment. The q0=0 case is included: both gradients vanish, the sequence is constant, and all inequalities still hold.

## Consequences and exact remaining gap

Telescoping for every finite horizon gives the infinite summability bound. A nonnegative summable sequence tends to zero, so the gradients vanish. Bounded finite-dimensional factor pairs have convergent subsequences; gradient continuity makes every subsequential limit critical. The running-minimum bound follows by averaging the finite sum. These statements do not require that the entire sequence converges to one point.

For B0=0 and a Gaussian A0, this provides an allowed positive step after observing the initialization, conditional on every full-row-rank design. It does not supply a single positive step independent of the unbounded Gaussian initializer. C013 shows that unconditional expected-limit risk with such an initialization-independent fixed step can diverge even at rank one.

Combining this bound with the already verified empirical strict-saddle landscape C010 is insufficient to conclude global optimization. One must additionally show that the specified zero/Gaussian initialization does not approach a nonglobal critical point, with all hypotheses of a saddle-avoidance theorem checked for its lower-dimensional initial support and step rule. Vanishing gradients do not establish that. Even convergence almost surely would not by itself justify passing to expected population risk; a failure-tail/integrability or finite-stopping argument is separately required. The usual full-ambient absolutely-continuous random-initialization theorem cannot simply be cited for the plane B0=0.

Independent reviewer audit and any novelty assessment remain pending. [Lemma 10 of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Let \(\gamma\in\Opendenseset_\alpha\). Then the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item For every \(j\ge1\),
\[
\partial_x^j\Psi^\gamma\in C_b([0,1]\times\mathbb R),
\]
and, for every \(j\ge0\),
\[
\partial_s\partial_x^j\Psi^\gamma
\in L^\infty([0,1]\times\mathbb R).
\]
In particular, for every $j\geq 1$,
\[
\partial_x^j\Psi^\gamma\in
C_b^{\alpha/2,\alpha}([0,1]\times\mathbb R).
\]

\item For every \(s\in[0,1]\), the function
\(x\mapsto\Psi^\gamma(s,x)\) is even,
\(x\mapsto\partial_x\Psi^\gamma(s,x)\) is odd, and
\(x\mapsto\partial_{xx}\Psi^\gamma(s,x)\) is even.

\item For all \((s,x)\in[0,1]\times\mathbb R\),
\[
|\partial_x\Psi^\gamma(s,x)|\le1,
\qquad
0\le \partial_{xx}\Psi^\gamma(s,x)\le1,
\qquad
|\partial_{xxx}\Psi^\gamma(s,x)|\le4.
\]
In particular, \(x\mapsto\Psi^\gamma(s,x)\) is convex.
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem thm:lamperti of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $f\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R})$ with $f>0$ and let $b$ be as in Theorem~(thm:opvol of the paper). Suppose
there exist a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism $g$ of $\mathbb{R}$ with $g'>0$, a constant $\sigma>0$ and
a function $\tilde b$ \emph{independent of the law}, such that for every compactly
supported $\mu$ with a density the spectral velocity field of $g(X)$ is that of a free
SDE with constant diffusion coefficient $\sigma$, that is
\begin{equation}
  g'(x)\Big(b(x)+f(x)^{2}H(f^{2}\mu)(x)\Big)
  =\tilde b\big(g(x)\big)+\sigma^{2}H\big(g_{\#}\mu\big)\big(g(x)\big).
\end{equation}
Then $g$ is affine and $f$ is constant. Equivalently, a non-constant state-dependent
sandwich volatility cannot be removed by any change of spectral variable.

Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y). If ran T has finite algebraic codimension in Y, i.e. there is a finite-dimensional subspace F of Y with ran T + F = Y and ran T ∩ F = {0}, then ran T is closed in Y. Consequently, closedness of the range need not be assumed in the definition of a Fredholm operator. (The hypothesis is genuine finite codimension; a merely dense proper range, such as that of a compact injective operator with dense range, has infinite codimension and is not closed.)
X and Y are Banach spaces (completeness of both is used through the open mapping theorem)
T: X -> Y is bounded and linear
ran T has an algebraic complement in Y of finite dimension

[Corollary 19 (Probabilistic representations for absorption probabilities) of arXiv:2608.16752, 'Absorption Probabilities for Random Convex Hulls: Distribution-Freeness via the Wall-Cross'] Let $U_2,U_3,\dots$ be independent random variables with $U_m\sim\mathrm{Bern}(1/T_m)$, where
$T_m=2m$ for the walk, $T_m=m$ for the bridge and $T_m=2$ for Wendel. Then
\[    \pwalk{n}{d}=\mathbb{P}\Big(\sum_{m=2}^{n}U_m\geq d\Big),
    \qquad
\pbridge{n}{d}=\mathbb{P}\Big(\sum_{m=3}^{n}U_m\geq d\Big),
\]
the sum for the bridge starting at $m=3$, and
\[
\pwend{n}{d}=\mathbb{P}\Big(\sum_{m=2}^{n}U_m\geq d\Big)
    =\mathbb{P}\left(\mathrm{Bin}(n-1,\tfrac12)\geq d\right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In information theory and coding theory, Reed–Solomon codes are a group of error-correcting codes that were introduced by Irving S. Reed and Gustave Solomon in 1960. They have many applications, including consumer technologies such as MiniDiscs, CDs, DVDs, Blu-ray discs, QR codes, Data Matrix, data transmission technologies such as DSL and WiMAX, broadcast systems such as satellite communications, DVB and ATSC, and storage systems such as RAID 6.

[Thm 225 (\textbf{main result}) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For the spherical projection pursuit problem \eqref{eq:proj-pursuit-def}, we have the following:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item 
        
        If $\mu \in \ocM^{\sph}(\alpha)$, for any $\iota > 0$ there exist $L$ large enough and $c$ small enough such that for sufficiently large $N$, there exists an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm that $(\iota,1-e^{-cN})$-attains $\mu$.
        \item 
        
        For any $\fq \in [1,2)$ and $\iotamsr > 0$, there exists small $\iotasol > 0$ such that the following holds.
        For any $L$, there exists small $c>0$ such that for sufficiently large $N$, all $L$-Lipschitz algorithms are $(\fq,\iotamsr,\iotasol,1-e^{-cN})$-confined to the set $\ocM^{\sph}(\alpha)$.
        \item 
        
We have $\ocM^{\sph}(\alpha) = \ocM^{\sph, \concave}(\alpha)$, i.e., concave $p$ suffice to achieve all endpoint measures of \eqref{eq:main-process-intro-general}.
    \end{enumerate}
The analogous results hold in the Ising setting, replacing $\ocM^{\sph}(\alpha), \ocM^{\sph, \concave}(\alpha)$
with $\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha), \ocM^{\Ising, \concave}(\alpha)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$ define $\hat f(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x) e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx$ for every $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$; the integral converges absolutely for every $\xi$. The map $f\mapsto\hat f$ is linear, $\hat f$ is bounded and uniformly continuous, and $\|\hat f\|_\infty \le \|f\|_1$. Symmetry rules (for $a,b\in\mathbb{R}^d$, $\lambda>0$): $x\mapsto f(x-a)$ has transform $e^{-2\pi i a\cdot\xi}\hat f(\xi)$; $x\mapsto e^{2\pi i b\cdot x}f(x)$ has transform $\hat f(\xi-b)$; $x\mapsto f(\lambda x)$ has transform $\lambda^{-d}\hat f(\xi/\lambda)$; $\overline f$ has transform $\overline{\hat f(-\xi)}$. The inverse transform of $g\in L^1$ is $\check g(x)=\int g(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,d\xi$. With this convention Plancherel reads $\|\hat f\|_2=\|f\|_2$. Convention warning: texts using $\int f(x)e^{-ix\cdot\xi}dx$ have inversion with a factor $(2\pi)^{-d}$ and $\|\hat f\|_2=(2\pi)^{d/2}\|f\|_2$; the unitary convention puts $(2\pi)^{-d/2}$ in front of both. Constants in Plancherel, Poisson summation, the uncertainty principles and Paley-Wiener depend on the convention, so check it before importing a constant.
f is Lebesgue integrable on R^d
convention: kernel e^{-2 pi i x.xi} with no normalizing constant
title: Fourier Transform on L^1(R^d)

[Lemma of arXiv:2411.14177, '\textbf{Invariant Sublinear Expectations}'] If $\Lambda$ is a Banach-Mazur limit, then
$$
\liminf _{n \rightarrow \infty} x_n \leqslant \Lambda(x) \leqslant \limsup _{n \rightarrow \infty} x_n
$$
for each $x=\left(x_1, x_2, \ldots\right) \in \ell_{\infty}$. In particular, $\Lambda(x)=\lim\limits_{n \rightarrow \infty} x_n$ for each convergent sequence $x$ (so every Banach-Mazur limit is an extension of the limit functional). [Lemma Lemma 4.1 in sethuraman-varadhan of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] Let $S$ be a standard Borel space, $Q$ a probability measure on $S \times S$ with marginals $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and $\pi(x,dy)$ a Markov kernel satisfying $Q(dx,dy) =
    \alpha(dx)\pi(x,dy)$.
    If $f \in L^2(\alpha)$ and $g \in L^2(\beta)$ satisfy
    \[
        \int f \,d\alpha = \int g \, d\beta = 0,
    \]
    then
    \[
      \Big| \int \!\! \int f(x)g(y)  \, Q(dx,dy)    \Big| \leq \sqrt{\delta(\pi)}  \, \|f\|_{L^2(\alpha)}  \,
      \|g\|_{L^2(\beta)}
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Complex form of Lemma 4.1 in \cite{sethuraman-varadhan}

[Defin 77 ($\epsilon$-cluster structure) of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Let $\eps>0$ and $\bs{n}_K=(n_1, \dots, n_K)\in (\mathbb{N}^*)^K$ with $\ov{\bs{n}}_K=\sum_{k=1}^K n_k = N$. One says
that $\bs{x}_N \in \R^{N}_{<}$ has the $\epsilon$-cluster $\bs{n}_K$  if the following is true.
Define $i_1=1$ and $i_k = n_1 + \dots + n_{k-1}+1$ for $k\geq 2$, so that $x_{i_k}$ is the leftmost particle in the $k^{\e{th}}$ cluster.

\begin{enumerate}
\item For all $k = 1, \dots, K$,  $x_{i_k + j} - x_{i_k + j-1} \leq \epsilon$ for all $j = 1, \dots, n_k -1$.
\item For all $k = 2, \dots, K$,  $x_{i_{k}}  - x_{i_{k} -1} > \epsilon$.
\end{enumerate}
We let $\mc{E}_{\eps}( \bs{n}_K)$ be the set of $\bs{x}_N \in \R^{N}_{<}$ that have $\epsilon$-cluster $\bs{n}_K$.
title: $\epsilon$-cluster structure

body:
[Lemma lem:centers of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ be nonzero and nonnegative, and set
$\kappa:=\|f\|_1$.  Then $\mathsf C(f)$ is nonempty and compact, and
$\mathcal A(f)<2\kappa$.  Moreover, the following statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item if $\operatorname{supp}f^*\subset B_r(\mathbf0)$ for some $r>0$,
then every $\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(f)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
  \int_{\mathbb R^2\setminus B_r(\mathbf b)}f
  \,\mathrm d\mathbf x
  \leq\frac12\mathcal A(f);
\end{equation}
\item if, for some $r,s>0$ and $\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^2$,
\[
  \operatorname{supp}f^*\subset B_r(\mathbf0),
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}f\subset B_s(\mathbf a),
\]
then
\begin{equation}
  |\mathbf b-\mathbf a|\leq r+s
  \qquad(\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(f));
\end{equation}
moreover, the mass center $\mathbf X_f$ defined by (equation eq:mass-center of the paper) satisfies
\begin{equation}
  |\mathbf b-\mathbf X_f|
  \leq\frac{r+2s}{\kappa}\mathcal A(f)
  \qquad(\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(f));
\end{equation}
\item if $\operatorname{supp}f^*\subset B_r(\mathbf0)$ for some $r>0$
and $\mathcal A(f)<\kappa$, then
\begin{equation}
  \operatorname{diam}\mathsf C(f)\leq2r;
\end{equation}
\item for any nonzero, nonnegative $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$,
\[
  |\mathcal A(f)-\mathcal A(g)|\leq2\|f-g\|_1;
\]
\item the set-valued map $f\mapsto\mathsf C(f)$ has a closed graph with respect
to strong $L^1$ convergence: if $f_n,f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ are nonzero and
nonnegative, then
\[
  f_n\to f\ \text{in }L^1(\mathbb R^2),\qquad
  \mathbf b_n\to\mathbf b\ \text{in }\mathbb R^2,\qquad
  \mathbf b_n\in\mathsf C(f_n)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \mathbf b\in\mathsf C(f);
\]
\item the set-valued map $f\mapsto\mathsf C(f)$ is upper semicontinuous\footnote{See
[AubinFrankowska2009] for this standard definition.} with
respect to strong $L^1$ convergence: for every nonzero, nonnegative
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ and every open set $O\subset\mathbb R^2$ with
$\mathsf C(f)\subset O$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that
\[
  g\in L^1(\mathbb R^2),\quad g\geq0,\quad g\not\equiv0,\quad
  \|g-f\|_1<\delta
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \mathsf C(g)\subset O.
\]
\end{enumerate}
title: Properties of optimal translation centers

[Theorem thm:vector-KP-nondegeneracy-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Assume that 
\(
\mathbb{E}(X_0+X_1)=1
\), 
and let 
\(
M=\lim_n M_n
\).

\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(\kappa_X<1\), then the following are equivalent:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \(\mathbb{P}(M>0)>0\);

\item \(\mathbb{E} M=1\);

\item 
\(
H^+(X)<\infty
\)
and 
\(
\gamma(X)<0
\).
\end{enumerate}

\item If 
\(
\kappa_X=1
\),
then the following boundary dichotomy holds. If
\[
X_0+X_1=1
\qquad\text{almost surely},
\]
then
\[
M_n=1\quad(n\ge0),
\qquad
M=1
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
If instead
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_0+X_1=1)<1,
\]
then
\[
M=0
\qquad
\text{almost surely}.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:vector-KP-nondegeneracy-paper of arXiv:2606.08683

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). In two-dimensional critical or near-critical percolation, RSW theory states that if crossing probabilities of n x n squares are uniformly bounded away from 0 as n grows, then crossing probabilities of rho n x n rectangles, for any fixed aspect ratio rho, are also uniformly bounded away from 0 (and from 1) by a constant depending on rho but not on n. The classical proof glues together several square-crossing events using the FKG inequality and translation and reflection symmetry of the lattice. RSW estimates are the essential multi-scale input for proving arm-exponent bounds, conformal-invariance-adjacent results, and, via the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, for establishing sharpness of the phase transition without relying on exact self-duality. RSW does not by itself prove existence of a scaling limit as n -> infinity, does not give the exact value of any crossing probability, only two-sided bounds; and the classical form required exact self-duality (p=1/2 on the square lattice), so extending the theory to general planar lattices or to p != 1/2 required a genuinely new, duality-free argument (Tassion, 2016). Typical failure: Assuming that RSW-type bounded-away-from-0/1 crossing estimates transfer automatically to a new planar model merely because it is monotone and planar; RSW requires either exact self-duality or the more robust but still nontrivial Tassion-style construction, and models without FKG, or with strong enough long-range dependence, can fail to admit the needed gluing arguments even though they look superficially similar to Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Russo, 1978, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Seymour and Welsh, 1978, Annals of Discrete Mathematics; Tassion, 2016, Probability Theory and Related Fields.
two-dimensional planar lattice model satisfying the FKG inequality
translation invariance and, in the classical gluing constructions, reflection symmetry of the lattice
an a priori lower bound on square-crossing probabilities, which is a hypothesis to be separately established, not a free consequence of RSW
independence, or at least positive association, of the underlying edge or site variables

Let Ω ⊂ R^n (n ≥ 2) be a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary, dS the surface measure and ν the outward unit normal (defined dS-a.e.), and let 1 ≤ p < ∞.

(1) Existence and boundedness. There is a unique bounded linear operator T : W^{1,p}(Ω) → L^p(∂Ω, dS) such that Tu = u|_{∂Ω} for every u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω) ∩ C(Ω̄). Tu is the trace of u, and ||Tu||_{L^p(∂Ω)} ≤ C(Ω, p) ||u||_{W^{1,p}(Ω)}.

(2) Kernel. ker T = W^{1,p}_0(Ω), the closure of C_c^∞(Ω) in W^{1,p}(Ω). A W^{1,p} function vanishes on ∂Ω in the trace sense exactly when it is a W^{1,p}-limit of compactly supported smooth functions.

(3) Range (Gagliardo). For 1 < p < ∞ the range of T is exactly the fractional Sobolev space W^{1−1/p, p}(∂Ω), and T has a bounded linear right inverse W^{1−1/p, p}(∂Ω) → W^{1,p}(Ω). In particular T : H^1(Ω) → H^{1/2}(∂Ω) is bounded and onto, and every g ∈ H^{1/2}(∂Ω) has an extension u ∈ H^1(Ω) with Tu = g and ||u||_{H^1(Ω)} ≤ C ||g||_{H^{1/2}(∂Ω)}. For p = 1 the range is all of L^1(∂Ω). Since H^{1/2}(∂Ω) ↪ L^2(∂Ω) is compact, T : H^1(Ω) → L^2(∂Ω) is a compact operator.

(4) Integration by parts with traces. For u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω), v ∈ W^{1,p'}(Ω) with 1/p + 1/p' = 1 (p' = ∞ for p = 1) and each i,
   ∫_Ω u ∂_i v dx + ∫_Ω v ∂_i u dx = ∫_∂Ω (Tu)(Tv) ν_i dS.
Hence for u ∈ H^2(Ω), v ∈ H^1(Ω) Green's first identity ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v dx + ∫_Ω (Δu) v dx = ∫_∂Ω (∂_ν u)(Tv) dS holds with ∂_ν u := ν · T(∇u) ∈ L^2(∂Ω), and for u ∈ H^1_0(Ω) all boundary terms vanish.

Where it fails. There is no trace operator on L^p(Ω): ∂Ω has Lebesgue measure zero, an L^p class has no boundary values, and an estimate ||Tu||_{L^p(∂Ω)} ≤ C||u||_{L^p(Ω)} is false (the full W^{1,p} norm is needed). For p > 1 the range is NOT L^p(∂Ω): a general g ∈ L^2(∂Ω) has no H^1(Ω) extension. The kernel and range statements use the Lipschitz boundary (a segment / extension property); for domains with cracks, slits or cusps the boundary is not Lipschitz and these statements need modification (a crack has two sides with two different traces). The trace of ∇u exists for u ∈ H^2(Ω), not for a general u ∈ H^1(Ω), so ∂_ν u is not defined in L^2(∂Ω) for arbitrary H^1 functions.
Ω bounded open with Lipschitz boundary, n ≥ 2
1 ≤ p < ∞ for existence, boundedness and kernel; 1 < p < ∞ for the fractional-space range description
Green's identity form: u ∈ H^2(Ω), v ∈ H^1(Ω)

$C_{\rm loc}=C_{\rm loc}(M,R)>0$ such that, whenever
$\varepsilon>0$ and $f\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ is nonnegative and satisfies
\[
  \|f\|_\infty\leq M\varepsilon^{-2},\qquad
  \operatorname{supp}f\subset B_{R\varepsilon}(\mathbf a)
\]
for some $\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^2$,
one has
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal D(f)\leq C_{\rm loc}\mathcal A(f).
\end{equation}

Let X be a random vector in a real separable Hilbert space with E||X||^2<infinity and covariance H=E[X tensor X]. Assume exact interpolation: Y=<X,theta_star> almost surely for a fixed theta_star in the Hilbert space. Assume R>0 and the operator fourth-moment bound E[||X||^2*(X tensor X)]<=R*H in positive-semidefinite order. Start theta_0=0 and use fresh IID examples with the single-example SGD update theta_(t+1)=theta_t-gamma*(<X_(t+1),theta_t>-Y_(t+1))*X_(t+1), where gamma>0 is constant during the run. Put D=||theta_star||^2 and f_t=E Rcal(theta_t), where Rcal(theta)=E(<X,theta>-Y)^2/2 =||H^(1/2)*(theta-theta_star)||^2/2; the outer expectation is over SGD samples. If 4*gamma*||H||<=1, then for each integer t>=1, f_t<=D/(4*gamma*t)+gamma*R*sum_(k=0)^(t-1) f_k/(t-k). The convolution is over preceding expected risks and does not assume that the last-iterate risks are monotone. No strictly positive smallest covariance eigenvalue is required.
Fresh IID noiseless samples, theta_star in the real Hilbert space, theta_0=0.
H=E[X tensor X] with E||X||^2<infinity; E[||X||^2*(X tensor X)]<=R*H for R>0.
4*gamma*||H||<=1.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:86a406c244efd15153f2a84c796a6f8cfa5c2e0bd5e467b74ef5175a50b3d563","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/86/86a406c244efd15153f2a84c796a6f8cfa5c2e0bd5e467b74ef5175a50b3d563.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:6555546a1811f821b8ee1f815217a67a34bd2c8a74b2a6c63a5ffbe7971c4eed","bundle_entry_key":"tripod-centered-rank-one-truncation-barrier","bundle_id":"population.w715-t276-truncation-barrier-unaudited","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Deep ReLU representation cost","draft":"w715/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.deep_networks:jacot-tripod-centered-rank-one-truncation-barrier-unaudited","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Single-layer rank-one truncations do not force normalized cost two

Target 2. Status: proof unaudited; route-failure result, not a network construction.

The setting is the dossier's exact tripod map f on the square. All norms below
are Euclidean or their induced operator norms, except the Frobenius norm.

## A uniform obstruction to scalar factorization

Every F=g composed with h, with h:[0,1]^2 -> R continuous, satisfies

    sup_x ||F(x)-f(x)|| >= 1/4.                                  (1)

Here g need not be continuous. To prove this, suppose the error is <1/4.
The three distinguished corner values f(c_i)=v_i/2 have pairwise distance
sqrt(3)/2, so F(c_i) are distinct. Thus h(c_i) are distinct. Choose j so
h(c_j) lies between the other two values. As in the dossier, there is a path
between the other corners outside the closed support triangle of leg j.
The intermediate value theorem gives a point q on this path with
h(q)=h(c_j), hence F(q)=F(c_j). But f(q) is zero or lies on another leg.
For its parameter t>=0, the squared distance to f(c_j) is

    ||v_j/2-t v_i||^2=1/4+t^2+t/2 >=1/4       (i != j).

It follows that ||f(q)-f(c_j)||>=1/2, whereas the assumed approximation
and F(q)=F(c_j) give a strict upper bound 1/2. This is a contradiction.
The support complement and tip facts are settled ground from Target 1.

## Necessary constraints on every layer

Let a depth-L biased ReLU network represent f exactly. The final layer is
linear, as in Jacot's model. Let s_{1,l}>=s_{2,l} be the two largest
singular values of W_l. All W_l have rank at least two: a rank-one weight
matrix, even with its bias and subsequent nonlinear layers, would provide
an exact scalar factorization of f.

Fix p0=(1/2,1/2), whose maximum distance to the square is R=1/sqrt(2).
Replace W_l by its top rank-one singular truncation W_l^(1), and replace
its bias by

    b_l' = b_l + (W_l-W_l^(1)) alpha_{l-1}(p0).

The altered network F_l factors through one scalar at layer l. Its raw
layer error at input x is

    (W_l-W_l^(1))(alpha_{l-1}(x)-alpha_{l-1}(p0)).

ReLU is globally 1-Lipschitz. Prefix and suffix Lipschitz bounds therefore give

    ||F_l-f||_infinity <= R s_{2,l} product_{k != l} s_{1,k}.

This estimate also holds when l is the final linear layer. Combining it
with (1), and squaring, yields for every l

    d_l product_{k != l} a_k >= c,
    a_l=s_{1,l}^2, d_l=s_{2,l}^2, c=1/8.                       (2)

## Exact optimization of these spectral constraints

Put t=product_l a_l. Constraint (2) says d_l>=c a_l/t. Thus the total
parameter cost C_L, including nonnegative bias costs, satisfies

    C_L >= sum_l(a_l+d_l)
        >= (1+c/t) sum_l a_l
        >= L t^(1/L)(1+c/t).                                  (3)

For L>=2 the derivative of the last expression, as a function of t>0, is

    t^(1/L-2) [t-(L-1)c].

Its minimum is attained at t=(L-1)c. Therefore these constraints give

    C_L >= [L^2/(L-1)] [(L-1)/8]^(1/L).                       (4)

The important finding is the limitation, not an improved finite-depth bound.
For each L>=2 the abstract spectral values

    a_l=[(L-1)/8]^(1/L),    d_l=a_l/(L-1),    all l,

satisfy 0<d_l<=a_l and EVERY inequality (2) with equality. Their summed
squared singular values equal the right side of (4), whose quotient by L
tends to 1. For L>=17 they also satisfy the ordinary product-of-top-singular-
values Lipschitz constraint product_l s_{1,l}>=sqrt(2) for this map.

Hence the collection of all centered single-layer rank-one truncation
inequalities (2), the singular-value order constraints, and the global
Lipschitz product lower bound cannot by themselves force R_infinity>=2.
The missing ingredient is consistency of the features and singular directions
across layers. The displayed spectral values are NOT a network representing f
and do NOT prove R_infinity=1. No lower bound stronger than the full problem's
known normalized lower endpoint follows asymptotically from this route alone.

For orientation, the right side of (4) is
L+log L+1-log 8+O((log L)^2/L). This expansion is not needed for the barrier:
the exact normalized expression already converges to 1 by taking logarithms.

## Checks and remaining step

The rank-one approximation uses a new bias so that prefix differences, rather
than unbounded activation magnitudes, enter the estimate. Every denominator
is positive because all layers have rank at least two. The scalar surrogate
may depend on the layer l, which is allowed in (1). Constraint multiplication
in the witness is deterministic algebra; no probabilistic independence is used.

scripts/check_truncation_barrier.py checks the witness constraints using exact
rational identities a_l^L=(L-1)/8, including L=2 and L=17, without approximating
an L-th root. The general argument is the algebra above, not a finite scan.

[Lemma 2 (Information equality for the ignoring estimator) of arXiv:2609.00774, 'Semi-Supervised Classification with Informative Missing Labels in Weibull Mixture Models'] Let
\[
 S_Y(\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p_Y(Y;\theta),
 \qquad
 S_{Z\mid Y}(\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(Z\mid Y;\theta),
\]
and let
\[
 \psi_{\mathrm{ig}}(\theta)
 =S_Y(\theta)+(1-M)S_{Z\mid Y}(\theta)
\]
be the score of $\ell_{\mathrm{ig},1}$. Under the conditional-independence assumption $M\perp Z\mid Y$ and the usual differentiability and moment conditions,
\begin{equation}
 -\E\left\{\frac{\partial\psi_{\mathrm{ig}}(\theta)}
 {\partial\theta^\top}\right\}
 =
 \E\{\psi_{\mathrm{ig}}(\theta)\psi_{\mathrm{ig}}(\theta)^\top\}
 =
 \J_{\mathrm{ig}}(\theta,\xi).
 
\end{equation}
If, in addition, $\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{ig}}\xrightarrow{p}\theta$, $\J_{\mathrm{ig}}$ is nonsingular, and the standard local regularity conditions for M-estimation hold, then
\begin{equation}
 \sqrt n(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{ig}}-\theta)
 \xrightarrow{d}
 N\!\left(0,\J_{\mathrm{ig}}^{-1}\right).
 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Information equality for the ignoring estimator

[Lemma 17 (Vanishing diagonal regularization) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let \(\widetilde H\) be a bounded centered array with zero diagonal and an
exactly stochastic, uniformly flat off-diagonal variance matrix
\(\widetilde S\).  Let \(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_N\) be independent, centered,
variance-one, uniformly bounded random variables, independent of
\(\widetilde H\).  For fixed \(\eta\in(0,1)\), set
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde H^{(\eta)}_{ij}
 :=\sqrt{1-\eta/N}\,\widetilde H_{ij}\quad(i\ne j),
 \qquad
 \widetilde H^{(\eta)}_{ii}:=\sqrt{\eta/N}\,\chi_i.
\end{equation}
Then the variance matrix of \(\widetilde H^{(\eta)}\) is exactly stochastic
and satisfies the uniform lower and upper bounds required by the
generalized-Wigner theorem, with constants allowed to depend on \(\eta\).
For every finite family of functions analytic near \(\Gamma\),
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\left|
 \E\Tr\varphi(\widetilde H^{(\eta)})
 -\E\Tr\varphi(\widetilde H)
 \right|&\le C_{\varphi,\Gamma}\eta,
 \\
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\Var\!\left(
 \Tr\varphi(\widetilde H^{(\eta)})
 -\Tr\varphi(\widetilde H)
 \right)&\le C_{\varphi,\Gamma}\eta.
 
\end{align}
Moreover, the Li--Xu expectation and covariance formulas converge to their flat
zero-diagonal versions in the order \(N\to\infty\), then
\(\eta\downarrow0\).  Consequently the joint CLT for

body:
[Theo 17 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] Let $(\nu_h)\in {\cal M} ( \gamma , \R^{2n} )$  with $\gamma <0$. Suppose that  the function 
  $\varphi $ in  (\ref{Four-mes}) is a quadratic form, namely,
  
   \be \varphi (u) = - \frac  {1}  {2} 
     \sum _{jk} a_{jk} u_j u_k = - \frac  {1}  {2}  (Au ) \cdot  u , \ee 
    
  where   $A=(a_{ij})$ is a symmetric  matrix with a   definite positive 
  real part.   Then, 
  
  
  i) We have for every  $F$ and  $G$ in  $ D_{\lambda h}(\R^{2n})$ 
  (with large enough $\lambda $),
   
  $$ F \sharp _h ^{\nu_h} G = R e^{h L^{\nu}(D)} (F \otimes G) ,$$
  
 where  $L^{\nu}$ is a quadratic form whose matrix also denoted by 
  $L^{\nu}$ is written as,
  
  \be 
    L^{\nu} =  \frac  {1}  {2} 
     \begin{pmatrix} 0 & B +  A   \\  B^T +  A  &  0  \end{pmatrix} 
    ,\quad B  = - \frac  {1}  {2} 
       \begin{pmatrix} 1 & i \\ -i &   1 \end{pmatrix}.  \ee 
       
       
       ii) For any  $F\in  D_{\lambda h}(\R^{2n})$
  (with $\lambda $ sufficiently large), we have the estimates, 
  
   $$ \frac {h^m}  {m!} \Vert ( L^{\nu}(D)) ^m F \Vert_{ D_{  h }( \R^{2n})} 
  \leq  \frac {C^{m+1}}  {(\lambda - 1) ^m}
  \Vert  F \Vert_{ D_{\lambda  h }( \R^{2n})}. $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

    When $p$ and $q$ are both sufficiently small, for some constant $c > 0$, the following holds with probability at least $1 - cq^{41}$.

[Theorem 7 (van den Berg) of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Suppose that $D$ is simply connected and that $\partial D$ is Minkowski nondegenerate with
Minkowski dimension $\msf d_M(\partial D)\in[1,2)$. That is,
\[0<\liminf_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}\leq
\limsup_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}<\infty,\]
where we define
\[\partial D_r=\left\{x\in\mbb R^2:\inf_{y\in\partial D}|x-y|<r\right\}.\]
There exists constants $c\in(1,\infty)$ and $\th>0$ such that
\begin{align}

c^{-1}t^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2}\leq\msf{A}(D)-\msf M_0(t)\leq ct^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2},\qquad t\in(0,\th).
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: For an odd prime p and integer a, the Legendre symbol (a/p) is 0 if p | a, +1 if a is a nonzero quadratic residue mod p (some x^2 = a), and -1 if a is a quadratic nonresidue. Euler's criterion gives (a/p) = a^{(p-1)/2} mod p; the symbol is completely multiplicative in a. It is the object of the law of quadratic reciprocity and generalizes to the Jacobi symbol for composite lower arguments.
title: Legendre Symbol

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered.
the members' predictions on the rows to be scored are available (transductive setting); their targets are not
the blend w(t) = (1 - t) w_simplex + t w_leastsquares is linear in t, so the cross-validated and bootstrap predictions of every t come from the two base estimators' predictions; the criterion is the 5-fold cross-validated squared relative error on the calibration rows plus the excess pairs-bootstrap variance (B = 8) of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows

	    {Sample $(S_0, (S_i)_I)$ from $\textup{QT}(\tilde{W}_1, \tilde{W}_2, \tilde{W}_3) \times \prod_{i\in I} (1-\frac{2W_i}{\gamma^2})\mathcal{M}_2^{\textup{disk}}(W_i)$ where $\tilde{W}_i = \max (W_i, \gamma^2 - W_i)$. Let $(D, \phi, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ be an embedding of $S_0$. For each $i \in I$, identify the first marked point of $S_i$ with the vertex $a_i$ of $S_0$, and forget this marked point. Let $S$ be the resulting three-pointed quantum surface. }

body: [Theorem 2.6 (Maximum–entropy characterisation) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Graphs'] Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$, latent positions $U=(U_{i})_{i=1}^{n}\in(0,1)^{n}$, and a finite index set $\mathcal{I}\subset\mathbb{N}_{0}\times\mathbb{N}_{0}$. Let $\Omega:=\{0,1\}^{\binom{n}{2}}$ and identify $A\in\Omega$ with an undirected adjacency matrix by setting $A_{ji}:=A_{ij}$ and $A_{ii}:=0$. Using the statistics $S_{00}(A)$ and $S_{rs}(A,U)$ defined in Section 2.4, fix target moments $m_{00}\in\mathbb{R}$ and $(m_{rs})_{(r,s)\in\mathcal{I}}$ and define $\mathcal{Q}(m):=\Bigl\{Q\text{ pmf on }\Omega:\;\mathbb{E}_{Q}[S_{00}(A)]=m_{00},\;\mathbb{E}_{Q}[S_{rs}(A,U)]=m_{rs}\ \ \forall(r,s)\in\mathcal{I}\Bigr\}.$ Assume $\mathcal{Q}(m)\neq\varnothing$. (i) Existence and uniqueness. There exists a unique maximiser $Q^{\star}\in\mathcal{Q}(m)$ of Shannon entropy $H(Q):=-\sum_{A\in\Omega}Q(A)\log Q(A),$ where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and $0\log 0:=0$. (ii) Exponential-family characterisation (attainable moments). For $\theta=(c,(s_{rs})_{(r,s)\in\mathcal{I}})$ define $P_{\theta}(A\mid U):=\exp\Bigl\{c\,S_{00}(A)+\sum_{(r,s)\in\mathcal{I}}s_{rs}S_{rs}(A,U)-\Psi_{n}(\theta;U)\Bigr\},$ with $\Psi_{n}(\theta;U):=\log\sum_{A\in\Omega}\exp\Bigl\{c\,S_{00}(A)+\sum_{(r,s)\in\mathcal{I}}s_{rs}S_{rs}(A,U)\Bigr\}.$ If there exists $\theta^{\star}$ such that $P_{\theta^{\star}}(\cdot\mid U)\in\mathcal{Q}(m)$ (equivalently, $\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{\star}}[S_{00}(A)]=m_{00}$ and $\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{\star}}[S_{rs}(A,U)]=m_{rs}$ for all $(r,s)\in\mathcal{I}$), then $Q^{\star}=P_{\theta^{\star}}(\cdot\mid U).$ In particular, if one restricts $\theta$ to the WL–ERG subfamily (e.g. by imposing symmetry constraints inherited from a symmetric coefficient matrix), then any moment-matching WL–ERG member must coincide with $Q^{\star}$ and hence is the unique maximum–entropy distribution under the constraints. The maximising distribution is always unique; the canonical parameter $\theta^{\star}$ is unique whenever the exponential family is minimal.
